items.title: Louise Glück’s Life in Restaurants
items.description: If Maria Rondeau and JuanMa Calderón were literalists, they might have put nasturtiums on the menu at Rosa y Marigold, the Peruvian restaurant they opened in April, in Boston. They took the name from the novella “Marigold and Rose,” the final book published by
items.author: Hannah Goldfield
paragraphs: If Maria Rondeau and JuanMa Calderón were literalists, they might have put nasturtiums on the menu at Rosa y Marigold, the Peruvian restaurant they opened in April, in Boston. They took the name from the novella “Marigold and Rose,” the final book published by their friend Louise Glück, the Nobel Prize-winning poet, before she died, in 2023. The story is told from the perspective of infant twins with divergent personalities—Rose is unguardedly buoyant, whereas Marigold is watchful and introspective. “The garden relied on nasturtiums, which Mother and Father ate,” the narrator observes. “It was strange to see the grilled fish with nasturtium butter melting over it. . . . But once you try it, Mother said, the taste is magic. The twins knew what magic was. It made the sun rise. Now they knew it had a taste.”

Rondeau, who grew up in Guatemala, is an architect; Calderón, her partner in life and in restaurants, is a filmmaker and chef from Peru. In September, I sat at Rosa y Marigold’s sleek U-shaped bar with Rondeau and the poet Dan Chiasson, a regular contributor to this magazine and another close friend of Glück’s, sharing thin strips of charred beef heart, tendrils of squid blanketed in a silky, lavender-hued olive mayonnaise, and a formidable mound of chaufa de mariscos—Chinese Peruvian seafood fried rice. To drink, Chiasson ordered his usual, a gin Martini, recalling fondly how Glück would fish the olives out of his glass. As an epileptic, she abstained from hard liquor, but she loved the flavor.

“The whole book is about this idea of duality,” Rondeau said. “It’s an allusion to her two grandchildren”—Glück’s only child, Noah Dranow, is the father of twins—“but it’s also Louise. I think many people are two sides.” Rondeau designed Rosa y Marigold’s dining room to have two sections, each with a mirrored-steel slab hanging overhead, slightly angled to offer a glimpse of the other side.

That afternoon, we’d visited Celeste, the couple’s first restaurant, which they opened in the spring of 2018 in a tiny triangular storefront in Somerville. Glück, whose apartment was nearby, soon became a regular, with a regular order: a cold beer, the arugula salad with lime and Parmesan, and the ceviche, sometimes followed by the sudado de pescado, a Chinese Peruvian dish of steamed fish and vegetables. She always came with a friend, occasionally two, and often requested that the music be turned down.

The couple knew little about her until, one day, Glück left behind an envelope return-addressed to Yale, and Rondeau looked her up, to get it back to her. After that, Glück made her reservations with Rondeau directly. “If anything was off—the salt, the lime, the fish—I would get a text,” Rondeau said affectionately. “She had a perfect palate!” Chiasson added. “She was our in-house critic,” Rondeau continued. “And I would always be extremely grateful, because she kept it real.”

One evening, Rondeau and Calderón mentioned that they’d been approached about writing a cookbook. The next time they saw her, she handed them a typewritten foreword, detailing how she’d first encountered Celeste in Boston magazine, which had published a photo of the ceviche. “It was a summer day and I wanted that ceviche immediately,” she wrote, admiring how it was “not drowned by the chef’s noisy creativity in shards of coconut or a confetti of pomegranate seeds / A very pure looking dish of glistening blue cod.” At the restaurant, Glück became “more like a citizen” than a regular, she wrote. “And Celeste is a world. But a world so much more wonderful and reliable than our real world.” Glück ate dinner at Celeste on the day she won the Nobel, surrounded by friends of Rondeau’s and Calderón’s, whom they’d invited to insure her privacy.

I first learned about Glück’s passion for restaurants in the spring of 2020. At the time, I was this magazine’s weekly restaurant critic, and I had shifted, suddenly, from dining out all over New York City to chronicling the industry’s attempts to stay afloat during lockdown. Glück e-mailed me to commiserate, and to ask if I had ideas for how to help. “Among so many horrors, the collapse of these enchanted worlds seems somehow desperately poignant,” she wrote.

I was lightly shocked to hear from her. I knew and revered her as one of the great living poets, and imagined her as particularly godlike, too high-minded to care about something as earthly as food. There was also the fact that she had struggled with anorexia as a young woman, which she wrote about in her 1989 lecture “Education of the Poet.” We struck up a sporadic correspondence. “I love to cook and have been a terrific and fastidious home cook,” she wrote with refreshing candor, but she yearned for the ritual of dining out. (Later, I learned that she’d bought a heat lamp for Celeste so that she could eat there outdoors.)

In “Education of the Poet,” Glück, who was born to a wealthy family in New York, in 1943 (her father, a Hungarian Jewish immigrant, helped invent the X-Acto knife), described her anorexia as an attempt to “establish a self with clear boundaries.” “The conflict played itself out most fiercely with my mother,” she wrote, who “only wavered when I began to refuse food, when I claimed, through implicit threat, ownership of my body, which was her great accomplishment.” By all accounts, Glück’s mother, Beatrice, was a wonderful cook; Glück’s papers, archived at Yale’s Beinecke Library, make clear that she grew up among people who loved to eat. In one letter from summer camp, addressed to her younger sister, Tereze, Glück wrote, “I miss—sundaes, shrimp cocktails,” next to tiny sketches of each.

Glück recovered from anorexia through years of psychoanalysis—years during which she also studied poetry with Léonie Adams and Stanley Kunitz. She published “Firstborn,” her début collection, in 1968, when she was twenty-five. Later letters detailed lavish hotel meals in Europe with her first husband and dinner parties in Plainfield, Vermont, where she taught writing at Goddard College and worked part time at a café, baking pastries in exchange for child care. (Noah, her son, grew up to be a sommelier.)

In 1980, John Dranow, Glück’s second husband and the director of the writing program at Goddard, co-founded the New England Culinary Institute, a small cooking school that operated restaurants in Montpelier. Glück sat on the board of directors until the nineties, when they divorced and she moved to Cambridge. In one poem from “Meadowlands,” an unsparing, darkly funny collection from that time, an unidentified husband and wife argue over food. “I stopped liking artichokes when I stopped eating / butter. Fennel / I never liked,” he says. “Living with you is like living / at boarding school: / chicken Monday, fish Tuesday.”

“Why do you call it rigidity?” she retorts. “Can’t you call it a taste for ceremony? Or is your hunger for beauty / completely satisfied by your own person?” The husband has the last word, accusing her of joyless pleasure-seeking: “When you make artichokes, / make them for yourself.”

The word “poet,” Glück wrote, “must be used cautiously; it names an aspiration, not an occupation. In other words: not a noun for a passport.” She could go years without writing, though she rejected the notion of writer’s block, perceiving instead a liminal state of waiting for poems to arrive. During fallow periods, Glück occupied herself with teaching, which she loved, gardening (she claimed to have read nothing but catalogues for two years), and eating at restaurants. “Dinner takes a certain shape,” the poet Katie Peterson, who ate with her frequently at Chez Panisse when Glück taught at Stanford, observed. “A familiar menu is like a rosary.”

In Cambridge, Chiasson pointed out Koreana, the restaurant where he, as a worshipful Harvard grad student, had first spotted Glück, in 1997, having dinner with the poets Robert Pinsky and Frank Bidart. (Bidart, Chiasson’s mentor, eventually introduced them.) Chiasson showed me an unpublished poem that he’d written for Glück after she died: “back before anything happened / yet it was still the bitter end / three poets sat around a lazy susan / kimchi, Tsing Tao, bibimbap, gossip.”

Earlier that day, we’d dropped in on the poet Henri Cole, in Boston’s South End. The two men, who had each shared countless meals with Glück, but never together, delighted in comparing notes, remembering her habit of sampling several wines before inevitably choosing something crisp and dry; her insistence that no meal was complete without greens; and the decisiveness with which she could turn on a place she’d loved. She almost always ordered the fish. She almost never ordered dessert, but would happily pluck the raspberry off of someone else’s crème brûlée. She preferred to eat early, and would wait outside her home, ready to be picked up.

Chiasson and Cole had last seen each at La Royal, another of Rondeau and Calderón’s restaurants, at a memorial for Glück, packed with her dinner companions. When Rondeau first told Glück, in 2021, that she and Calderón were considering opening a new place, Glück advised against it, then immediately changed her mind on a visit to the empty storefront, in a beautiful brick building from 1910, facing Royal Avenue in Cambridge. Not long before she died, Glück weighed in on the menu—both the dishes served and the printed layout—and chose the restaurant’s name.

Chiasson theorized that his friend’s love for both restaurants and poetry stemmed from her interest in “primal urges.” “We build these institutions to contain them and express them,” he said. “Marriage, restaurants, homes—they’re frames for containing all this passion.” In 1999, Glück imagined a creation story of sorts, describing small worlds that appeared in the fissures of a larger, shattered one. “On Huron Avenue they became / a block of stores,” she wrote, “whatever / they were or sold, they were / alike in their function: they were / visions of safety. Like / a resting place.” She called the poem “Formaggio,” after her favorite cheese shop, in Cambridge. ♦

items.title: The Bari Weiss Effect on “60 Minutes”
items.description: Close to Christmas in 1968, the journalist Mike Wallace went to Atlanta, Georgia, to the home of Martin Luther King, Jr. Earlier that year, King had been assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee. Now Wallace, filming a segment for a new magazine-style news program c
items.author: Vinson Cunningham
paragraphs: Close to Christmas in 1968, the journalist Mike Wallace went to Atlanta, Georgia, to the home of Martin Luther King, Jr. Earlier that year, King had been assassinated in Memphis, Tennessee. Now Wallace, filming a segment for a new magazine-style news program called “60 Minutes,” on CBS, sat on the King family’s handsome couch with one leg perched on the seat, looking somewhat ill at ease. A well-appointed Christmas tree feebly defied the air of sorrow in the room. Across from Wallace sat Coretta Scott King, the Reverend’s widow. The King kids were quiet and poised, letting the camera inspect their faces, putting on a show of mild bravery for the nice reporter and all the people out there watching at home. Wallace asked after the family. Was the season sad? Then, zooming out:

King answered in her artful way, assuring Wallace that there were “many more people” who shared her husband’s commitment to nonviolent struggle than there were young Black radicals of various stripes ready to resort to violence.

The King-shaped moral vacuum had given Wallace a kind of civilizational anxiety. Without the charismatic clergyman, what kind of unruly Black-underclass anger would take the stage? That fear didn’t belong solely to Wallace. “60 Minutes” had come along at just the right time to draw a picture frame around a particularly perilous passage in the landscape of the country. Part of its purpose, from the beginning, was not only to deliver new facts but to interpret ragged events for a nervous audience of relatively prosperous, largely white viewers who shared Wallace’s concern about the shape and tenor of the future. That cohort’s curiosities and anxieties were, it seemed, the unspoken rationale for the new show’s existence. Could America, they all seemed to be asking vicariously, through Wallace’s stentorian voice, ever just be normal again?

The fifty-ninth season of “60 Minutes,” which premièred in September, arrives at a similarly disorienting juncture in the life of the American polity. CBS, the country’s unofficial home for geriatric entertainments—stuff like “NCIS” and the shuffling-zombie game show “The Price Is Right”—has become an unlikely protagonist in a morphing media scene. Last summer, its parent company, Paramount, completed a merger with Skydance Media, an outfit founded by David Ellison, an actor turned media mogul whose father, Larry Ellison, happens to be one of the richest people on the planet. Ellison fils’s most high-profile hiring decision was to enlist Bari Weiss—the former Times Opinion editor and founder of the center-right publication The Free Press—as editor-in-chief of CBS News.

Weiss has her own particular vision of American and international normality. Last year, not long after assuming her role atop CBS News, she appeared on a panel at the conservative Jewish Leadership Conference. She understood her new job, she said, as an opportunity to “speak for the seventy-five per cent” of people on the center right and the center left, marginalizing figures like the leftist streamer Hasan Piker and the former Fox News star Tucker Carlson. She wanted to invite into “the room”—the great national agora symbolized by CBS’s airwaves—eminences who could stand at the “forty-yard lines” of reasonable discourse. She’d recently hosted a debate between the permanently discontented lawyer and Epstein pen pal Alan Dershowitz and the conservative polemicist and former N.R.A. spokeswoman Dana Loesch. You know, people like that.

This deserving three-quarters of the population, as construed by Weiss, includes people who don’t believe in “the world as propagandists and ideologues imagine it to be” but want to know “what’s actually going on in the world”—a world that “used to just be normal.” As my colleague Clare Malone has reported in this magazine, Weiss first came to public attention in college, as a consequence of her support for Israel and consistent denigrations of the Palestinian cause. But perhaps she has always, more fundamentally, been auditioning for a role as a propagandist for a dusty vision of a bygone postwar United States, whose faintly familiar personae and aging slogans masquerading as common sense—“individual responsibility,” “the American project,” “Alan Dershowitz”—are putting up a well-funded fight against the fiercer energies of the age.

You can detect the strain of the effort to erect this cardboard version of the country in the early episodes of the new “60 Minutes,” helmed by executive producer Nick Bilton, who, like Weiss, is a Times alum. Visually, the show looks a lot like it did before. Each hyper-competently produced segment opens with a journalist standing with wary authority like the Ghost of Christmas Future, inviting viewers to cross the threshold into some harrowing or heartening new way of apprehending reality. The first segment of the new season, hosted by Norah O’Donnell, was about a fighter pilot, code-named Bravo, whose plane was shot down over mountains in Iran. His interview with O’Donnell relates his story—a faulty parachute, a tough crash, a long bloody hike, and survival until he was rescued by an American plane—in a genuinely moving way. Pete Hegseth is interviewed, too, recalling his reaction to the news of Bravo’s crash—“Shit!”—and insuring that the tale is interpreted as an instance of American power wielded nobly and bravely, with a masculine, sporting élan. Early in the segment, O’Donnell calls the ongoing war with Iran “unpopular,” but the rest of the story does nothing to interrogate just why an American fighter jet was zooming through Iranian skies, and whether the exercise was, in the end, worth the very possible loss of Bravo’s life.

One of Bilton and Weiss’s signature new on-air hires is the conservative writer Ross Douthat, formerly an opinion columnist for the Times. His method is often to approach cultural or political phenomena, progressive or reactionary, with a mix of Gen X irony and sincere moralism which, by degrees, subtly shifts the frame of the discourse to the right.

A few episodes into the new season, Douthat interviewed the Republican senator Thom Tillis, of North Carolina. Tillis is the rare Republican lawmaker who has put up some measure of resistance to Donald Trump, opposing the President’s One Big Beautiful Bill. Recently, he called Hegseth’s initial plan to publicly execute the Fort Hood shooter, Nidal Hasan, “beyond disgusting.” Douthat’s interview portrays Tillis as a robust, independent-minded figure, the kind of guy you might dream up in a fugue state of acutely missing John McCain. At one point, Tillis dares Douthat to jump across the tracks of Congress’s private subway system. Douthat, not known for his athleticism, makes it across. So does, of course, the hale Tillis, whose physical fitness, at sixty-six, is mentioned more than once in the segment. Tillis, scrutinized in this very friendly way, seems like the ideal political representative of Weiss’s “seventy-five per cent,” a guardian of an order whose foundations have long since rotted away. In the version of America in which, say, Mitt Romney hadn’t been exiled from the good graces of the Republican base, Tillis might be gearing up for a successful, quite “normal” bid for the Presidency. As the real world stands, he is a man without an obvious wider constituency, whose highest feasible ambition might be the continued admiration of Douthat and Weiss.

On a recent episode, the longtime correspondent Lesley Stahl reported from the West Bank, where a group of Israeli shepherds called the Hilltop Youth have carried out a series of violent attacks against Palestinian families, attempting to take and settle their land by force. It’s an excellent report, framed by the imminent elections in Israel and the U.S., drawing an implicit portrait of an uncertain but surely bloody future. Soon after that episode aired, it was reported by the media newsletter Status that the in-house screenings for Stahl’s segment had grown “extraordinarily contentious,” with Weiss taking a “very, very hands-on” role in fisking the piece, causing Stahl to consider joining her onetime colleagues Cecilia Vega, Sharyn Alfonsi, and Scott Pelley (who have all been fired since Weiss took over) as former employees of “60 Minutes.” (CBS News has denied the Status report, and defended its own editorial rigor.)

The fracas makes sense: the war in Gaza, with its wake of corpses and depths of ongoing violence, suggests no neat, reassuring, or “normal” solutions. To move forward and, one day, make reparation would surely mean including voices that might have made Mike Wallace nervous, and perhaps fall well outside Weiss’s favored forty-yard lines. To make “60 Minutes” worth the cost of so much reliable prime-time air would be to admit that we will need to envision, together, somewhere down the line, a new world. ♦
An earlier version of this article misstated the timing of Nick Bilton’s departure from the New York Times.

items.title: The Scourge of A.I. Rapping Videos
items.description: When I first heard “Versace,” the 2013 breakout single by the Atlanta trio Migos, it was like seeing a rainbow for the first time. The hook is just Quavo saying the word “Versace” over and over, saccadic and uninterrupted: “Versace, Versace, Versace, Versace!”
items.author: Brady Brickner-Wood
paragraphs: When I first heard “Versace,” the 2013 breakout single by the Atlanta trio Migos, it was like seeing a rainbow for the first time. The hook is just Quavo saying the word “Versace” over and over, saccadic and uninterrupted: “Versace, Versace, Versace, Versace!” It’s not the repetition of the designer name itself that gives the song gravitas but how Quavo and his bandmates, Offset and Takeoff, accent and manipulate the word into eighth-note triplets. They didn’t invent this style of vocal performance, but they did revolutionize its use in hip-hop and popular music, with everyone from Taylor Swift to Ariana Grande adopting iterations of what came to be known simply as the “Migos flow.” In the years following “Versace,” the group notched two No. 1 albums, tied a Beatles chart record, and set off multiple online trends. They popularized the Dab, a dance that became so culturally inescapable that Hillary Clinton, when campaigning for the Presidency, in 2016, did it during a guest appearance on “Ellen”—effectively killing the craze on the spot. Their hit “Bad and Boujee,” from the same year, became one of the defining songs of the decade. As the critic Meaghan Garvey wrote for Pitchfork, in 2018, Migos had “officially infiltrated the mainstream without going pop; instead, pop had gone Migos.” Even after years of creative stagnation, a hiatus, and, tragically, the death of Takeoff, in 2022, Migos had already cemented themselves as cultural icons perennially synonymous with everything cool. Others could imitate but never replicate; their coolness was predicated on their originality.

Imitation, of course, once precluded becoming—a distinction that has dissolved in the age of A.I.-generated deepfakes. In the not-so-distant past, people could dress like Quavo, do the Dab like Offset, or mimic Takeoff’s ad-libs (“Mama!”), but they could not inhabit their movements or voices, could not imagine themselves into their bodies. Now, with the help of A.I., people are doing far more than imagining: in a recent viral trend, users have begun to digitally transplant themselves—and their favorite television characters, celebrities, athletes, politicians, and pets—onto Quavo and Takeoff in a studio performance of their 2022 song “Hotel Lobby.” The original video, which aired on the YouTube series “A Colors Show,” features the duo standing before a bright-orange backdrop, positioned on either side of a dangling microphone. They perform a series of nonchalant dance moves while rapping about diamonds and drugs and experiencing the world in technicolor clarity. But, as it turns out, if you replace Quavo and Takeoff with literally anyone, or anything, the stand-ins manage to channel the same powerful aura as their originators, even if, in real life, they could never dream of achieving such coolness. The tech C.E.O.s Sam Altman and Dario Amodei, two of the more physically awkward and swagless people in public life, suddenly seem loose and inspired when superimposed into the “Hotel Lobby” video; Donald Trump and Elon Musk, hardly known for their fluidity of movement, also assume an effortless cool when becoming Quavo and Takeoff. Deepfakes are controversial, sinister even, given their ability to be used for misinformation or sexual exploitation. But these rapping deepfakes are openly satirical and seemingly inane—is there really any harm in chuckling along with their absurdity?

And people do seem to be chuckling along. After the popularity of the “Hotel Lobby” meme, the deepfakers have turned their attention to the music video for Drake’s “Burning Bridges,” which shows the Canadian rapper and his friends in the back room of a dimly lit restaurant, grinning and staggering around, pointing at the camera and clinking their freshly topped-off shot glasses. Dressed in a black leather headband and jacket, Drake playfully mimes his lyrics: covering his face with his hands, grabbing his chain, swaying about with his arms around his pals. Unlike Migos, Drake has often been accused of trend-hopping, rather than trend-setting, a “culture vulture” who adapts regional sounds and styles for personal gain. (This critique, aggressively weaponized by Kendrick Lamar in diss songs such as “Not Like Us,” tends to be a bit overstated—much of pop music now sounds the way it does because of Drake’s curatorial trailblazing.) But the video’s unmistakable radiance—its delectable sense of place and community, its humor and bluster—has become fodder for a seemingly endless trove of memes that present, for example, the cast of “The Sopranos,” the New York Knicks’ starting five, or any ordinary group of friends as Drake and his buddies: turned up in a restaurant, mean-mugging the camera, slicker and more confident than anyone has any right to be. How novel, and exciting, it must be for the random internet user to consign familiar characters to a rap video, a venue that, until very recently, had a fairly obvious barrier of entry: you had to be the one doing the performance, whether as karaoke or as an original routine. The deepfake meme has removed that barrier. Anyone can now become Drake or Quavo or Kanye West. (A.I.-generated spoofs of West with his Sunday Service choir are the latest rap videos to go viral.) Are you laughing yet?

The initial concern with deepfakes, which emerged during Donald Trump’s first term as President, was that they would mirror reality so closely as to render fact and fiction indistinguishable. Adam Schiff, at a 2019 U.S. congressional hearing, warned that deepfakes would perpetuate “nightmarish scenarios that would leave the government, the media, and the public struggling to discern what is real.” But, as Daniel Immerwahr wrote for The New Yorker in 2023, this wellspring of panic was probably misplaced. “Doctored videos online delight, taunt, jolt, menace, arouse, and amuse, but they rarely deceive,” he argued. Written misinformation and conspiracy theories, for instance, proved more challenging to dispel and dismiss than deepfakes; narratives are interpretive frameworks that messily collage anecdotes and data and ideology together, whereas a manipulated video can often be snuffed out. This is perhaps why, at least so far, deepfake technology has mostly been wielded as an elevated form of shitposting.

But, even when deployed as satire, there remains a revealing tether between deepfake technology and the tech world’s obsession with transhumanism—the belief that humans can evolve with technology to transform into beings no longer dependent on biological bodies. The A.I. scientist Ray Kurzweil told the Guardian, in 2024, that he intended to use mind-uploading technology to “create a replicant of myself, which is an option I think we’ll all have in the late 2020s.” He planned to live forever, he said, even as his body aged and he approached death. Beyond keeping his consciousness alive, he also sought to defy death in other ways, namely by resurrecting deceased loved ones, like his father, as A.I. avatars. “The capability to bring back departed humans digitally will bring up some interesting societal and legal questions,” he said, as if the outcome were inevitable. Altman, writing on his personal blog in 2017, described the “merge” between humans and machines as already starting, though a “gradual process.” He argued that “brain-machine interfaces are going to happen” and that only “arrogance” allowed dissenters “to assume that we will never build things smarter than ourselves.” With this logic, the deepfake meme operates as a soft launch to more odious uses of the technology. In Altman’s and Kurzweil’s visions of the singularity, existence transpires in a simulated reality; if we want to be Quavo in this space, then surely we can be Quavo. The limitations of our earthly world no longer bound us—“we could live forever in computers,” according to another Altman blog post.

Simulated reality, as enlightened as the tech executive may make it sound, is not immune to the baseness of racial and cultural appropriation. It’s revealing that some of the most popular A.I.-generated deepfake memes position Black performers as vehicles for comedic and parasocial fetishization. When I first started seeing the “Hotel Lobby” meme pop up on social media, my immediate thought was that it was a new form of blackface minstrelsy. And there was something, too, about how the internet hive mind selected rap-music videos as its preferred meme-able objects—the creator of the deepfake could inhabit, or imagine others to inhabit, the aesthetics of the Black rapper without having any of the historical or cultural experience of being Black. The long-standing desire to appropriate Black art, according to the critic Wesley Morris, connects to a deeply rooted urge to embody the freedom and authenticity endemic to its most popularized forms. Writing for the Times, in 2019, Morris noted that “particular to black American music is the architecture to create a means by which singers and musicians can be completely free, free in the only way that would have been possible on a plantation: through art, through music.” Even when deepfake memes project other Black people onto Black rappers—such as Zendaya’s character Rue, from the television show “Euphoria,” as Drake, or Barack Obama as Takeoff—an uneasy tension persists. The Black performer remains the template of the parody, a canvas to characterize and deform in whatever way the meme-maker sees fit.

Perhaps the clearest precursor to the complicated racial dynamics of deepfake memes is what happened on TikTok at the turn of the decade. The social-media platform became a beacon of youth culture in large part owing to dance, particularly dances created by Black people, set to music by Black artists. White teen-agers performed moves like the Whoa and the Renegade, and twerked to Jersey club and Chicago drill, not in homage to the cultures that created them but as breezy, frictionless paths to virality. Of course, users of all races engaged with these TikTok trends, but the most visible accounts tended to be those of white influencers. As Jon Caramanica wrote for the Times, in 2019, “TikTok all but eradicates traditional norms about cultural ownership.” Once a trend or a song blew up on the app, it divorced itself from history or lineage and instead became the possession of the platform, a context-free artifact that any user could assert a claim of. Deepfake memes grant a similar carte blanche to their creators, while introducing even pricklier questions about race and authenticity. It was easy to criticize the white teen for booty-shaking and hip-thrusting to regional rap music, but the overtly manufactured nature of face-swapping videos affords many of its makers anonymity, or at least plausible deniability. (They aren’t the ones pretending to be Quavo; it is their A.I. avatars.) Appropriation can almost feel beside the point, though, not because it doesn’t matter but because A.I. has made it the default. This is the technology’s operating principle—human expression reduced to raw data for machine manipulation; peoples’ likenesses rendered nonconsensually and frivolously; creativity concentrated into prompts and preëxisting templates, with little social incentive to make anything new or risk vulnerability—and the harms extend to everyone.

Last week, the Atlantic Coast Conference posted a video to social media showing college-basketball players from its member schools performing an in-person rendition of the “Hotel Lobby” meme. It’s joyfully clumsy; nervous and stilted, the athletes stand before a white backdrop, dressed in their uniforms, tepidly rapping along to Takeoff’s verse and haphazardly mimicking Quavo’s dancing. They do not look as cool and put together as the rappers they imitate, and they sound nowhere near as good. They are confined to their bodies, rife with their many flaws and inadequacies. But the earnestness of their performances, the texture of their hesitation, makes the video far more compelling than any of its deepfake counterparts. When a trio of players from Virginia Tech get their turn on the camera, their exuberance is palpable—they shimmy and stampede around the set, shouting along to the lyrics as if they were at a concert. They are not pretending to be Quavo and Takeoff, because why would they? They, as themselves, are interesting characters in their own right. ♦

items.title: We Can Never Understand Elizabeth Holmes, or Nathan Fielder
items.description: The comedian Nathan Fielder loves to sit just a hair too close to people. Often, these are people he barely knows. In an episode of “The Rehearsal,” his mind-bending, genre-defying HBO show, in which he helps participants prepare themselves for meaningful life
items.author: Naomi Fry
paragraphs: The comedian Nathan Fielder loves to sit just a hair too close to people. Often, these are people he barely knows. In an episode of “The Rehearsal,” his mind-bending, genre-defying HBO show, in which he helps participants prepare themselves for meaningful life events before they take place, we see Fielder recline in his stocking feet on the twin bed of a young pilot he’s just met, his legs tucked girlishly, as the other man perches uncertainly beside him. In the finale of “Nathan for You,” the Comedy Central show in which he offers ludicrous advice to failing small businesses, he shares a small hotel room with an elderly near-stranger whom he’s helping search for a long-lost love. (“This is kind of a fun trip, huh? Just the boys?” Fielder goads the expressionless senior.) Later in the episode, when Fielder brings an escort back to the room, he scoots near her on one of the beds, making unbroken and unnerving eye contact all the while.

There’s something inherently comical about this insistent, creepy overfamiliarity. (It’s not surprising that a screenshot of the bed scene from “The Rehearsal” has become a popular meme.) Fielder’s willful disregard of conventional social norms—his comfort with an atmosphere of discomfort, to the extent that he is able to carry on as if nothing is amiss—elicits laughs in the same way as the punch line of an old joke that I recently heard: a urologist tells his patient he must stop masturbating. “Why?” the patient asks. “Because I’m talking to you!” the doctor responds. (Fielder, of course, is the patient.) But there’s also something puzzling, and unsettling, about the forced intimacy that Fielder likes to enact: it creates a tension that fuels his comedy but that lingers long beyond the laugh. What game is he playing, we wonder, and to what ends?

In his odd, gripping, and entirely original new documentary, “You Can See Everything,” which he co-directed with the filmmaker Lance Oppenheim, Fielder’s penchant for invading his interlocutors’ personal space is more pronounced than ever before, and, at nearly three hours long, the film gives us ample time to try and figure out his motives, as well as those of his subjects. Unlike his past work, however, “You Can See Everything” isn’t very funny at all. Instead, it’s a haunting exploration of the limits of other people’s knowability. How close can we really get to those around us? Where do we begin and where do they end? Are each of us, ultimately, all alone in the world, mere islands unto ourselves?

The documentary starts in medias res, with a man’s face in tight closeup as he speaks on the phone. This is Billy Evans, a Silicon Valley entrepreneur and the life partner of Elizabeth Holmes, the disgraced founder and onetime C.E.O. of the health-care startup Theranos, who, in 2022, was convicted of four counts of fraud. (Holmes deceived investors by making false claims about the capabilities of Theranos’s proprietary blood-testing device, which, she said, could detect a whole slew of ailments with just a pinprick’s worth of blood.) It’s now April, 2023, just more than a month before Holmes is set to begin serving her eleven-year federal prison term, and Evans, as he tells whomever is on the other end of the phone line, thinks that people need to understand who Holmes really is. If they did, they certainly would see that she is “so true and so good,” as he murmurs to her, a bit later. To that end, the couple have invited Fielder, Oppenheim, and a film crew into their Del Mar, California, beachfront rental, to document their lives with “radical transparency” and “as much access as possible.”

The film finds its subjects at a very fraught moment. Holmes, who is still nursing the younger of the couple’s two small children, is filing challenges to her conviction and taking calls about what to expect in prison. Evans, meanwhile, is focussed on getting “the band back together” to continue developing, with Holmes’s help, a new device providing low-cost blood-testing, which he refers to as “Theranos 2.0”—a startling example of Silicon Valley hubris, considering how well 1.0 turned out. For the couple, however, this makes sense—Holmes, they both insist, is completely innocent. (The implication is that her former partner in both love and business, the much older Ramesh [Sunny] Balwani, Theranos’s C.O.O., who was convicted of twelve counts of fraud, is the one responsible for the company’s wrongdoing.)

“The world believes a reality about me that isn’t true,” Holmes tells Fielder. He isn’t convinced by her protestations (“there is a lot of evidence that points to the fact that you defrauded investors and also deceived, you know, regulators and the public and patients,” he says), and he skulks around darkly, his surveilling presence casting a pall on the Holmes-Evans ménage. In scene after scene, Fielder, who fully moves into the house, grills the pair, together or separately—in their kitchen nook, in their marital bed, on their living-room couch—often at such proximity that they can surely feel his warm breath on their cheeks. A bit of this is still comical, and it certainly serves as a self-conscious callback to Fielder’s popular reputation as a possibly sinister weirdo. Running roughshod over domestic conventions, he sometimes seems like the couple’s overgrown son, recalcitrant and lacking in boundaries. (I laughed when, a few hours before Holmes is scheduled to surrender to the authorities, the comedian finally offers to give the couple some space so that they can “have sex,” and proceeds to go sit in his car with the music blasting—a move that reminded me of his “Nathan for You” scheme to create a “sex box,” in which parents can have intercourse while on vacation with their children.)

Mostly, though, we’re dealing with dead-serious business here. This is certainly the first time that a Nathan Fielder project has reminded me of a Bergman film, and that might be at least partly because of Oppenheim’s involvement. In his previous documentaries, such as “Some Kind of Heaven” and “Spermworld,” and in his recent narrative feature “Primetime,” Oppenheim is a stylish visual thinker and a master of vistas; in “You Can See Everything,” he turns largely to the vista of the human face. With the help of David Bolen’s eerily beautiful cinematography, Oppenheim, like Fielder himself, aims to get as close as possible, homing in, “Persona”-style, on the protagonists’ features, expressions, and gestures as a kind of window into their souls.

Holmes’s soul, however, remains a cipher. Who is this woman, with her wide, unblinking, cornflower-blue eyes, with her frequent tears and earnest proclamations, who keeps insisting on her utter sincerity—going so far as to say that she can’t remember telling a single lie? “She’s really weird. She’s just not normal,” Evans tells Fielder, while attesting to Holmes’s honesty, but the idea of full transparency—the notion that one can and will see everything about another person if there is willingness on both sides to do so—is both troubled and troubling in the film. The more access Holmes allows, the less Fielder is, seemingly, able to know her.

One pathway to enter another person’s consciousness is through the figure of the double—or Fielder, at least, seems to think so, when he tries to understand Holmes via the lens of his own subjectivity. “I’m a bad communicator,” he tells her at one point. “I don’t know a lot of words. Is that what you’re like?” (He also echoes a common reaction to his own tactics in the course of his career, when he wonders whether Holmes is “fully sincere” or “the most manipulative person who ever lived.”) Later in the film—and be warned of some spoilers from here on out!—he attempts to understand his subject by engaging with another double of hers, the actress Amanda Seyfried, who portrayed Holmes in the 2022 Hulu series “The Dropout.” It also becomes clear that Holmes and Evans see themselves as doubles of each other, claiming that the connection between them is practically telepathic.

Is this type of thinking delusional? Does it, at the very least, involve some mangling of an individual’s dearest, most private core? “You’re a very talented actress, very good performer, but, you know, you’re not her,” Fielder tells Seyfried, a rare admission by the comedian that his method has limits: a double, however convincing, may obscure its subject just as much as it reveals her. He recounts a conversation he had with Holmes, in which he compared his uncertain feeling while talking to her—was she telling him the truth or fooling him?—to a magic trick that he once saw David Blaine perform. Blaine appeared to be driving an ice pick through his hand, which viewers assumed relied on smoke and mirrors. In fact, Fielder says, Blaine was literally stabbing his hand, puncturing his own flesh to create the illusion of an illusion.

Watching this scene, I thought of Theranos’s promise to provide people with crucial medical knowledge through a tiny blood sample. This promise, as we now know, was fraudulent. No puzzles were solved; blood, it turned out, would not tell, and the mysteries of the self remained locked within it. Fielder, too, resists being known: after spending weeks trying to get into his subjects’ heads, he dismisses the possibility that they’d be able to get into his. “I know what you’re feeling,” Evans tells him, at one point in the film. Fielder’s response is immediate, and notably heated: “No, you don’t.” ♦

items.title: Why Is It So Hard to Sit Still?
items.description: Long ago, when I was a fledgling journalist, I learned from an eminent editor about the concept of Sitzfleisch. It was a German word, he explained, that referred to the ability to sit still for a long time. “If you want to be a professional writer, you need Si
items.author: Joshua Rothman
paragraphs: Long ago, when I was a fledgling journalist, I learned from an eminent editor about the concept of Sitzfleisch. It was a German word, he explained, that referred to the ability to sit still for a long time. “If you want to be a professional writer, you need Sitzfleisch,” he told me. Although it was important to “get out there” and “report,” it was also inevitable that I’d have to plant myself at a desk for whole days and weeks, focussing unremittingly on the production of words; many talented writers, he suggested, had failed to progress because they wrote beautifully but not for long enough.

Under different guises, I was already familiar with Sitzfleisch. In a prior life, as a graduate student in English, I’d spent entire days reading. This was reading for work, not for fun, and I frequently had to force myself to occupy the same library armchair from morning til night, squinting at the pages until my vision blurred. I’d discovered, during this period, that not all Sitzfleisch was created equal. You could succeed at sitting in a chair while your mind wandered. Often, it was movement that pushed you out to sea. In those days, I read lots of productivity books, and one of them, “How to Work the Competition Into the Ground and Have Fun Doing It,” was particularly centered on the struggle against “mind drift.” Its author, John T. Molloy, had carefully observed himself at work, and determined that episodes of drift began when he leaned back in his chair. Accordingly, he placed a sign that read “GET BACK TO WORK” near the ceiling, at the exact spot where his gaze tended to alight when he reclined. Seeing it, he’d immediately lean forward, returning to a state of Über-Sitzfleisch—the higher kind of sitting.

The problem is an odd one, fundamentally. Newton’s first law of motion holds that bodies at rest stay at rest. But it doesn’t apply, apparently, to human bodies. Why are we so antsy? Why can’t the body content itself with stillness, leavened, perhaps, by the fluttering of fingers over a keyboard or the occasional arcing turn of a page? When I attempted extended Sitzfleisch, I sometimes felt as if every joint in my body had its own will, my fingers wanting to bunch and unbunch, my legs to cross and uncross. Standing and pacing were just an eyeblink away.

This past June, I broke my ankle, and so had to spend much of the summer in bed. The desire to move—even to move the broken ankle itself—became, at times, overwhelming. This was the problem of Sitzfleisch, amplified. And yet my nervous energy could be temporarily suspended by meditative breathing, or extinguished for hours by a fast-paced book or an absorbing show on Netflix (or, on good writing days, by the flow of work). What was sometimes impossible was at other times effortless. Just sitting there, it turned out, was complicated.

“Why do we and other animals have brains?” the neuroscientist Daniel Wolpert asked, in a 2011 TED talk. You might think that brains are for perceiving the world, or for having ideas, but this would be wrong, Wolpert said: “We have a brain for one reason and one reason only, and that’s to produce adaptable and complex movements.” At bottom, brains help us figure out where and how we’ll move next; even perception and communication are forms of movement (the saccade of an eye, the enunciation of a syllable). In general, living things that don’t move don’t have brains. The sea squirt, Wolpert pointed out, has a brain, and uses it to find a good rock on which to make its home—but then it immediately digests most of its brain, because it never needs to move again.

Learning this, you might imagine the brain as an issuer of clear movement commands—as a general, or a choreographer. But this doesn’t capture the full story. In reality, the brain is a collection of subsystems that are, to varying degrees, interconnected and autonomous. Many of these subsystems hatch their own individual movement plans, creating a range of possibilities, all competing. The competition is adjudicated in the basal ganglia, structures deep inside the brain that repress all the plans except one. The basal ganglia get better at their job during the first thirty years of life; this is partly why kids are more impulsive and restless than adults. Disorders such as Parkinson’s and Tourette’s involve a malfunctioning of the basal ganglia. So we might say that, beneath the surface of stillness, there’s an ambitious cacophony that must be controlled. Our brains are wild, and yet rein themselves in.

Instead of imagining a binary between motion and stillness, should we picture a spectrum of activity, ranging from the brashest, biggest movements to the minute ones that we use to investigate the world or put down our thoughts? My eight-year-old son seems to sit still while playing Minecraft; when he’s not doing that, he runs laps around the house. But, when he’s Minecrafting, is he really still? Actually, he’s immersed in a flow of typing and mousing, imagining and deciding, venturing and inspecting; with his eyes and hands, he is in constant motion. Similarly, he can curl up in a chair for an hour, trying to get faster with his Rubik’s Cube. Is that Sitzfleisch? If so, Sitzfleisch is really about maintaining momentum. You don’t lean back in your chair when you’re making progress on the problems you’re facing; you do it when you’re stuck.

In a short story called “Catch That Rabbit,” from 1944, Isaac Asimov imagined a futuristic scenario in which engineers test a robot nicknamed Dave, which controls six “subsidiary” robots, orchestrating their movements in the excavation of a mine on an asteroid. Dave is supposed to be able to operate without human supervision. But whenever he encounters a truly vexing or overwhelming problem—an imminent cave-in, say—his subsidiary robots act strangely, performing what, to trouble-shooters, look like “callisthenic exercises.” Why is the team of robots working hard one moment, and marching in formation the next? The engineers conclude that, when Dave doesn’t know what to do, he enters a “moronic maze” and starts “twiddling his fingers.” This reverses the picture we might have of Sitzfleisch. My editor presented it as though people with Sitzfleisch stay in one place so that their minds can work. But it might be because your mind is working that you can sit in place.

In “The Principles of Psychology,” from 1890, William James compared our thoughts to a river. On the whole, he wrote, “easy simple flowing predominates in it.” Yet “at intervals an obstruction, a set-back, a log-jam occurs.” This “stops the current, creates an eddy, and makes things temporarily move the other way.” If a river were self-aware, how would it feel about those eddies? James thought it would experience them as “places of effort”:

The sensation of mental effort isn’t necessarily bad. In fact, James thought, “the whole feeling of reality, the whole sting and excitement of our voluntary life,” comes from the sense that we’re the ones pushing our mental lives forward. From this perspective, it’s because Sitzfleisch eludes us that we know we exist. If you’re not struggling to sit still, are you even alive? Or are you just a sea squirt, happily brainless on its rock?

In schoolrooms and offices, there are worksheets and spreadsheets to be done; around the world, there are probably millions of Google Docs open in millions of browsers, cursors blinking. There are lots of reasons to try to repress our nervous energy, and so it’s no surprise that there’s a big-time campaign against mind drift. I’ve certainly profited from honing my Sitzfleisch skills. I know when not to lean back in my chair, lest it lead, God forbid, to going for a walk.

But it’s worth noting that sitting still and doing just one thing for a long time is, in many respects, at odds with the essential nature of the human mind. And it’s also good to ask whether, for many tasks, it’s capability, rather than discipline, that allows us to concentrate. When you can’t move, you desperately want to fidget; it’s when you don’t know what to think that your mind darts to something else. Often, you want to get up from your desk because you’ve stumbled across the limits of what you know how to do. You can respond by forcing yourself to sit there, banging away at the problem with whatever resources you have. Or you can get up, do the dishes, and hope that the solution will come to you. Maybe, the next time you encounter a logjam, you’ll be able to stay in the flow a little longer. ♦

items.title: The Amazon Coat: An Oral History
items.description: Even with a decade of trendspotting, deal hunting, and expert interviewing behind us, few stories compare to that of the Orolay coat. As the tale goes, in March 2018, former New York fashion director Amy Larocca appeared behind features editor (then–associate
items.author: Bella Druckman
paragraphs: Even with a decade of trendspotting, deal hunting, and expert interviewing behind us, few stories compare to that of the Orolay coat. As the tale goes, in March 2018, former New York fashion director Amy Larocca appeared behind features editor (then–associate editor) Katy Schneider’s desk with a hot tip: “There’s this coat I need you to look into. It’s $89, and every woman I know on the Upper East Side has it.” In the months and years following Schneider’s reporting, the coat became so ubiquitous in the city that it earned its own nickname: “the Amazon Coat.” Here is an oral history of the Orolay coat — from its uptown origins to its eventual banishment to Buffalo Exchanges — according to the whisper network of women who set off the trend, the New York staffers who broke the story, and several folks who covered the coat’s unlikely takeover of the city.
“Women were crossing the street to ask me where I got the coat.”
No one knows exactly who bought the Amazon Coat first, but a daisy chain of women shared the link with friends and strangers until it caught our attention as a thing.

Jessica Reich, teacher: “It was actually in 2016 that I purchased the coat, so it’s been about ten years. It’s crazy. I was planning a trip for a joint 30th birthday with my boyfriend at the time to Iceland. I was just doing what I do whenever I’m going to travel to a new place, which is look around and see what gear I need. I was going in March, so I was really interested to see what type of winter gear I would need, and I found this blog — I don’t know if she’s around anymore, but it was called The Blonde Abroad. This was obviously back when you didn’t necessarily go on someone’s Instagram to find clothes and stuff. You were literally going to their blogs. So I was probably just searching ‘Iceland fashion,’ something along those lines, and she popped up. She had this coat and linked it, and I was like, This is amazing. So I just bought it through her link.”

Kiki Rich, author of The Blonde Abroad: “It came from this picture of me in Whistler. We had helicoptered into this snowy mountain peak, and that picture — this was pre–the term, even, viral, I think — it just got so much attention. Then even my own audience was like, ‘Where’s that from? Where’s that from?’”

Fernanda Niven, founder of homeware brand the Bouwerie: “I found out about it because a friend of mine had one and I saw her in it and nobody else was wearing it. I think she just discovered it on Amazon. I loved it, and I said, ‘Can I find out where you got that coat?’ She told me and I bought one immediately and I started wearing it around the Upper East Side. It was unbelievable. Women were crossing the street to ask me where I got the coat.”

Reich: “I kept wearing it. It just started to become a thing. I was a teacher at the preschool at the 92nd Street Y at the time. So the moms at school and the other teachers were like, ‘Oh, tell me about the coat.’ And then at the time, it was relatively, from my standpoint, inexpensive. It’s funny the article has updated itself to reflect the current price. But I think back when I got it, it was well under $100. It might have been $70, $80 at the time.”
Niven: “I’ve never had anything like that happen to me before, where it was just like girl after girl, woman after woman asking me, ‘Wait, I’m so sorry to ask — where is that coat from?’”
“It was like our Watergate.”

One March morning, then–New York fashion director Amy Larocca was discussing the latest trends with her friend and former market editor Gretchen Fenton. The coat she’d be seeing around, it turned out, was from a then-unknown brand you could find on Amazon called Orolay. When she got back to the office that day, she tipped off Schneider (now features editor, then associate editor) and Alexis Swerdloff (now deputy editor, then Strategist editor), who got right to work.

Amy Larocca: “Gretchen was like, ‘Do you know about this coat?’ I was like, ‘Yes, I have seen this coat.’ And she was like, ‘Do you know the thing about it?’ And I was like, ‘What about it?’ She was like, ‘It’s from Amazon.’”
Katy Schneider: “We immediately knew it was such a great story. We were super freaked out about getting beat.”
Larocca: “I was always telling Alexis and Katy things. I’m sure I probably just got back to the office and I was like, ‘All right, guys. Hot tip.’ I did not think it was gonna be this hot a tip.”
Alexis Swerdloff: “It was like our Watergate.”
Schneider: “It was a perfect daisy chain. Every single person told me someone else to call and gave me their number. It’s not so easy to get this kind of reporting or to get quotes like this.”
Niven: “I felt like if someone was calling to talk to me about it, it meant that clearly she had been noticing it around.”

Schneider: “I was going the next day to Florida for a family trip. I was just like, ‘I am so determined to figure out what’s going on with this Amazon coat that I’m not letting it go.’ I remember I was with my family and I was at the airport sitting at a table on the phone with one or two of those women from the lede, just being like, ‘Tell me where you got the coat.’”
Larocca: “I think it’s the ultimate Strategist thing because it was cheap. I think that was so in the spirit of the Strategist — like, ‘Amazing finds. We do the hunting for you.’”

Schneider: “It was just one of these things where Amy had stumbled upon such a phenomenon. That was evident immediately when I started reporting. Every single person who I called immediately knew what I was talking about, immediately had another person to connect me to. And it came together super quickly.”
“It was so much bigger than anyone could have imagined.”

After our story went live, dozens of publications covered the coat’s unlikely rise to popularity — and more people bought the coat than we could count. One woman even made an Instagram account under the handle @theamazoncoat that accrued more than 10,000 followers as it documented the women and men wearing the coat across the country.

Schneider: “It was so much bigger than anyone could have imagined. I remember it being very strange to see the effect of that in real life over the next couple of not just months but years. For years after that story, seeing people wherever I went in that coat on the street was crazy.”
Swerdloff: “You’d walk down the street and you’d be like, We did this. For better or for worse.”
Larocca: “I always thought, All my years at New York Magazine and my biggest contribution is the frickin’ Amazon Coat.”

Swerdloff: “It was a little secret you’d have. I remember being in a room with all these people being like, Well, you’re wearing this sort of because of me. I mean, not me, multiple people, but it was a very strange feeling to have.”

Lucy Handley, freelance journalist who covered the coat for CNBC: “We had this stand-up meeting with a couple of editors and maybe 12 journalists who wrote for the website, and I remember saying, ‘Oh, there’s this Amazon coat.’ Immediately, my editor went, ‘What’s the Amazon Coat?’ There was this level of intrigue because I guess at the time you might not have associated Amazon with fashion.”
Making its Good Morning America debut.

Reyhan Harmanci, executive director at Wired who wrote about the coat for the Times: “I totally bought it. I couldn’t believe the price. It was so cheap, and it was really, really warm. But it was then a bit uncanny to be wearing the same thing as literally every other woman I could see.”

Handley: “It’s a baggy, kind of casual, a bit oversize style that I think is still fashionable now. I can see the picture I used. The model in the picture was wearing skinny jeans, and that was the big trend. Athleisure was just starting, so yoga leggings with a big top.”

Swerdloff: “This idea of a viral item wasn’t really a thing at the time. The only other thing I could think of at the time that was sort of like that was the Instant Pot. There just weren’t items that went viral on the internet in that way. It was really one of the first that I can remember like that and that you would just see out in the world and everywhere. That happens now all the time.”
Harmanci: “This was before lanternflies, but it had the invasion kind of vibe.”

Larocca: “My kids were pretty little, and they would be like, ‘Mom, the coat, the coat!’ It became a family joke. I remember sitting in the subway and being like, Oh my God, there are multiples in this car. What is happening? That is so crazy. This just sort of blasted in out of nowhere.”

Lauren Posner, creator of the @theamazoncoat Instagram account: “A lot of my friends and people I knew had the coat, so I just thought, Oh, why don’t I just start taking pictures of people wearing the coat? And if they want to answer a question — why they bought the coat, what drew them to the coat, why does it inspire them or something quirky — and just put it on Instagram, it would be fun. But that was also a time when a lot of Instagram accounts like that were coming about.”
Harmanci: “I somehow managed to write about this at least a year after you guys had done multiple stories, so it’s really amazing anyone let me write about it.”

Posner: “There were people who did outrageously creative things. Someone made a cake that looked like the Amazon Coat, and they used the hashtag #theamazoncoat. I would also look for posts that had the hashtag and repost them.”

Harmanci: “Everyone I talked to seemed to have a different way into it. Like, some people had seen the New York Magazine story, but a lot of people just saw it on the backs of their friends or saw a picture of it or it was a hand-me-down coat from somebody. It just seemed like no one really knew where the coat came from.”
“I remember seeing the coat at Buffalo Exchange, and I was like, Okay.”

Over the years, Orolay released ankle-length and cropped versions, a fleece-lined variation, and even a line for kids, but the Amazon Coat was eventually demoted to the back of closets or pawned off to Buffalo Exchange during the pandemic. Still, the original coat has amassed more than 29,000 reviews on Amazon (that’s up from 6,000 in 2019) with an impressive four-and-a-half-star average rating. Every Prime Day when it goes on sale, readers still buy it. Will it ever have a nostalgia-fueled resurgence?

Harmanci: “It was two winters. First winter was early adopters. Second winter was the rest of us. And then it was kind of gone. I do think that all of the new variants helped kill it. One of the fun things about the coat originally was that it was so basic. You had two or three colors, maybe — no other options. It was at a moment where you had these formfitting puffy coats. It was a real choice to be wearing this puffy square, essentially, with these pockets hanging out. It was not an elegant coat, but it was extremely comfortable and extremely warm. I think that helped its lanternflylike recognizability because it was so differently and awkwardly shaped.”
Emily Gould, New York features writer: “When I would first see an Amazon Coat in the wild, I would be like, Oh, she’s got the Amazon Coat. And then it eventually just became ‘the Coat.’”

Megan Reynolds, freelance writer and editor who wrote about the coat for Jezebel: “It’s like the Spider-Man meme — you’re all pointing at each other in the same fucking outfit. To me, that’s kind of what killed the coat.”

Niven: “I wore it so much, and I kind of got sick of it. Then seeing it everywhere, you’re wearing it and you’re seeing it, so it’s overload. But I still love the navy one. I still have it, and every once in a while, I break it out.”
Reich: “It definitely will always have a place in my closet.”
Larocca: “I never wanted to see it again.”
Posner: “Believe it or not, I still wear it occasionally, especially on really cold days. I still see plenty of people wearing it as well.”
Swerdloff: “I remember seeing the coat at Buffalo Exchange, and I was like, Okay.”
Reich: “I wonder if some people will think, Oh, I just came upon this, not knowing that it’s been around for so long. Or other people might be like, Wow, this is a throwback.”
Larocca: “Is the Amazon Coat going to have one of those hilarious revivals of ‘It’s so pre-COVID’ or whatever they decide to call that era?’”
Swerdloff: “Is it gonna come back in style? Is it going to be like suddenly you’re going to see Liana Satenstein wearing the Amazon Coat? I don’t know.”
