items.title: Angie Nixon Won’t Stop Fighting
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Zak Cheney-Rice
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

It is one month before Election Day, and a crowd of faithful Democrats has gathered near Fort Lauderdale, Florida, for what should be a tense occasion. The audience in the Lauderhill Performing Arts Center is mostly older and white, the kind of “Vote Blue” stalwarts from surrounding Broward County who sport I MISS BARACK caps and pine for the days when the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool was algae free. Angie Nixon, the candidate here to address them, is running what looks like a doomed campaign for the U.S. Senate. She has significantly less money than her Republican opponent, is trailing in most polls, and has broken with party leaders in almost every internal dispute of the past ten years, from Bernie versus Hillary in 2016 to whether Israel is committing a genocide in Gaza.

And yet inside the air-conditioned lobby of the auditorium, a minor miracle is occurring. These partisans love her. “You finally feel a momentum,” says a delighted John McRae, who’s there with his wife, Nancy. “She’s very exciting,” says Deborah Webb, a local substitute teacher, practically giddy. “She’s kind of like Christ coming into the Temple and throwing over the tables,” says Tim Singer, who plans to volunteer for Nixon, leaning closer to be heard over the buzzing crowd.

The fact that Nixon has this audience so amped up might surprise national Democrats. Her reputation as a bullhorn-toting agitator in the Florida house of representatives made Nixon a divisive figure in the state party. She won her seat by primarying a fellow Democrat, Kimberly Daniels, and has conducted protests on the house floor without the say-so of party leaders. After a policy disagreement, Nixon and one colleague, state representative Michele Rayner, did not speak for two months. (Rayner, now an adviser to Nixon’s campaign and a close friend, admits Nixon was right.)

Many of the party’s moderates were against Nixon’s Senate bid during the primary. And in general, Establishment Democrats have been “not supportive” of her confrontational methods, Rayner tells me. They worry she will push out faithful, if centrist, Democrats. In 2023, Nixon introduced a cease-fire resolution to halt Israel’s destruction of Gaza. It infuriated the Democratic state senate minority leader, Jason Pizzo, who went so far as to publicly apologize to Israel’s consul general to Miami. A year and a half later, Pizzo declared the Democratic Party in Florida “dead” and dramatically quit to become an independent.

In spite of these concerns from party officials, on August 18, when given the choice between her and Alex Vindman, a stiff, poll-tested moderate of the kind Democrats have been foisting upon Floridians for years, voters chose Nixon by a decisive 12-point margin. The result shocked national commentators. Vindman is a retired U.S. Army lieutenant colonel who became an MSNBC darling after testifying at President Trump’s impeachment hearings. He had out-fundraised Nixon 16-to-1 and was so confident she posed no threat to his nomination that he barely bothered to campaign against her. It was a testament to how poorly Vindman understood Florida — “He says he’s lived here for three years,” Nixon tells me, “but I had never heard of him” — that he failed to see what was obvious on the ground: Democratic voters were fed up with the status quo.

For them, the past decade has been one agonizing defeat after another. Since 2016, what was once the most prized swing state on the electoral map has become a reliable GOP stronghold. Trump has carried Florida in three consecutive presidential elections, increasing his margin of victory every time. The 2022 midterms were such a bloodbath for Democrats — Governor Ron DeSantis and then-Senator Marco Rubio won reelection by 19 and 16 points, respectively — that strategists and donors started to write off the state. “Florida is off the board,” DeSantis bragged to Fox News in 2024. “It is a Republican state.”

Nixon, a dynamic 42-year-old Black single mother turned union organizer, has premised her campaign on the idea that GOP rule has been a disaster. Florida has become more repressive, with bans on abortion and public-school-curriculum materials going into effect, and less affordable, with analysts ranking its housing markets among the most hostile in the country toward renters. She caught fire because she seems to understand better than any other candidate that this election is about “rent, gas, food, and how Florida has become the Hamptons of the United States,” as one longtime Democratic donor, Mitchell Berger, puts it. The Democrats’ go-to response over the past 30 years has largely been to run the most anodyne candidates they can find, only to watch Florida become redder. Nixon has taken the opposite approach, seizing on a polarizing agenda of bigger government and universal programs that pundits long assumed would exclusively resonate in deep-blue states like New York.

Her primary win should be exciting for the party. She is an authentic working-class candidate with charisma, the kind of populist whom political strategists have salivated over this midterm season. “Donald Trump’s net worth has increased by over $4 billion since he’s been back in office. What y’all bank accounts look like?” Nixon asks the crowd. “I mean, seriously, what do your bank accounts look like?” People start calling out numbers. “Somebody said, ‘Double zero.’” Nixon bows her head in pity. “Lord. We going to work on that.” But the national party was initially cool to her efforts. It was galling for Nixon, in part because of Democrats’ lip service to how much they owe to Black women. “It’s like they want our labor,” she tells me, “but they don’t want our leadership.” It also seems shortsighted. For Nixon, November 3 will mark not the end but another beginning. The deeper reckoning comes after the election. She wants to reshape Florida politics — win or lose, with or without national Democrats’ approval.

When Nixon announced her Senate bid in January, she’d spent months trying to recruit someone else for the job. She had lots of good options, she says, including colleagues in the state legislature who she knew “had the back of the community and weren’t going to sell out.” But none of them could be convinced a statewide race was worth the headache. “They kept saying, ‘Where am I going to get the money from? It’s Florida; it’s deep red.’ They felt like it was just a suicide mission.” That Nixon rejected their defeatism is consistent with her longtime approach to politics. Rather than despair at subpar leadership, she runs for office herself, even when it means dispatching fellow Democrats. “I have no problem primarying people,” she says. “That’s what I have always done.”

The joke around Florida is that Nixon’s is a “friends and family” campaign. It heavily relies on her decades-old alliances and personal relationships instead of the usual consultants and party-assigned staffers. Former colleagues from the state legislature and SEIU and even Nixon’s eldest daughter, Natalie, who is 19 and joined her mom at a recent rally at the University of South Florida, can regularly be seen piling out of her pink-and-yellow campaign Sprinter van.

Still, Nixon does want the support of national Democrats. Days after winning the August primary, she spoke by phone with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer. She says she asked Schumer for his help; Nixon wanted introductions to donors and assistance with press. (Florida, with its ten major media markets, is one of the most difficult and expensive states in which to advertise.) “We’ll see” was the gist of Schumer’s reply. His noncommittal answer became a minor cause célèbre in progressive corners of social media. The outrage appears to have motivated the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee to act: Kirsten Gillibrand, Schumer’s fellow senator from New York who runs the organization, hosted a virtual fundraiser for Nixon earlier this month. Schumer and the DSCC are “now being supportive,” Nixon says, although it came late and only after a public campaign for help. “Elected officials don’t like bad press,” she says.

Most of the issues Nixon is running on — Medicare for All, the “Green New Deal,” free child care, Bernie Sanders’s proposed tax on billionaires — are factional third rails, emblematic of years of infighting between Establishment moderates and progressive insurgents. Many fellow Democrats, both national and local, believe these stances will torpedo her candidacy. Nixon’s polling numbers have been a grab bag, ranging from almost tied to a double-digit deficit. And she faces in Republican opponent Ashley Moody a candidate running with the unwavering support of her party.

A former state attorney general, Moody has never lost an election. She is the rare Republican official who has outrun DeSantis in statewide races. Her alliance with the governor is a prime expression of the Florida GOP’s sense of impunity over the last decade. Moody defended DeSantis’s unpopular campaigns against abortion and recreational marijuana. In 2023, she signed off on a deal that routed $10 million from a Medicare settlement payout to Hope Florida, a charity affiliated with the governor’s wife, Casey; the money was then used to fund Republican political action committees. A grand jury this summer found that the transfer was an illegal misappropriation of the funds, but jurors could not determine who was at fault, so no criminal charges were filed. (Moody has called attacks on her involvement “disingenuous.” In October, an appellate court ordered the grand-jury report to be expunged, saying the panel overreached.) Meanwhile, Moody’s political fortunes have continued to rise. In 2025, when Rubio joined Trump’s Cabinet as secretary of State, DeSantis appointed her to his vacated Senate seat. Moody became a reliable pro-Trump vote on Capitol Hill, backing the president’s refusal to extend Obamacare subsidies, his pillaging of Venezuela’s oil reserves, and his ongoing war on Iran.

Nixon is juggling making the case that Moody is corrupt with a frenetic campaign schedule that leaves her relative lack of resources more pronounced. When I meet her in Tampa between campaign stops, she has slept only two hours, has been on the road nonstop for the past week and a half, and hasn’t seen her youngest daughter, 5-year-old Ashanti, in as many days. Seated on a couch in the Black English Bookstore on East Oak Avenue, she lets loose about how frustrated she is with the party leadership. Nixon tells me about the list she’s been keeping of people who have slighted or undermined her. “Former colleagues. Some chairs of Democratic executive committees. Mm-hmm. Some chairs or presidents of caucuses. Oh yeah. Oh yeah. There’s a list that has been kept,” she says with a laugh. “After the race, we going to have some nice conversations.” I ask if she’ll share some of the names with me. “I don’t wanna name names right now,” she says. “I’m just trying to win.”
Three of the names that could be on Nixon’s list are easy enough to guess.

There are the Vindmans — Alex, her Democratic primary opponent, and his wife, Rachel, a politics Substacker who until 2024 co-hosted a podcast called The Suburban Women Problem. When Nixon started to seriously consider running for Senate, she was told the DSCC was already recruiting Vindman. She found his contact information and called him to gauge his interest. At the time, he was relatively unknown in state politics and had never run for public office. Vindman and Nixon never spoke at length about the run, and when Nixon asked around the state party, she got what sounded like a definitive answer: He wasn’t interested. She launched her campaign on January 22. On January 27, Vindman launched his.

It was an awkward way to kick things off, and it only grew more fraught as it became clear he intended to act like Nixon’s campaign didn’t exist. “I saw Vindman in Orlando for an event — it was at the Pulse-nightclub-shooting remembrance, so this was back in June,” says Wes Hodge, the treasurer of the Florida Democratic Party. “And he made a comment like, ‘Well, we’re looking at November and the race against Moody.’” Hodge was incredulous. “I was like, ‘Dude, you don’t have that luxury! You have an opponent in August who you need to take seriously.’” Vindman approached a potential debate with the same attitude. “We’re happy to let you know the second we make a decision,” his campaign manager, Blakely Wall, told reporters in July when asked if Vindman would participate. (He never agreed to a debate.) This posture rankled Nixon, one of whose many criticisms of “unelected Ashley Moody,” as she refers to the GOP incumbent, is that she, as an appointee, did not earn her office. Here was Vindman acting just as entitled, carrying on as if the nomination were a foregone conclusion and their primary just a formality.

By the end of July, Nixon’s momentum was harder to ignore, and at least one of Vindman’s surrogates decided she was worth taking on. His wife, Rachel, who had previously inspired a right-wing outrage cycle by posting a joke about Trump getting shot, went after Nixon on Threads. “If your campaign events with less than 20 people devolved into you making personal attacks on your opponent, you are a shitty human,” she wrote in a since-deleted post. “Also, buy some professional clothes for the love of everything (shoes included).” It’s unclear which personal attacks Rachel was referring to. Nixon replied with a cheeky photo of herself in heels. “Are these OK?” she wrote. Rachel later apologized, and her husband has not publicly addressed his wife’s remarks. After losing the primary, Vindman endorsed Nixon, introduced her to his donors, and made a $400,000 contribution to the Florida Democratic Party.

The Friday after the primary, Nixon got on a call with FDP chair Nikki Fried — the third possible name on her list — whose official stance on the Democratic nomination was neutral. “We stay out of all those primaries,” Fried tells me, “and we make sure that everybody’s getting a fair shake.” The call between Fried and Nixon did not go well. According to Axios, some in the party believed Fried was disappointed when Nixon won, and their conversation, which Fried says started out as congratulatory, devolved into a heated disagreement. “Unfortunately, it became tense,” Fried tells me. Nixon reportedly bristled at the chair’s attempt to give advice, telling Fried, “You never gave a care about me from the beginning, and now you’re telling me how to run my campaign?”

Fried tells me one of the concerns she raised was about Nixon’s association with the Democratic Socialists of America and what Fried describes as the celebratory response by some chapters to Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel: “I was just making sure I was relaying messaging to her of concerns that I have been hearing, not only from demographics in our coalition but from some electeds, too, that were worried.” Fried assures me she is encouraged by Nixon’s distancing of herself from the most controversial parts of the DSA platform, namely abolishing the police and prisons. Nixon is not a socialist, and she tells me she joined the organization this summer purely because her campaign “needs to be all hands on deck” to beat back the right. While Fried seems intent on striking a conciliatory tone — “The most important part is that everybody’s united” — Nixon is less interested in doing so. “We are running a coordinated campaign,” Nixon tells me when I ask for more details about the call. Was she really upset that Fried gave her advice? “We are running a coordinated campaign,” she repeats.

Nixon has always done things her own way. She ran her first campaign as a candidate — for a city council seat in her hometown of Jacksonville — right after graduating, in 2008, from the University of Florida. She had come back from school with her daughter Natalie, who was less than a year old, and found herself unhappy with local leadership. The Moncrief neighborhood where Nixon grew up had barely improved since she was a child. The community was on top of a Superfund site. The soil was toxic, and the local schools were in the same rough shape as when Nixon’s mother deemed them inadequate and had her bused across town. Nixon’s cousin was shot and killed when they were teenagers. “If he would’ve got bused across town like me,” she says, “I think he still would be alive.”

After Nixon announced her candidacy, she went door-to-door, pushing Natalie in a stroller. “It wasn’t about being in charge,” she says. “It was about wanting somebody that was going to do the job correctly.” She adds, laughing, “Damn, I’m really anal. I’m kind of type A.” She and Rayner, who is sitting beside Nixon as I ask about her start in politics, begin cackling. “I’ve learned a lot about myself on this campaign.”

Nixon lost the election, but she spent the next decade shuffling among positions in Duval County politics — as a district aide for a state representative, then as a field director and political director for the mayor of Jacksonville — and, eventually, as an organizer for policy nonprofits, like the advocacy group New Florida Majority, trying to boost civic engagement among Black and brown Floridians. In 2016, Nixon helped run Black outreach for Sanders’s 2016 presidential campaign in Florida, a gig that came full circle when the Vermont senator committed $250,000 to back Nixon’s Senate campaign in early October. “I met Bernie maybe twice,” she says.

In 2018, SEIU’s Florida chapter recruited Nixon as a field director. She worked on various campaigns, including the push for a $15 minimum wage. (A law accomplishing just that went into effect last month.) Later, she was moved to a SEIU local that organizes college Head Start workers, the people who provide child care and early education for the children of low-income students. “I do not have words to describe how hardworking Angie is,” says Afifa Khaliq, the local’s president. In 2020, Nixon ran for state representative and won. She launched her Senate campaign as her third term in the legislature was ending.

What appears on the surface to set Nixon apart as a lawmaker is her pugnacity. She loves to fight. She has a line of tattoos along her right forearm — one is the Adinkra symbol for “call to war” — because that was the arm most visible to her colleagues when she addressed the legislature. “I wanted them motherfuckers to see this while I’m talking,” she says, cocking her arm like she’s holding a microphone. A few weeks before we meet, Nixon agreed to a $250 fine and 15 hours of community service to resolve two misdemeanor charges — trespassing and resisting arrest — from her refusal in May to vacate the governor’s office. She had been demanding a meeting about a recent Republican gerrymander in the state that reduced the number of Democratic-leaning congressional districts from eight to four. Nixon didn’t want a trial on the charges to distract from her campaign, so she took the community service and moved on. But if she had not been in the middle of the campaign? “She wanted to continue to fight,” says her lawyer, Mutaqee Akbar.

Her facility with conflict has proved a useful quality at a time when right-wing politics are distinguished more by their rancor than their substance. Laura Loomer, the influential pro-Trump conspiracist who successfully lobbied the president to fire several top aides last year, called Nixon on X “a ghetto, black, communist.” Vice-President J. D. Vance traveled to Florida on October 1 and told a rally crowd in Lakeland that Nixon doesn’t “belong in America.”

But what genuinely makes Nixon different, according to people who know her, is that her public brawling is matched by her shrewdness and stamina as an organizer. “Angie won the Democratic primary because she has been knocking on doors, talking to people, alongside people, for decades,” says Phillip Agnew, who met Nixon when he was part of the Dream Defenders, a Black Lives Matter–era youth-activist group. She is unafraid to talk to anyone. Nixon says right-wing voters are often shocked to discover she’s “not this horned beast” when she shows up at their doorsteps. Representative Maxwell Frost, the congressman from Orlando, says every Nixon event has a canvass attached to it. This is rare in Florida. “What it usually is,” he says, “is you show up, you go to the rally, they get your information, and then they ask you, like, a day or two later, ‘Can you come back and canvass with us?’ And the difference is, because Angie’s an organizer, she knows that every little hurdle you add in front of someone doing something makes it less likely that they’ll actually volunteer.” Instead, Frost says, people show up to her events as spectators and leave as door-knockers.

Nixon is convinced some Democrats don’t want her in D.C. because they’re lazy. “I would force them to do more work,” she told The Breakfast Club in September. She’s known in Duval County for her hands-on approach to constituent services. Brandon Davis, her senior adviser and media consultant, remembers her once taking time between campaign stops to help someone whose apartment ceiling had collapsed and who couldn’t get a response from their building-management company. Nixon wants to scale this approach if she’s elected, deploying aides across the state for weekly listening sessions and personally hosting town halls in a different part of Florida every month. “We’re going to have community office hours where we go to libraries and coffee shops and small businesses and welcome people to come talk to us about different issues,” she says.

Even Nixon’s opponents have admitted she is uniquely industrious. “Angie was working 24/7,” says Mitchell Berger, the donor, who backed Vindman in the primary. “Not that Alex wasn’t working, but there is something to knocking on doors and showing up at community events as opposed to just working the phones for money and showing up at financial events.”

Nixon’s strong ground game helped make up for an astonishing spending gap. In July, Nixon had a little less than $975,000 on hand. Moody had $11 million, which she has used to fund ads falsely accusing Nixon of being a socialist who wants to abolish the police and prisons. (Nixon’s retort is that she doesn’t want to abolish prisons, she wants to put Moody in one.) This ability to define the opposition is key: A Stetson University poll in September found that 32 percent of Floridians surveyed — close to one-third — still don’t know who Nixon is, compared with just 19 percent for Moody. “Nixon’s not getting anywhere near the resources to run a statewide race,” Susan MacManus, a veteran political analyst who has taught at the University of South Florida, said earlier this year.

That Nixon offset her disadvantages enough to be even slightly competitive with Moody holds lessons for her fellow Democrats — including her skeptics. In the primary, she showed that she could win with less by outworking an Establishment-favored opponent and leveraging relationships unconnected to party leadership. In the general election, she is proving she has the force of personality to bring national attention, and even national money, to a campaign that donors and strategists were inclined to write off. Nixon’s most recent FEC report indicated that she pulled in close to $7.2 million. (Moody, who raised just $1.8 million in the same period, still has a roughly $5 million advantage.) She accomplished it by prodding moderates and galvanizing progressives. Ro Khanna is planning to campaign for Nixon in Florida later this month. Sanders, Chris Murphy, and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez have already done so. Most important, the base has bought in, undeterred by Florida’s red hue.

The last time Democratic voters in Florida were this excited was in 2018. Like today, President Trump was on the defense, and the national spotlight was on a statewide race: the gubernatorial campaign of Andrew Gillum, then the mayor of Tallahassee.

Gillum is an obvious template for Nixon; Davis, her adviser, was Gillum’s campaign manager. Both are Black multigenerational Floridians to the left of their party with a talent for public speaking. Both had a similar projected path to statewide victory: overperforming in Jacksonville and the panhandle while running up the score around college areas in Tallahassee and Gainesville and banking on kitchen-table appeals attracting more South Florida voters than the GOP’s red-baiting scared away. And both share a maximalist campaign philosophy. “Just making sure we go everywhere,” Nixon says. “Making sure we have an aggressive 67-county strategy. Making sure I spend every dollar that I have.” Gillum lost to DeSantis by one of the slimmest margins in Florida gubernatorial history — a 0.4-point, 33,000-vote defeat.

Eight years later, the Gillum moment has become easy to dismiss. After the election, he spiraled into depression and was found inebriated in a motel room with a male escort. He checked himself into rehab, reportedly got sober, and launched a somewhat successful podcast. Then, in July, he was arrested on meth charges in Alabama. The fortunes of Florida Democrats have followed a parallel trajectory. After 2018, they fell into a now familiar pattern, running moderate statewide candidates like Val Demings and Debbie Mucarsel-Powell — and getting clobbered. The party hemorrhaged talent as the people and money that had coalesced around Gillum 2018 disappeared. By 2024, the idea that Kamala Harris could compete in Florida was never seriously considered.

How did things get so bad so quickly? It’s conceivable that a strong state party could run back the Gillum playbook with more success and assimilate internal disagreement without things spilling over. But the reality is that Nixon has had to build most of her own campaign infrastructure because it did not exist. Steve Schale, the longtime strategist who directed Obama’s victorious statewide operation in 2008, scoffs at the idea that Florida’s Democratic Establishment was aligned against Nixon — that would imply some meaningful measure of organization and influence by the party. “You wield power with sticks and carrots, right?” he says. “What happens when you have no sticks and you have no carrots?”

The ability of a state party to exert influence depends entirely on the scope of its electoral power. And Florida Democrats don’t have a senator, a governor, or any statewide officials. Their most influential figure in the House of Representatives is Debbie Wasserman Schultz, who is probably better known for being ousted as chair of the Democratic National Committee months before Hillary Clinton fumbled Florida in 2016. Democrats are a superminority in the state legislature, which is part of the reason Nixon’s weapon of choice has been the bullhorn rather than the backroom deal. The fact that the state party is carrying $6,000 in debt instead of the more than $800,000 deficit it was running in 2020 is arguably its biggest success story of the past ten years. Without electoral power, the board that votes on how the party should proceed is “just a whole bunch of people with opinions,” Schale says. It couldn’t tip the scales of a primary if it wanted to.

Another problem is that, for Florida Democrats, the people and institutions planning, funding, and running elections are extremely transient. “The only partisan infrastructure that’s ever existed here is whatever got built around whatever presidential election was happening at that point,” says Schale. “The other 42 months of that four-year cycle, the party can barely keep the lights on.” Diminishing returns — the last statewide office Democrats won was when Fried was elected commissioner of agriculture in 2018 — has put the party in a kind of death spiral. “I will be 25 years old in less than a month,” says Jackson McMillan, a Tampa-based Democratic strategist who runs a firm called Key Lime Strategies. “And I am considered a veteran strategist here in the state of Florida because I’ve been doing this for, like, eight years.” That’s how you get a campaign like Vindman’s, much of whose staff was chosen and imported by the Washington-based DSCC. The problem is compounded for progressives like Nixon because they have access to so much less money. “The president of Florida’s progressive caucus,” says McMillan, “works multiple jobs and lives with roommates.”

Fried is the eighth FDP chair since 2010 and — at nearly four years into the job — has one of the longest tenures of this century. “We have to acknowledge first and foremost that that job sucks,” says McMillan; you spend a lot of time getting yelled at by activists who think you can do more than you can. People I spoke with credit Fried for being the most productive chair in a long time. From September to October, Democrats outpaced Republicans in month-over-month party registration for the first time in five years. But at this point in the election cycle, that’s like playing catch-up on a hamster wheel. I ask Nixon how this race might look different if the FDP were not “dysfunctional,” as she says. “They would be registering a shit ton of voters and running commercials attacking Ashley Moody left and right, like the Republican Party does,” she says. “My campaign shouldn’t be going negative. I should just be speaking affirmatively about my policies.”

Some of these challenges might be surmountable in a less complicated state. But winning a statewide campaign in Florida is like assembling a “jigsaw puzzle,” says MacManus, the professor and political analyst. items.title: Go Ahead, Pity Elizabeth Holmes
items.description: There is something stunted, almost upsettingly so, about the way we talk about You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Critics agree the movie is extraordinary, but they te
items.author: Ryu Spaeth
paragraphs: There is something stunted, almost upsettingly so, about the way we talk about You Can See Everything, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary about the disgraced Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. Critics agree the movie is extraordinary, but they tend to be rather elliptical when explaining why. There is a lot of musing about the slippery distinction between performance and being, and about the fundamental unknowability of other people, tropes of such longstanding tenure in the arts they verge on clichés. This mental block, it seems to me, comes from our collective confusion about how to feel about Holmes herself.

On the one side, you have John Carreyrou, the reporter who broke the story that Theranos was a fraud. Carreyrou argues that You Can See Everything is a devastating exposé of an inveterate manipulator and liar, one who can bring forth tears on command to elicit our sympathy. By “subjecting herself to Mr. Fielder’s polite but insistent questioning,” he writes, “Ms. Holmes handed them — and us — a microscope with which to observe and dissect her lies.” Carreyrou’s interpretation of a much-discussed scene in which Holmes fails to understand Abbott and Costello’s famous sketch “Who’s on First?” takes a typically hard line: She pretends not to get the joke so she can cast “herself as the neurodivergent entrepreneur who operated on a different wavelength,” as opposed to a scheming criminal of the tawdriest kind.

On the other side, you have what Carreyrou describes as “cinephiles’ lofty debates about truth and art.” These debates revolve around how we should feel about the obvious but bizarrely repressed fact that Holmes is totally captivating, the source of the film’s eerie power. She is both a loving mother and a cartoon character with her Looney Tunes eyes, possessed of a dreamy gaze that is common to saints and madwomen alike. When the tears slide across the plane of her face — which under Oppenheim’s zoom lens takes up the entire screen, the entire world — it is as if we can see something fracturing inside her, some horrible realization taking hold as she prepares for life in prison. For those who don’t share Carreyrou’s unforgiving take, this “glimpse into her soul” presents a problem: What if we’re being duped? What if we ourselves are exposed as sentimental fools? The result is a wary coolness flowing under the warm effusions of praise for the movie, as critics warn that “one’s empathy may easily be exploited.”

I say let the feelings flourish. You shouldn’t feel bad for feeling bad for Elizabeth Holmes. Not because maybe she is neurodivergent, or because she appears to be surrounded by men, including Fielder and Oppenheim, intent on using her for their own ends. Rather, because she represents something all too knowable and familiar.

This is not to say that, under the camera’s watchful gaze, Holmes transforms into an honest broker. Quite the contrary. In another instantly notorious scene, she tells Fielder that she has never told a lie — which is, of course, a lie. It is so bald-faced, so ludicrous, so unlikely to convince Fielder or anyone else, that you start to realize Holmes’s issues go beyond mere falsity, mere calculation, into the ruinous regions of self-deception, where she is struggling mightily to maintain some fiction of herself: namely, that she is not the sort of person who tells lies. She is not a liar, which is not something anyone wants to be. And here is where I find myself identifying with Holmes. I also believe that I am not a liar, even though I tell lies all the time. I probably lie every day. In a certain light, you could say that is in fact what I am, a liar.

I felt a similar pang of recognition in the scenes in which Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, attempt to resurrect Theranos, all hot-blooded purpose as they work the phones under the insane belief that they can relaunch a tarnished company whose founder is days away from entering prison. I am a writer after all. How many essays have been forged in the throes of manic inspiration, fired by the fantasies of tens of thousands (no, hundreds of thousands!) of readers, only to be met by the editor’s withering glare and the indifference of audiences? How could any of us do anything without a healthy dollop of self-deception to help us along the way?

The movie’s most poignant scene involves Fielder compelling Holmes to watch The Dropout, a televised dramatization of the Theranos scandal in which Holmes is played by Amanda Seyfried. As Seyfried gamely fangirls to Steve Jobs and shouts, “Get the fucking money!” and lets her former lover and Theranos partner Sunny Balwani fondle her, Holmes collapses in sobs and says she can no longer go on. Perhaps, as Carreyrou suggests, this is all for show, a plea for our mercy and affection. But let’s grant for a moment that her tears are genuine. Is Holmes upset because the television show is a true depiction, smashing the carapace of denial she has built around herself? Or is it rather that none of us could bear realizing what the world thinks we are like, which invariably is at odds with how we view ourselves?

Fielder and Oppenheim are not ones to open their thematic aperture too wide. As the documentary goes on, it becomes ever more narrowly focused on the question of whether Holmes is aware that Evans is trying to profit from the movie. But there are hints everywhere of a broader malaise emanating from Silicon Valley: Tesla Cybertrucks in a parking lot, a WeWork that Evans uses as his office space. These are (or were) companies run by men animated by delusions of grandeur, who like Holmes are not inclined to see themselves as bad people. Like everyone else, they have their reasons and excuses for their behavior. What I struggle to comprehend is a form of moral superiority that suggests we can’t possibly understand Elizabeth Holmes when we can — not only because her way of living is all around us, but because it’s inside us, too. That is what makes her tragic, if that is not too grandiose a word: a real-life Emma Bovary for the technological age.

For me, at any rate, that is why this odd bit of journalism (for that is what it is) is so moving, so transfixing. As the movie creeps toward its conclusion, there are surreal flashbacks of Fielder and Holmes swimming together in the frigid Pacific Ocean. At times they seem to be playing, frolicking almost; at others, she seems to be beseeching him, or he seems to be dragging her along. It is an image that can be interpreted in all kinds of ways: attraction and repulsion, forgiveness and betrayal, two creatures trapped in the same soup.

items.title: Trump Loyalists Wage ‘Blood Feud’ Over Missing Millions
items.description: In the span of a little more than a week, the Trump administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece over an alleged pay-to-play scheme, scrapped Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution, and introduced new press secretary Katia Zacharia b
items.author: Bess Levin
paragraphs: In the span of a little more than a week, the Trump administration fired Kimberly Guilfoyle as ambassador to Greece over an alleged pay-to-play scheme, scrapped Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream an execution, and introduced new press secretary Katia Zacharia before showing her the door just five days later. With all that going on, you might not have noticed another unfolding Trumpworld scandal or thought it was even possible for a fourth shitshow to simultaneously be occurring. But it is, and it’s a classic, in that it involves two Trump loyalists accusing each other of wrongdoing, an alleged promise of pay-for-access, $17 million that supposedly went missing, and a 29-year-old who claims to be a billionaire but might not actually be either.
The parties: Richard Grenell, Alina Habba Mildon, and Habba Mildon’s new husband

Grenell is Donald Trump’s presidential envoy for special missions. He previously served as U.S. ambassador to Germany, acting director of National Intelligence, and interim director of the Kennedy Center. In another lifetime, he was a foreign-policy advisor to Mitt Romney’s 2012 presidential campaign, and in 2020 he was described by top Obama adviser Susan Rice as “one of the most nasty, dishonest people I’ve ever encountered.”

Alina Habba Mildon joined Trump’s legal team during his first administration, replacing a longtime litigator who had quit. (Per the Washington Post, her previous experience included “being general counsel for a parking garage company.” She also represented a cast member of The Real Housewives of New Jersey in a dispute with Facebook.) In 2024, a judge threatened to send her to jail during the E. Jean Carroll defamation trial. In 2025, she was disqualified from serving as acting U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey.

Turhan Mildon is a Turkish businessman who Habba met in 2025, and they were married at the Waldorf Astoria last month. (Nelly performed.) According to the New York Times, Mildon “portrays himself as a billionaire,” the suggestion being that he may not actually be one. He has a cement business in Venezuela and “told Forbes Turkey that he produces 4.5 million tons of cement a year” there, though “data seen by the Times shows that Venezuela’s entire annual cement output is about a third of that figure.” The Times also raised questions about Mildon’s comments about his shrimp business; a spokesman for Mildon told the paper he was misquoted by Forbes. And while Mildon says he’s 29, U.S. and British documents list him as 25, per the Times. Mildon and Grenell reportedly first met in late 2024.
The claim: Missing millions that were earmarked for the Kennedy Center

Last Friday, the new Mrs. Mildon, who “has maintained a close relationship with the president,” according to the Times, “stormed into the Oval Office intent on taking down” Grenell. There, according to Axios, she alleged that at Grenell’s urging, her husband wired $17.6 million to a defense company called Texas Armament & Technology, explaining that part of the money would go to a contract with the Democratic Republic of Congo involving software and $5.6 million would go to the Kennedy Center.

Habba Mildon told Trump that she recently learned that the money never made it to the Kennedy Center. Grenell also allegedly sent a text to Mildon promising access to “POTUS,” “VIP events” and Trump officials, according to a text message. “Once the money comes to the company here, I will arrange the donation to Kennedy Centre [sic], and you’ll be joining the VIP events and get close with the administration, even with POTUS,” the text from May 3, 2025, reportedly reads.

Though the wire transfer allegedly occurred some time ago, “Mildon never checked to see if it was deposited” because “he believed it had been credited because he was treated like a VIP donor at the Kennedy Center,” according to Axios.
What Grenell has said about the claims

Speaking to Axios, Grenell called Habba Mildon’s claims “absurd,” adding: “I’ve never asked for one cent to be sent somewhere else pretending it was for the Kennedy Center, and I’ve never received any payment from him at all. Make him give proof to what he is saying, not make these absurd allegations.”
The proof, according to the couple
A lawyer for the Mildons sent the White House a “2025 text that discussed the Kennedy Center donation and Congo ‘software,’” according to Axios.

In the text to Mildon, the sender also says, “There is an e-mail that was sent to you, can you please take a look at it for me ?” That email also was furnished to the White House, as was a May 29, 2025, financial record showing $17.6 million was wired to the company, known by its initials TXAT, sources said.
The weird bits that don’t make any sense

There are many! For starters, while Habba Mildon initially indicated the $17.6 million originated in her husband’s bank account, it actually “was wired to TXAT from Congo’s “Ministère des Finances” in Kinshasa, the capital city, where Mildon has business and access to finances according to a White House official who spoke to Axios. (A spokesman for Mildon declined the site’s request for comment, while representatives for TXAT and the Congolese government could not be reached.)
Meanwhile, Habba Mildon is said to have initially claimed that the full $17.6 million was supposed to go to the Kennedy Center but then said it was $6 million.

Lisa Dale, who was in charge of the Kennedy Center’s finances at the time, told the site that while there was a record showing an outstanding donation of $270,000 from Mildon, “There was nothing about $6 million. I would have heard about that.”
What the White House is saying

One administration official told Axios that “POTUS doesn’t want to deal with this,” but “if there is missing money, this is a big, big problem.” (The White House’s general counsel has reportedly launched an investigation.) Another official noted “these are only allegations,” while a Trumpworld insider summed up the drama: “This is the ultimate MAGA blood feud.”

items.title: Polls Show a Blue Wave Downballot, Too
items.description: Even in an era of increasing partisan polarization and straight-ticket voting, state elections have their own logic and rhythm, in part because salient issues at the state level can be different from those prevailing nationally and also because some state pols
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: Even in an era of increasing partisan polarization and straight-ticket voting, state elections have their own logic and rhythm, in part because salient issues at the state level can be different from those prevailing nationally and also because some state pols — notably governors — are news-commanding celebrities in their own right. But the national political environment still affects downballot elections if only by affecting turnout patterns. So Democrats anticipate at least modest gains in the 36 gubernatorial elections being held this year and in the 88 state legislative chambers with some or all of their members facing voters in November.

Exactly half of those 36 gubernatorial elections are for positions currently held by each party, though incumbents (nine Democrats and eight Republicans) are running in only 17 of them, thanks to voluntary retirements and term limits. The Cook Political Report currently rates 12 races as competitive with five leaning Democratic (Alaska, Arizona, Iowa, Michigan, and Oregon), three leaning Republican (Florida, Kansas, and Texas), and four toss-ups (Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, and Wisconsin). If the “leaners” go the way they are leaning, Democrats would net one additional governorship (picking up Alaska and Iowa but losing Kansas). A Democratic sweep of the toss-up races would net three more (Georgia, Nevada, and Ohio). That’s impressive in no small part because 11 of the 12 competitive races (all but Oregon’s) are in states carried by Donald Trump in 2024.

Polling of the gubernatorial races reinforces most of Cook’s analysis. Using the Silver Bulletin polling averages, Democrats have robust leads in four of the five Lean D races. In Alaska, a complicated race because of that state’s top-four primary system with ranked-choice voting in the general election, Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins has 45.6 percent to Republican Bernadette Wilson’s 23.6 percent and Republican Dave Bronson’s 15.7 percent. (Another Democrat who qualified for the general election dropped out.) In Arizona, incumbent Democrat Katie Hobbs leads Republican Andy Biggs by 9.1 percent. In Iowa, Democrat Rob Sand leads Republican Zach Lahn by 7.3 percent. And in Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson leads Republican John James by 8 percent. The closest race of the batch is actually in deep-blue Oregon, where incumbent Democrat Tina Kotek has a 1.6 percent lead over Republican Christine Drazan.

All of the Republican-leaning races, however, are relatively close. In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds was expected to win easily against Democrat David Jolly but leads by only 4.4 percent. So too was Texas incumbent Republican Greg Abbott, but he leads Democrat Gina Hinojosa by just 2.4 percent. Aside from Oregon, the best chance for a GOP flip is in deep-red Kansas, where Republican Ty Masterson leads Democrat Cindy Holscher by 4.3 percent for the office being vacated by term-limited Democrat Laura Kelly.

The four toss-up gubernatorial races are predictably tight, per the Silver Bulletin polling averages. In Georgia, billionaire Republican Rick Jackson leads Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms by one percent. In Nevada, Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo leads Democrat Aaron Ford by 0.8 percent. But in Ohio, Democrat Amy Acton is leading heavily financed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy by 4.4 percent, and in Wisconsin, upset primary-winning Democrat Michael Crowley leads Republican Tom Tiffany by 3.6 percent.

Two other gubernatorial races where the GOP is favored (rated as “likely Republican” by Cook) bear watching for a possible upset. In Nebraska, incumbent Republican Jim Pillen has a relatively narrow 4.4 percent lead over Democrat Lynne Walz, while in Vermont, five-term maverick Republican incumbent Phil Scott has a surprisingly small 2.2 percent lead over Democrat Amanda Janoo.

Let’s say a big blue wave hits gubernatorial races and Democrats win all the competitive contests plus the two “upset specials.” In that unlikely but theoretically possible event, they’d net nine new governorships and hold 33 of 50 overall.

Control of state legislative chambers is harder to predict given the complexities of each state’s elections and sparse relevant public polling. But according to estimates from Larry Sabato’s Crystal Ball, 15 state legislative chambers are in play in November.

Democrats hope to flip the Arizona house and senate, the Georgia house, the Michigan house, the New Hampshire house and senate, the Pennsylania senate, and the Wisconsin assembly. Republicans hope to flip the Maine house, the Michigan senate, and the Minnesota senate. Both parties are battling to control the currently tied Minnesota house. Given the environment for both gubernatorial and legislative races, Democrats are hoping to bust up Republican “trifectas” in Florida, Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio, and Texas while building their own trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Vermont, and Wisconsin. Republicans hope to disrupt a Democratic trifecta in Maine and build their own in Kansas.

So once again, a blue wave could significantly reconfigure American politics at the state level (particularly with a new decennial redistricting cycle approaching in four years) as well as in Washington.
- Polls Show a Blue Wave, But Beware All the Close Races
- Trump’s Popularity Is Circling the Drain

items.title: Art, sound and a very small house: Three Tokyo exhibitions to see in October
items.description: Tokyo’s creative scene is in full swing this autumn. Monocle stops by three galleries to peruse a graphic design survey, sample an immersible audio visual installation and explore a fresh take on a literary classic from 13th-century Japan.
items.author: Ben Davis; Tabitha Sipp
paragraphs: Tokyo’s creative scene is in full swing this autumn. Monocle stops by three galleries to peruse a graphic design survey, sample an immersible audio visual installation and explore a fresh take on a literary classic from 13th-century Japan.
‘Ryuichi Sakamoto + Shiro Takatani: Ambient Kyoto’

Azabudai Hills Gallery is the setting for the latest presentation of a site-specific work by the late musician and composer Ryuichi Sakamoto and visual artist Shiro Takatani. Based on Sakamoto’s 2017 release Async, the “Async Immersion” installation builds on his concept of secchi-ongaku (installed music), the spatial experience of sound that he envisaged during the album’s production.

Sakamoto’s 14-track album is accompanied by a 26.4 metre-wide screen that shows Takatani’s visuals. The imagery includes pianos, equipment from Sakamoto’s studio and landscapes that unfurl across the screen while remaining out of sync with the soundtrack. The result is a spatial experience that feels a world away from life beyond the gallery’s walls.

“Experiencing the work within the flow of the ever-changing interplay of sound and image is like watching waves or ripples in the rain,” writes Takatani. It’s “an experience that, while repetitive, never happens in the same way twice.”
‘Ambient Kyoto’ is on view until 25 October 2026; ambientkyoto.com
‘Yoshihisa Tanaka: Archive / Achieve’

The work of prolific 46-year-old art director Yoshihisa Tanaka takes centre stage at Ginza Graphic Gallery this month. Over the past two decades, Tanaka’s work across contemporary art, architecture, photography and fashion has expanded to include explorations in paper as material and medium. In recent years, he has experimented with creating paper trainers with New Balance and designed an installation using pleated and folded Japanese washi paper to create undulating forms for Issey Miyake’s spring/summer 2024 show in Paris.

Tanaka’s enquiries into the possibilities of paper as not only a medium for print but a material in its own right appear throughout this survey. The basement gallery is filled with publications, posters and invitations spanning the past two decades. Meanwhile the ground-floor space presents design materials from the archives of businesses and universities in containers, display fixtures and other storage designed by Tanaka and made with washi. By reimagining the archive, he considers the cultural value of preserving graphic design and passing it on to future generations.
‘Archive / Achieve’ is on view through 21 October 2026; dnpfcp.jp
‘Learning from “Hojoki”: Tiny Architecture Reweaves Life’

The celebrated 13th-century essay “Hojoki” (“The Ten Foot Square Hut”) has long inspired people from various walks of life. The nonfiction essay, written by Kamo no Chomei, details the political and environmental situations that moved him to live in a secluded hut in Hino in the Kyoto mountains. Eight centuries after Chomei left society behind, his musings on living in an impermanent world have informed the latest show at 21_21 Design Sight in Roppongi.

Directed by Atelier Bow Wow co-founder Yoshiharu Tsukamoto, the exhibition uses Chomei’s work as a lens for examining the essence of architecture. The exhibition asked designers, builders, artists and architects to create interpretations of Chomei’s 10-foot-square dwelling, drawing from their own tools, materials and perspectives on contemporary life. Yusuke Obuchi and Jun Nakamura refashioned an abandoned feed silo into “walking architecture”, while Yusuke Omuro and Kawacho-Gumi created a storage shed based on the writings of the late novelist Chotaro Kawasaki.

Each tiny dwelling explores ideas around society and architecture in light of the challenges of contemporary life. “In order to overcome such dilemmas and anxieties, we would do well to fundamentally rethink the lifestyles to which we have become so accustomed,” writes Tsukamoto.
‘Learning from “Hojoki”: Tiny Architecture Reweaves Life’ is open until 11 January 2027; 2121designsight.jp

items.title: A tour of the world’s best autumn/winter menswear collections and collaborations
items.description: Menswear brands have dropped trousers and more. But what has caught the eye this season? It seems that clothiers have fallen for popped collars again and – encouragingly – remain certain that quality fabrics are a non-negotiable. And for those who have also fl
items.author: Jack Simpson
paragraphs: Menswear brands have dropped trousers and more. But what has caught the eye this season? It seems that clothiers have fallen for popped collars again and – encouragingly – remain certain that quality fabrics are a non-negotiable. And for those who have also flicked through hundreds of brands’ lookbooks this autumn, I ask you this: why is every collection being shot in Scotland this year? Seriously, the Hebrides have never been better dressed – or better-looking. But before trekking up there, let’s start off by checking in with the Antipodeans:
Pick up fine fabrics from Asha Jasper

When it comes to building the best menswear collections, sourcing deadstock threads and knowing the right mills have become just as important as fashioning a well-crafted garment. Asha Phillips, founder and creative director of Sydney-based brand Asha Jasper, designs collections from the weave and weight of textiles hand-picked from Japanese and Italian mills. With the perfect fabric to hand, Phillips shapes pieces using classical tailoring methods and modern utilitarian references. We particularly like Asha Jasper’s straight-cut, made-in-Australia trousers that would fit everything from a boardroom to a bar.
Ride on Japanese clothier Niceness’s coattails

Tokyo-based Niceness has, for yet another season since its 2017 debut, produced a range of outwear that’s the envy of all those who thought last year’s coat would do. Among rails of beautiful wool suiting, silk shirting, knits and accessories for men and women, it is the outerwear pieces that form the new collection’s coat stand of showstoppers.

The E Calder coat is one of many (do check out the Rowan and Dieter shapes too) that takes traditional silhouettes a little further. Inspired by British military macs and made from US Sea Island cotton, it’s a nod to 1950s and 1960s design, with side slits to access trouser pockets. Last year’s coat will not do.
NN07 and Fracap’s latest collection has a foot in many camps

Danish clothier NN07 and Italian bootmaker Fracap have been in lockstep for years. In their third collaboration, the brands reimagine Fracap’s M127 silhouette with three new boots that, for the most part, reflect NN07’s penchant for pared-back aesthetics.

Two of the designs, which come in traditional brown and black leathers, are quite at home on a steep alpine edge, pounding inner-city pavements or mucking out the stables in the country. The third pair – though it wouldn’t struggle with these tasks – might make you forever conscious of scuffing your prized, dark-grey ponyhair shoes. The choice is yours.
Stone Island Ghost will blend seamlessly into your wardrobe

Stone Island’s Ghost collection draws on the brand’s extensive material research and garment-dyeing capabilities to create pieces inspired by the art of camouflage. Its approach is pared-back but delivers striking monochromatic and tonal looks.

The David-TC is a padded jacket with an inviting shearling-trimmed collar, woven from a star-shaped Japanese polyester that mimics vintage military motifs. It’s one for cooler months, to be worn for years to come.
Stride into the new season with Tarvas hiking shoes

Finnish shoemaker Tarvas has found its footing at the top of the crossover between hiking boots and trainers. With its topographical layering of leather, rubber and mudguard, the brand’s Easy Hiker is now a recognisable silhouette on the streets of Paris, Tokyo and beyond.

The Wanderer is the Hiker’s slender cousin. With a generous Vibram sole and a Jacques Solovière-like upper side that forms a calfskin pleat through its centre, it’s ideal for both the fleet-footed city flâneur and the forest trail explorer. If you can’t decide, the Explorer and new Derby shapes provide a middle ground with a more classic look. Picking which style to buy might be your only uphill battle for a while.
Toast the season in classic, warm-toned pieces from Forét

Without wishing away the ease of summer styling, we’re now in the sartorial “good bit”. The part of the year when layered pieces form pleasing depths and contrasts in outfits. Wardrobe staples form new affinities: that old woolen jumper pairs rather well with that new, popped checkered collar.

Forét’s autumn collection picks a perfect country colour palette of cumin, sage and wooded hues to complement city silhouettes and styling. Outerwear ranges from Harris Tweed macs to lighter twill and herringbone jackets made in Portugal. And we particularly like its high-necked, ribbed knit in thyme and flannel shirting in navy and rust.
Put down your roots in attire from Nikawi and YMC

Our Chiltern Street neighbours Niwaki do much more than make the perfect set of secateurs. The gardening brand also creates thoughtful pieces of kit for everyday life, from lunchboxes to stepladders. And, on this occasion, it’s a limited-edition clothing collection in partnership with UK label YMC that has caught our eye.

The Gardener’s Jacket is a reinvention of one of YMC’s staple silhouettes, featuring a water-resistant shell, a more generous hood and a reconsidered pocket placement for tools. The Suedehead Jumper is made from Scottish lambswool and comes in alluring pink and understated pine colourways. Naturally, there’s also a set of YMC x Niwaki Higurashi Secateurs with a leather belt and holster. Whether you’re working on the allotment or tending to your monstera, it’s a collection that celebrates urban gardening.
nikawi.com; youmustcreate.com
Mix up your wardrobe with Auralee’s two-sided coat

Running gear by District Vision or Satisfy might be the best kit while you’re on a run – but what if you’re on the run? If a leather jacket is too conspicuous, Tokyo’s Auralee has a reversible coat that enables you to switch up your look fast.

But it also suits a stand-up citizen wanting to turn heads, with its two-sided, stand-up collar. One side boasts a smooth Pakistani sheep leather, while the other comes in either a khaki or brown chambray for a more elegant, draped finish. For something a little more traditional, opt for a blue tweed blouson jacket or the brand’s ultrafine, wool twill trench coat with detachable lining.
Layer up in fine fabrics by Oliver Spencer

Oliver Spencer’s autumn collection is a nod to the brand’s city origins. Elegant trenches feature rear-dart detailing, allowing the coats to drape and move as you walk. Softly tailored suits create a less stuffy silhouette that won’t look out of place during an alfresco business lunch or the commute home. For layered looks with texture and depth, try checked wool coats, bright alpaca knitwear and shirts in corduroy and brushed cotton. It’s a range that you’ll fall for.
Look sharp on hairpin bends and out of the saddle too in Pas Normal Studios

Copenhagen’s Pas Normal Studios makes cycling gear Copenhagen’s Pas Normal Studios make cycling gear that looks good even when you’re just a blur, clocking 45km/h on a steep descent in Palma de Mallorca. But the brand’s racing jerseys and speedsuits can look a little too taut once you’re back in the city.

Its new Off-Race collection is designed for all of those quieter moments when you’re not pedalling to your destination: think lightweight jackets made from Japanese seersucker, boiled-wool fleeces, musette bags and packable down jackets. One standout is a merino-wool half-zip made in tandem with fellow Danish brand and knitwear specialists SNS Herning.
Stride out in a pair of Jacques Solovière

This season’s grained leather Raymond shoe adds even more depth to an iconic silhouette that already folds and puckers just so. Unlike many French-made leather shoes, Jacques Solovière’s kicks are extraordinarily light to keep you fleet-footed through the winter if a boot isn’t your thing. And if the calf leather and single laced eyelet makes too subtle an impression, the Boldie offers a perforated, brogue version for a little more bulk.
CDLP are an underwear brand that gets the brief
Not all men are underwear models and most work in industries where trousers are encouraged. So it’s odd that the majority of brands seem to approach boxer-short design like an advertising campaign.

Stockholm’s CDLP, however, makes drawers that put fabric and feel before all else. Its Tencel Lyocell boxers are silky and tailored for comfort. And if you’re one for a Y-shaped brief or baggier short, CDLP will have you covered.
Upgrade your journey with DB’s new Rameverk luggage range

Are you off anywhere chasing sun or embracing the elements? Well, Oslo-based baggage experts Db understand how to cart your kit from A to B in one piece. The brand’s Rib-Cage Construction technology means that its luggage proudly holds form, no matter which bellboy or air steward is hoiking it around. Db’s new Ramverk aluminium range has a zip-free frame that’s built to protect your belongings – including all of these new purchases – for a lifetime. But better than that, isn’t it rather fetching?

items.title: Our Entrepreneurs special proves why starting a business is always worth the risk
items.description: Why would you want to start your own business? Being an entrepreneur has a certain allure; it certainly makes for a better introduction when you meet someone at a party. But the sweat and stress that come with this job title should not be underestimated.
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Why would you want to start your own business? Being an entrepreneur has a certain allure; it certainly makes for a better introduction when you meet someone at a party. But the sweat and stress that come with this job title should not be underestimated.

At the start-up stage, there’s money at stake (and often funds contributed by friends and family who wouldn’t mind seeing it come back to them one day). In the up-and-running years, questions about stamina arise: can you really keep working seven days a week? Then, when you hit your stride, there are additional anxieties to contend with. How can you continue growing at pace? Should you bring in investors – or even sell?

But, every year, hundreds of Monocle readers decide that it’s time to say farewell to the corporate life, give up on salary security and do their own thing. Though I imagine that most of them would like to make enough money to lead a comfortable life, for many there are other important factors to consider: a sense of freedom, doing something that they are genuinely passionate about and taking a chance.

And these are the ideas, the draws, that we unpack and investigate over the following pages. This is a magazine for entrepreneurs at every stage of the self-driven adventure. Across its pages, it offers encouragement, advice and some amusing asides.

One idea that becomes apparent is that you don’t have to come up with a crazy new idea to succeed. Often finessing something that already exists is the way to go – so don’t hold back while you search for that elusive gap in the market. In this issue, you will meet the switched-on team that has revitalised an old East German lighting brand and the crafty folks who are continuing centuries-old trades with the support of guilds.

There are also plenty of modern innovators who we would like to introduce you to, from a maker of tiles in Shanghai who uses recycled plates and pottery to the business exploring how co-working and homes for seniors can create a powerful union in Hamburg. There’s much to discover.

Then there’s the question of where you should run your business from, the places that will foster an entrepreneurial flair. We’ll take you on a tour of two Spanish outposts that are attracting design-minded start-ups: Galicia and Valencia. We walk you around a Jakarta market that has become a hothouse for generating new brands in Indonesia and more places besides.

Every entrepreneur needs to start their journey somewhere. Perhaps yours will begin after you finish reading this copy of The Entrepreneurs. Your business won’t be easy but it will be worthwhile. And it will be yours.
For more on starting up and running a company, ensure that you listen to Monocle’s weekly podcast, The Entrepreneurs.

items.title: Sophie Monaghan-Coombs - Monocle
items.description: The opening of Frieze London is casting the world’s art market in a positive light – and catching the eye of eager buyers.
paragraphs: The opening of Frieze London is casting the world’s art market in a positive light – and catching the eye of eager buyers.
Forget the usual business books. If you really want to get ahead, take some advice from Cruella de Vil, Tom Ripley and other entrepreneurial characters from the world of fiction.
Part workspace, part residence, the communal facility by Jan Garde and Henning Weiss is bringing people in all stages of life together in style.
This month’s highlights include an irreverent novel about contemporary art, an exhibition of one of today’s most exciting fashion photographers and a Tom Cruise disaster movie.
To help you pick the right books for your summer reading list, we asked an array of cultural figures to share the titles old and new that have inspired them.
The preview week of the world’s most prestigious exhibition of contemporary art was an unruly spectacle – charged by political dissent, moments of beauty and works shining brightly through the chaos.
In recent years the art world’s largest commercial fair has painted itself into a corner. But satellite shows and new initiatives at this year’s event are helping to offer fresh perspectives.
The world’s biggest space dedicated to illustration has opened in London. Can it help to protect the art amid rising threats from AI?
There’s more to collecting than following markets and speculating on value appreciation. We meet the people at the heart of the action, from a veteran auctioneer to a design-fair director.
Artsignal, the AI-assisted service built for auction houses and collectors, is a first-of-its-kind research tool helping art professionals gather market-level insights.

items.title: Issue 61 - Kinfolk
items.description: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute
paragraphs: Kinfolk’s Sixty First Issue examines play as a way to move through adulthood with greater joy, curiosity and wonder. “We don’t ever lose the desire to play; we’re just socialized to stop playing in certain ways,” Mia Sundstrom, who leads the National Institute for Play, explains to us on page 154. Throughout the issue, we explore pathways to play, including expert advice on rediscovering your own play type as a busy adult and, failing that, five games devised and demonstrated by artist Carsten Höller for those who don’t know where to begin.

In a study of architects, psychologist Donald MacKinnon found that those considered most creative by their peers were often those who knew how to play; this is certainly true of John Outram, whose over-the-top masterpiece, Sphinx Hill, we visit on page 70. Painters play with color and line—a type of immersive flow state our fashion editorial explores on page 60. And musicians improvise and experiment, a process familiar to the band Balming Tiger (interviewed on page 78), whose alternative approach to K-pop subverts the genre’s perfectly synchronized image.
176 pages, offset-printed and perfect bound, full color on uncoated and coated paper. Printed in the United Kingdom.
