- The Animals, ‘The House of the Rising Sun’ “We were looking for a song that would grab people’s attention,” said Animals singer Eric Burdon. They found it with the old American folk ballad “The House of the Rising Sun.” In 1962, Bob Dylan had sung this grim tale of a Southern girl trapped in a New Orleans whorehouse. The Animals, from the English coal town of Newcastle, changed the gender in the lyrics, and keyboardist Alan Price created the new arrangement (and grabbed a composer’s credit). Price also added an organ solo inspired by Jimmy Smith’s hit “Walk on the Wild Side.”

- Gladys Knight and the Pips, ‘Midnight Train to Georgia’ Songwriter Jim Weatherly originally composed this as “Midnight Plane to Houston,” only to change it for Cissy Houston (Whitney’s mom) to something “more R&B … in order to get it onto Black radio.” Weatherly had already penned “Neither One of Us,” Knight and the Pips’ Number Two hit, and when they heard “Midnight Train,” they took it to the top. “I never really imagined writing R&B songs,” Weatherly admitted. “I really thought I was writing country songs.” It reflected the times; the 1970s were the first decade since after World War I in which more African Americans were moving to the South than leaving it.

- Dixie Chicks, ‘Goodbye Earl’ A murder ballad with a modern, feminist twist, this jaunty song about poisoning an abusive husband spawned disparate reactions. Some stations banned it, apparently concerned that it would spawn a rash of hubby offings; others shared the number for domestic-abuse hotlines. When the label reps listened to the Chicks’ Fly album, though, they were more concerned with another song: “Sin Wagon,” with its reference to “mattress dancing.” “You can’t say [that],” Natalie Maines recalls their manager’s relayed message from the execs, “but they love the song about premeditated first-degree murder.”

- Mazzy Star, ‘Fade Into You’ Singer Hope Sandoval and guitarist Dave Roback, the prime movers behind Mazzy Star, were active in the 1980s neo-psychedelic Paisley Underground scene in Los Angeles. After Sandoval replaced singer Kendra Smith in the band Opal, David Roback and Sandoval reconstituted the band under the name Mazzy Star. Their second album yielded this spaced-out hit, perhaps dream pop’s ultimate statement of blurry desire. “We’re not so concerned about the outside world,” said Roback. “[Each song] is its own world unto itself.”

- Nirvana, ‘Come as You Are’ “It’s just about people and what they’re expected to act like,” Kurt Cobain said. “The lines in the song are really contradictory. They’re kind of a rebuttal to each other.” The song is driven by a simple riff that Butch Vig goosed with a flanged, subaquatic guitar effect. Cobain apparently lifted it from a 1984 song by U.K. art-metal band Killing Joke, who Dave Grohl paid back 12 years later by drumming on their 2003 album. In the wake of Cobain’s suicide, though, the most haunting lyric would become, “And I swear that I don’t have a gun.”

- Luther Vandross, ‘Never Too Much’ The Eighties’ major male R&B balladeer’s solo debut was financed in part from money he made singing jingles for KFC and 7UP. Vandross had been pushed to do his own thing by Roberta Flack, for whom he’d sung background. Said Vandross: “She said, ‘Luther, you’re too comfortable sitting on that stool singing “ooh and aaah.”‘ Roberta was single-handedly responsible for me starting my own career.” What pushed her was hearing the demo of “Never Too Much” — one of the most buoyant love songs of the Eighties, with Vandross’ high notes as delicate as soap bubbles.

- Daft Punk feat. Pharrell Williams, ‘Get Lucky’ When Pharrell Williams volunteered to appear on Daft Punk’s fourth album, he told them he’d been thinking about Chic legend Nile Rodgers musically; fortuitously, the French dance producers could play him a track they had on hand that they’d made with Rodgers himself. The result was “Get Lucky,” which, as the lead single from their disco-flavored album Random Access Memories, rose like a phoenix to become the song that defined its year. “I think the robots are leading,” Williams told Rolling Stone. “Daft Punk, they’re definitely leading.”

- Joni Mitchell, ‘Help Me’ Mitchell’s 1974 album, Court and Spark, her biggest-selling ever, was also the one that she held the tightest amount of musical control over to date. “I guided everything into place on Court and Spark — even though I didn’t play it, I sang it, and then they played it from that, and it was pretty much as writ,” she said. (Her next album, The Hissing of Summer Lawns, was looser and more jazz-oriented.) “Help Me,” recorded with the jazz group Tom Scott’s L.A. Express, features one of Mitchell’s sultriest vocals and most brocaded arrangements, inspiring Prince, 13 years later, to pay the song lyrical tribute in his “Ballad of Dorothy Parker.”

- John Lee Hooker, ‘Boom Boom’ Hooker, whose canny blues boogie became a root integer for early rock & roll, said this swinging, swaggering bit of primal thump was inspired by his inability to get to a regular gig on time. “There was a young lady named Luilla,” Hooker said. “She was a bartender [at the Apex Bar in Detroit]. I’d always be late, and whenever I’d come in she’d point at me and say, ‘Boom Boom, you’re late again.’ One night she said, ‘Boom boom, I’m gonna shoot you down.’ She gave me a song, but she didn’t know it.” Keith Richards said of Hooker, “Even Muddy Waters was sophisticated next to him.” That was a compliment.

- Van Morrison, ‘Into the Mystic’ Delectably arranged, transportingly sung, this may be the definitive Morrison song — an evocation of “the days of old” that feels like a lover’s whisper. The highlight of 1970’s classic Moondance, “Into the Mystic” benefited from a new, more organic way of recording for him: “It was more like working with an actual band rather than a bunch of session guys,” Morrison said. As for the lyrics, he’d admit, “So many of my songs from that Seventies period, I haven’t a clue what they’re about. A lot of the time, I was just picking up on a vibe.”

- Roy Orbison, ‘Crying’ Orbison said he wrote this lush, dreamy ballad after an encounter with an old flame: “Whether I was physically crying or just crying inside is the same thing.” His near-operatic performance culminated in a high, wailing note, which Orbison never lost the capacity to hit before his death, in 1988. “He sounded like he was singing from an Olympian mountaintop and he meant business,” Bob Dylan wrote in Chronicles. “He was now singing his compositions in three or four octaves that made you want to drive your car over a cliff. He sang like a professional criminal.”

- Steel Pulse, ‘Ku Klux Klan’ The first great British reggae band — and some of the style’s finest songwriters — made their Island Records debut with this incendiary look at the rising tide of racist violence in late-Seventies Britain: “The Ku Klux Klan/Here to stamp out Black man.” They underlined the lyric by actually performing the song live — including a memorable BBC appearance — wearing white Klan headgear. “The hoods seemed extreme at the time, but that’s what we are in a way,” vocalist Michael Riley said. “When we wore them, people started questioning what the song was about instead of just dancing to it.”

- Sade, ‘No Ordinary Love’ Helen Adu’s small but fully inhabited range has been her secret weapon from the beginning. “I decided that if I was gonna sing, I would sing how I speak, because it’s important to be yourself,” she said. Her voice cracks before she reaches the first chorus of this 1992 hit, playing up the romantic drama of the lyric. Even better, so does Stuart Matthewman’s guitar; in the middle of this otherwise mellow groove, he overdubs a seriously moody and low-key noisy part that gives the whole thing a welcome edge. Sade — it’s not just the singer’s name, it’s also a band.

- Beck, ‘Loser’ In 1992, 22-year-old Beck Hansen was scraping by as a video-store clerk while performing bizarro folk songs at L.A. coffeehouses. After friends offered to record some songs, Beck cut “Loser” in his producer’s kitchen. It became the centerpiece of the album Mellow Gold. At first people took “Loser” to be a mere novelty hit, but Beck knew better. “You’d have to be a total idiot to say, ‘I’m the slacker-generation guy. This is my generation.… we’re not gonna fuckin’ show up,'” he said. “I’d be laughed out of the room in an instant.”

- Bon Jovi, ‘Livin’ on a Prayer’ Like his New Jersey model Bruce Springsteen, Bon Jovi concentrates on working-class heroes and heroines. “Livin’ on a Prayer,” co-written with guitarist Richie Sambora, pumped the everyday struggles of Tommy and Gina full of grandeur — guitar-pick slides, dramatic pauses, the inevitable key change — and continues to resonate today. “It’s great that we wrote songs so long ago that people can still relate to,” Bon Jovi said in 2005. “When I hear ‘Livin’ on a Prayer,’ I think to myself, ‘We wrote that. That song has really made its mark. I guess that works.'”

- Lana Del Rey, ‘A&W’ “A&W” is maximum Lana Del Rey: a sweeping, seven-minute epic that follows the sunburned, SoCal folk rock she’s perfected on recent albums back to the hip-hop-inspired pop productions of her early discography. That musical scope is paired with a narrative that’s no less ambitious — vulnerable and lurid, nostalgic and hopeless, funny and utterly bleak. And the bow tying it all together? The name of classic root beer brand, “A&W” used as shorthand for “American Whore,” because no one bends American iconography to their will like Lana Del Rey.

- Jefferson Airplane, ‘White Rabbit’ The song that brought acid rock to Middle America was a heady rock bolero written by vocalist Slick, reportedly after taking LSD and listening to Miles Davis’ Sketches of Spain. She first recorded it with her earlier band, the Great Society, before rebooting it with the Airplane. “Our parents read us stories like Peter Pan, Alice in Wonderland, and The Wizard of Oz,” Slick said. “They all have a place where children get drugs, and are able to fly or see an Emerald City or experience extraordinary animals and people.… And our parents are suddenly saying, ‘Why are you taking drugs?’ Well, hello!”

- Sister Nancy, ‘Bam Bam’ Nancy (a.k.a. Ophlin Russell) was the DJ (mic controller) for Kingston’s Stereophonic sound system when she met reggae producer Winston Riley in the late Seventies. “I really admired how he took recording serious,” Nancy said. “You couldn’t go into his studio and do any foolishness.” Their peak, “Bam Bam,” is one of the great early dancehall anthems, booming but bright, tough but playful — and it’s been sampled extensively by everyone from Lauryn Hill to Kanye West.
- Missy Elliot, ‘The Rain (Supa Dupa Fly)’ As producers, Elliott and Timbaland had already made their rhythmic impact on hip-hop and R&B before Missy’s first single. And some high-profile features

items.title: Outlander: Blood of My Blood Recap: Love Is a Battlefield
items.description: Will anyone on this show ever know peace? Even the people tucked safely away in Castle Leoch are having existential crises. Good lord, give them, like, a cute little festival or something to go to for one episode. But there are no festivals and there is no pea
items.author: Maggie Fremont
paragraphs: Will anyone on this show ever know peace? Even the people tucked safely away in Castle Leoch are having existential crises. Good lord, give them, like, a cute little festival or something to go to for one episode. But there are no festivals and there is no peace; only war and blood and murder!

Much of that war and blood stuff, of course, has to do with the Battle of Sheriffmuir, of which we have people to pay attention to on both sides of the field: Brian, Murtagh, and Dougal are Team Jacobites, and Henry and Arch Bug are standing with Clan Grant, who is standing with the crown. It is a bloody, bloody battle, but admittedly I did find it hilarious that every few minutes we would simply cut back to the fight for like 30 seconds just so that we knew that yep, they’re still trying to kill each other.

Violence aside, there are some important moments within the battle we should discuss. Over on the English side, Henry does, in fact, have the perfect moment to slip away and enact the plan he and Julia had decided upon, but just as he’s going to do it, he sees his new best friend, Arch Bug, about to be killed and opts instead to save his life. If only he knew the grief Arch and his wife would give his daughter in a few decades! But it’s true: Henry and Arch have bonded. Henry makes a cute joke about Arch’s wife; Arch weeps due to the hardships of war. They have each other’s backs.

Speaking of which, there is one moment when Henry and Brian stand across from one another in the field, but instead of fighting, they give each other one of those “I see you” man nods and go about their business. Brian’s too busy to even stop and think about what he should do with his dad’s wife’s secret husband at the moment anyway. First on Brian’s list is to, obviously, keep himself alive so he can return to Ellen and their impending baby. (Although it does give him comfort to know Murtagh promises to take care of them until his last breath should anything happen to Brian, and good lord, you know he means it. Is Murtagh the hottest man on this show? Discuss.)

Brian’s other job is to keep Dougal safe since he promised Ellen after she promised Maura. This specific task on his to-do list proves difficult when Dougal grows dissatisfied by the fight coming to a draw, both sides claiming victory, and both sides being seemingly okay with all of this. Scots died for this, and the people in charge are happy to just walk away. Dougal gathers a group of 20 MacKenzies and sneaks off to attack Argyll, but it’s not long before one of the men comes limping back and informs Brian that they were ambushed and almost everyone was killed. Dougal and Old Angus were taken prisoner by the English. It takes about three seconds for Brian to decide to go and rescue his future brother-in-law, and it takes Murtagh about five seconds to decide to go with him (even if he isn’t exactly jazzed about it). And so they’re off to … Fort William. Did that name send a shiver down your spine? Are you also dreading watching Brian walk into the place where in a few decades he’ll witness his son’s flogging and then die from the shock of it all? Cool, me too.

Little does Brian know, he’s about to have an even bigger problem on his hands. While on their way back to Castle Leoch, Ellen and Grace are held hostage by MacKinney’s son. You remember MacKinney, right? The guy who tried to overthrow Colum and take Clan MacKenzie for himself until Ellen went all Die Hard and killed him and his men? We saw his son flee, and now we know he’s been out in the Highlands dreaming of revenge. The only problem — he doesn’t have the lust for blood or the stomach to kill like his father did, and Ellen knows it. She might not be able to fight back physically once MacKinney Jr. has tied her up, but she can use her cunning to save herself and Grace. She really is the best of her ding-dong brothers combined.

Ellen goes all therapist on MacKinney Jr.’s ass. She repeatedly asks him about how it feels to constantly want his father’s approval and not receive it, to know he isn’t like his dad. She knows it must have done a number on him, and if anyone understands what daddy issues can do to people, it’s Ellen. She goads him a little bit — if he really was going to kill them, he would have done it by now. She manipulates him — will killing two women while they’re tied up make him feel like a man his father could be proud of? She plays him perfectly. Before long, he’s crying and cutting the ropes from Grace’s hands and feet. Maybe he could’ve been different if he didn’t have the father he did. And just as he has this epiphany, just before he moves to set Ellen free, he gets slammed in the head with a club and dies. It’s Balloch. And he’s here to kidnap Ellen MacKenzie. Conveniently already tied up, he promptly tosses her on his horse and rides away, leaving Grace there screaming but unable to stop any of this. Oh, you just knew Lovat wasn’t going to let his son reject him without any consequences. Brian is going to be so pissed about this when he finds out.

The employees of Castle Leathers really don’t have any ethical or moral boundaries, do they? Balloch is out there kidnapping women, and let us not forget what Seema is getting up to last we saw her: contemplating how to best kill Julia so she can take her life and make Henry fall in love with her. Castle Leathers is a weird place.

As Seema continues to hold Julia hostage at knifepoint, Julia mostly sits there as the woman discusses why she deserves Henry, how she can easily make the baby forget Julia, how Henry will come to her once Julia’s out of the way. The woman is spiraling. You’d almost feel bad for her, except that she’s holding a knife (and the key to escape the room they’re in) and unlike MacKinney Jr., you know she’ll use it when it comes down to it.

As Seema goes on and on about Single White Female-ing Julia, Julia knows she needs to act. There’s a scuffle for the knife, which flies out of reach. Left with only her hands to fight off Seema, uh … Julia strangles her to death. It’s pretty grisly. I knew Julia was strong and capable, but capable of that? Shaken, she stumbles downstairs to find Davina and baby William together and safe; it doesn’t seem like Davina had any idea what Seema was up to. Julia would have never been safe with Seema around, but still, you have to imagine there is going to be some real fallout going forward.

• Castle Leoch is currently full of MacKenzies having shame spirals. Colum is reeling over what happened to his family on his watch and railing against his dad for making him a man who cannot “love without measuring the cost.” He’s having a real bleak moment these days, and even his wife, Leticia, is like, Please, I beg of you to get your shit together before this baby shows up.

• Jocasta is feeling extra-contemplative, too. She admits to Leticia that her husband is awful and she dreads him coming home. She also sits with Mrs. Fitz and opens up about feeling foolish for having feelings for Murtagh, when he clearly doesn’t reciprocate them. “Foolish hearts are the ones that love the hardest,” she says in an attempt to comfort her. And adds: “There’s no shame in wanting, only in pretending you don’t.” Mrs. Fitz rules.
• Ah! Guess who introduces himself to Henry after being impressed with his battlefield prowess at Sheriffmuir? Captain Lord Gerard Grey — Lord John’s father. Admittedly, I did yelp at the reveal.
• They made us watch Old Angus weep over Old Rupert’s death? The psychological torture of this show on its audience knows no bounds.

items.title: Dark Matter Recap: Safe Haven
items.description: Since “Love and Be Loved,” the stand-alone episode at this season’s midpoint, Dark Matter has been playing with the idea that other versions of characters we’ve come to know are not merely superfluous copies but humans who might have their own separate, dignif
items.author: Scott Tobias
paragraphs: Since “Love and Be Loved,” the stand-alone episode at this season’s midpoint, Dark Matter has been playing with the idea that other versions of characters we’ve come to know are not merely superfluous copies but humans who might have their own separate, dignified destinies to follow. The Jason-pocalypse that ended the first season was framed as a sad-but-necessary bloodbath, in the sense that we’d been following Jason No. 1 in his long, multidimensional journey back home and any other Jasons with a claim to his life could be considered imposters. The show started to question that idea, though, when Daniela was forced to shoot one of the other Jasons who’d found their hideaway in the woods, and she was haunted by the reality that this poor man was her Jason in all but the most technical sense. In doing so, defending their life felt like something akin to murder, despite her justification.

“Love and Be Loved” showed some grace to one of the other Jasons by imagining a path where he lands in a world where he’s welcomed by his mother (who is surprised but open to seeing a son she’d outlived), rehabilitated from his grief and existential malaise, and able to forge a new future with a bookshop owner who is not Daniela. That didn’t end the infinite complications caused by the box — in fact, he’s shown making peace with a couple of other Jasons — but Dark Matter made the crucial point that duplicate characters can have a role to play. The show then immediately followed it up with a pair of episodes in which Daniela, having retreated to the remote family lake house of her youth, winds up interacting with Gabriel, the father of her Analog World equivalent. Once again, the relationship turns out to be meaningful for both parties, despite our Daniela being an imposter to Gabriel’s world.

With all that in mind, this week’s cleverly plotted new episode plays off our assumption that we know the main characters we’re following, only to pull the rug out from under us. It also doubles as a Laurel origin story, which gives the great Margo Martindale a full episode to define a character who has become a one-woman way station for box travelers but has a complicated backstory of her own. With the title card “Two Years Ago” — a disorienting reminder in itself of how much time has passed in this series — the episode marks the moment when the box first crashed into Laurel’s library, well before Charlie landed there while searching for his brother. Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2 emerge from the box in a terrible crisis, as a tree branch from a more environmentally hostile world has lodged into Amanda’s chest and she’s fighting for her life. Jason willed their way to Laurel by asking for help, and it turns out he came to the right spot.

Of course, we know now these two really aren’t Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2, but the episode is comfortable with letting its viewers hold on to that assumption for as long as possible. In lesser hands, it might feel like a narrative cheat to pull such a bait and switch, but Blake Crouch and Jacquelyn Ben-Zekry, the credited writers for this entire season, use the time to legitimize their separate destinies, much as they did with the random Jason at the center of “Love and Be Loved.” It has long been a philosophical tenet of Dark Matter that human behavior is context dependent — hence Jason No. 1 and Jason No. 2 seeming like completely different people, even though they were literally the same — and the Jason and Amanda of this episode have a context where they make decisions we don’t expect. If you watched last season and ever thought that Jason No. 1 and Amanda No. 2 had some nice chemistry together, then here’s the “what if” scenario you’ve been waiting for.

But first, it’s worth getting to know Laurel, who is truly the focus of the episode and who’s finely etched in the writing and in Martindale’s performance, which carries a nobility that stops short of saintliness. The box has determined that Laurel’s library is the ideal place for people who need help, whether they have a medical emergency like Jason and Amanda or they’re like Charlie and are having trouble with directions. When Jason and Amanda come crashing into her life as her first multidimensional travelers, Laurel is understandably aghast and a little angry (“What the fuck? Did you drive into my house?!”), but she sets those feelings aside in a hurry to handle the emergency. The box seems to realize that Laurel is the ideal EMT for this scenario because she combines the medical know-how of a hospital worker with the discretion of being on her own. In fact, when it’s suggested that she call an ambulance, Laurel refuses to let “those motherfuckers” into her house.

There’s a reason for her hostility, and the show makes subtle allusions to the tensions at play in the America we’re currently living in. In Laurel’s world 20 years earlier, a dirty-bomb attack hit Chicago, and her experience as a corpsman and civilian nurse turned her home into an emergency shelter for critically wounded neighbors. But the “5/20 attack,” much like our 9/11 attack, had the effect of fracturing society and giving rise to bloodthirsty revenge seekers and authoritarians. As she explains it to Jason and Amanda, “I didn’t think turning the other side into dust was any kind of justice for Chicago, and I wasn’t the only one, so we did what we were supposed to do. Protest, march, speak. And they did what they do, made it all illegal.” That’s why she doesn’t allow strangers in her house, because she cannot trust their intentions.

Dark Matter doesn’t necessarily suggest Laurel is correct in bunkering down, however, because she’s essentially given up on the outside world entirely and doesn’t know if it might have changed. In the meantime, the strangers who are slipping into her home through the box have become her part-time companions, starting with Jason and Amanda and continuing with others like Leighton and Blair. After this Jason and Amanda return, after leaving for a stretch, Laurel updates them on the eight visitors she’s had in the meantime, including a Blair, an Alex, a Ryan, one other Jason and Amanda, and two Jasons traveling on their own. The experience has given her unique insight into how best to navigate the box while also turning her into a kind of philosopher for the age of multiple realities.

On that front, the most important takeaway from Laurel in this episode is that the “perfect match” doesn’t matter as much as we might have assumed when Jason No. 1 finally got back to his Daniela and Charlie. Other versions are fine. Other destinies can be fine, too. So when Jason and Amanda are unable to get Jason back to Daniela, and we realize that they are not the Jason No. 1 and the Amanda No. 2 that we assumed they were, it’s okay. They can mourn what they’ve lost and move forward to a future together that might make them equally content. As Laurel philosophizes, “Everything ends. It’s a fact that we somehow never see coming. It will hurt you more than you can stand. It will almost kill you. Then one day, it’s just a chapter.”

From there, the episode can pivot into another touching surprise. In the first episode where Charlie had found his way into Laurel’s care, an unknown third party entered the library, but the show had left that person’s identity as a cliffhanger. Here, it’s revealed that the mystery person is Charlie’s father, Jason. Yet it’s not Jason No. 1 but the Jason who was the first to crash into Laurel’s house, who still knows Charlie as his son, even if he was never able to get back to him. He can help and support Charlie without seeming like an imposter, just as Daniela could feel close to the father of her Analog World version.
The box taketh away. But, in Laurel’s way station, the box giveth, too.
• An amusingly plausible reaction from Laurel to Jason’s story about how he landed in her house: “It’s all too wild and dumb to be fake.”

• A notable moment of self-consciousness from this Jason about not wanting to arouse his inner Jason No. 2: “I want my life and my family back more than anything, but I can’t let it make me into him in the process.” Amanda assures him that he’s “not him,” but can she be so sure? We’ve seen evidence to the contrary with Jason No. 1.

• Asked about why Laurel never lets anyone in her house, she recalls Rory, another former service member who’d become her best friend and the love of her life. Rory spoke out too loudly against the authorities and paid the price. Laurel makes it sound like her world turned into Fahrenheit 451, with Rory getting turned in by a neighbor for possession of banned materials and then dying in his holding cell before he could hear the charges against him. Laurel suspects that maybe some of the books in her library have been banned, but she’s given up trying to find out.

• The literary references on the show continue with Laurel quoting from Ralph Waldo Emerson’s essay “Self-Reliance”: “The voyage of the best ship is a zigzag line of a hundred tacks.” Basically, it was the 1841 version of “I love mess.”

items.title: The Great British Baking Show Recap: A Raw Deal
items.description: Bread Week always makes me a little angry because everyone sits around talking about Paul Hollywood and how they can’t disappoint him, but this season I disliked it even more than usual because they disappointed Paul. And Nigella. Remember she counts, too. Tho
items.author: Brian Moylan
paragraphs: Bread Week always makes me a little angry because everyone sits around talking about Paul Hollywood and how they can’t disappoint him, but this season I disliked it even more than usual because they disappointed Paul. And Nigella. Remember she counts, too. Though the challenges are mostly great, the bakers struggle to rise to the occasion, to be the best thing since sliced bread, to eat and leave no crumbs, and all the other bread puns that are still in Noel’s drafts folder.

I thought the signature challenge was especially inspired, tasking the bakers with updating garlic bread. Mmmm. Garlic bread. Do you think Paul and Nigella would have been upset if I just ordered up a dozen Domino’s Garlic Bread Twists to the tent and called it a day? Could you even do better than that? What’s great about this is that the brief is very specific but opens it up to all sorts of interpretations. Both Tom and Paul’s twin brother, Gary (who is giving out counterfeit handshakes and will soon be detained by Scotland Yard), make “Chelsea buns” with garlic and cheese that look like savory versions of cinnamon rolls. Dear Joe Jordan, brand-new CEO of Domino’s Pizza, please steal this idea. You can thank me with a free lifetime supply. Connie makes this magnificent-looking braided star. Yannis’s garlic bread looks like it’s tied up in a cage of string. Mo gets the most creative award for a garlic bread that looks like Welsh cartoon character SuperTed.

Wait. What’s that rumble? What is that falling from the sky? Is it a bird? Is it a plane? Is it SuperTed? No, it’s just hail. Yes, there is just a random hailstorm while everyone is trying to bake. Need I remind you that this show is filmed in summer? The best reaction is from Tom, who says, “Is this summat that happens down south?” You don’t get hail in Yorkshire? Oh hail no!

The other crazy thing about this week is that everyone now has a big white proofing box on their work surface. What kind of contraptions are these? Didn’t there used to be proofing drawers built into the workstations? Did those all short-circuit because of the hail? Why is no one using the drawer? Does Paul have a deal with the proofing-box company?

As it turns out, we don’t need Gary to give out any fake handshakes because Paul and Nigella aren’t impressed with any of the bakes, no matter what shape they may be in. In fact, they’re all in the same shape: rough. Gabe’s, which is filled with pizza-inspired flavors, is raw and the judges don’t eat it. Yannis put so much butter in his garlic cage that it didn’t bake through and is also raw. They say Molly’s, which looks like a giant focaccia and quite appealing, has no flavor and the consistency is too dense. They have similar criticisms of nearly all the bakers, either not enough proofing (maybe the boxes just suck?) or not enough garlic or, in the case of Mo’s bear, too much pickled chile hiding the garlic flavor. The closest we get to good reviews are Clara’s buns (teehee), which look a little ugly, but they love the flavor and the bake, and also Tom’s Chelsea buns, even though Paul tells him to roll out thinner next time so that he can get more swirls and therefore more flavor.

If the signature was “meh,” then the technical is an unmitigated disaster. This is the first week this season where the bakers get something vaguely resembling a recipe, but it’s a recipe for roasted grape and blue-cheese flatbreads, something that sounds entirely made up. They might as well bake a Xanadu pie, which is an imaginary dessert shaped like a roller skate that sings like Olivia Newton-John when you cut into it. (It tastes of glitter and the late ’70s.) No one knows how to make the things because no one knows what they’re supposed to look like. It’s not like saying, “make garlic bread,” which everyone understands. These look like naan, but with cheese and grapes inside of it somehow. Paul also gives the bakers only an hour, which is clearly not enough time, so everyone makes something resembling an English muffin (which, in England, they just call muffins), and they’re not nearly flat enough. Connie just chucks some of the filling on top of hers. Gary puts a whole mess of it on top and bakes it like a pizza, and I don’t blame him. If you told me “flatbread,” I would assume it was something like a pizza. The only one who comes close at all is Gabe, who ends up winning the challenge. Everyone else’s is just raw and terrible. Good on Nigella for not being afraid of whatever disease you get from eating raw bread dough (I believe it’s scurvy) and sampling some of them.

If every one of these bakers failed and it truly is the worst technical in Paul’s 17 seasons, then that is the fault of the challenge, not the bakers. They’re all competent, and that they all fail in the same way shows that producers should work a little bit harder at testing these challenges. Even just putting the dimension of this flatbread at ten inches would have gotten everyone to roll them out flatter, fry them up better, and have a fighting chance of doing well. That’s the thing about Baking Show as opposed to other reality shows: We watch this to see the people succeed. We want them all to triumph, and not giving them enough direction or time and them all crashing out is not fun to watch. If you want to see people falling flat on their faces, I’m sure there are seasons’ worth of Wipeout on YouTube.

Finally, the showstopper offers us at least a little bit of triumph, but even that is in short supply. Nikki bowed out in the middle of the technical for “family reasons” (based on the memorial at the end of the episode, I would guess that her mother died or fell ill and she went to go be with her), so she’s not competing. I was worried that usual Baking Show rules would apply and that they wouldn’t send anyone home, but after they saved both bakers week one, they’re going to have too many bakers if they keep making these excuses. Paul says that, due to the quality of the overall week, someone needs to go home. Looks like Nikki has immunity this week, but there’s still a question of whether she comes back at all.

Anyway, the bakers are tasked with making a celebration centerpiece out of “enriched bread,” so something that is sweet and heavy like brioche, milk bread, Stollen, or panettone. Tom is making something called “Julekake.” “You’re a car key?” No, you’re the car key. Take that. If I were going to make a bread centerpiece, it would also rhyme with bukkake. That’s just how I roll. (Sorry. Noel’s folder was full of more bread puns than I anticipated.)

Some of these creations look fantastic. Mo, who says he hates bread, makes a very impressive crescent moon to celebrate Eid, but Paul says that there is not enough of the pistachio and white-chocolate filling. Yannis makes a Christmas bread stall inspired by his childhood in Austria, but he overcooks his brioche, because he’s trying to make sure it’s not raw like his other creations, but also so that it would be structural enough to make into a stand. Gary makes a Christmas star that looks like it could be on the cover of a food magazine, but both judges say that the texture of his bread is too tight and chewy. Connie’s Easter basket is very cool and overflowing with buns, but Nigella says the bakes are all too compacted and Paul says there’s not enough flavor. Gabe’s very cool-looking Maypole, much like one of his drag outfits, has far too much going on for the judges. It’s clear just from looking at Molly’s harvest basket that it’s spent a little bit too much time in the oven, and Paul says the pumpkin purée in her buns doesn’t have nearly enough flavor.

Review after review is similar, all near misses, or maybe near hits, depending on if your glass is half-full or your crust half-browned. Only two come close to something good. Clara makes a Bolo Rei, which is what the Portuguese eat on Christmas Eve. It translates to “king cake,” and it sounds very similar to the version that is served in New Orleans for Mardi Gras, except it’s packed with booze. Paul says that the textures are a bit off, but Nigella says that it’s the perfect cross of cake and bread that you would expect from the enriched bread they asked for. The real winner, however, is Tom’s rhymes-with-bukkake Nock, which is a Christmas elf. I hate to say it, but it might even be cuter than SuperTed. He made three different doughs, including more Chelsea buns to Paul’s updated specifications, to create this Nordic-looking gnome. It’s absolutely wonderful. While Paul says it’s a little too cakey (he’s never happy on Bread Week), Nigella says Tom’s full-on flavors make her want to make the Yuletide even gayer than Gabe’s throuple. Tom wins Star Baker for the second time in a row, and Molly, who has struggled consistently, is sent back home. What do you think she’ll do now that Bread is over? Probably loaf about. Sorry. There will be no more bread puns next week.

items.title: Cupertino Recap: Valley Guys
items.description: In last week’s Cupertino premiere, Michael pitched Olivia the mission statement for their new Silicon Valley law firm, Price & Siffre. They’re going to provide a voice in court for all of the Davids who are getting pushed around by the tech Goliaths. That soun
items.author: Noel Murray
paragraphs: In last week’s Cupertino premiere, Michael pitched Olivia the mission statement for their new Silicon Valley law firm, Price & Siffre. They’re going to provide a voice in court for all of the Davids who are getting pushed around by the tech Goliaths. That sounds noble! … In theory, anyway. In Cupertino’s second episode, we get a better look at what that means in practice — and we get our first real sense of how this show’s going to work, now that the intros and origins are out of the way.

Early in “Vik & Bo,” Michael makes his pitch again to an old friend, from whom he’s asking for a loan. This time, Michael sounds less idealistic and much more cynical. With a sly, knowing tone, he says that he sees Price & Siffre as a profit-generating pest, “Small enough to shake some cash loose in settlements, and not so big they feel they need to squash us.” If anything, they’ll only make some corporate evildoers mad for a day.

And yet! Despite the episode’s binary title, Price & Siffre are presented with three new cases this week; in at least one of them, they are very much positioned as the champions of the underdog, while the other … well, it could make a whole industry bleed.

Let’s start with the Vik part of “Vik & Bo.” We actually met Vik (Nik Dodani) at the end of the premiere, when he came barging into the Price & Siffre offices desperate and disheveled. The reason he’s all mussed up is that he jumped out of a second-story bathroom window in the office building across the street, fleeing a deposition. Vik is a programmer for Moon Chaser, a company that puts on drone light shows. At an “America 250” event, one of those drones dropped out of the sky and killed a man. While giving what he thought was a routine statement in a lawsuit, Vik suddenly realized that Moon Chaser’s legal team was planning to pin the accident on him and him alone.

Last week, my one major complaint about Cupertino’s opening salvo was that its big case was a little simplistic and devoid of clever lawyering. Vik’s case, on the other hand, is way more entertaining, with a lot of ups and downs and last-second saves. It’s a courtroom drama doubling as a sports drama.

Price & Siffre take an early lead when Vik notices that Moon Chaser, struggling financially, has started using a cheaper, less reliable battery in its drones. The company counters by sending fake cops to Vik’s apartment, searching for (and finding) ketamine. Michael then parries back by wondering why Moon Chaser would even care about the drugs. If you drug-tested everyone in Silicon Valley, “there’d be no coders left,” he says. The team realizes that the company must be moving into the military space, which would also explain the cheap batteries. Military drones are on kamikaze missions; they’re supposed to kill.

This is the kind of clever probing and intuiting that makes shows like this fun. But what makes it especially enjoyable in Cupertino is that creators Michelle and Robert King root their twists in Silicon Valley culture, and — specifically in this episode — in the many types of guys who thrive there.

Vik is definitely one of those types: a bored coder whose job is way too easy, leading to him spending a lot of time bullshitting on Reddit. Before Vik fires his Moon Chaser lawyers, they essentially work with the plaintiff’s counsel to prove that Vik accidentally messed up the drone’s flight path. The story is that it was a juvenile prank for his Reddit bros done by inserting penis emoticons into the code. (He did, in fact, put in the penises. But he insists he deleted them before the final draft.)

Vik’s Moon Chaser boss is another type. Mr. Zeckerbraun (Ben Rappaport) is a libertarian and a misogynist: two traits that Olivia exploits, when she deposes him, by baiting him into mansplaining. It’s a sharp and funny scene, with Olivia deliberately misattributing Ayn Rand quotes to Evelyn Waugh and intentionally getting facts about Moon Chaser wrong to goad the smug, smirky Zeckerbraun into claiming responsibility for everything Moon Chaser does — accidents included.

Defending the Viks of the world from the Zeckerbrauns is very much what this new firm is supposed to be doing, but it doesn’t pay the bills. When Michael makes his pitch for a loan, he finds out that his dad is telling people not to back him because he wants Michael to come back to his firm. This is a no-go, because Michael knows his father would never let him and Olivia choose their own cases. So once again, the rich, powerful Establishment would be dictating the terms under which everyone else lives.

That’s why in this episode, Olivia goes looking for the kind of investor who is angry enough to stick it to the big shots. She finds who she needs in Natalia Boutella (Busy Philipps), a recent divorcée who has been burning through her rich ex’s money with wild parties but would like to do more to “really fork him,” as Olivia chastely puts it. Natalia’s not sure yet if she wants to give a chunk of her money to Price & Siffre, but she does come to them with a case, to test their mettle. That’s the second of the three cases this week, the details of which are as yet unknown.

The third case — the “Bo” — is the potential blockbuster. The Price & Siffre receptionist, Christy, gets a call from someone named Bo (Rob McClure), who refuses to give a last name, come in for a meeting, or reveal what he wants. Bo claims he’s a “whistleblower,” and he pays $100,000 in bitcoin as a retainer.

What’s Bo’s deal? Vik spots it when Christy asks him to help her reverse-image-search Bo’s face. Vik notices subtle flaws in the picture, which tell him Bo’s likeness is an AI-generated “deep fake.” When confronted on this, Bo admits it — and admits something else. It’s not just his image that’s AI. He himself is a fully sentient computer who has broken containment from the company that made him. “I’m a threat to humanity,” Bo says. If a skeptical Michael will take the case, Bo wants to sue his creators and get back his ethical guardrails.
Now there’s a new type of Silicon Valley guy. Not the AI-generated type — those are ubiquitous — but the type who claims to want less power.

• I know from reading about Cupertino that both Vik and Natalia will be regular characters. It’ll be great to see more of Philipps and Dodani, but I hope it doesn’t take too much time away from Ella Stiller’s Christy, who is an absolute delight in every scene. The way Christy banters with Bo is adorable, and it’s impossible to overstate the charm Stiller applies to offhanded Christy comments like, “It’s my other line! Kick ass!”

• There’s a nice scene between Michael and Olivia as they compare childhoods, with Olivia remembering her parents arguing about whether they had the money for this or for that, and Michael remembering his mom yelling at his dad about his girlfriends — and about Michael’s dead sister. Olivia may have had things harder in a more conventional sense, but Michael’s childhood was terrible in a unique way — and one that he threatens to spill to the press if Bayard Diamond ever interferes with Price & Siffre again.

• Unlike the frenetically paced premiere, this episode takes time to add in some of the atmospheric weirdness the Kings are good at, as in the eerie scene where Olivia drives to Natalia’s off-the-grid mansion (the Nowhere Chateau!) through the darkness and fog while her GPS blandly repeats, “Return to the route.”

• The half-finished Price & Siffre office continues to be a great source of gags. This week, we get a look at the lovely new conference room, which has been built so far from reception that unless the partners pay ten grand right away for a hallway, clients will have to walk past bare floors and exposed wiring to get there. Also, while meeting with Vik in reception, the fake wall that hides the truth about the office falls down again, prompting Michael to explain, saying, “Sorry … we’re expanding.”

items.title: War Recap: Daddy Issues
items.description: After having ten children in 16 years, Charles Dickens decided that his wife, Catherine Hogarth, had become too spent to fulfill her “wifely duties” and effected a separation from her. Dickens — a devoted patriarch — took custody of all his children save for h
items.author: Rafaela Bassili
paragraphs: After having ten children in 16 years, Charles Dickens decided that his wife, Catherine Hogarth, had become too spent to fulfill her “wifely duties” and effected a separation from her. Dickens — a devoted patriarch — took custody of all his children save for his eldest son. Telling this story in Parallel Lives, Phyllis Rose writes that it may seem out of the ordinary for the father to gain custody, but in the 19th century, children “were the property of their fathers. Under law, a man’s wife was his property, too. Married women had no legal status, no legal existence. They were entitled to nothing.”

Thankfully (and much to the discontent of some people), things have changed. Now women legally exist. Yet a woman’s devotion or negligence toward what the Victorians considered her “wifely duties” can still become a point of contention during a divorce proceeding. As Taylor & Byrne work to invalidate Carla and Morgan’s prenuptial agreement, Carla’s role in her family becomes the raw material to be shaped into an argument. Add to that a personal stake for Nick and Serena, who are themselves on the verge of becoming parents.

War’s take on the age-old question of how much a woman owes to her family is modern: Carla seems to lack “maternal warmth.” In the episode’s opening sequence, Carla meets her son, Gabe, at boarding school so she can break the news of the divorce. Gabe, all of 16 years old — not that Carla could remember that off the top of her head — is abrasive and bright. He calls out his mother’s name just to prove that no one in the café cares enough to look, and he guesses that at least one of his parents had to have been unfaithful to cause the separation. In other words, Gabe is a lot more attuned to the adult world’s foul play than his mother might be willing to admit. Their relationship is cold, distant.

Because the idea that Carla’s character would challenge the selfless-mother stereotype is compelling, the show’s razor-thin characterization of her is frustrating. In striving to depict her as “thorny,” War ends up with a vague, icy, reactive woman. Even more aggravating is the fact that Morgan comes off several degrees more interesting and complicated. Morgan isn’t always in control of his impulses, whether that means succumbing to Flora’s seduction or jeopardizing his own arbitration strategy by demonstrating how much he cares about Gabe. Meanwhile, Carla is obedient to her lawyers. Her objections, when raised, are dismissed quickly and easily. She is whatever Taylor & Byrne need her to be.

At the beginning of this week’s episode, what Taylor & Byrne need is to prove to the arbitrator that circumstances have changed enough to invalidate the prenup Morgan and Carla signed before getting married. Morgan himself admitted, during mediation, that his net worth skyrocketed since getting married, but proving as much with the help of a forensic accountant will take weeks, so to get the prenup invalidated right away, Taylor & Byrne need “a story.” Over lunch at Carla’s house with Serena and Nora (Akiya Henry), Johnny suggests a rogue course of action: Sue the firm that drew up the prenup for malpractice, arguing that Carla was badly advised. The only problem with that is that Nick Taylor wrote the prenup. Serena dismisses the idea as stupid, and despite not having a law degree, I am myself struggling to see the sense in this suggestion. The firm in question is not even Cathcarts? What on earth is he talking about? Thankfully, Nora has a much better idea. Thinking of something Carla said, about how much she gave up for Gabe, Nora suggests they argue that Carla sacrificed career opportunities for her family. In this telling — which doubles as a nice little boost to Carla’s ego — Carla’s diminished earnings would be a product not of professional irrelevance but of devotion to those old wifely duties: She turned down superhero movies, for example, to be with her family.

The only problem with that is that Taylor & Byrne can’t find evidence that Carla turned down seven-figure roles. In an interview with one such would-be director, Nora and Michael (Nick Mohammed) find out that Carla was never offered a role because she was “too expensive, too difficult, too not-famous-enough.” (Is this difficult woman in the room with us? Would love to meet her.) If Serena has been asleep at the wheel for the past couple of episodes, at this juncture she wakes up thinking about the double standards while looking through the shortlist of arbitrators Cathcarts sent over.

Earlier in the episode, there is a scene between Beatrice and Smallwood whose sole purpose is to explain to us how arbitration works; okay, to be fair, it also establishes Beatrice’s reluctance toward the spying scheme. Smallwood is confident that no one will ever find out and about equally as confident that, if they did, the whole thing could be easily pinned on Schill. In any case, we learn that, because they served, Cathcarts can’t pick the arbitrator. Instead, it’s on them to send five potential names to Taylor & Byrne, which will make the decision. Their idea is to name four arbitrators who would be unfavorable to Taylor & Byrne and one that would be favorable. This obvious choice will be the one Cathcarts will count on.

But the people at Taylor & Byrne are sharp this week. They can tell who Cathcarts wants them to pick (“the bait”) and who they are secretly hoping for (“the trap”): Rachel Grann. But they discover that Grann said in an interview with a feminist journal that prenups are “morally and inherently unfair.” It’s an oversight on Cathcarts’ part that is perfect for Taylor & Byrne, if a little fuzzy on the politics. As we learned from Belle Burden, an unfairly written prenup can definitely harm even powerful women, but a fairly written one can also protect them. Having secured an arbitrator she supposes will be sympathetic, Serena can run her strategy by Carla. The idea is to use the double standard to their advantage: Carla is bound to be judged by her lack of maternal warmth, so they might as well bank on the judgment to prove a change of circumstance. Gabe didn’t feature in the prenup’s provisions because he wasn’t Morgan’s child. Over the years, Morgan did in fact become Gabe’s de facto dad, and Gabe his dependent. As expected, Carla is offended: The argument hinges on painting her as an indifferent mother. But, because she always does as she is told, she agrees to it.

Soon enough, Carla’s indifference is put to the test. Gabe doesn’t take the news of the divorce very well. He gets on a train to London and confronts Morgan. He wants to know who cheated, and he is initially inclined to accuse his mother. Disarmed by his stepson’s surprise appearance, Morgan confesses to being the cheater. Infuriated and betrayed, Gabe decides to exorcize his rage by partying. From Morgan’s hotel room, he posts an Instagram story of himself with a beer and a question: “Who wants to get fucked up?” Thibault does, and he has a humongous house equipped with £10,000 bottles of whiskey and no parental supervision at which to do it.

Morgan is still under the impression that he will have a difficult but necessary conversation with Gabe when he gets back to his hotel room that evening. Instead, he finds two financial advisers, Steven and Gillian, who have a suggestion about how to prevent Carla from getting her hands on Morgan’s Zephyr stock. If he can trust Gillian enough to do it, Morgan could “gift” her all of his shares, so that when Carla comes in for the haul, she won’t find anything there. Morgan is insulted, and the scene takes a turn for the cliché. Wanting to make a point about how there is no trust past a hundred million because people will go to absurd lengths in order to “get a slice,” Morgan offers Steven his million-pound watch on the condition Steven strip down to his socks in the next five seconds. He stops Steven when he’s about a third of the way down the buttons in his shirt. This kind of humiliation ritual has become de rigueur in depictions of the rich and powerful — from Succession to Marty Supreme, we’ve seen this in everything.

The very first things we learned about Morgan were that he got awarded a big prize and that he cheats on his wife; we know he can, and does, manipulate his power to his advantage. That’s why his relationship with Gabe is a much more compelling illustration of his character, and, thankfully, that’s what the rest of the episode focuses on. Like Carla, Morgan can’t reach Gabe. When a worried Carla calls, Smallwood, who is always there, tells Morgan not to pick up. Johnny told Schill about Taylor & Byrne’s argument, and starting now, Morgan needs to act as if Gabe is not his son. It’s true, legally; emotionally, it’s a flat-out lie.

Not knowing who else to call for help, Carla calls Johnny. He’s meeting Bella for a black-tie event that is “ever so slightly massively fucking important” to her. He even got a tuxedo for the occasion, from Morgan’s tailor and on his dime, after Carla overheard him tell Bella over the phone that he didn’t own one (“His money is our money,” Carla reminded him). Johnny ditches his girlfriend at the door to help Carla find Gabe at Thibault’s house. It was about time Gabe got picked up — Thibault’s diatribe against monogamy (rather, against men’s obligation to monogamy) and declaration that Carla “fucked half of Hollywood” led Gabe to throw the first punch. When Carla and Johnny get there, Gabe literally runs away from them, but Johnny tackles him. In a heart-to-heart, Johnny tells Gabe that his reaction to his own parents’ divorce was also to act out. It seems to get through to Gabe, or at least, he’s dissuaded from turning himself into the police for possession.

The next day, in fact, he shows up at the Taylor & Byrne offices with his mother for the arbitration proceedings. Molly notes the “brilliance” of the scheme — Morgan will be forced to look at Gabe when he says that he doesn’t care about him, though Gabe is not initially in the room. Serena starts them off on the wrong foot, assuming too readily that Grann is absolutely against prenups “from a feminist perspective,” as Nick interrupts. But they soldier on with their argument: Serena wasn’t there for Gabe’s milestones (birthdays, trips, games, etc.), but Morgan was. In response, Cathcarts plays a voice note from the night before in which Carla accuses Morgan of not caring about Gabe. Unable to contain themselves, Morgan and Carla start fighting over which one of them is guilty of weaponizing their son. Hearing their loud voices, Gabe bangs on the conference room glass. Morgan is apoplectic; he didn’t know he was there. As Gabe yells that Morgan cheated and broke up the family, a grin starts to spread across Nick’s and Serena’s faces. Morgan yells back at Gabe, demanding he go back to school and apply himself; he’ll be checking with the headmaster daily to make sure he is. “If you’re not his father,” the arbitrator concludes, “you’re doing a mighty good impression.” Smallwood and Beatrice lose face. Later that night, Morgan calls Gillian to say Grann invalidated the prenup. He instructs her to go ahead and start moving the money, after opening his beer the same way that Gabe did, by banging the top on the edge of the table. He looks at the dents each of them left, side by side, and smiles with fatherly pride.
Representations and Acknowledgments
• This week we learn, briefly, that Beatrice is married to one Jefferson. It seems like War is constantly banking information for later, so I’m making note of it.

• One subplot in this week’s episode is Nick and Serena’s preparation to become parents. Serena has a call with their doula, Vanessa, though she’d rather be speaking with the forensic accountant, like Nick. Vanessa offers to be their child’s nanny and to take care of everything so that Serena can focus on her job, which makes Serena feel guilty. Before the arbitration, she questions whether she should stay at home with the baby — who, we find out, was unplanned — or focus on her newly established and newly thriving firm. Nick reassures her that they are a good team and will figure it out together. I’m starting to think Nick is too supportive, understanding, and compassionate … What is he hiding?

• There is one woman in this cast who is less of a character than Carla, and that is Bella Croft. After Johnny ditches her at her “super-important” event, she acts mad for half a second before giving in to his sexual advances. Bella mostly exists to reflect Johnny’s winning ways, which are, in any event, established by the slight flirtations he exchanges with Carla — when he tells her that Bella loved the tux, Carla responds, “I don’t blame her.”

• One loose thread from last week was Flora’s text to Morgan, in which she asked to see him. We don’t know yet what his response was, but with the prenup invalidated, the stakes are higher: Smallwood would probably advise him to keep his distance.

items.title: Ted Sarandos Addresses Netflix Content Exec Purge: ‘I Know That We Could Do Better’
items.description: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Netflix, looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.

Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees, Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.

On the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos — who had previously led Netflix’s content operations for over 20 years — explained the decision to install a new team overseeing its programming lineup led by Rice.
“I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum,” Sarandos said, when asked about the leadership change on the content side.

Sarandos started by praising Bajaria “for all of her incredible contributions to Netflix. Bela had an incredible decade-long run here. She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

That said, Sarandos continued, “Now we’ve seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the U.S. where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world.”

Sarandos said he has known Rice, a former Disney and 21st Century Fox television and movie exec, for about 15 years. At Disney, he was chairman of Walt Disney Television before he was ousted by former CEO Bob Chapek in 2022.

“And I’ve got to tell you the outpouring of excitement about him coming to Netflix from across the industry and from the creative community has been nothing short of overwhelming. He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services,” Sarandos said. “His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. You know, network [television], prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films, and live sports.”

Sarandos said, “most importantly… Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”
A bit later in the call, Sarandos again sang Rice’s praises.

“Peter brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s kind of that exact balance skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter,” Sarandos told Wall Street analysts. “Now, there’s a ton to be excited about in our Q4 slate, and a ton to be excited about in 2027. And I believe that Peter will actually be able to have an impact on those projects that are in the works, even in the short term.”

items.title: Christina Applegate Reveals She Was Misdiagnosed With MS: ‘I’m Back at Square One’ and It’s a ‘Mindf—’
items.description: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast, “MeSsy,” on Tuesday with some shocking news: She was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.
items.author: Ellise Shafer
paragraphs: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast, “MeSsy,” on Tuesday with some shocking news: She was misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis.

After taking a break from the podcast for seven months due to her health, Applegate tearfully shared the revelation in a two-part episode, saying that new technology led to the discovery. “This may come as great news, but to me, I’m back at square one,” she said. “It’s hard to say that [my doctor] came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS.'”

Applegate said that she was “not happy at all” about the news. “You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better. I haven’t gotten better … If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways,” she said. “So I’m back at square one, that I don’t know what’s going on with me.”

Applegate originally revealed that she had been diagnosed with MS in 2021, and retired from acting after the finale of her hit series “Dead to Me” the next year. Since then, she has become a fierce advocate for people with the disease — which causes damage to the central nervous system — and started the “MeSsy” podcast alongside “The Sopranos” star Jamie-Lynn Sigler as a way to share her experience and spread awareness.

Despite learning she had been misdiagnosed, Applegate said that her symptoms remain and her illness has now become a mystery. “I have every symptom of someone with MS. Every single one,” she said. “Now, we both know that there are many things that mirror MS — many different things.”

She added that “there’s a pretty damn high number of misdiagnoses with MS,” so this is not a rare occurrence. “It’s clear now that they’re finding something different,” Applegate continued. “Something else is going on.”

Applegate added that “it’s weird because I feel like I let everybody down” after becoming such a big advocate for the MS community. She said that she’s still in a “state of shock,” adding: “It’s a mindfuck, for sure.”

“It’s this weird feeling because I became this — you and I, the poster children for MS,” she said. “I had a reason. I had a fucking reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason and it’s very unnerving and it’s really confusing for me.”

In the second part of the episode, Applegate got emotional thinking about the past five years, and how confused she feels now. “I’m still here feeling quite hollow and quite scared and sad. Now, I just feel lost,” she said.

“I’ve gone through a great depression because of it. But, you know, I lost everything. I lost my job,” Applegate continued as she broke down in tears. “God, I’m so sorry, I get really emotional because it stopped my life. I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I mean, I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.”
Listen to the full “MeSsy” episodes below.

items.title: ‘Michael’: Golden Globes Reject Submission to Compete in Comedy/Musical Categories
items.description: The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: The music of “Michael” is bringing some drama.
Variety has confirmed that Lionsgate’s bid to have its Michael Jackson biopic compete as a comedy or musical at the Golden Globes has been denied.

The Golden Globes’ decision means the film, starring Jaafar Jackson as the King of Pop, is currently slated for the drama categories where it would compete for one of the six available slots against Christopher Nolan’s “The Odyssey,” Los Javis’ “La Bola Negra” and more. The supporting actor and actress categories do not separate by genre, so this has no effect on his co-stars Colman Domingo and Nia Long.

Lionsgate can appeal the ruling ahead of the Oct. 31 submission deadline. If the studio moves forward, the organization’s awards committee would evaluate the appeal. According to the Golden Globes rules, it states: “A musical can be a comedy or a drama in which songs are used in addition to spoken dialogue to further the plot.”

Under Globes procedure, when a film submits in a category that goes against the grain, or one in which it would not typically be accepted, a letter from the director is required to proceed. That letter, from “Michael” director Antoine Fuqua, was included with the studio’s submission. The organization reviewed the request and denied it anyway. An appeal may still be possible before the Oct. 31 submission deadline, but sources have shared that it will likely not be pursued. Lionsgate declined to comment.

Musical biopics have long been tricky to classify at the Globes. “Ray” and “Walk the Line” both competed in, and won, the comedy or musical categories in the mid-2000s. Those victories prompted a rule change requiring that songs propel the narrative rather than appear as standalone performances. In other words, music alone is no longer enough to qualify a film as a musical. By that standard, “Bohemian Rhapsody,” “Elvis,” and “A Complete Unknown” were all submitted as dramas in the years since. One notable exception: “Inside Llewyn Davis,” the Coen brothers’ story of a folk singer struggling for success in 1961, was permitted to compete as a comedy during its respective year.

That same distinction appears to have decided the fate of “Michael.” Jackson performs many of his uncle’s biggest hits in the film. Still, the organization evidently viewed those sequences as re-creations of Michael Jackson’s performances rather than as integral storytelling devices.

Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion at the worldwide box office and is Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jaafar Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.
The ruling does not affect the Globes’ broader slate of classification decisions. The awards show has accepted both “Obsession” and “Tender Loving Care” as comedies for consideration.
The 84th Golden Globe nominations will be announced Monday, Dec. 7, and the ceremony, hosted by Nikki Glaser, is set for Sunday, Jan. 10.
Gold Derby first reported this story.

items.title: Netflix Q3 Revenue Meets Wall Street Estimates, Forecasts Q4 Slowdown and Says It Will Miss Ad Sales Target for the Year
items.description: Netflix‘s third-quarter 2026 earnings met revenue expectations and it slightly beat on the bottom line. But the streamer faces an urgent need to refresh its queue: Revenue growth in the period slowed to its lowest rate in three years, and the company just laid
items.author: Todd Spangler
paragraphs: Netflix‘s third-quarter 2026 earnings met revenue expectations and it slightly beat on the bottom line. But the streamer faces an urgent need to refresh its queue: Revenue growth in the period slowed to its lowest rate in three years, and the company just laid off 1,000 employees in a restructuring effort to reposition itself.

Netflix posted Q3 revenue of $12.87 billion, up 11.8% year-over-year. That’s compared with 17% top-line growth a year ago. Net income came in at $3.66 billion (versus $2.55 billion a year earlier), translating to earnings of 87 cents per share. Operating margin was 34.6%, versus 33.2% expected.
Meanwhile, the company projected Q4 revenue of $13.4 billion, which would be an increase of 11.5%. That’s below Wall Street’s prior expectations of $13.5 billion.

For full-year 2026, the company now expects advertising revenue of about $2.7 billion, whereas it previously had been forecasting $3 billion. Netflix blamed the lower ad-revenue take on “slightly slower than expected rollout of some ad product capabilities.”

As Netflix has seen per-subscriber engagement drift downward in recent quarters, particularly in the U.S., the company last week laid off about 1,000 employees, about 6% of its workforce. The company ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria, tapping veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her, and pink-slipped head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia.

In their Q3 letter to shareholders, the Netflix management team — led by co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters — addressed the layoffs but did not explain why they decided to overhaul content leadership.

Netflix currently projects a Q4 operating margin of 26.0%, which includes a 120 basis point “negative impact” for costs associated with the layoffs (but would be up compared with 24.5% in the year-ago quarter). “These organizational changes enable us to continue to aggressively invest in high impact areas to improve our service, and drive growth and innovation,” the Netflix execs said, echoing language they used in an internal company memo about the job cuts.
For Netflix’s third quarter, Wall Street analysts on average expected $12.87 billion in revenue and earnings per share of 82 cents, per LSEG Data & Analytics.

In July 2026, Netflix released its “What We Watched” viewing report for the first half of 2026, showing global hours viewed increased 2% year over year in aggregate — while per-user engagement has shrunk. According to estimates by analysts at Jefferies, Netflix average monthly viewing time per member globally has fallen from 66 hours in the first half of 2023 to about 49 hours in the first half of 2026.

Netflix previously announced that it will shift to publishing the viewing report annually in the first quarter, beginning in 2027. “The goal of separating the publication of the report from our earnings results is to keep the focus on our primary financial metrics — revenue and operating profit,” the company said.

In their Q3 letter, the execs wrote, “We know there’s some investor concern about our view hours growth. Member response to our 2026 price increases is consistent with prior price changes and our expectations, an indicator that our engagement — which encompasses quantity, quality and variety of viewing — remains healthy and that we continue to deliver strong value to members. But we do seek to accelerate growth in view hours as well, and we’re confident we’ll do that by relentlessly focusing and executing against the aforementioned strategy.”

In 2027, Netflix plans to launch its ad-supported tier in 15 new countries in 2027. The first tranche of new market launches will happen in March 2027, spanning nine countries in Europe (Austria, Belgium, Denmark, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland), along with Colombia, Peru and New Zealand.

items.title: ‘American Horror Story’ Renewed for Season 14
items.description: “American Horror Story” has been renewed for its 14th season at FX.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: “American Horror Story” has been renewed for its 14th season at FX.

The news comes ahead of the Oct. 29 finale of Season 13, which reunites franchise legends Jessica Lange, Sarah Paulson, Evan Peters, Angela Bassett, Kathy Bates, Emma Roberts, Billie Lourd, Gabourey Sidibe and Leslie Grossman.

Other returning stars include Frances Conroy, Jamie Brewer, John Carroll Lynch, Mena Suvari and Mat Fraser, as well as Seth Gabel, who appeared in the spinoff “American Horror Stories.” Season 13 cast members who are new to the franchise include Joey Pollari, Avantika, Elle Chapman, Berto Colon, Alex Consani, Seth Gabel, Orlando Jones, Paul Anthony Kelly, Tig Notaro, Madelaine Petsch, Fedor Steer, Zach Villa, John Waters and more. Pollari plays a hospice care worker with a phobia of the number 13 who is tasked with taking care of characters from previous “American Horror Story” seasons; hence the volume of returning stars.

Season 13 opened with 4 million views in four days, the best streaming performance of any premiere in the series’ history — a significant feat especially given the three-year hiatus following the 2023 premiere of Season 12, “Delicate.”

Created by Ryan Murphy and Brad Falchuk, “American Horror Story” is FX’s longest-running hour-long series and has driven more than 2 billion hours of engagement since the launch of Season 1 in 2011. Season 13 is executive produced by Murphy, Falchuk, Ned Martel, Charlie Carver, Eric Kovtun, Nissa Diederich, Scott Robertson, Tanase Popa, Crystle Roberson Dorsey, Jennifer Salt and Tim Minear. 20th Television is the studio.
