items.title: Netflix: “We Need Better Execution” in U.S., and Peter Rice Can Deliver It
items.description: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said Wednesday that while the streamer’s strategy for continued growth is sound, it needs “better execution” of that strategy — particularly in the United States.
items.author: Rick Porter
paragraphs: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos said Wednesday that while the streamer’s strategy for continued growth is sound, it needs “better execution” of that strategy — particularly in the United States.
He also said that incoming chief content officer Peter Rice will provide the leadership to deliver on that promise.

“The business and the business flywheel are working. There’s no need for a fundamental shift in strategy,” Sarandos said on a call to discuss Netflix’s third quarter earnings. “We do need better execution in the U.S. Our content around the world is largely working. … The U.S. is also working. It’s just not growing as fast as it could or as fast as we’d like.

“We had some really solid doubles and triples this year,” Sarandos continued, referring to Netflix’s 2026 releases. “But the other territories count on some of those titles being home runs so they’ll travel around the world. So we’re really focusing on that execution.”

Rice, a former Disney and Fox executive, was hired as chief content officer last week — he starts the job on Oct. 26 — after Bela Bajaria was let go. Sarandos praised Bajaria “put a lot of hits on the board” and built the international team that has contributed to Netflix’s growth outside the U.S. and Canada. But as U.S. growth has slowed, Netflix made a change.

Sarandos noted that reaction to Rice’s hiring within the industry has been very positive, and that his experience in all aspects of the business — movies and television, linear and streaming — is what Netflix needs.

“His creative instincts and business acumen are remarkable,” Sarandos said of Rice. “He’s an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. … Most importantly, Peter Rice understands talent relations. In a competitive market, creative talent have choices where they want to work. We want Netflix to always be the place that they do the best work of their lives. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world.”
Co-CEO Greg Peters also addressed the layoffs of 1,000 employees last week, saying there were some areas where Netflix had “overinvested.”

“When you’ve driven considerable top line growth as we have over the last several years, and you’re in a highly dynamic market that’s constantly changing, I don’t think it’s unusual then to find that there are some areas that we built quickly and we ended up overinvested in, or there are opportunities to adjust how we are operating to best drive the business through the next stage of growth,” Peters said.

The Netflix co-chief added, “We prefer to make these adjustments organically and iteratively. That’s the best way to do it. We think it’s our mission basically to constantly be trying to tune and adjust, but sometimes the team needs a forcing function. The company needs a mandate that requires the whole organization to ask hard questions about where can we be more efficient, where can we make tough decisions about where we can trim or redirect how we’re investing.”
Additional reporting by Caitlin Huston.

items.title: ‘Phony’ Review: Connie Britton and Sam Nivola Lead Hulu’s Likably Quirky and Beguiling Paranoid Mystery Series
items.description: One of the consequences of pervasive social media use and video calls or meetings is that we’re perhaps more attuned to faces — our own, our loved ones’, even strangers’ — than ever before.
items.author: Daniel Fienberg
paragraphs: One of the consequences of pervasive social media use and video calls or meetings is that we’re perhaps more attuned to faces — our own, our loved ones’, even strangers’ — than ever before.

It’s nearly impossible for a blind date to be truly “blind.” High school and college reunions have become borderline superfluous. If somebody gets bangs or grows a beard or goes on Ozempic or remains bizarrely untouched by the ravages of time, we tend to be aware. It’s harder to go incognito in the world, and it’s difficult for somebody to change without our noticing.
Cast: Connie Britton, Sam Nivola, Myra Syal, Grace Brennan, Mahaela Park, Maliq Johnson, Colter Lee
The very modern discomfort and sense of the uncanny provoked by an unexpected and nearly imperceptible alteration is at the heart of Phony, a new genre hybrid from Hulu.

Half paranoid thriller and half coming-of-age comedy, Phony isn’t exactly gripping and it’s rarely hilarious. Instead, it initially occupies a very likable middle ground in which life and death stakes, a young ensemble of perfectly cast relative unknowns (plus Connie Britton and Sam Nivola), and a dildo-hoarding beaver can engage and intersect.

Critics have been sent four episodes from the eight-episode first season — exactly the right amount for me to know I’ll be checking out the second half of the season to see which of various landings the show’s creative team is able to stick. At the same time, it’s easy to see all the ways Phony could fall apart, from an unsatisfyingly resolved central mystery to the contrasting sins of deciding to take itself too seriously or not seriously enough.

For now, though, the potential of this clever and brisk series, which calls to mind everything from TBS’ Search Party to Apple’s Maximum Pleasure Guaranteed to Amazon’s recent reimagining of Carrie, is ample.
Phony was created by Nick Paley, one of the writers of the brilliantly pensive Marcel the Shell With Shoes On, with Anthony King (the second Jury Duty season) serving as co-showrunner.
The White Lotus breakout Nivola plays Sonny, an endearingly dorky-yet-popular student at a high school somewhere in the Northwest. (Oregon, I think?)
Sonny has found a way to be friendly to and friends with much of the school, paying close attention to his classmates’ personal dramas and helping out whenever possible.

He’s best friends with a temporarily injured jock (Maliq Johnson’s Vogel) and he and his girlfriend (Mahaela Park’s Chloe) are about to take the next step in their relationship. (Sex. They’re about to have sex.)

The key figure in Sonny’s life, though, is his mother Ellen (Britton). As a single mom and principal at Sonny’s high school, Ellen is very, very intimately involved. And that’s okay, since their relationship is thoroughly sweet, albeit co-dependent.
Then, a downed tree — the handiwork of the aforementioned dildo-loving beaver — causes Sonny to drive off the road, totaling his car and putting him in a coma.

After a week, Sonny regains consciousness. Everything seems normal, except for a pretty big problem: Sonny is convinced that his mother has changed — that she is, in fact, an imposter pretending to be his mother.

Naturally, there’s a lot of skepticism, which causes Sonny to reach outside of his main friend circle, forming a bond with Mallory (Grace Brennan), a Seventh-Day Adventist returning to school after several years of home-schooling; Mallory’s geeky and open-minded cousin Weldon (Colter Lee); and Sharla (Meera Syal), a conspiracy-theorizing private investigator.

The questions raised so far include whether or not Ellen is or isn’t an imposter of some sort; if she is an imposter, what the imposter’s motivations are; and if she isn’t an imposter, what it means in terms of Sonny’s post-accident trauma.

Paley, who wrote and directed the first two episodes, quickly establishes a mood of uncertainty, and Nivola’s performance swiftly takes him from appealing Everyteen to a Hitchcockian ordinary (young) man caught up in an extraordinary situation. By the end of the four episodes I’ve seen, a lot of the ambiguity has been stripped, some of it by cheating away from Sonny’s exclusive perspective in a way that I don’t think benefits the storytelling.

Part of that is because with shows like this, I will always err on the side of uncertainty and textual openness, while those same shows tend to err on the side of giving answers to impatient viewers. Watching Phony, I was caught up in the nebulous mystery and, thus far, less and less intrigued by the concrete mystery. A lot of my pleasure came from Paley refusing to come out and underline ways that Ellen might or might not have changed, letting viewers spend a lot of time staring at Britton, unable to tell with complete certainty if anything was done to augment her appearance.

You could tell me that in some shots she’s wearing contacts or that her eyebrows were colored and I’d believe you. But I’d be just as credulous if you said that Britton’s face is like one of those words where the longer you look at it, even the correct spelling begins to look wrong. Britton is resisting playing anything conclusively, and the show is all the better for the built-in warmth that TV viewers feel for any Connie Britton role. Like Sonny, we think we know what to expect from her.

At some point, Phony is going to simply come out and say, “Here’s what happened and here’s how we either did or didn’t trick you and why,” and I’m not eager for the clarification. Other viewers, I’m sure, will be looking for hints and clues, trying to figure out the story.

I made no effort to figure out the story, in part because, as a high-school dramedy, Phony is quite satisfying. Nivola escalates his performance well, and I think it’s by design that Sonny feels like a character in a TV show or movie while every other young person in the cast just feels like a normal teen. Brennan, Park, Lee and Johnson convey effortless naturalism, even if their characters are just a hair prettier and quippier than your average kid. Even when Sonny begins investigating with Mallory and Weldon, they make a set of dumb mistakes and flawed logical leaps that befit their age and academic level, rather than instantly becoming adept junior gumshoes.
Add American Vandal and A Good Girl’s Guide to Murder as comparisons one might happily make to Phony.

There’s a darkness at the show’s center, but Paley and subsequent director Tazbah Chavez (Reservation Dogs) never let anything become too solemn. So far. Episodes are all in the half-hour range, and they move fast. I thought, a few times, that I wouldn’t mind a few extra minutes per episode to live in this world, to acknowledge the different background members of the high-school ensemble. But I usually came back around to liking that we know a little about the kid who’s constantly juggling or doing magic just outside the main narrative, but not too much. Or that we don’t get bogged down in the psychology of a boy named Shovel whose response to possibly spotting a dead body is to throw a dead body-themed party, rather than going to the police.

So far, the show has done well keeping its thematic underpinnings subtle and unarticulated. It’s a show in which the very modern idea with which I led this review is there, but nobody needs to say it. Nobody needs to talk about high school as a place where everybody and everything is changing, but that changes to the grown-ups around you would be most unnerving. It’s all just baked in.

I hope that Phony can remain light on its feet going forward. The truth about Ellen is inevitable and how Paley and company handle that truth will determine if Phony is a quirky little yarn or something better and more substantive. I’ll be curious to see where it lands.

items.title: Katt Williams Was Sure He’d Be Dead by Now
items.description: Katt Williams, who long ago sold flowers to help make ends meet, is tonight sending bouquets of appreciation to his comedic rivals.
items.author: Timothy Bella
paragraphs: Katt Williams, who long ago sold flowers to help make ends meet, is tonight sending bouquets of appreciation to his comedic rivals.

It’s after 10 p.m. in October on a steamy South Florida night, and the comedian has had a long day, recording the audio version of his upcoming memoir and preparing to launch an original Netflix podcast. Now, in between drags of Newports and the blunt he smokes in the backyard of a rented luxury estate, he is being asked to reflect on his past opponents.
And mostly, the comedian known for his savage takedowns and viral beefs is keeping his cool.

Rickey Smiley, who Williams once said “can’t act” after the radio host claimed the part of Money Mike was stolen from him in the 2002 film Friday After Next, is now “funny.” And Kevin Hart, whom Williams called an “industry plant” and a “Hollywood puppet” while questioning the credibility of the actor’s rise to stardom, is tonight a “nice guy.”

But when asked about Steve Harvey — the radio personality and Family Feud host Williams accused of stealing jokes and previously described as “a country bumpkin Black dude that can’t talk good” — Williams struggles.
“Well, this took a turn,” he says, taking a drag from his fourth cigarette. “I did so well with Rickey Smiley, too.”

This is the point when you’re expecting Williams to bury Harvey like the latter did him (and seemingly half of Hollywood) in a 2024 episode of Shannon Sharpe’s Club Shay Shay podcast that’s been viewed more than 94 million times. But on this night, the 5-foot-5 giant of comedy lays down his verbal shovel and decides not to toss more dirt on Harvey.

“The statistics will show nine out of 10 times, no matter who it is, I’m going to find something wonderful to say. Because if you don’t have anything good to say, don’t say anything at all,” Williams says in a quiet pitch, almost as if he’s about to tell you a secret. “But in this case …”
After two minutes, the nicest, or most respectful, thing he can say about Harvey is that “he’s a cautionary tale.”

This is what you get when you’re around Katt Williams: You’re never quite sure what he’ll say, who is going to be the target of his ire or what devastation he might leave in his wake, but he speaks with absolute conviction in pursuit of the truth.
“More now than ever, truth is really at a premium,” he says.

For nearly a quarter century, Williams has been one of comedy’s most combative, persistent and unexpected raconteurs — stealing scenes in films like First Sunday, emerging as an improv force on MTV’s Wild ‘n Out, winning an Emmy in 2018 for his guest appearance in FX’s Atlanta and cranking out 14 stand-up specials.

At 55, parts of his life could be mistaken for the kinds of myths in one of those rags-to-riches books you read in school: an emancipated and homeless teenager who fled from Cincinnati to Miami and supported himself by cleaning at an upscale restaurant and stealing car radios; a door-to-door magazine salesman who simultaneously learned how to take rejection and make money by talking; an aspiring comedian fueled by gas-station burritos as he scribbled jokes on the back of his eviction notice. He has faced a fraught history of unflattering headlines about him being volatile and erratic, criticism that his claims of being blackballed by Hollywood are overblown and a litany of legal issues that include 39 arrests — by his own count. (He maintains that he has no felony convictions on his record.)

Now, though, Williams has found some stability in his life. A father of 10 and a grandfather of five, his last known legal entanglement was almost a decade ago. He regularly sells out arenas. He claims to make about $100,000 for each show on tour and roughly $10 million for each of his four comedy specials on Netflix — the platform will also launch his podcast later this year. Williams reflects on how he got here in his new memoir, Nine Lives, No Wives, and 69 Concubines, out Oct. 20.

“There’s never been anyone like him, and I doubt that there’ll be anybody like him in the future,” says Luenell, the comedian, actress and longtime friend who performed in many of the same California clubs as Williams nearly 30 years ago. “Individuality is key because there are so many cookie-cutter, play-by-the-rules people out here, and I just love me a renegade. That’s what Katt is.”

Mo’Nique, the Oscar-winning actress and comedian who has been friends with Williams for more than two decades, says, “I am attracted to the underdog, and when you see this little guy onstage and he’s so fearless and so full of confidence, you cheer for that.
“Now, I don’t know if he considered himself an underdog,” she concludes, cackling.

So, what exactly is Williams chasing now that he has unlocked more mainstream respect as one of his generation’s foremost virtuoso ranters? It’s to live out a life as, in his words, “a motherfucking truth-teller with a microphone,” that he believed would ultimately be cut short.

“I never assumed that I was going to make it further than Tupac and Kurt Cobain,” he says of the music legends who died in their 20s — a feeling that’s never fully left him. “I had been led to believe that the good die young, and I had seen enough examples.
“I just assumed that was going to be my lot in life, which meant I needed to be more.”

The first time that Micah Sierra Williams stepped to the microphone of a hole-in-the-wall comedy club in Florida that he remembers reeking of cigarettes and “broken dreams,” he was trying not to get thrown out.

The 16-year-old was underage and wasn’t supposed to be there, and he had no material planned when he sneaked into the joint with his friends in the late ’90s. His intent was to get into a bar and have a good time, not make people laugh. But there was an open mic and he took it.

The then-teen wondered what the hell he was going to talk about for three minutes. He hadn’t lived a long life to that point, but he wasn’t short on material either, not after he had knocked on strangers’ doors as a Jehovah’s Witness at 7, gotten advice on women from Prince (yes, that Prince, who, at 18, was dating Williams’ cousin), escaped his parents’ basement beatings at 13, and was rejected from the U.S. Marine Corps because he was too young. His childhood was so insular in his strict Jehovah’s Witness home that he thought that Richard Pryor, who later lauded him for knowing “exactly who the fuck you are,” was a regular guy caught on tape being hilarious.

In a crowd he remembered as being “whiter than a Canadian blizzard except for one sister in the back,” the only joke he knew was a reliable one: “Being the only chocolate drop in a town of vanilla wafers.” Years later, Williams realized the steady laughter meant he killed, even if it wasn’t immediately apparent to him.

“I was having a conversation without racism, and I get why it was funny to them. I haven’t heard anybody talk like that,” recalls Williams, who was also selling flowers in the community to make some money. “I didn’t rush to do it again for what seemed like forever because I wasn’t really sure how well I had done. I just chalked it up to, ‘He’s the only Black guy there, we might as well let him win.’”

After he finally gave comedy a real shot in Oklahoma — where he played clubs with the likes of Jeff Foxworthy and Larry the Cable Guy (while also acting in a “pimp adjacent” role to a group of “intimate entertainment specialists” for a couple of months) — he moved to California in 2000 to see if his act would play in Hollywood. “He wasn’t chuckle funny. He was spill-your-drink funny,” Luenell says of her first impression of him. Yet, he was a single father struggling to break through in film and television who had received a cease-and-desist letter from Dr. Seuss over his use of “Katt in the Hat,” his stage name at the time. Williams knew time was short.
“I knew that I only had five years to become a star in L.A., or I’m fucked,” he says of that period. “That’s just how it works.”

By the time he broke through in the Ice Cube-led Friday After Next in 2002 as Money Mike, a pimp who felt authentic thanks to Williams’ own time as a “pimp adjacent,” he was “right on schedule, and not a moment too soon,” he says. Known for his meticulous delivery based on a calibrated tone of mock outrage, lavish fashion sense and a signature straightened perm hairstyle, Williams became a consistent comedic presence in film and TV over the next two decades — a mainstay on TV in The Boondocks and scene-stealer in films like Norbit and The Perfect Holiday.

Williams had found fame and legal trouble. Between 2006 and 2018, he faced charges that included gun possession, assault, battery and theft. A stolen gun was found in his briefcase at LAX in 2006, and he pleaded no contest to a misdemeanor. When he was accused of acting in a threatening and violent manner at a Seattle bar before resisting arrest, he announced he was retiring from comedy in 2012. That lasted all of three days.

While he admits he has messed up plenty in his life, joking that his rap sheet is so long that it rivals the Bible, Williams says that he blames his parents and former members of his team for pushing a narrative that he was abusive and unhinged. In his memoir, Williams details how he spent a day at Rikers Island on gun charges before performing at Carnegie Hall in November of 2008. (The charges were dropped.) After the performance, he was involuntarily committed to a mental institution in South Carolina for about a week, he writes in the book. Williams claims in his memoir that his family and members of his inner circle wrote letters “saying I had exhibited violent behavior, I’d threatened them, and they feared for my safety.” Years later, Williams denies much of what’s been said about him and shifts blame to the group of people he refers to as “the Betrayal All-Stars.” He doesn’t deny that he owns guns or has a long history with weed — he is, after all, smoking in front of me for nearly two hours — but he rejects that he was abusive or ever lost his mind due to drugs.

“In none of the situations was I in a mental position where I didn’t know what was going on or what was happening. I wasn’t,” he says. “As a comedian, I’m not coming to your town to do any harm whatsoever. I’m not selling any drugs. I’m not buying any drugs. I’m not supplying any guns. I’m not committing any offenses.”
Among those betrayers were his parents, who are still alive but remain distant.

“I know it’s going to seem weird, but I’m grateful for them. I’m thankful that I had parents,” he admits, chuckling. “I didn’t get this far by holding on to turmoil and traumas. I’ve already flipped it for my benefit. If you’re turning the negatives into positives, then you can’t really dwell on the negative.”
The challenge from Mo’Nique in February of 2025 was one Williams couldn’t resist.
I bet I can beat you in a race, Katt.

“Mo,” Williams replied, “you don’t want none of this.” After all, his Emmy win for Atlanta featured him displaying near-perfect sprinting technique in the role of Alligator Man, who is shown running away after he illegally kept both his girlfriend and alligator locked up.
“No,” Mo’Nique replied. “You don’t want none of this!”

Mo’Nique, who was still getting her hair and makeup ready before she went onstage in Houston as part of Williams’ Heaven on Earth tour, had a head start as she sprinted toward the makeshift finish line backstage at NRG Arena. So, when Williams, who had bragged that he could run a 40-yard dash in less than five seconds, streaked by her in his electric blue sweatsuit in back-to-back races, Mo’Nique found out that he was “competitive as shit.”
“His ass was coming so fast that it scared me!” she says.

As Mo’Nique listened to Williams’ interview on Sharpe’s podcast the previous year — the one in which Williams accused Cedric the Entertainer of stealing his closing joke, suggested he turned down $50 million so he didn’t have to party with Sean “Diddy” Combs and claimed that Ludacris was part of the Illuminati — she thought to herself that she had found her long-lost, fraternal, truth-telling twin. Mo’Nique identified with Williams’ claim that he had been blackballed in Hollywood after she said she experienced similar treatment for not wanting to campaign for Precious, the 2009 film that won her the Academy Award for best supporting actress.

“No one has ever come out and said, ‘Katt Williams is lying,’” Mo’Nique says. “I believe Katt Williams will go down as one of the greats. The truth-tellers never, never die because the truth never dies.”

There are many books that have shaped and saved Williams’ life, including The Swiss Family Robinson and Robin Hood. He gets lost talking about these stories: “All of the stories had the same line: Where somebody is a regular person, just like me or you, and they are dealing with some extraordinary circumstances, which seem like are going to be too big for them. And we get a chance to see them get beat up. Then, simply because they persevere and keep going at whatever it is they’re doing, they get to the other side of that, and we find out what they truly were the entire time.”

He believes the person he really was the whole time was revealed on that episode of Sharpe’s podcast. When the topic of the Sharpe interview comes up, Williams relights his blunt to talk about another book he’s turned to in moments featuring chaotic or adversarial elements: Sun Tzu’s The Art of War. For all the specials he’s had and movies and TV shows that he’s appeared in, the Sharpe interview remains unarguably the biggest cultural touchstone of this point of his career. The comedian is cool with that.

“If I got up there and lied 17 times, then I should expect some retribution,” he says. “But not if I go up there and tell some uncomfortable truths.” He adds of the cultural fallout from the interview, “There was little for me to gain if it wasn’t done correctly.”

As Williams aims to carve out a space in the oversaturated podcast field, he’s wondering what his audience wants him to do next. On his website in 2007, he wrote that his goal was to “build a comedy empire and help restore dignity to our profession.” He grins at the reminder of the goal.

So … did he do it? As the silence of the dark South Florida night is filled only by the chirping of crickets and the gentle humming of the air conditioning, Williams exhales smoke from his last Newport and, like he’s done since he was 16 and that first time onstage, he delivers his truth into the mic.
“I don’t think I could be a fair judge of if I did that. I think that was my intention,” he tells me. “Hopefully, I didn’t hurt the cause.”

items.title: The Real-Life Wardrobe of Quil Lemons, Who’s Feeling Inspired by 'The Boondocks'
items.description: There hasn’t been a moment when Quil Lemons wasn’t interested in making pictures. “Photography has always been like speaking,” he says. “It has helped me digest this mortal coil of what is going on here. My interest starts with art, and then photography became
items.author: Christopher Fenimore
paragraphs: There hasn’t been a moment when Quil Lemons wasn’t interested in making pictures. “Photography has always been like speaking,” he says. “It has helped me digest this mortal coil of what is going on here. My interest starts with art, and then photography became the vehicle for me to have something to say.”

If you’ve glanced at a fashion magazine in the last half-decade (including this one), you’ve probably seen Lemons’s images. In 2021, at the age of 23, the photographer and fine artist became the youngest person to shoot a Vanity Fair cover, and his work has been shown at the Philadelphia Museum of Art and the International Center of Photography, among others. One such show was his first solo exhibition in 2023 called “Quiladelphia”—a portmanteau of his name and his native city—which also serves as the namesake of his first photography book, which drops on October 28 through IDEA.

Quiladelphia, the book, expands on the themes of that show: what it is to be Black, queer, and masculine, what it is to love another man, romantically and platonically; his native city’s grit and boundaries. It features a forward by writer Brontez Purnell, an essay by Lemons, and conversations with the artist Lyle Ashton Harris as well as singer-songwriter (and fellow Philly native) Santigold.

As a seasoned fashion photographer, Lemons is also deeply interested in clothing and personal style. Ahead of his upcoming book tour, I met with him in Brooklyn to chat about photographing stars like Ice Spice and Lindsey Vonn, his first pair of Margiela Replicas, and why he’s been “fucking with Buck Mason” lately.

Quil Lemons: I studied journalism—I’m always asking who, what, where, why. That’s originally what it started off for me. How could I answer those questions through an image? Fashion has been really fun to play around with; fantasy and myth and what that means in relation to Blackness, what that means in relation to pop culture. How it’s evolved. Patience is something that I’m leaning more into these days. I’m not jumping to make as many images that don’t say as many things, like some of my contemporaries. I’m really interested in images that you can sit with for some time, like a painting. That’s how I look at my photography now.
Oh, yeah. Paul Strand shot this image of an African girl with books on her head. I just thought that said so much.

To the point of journalism, I ask: Is this story important to tell now? I’m asking myself that a lot with putting out a book and I think it’s the right time. How I pick a subject… I feel like most times they find me. We’re in the same tribe of people. If humans were put into different pods by God, I think I would be in the pod with these people. We have a lot of fun.

There’s a shared sensibility to life and sometimes that’s queerness, sometimes that’s Blackness. Sometimes those are one and the same. Sometimes they fight. I like tension and friction because that’s where I [find] a real sense of humanity is. I like people that aren’t necessarily taking the easy route and that are trying to be subversive to whatever space they’re in. That’s why I say we are all in the same tribe of people.

Punctuality. It’s really important being on time. So, me and my crew come about two hours before the talent gets there just to make sure our setup is great. We also like to have a really strong sense of etiquette. I don’t want you to come onto a messy set. This is a workspace; let’s get you in and out. I don’t want to spend a bunch of time making an image because we have eight hours with you, so we need to be on it.

Fashion isn’t what it used to be. We don’t have two days to do a shoot. With some publications I am given a lot of time, but I would say that’s rare and it’s something I do try to push for, but there are realities. So, I just want to make sure it’s easy because there are a lot of distractions in not being prepared. Then I can’t really meet my subject in the best way.
Oh, for sure. I also ask my talent what they want to listen to because I need you to feel good. Most times we’re pretty aligned or they trust my taste.

I was really into Loe Shimmy. Loe Shimmy’s BPM is really trance-like in a really fun way that conjures sexiness. I listen to a lot of PinkPantheress, listen to a lot of Syd. Syd was played a lot during my wedding; I remember those months I was listening to a lot of her project [Beard] before it came out. Charli [XCX], because Charli gets you into that cunty space. I listen to a lot of female rap, like Karrahbooo, Anycia. It’s a fun playlist.

Rihanna is always playing on set. Rihanna’s my favorite right before we shoot because everyone loves Anti. It’s a great set album because everyone knows exactly where they were [when it came out]. It’s a really good conversation starter. Everyone has a favorite song. So I really appreciate Rihanna for making my sets the most beautiful to start.

On [the podcast] Throwing Fits, they asked me how it was looking at Ice Spice’s badonkadonk. Ice Spice’s ass is so natural. It’s insane, the way it vibrates, and I think she would appreciate me for saying this. But I feel like a lot of people focus really heavily on her butt because we haven’t seen a natural ass in a long time. But also my favorite part about Ice Spice is that the face and the ass match each other, and it’s equally as beautiful.

Craziest thing I shot recently was Lindsay Vonn for Vanity Fair. Lindsey Vonn had just regained the ability to stand from a really crazy injury. I’m always in awe of strong women, but that was such a feat to see her be able to walk again after not knowing if she was going to be facing a double amputation. That’s what made that story really special to me—her resilience. I got to meet Miguel’s son this year and that was really sweet because Miguel meant a lot to me growing up. I loved his music. I just loved the visual of Miguel. He’s so handsome, and to meet his son was so sweet. I’m just thinking, like, We heard how you were created.

We’re still dismantling it. It’s really fun now because I feel like I was saying shit in 2023, like, “Go vote.” And people were like, “What?” And I’m like, “Yeah, you should go out and vote because we’re going to start losing rights.” Our country has gotten even more radical. I did a group show called “American Faggot Party” in Provincetown the summer of ’24, right before the election, just because I was scared as to what Donald Trump’s administration was going to do to all spaces that supported Blackness and queerness. I’m never going to say I told you so, but I was definitely picking up on what was in the undercurrent. It’s fun to be in this space because I’ve been prepared and a lot of people go, “Oh, you’re so brave for saying something like that in 2023.” But I feel like people forget that bravery is a choice, and I choose to not be a pussy to conversations that are happening in front of my face. My art has become even more potent in that.

Quiladelphia explores what it means to be a Black man in America. I’ve grown an Obama-era optimism, so there is no ceiling. In the book you will get to see the multitudes of Blackness, masculinity, queerness and how they all intertwine and intermingle because they all exist within me. Quiladelphia is just a really fun play on the fact that I was born and raised in Philadelphia, the City of Brotherly Love, and it was the title of my 2023 show. I think when people saw that show, they saw what my future in art looked like, and I don’t think they could have predicted what it was going to look like. I still think that that’s the question and why everyone’s interested right now.

Inherently, clothing and Blackness go hand in hand when you have to code-switch to be socially viable in our country’s educational spaces and in our workforce. I grew up in a very blue-collar city, so I knew people that came home in a uniform and then they stepped right back out of the door in some fly shit. I’ve always taken that ideology into who I am as a person. I also grew up watching Pootie Tang, and Pootie Tang was so fantastic in presentation, but I feel like you have to be that to subvert stereotypes as a Black man and to be seen other than those stereotypes. That’s why I like getting dressed.

Completely. I look back at certain eras. I feel like each era, you can see the things that I am challenging within the art. There [was] Glitterboy and then there was a post-Glitterboy, like, I’m going to challenge femininity. When I was doing Quiladelphia, it was really fun to engage with the language around sex work, leather, queer codes of dressing and communication. Now I am at a point where I’m just reflecting Quil and I’m really interested in showing what it is to truly be African American.

I was a Jordan kid. Jordans every Saturday. So, I was cool with paying $160. But when I was 16, I had a job at a Walgreens and I saved and bought a pair of Margiela Replica sneakers. That’s when I knew I was really in it.
They were metallic, black and silver. I still own that decision. I was hesitant [to admit it], but I still do, because I think I could freak it.
Same. They’re so classic. But also, I’ve heard from the kids on TikTok that they’re calling them an “unc shoe.” Or a “dad shoe.”
Same. It is what it is. That was my hesitation.
See, it’s really funny. I haven’t really bought clothes.
People give me a lot of things! So, I’m really going to have to think about when I did, because I think that does say something.

I’m really into cashmere. I’ve been fucking with Buck Mason. I’ve been into the quality of the clothing there. I’m trying to think of what was the last thing that I actually bought. Probably my wedding ring by Bernard James.

I love Margiela just because it’s always been really chic. In the past year, I’ve been loving Comme [des Garçons]. That’s my new shit. I’ve always been a fan of Commission. They make really good clothes. They kind of cut them to my body. When I find a brand, I end up in there every day and I’m so nosy. I want to know everything about it. So, we kind of become a pair in a way; Commission has been dressing me for a lot of my openings. Same thing with Simone Rocha, but Simone is a little bit more of when I am embracing and I’m feeling a little bit more feminine, but not, but just wanting to be fully embodied is when I feel like I want to wear Simone.

It’s so important, especially with communicating Black masculinity. It’s so specific. The person that I’ve been working closely with has been my husband [stylist Parker Harwood], because our language just never stops when it comes down to reference points. And in a lot of the new work, I am playing around the characters of Gangstalicious and Thugnificent from The Boondocks. They were so ripe to me, and it’s so funny looking back at their predictions for what has now become so true to what Black male aesthetic is. I’ve always been interested in luxury and communicating that, and those two things are really fun for me to toggle between—and by luxury, I mean there are certain brands that just naturally exude that, but also tailoring. One of the oldest forms of luxury is being able to buy a suit. It says something when a Black man is in a suit. So, going back and forth between these two archetypes that exist as parallel twins for Black men in our country are two things I’m dancing with.

It’s so funny. I’ve been re-watching a lot of his speeches lately. I made my own version of a commencement, a State of the Union address for the show that I did in Provincetown, and it was really fun to kind of declare it. I was referencing [the artist] Zoe Leonard who wrote, "I want a dyke for president,” so I was like, “I want a fag for president.”
We are in a desert of empathy.
We? I don’t know if it was me. But I do think that that says a lot in terms of how we understand femininity.
Running the country. We could go on.

items.title: America Is Officially Back in the Selvedge Denim Business
items.description: Mike McLachlan, the founder of the Connecticut clothing brand Manresa, has owned many pairs of selvedge denim jeans over the years, but the ones he’s wearing right now are by far the closest to his heart. “Selvedge mills tend to lean more towards more characte
items.author: Jeremy Freed
paragraphs: Mike McLachlan, the founder of the Connecticut clothing brand Manresa, has owned many pairs of selvedge denim jeans over the years, but the ones he’s wearing right now are by far the closest to his heart. “Selvedge mills tend to lean more towards more character-rich neppy, slubby denim,” he says, referencing the textural characteristics prized by many selvedge enthusiasts. “But I've always been more of a fan of what Levi’s would have been using in the middle of the century. It’s fairly flat and uniform, and it’s a style of denim you don’t find very often anymore. It’s as traditional as it gets.”

For McLachlan and many others, selvedge denim—the old-school-style cotton twill woven on antique narrow looms—is both aesthetically and ideologically superior to the stuff most jeans are made of today. Not only does it take on more character as it wears and fades, it represents a direct connection to the authenticity of denim’s golden era, before it was consumed by the modern global fashion industry. McLachlan’s new favorite jeans are a one-of-one prototype, but thanks to the efforts of Trion, Georgia’s Mount Vernon Mills, and a room full of painstakingly restored antique shuttle looms, anyone in search of the kind of no-nonsense dungarees one might have bought at Sears in the 1950s will soon have plenty of options.

In early November last year, Mount Vernon Mills, a 180-year old fabric mill and America’s largest denim producer, posted an Instagram video of a semi truck backed into a loading bay, its cargo shrouded in a white plastic sheet. The video, set to the opening chords of AC/DC’s “Hell’s Bells,” didn’t reveal much, but for those attuned to the fate of American-made selvedge over the last few years, it marked a major milestone. Under that white sheet was one of 40-some Draper X3 looms salvaged from the legendary Cone White Oak denim mill in Greensboro, North Carolina. To those who worship at the altar of 20th century workwear, it represented nothing less than the salvation of American denim. A little less than a year later, that machine and 20 others like it are up and running, fabric samples are being shipped to clothing brands across the country, and a new chapter in a 120-year story is beginning.

“It has been a crazy ride,” says Tim Harris, the director of marketing and specialty sales at Mount Vernon Mills, and the company’s de-facto social media manager. He’s the one who posted the video of the looms arriving last November, and he’s been documenting their progress on TikTok and Instagram in the months since. The equipment, some of which had been in storage for nearly a decade, was in rough shape. “There were some full looms there, but there were also these bins of parts that had 6000 springs and levers in them, things that had not been made since the 1970s,” he says. “It was like, ‘Here we go!’”

The Draper looms’ journey to their current home was long and fraught. The looms—some of which date back to the 1950s—were originally used at the Cone White Oak mill, which opened in 1905 and was the official supplier of selvedge to Levi’s, Wrangler, and many other storied American brands for most of the 20th century. Before White Oak closed in 2017, it had been the last remaining commercial producer of selvedge denim in the United States, and many feared the legacy of American-made selvedge would disappear with it. Enter Vidalia Mills, an ambitious textile startup, which purchased White Oak’s equipment, moved it to Vidalia, Louisiana, and promised a glorious return to form. That never quite came to pass, however, and when Vidalia’s assets went up for auction last year, Mount Vernon Mills bought the lot.

Given its history and its size, Mount Vernon Mills is perhaps the only company with both the resources and the skilled workers necessary to resurrect American selvedge, but restoring the looms to their former glory was no small feat. Pickers scoured barns and warehouses for spare parts, and a crack squad of technicians from Greensboro decamped to Trion to teach Mount Vernon’s staff how to keep the antique machinery running. As of now, Harris says, about 20 of the 45 Draper looms are operational, and each has been christened with the name of a golden-era American cultural icon: Elvis, Aretha, Lucille.

Because antique shuttle looms like the Draper weave at a fraction of the pace of their modern equivalents and require far more maintenance, running a selvedge production line represents a significant investment for a relatively small output. To put it in perspective, Mount Vernon hopes to produce 20,000 yards of selvedge per week at full capacity, the same amount of time it takes its modern looms to churn out millions of yards of conventional denim. Despite this, Harris says, there is no shortage of buyers excited to turn its new selvedge into jeans. “The outpouring we have received for this crazy idea of bringing these old things back to life, and doing this in America, has been amazing,” he says. “Folks are reaching out. They want to be a part of it. We could not have asked for a better reception.”

One of those reaching out is Kyle Moredocks, who recently got his hands on a sample of Mount Vernon Mills selvedge. Moredocks is the founder of an eponymous Portland-based brand that makes customized jeans, jackets, and shirts to order (his Cowboy Jean recently got a shoutout from Derek Guy). Because Moredocks’ concept is based on on-demand production, he doesn’t buy huge quantities of material, and that makes it difficult to meet the minimum orders of large textile mills. “If you can go straight to the mill and meet their volume requirements then obviously that's easier. But if you're someone our size making less than 100 pairs a year, it's more challenging,” Moredocks says. At Mount Vernon, however, the new selvedge program is distinguished by being available to small brands like Moredocks and Manresa at minimums far below the industry standard.

“These [brands] are the ones keeping this thing alive—the romance and the stories behind these jeans, and they look for craftsmanship.” Harris says. “This is not cookie-cutter-every-yard- looks-the-same denim. This is handcrafted by artisans, and it’s different. This is the $300 Pappy Van Winkle, not the $25 Wild Turkey.”

Harris alludes to bigger deals with high-profile clients that he can’t name, but to anyone familiar with the recent surge of special-editions made from White Oak’s remaining American-made selvedge, it’s not hard to guess who the list might include. Mount Vernon is initially offering two standard sanforized (i.e. washed and pre-shrunk) denims: the Revere, a 13-ounce dark indigo, and a heavier 15-ounce Franklin. “We wanted to do old revolutionary names because we were doing something revolutionary,” says Harris. “Mr. Revere came and told us that the revolution was coming.”

At Manresa, McLachlan is working through his last remaining yards of Japanese selvedge, and plans to release his signature 207 jeans in Mount Vernon Mills denim in the coming months. “We'll make Mount Vernon 15-ounce during the colder months, and the 13-ounce during the warmer months,” he says. “Then maybe a field coat, maybe a barn coat, maybe a jean jacket somewhere down the line.”

In the meantime, McLachlan has been wearing his prototype Mount Vernon 207s every day. “They have a little bit more drape than a Japanese counterpart might, and they just feel comfortable as soon as you put them on,” he says. “I feel very lucky to be able to be wearing a pair.” McLachlan also boasts that as one of the first people in the world to have a pair of Mount Vernon selvedge jeans, he’ll have a head start on the fade competition that will inevitably ensue.
“I’m going to wear them every day, so nobody's ever going to catch up to me in terms of my fade,” he says. “So I’m pretty proud of that too.”

items.title: Why This New Hublot Is My Favorite Watch of 2026
items.description: The older I get, the simpler my tastes are becoming. But don’t confuse simple with boring. Simple can be stunning—just look at this new Hublot.
items.author: Mike Christensen
paragraphs: The older I get, the simpler my tastes are becoming. But don’t confuse simple with boring. Simple can be stunning—just look at this new Hublot.

It’s mid-October; I’ve seen a boatload of new watches since the start of the year, and people are already talking unapologetically about Christmas plans, so I feel all right about making some “best of 2026” calls. I know there was a much more fun release from the brand just last month, but this Hublot Classic Fusion Tributo—specifically the one in yellow gold, but the white gold version is also fit—might be that watch for me.

I remember when I first tried on a Classic Fusion. It was in 2018, when Baselworld was still the king of the watch fair scene. I liked it because, unlike many watches, the dial was clean. There was hardly anything going on with the Hublot, and the porthole shape of the case and bezel hit different. There was a bit of AP Royal Oak sniffing around, but it was more stripped back and less showy. The casual nature of a sporty black rubber strap cozying up against the pimping gold case immediately felt quite me; like the horological equivalent of dressing for business up top, party down below.

I reckon this new Classic Fusion is the most complete version of the original ever made. The OG was a 1980 creation by a young Italian gentleman called Carlo Crocco, and the story behind the making of this watch is one of my favorites, and not just because it’s essentially the watch Hublot was founded upon.

When Crocco started working in watches for his family’s company in 1969, he was tasked with “developing entry-level products," he says. But he had greater ambitions: he wanted to create more beautiful things. So in a fitting tribute to his wife Marie-Danielle, he decided to do exactly that.

Crocco's philosophy was simple: “To remove rather than to add.” With that in mind, he came up with a design that used twelve screws to hold it together while also telling the time. Who needs hour markers on a dial? Not Crocco. He wanted to make something innovative that kept the “classicism and know-how of the Swiss industry," he says, while “adding something different and special to it."
Thirty-eight years prior to my first Baselworld, Crocco walked up to that same fair to debut his new creation (the MDM stood for “Marie-Danielle Montre,” montre being watch in French).

Vacheron Constantin’s distributor in Italy told the designer, “You are crazy!” according to Crocco. Meanwhile, Cartier’s director came by and said, "This is the product we should have had," says Crocco. The timing of the watch's release was crucial, though. Many Swiss watchmakers were freaking out about the Quartz Crisis—the arrival of the new more-accurate and easier-to-mass-produce technology in 1969 decimated the luxury industry in the '70s. “We arrived at that moment with a high-end watch equipped with a Swiss quartz movement," says Crocco. "It was the ideal time to introduce a new model.”

Fast forward to 2026, and only one of those directors was correct. Without the Classic Fusion, Hublot wouldn’t be the disruptive powerhouse it is today. Its willingness to combine the precious luxury material with a rubber strap may seem old hat today but it's only because Hublot kickstarted the movement more than four decades ago. And this new tribute version brings back the MDM logo on that polished black onyx dial at 6 o’clock, as well as the 12 screws that hold it together and tell the time. I’m all for the 38mm case (the OG was 36mm) as that size better fits my wrist, especially when a watch has lugs like these. But crucially, it is powered by an in-house movement indicative of how far Hublot has evolved technically in the past 46 years: the HUB1711 Manufacture Self-winding Caliber, with 50 hours of power reserve.

“Minimalism by design” and “horological depth” are two things Hublot CEO Julien Tornare holds in high regard, and this tribute has both in abundance—honoring Crocco’s original not “by freezing it in time, but by keeping it in motion," Tornare says.
My review is in: 10/10 for pure, unadulterated simplicity that's never boring.
This story originally appeared on British GQ.

items.title: Noah and Timex’s Newest Watch Channels Vintage Patek Philippe
items.description: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: Want more insider watch coverage? Get Box + Papers, GQ's newsletter devoted to the watch world, sent to your inbox every Friday. Sign up here to get it free.

Ever since their Sun and Moon watch sold out in a snap in 2014, Noah and Timex have nurtured a growing collection of affordable timepieces to cement themselves as one of the most fruitful and popular collaborators in the watch world.

Now, the pair are back with perhaps their most elegant watch yet: the Boatswain. For those of you who didn’t grow up scrubbing the poop deck, a “boatswain”—pronounced “bosun” or “bos’n”—is a senior petty officer on a ship who is in charge of maintenance, operations, crew management, and the like. Like the Anchor watch from earlier this year, the name strikes a nautical to but the Boatswain is cocktail-party ready. The $228 watch is launching October 15th at 11 a.m. EST on Noah's website.

The watch’s Oval shape captures the look of the thin, beloved Golden Ellipse Patek Philippe has made since the 1960s. Noah and Timex have used this shape before, but this dial does away with the lighthouse design and even the moon phase complication for the simplest execution yet. Measuring 31 x 35 mm with an 18mm lug width, the elliptical case comes in steel or gold-tone steel with soft edges, a flat crystal, and a small crown. The dial is pared down to the essentials: an eggshell background is overlaid with black Roman numerals and a black pencil handset. But if you look very closely at what would typically be a railroad-shaped inner minute track on, say, a Cartier Tank, this one is actually shaped like a length of coiled rope, neatly knotting together the watch’s nautical theme.

Powered by a quartz movement and available on a brown leather strap in steel and a black leather strap in gold tone, this is Noah and Timex’s cleanest offering yet—and one of their best-looking. Though 2025’s Lighthouse Watch featured a similar silhouette, this one’s classic dial offers a more restrained take on the partnership’s aesthetic. And at $228, every burgeoning collector fresh to the workforce is almost guaranteed to scoop one up to strap on for work, play, and just about everything else.

The arc of Noah’s Timex projects has been fascinating to watch precisely because they didn’t necessarily resonate widely right off the bat: handsome as the first couple of Weekender-type watches were, they didn’t explode into the popular consciousness with the impact of a sartorial bomb. But ever since the Sun and Moon—followed by the Rectangular Moon Phase Watch, the Lighthouse Watch, Oval Moon Phase Watch, and others—the two brands have been on an absolute tear. Something about the dressier, unisex silhouettes; the playful complications; and the affordability has been right on trend in the watch industry. Plus, it gave younger or more budget-minded collectors the chance to get a taste of the elegant vintage Cartier and Patek Philippe watches that are typically the exclusive province of deep-pocketed buyers.

If Noah founder Brendon Babeznian, a self-professed non-watch guy, has hit upon anything, it seems to be that a great-looking, everyday watch doesn’t need to be a precious heirloom piece that you keep in a safe and only take out for weddings, bar mitzvot, and anniversary dinners. Rather, it can be funky, not too expensive, and nearly perfect.

items.title: 7 Expert Habits to Build a Better Social Life from Psychology Professor Julianne Holt-Lunstad
items.description: This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.
items.author: Ecleen Luzmila Caraballo
paragraphs: This is Expert Habits, a regular column in which thinkers, leaders, and other high performers talk about the habits and routines that help them live a better life.

If you’ve heard the stat that loneliness is as dangerous to your health as smoking 15 cigarettes a day, you’ve heard of Julianne Holt-Lunstad's work. A distinguished professor of psychology and neuroscience at Brigham Young University, Holt-Lunstad has spent her career proving what most of us feel intuitively but rarely act on: that our relationships are not just a nice-to-have, but one of the biggest levers we have over how long—and how well—we live. In addition to being a professor, Holt-Lunstad advises the World Health Organization, and is the co-founder of the Foundation for Social Connection and The Connection Institute.

Her focus is especially relevant as loneliness remains a prevalent problem in the US. A new study shows that 40% of Americans report moderate to severe loneliness. The good news is that Holt-Lunstad’s meta-analyses have found that measuring people's positive social connection—the breadth of their social network, whether they have someone to confide in, how satisfied they feel in their relationships—predicted a sense of feeling alive even more powerfully than measuring the negative effects of the absence of connection. Social connection was associated with a 50% increase in prolonged life whereas isolation, on the other hand, was linked to a 32% increased risk of mortality, and loneliness to a 14% increase. She says it’s important to recognize, “not only the dangers when [relationships] are absent or poor quality, but also looking at the incredible effects and benefits they bring."

Holt-Lunstad herself practices what she preaches (and researches) in her own daily life. We spoke with the professor about how she fills her calendar with intentional moments of connection, defaults to inconvenient choices for the sake of face time, and gives with no expectations.

Julianne Holt-Lunstad: “One of the things that I try to do is nurture the relationships across different aspects of my life. We can think about different circles of our social lives: our really close relationships with family and close friends, and then the broader friends and acquaintances, and then there’s neighbors, coworkers and things like that. Because we know that consistency is important, I have tried to establish routines. I have a group of friends that we get together once a month, and we schedule out the whole year and we have it on the calendar, and so [our gatherings] always happen.

“I have two boys that are now grown, and we try to do it more frequently, but we have scheduled weekly calls so that I’m always knowing what’s happening. On my way to work, I have a commute, and every single time I use that to either call one of my sisters or one of my friends. I always check in. It’s a nice time because it’s quiet, and it’s just dedicated time that we can catch up.

“Sadly, my parents passed away a couple of years ago, but before they passed away, every night when I would make dinner, I would call them while I was making dinner. I would talk to them every single day and knew what was going on. And in fact, when they passed away, it was kind of weird because I didn’t know what to do with myself when I was making dinner. I was always used to having this conversation.”

“Whenever I’m thinking of someone, I’ll send them a message. I’ll say hi or let them know—because sometimes we can think about people and it passes and you never actually connect. It’s a very low lift—certainly not as much as picking up the phone and making a call. One thing I’ve started doing recently that I’d never done before is leaving voice memos, because sometimes just hearing people’s voices can convey so much more than just a few words.”

“When there’s something important in people’s lives, I will go out of my way to be there for it. Sometimes it’s incredibly inconvenient, but it's important to be there, to show up. Every time I do show up, I’m glad I did. Because I often end up having a conversation with someone I didn’t expect to. And it might be someone who is either a complete stranger or even someone I barely know, but the connection not only sparks a new familiar face that can lead to other conversations down the road, but also helps me recognize what incredible people I’m working with or are in my neighborhood, that you sometimes take for granted.

“People are opting for convenience, which often takes you away from other people. And so opting for in-person when possible, whether that is the in-person meeting or actually going to the grocery store instead of ordering online, or going out to a restaurant instead of ordering [a meal] online, going out into your community.

“In my Social Connection in America project, we see that the majority of Americans are disconnected—they rarely get together in person with people who matter to them. I also did a study with Eventbrite looking at different types of events that create connection, and what we found is that in-person is better than virtual. We have new data coming in our Social Connection in America 2026 report showing that most Americans report that interacting virtually doesn't satisfy their social needs at the same level as interacting in person.”

“As a professor, I start every class with what I call a connection moment. Every day we take two minutes—I literally set a timer—for a different fun prompt each day. Even in my meetings, I'll try to start with something similar, where we have a moment to connect as humans before we get into the business of what we need to do.

“It helps us get to know each other and create a safe, trustworthy environment so learning can happen better—where students feel more comfortable participating in class and feel a greater sense of belonging and motivation to participate. In meetings, it can also defuse what might be a potential tension over difficult decisions, because now you can see the shared humanity that we have. There's less ‘my position’ in it. You recognize that we’re in this together.”

“We have evidence that participation in groups is associated not only with better health outcomes, but there’s even the work of [political scientist and author] Bob Putnam on how it influences democracy. When we think about groups, the mechanisms can be exposure to different types of people in different settings, but also the fact that groups often have a regular cadence—weekly worship attendance, a daily fitness class, your monthly book club—and a consistency in who's participating.”

“When we do small acts of kindness or service or support for others, or just even showing up for a friend, that can not only give us a sense of purpose and meaning, but also can serve to strengthen those bonds with that person. We know that closeness or intimacy in a relationship is often reciprocal. And so, as we give, others are more likely to give in return, and that reciprocation can often build that closeness and intimacy in a relationship.”

“We asked people to do small acts of kindness for their neighbors, and what we found was that this significantly reduced loneliness. What's so fascinating is that presumably the person on the receiving end benefited too, although we don't know—we only measured the person providing the act of kindness. This is consistent with several other studies showing that, as the old saying goes, it's better to give than to receive. We actually show measurable benefits when we're providing help and support and service to others. And in some cases, that is equivalent or even stronger than actually receiving any help ourselves.”

items.title: Pierpaolo Piccioli on His Vision for Balenciaga & the Power of Starting Over
items.description: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection
items.author: Eric Wilson
paragraphs: It takes less than a minute for Pierpaolo Piccioli to steer a conversation about fashion into one about philosophy. More than a year into his tenure as creative director of Balenciaga, during an interview on the day after he showed his first couture collection for the house in July, Piccioli explains how he has navigated a role that is both familiar and foreign to him by first quoting Friedrich Nietzsche and the concept of oblivion—oblio in Piccioli’s native Italian.

“Oblio is a moment when you are aware of your past, but you kind of forget everything for a moment and you see everything with new eyes,” says Piccioli, seated at a large conference table in his office suite on Avenue George V, in Paris. “And that’s what actually happened to me.”

For most of his career, over a quarter century, Piccioli was associated with one designer: Valentino Garavani, who made a lasting impression on his life and his eye. Starting in 1999, Piccioli, then in his early 30s, and his longtime collaborator, Maria Grazia Chiuri, rose through the ranks at Valentino, becoming co–creative directors in 2008, a year after Valentino announced his retirement. Then Piccioli led the Roman house solo from 2016 to 2024, while Chiuri served as creative director at Dior. He knew the seamstresses by their names, their skills, their peculiarities, and their very Italian way of working, and he adopted the rhythms and rituals, if not the formality, of Valentino himself. This would have been a lot to leave behind for a designer taking on the mantle of another legendary brand—let alone that of Cristóbal Balenciaga. That house’s own rich history includes two wildly successful modern interpretations, first under Nicolas Ghesquière, then under the now mononymous Demna. But in the words of Nietzsche, “Man will desire oblivion rather than not desire at all.” “I didn’t want to come here to find the same people with the same experiences,” Piccioli says. “I wanted to face something new.”

At his couture show the day before, under the blazing sun in a garden on the outskirts of Paris, Piccioli showed 52 looks that were captivating in their strange beauty. Some of them were outrageously glamorous in the bold style that Piccioli had once championed at Valentino: He opened with a cloud-shaped jacket trimmed with a flock of intense red feathers, worn over a white oversize silk duchesse satin T-shirt and voluminous beige trousers; another look consisted of a dark red shirt styled with big pink pants. But many others represented new territory for the designer, like a floor-length coat the color of a yellow highlighter, which he showed backward, slung over matching pants. There was a fluorescent pink silk “balloon bolero” dress trimmed with feathers made of tiny strips of curled organza. The designs seemed to demand close inspection to be fully understood.

“It felt like a real celebration of artistry,” said the actor Lily Collins, who has known Piccioli for more than a decade, since they first attended a Met Gala together. “Pierpaolo and Balenciaga are the perfect mix.” Naomi Watts headed backstage, where she raved about a tailored black dress adorned with a white ribbon scarf. “That’s the sort of dress I look forward to wearing in my 50s, 60s, 70s, and then some,” she said. Demi Moore, who wore a Piccioli-designed Balenciaga couture ensemble at Cannes in May, circled the boards showing photographs of the models in each of their looks, while Hudson Williams, who appeared in one of Piccioli’s first Balenciaga advertising campaigns, stood nearby, waiting to offer his congratulations.

“This collection is the result of a feeling,” Piccioli wrote in a printed program composed of 20 narrowly spaced pages, including detailed descriptions of all the looks, along with the names of the members of his atelier who helped realize them—Victor, Thomas, Léa, Margherite, etc. “We worked while getting to know each other, learning to understand one another,” Piccioli wrote. It was part of his broad effort to humanize the couture-making experience, which can feel cold and anonymous to anyone living outside that bubble.

The week before the show, Balenciaga wiped its social media history and then posted portraits of some 40 members of its atelier, all dressed in their white Balenciaga Couture work coats. Many of them appeared to be quite young, though a few were established hands and familiar faces, including Bruno Sialelli, formerly the creative director at Lanvin. Philip Treacy, the milliner, was also credited in the couture program for contributions that included a pink ostrich-feather headpiece that spiraled from the crown and around the torso, turning the model who wore it into a swan.

This meeting of minds, among Piccioli, his seasoned collaborators, and his younger team, has become as much a part of his vision for Balenciaga as the clothes seen on his runway. “When you don’t know the rules, you are more open to experiment,” he says. “And that is the key for me to interpret Balenciaga. I didn’t want to go back to any of the old shapes but to try to invent a new shape that could have been that of Cristóbal.”

The day after the show, the couture salon is packed with visitors examining the looks. Patti Wilson, the stylist, has been there for more than an hour. Amal Clooney is spotted among the mannequins. When he arrives, Piccioli, who is 59, is dressed in his usual uniform of a black T-shirt and trousers, with a necklace of coral amulets worn as protection from bad energy. He has a pack of cigarettes in hand and is still very much the picture of a Roman designer who cooks his own pasta most nights, now at his new home just across the Seine. “I’ve got my Roman ways in Paris,” he says. “It’s a sort of effortless approach that is maybe less formal than expected, more direct and more human.”

On his first day at Balenciaga last year, Piccioli traveled to Getaria, the tiny fishing village in the Basque region of Spain where Cristóbal Balenciaga was born in 1895, and where a museum dedicated to the master’s work today offers access to an enormous array of designs collected by his staff and clients. As Piccioli immersed himself in Balenciaga’s world, he began to understand that designs he had perceived through images as austere or strictly linear were, in fact, quite light. That would be his starting point for Balenciaga couture. “In every one of his silhouettes, the body was the protagonist,” he said.

To achieve similar results in new ways became an obsession for Piccioli, and this is where having a younger atelier was an advantage—the team was willing to experiment with techniques that break with the strict traditions of couture. Perhaps the biggest change was replacing standard Stockman mannequins with custom forms created from 3D scans of models’ bodies. Those ghostly plastic forms were used to shape fabrics through a complex process of layering cashmere upon leather that had been washed, stretched, and allowed to dry in place to hold its shape. Each mold took as long as a month to create, but eliminated the need for darts or seams. Piccioli also wanted to play with new fabrics and materials, using a lab-grown silk called AMSilk that purports to be fossil fuel–free and stronger than steel.

Despite these technical innovations, Piccioli believes in the classic model of couture as the pinnacle of fashion. “When you talk about couture, you talk about an approach in which there are no maps. A 3D conversation with the body can then apply to denim, T-shirts, and tailored jackets from prêt-à-porter. To me, a T-shirt has to be a T-shirt, as much as a pair of jeans has to be a pair of jeans. But if you meld couture and industrialization, you can make a more modern garment.”

Like most designers of his generation, Piccioli was raised to worship at the altar of the great Cristóbal Balenciaga, who worked in Paris from 1937 until his retirement, in 1968. The first image Piccioli posted on his personal Instagram account, in 2018, was of a 1967 Balenciaga wedding ensemble that had been included in the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Costume Institute exhibition “Heavenly Bodies” that year. “Simplicity is a solved complexity,” Piccioli wrote in his caption, paraphrasing the sculptor Constantin Brâncusi. It did not escape Piccioli’s attention that the wedding dress had been designed by Balenciaga the same year Piccioli was born. And although his reverence for Balenciaga is rooted in the maestro’s innovations, Piccioli made clear upon his arrival at the house that he respected the label’s more recent history as a modern luxury brand as well. Balenciaga is now a commercial behemoth that has been redefined by other famous designers. Ghesquière gave Balenciaga heat in the new millennium; Demna brought the house to the street over the past decade, and his flair for disruption ultimately drove Balenciaga well past $1 billion in sales. Both are difficult acts to follow.

With his initial ready-to-wear shows, Piccioli laid some of the groundwork. His spring 2026 collection was based on Balenciaga’s 1957 sack dress, which had a lightweight and unrestrictive shape that was revolutionary at the time; the following season was an ode to “finding lightness in the dark,” as illustrated by inky black skirts and coats, a few pieces rendered with imagery from Sam Levinson’s Euphoria. Piccioli also alluded to his personal love of sports with a techwear-meets-couture pre-fall collection, and with the introduction of a collaboration with the NBA in January that included four-figure varsity jackets, as well as hoodies and sweatpants that would not have looked out of place in the luxury streetwear oeuvre of his predecessor.

As Piccioli steers the future of Balenciaga while learning to embrace his own, he is facing change on a personal level. Valentino Garavani, to whom Piccioli remained close long after his retirement, died in January at the age of 93. Piccioli’s former design partner, Chiuri, has since left Dior and returned to Rome, where she made her couture debut for Fendi the same week Piccioli was presenting his for Balenciaga. His children, Benedetta, Pietro, and Stella, are all now adults and starting their own lives. Just as before, he returns to Italy to spend his holidays with his wife, Simona, and their family at their seaside home in the small beach town of Nettuno, near Rome, but their days there are more limited than they were before.

In Piccioli’s loose interpretation of Nietzsche, a designer might be able to forget his history out of necessity for a moment, but the past remains around him all the same. Acknowledging as much, Piccioli has kept the office he inherited mostly untouched. Its decor is aggressively gray, just as Demna left it last year when he was tasked with righting the ship at Gucci, which, like Balenciaga, is owned by the luxury goods conglomerate Kering. Piccioli layered some brightly colored rugs on the floor and retrieved from his own storage a three-person desk designed by Gio Ponti. Against the far wall is a billboard-size poster of a famous photograph of the same Balenciaga 1967 wedding ensemble Piccioli posted on Instagram, which shows the dress in such stark black and white contrast that its sharp silhouette forms an almost perfect triangle. Leaned against the photo is a bright pink surfboard designed by Piccioli for Zara’s 50th anniversary last year.

“I’ve added some elements and taken out others, but this is kind of metaphorical of what I’m doing here at Balenciaga,” Piccioli says of the office. “They are contradictory in the space, but in a way I feel that they have found their own harmony. I didn’t want to deny what has been done before me. I’d rather layer on top of that and create a bridge so that Balenciaga can go somewhere else.”

Hair by Benjamin Muller at MA+ Talent; makeup by Lucy Bridge at Streeters; manicure by Fanny Santa Rita for Essie at Call My Agent. Model: Lydia Hall at Ford Models Barcelona. Casting by Ashley Brokaw Casting. Set design by Rafael Medeiros at the Wall Group.
