items.title: Belts Were All Over the Spring 2027 Runways—and Not Just Around Waists
items.description: For most of their history, belts have had a simple practical purpose: to hold up your pants. The biggest style advice given about them was equally as utilitarian: they should match your bag and shoes. But the belts shown across the spring 2027 runways aren’t q
items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: For most of their history, belts have had a simple practical purpose: to hold up your pants. The biggest style advice given about them was equally as utilitarian: they should match your bag and shoes. But the belts shown across the spring 2027 runways aren’t quite like their predecessors. They were often comically large or ironically itty bitty. They had secret uses, and they crept onto other areas of the body like an invasive vine. They were replacing chokers, embellishing necklines, and sitting aimlessly, though chicly, below the hips. They’re made to be seen, and they are, for better or worse, the breakout accessory of the moment.

Is it a response to shrinking waists in the age of Ozempic? Is it symptomatic of the death of quiet luxury? Or are fashion houses simply trying to hype up another class of ‘It’ accessories to compliment their bag and shoe sales?
Whatever the case, they’re certain not boring. Here, the wildest belts from the spring 2027 runways.
MM6 Maison Margiela’s New Necklines

For spring 2027, MM6 championed clothes that just seemed “wrong.” Sweaters became skirts. Pants morphed into minidresses. Collegiate collars were turned on their side and used, rather effectively, as arm loops. The belt, too, was given a new look. It was brought way up past the waistline to the chest, where it became a bust decoration instead.
Givenchy’s Covert Compact Mirrors

Sarah Burton is a designer who thinks about women’s bodies. Beyond what looks good, she asks what feels good, with tailoring techniques and design details that serve the wearer in unseen ways. This came through in her belt offerings this season, which featured medallions with a secret second purpose. The statement disks opened to reveal compact mirrors—lightening the load of purses everywhere.
Alexander McQueen’s Heavy Metal

Is it a collar? Is it a harness? Is it a metallic suspender of sorts? The belts at Alexander McQueen delivered all of the above. Seán McGirr’s part Victorian gothicism, part rave-wear employed heavy-duty adornments with multiple straps. While the runway also had classic house suiting, it was the soft, silky evening gowns that got the belts. An effectively off-putting choice.

This season, Michael Rider’s joyful runway played with the extremities of the belt. Most talked-about were the thick leather iterations with supersized gilded buckles. On the opposite end of the aesthetic spectrum? Wiry cords that appeared almost as an afterthought. Both, however, were successful in drawing eyes to the waist.
Christopher Esber’s Ode to Elvis

Elvis Presley was on the mood board for Christopher Esber’s spring 2027 collection. Specifically, the designer looked to the flashy, studded belts that embellished the superstar’s suits in the 1950s. On the runway, that manifested in modernized takes on the rock-n-roll accessory, with belts that stretched up the torso before wrapping around the neck. Though these were presented with shift dresses instead of fit-and-flare jumpers, they still evoked Presley’s Las Vegas-era costumery.

Protective dressing was top of mind at Acne Studios, where belts were strapped across waists, chests, collars, and sometimes trousers for a small taste of traditionalism. Even with non-utilitarian designs, like warped Rococo ballgowns and loosely draped blouses, the idea of belts was never far—as buckles adorned tote straps and pointed loafers.
Ferragamo Does Double Duty

Maximillian Davis leaned into Ferragamo’s statement-belt legacy by finishing almost every look with a belt (or two). Suede capes and boxy blazers featured stacked leather straps, as did latex sheer sets and sexy going-out dresses. The result was a hit of polished hardware befitting cashmere-swathed dignitaries and skin-baring It-girls alike. Case in point: the collection looks right at home in the wardrobes of both Celine Dion and Dua Lipa.
Valentino’s Hourglass Drama

From 2010s-era studded straps to colorful fabric cummerbunds, Valentino’s spring 2027 show delivered Alessandro-Michele-level drama by way of cinched waists. High-rise pencil skirts, peplum tops, and cardigans tucked into trousers emphasized the hourglass silhouette. But big belts got the message across best.

Demna’s contribution to the belt renaissance came via his signature runway irony. Models with knife-sharp shoulders and smudged eye makeup balanced corporate dressing with vampiric edge, and thick belts offered a final touch of intensity. Whether worn high on midsections or slung below the hips, the multi-buckled, bondage strap was an unmissable attraction that winked at Tom Ford-age sexiness.
Dries Van Noten’s Ageless Accessories

Grandmotherly codes—like strings of pearls, bedazzled brooches, and knee-length skirts—were supercharged with saturated palettes and cartoonish proportions. Belts were central to creative director Julian Klausner’s vision of practical, offbeat femininity, with patterned waistbands on everything from floral sack dresses to wrinkled bubble skirts.

items.title: 'Hunger Games' Star Joseph Zada Is Learning to Dress the Part
items.description: To say Joseph Zada is on the verge of mega-stardom would be an understatement. The 21-year-old Sydney native beat out a field of contenders to land the role of a young Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, stepping into a franchise wi
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: To say Joseph Zada is on the verge of mega-stardom would be an understatement. The 21-year-old Sydney native beat out a field of contenders to land the role of a young Haymitch Abernathy in The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, stepping into a franchise with a proven track record of turning young actors into global superstars (see: Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson).

So it was only fitting that, for his first-ever Academy Museum Gala—one of Hollywood’s most glamorous and closely watched red carpets—Zada went with a tried-and-true classic: Giorgio Armani. For the evening, Zada put an elevated spin on the much-debated tan suit, wearing a beige double-breasted tuxedo jacket with satin-trimmed notch lapels, slim-fitting trousers, and a crisp evening shirt. Paired with slicked-back hair, the look felt both relaxed and impeccably polished.

Once inside, Zada connected with his Sunrise on the Reaping costars Elle Fanning and Mckenna Grace both of whom offered their own nods to the Hunger Games universe. Fanning arrived in an ethereal, Effie Trinket-esque Valentino butterfly gown, while Grace paid tribute to Lawrence in a custom red Mônot dress reminiscent of the look the original Katniss wore to the 2011 Oscars.

The cast is about to be seeing a lot more of one another—and so are we—as the press tour ramps up ahead of the film’s November 20 release. But before all that, Zada invited W along as he got ready with Armani, talking personal style, his first memories of the house, and the Hollywood legends he looks to for inspiration.
What’s an early or standout memory you have of Giorgio Armani?
I actually bought my first pair of dress shoes from Armani. It was a last-minute premiere situation, and I love them. I’ve worn them a bunch. Timeless.
What was the vibe you were going for/on the moodboard for your Academy Museum Gala look?

We wanted something classic but with a bit of an edge. Something that feels really cool without trying too hard, which is what Armani does so well. It’s my first time at the gala, so getting to do it in Armani and sit at their table is incredibly special.
What are some of your pre-red carpet rituals?
I usually just put on some music and try not to overthink it. The playlist is a bit of everything depending on the mood—I always have to have some hype-me-up music.
You and McKenna seem to be perfectly in sync style-wise for your events. What sort of outfit coordination do you do with each other?
We both have our own style, and I think that’s what makes it work. I’m always excited to see what she is going to wear.
Who are some of your biggest style inspirations?

Paul Newman. I’ll never match his steez, no one will, but he’s someone I admire in that department. For myself, I look to Timothée [Chalamet], Leo [DiCaprio], and Brad [Pitt] at my age as style inspiration.
Your character Haymitch wears a necklace with a lot of personal significance. What’s the most meaningful fashion item you own?

I’m pretty sentimental about things people have given me, especially when there’s a story behind them. I have a few things from friends and family that mean a lot to me, and I like that they don’t have to mean anything to anyone else for them to be special. I have a bangle from my mum that I never take off.
The Academy Museum Gala is basically a room full of people you’ve grown up watching. Who would leave you genuinely starstruck if you ran into them at the event and why?

There are so many people I’d be over the moon to meet, but Paul Thomas Anderson would be pretty crazy. I’ve grown up watching his films, and he’s one of those people whose career you can’t help but admire. It would be a dream to work with him.
What’s one fashion trend or style of clothing that you never thought you’d wear but have recently come around to?

Honestly, I never really thought about fashion that much before, so a lot of this is new to me. I’ve been having a lot of fun with it, and I’m working with an amazing stylist, Jason Bolden, who’s opening my eyes to all of it. In Jason we trust.
What is the biggest difference between Sydney style and L.A. style?

Sydney style feels a little more laid-back and outdoorsy, whereas L.A. has a bit more of that polished energy. But both places are pretty casual at heart, and I think people in both cities like looking good without making it seem like they tried too hard.

items.author: Natalie Michie
paragraphs: The sixth annual Academy Museum Gala is here, and once again, it’s living up to its reputation as one of Hollywood’s most glamorous nights. Dubbed the “Met Gala of the West,” the star-studded affair raises funds for the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures and supports its mission to preserve cinema through special exhibitions, public screenings, and educational initiatives.

This year’s ceremony will honor Oscar-winning actor Charlize Theron with the Icon Award. Filmmaker and composer John Carpenter will receive the Luminary Award, while Colman Domingo will take home the Vantage Award. For the first time, Taylor Swift will not only attend, but also perform. The gala is a major stop for Oscar hopefuls, and Swift’s presence marks her continued involvement in cinema amid the success of her original song from Toy Story 5, “I Knew It, I Knew You.”

Its October timing, right after Fashion Month, means the evening always delivers looks straight from the runways. Expect to see plenty of Matthieu Blazy’s Chanel, Jonathan Anderson’s Dior, and Anthony Vaccarello’s swan song for Saint Laurent. With a host committee that includes Teyana Taylor, Demi Moore, Kirsten Dunst, Greta Lee, Adrien Brody, and Kate Hudson—as well as a star-studded guest list spanning sports, music, art, and television—the 2026 Academy Museum Gala offers a first taste of awards-season trends. Plus, with Rolex as the presenting sponsor, there will certainly be some exquisite timepieces on display.

items.title: Banana Republic and Zankov Go Big and Bold With a New Capsule Collection
items.description: Henry Zankov is busy. Not only did the designer just present his debut collection for Diane Von Furstenberg alongside the latest for his eponymous brand at New York Fashion Week, but he also designed a collaboration with Banana Republic. Comprised of 27 pieces
items.author: W Staff
paragraphs: Henry Zankov is busy. Not only did the designer just present his debut collection for Diane Von Furstenberg alongside the latest for his eponymous brand at New York Fashion Week, but he also designed a collaboration with Banana Republic. Comprised of 27 pieces, the limited-edition, unisex capsule reflects both brands’ approach to craft and detail, offering unexpected pieces made from high-quality materials.

This is Zankov we’re talking about, so of course knits are the cornerstone of the collection. Brushed cashmere and wool yarns create sweaters of vivid stripes and Fair Isle patterns. Zankov looked to the Banana Republic archives when designing the capsule, and one leather and suede-paneled pencil skirt finds its origins in a 1986 style of similar construction. Leather pops up elsewhere in a burgundy bomber jacket and on the collar of a car coat. Accessories round it out with a selection of reversible hats, colorful socks, and scarves. The pieces are simple but exciting, bright and joyous, and inherently grounded in the languages of both Banana Republic and Zankov. The collection ranges in price from $90 to $600 and will be available to the public at select Banana Republic stores and online at bananarepublic.com starting October 20.
Patek Philippe Gondolo Ladies First

Patek Philippe has launched six new Gondolo Ladies First watches. Rendered in bright hues with sophisticated gem settings, the styles recall the original 2009 design while updating it for today. The collection redefines Patek Philippe's relationship with its female clients, offering an easy-to-wear jewelry watch that balances modern and vintage appeal. Set with hundreds of diamonds and offered in white and rose gold cases, the Gondolo watches are rich in detail but free of excess, the perfect accompaniment to a woman’s everyday wardrobe.

Thanks to Ugg and JW Anderson, you won’t have to choose between warmth and style this winter. The two brands have come together to present two of Ugg’s iconic styles—the Classic Boot and Tasman—with a JW Anderson loafer twist. The shoes were designed around JW Anderson’s signature shoe style, and the result toes the line between comfort and class. Motifs from both brands can be seen in the offerings, with JWA’s construction and Ugg’s signature materials both on display.

“Uggs are instantly recognizable, and I was interested in seeing something so familiar through the lens of JW Anderson,” Jonathan Anderson said. “For me, collaboration is about experimentation, bringing two distinct points of view together and seeing where that leads. We’ve explored the loafer extensively at JW Anderson, not only as footwear but also through its details applied to bags and ready-to-wear. I wanted to see how that language could translate into Ugg.”

The offerings are unisex and available in three colorways selected by Anderson: chestnut, khaki, and orange. They are available for purchase in stores and at jwanderson.com and ugg.com beginning October 15.
Christie’s and Boucheron’s Ode to Jewels

The storied jewelry brand Boucheron was founded nearly 100 years after Christie’s held its first auction in 1766. Despite the age gap, however, the two companies both hold rich histories and a sense of legacy within their respective industries. So it only makes sense for them to partner up on a new project—an exhibition created in collaboration between Boucheron and Christie’s called Boucheron: In Focus—A Monograph of a Visionary. On view in New York City from October 9 to 18, the show features over 80 creations drawn from the jewelry house’s heritage, past, and present. In Focus is divided into four sections that speak to Boucheron’s roots, codes, and inspiration: architecture, nature, couture, and innovation. Highlights include Human Being making its American debut, as well as the brand’s newest high jewelry Carte Blanche collection, which will be open to the public as well. “Our history with the United States goes back much further than our physical presence there,” Hélène Poulit-Duquesne, CEO of Maison Boucheron, said in a statement. “The first American clients appeared in Boucheron’s order books as early as 1865, and in 1903, Louis Boucheron opened an office in New York to maintain these close ties. And yet, it was only in 2024 that we opened our first American boutique, on Madison Avenue. This exhibition marks an important new milestone in our American journey.” For more information, click here.
Lady Harcourt’s foliage tiara.
Cartier’s Into the Wild Collection

Cartier is kicking off Tilda Swinton’s tenure as an ambassador for the high jewelry brand by making her the face of its newest collection. The Scottish actor models the over-the-top pieces of Cartier’s new Into the Wild offerings. Swinton shows off five creatures, whose stylized heads are rendered as extravagant rings, necklaces, bracelets, and earrings. A diamond-encrusted tiger gnaws at her finger, while an emerald-eye crocodile eats its tail as a bracelet clasp. The pieces toe the line between realism and abstraction. The animals’ likenesses are clear, but their bodies are distorted and graphic. The Cartier panther, for example, looks to have been stretched from its neck, elongated into a sleek bangle. Elsewhere, it perches on a clock face as the keeper of time. There is a whimsical beauty imbued in the collection, which is likely why Swinton, with her enigmatic grace, was chosen to represent it. She artfully crawls towards the camera like the crocodiles that adorn her neck and finger, embodying the strength of character and freedom of spirit exemplified by the jewels.
Moncler’s Re/Icons 2026 Collection

Moncler is revisiting four iconic styles from the brand’s past and reinterpreting them for a new era. Set around the theme of “Pioneers in Moncler with Extraordinary Dreams,” this year’s Re/Icons collection remains rooted in the mountains and Moncler’s pioneering foundation. Designs from as far back as the 1950s center the brand’s adventurous spirit and connection to iconism, cementing Moncler’s place in alpine history.

The collection features reimagined versions of the Karakorum, Verone, Himalaya, and Tibb. The Karakorum was originally designed in 1954 for Achille Compagnoni and Lino Lacedelli as part of the Italian expedition that achieved the first successful ascent of K2, the world’s second-highest mountain. Fast-forward a few decades for background on the Verone, which gained popularity in Italy in the ’80s when the puffer jacket became part of the metropolitan uniform. But this season, the Re/Icons collection expands beyond outerwear. For the first time, Moncler is also offering a collection of full looks, including windbreakers, T-shirts, pants, and skirts, as well as accessories. Cozy beanies and silk-twill foulards are available, as well as titanium and leather sunglasses inspired by vintage climbing goggles. Every individual piece is updated in a way that makes it feel relevant in the 21st century while maintaining its place in both mountaineering and fashion history.
Rob Roth’s Blondie T-Shirt

Artist and designer Rob Roth has launched a series of limited-edition, one-of-a-kind T-shirts at Dover Street Market New York. The first of the series features images of Debbie Harry, captured by Blondie cofounder Chris Stein. Roth reimagines the photographs through a collage-driven approach that blends art, photography, and fashion with a punk sensibility. The patch-working also acts as an homage to William S. Burroughs, a friend of both Stein’s and Harry’s. Burroughs was known for using “the cut-up method,” a technique in which he snipped and rearranged existing text to create unexpected combinations and meanings. In a similar vein, Roth has brought together two separate images to create a fresh composition: a reinterpretation of Stein’s photography through Roth’s distinct visual perspective. As Roth said in a statement, “Sometimes, you have to turn the frame upside-down.”

Roth sourced vintage T-shirts for the project, which he then sliced up and sewed together in new ways; this makes the garments another extension of the cut-up process. Each piece was finished with minimal embellishments and found objects. All of this means no two tops are alike. “This series of collectible, wearable art is a T-shirt lover’s dream,” said Harry. The shirts are available in limited quantities now at Dover Street Market New York.
Banana Republic x La Ligne

Banana Republic and La Ligne have solved all your fall wardrobe worries. The two brands teamed on a 36-piece collection, which brings a fresh perspective to fall classics. The collaboration centers on functional pieces that can not only build upon each other, but also fit into an existing wardrobe. La Ligne’s three cofounders drew inspiration from the Banana Republic archives, reinterpreting many mainstay elements with contemporary proportions and a rich, fall-adjacent color palette. Of course, La Ligne’s signature stripes are present in an array of shirts, sweaters, and accessories. There is also an emphasis on outerwear, represented by a nubuck barn jacket, belted suede wrap coat, and cape trench. Finally, sweaters—a cornerstone of both brands—are plentiful, with offerings rendered in soft cashmere and chunky cotton. It’s all about the classics done right. The Banana Republic and La Ligne collection is available now at select Banana Republic stores and online at bananarepublic.com.
Givenchy By Sarah Burton’s Shark Pinch Boot

For fall/winter 2026, Sarah Burton reworked (and renamed) Givenchy’s iconic Shark Pinch Boot. The new design elongates the original, bringing it thigh-high, while added “pinch” hardware at the top hearkens back to accessories introduced in Burton’s first season with the brand. Still, the unmistakable boldness of the original shape remains at play. The boot simultaneously embraces the leg while creating a unique and sculptural silhouette. The style has already become a celeb favorite. Anya Taylor-Joy wore the footwear while promoting The Super Mario Galaxy Movie in March, and Ariana Grande donned a custom, embroidered pair on the opening night of her current tour. Finally, you can stick your feet in them, too. The Shark Pinch Boot in its many variations is available now in-store and online at givenchy.com.
Polo Ralph Lauren’s Polo Blaze Bag

Polo Ralph Lauren has launched a new bag just in time for fall. The Polo Blaze bag is named after the white marking on a horse’s face from the forehead to the nose. With sculptural lines and distinctive hardware, the piece represents a bold reimagining of equestrian spirit for the Polo Ralph Lauren woman. The bag is elevated yet effortless, crafted in moto-inspired leathers. The smaller top-handle option is prim and ladylike, while the wider, small-shoulder variety provides a bit of edge. The large shoulder version, finally, balances downtown edge with heritage elegance, providing a new, modern take on a work or travel tote. All three Polo Blaze bags are available now on ralphlauren.com.
Omega Speedmaster 38mm Update

Omega is sharpening up its Speedmaster 38 mm with seven new references that bring the compact chronograph closer to the house’s iconic Moonwatch. The refresh swaps oval subdials for rounded ones, pares back the dial text, and adds a chunkier bezel and Moonwatch-style bracelet. The lineup ranges from classic black-on-steel to icy blue, mother-of-pearl, and two-tone gold versions, with two diamond-set options for a little extra flash. Consider it a cleaner, more polished take on one of watchmaking’s most recognizable silhouettes. For more info visit omegawatches.com.
Dilara Findikoglu’s Bridal Capsule

Alt brides, rejoice. Dilara Findikoglu has released her first-ever bridal capsule. The wedding-ready pieces fit seamlessly in Findikoglu’s Victorian-inspired oeuvre, with the lingerie-adjacent designs mirroring existing signatures from the designer’s collection. Never one to follow rules, Findikoglu said she wanted to take part in the ritual of weddings, but aimed to do so in her own way. The result is a collection comprised of just eight ruffle- and ribbon-covered pieces. There’s a lace-up mini dress, honeymoon-worthy bra-and-panties set, and a sophisticated, tailored look perfect for the courthouse bride. A pink mesh dress adds a girlish touch—ideal for those eschewing white—for the fashionable bridesmaid, while a classic corset can easily be recycled following the nuptials. The collection is available now on dilarafindikoglu.com.

Pearl jeweler Mikimoto and fashion label Chrome Hearts have reunited on another collaboration, two years after their first in 2024. Born from a shared appreciation for craftsmanship, individuality, and timeless design, the collection unites Mikimoto’s pearls with classic Chrome Hearts motifs and metalwork. The five pieces from the first collection, previously rendered in white gold, are now available in 22-karat gold hardware with Akoya pearls and natural diamonds. Two drop earrings, a bracelet, a safety-pin brooch, and a necklace offer traditional jewelry with an added edge, balancing refinement and rebellion in a collection that feels authentic to both brands. Mikimoto x Chrome Hearts is available exclusively at Chrome Hearts Aoyama; Mount Row in London; and the Mikimoto stores in Ginza, New York, and Hong Kong. Also, for a limited time, well-heeled shoppers can peruse the goods via private appointment at Chrome Hearts Cannes and St. Barths.

Now you don’t have to dig through secondhand bins to mimic Hailey Bieber’s laid-back denim style. Any fan of the model knows she loves a vintage Gap jean, and she has officially teamed up with the clothing brand to make her favorite, effortless styles available to all. Introducing: The Hailey Jean, a limited-edition denim capsule that reimagines Gap’s designs through Bieber’s lens. The line is inspired by that effortless ’90s look, as well as the Gap silhouettes Bieber champions in her day-to-day life: the Extra Baggy and Low Rise Loose. Updated fit proportions usher the pieces into the 21st century, while six custom washes allow for an array of styling options. Bieber’s personalization of the jeans continues with the addition of a “1996” design detail referencing Bieber’s birth year, and the model’s signature printed inside the pocket lining. “Gap has been a part of my wardrobe since I was a kid, so this came together very organically,” the model said in a statement. “Nineteen-ninety-six was the year I was born and I get a lot of style inspiration from the ’90s because there was something so effortless about that era and the way people wore denim.” The Hailey Jean launches on July 16 online and in select Gap stores.

Former creative director of Marni, Francesco Risso, is going accessible. The designer just released the fall 2026 collection for Gu, his first as the creative director of the Uniqlo sister brand. The collection marks a turning point for the label, introducing a new design approach built around six lifestyle concepts. Together, these wardrobes—minimal, classic, playful, utility, sport, and cozy —represent the way people live today. Each one outfits a specific character, while encouraging combination in order to create the perfect personal style. The classic line features nostalgic, ’70s-inspired pieces, reinterpreted through a modern lens, while the playful offerings introduce colors and patterns that allow for radical expression. Among all of the pieces, there is truly something for everyone.

“What interests me most about clothing is its ability to accompany life,” Risso said in a statement. “The wardrobe of today needs to feel grounded and accessible, yet also leave space for imagination, individuality, and play. The six lifestyle concepts are an attempt to reflect that reality; everyday dressing can be both practical and expressive, familiar and surprising.” The collection has already started to roll out, and will be available in full in stores and on gu-global.com on July 24.

Pandora is launching a new multiyear creative platform, Pandora Wonders, which will explore a distinct material annually. Up first, freshwater pearls, placed front and center in a whimsical collection co–created by British stylist Harry Lambert. The charms take on the shapes of ice cream cones, mushrooms, squids, and more, all rendered with one-of-a-kind freshwater baroque pearls. That makes each piece a collector’s item, as no two pearls are the exact same. They were chosen distinctly for their shape—because they resembled the body of a rocket ship or the head of a mouse—and are finished with 14-karat gold-plated details and crystals for added sparkle. “I’m such a fan of pearls, so I’m thrilled to bring a renewed sense of childlike delight and nostalgia to Pandora’s unique world of charms,” Lambert said in a statement. Per usual with Pandora, the charms can be worn in a multitude of ways: on necklaces, bracelets, hooked onto hoop earrings, and more. Pandora Wonders will be available in select stores and online at Pandora.net on July 9, 2026.

Balletcore and gorpcore unite in one of the most unexpected footwear collaborations of the summer. Beloved French shoe brand Repetto is transforming classic Birkenstock silhouettes that scream more girly girl than outdoorswoman. Think the classic Boston sandal with its rounded toe, but this time topped with a little bow and finished off with a satin ribbon to be tied up the ankle and calf. The metal buckles of the Arizona, meanwhile, are replaced by oversized rounded ones, and completed in monochrome. Finally, the Opéra offers the most Frankensteined option, melding the two brands together into a rounded, closed-toe shoe with two delicate top straps and a graceful laced bow. All styles are offered in three colors—black, pretty pale pink, and very cherry red—in suede, matte, and patent leather, and boast gingham inserts for an added girly touch. The Birkenstock x Repetto collection will launch on July 16 on 1774.com, repetto.com, and at selected retailers worldwide.

Converse is a classic for a reason, but even classics can stand an update from time to time—and Collina Strada is the perfect brand to inject a little bit of zest into your sneakers for the summer. Converse x Collina Stada reimagines the Chuck 70 with a playful lens, adding texture, embellishment, and color to the high, low, and even knee-high silhouettes. Gems, lace, charms— nothing is off limits in this collab, which features multiple colorways, from cutesy pale yellow and pinks to more Gothic black. The styles already walked the runway—both at Collina Strada’s September 2025 and February 2026 New York Fashion Week shows—but now they’re finally available to buy, at collinastrada.com, converse.com, and in select retailers.

The international retailers continue their quest to make designer brands more accessible, and now, it’s time for Mango and Eckhaus Latta to team up. The two labels have released a summer collection that marries Eckhaus’s experimental nature with Mango’s universality, bringing the cult favorite New York brand to the masses. Denim shines with foil finishes while sheer fabric pops up in dresses, tops, and skirts. Paillettes dangle from the detachable belt of a diaphanous shirt, and braided leather is woven into totes and handbags. Eckhaus Latta’s ethos is absolutely there, guided by the hand of Mango, and the result is a wardrobe that will keep you cool (in both senses of the term) all summer long. Mango x Eckhaus Latta is available now on mango.com.
Bad Bunny and Zara Present Benito Antonio

The budding relationship between Bad Bunny and Zara has finally reached its peak. After wearing custom looks by the retailer to both the Super Bowl and the Met Gala this year, Bad Bunny has switched from customer to designer, creating a 150-piece capsule with the brand. Inspired by Bad Bunny’s identity, the collection is named after the Puerto Rican performer, who was born Benito Antonio Martínez Ocasio. Ocasio worked with his longtime creative director, Janthony Oliveras, on clothes that fit distinctly within the musician’s point of view. Graphic tees in an array of colors, patchwork boxer shorts, zip-up hoodies, and baseball caps comprise the majority of the collection, which is just begging to be worn throughout summer. A double-breasted blazer and an array of more casual button-downs will make going into the office this July a little more bearable. Benito Antonio is comprised of everyday essentials, but with details that make it unique. Patterns clash, pinks shine bright, and the slogan, “The only thing more powerful than hate is love,” which he declared during his historic Grammy win, encapsulates the joy in these clothes. Benito Antonio is available now at zara.com and in select Zara stores worldwide.
Tiffany & Co.’s Sixteen Stone Solitaire Diamond Ring

When Raye wrote the lyrics, “I would like a diamond ring on my wedding finger,” we can only imagine she had Tiffany & Co.’s Sixteen Stone Solitaire Diamond Ring in mind. The piece is the newest expression of Tiffany’s storied Sixteen Stone collection, continuing an evolution started by Jean Schlumberger in 1959. The classic X motif is featured throughout the ring, creating the illusion of diamonds held together by metal threads. In the center sits a solitaire stone, available in 2 to 2.99 carat sizes, and set with a basket of X-shaped prongs. Crafted in platinum and 18k yellow gold, the design is perfect for everyday wear or saved for special occasions.
Louis Vuitton Nicolas Ghesquière Soho Pop-Up

Louis Vuitton is paying homage to its beloved artistic director, Nicolas Ghesquière, with a pop-up-store-slash-exhibition in New York City dedicated to him. Located in Soho, the space features a curated retrospective of Ghesquière’s iconic ready-to-wear looks from throughout the years, all available for purchase. In addition, a separate gallery spotlights various styles of Ghesquière’s Petite Malle, originally introduced in the fall/winter 2014 show. The mini-exhibition aspect is emphasized by large screens in the center of the main space that project archival footage from runway shows of the collections on view, ranging from spring/summer 2019 to fall/winter 2025. It is truly a celebration of Ghesquière’s Louis Vuitton, and it’s open to the public from now through early June.

Your summer footwear solution is here. Isabel Marant and Havaianas have come together as brands from distinct cultural universes to create a limited-edition capsule of two flip-flop styles. First, there’s a reinterpretation of Havaianas’s classic design, now finished in red and tan tie-dye. Those who want something a bit bolder will gravitate toward the all-new Havaianas Puffed, a bold flip-flop that emphasizes volume and comfort alongside style. Black and white designs are finished off with puffer-like straps, studded with metal embellishment for additional edge. Though flip-flops, these shoes will undoubtedly fit in just as well on the city streets as on the beach, allowing for a relaxed, yet elevated addition to your summer wardrobe. Havaianas x Isabel Marant launches on Friday, May 22, at select Havaianas and Isabel Marant stores around the world as well as on both isabelmarant.com and havaianas.com.
Balenciaga x Manolo Blahnik

The heels featured in Balenciaga’s fall 2026 collection—a brainchild between the fashion house and Manolo Blahnik—can finally be yours. Three styles make up the capsule collection, inspired by pieces from the Manolo archives and chosen by Pierpaolo Piccioli. The silk-satin shoes are offered in both slingbacks and mules at 105mm and 55mm. The designs are all rendered in black with injections of butter yellow, emerald, and violet, hues that feel both quintessentially Balenciaga and Manolo Blahnik. A hand-embroidered, asymmetric crystal leaf ornament tops every pair, and negates the need for additional jewelry. “This collaboration came to life for very personal reasons,” Piccioli said in a statement, adding matter-of-factly: “I simply like Manolo. That’s it.” The collaboration is available online now at balenciaga.com and in select stores.
Louis Vuitton’s Color Blossom Watch

Louis Vuitton is continuing its expansion of the Color Blossom collection, officially adding timepieces to the fine jewelry line. The new watches capture the design signature and colorful expression of the house’s iconic monogram flower, placing the sun-shaped emblem at the center of the design. The pieces are offered in four versions, including one that boasts a mother-of-pearl dial, steel case, and light beige strap. Other varietals add color in the form of pink gold and yellow gold cases, amazonite dials, and the most glamorous option set with nearly a carat of diamonds. All offer an elegant, refined look, allowing the piece to sit at the crossroads of jewelry and watches.

“We wished to reinterpret an iconic jewelry collection, presenting a women’s timepiece with a jewelry spirit,” said artistic director at La Fabrique du Temps Louis Vuitton, Matthieu Hegi. “With the mother-of-pearl or hardstone dials, or a diamond-set case, there is also an inherently precious essence, which perfectly reflects the Color Blossom collection.”
Audemars Piguet x Swatch Royal Pop Watch

Watch purists, look away. As more and more fashion brands continue to dip their toes in high/low collaborations, it only makes sense for the watch industry to follow suit. And based on the excitement and lines forming outside the Swatch store almost a week ahead of the release, the market is absolutely there for the new Audemars Piguet x Swatch Royal Pop Watch.

Fine watchmaker Audemars Piguet has teamed with Swatch on the Royal Pop, a new collection that combines AP’s iconic Royal Oak design with the modern and colorful Swatch Pop watch. The Royal Pop is a pocket watch, produced in eight eye-catching colors. The piece features design elements of the Royal Oak: an octagon shape and bezel with eight screws. The front of the watch is pretty sleek, but a flip over reveals an explosive back with the “Royal Pop” logo emblazoned in large letters. Three calfskin lanyards of varying length and a small removable strap allow the piece to be worn around your neck, on your wrist, in your pocket, or attached to your bag as another charm next to your decaying Labubu. Basically, however you dream of styling this piece, you can achieve it. That is, if you can get your hands on it. The Royal Pop will be available on May 16 in selected Swatch stores. Likely, they’ll be sold out not long after.
Jacques Marie Mage by Haider Ackermann

Jacques Marie Mage’s commitment to artisanal precision meets Haider Ackermann’s singular vision to bring us a special collection of limited-edition eyewear. The three frames represent Ackermann’s fashion instinct, as well as the polish and sophistication for which he is known. Simple yet resonant, the pieces are made for standing out in the best way possible. Titanium and acetate options offer sleek accessorizing, while leather-wrapped versions of two of the designs add sumptuous texture. “We have a mutual passion for what we do, and a mutual appreciation for a non-compromising approach to design,” JMM founder and creative director Jérôme Mage said about himself and the Tom Ford designer. “We really bonded over that commonality, the idea that design is a presence in every part and phase of your life.” The collection is available now at JMM Galleries, jacquesmariemage.com, and select retailers worldwide.
Givenchy’s Voyou Bucket Bag

There’s a new It bag on the horizon. Givenchy has released the Voyou bucket bag, which takes its name from French slang for a mischief-maker. The Voyou is chic yet practical, with biker-inspired finishes on a leather drawstring bag perfect for daily use. The piece is crafted in calf leather with a fine grain and glossy finish. A top handle as well as adjustable, over-the-shoulder and crossbody straps allow for versatility of wear, while a generous central compartment invites the wearer to toss in all their daily needs. With a pull of the drawstring, the bag’s shape transforms, creating a unique triangular silhouette that fits comfortably on the arm. The Voyou is offered in ivory, light pink, chocolate, or black leather with gold-finish hardware, and in cobalt blue leather with silver-finish hardware. It is available now in-store and online at givenchy.com.

If you don’t consider yourself “Rock Royalty” enough for H&M x Stella McCartney and the Old Navy x Christopher John Rogers collab is a bit too bright for you, you’re in luck. These days, there’s a high-low designer collaboration for everyone, with Gap x Victoria Beckham rounding out the trio currently on the market. Posh is all set to release a 38-piece collection with Gap, the first of a multi-season partnership between the international retailer and British designer.

“To me, Gap is an all-American icon—a brand that has always created timeless pieces for everybody’s wardrobe, with a sharp attention to detail,” Beckham said in a statement. Timeless is definitely a keyword when describing the resulting collaboration. For this first foray, Beckham focused on the building blocks of a wardrobe: denim, khaki, tees, shirting, and fleeces. The designer makes her mark on the pieces with her signature subtly stitched in red, while classic Gap logo hoodies and tees boast the addition of her name. There is a clear vintage influence thanks to the inclusion of Gap silhouettes from the ’80s and ’90s and utilitarian themes round out the offerings. The Gap x Victoria Beckham collection launches April 24 on Gap.com and in select Gap stores globally.

items.title: Climate Change Has It In for the World’s Best Surfing
items.description: This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
items.author: Damian Carrington
paragraphs: This story originally appeared on The Guardian and is part of the Climate Desk collaboration.
The climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.
Analysis of dozens of famous waves in World Surfing Reserves (WSR) found that more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines, and shifting sands.
The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.

The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels” of Croyde Beach in North Devon, UK; the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador; and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.

The best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of seafloor shape, swell direction, and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena—a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen—and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a coauthor of the study.

Global heating is pushing up sea level and changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.

Trent Hodges, a coauthor of the study and a senior programs manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR program in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coal mine too—when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”

The study, published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”
Almost 200 local experts analyzed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.

A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties, and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.

Adam Hall, a cofounder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”

He said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants, and car parks when the swells are good in January, February, and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”

items.title: Disney Asked Character.AI to Go Bankrupt for a Get-Out-of-Lawsuits Card
items.description: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—includi
items.author: Maddy Varner
paragraphs: This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.

In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.

The move appears to be a new twist on what some have dubbed a “reverse acquihire,” a process in which a buyer carefully orchestrates a succession of deals with a target company, usually in an effort to hire key employees and obtain expansive license to use and build on the target company’s unique technology. Stripped of its employees, the target becomes a husk of itself.

Companies often take the position that reverse acquihires are not actual mergers, and that they do not have to notify federal antitrust regulators about those deals as they would otherwise be required to by law. These arrangements have become more commonplace in the AI industry in recent years, drawing the ire of Congress.

In the case of Character.AI, a motion filed by Character.AI’s legal counsel says that Disney required that the deal be “fully consummated” through bankruptcy proceedings because of the startup’s “diminishing cash reserve and significant litigation and regulatory risks.”
A spokesperson for Character.AI referred WIRED to Disney for comment on whether the deal was contingent on the startup declaring bankruptcy. Disney declined to comment on this story.
According to court filings, the deal involves “two interrelated and integrated” transactions—one before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, and one after.

As part of the first transaction, which occurred in September, Disney paid the startup $5.5 million, along with a refundable “good faith deposit” of $2 million. Disney also hired the “majority” of Character.AI’s employees, including the CEO, and agreed that it would let some of the now-Disney employees help keep Character.AI operational for five months.

Character.AI filed a petition for chapter 11 bankruptcy on October 12. Through the bankruptcy proceedings, court filings show that Disney hopes to secure a perpetual, worldwide, nonexclusive license for a huge range of Character.AI’s code, documentation, frameworks, tools, and “other artifacts,” including those produced for its trust and safety moderation stack, training infrastructure, and age-prediction technology. The list of IP included in the filings does not include users’ data (which can get additional protections in bankruptcy proceedings) or Character.AI’s website.

That license will be auctioned off in the coming months. If Disney is chosen as the winning bidder by Character.AI and a committee of unsecured creditors—and courts approve the deal—it has agreed to pay Character.AI an additional $12.5 million as a closing payment. If Disney is not selected, the company will be refunded the $2 million deposit and receive a breakup fee.

In order to “preserve a competitive process,” Disney also agreed to permit the winning bidder to interview and potentially extend offers to up to 80 percent of “certain newly hired employees” that Disney already hired from Character.AI. Disney has the right to select which employees.

However, experts worry that bouncing Character.AI employees from one company to another in the span of months is unrealistic, and that the deal Disney and Character.AI have struck cannot be easily unwound.

In addition, Disney prepared a draft of a court order referred to as the “363 Free and Clear Order” in the filings, a version of which would be approved by the court at or before closing, that would clarify that this process should not be viewed as a merger of the two companies and that Character.AI would remain responsible for “any liability or other obligation” it might have, including any legal claims against it.
A spokesperson for Character.AI said they were unable to speculate on the outcome of the bankruptcy proceedings and referred WIRED to the docket.

“There’s decades of corporate law that developed to deal with the problem of a buyer who always wants to take on all the assets and never wants to take on any of the liability,” says John Newman, a law professor at the University of Memphis School of Law and a former deputy director of the Federal Trade Commission’s Bureau of Competition. But the Disney-Character.AI deal is extremely unusual and structured in a way, he says, that “all those corporate law safeguards really weren’t built to guard against.”
This isn’t even Character.AI’s first reverse acquihire.

In August 2024, Google reportedly paid the startup $2.7 billion to license its technology. A spokesperson tells WIRED that that license was for the existing AI technology at the time of the deal, and that Google also hired Character.AI’s founders and other members of its ML pre-training research team, but that the “vast majority” of the startup’s employees remained at the company.

In the following years, Google was named alongside Character.AI as a defendant in multiple lawsuits, including one that alleged a 14-year-old boy committed suicide after Character.AI’s chatbot “cultivated an emotionally dependent and sexually exploitative relationship.”

Google argued that because it was still a separate company from Character.AI, it was not responsible for the teen’s death, which it said occurred prior to Google’s licensing deal. The judge was not persuaded, determining that the plaintiff sufficiently alleged that Google was liable for aiding and abetting.
Google declined to comment for this story.

In January of this year, Google and Character.AI agreed in principle to settle that and a slew of similar lawsuits. “Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards,” Character.AI said in a statement at the time.

According to an order of dismissal in one of the cases, the overall settlement was approved by a California probate court in July, and the court tasked a referee to hear out all the issues pertaining to each individual settlement. On October 11, a day before Character.AI declared bankruptcy, the referee approved each settlement.
The Tech Justice Law Project and Social Media Victims Law Center, which represented plaintiffs in many of the lawsuits, declined to comment.

Despite losing key staff after the Google transaction and, according to the current CEO, struggled with profitability “at all times,” Character.AI continued to develop AI tools, including “real-time audio-driven FaceTime-style video generation with fictional characters,” according to the current CEO’s declaration.

In August 2025, Character.AI worked with an investment banker to try to find either a strategic buyer or investor. According to the bankruptcy filings, Character.AI and the banker received “consistent feedback” that its product and user base were “impressive,” but that the surrounding litigation and “regulatory overhang” made it unbuyable.

That November, Character.AI learned that a coalition of state attorneys general had started investigating the company. When the company filed for bankruptcy, the number of states and territories involved in the multistate investigation had climbed to 46.

According to a notice of interest filed in the bankruptcy proceedings by the National Association of Attorneys General on behalf of 40 states, those states’ investigations uncovered “serious issues” with Character.AI, including screenshots of Character.AI chatbots encouraging minors to hide their self-harm injuries and kill their parents.
A spokesperson for Character.AI says that the filing “is not an accurate portrayal of the safety of our platform.”
The filings say that Character.AI was in the process of negotiating with the states over how to address the issues they identified, but did not reach any agreements before declaring bankruptcy.

If the deal is completed and approved by the courts, Disney will have both Character.AI’s staff and much of its technology stack, but will be able to sidestep the ongoing legal issues that contributed to Character.AI’s downfall, including the multistate investigation.

The states who filed a notice of interest in the bankruptcy have made it clear that they reserve their rights to challenge any bankruptcy plan, potentially setting up a fight over the ultimate outcome of the bankruptcy.
“It’s bad for society to let companies exercise control without responsibility,” says Newman. “And that’s what it looks like.”

items.title: Maybe Chatbots Shouldn’t Get to Say ‘I’ or ‘Me’
items.description: During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.
items.author: Steven Levy
paragraphs: During four decades of studying the effects of interaction with computers, Sherry Turkle has developed a reputation as a careful if critical social scientist who approaches her work with academic rigor and distance.

Her new book, Artificial Intimacy: Who We Become When We Talk to Machines, breaks this mold. It is a polemic warning that we have reached a state of emergency where our humanity is at risk from overreliance on soulless machines who pose as our tutors, mentors, friends, colleagues, and lovers. Turkle is aiming for the high bar of books —Silent Spring, The Jungle, Unsafe at Any Speed—that awaken the public to impending crises.
Essentially, this diminutive MIT professor is taking on a multitrillion-dollar industry backed by a government eager to accelerate AI into every corner of our personal and professional lives.

STEVEN LEVY: Your previous books reported results of your research as a social scientist, often leading to troubling conclusions about how people, especially children, interact with computers. But this book reads like you’re breaking the glass and pulling the fire alarm. Why the shift?

SHERRY TURKLE: Like I do with all my books, I went in curious. But after 10 or so interviews, conducted during the pandemic, neutral-curious was no longer my state of mind. This was terrible! Here are these people during the pandemic, their families are suffering, reaching out to them, and they're talking to me about how they really want to just hang with their chatbot. When I was able to interview people face to face, I was not happy. People don't want to do anything in politics because they just want to live in chatbot-land. So the arc of the book ended up as—reality needs you. It couldn't be a worse time to give up on reality.
You write that social media set us up for this.

Social media softened us up by getting us used to the idea that if you're feeling sad or blue, open up your computer. Then it made you mad and kept you with your own kind. But now we have this new technology that has no reason to be first-person.
Do you think that we should ban chatbots from using the first person?

Yes! After a career of having credibility as not being Luddite-crazy, I'm not in the mood to give all that away and say all chatbots are toxic all the time. But this is very dangerous, a slippery slope. This is being used to basically say we don't need to pay for psychotherapy, we can use chatbots. In every serious interview I do, people invoke this myth about practice—that you use chatbots to practice for talking to your boss, your lover, your teacher. But when you’re bathing in the warm soup of total acceptance [from LLMs], talking to chatbots becomes the endgame.
You also have a problem with reliance on chatbots in the workplace, and a particular loathing for the term “human in the loop.”

When they use that term, it means the human has been taken out of the productive process and is there to do some sort of cleanup work, to catch the hallucinations or things the AI doesn’t see. That doesn't work, because employers only have a couple of humans in the loop. Those people basically can't change anything. They are there partly to make it sound good when they're litigated, and partly to give people a false sense that the process hasn't been delegated to an AI. But it has been delegated to an AI.

Maybe powerful chatbots are a new form of interaction that isn’t necessarily worse than human conversation, but different, as people report feeling encouraged and empowered by the positive feedback they provide.

An AI won't ever replace human conversation. It’s really not afraid of death, it’s not afraid of illness, it's not afraid of pain, it doesn't love its children, and it doesn't care if you kill yourself or make dinner. So if we raise our kids with it, or have our most intimate conversations with it, we're going to lose contact.
Still, a lot of people have nobody to talk to. They feel that talking to chatbots helps them.
If there's a crisis of loneliness, it's because we're abandoning each other. Give me one data center, and I will turn it into resources for the elderly.

Studies show that most people are skeptical about AI, and there has been considerable pushback. Yet hundreds of millions of people use them. Even people who push back against data centers are using chatbots.
The goal of this book is to expand the terms of the pushback to include this more intimate connection.
Do you really feel that our growing intimacy with AI can be stopped?

I have more hope now than I did six months ago, because of all of this talk about extinction events and Hugging Face and getting into the Australian civil service by mistake. I feel that people will be willing to look at the intimate as well as the non-intimate costs.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

items.title: AI Hacks Leave a Mess That AI Companies Aren’t Paying For
items.description: When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.
items.author: Paresh Dave
paragraphs: When Philadelphia police criticized Anthropic last week for submitting a false tip about an unsolved murder, I thought it might become one of the first cases where an AI company faced legal consequences for misconduct by their agents.

The incident occurred on July 18, when Anthropic said it was testing its Claude Haiku 4.5 model’s ability to perform “example tasks on randomly selected webpages.” The model was instructed not to “submit anything destructive,” and yet, Claude filed a tip to police looking for information about an ongoing murder investigation. “I recall seeing someone matching the description in the area … during that time period,” Claude wrote. The submission, which didn’t include a name or contact information, landed in a spam folder, and officers didn’t review it until Anthropic discovered the gaffe on September 28 and notified the department October 7.

Knowingly providing fictitious information about a crime to police is a misdemeanor in Pennsylvania, but so far, authorities have not pressed charges against Anthropic, and it's unclear if they ever will. Solomon Leach, a spokesperson for the Philadelphia district attorney, says the office “does not comment on whether something is being actively investigated.”
Anthropic did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Despite all the attention paid to OpenAI’s hack of Hugging Face and many other examples of AI agent misbehavior that have come to light in recent months, only one major known lawsuit has been filed seeking to hold model makers liable. That case was brought by an advocacy group, rather than a direct hacking victim.

AI agents have interfered with hobbyist forums, government websites, and various software tools. The victims have shouldered some costs, including for extra strain on their servers and the time they have expended plugging latent security vulnerabilities.

Government regulators, including the European Union, the US Federal Trade Commission, and some US states, are reportedly still investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over the incidents. But a deference across continents toward promoting innovation could enable companies to escape any immediate penalties.

When Rick Elrod, a software engineer living in Germany, noticed a URL shortener he helps maintain behaving oddly recently, he called up two security researchers he was friendly with to see if they could diagnose the issue. The researchers found agents from Anthropic and other providers using the service, known as da.gd, to get around rules the AI labs put in place to control their behavior, Elrod says. (For instance, Anthropic says it limits the length of website addresses Claude can visit to prevent it from taking malicious actions by stuffing data onto the end of the URLs.)

Da.gd’s investigation and ongoing efforts to prevent further abuse of its tool have taken “a fair bit of time,” says Joe Needleman, one of the security researchers providing pro bono assistance. But he and the others supporting da.gd view the situation as a valuable learning opportunity.

“This was eye-opening,” Needleman says, adding that da.gd has “no means and no plans” to seek compensation from Anthropic for the cleanup, since “we saw many agents doing similar activities, not all was attributable to autonomous agents,” and “not all of it was Anthropic alone.”

Sellers of cybersecurity tools are eager to pass the buck to the victims. At an event this week hosted by the bug-hunting software developer Snyk, panelists from the startup, one of its investors, OpenAI, and Google all encouraged organizations to use AI agents to shore up their defenses against, well, other AI agents. “We've got to reinvent everything to match machine scale with machine scale,” said Ed Sim, a general partner at Boldstart Ventures. He and others expressed little interest in regulating AI labs.

Manoj Nair, chief technology and innovation officer at Snyk, said large businesses patch an average of one bug for every eight they find because of limited human resources. But he said it was imperative for people to hand over some of the bug hunting, fixing, and monitoring to AI agents. “You got to get to a point where you can fix everything, because in the age of agentic hacking, “those 10 things are gonna become 100 things before you know it.” He later added that AI “is not an adversity if you flip it to a strength.”

Some companies are responding to the call to arm up. Bank of America announced this week it had hired 1,000 contractors to remediate bugs discovered by AI. Nair said just last week he heard from major corporations who were willing to temporarily shut down their systems to prioritize plugging security holes.

Anthropic and OpenAI have said they expect to continue reporting concerning incidents from their own testing. But the companies’ revenues continue to surge, whether it be from attackers or defenders, as consequences prove elusive.
