items.title: How ‘Final Fantasy VII Revelation’ Strikes the Balance Between Old and New
items.description: If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influ
items.author: Matt Kamen
paragraphs: If you're on the brink of completing one of the most ambitious projects in video game history, you're probably stressed. If said project is the decade-spanning Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, a ground-up rebuild and drastic expansion of one of the most influential games of the last 30 years, you’d probably be even more anxious.

Naoki Hamaguchi doesn’t seem stressed, though. When I ask the Square Enix studio head and game director how he’s feeling as the release of Final Fantasy VII Revelation draws near, capping a series he’s worked on for over a decade, the only reply is a wry “I was just so focused, it really felt like it passed in a flash.”

Hamaguchi’s calm demeanor is all the more surprising given the weight of expectation surrounding the project. The original Final Fantasy VII, released on Sony's PlayStation in 1997, was a pop-cultural phenomenon—not the Japanese-RPG series’ first Western release, but undeniably its breakthrough title; one that arrived right as gaming was growing out of its kids-only niche and into a mainstream medium.

It’s still regarded as one of the best Final Fantasy entries, and its tale of reluctant hero Cloud Strife and his scrappy band of eco-warrior friends battling an all-powerful corporation destroying the planet is more relevant than ever.

A remake has been brewing since the PlayStation 2 era, and even teased with a cinematic tech demo alongside the PS3 reveal. Yet when Final Fantasy VII Remake finally arrived in 2020, toward the end of the PS4’s lifespan, it came with a twist—this wasn’t the same game with modern visuals and mechanics, but rather a glimpse of an alternate reality, one where events could potentially play out differently.

The idea was expanded on in 2024’s second chapter, Final Fantasy VII Rebirth, which saw characters hopping between timelines—but Hamaguchi is keen not to label it his attempt at a Marvel Cinematic Universe–style Final Fantasy VII multiverse.

“When we started approaching these things, seven years or more ago, I don't believe there were so many other pieces of media tackling those same themes at the time,” Hamaguchi laughs. “We don't really tend to use the word ‘multiverse’—we talk about [the story being] ‘multilayered.’ Actually, the word that comes up most often is ‘reunion.’”

That word may resonate with fans of the original, where test subjects experimented on using cells from an alien named Jenova, including Sephiroth, were drawn to each other (and that’s the shortest possible explanation).

Does that hint at where Revelation’s increasingly complex, layered narrative may be heading, with cosmic variations on Final Fantasy VII’s events all merging? Hamaguchi won’t be drawn, but offers that developer Square Enix is “looking at it from the perspective of these layers coming back together and reuniting—quite a unique perspective within the lore that we have.”

Other lore changes include the vastly expanded three-act structure of the Remake trilogy, which allows—or sometimes necessitates—reshuffling characters, locations, and events, placing many out of sequence from the original.

One of the biggest examples is the nation of Wutai, home of Yuffie, a teenage ninja who becomes an ally to Cloud. In the original game, she was an optional recruitable character, and Wutai was two huts on the world map, with only a few screens worth of houses and temples to explore when players entered it. In Revelation, it’s vast. This Wutai is a thriving city with people to talk to and secrets to uncover; you’ll even need to use Chocobos (Final Fantasy’s signature yellow bird mounts) to explore. It’s also somewhere players can actually believe is caught in a war with Midgar, the urban megalopolis where Remake took place. A lot more is going on here than there was back in 1997.

Some may think that holding Wutai (and Rocket Town, another key location) back for the third Remake entry was a way to pad out the equivalent of the original version’s third disc, which mainly left players to mop up side quests and chase down some optional boss battles before the finale. However, Hamaguchi says the opposite was true—even after two 100-plus hour previous games, he was worried about how much was still left to fit into Revelation.

“I did see people online talking about things after Rebirth, saying, ‘Are you going to have enough to fill up another game? What's gonna happen?’” he says. “I was sat there like, ‘No, this is the opposite problem!’ I'm looking at everything we've still got to put in, and how are we going to get it in there? We actually had to be quite careful with what we put in there to avoid having too much content.”

Revelation may still feel crammed, though. It brings in the final two playable characters from the original game, aeronaut Cid Highwind and were-beast gunman Vincent Valentine, expanding party options and battle combos. It also adds its own twist on the memorable Emerald, Ruby, and Ultima Weapon super-boss battles—incredibly challenging fights against literally god-tier foes, often with strict constraints to test players’ skills.

Along with the sizable new areas, the world is far more open, with returning locations from the prior two games promising extra story avenues and battles to pursue when revisited. Players can soar the skies in Cid’s airship, the Highwind (points for personal branding), before parachuting back down to explore further. “I'm not sure if there's anything other than Revelation that is really an open world on a truly ‘world’ scale, on a planetary scale,” Hamaguchi boasts.

On top of that, Hamaguchi has previously said it may take multiple playthroughs to see everything in the game. That might sound like a daunting time sink to some, but Hamaguchi isn’t fazed. “Personally, I don't have any reservations," he says. "I do understand that there were some people who said there's too much content in Rebirth, but I think essentially that boils down to preference.” Variety matters more than volume, though, and Hamaguchi says the scale has expanded with diverse gameplay.

There are a few olive branches for players who like their games big but not all-consuming, though. That multiple-playthrough requirement will take the form of a chapter select, so you can revisit specific scenes and see events from different perspectives. Rebirth's notoriously difficult and often repetitive trophy requirements are also being toned down, but Hamaguchi says “that's not to say that the achievements are easy—not just anyone is going to be able to get all of them.”

If there’s one thing Hamaguchi actively does want to change with Final Fantasy VII Revelation, it’s players’ perspectives on what Final Fantasy fundamentally is. Even though the series has evolved over the years—to the point where 2023’s Final Fantasy XVI was more of an action game than an RPG—outsiders often still see it as staid and formulaic.

“I think that a lot of people have the image or preconception about the Final Fantasy series, that it tends to be quite story-focused,” Hamaguchi says. “That is, of course, fantastic, but I also wanted to really showcase the gameplay and to show that Final Fantasy as a franchise, as a series, could stand alongside other open-world titles that are really celebrated for their gameplay, and I thought that would bring in more fans.”

“Showcase” seems right—although my playtest of Revelation barely scratched the surface, there’s clearly a panoply of stuff to do at every turn, with almost every activity offering a fresh way to engage with the world. Yet for long-term fans, warm nostalgia weaves through, as with the new “Function Integrated Tactical Suitwear” system. This fashion-focused (clock the acronym) tweak to the combat system lets players dress the cast as RPG character classes from the pre-FF7 games—think Knights, White Mages, Summoners, and sundry other Final Fantasy figures—allowing for extraordinary customization over who you bring into battle and how they function. It feels retro but modern, and just one way Revelation writes a love letter to the whole series.

A balance of old and new feels like the perfect capstone for a project like the Remake trilogy, celebrating the industry-shaking original Final Fantasy VII while shaping the franchise's future. More importantly, it’s already attracting the people who will help build it.

“It's been over 10 years since the Remake announcement now, and I’m starting to come across people who are saying ‘Final Fantasy 7 Remake inspired me to get into the games industry,’” Hamaguchi says. “They're coming up now, and they're saying, ‘I want to make Final Fantasy, I have these ideas.’ I think that's wonderful. Nothing could make me happier, and I'll just keep trying my best on the cutting edge to push things forward.”

items.title: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason
items.description: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought
items.author: Thore Graepel
paragraphs: On an afternoon in Seoul in March 2016, I watched a program I helped build put a stone on the fifth line of a Go board in what looked like a gift to its human opponent. Move 37 in game two of the five-game match looked so absurd that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch.

It wasn’t. AlphaGo won the game, ultimately triumphing 4-1 over Lee Sedol, one of the greatest professional Go players of all time. “I thought AlphaGo was based on probability calculation and that it was merely a machine,” Lee said afterwards. “But when I saw this move, I changed my mind. Surely, AlphaGo is creative.”

When Deep Blue defeated then reigning world chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997, it did so by looking six to eight moves ahead per player and evaluating 200 million chess positions per second, using rules hard-coded by humans. Go is a vastly more complex game. A stone’s worth depends on how distant groups and territory unfold over dozens of moves. Computing even a fraction of the possible outcomes would take a supercomputer billions of years. To win, AlphaGo had to sense who was ahead at a glance and even invent moves no human had thought to play.

That is why many accounts of AlphaGo’s match against Lee portray move 37 as a flash of pure machine intuition. But that is a misunderstanding. It was actually AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. If we want future AI systems to produce trustworthy results and really novel insights in fields like science and medicine, we need to equip them with genuine reasoning capabilities of this kind.

AlphaGo is made up of two systems. The first, its policy network, was trained to guess what move a strong human would play. This “intuitive” part regarded move 37 as nothing special—a play that had a roughly one in 10,000 chance of being made by an expert human player. What made AlphaGo choose it was the program’s search machinery, which looked beyond immediate plausibility and weighed the future consequences of proposed moves. It explicitly constructed and searched a game tree with thousands of branches, each representing a different possible future.

A well-known theory in the behavioral sciences, popularized by Daniel Kahneman, distinguishes between two modes of human thought: System 1 is fast, gut-level, effortless; system 2, slow, step-by-step, and deliberative. AlphaGo offered a striking machine analogue of that split. Its networks supplied the hunches—this move looks promising, this position looks won—and its search supplied the deliberation, testing those hunches against the moves and countermoves that would follow. As in human cognition, neither half works alone. Intuition alone would never have opted for move 37, and brute-force search would have struggled to sieve through all the many possible moves.

This is strikingly different from the way today’s AI models work. A large language model picks the next token, over and over. That amounts to system 1 in action—fast, associative, and surprisingly good pattern completion across almost every subject people write about.

Not long after ChatGPT debuted, the field realized that language fluency alone falls short of true usefulness. The apparent solution was to make models that deliberate: Instead of answering immediately, they can now generate intermediate steps that decompose a problem, carry forward partial results, and influence subsequent reasoning—a process known as chain of thought.

The gains have proved real, above all in mathematics and coding. But unlike AlphaGo’s search, this does not introduce a genuinely separate reasoning mechanism: The intermediate reasoning is still produced by the same next-token prediction process, iterated for longer before the model commits to an answer.

Three shortcomings prevent what chatbots do from qualifying as reasoning (in a way that a scientist might recognize). First, these models typically maintain no explicit, persistent, and inspectable epistemic state. There is no open ledger that lays out the hypotheses a model is considering, the confidence it has in various explanations, the evidence it’s weighing, and the unresolved questions it’s holding onto—all things that should be systematically revised as new information arrives.

Second, they lack a clean separation between what the system knows and how it manipulates that knowledge. Knowledge and reasoning are inextricably interwoven in the weights of the neural network—there is no independent, explicitly represented set of beliefs. Third, while the chains of thought chatbots produce look like deliberation, research has demonstrated that the bots often concoct them after the fact, reaching an answer by one route but reporting another.

This is a problem because in the high-stakes applications we all care about, such as medicine, engineering, and scientific research, it matters not only what a system concludes but also how it arrives at its conclusion. When mistakes happen—for example, in medical diagnosis and treatment—we need to be able to pinpoint what went wrong: Was the system’s reasoning at fault, did it draw on invalid evidence, or did it make incorrect assumptions?

This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning—one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture. AlphaGo maintains a record of what it knows about a given position: the game tree. This data structure contains all the variations, the possible futures, that AlphaGo has considered, each move and position being annotated with judgments made by its neural networks. As its reasoning progresses, AlphaGo updates the game tree and eventually synthesizes the information in it to decide which move to make.

Similarly, for general reasoning a system should maintain an epistemic state that represents what the system holds as settled, what it doubts, what it has ruled out, which questions stay open. Reasoning can then be understood as a sequence of moves that change the epistemic state to advance knowledge and reduce uncertainty: deducing consequences, breaking problems into parts, and—crucially—deciding what question to ask, calculation to perform, or experiment to run next.

Of course, open-world reasoning is harder than playing a board game such as Go or chess. In the real world the current state of affairs is only partially known, the set of available actions is large and variable, and the consequences of actions are stochastic or unknown.

But recent advances in LLMs and other neural models now give us the capability to take on such general reasoning problems. For example, LLMs can suggest ways of tackling a problem on the basis of what is known and what resources are available. They can interact with tools via APIs or code and help assess whether a claim is supported by available evidence.

Most important, to keep the system honest, an independent part of the system must evaluate each move by how much it actually resolves uncertainty, updating beliefs only when the change is backed by evidence. Once these rules are enforced, the model can accumulate certified knowledge and improve its reasoning policy by learning from past reasoning experiences. You can think of such a system as the scientific method on steroids, with the purpose of producing knowledge that can withstand scrutiny.

I do not think we reach trustworthy machine intelligence by making system 1 bigger. Scale sharpens intuition, but it does not make intuition more deliberative. Move 37 mattered because a machine held a position, weighed the possible futures, and chose the move its artificial instincts would likely have rejected.

Society needs such creative moves in drug discovery, materials, climate, diagnosis—fields where the board looks nothing like a Go board and nobody hands us the rules. We will get such insights only from systems that reason—systems whose conclusions arise from an auditable sequence of evidence, inference, and belief revision rather than from a convincing story told after the fact.
Thore Graepel is chair of machine learning at University College London. He was a core member of the AlphaGo team at DeepMind and works to ensure that AI benefits human flourishing.

items.title: 2026 Climate Tech Companies to Watch
items.description: Each year, the MIT Technology Review team puts together a list of some of the most promising climate tech companies in the world. Whether early-stage startup or multinational corporation, the businesses we’ve chosen are working on technologies to help us addre
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: Each year, the MIT Technology Review team puts together a list of some of the most promising climate tech companies in the world. Whether early-stage startup or multinational corporation, the businesses we’ve chosen are working on technologies to help us address climate change or adapt to our warming world.
There’s an urgent need for these innovators: We must begin to drastically reduce emissions to avoid the deadliest impacts of climate change, while also contending with its harmful effects.

We hope that this list highlights the progress the world is making to tackle the climate crisis, as well as the breadth of solutions required. From energy storage powered by carbon dioxide to cleaner ways to make cement and refine critical minerals, these companies are building technologies to address the acute challenges we face.
This is the fourth annual edition of this list. Learn more about how we chose the 2026 slate.
Sign up for our weekly newsletter to understand the innovations, policies, and trends shaping climate tech today.

items.title: Here’s how our climate team picked 10 promising companies to watch
items.description: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.
items.author: Casey Crownhart
paragraphs: As the team at MIT Technology Review set out to choose companies for this year’s edition of our annual list of Climate Tech Companies to Watch, the challenge felt more daunting than any year since we started compiling the list in 2023.

This year is shaping up to be one of the hottest ever recorded. The world must begin to reduce greenhouse-gas emissions to address the climate crisis, which is already affecting communities around the globe. Wildfires, floods, and other climate-fueled disasters are killing thousands and costing billions of dollars. At the same time, political shifts and international conflict have stalled progress, particularly in the US.

Technology alone can’t solve climate change. But we believe innovations can help us make real changes and improve lives around the world as we try to address one of the most pressing challenges of our time.

In this project, we look for companies developing technologies that can help us face the climate crisis. Some are driving down the greenhouse-gas emissions fueling climate change; others are working to reduce the dangers that communities face from extreme heat, drought, or other shifts brought on by a warming planet. We focus on companies that have established a track record, whether through research findings, capital raised, or deployments.

When we set out to build our list, we start by soliciting nominations from our team of reporters and editors. We ask experts for suggestions and reach out to academics, researchers, investors, and analysts. Once we have a pool of nominees, we then consider each one, digging through literature, reports, and patents to vet both the technology and the business.

We judge each company not only on its own merits, but also on how it might fit into our list overall. We want the final slate of companies to represent a range of industries and include firms based around the globe that are at different stages of development. We also aim to strike a balance between highlighting companies previously included and introducing new names. Finally, we consider some of the most important trends and events of the year and look for nominees that reflect those developments.

The dismembering of US federal regulations and cuts to financial government incentives for innovation means that the country is no longer a leader in climate tech. Like last year, the 2026 list is largely composed of companies that are based outside the US. China is an obvious hotspot for technological innovation across energy and climate. This year’s list includes two Chinese companies: WeLion is building semi-solid-state batteries for electric vehicles, and Envision Energy is installing huge amounts of wind power and energy storage in China and around the world.
Several sectors stood out this year as being of particular importance. One of the biggest stories of the year is the rising demand for electricity, driven in part by AI data centers.

Energy storage is a key piece of that puzzle because it can smooth out variations in the electricity supply as grids incorporate more renewable power. We’ve included several energy storage companies on this year’s list. Energy Dome is building long-duration energy storage systems on the grid that rely on compressed carbon dioxide. Moment Energy is a Canadian company working to repurpose EV batteries for grid-scale storage. And Form Energy, which we also included in the 2024 edition of this list, is producing iron-based batteries that can store energy for multiple days.

A wide range of technologies is represented here: everything from mobile flood barriers to next-generation nuclear reactors. Some of the awardees might be familiar from our past coverage; others are just emerging and may be less well known.

We believe we’ve put together a list filled with businesses that are rising to the challenge of this moment. Political will has weakened even as the damages wrought by climate change continue to mount. By helping us make progress on tackling the climate crisis in such difficult times, these companies point to a better way forward.

items.title: Fervo Energy and its plan to streamline geothermal power
items.description: Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power far beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company is looking to work with large data center operators like Google to develop its enhanced geothermal power plants across the US,
items.author: Eshan Raul
paragraphs: Fervo Energy wants to expand geothermal power far beyond the handful of places where it has traditionally been practical. The company is looking to work with large data center operators like Google to develop its enhanced geothermal power plants across the US, and drive down costs in the process to compete with fossil fuels.

Fervo Energy is looking to expand the geographic range of geothermal energy. Instead of building power plants in the few places where hot water can readily travel through underground rock and carry heat to the surface to generate electricity, Fervo uses horizontal drilling and hydraulic fracturing to open its own pathways through the rock. This could make geothermal development possible in far more places.

After demonstrating this basic approach in 2023 at its Project Red facility in Nevada, Fervo is now developing Cape Station, a much larger plant in southwestern Utah expected to reach full commercial operation in 2028. The plant’s first phase began selling power in late September.

But the bigger change at Fervo this year is how much money it has available—and how much electricity demand has grown. The company went public in May, raising roughly $2.2 billion in one of the largest clean-energy IPOs in history. Fervo now plans to invest in accelerating its pipeline of larger geothermal projects.
- Industry: Geothermal energy
- Headquarters: Houston, Texas, US

- Notable fact: Fervo's recent agreement with Google provides a plan for the companies to pursue as much as 3 gigawatts of enhanced geothermal projects through 2033. That’s equivalent to roughly three-fourths of the total geothermal energy capacity operating across the US today.
One particularly large new group of potential customers is made up of the companies behind the AI boom, which operate enormous fleets of energy-hungry data centers.

This year Fervo expanded its years-long relationship with Google. In March, the companies signed an agreement to pursue more geothermal plants. Under these terms, Fervo will propose at least 1 gigawatt—roughly the generating capacity of an average nuclear power plant—worth of projects within two years, with Google then deciding which ones it wants to buy power from. In September, the tech giant agreed to purchase at least 396 megawatts of power from Fervo’s Cape Station to fuel a potential data center in Utah.

Fervo believes this buildout will allow it to drive down costs. Rather than engineering an entirely different facility each time, the company wants its engineers to work from a common design that can be refined from project to project. Each unit, which Fervo calls a GeoBlock, is designed as a roughly 50-megawatt power plant; combining several can create projects hundreds of megawatts in size.

The company measures its progress in part by its installed cost per kilowatt; this is, essentially, how much money it needs to spend to build each unit of a power plant’s generating capacity. Fervo is targeting about $7,000 per kilowatt for Cape Station’s first 100 megawatts and $5,500 for the next 400 megawatts. This is on the way toward its long-term goal of $3,000 per kilowatt—a level the company says will allow it to meet, and eventually undercut, the cost of a new natural gas power plant, without the ongoing expense of buying gas to generate electricity.

The catch is that Cape Station’s next 400 megawatts are being built directly beside the first 100 in Utah. While success there would provide evidence that Fervo can economically scale its energy output, it doesn’t mean this tech will easily carry over to another part of the country, says Shuvajit Bhattacharya, research associate professor at the University of Texas at Austin’s Bureau of Economic Geology.

This distinction matters because the Earth’s subsurface is not a uniform assembly line for power plants. Different places have different underground conditions, which determine where it makes economic sense for Fervo to drill and how deep its wells must go. The company will need to demonstrate that its approach will work in more places than Utah and Nevada.

The next few years will put Fervo’s strategy to the test: The company must prove it can lower costs as it finishes Cape Station, turn its discussions with data center companies into operating power plants, and ultimately replicate its success in other geological settings.

Fervo's nearer-term target is to have one gigawatt operating by the end of 2030. Five years after that, the company hopes to have five gigawatts up and running in total—which is more than the entire current US geothermal energy supply.
Update: We've added information about the commercial timeline of Fervo's Cape Station plant.

items.title: WeLion New Energy and its semi-solid-state batteries
items.description: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones.
items.author: You Xiaoying
paragraphs: WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The company’s semi-solid-state cells could improve safety and offer greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries to power electric cars, boats, and drones.
From the EVs that carry commuters home to the ships that transport goods across countries, more and more vehicles around us are powered by batteries.

Lithium-ion batteries are commonly used to power personal devices and vehicles today. But as the need for batteries surges, there’s a growing appetite for cells that can store more energy on a single charge.
Also, in lithium-based batteries the electrolyte, which facilitates ion transfer, uses a flammable liquid that can create a fire hazard.

Several companies, including WeLion New Energy, are working to make solid-state cells, which use a solid electrolyte instead of a liquid one. This could increase the energy density of batteries, as well as improve their safety. Fully solid-state cells are extremely difficult to manufacture, though. So WeLion currently focuses on developing and producing semi-solid-state cells, which have a part-liquid, part-solid electrolyte.

On that front, they have made steady progress. In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack in partnership with Shanghai-based EV-maker Nio, best known for its battery-swapping technology. The pack had an energy density of 360 watt-hours per kilogram (wh/kg), significantly higher than the 200 wh/kg average for lithium-ion packs today. That translated to a range of over 1,000 kilometers (621 miles). However, only about 200 of the battery packs were manufactured due to their high production cost, but they are still being used by Nio, WeLion says.

WeLion has also built batteries to power cargo ships and ferries through a subsidiary. And the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density too. WeLion’s engineers made a semi-solid-state battery that achieved a remarkable energy density of 824 wh/kg during testing in 2025, more than three times that of a standard lithium-ion battery available today.
- Industry: Energy storage
- Headquarters: Beijing, China
- Notable fact: WeLion’s cofounders include Chen Liquan, a scientist at the Chinese Academy of Sciences who led the development of the country’s first all-solid-state battery back in 1988.

China emits more carbon dioxide than any other country, and its transportation sector accounts for around 10% of that total. Scaling up the production of safer, higher-capacity batteries could help switch more vehicles away from fossil fuels.

Batteries that power electric ships could be especially helpful—the carbon dioxide emissions from vessels that move goods along China’s lakes, canals, and rivers are projected to grow by around 25% in this decade alone, reaching 18.7 million metric tons by 2030.

One big challenge WeLion faces is scaling up production of its semi-solid-state batteries and competing on cost in a crowded battery market. WeLion says that its semi-solid-state batteries are more expensive than conventional lithium-ion batteries made by larger Chinese battery companies such as CATL.

And while laboratory tests showing high energy density are impressive, it can be difficult to translate laboratory results to the real world. The company declined to give more details about the experimental results from its 2025 prototype, which it says is far from commercialization. Key details remain unclear, including how many times the cell can be charged and discharged and how capacity degrades over its lifetime.

WeLion plans to bring a new semi-solid-state battery for drones to market with an energy density of 410 wh/kg by the end of this year. It also intends to introduce its first all-solid-state battery for cars in 2027, which is expected to have an energy density of 400 wh/kg.

Two inland cargo ships powered by WeLion’s batteries are expected to launch in October 2026 in Huzhou, a city in eastern China. The battery pack of each of these ships will be able to carry nearly 4,000 kilowatt-hours of electricity, enough for them to sail for up to 250 kilometers (155 miles), the company says.

Today, WeLion has an annual manufacturing capacity of 11 gigawatt-hours (GWh) spread between four production bases in China. Two additional plants with a combined yearly capacity of 18 GWh are under construction.

items.title: The Chrome Hearts Hustle
items.description: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.
items.author: Ezra Marcus
paragraphs: This article was featured in New York’s One Great Story newsletter. Sign up here.

On a hot afternoon in August, I step off an elevator into a fluorescent-lit showroom on the second floor of an office building in the Financial District. Jack Jiang, the shop’s 19-year-old proprietor, is sitting behind a glass countertop, wearing gray sweatpants and a black hoodie that reads GO FUCK YOURSELF in lime-green cursive. There is no security guard, even though Jiang is surrounded by millions of dollars’ worth of luxury clothes and accessories: a Supreme x Ducati motorbike, a shelf full of Hermès Birkin bags, and racks and racks of Chrome Hearts. The brand’s signature crosses are everywhere: on jeans, biker jackets, and hoodies; on silver handcuffs, a stapler, a hacksaw, and a baseball hat. While giving me a tour of the space, Jiang pulls out a toilet plunger carved from ebony wood and capped with a silver cross, listed for $8,500. “It’s been used!” he tells me.

Jiang moves more than $20 million worth of product a year. Under the username Legos, he posts videos on TikTok of himself tracking down the items he later off-loads to his showroom. In one video, he shows up at a Beverly Hills high-school party. “We gonna finesse all these rich Beverly Hills kids’ Chrome!” he says to the camera. Inside, the attendees scream his name and clamor to sell him the clothes off their bodies. One says the diamond-studded necklace he’s wearing was a gift from his grandmother and he wants at least $2,500 for it; another strips off his Chrome Hearts pants while standing on a table. In another video, Jiang shows off a Chrome Hearts beanbag chair the rapper Bhad Bhabie sold him. He’d later resell it for nearly half a million dollars.

Jiang is not the only one buying and selling Chrome Hearts for exorbitant prices, nor is he the only one posting these interactions online. The brand has become extremely popular over the past few years among the young and wealthy and especially among crypto entrepreneurs fresh off absurd windfalls from meme coins and NFT projects. “A lot of young teenagers, they’re making $10 million, $50 million at the age of 19, 20 — it’s instant, so a lot of them don’t know how to spend it,” Raphael Badalov, a 22-year-old reseller who goes by the handle byraph, tells me recently, fingering his Chrome Hearts Star of David necklace. We are standing in the middle of a massive floor-through space overlooking West 25th Street, soon to be his new showroom. These same kids have spent the past half-decade “seeing their favorite rappers onstage in head-to-toe Chrome Hearts,” another reseller, Vincent Ferraro, says. “They wake up rich overnight. Like, why not live your dream? Get your dream car, get your dream jeans.”

Except they can’t. As with Hermès, according to the resellers and collectors I spoke to, it is impossible to purchase much of anything at a Chrome Hearts store unless you’ve cultivated a yearslong relationship with the brand. “You can go in these stores with a million dollars in cash and you’ll get nothing and then another guy will come in that has a relationship and they’ll offer him a bunch of cool stuff,” says longtime collector Mason Balbier. He would drop by the store and hang out with the salespeople, and eventually, “it just started happening,” he says. (The brand denies their pieces are dispersed based on “status.”) To get your hands on Chrome Hearts as a new buyer, then, your only option is to turn to resellers like Jiang, who charge whatever they feel like — five figures for jeans and leather jackets, higher for rarer pieces. The comment sections of Jiang’s reselling videos are full of people mocking the high prices. “Is it really worth that? I would say it’s not,” Jiang says. “I feel like it’s retarded.” Still, he added, “if there’s someone willing to pay that price, that means there’s logic behind it. There’s a saying in China: It makes sense if it happens.”

Chrome Hearts was founded in 1988 in Los Angeles by a carpenter, Richard Stark, and his two friends, the jeweler Leonard Kamhout and the leather craftsman John Bowman. They sold studded leather pants and custom motorcycle gear to other friends; in the beginning, they designed the costumes for a low-budget horror movie. After a few years, they managed to open a shop on the Upper East Side, which they filled with silver fleurs-de-lis, Gothic-style belt buckles, and handmade chaps. Cher and Lenny Kravitz were early fans, as were members of Guns N’ Roses and Aerosmith. By the mid-’90s, Stark and his wife, Laurie Lynn, had grown the brand into a multimillion-dollar company, opening stores in Tokyo and West Hollywood and collaborating with Rei Kawakubo and Rick Owens. Chrome Hearts continued to operate like a small family business, never releasing collections on a schedule, gifting to celebrities, putting on a runway show, or even expanding production outside its L.A. factory. In the aughts, as other companies began expanding their web presences, Stark and Lynn opted not to sell online.

The Starks’ three children, Jesse Jo, Frankie Belle, and Kristian, became involved in their parents’ company as they got older, roping in friends like Bella Hadid and Young Thug to model for the brand’s magazine and wear the clothes. Lil Uzi Vert’s 2020 album included the song “Chrome Heart Tags”; the YouTuber FaZe Banks got the brand’s cross tattooed on his kneecap. “The family’s ability to market without really marketing is flawless because they’re very, very good at seeding,” Badalov tells me. “They did everything in their power to make sure that wherever you go, you’ll never not see the brand, but you’ll never see the brand directly from the brand.” Eventually, Chrome Hearts became a sort of young-money uniform: Kim Kardashian wore it to the 2025 Met Gala; Timothée Chalamet, another friend of Kristian’s, wore it to a series of NBA games. Limited-edition collaborations only drove up the hype: triple-white Air Force 1’s, a limited-edition drop with Drake at the Aspen store.

The resellers have been swarming the internet since the early 2020s, cashing in on the fact that no one could get any of this stuff. Badalov remembers the moment he decided to go all in on reselling the brand. He was 17, working at a luxury vintage showroom. “One day, a client comes into the showroom I was working at and he brings in a bunch of Chrome Hearts rings,” Badalov says. He watched the man sell the collection for thousands of dollars. “I had an intuition. I’m like, This is going to be the biggest brand of our generation, guaranteed.” He started building his relationship at the Chrome Hearts store and snapping up pieces he knew he’d be able to resell.

The brand responded to the surge of resellers by bolstering efforts to shut them down — banning them from stores, introducing an appointment-only booking system, and training salespeople to look out for suspicious customers. Badalov had been selling for about a year when he was banned, but by that point, he’d established a customer base and a name for himself. Over the next few years, he managed to sell millions of dollars of Chrome Hearts, mostly jeans. On his Instagram, he posts his celebrity clients, including Playboi Carti, Central Cee, and Fabolous. He’s attuned to the absurdity of his life. “I’ve sold jeans for $300,000 before, and you and I are having a regular conversation about it. But let’s not forget that’s fucking insane,” he says. His prices come down to instinct. “There’s one-of-one jeans with Travis Scott’s name tag in them — those jeans you can get half a million for right now,” he says. “If you buy the Chrome Hearts Levi’s with green patches, those are probably worth $30,000 to $35,000. The same pair with crocodile patches is $100,000. It takes one person to buy it secondhand, and as soon as somebody does, word gets out and then boom — we have a market price.”

Jiang started his reselling career as a middle-schooler at a boarding school in Massachusetts. He followed sneaker resellers on TikTok and thought he could make some extra money. He started small, waiting on line at Foot Locker to buy shoes to flip, but quickly moved on to rarer kicks: sought-after editions of sneakers from Jordan, Off-White, and Yeezy. He made his first million at 16. During his sophomore year of high school, his friend offered to trade him a pair of Chrome Hearts jeans for two pairs of rare sneakers; he quickly off-loaded the pants to another reseller for a $4,000 profit. This never would have worked with sneakers, he realized, where the pros are sensitive to margins and obsessively track prices on resale sites like StockX. But with Chrome Hearts, there was a convenient information asymmetry. “You can’t find those details online. People who have Chrome Hearts, a lot of them don’t post it,” he says. “You might see a listing for $25,000, but I’m only selling for $15,000. So what’s the real price? You can’t really determine that.”

Also helpful was the fact that some of the items were produced in extremely low quantities, a core part of Chrome Hearts’ business model: only a handful of exclusive jeans made for a particular store or one-offs created for celebrities like Drake. This meant the resellers could set the market price wherever they wanted. All they had to do was find product. When they posted online that they were on the hunt, people with closets full of items they’d bought decades prior were more than happy to sell their jeans to a high-schooler offering ten times what they’d originally paid. As a teenager, “I would fly around the country,” Jiang says. “If today there’s a 40-year-old guy in Scottsdale, Arizona, who bought $400,000 worth of Chrome Hearts back in 2010 — all one-of-one pieces, gold — the advantage I provided was I would literally pull up to his house, wire ready.” He once spent $2.5 million buying out a single collection. Documenting the search turned him and his fellow Chrome Hearts traders into minor celebrities. In his videos, people scream after him and ask for selfies. Online, “Chrome Hearts reseller” has become yet another recognizable Gen-Z digital hustle, as familiar to the kids as “peptides booster” or “OnlyFans creator.”

Jiang breaks his clients into tiers. “If we’re talking about people spending more than $50,000 per item, then I have, like, 30 to 40,” he says, “mainly overseas buyers in Thailand, China, and Japan. Middle-aged, successful businessmen who love the brand. I’ll get a $100,000 item and it will sell within ten seconds because no one else has it.” Then, he says, he has the “$10,000-to-$50,000 range. Those are the 13-year-olds who can spend $20,000, the crypto kids, and the college athletes who are getting paid through NIL.”

He does whatever he needs to get the rarest items for his customers. In one recent TikTok clip, Jiang can be seen sitting on a couch in a palatial showroom, buying Chrome Hearts from a teenager recently embroiled in a crypto scam. “My boy used to buy Chrome when he was up!” Jiang jokes. The two haggle over the price of a pair of pants; Jiang ultimately buys them for $9,000. Then the boy pulls out a pair of women’s boots. “I found them in my mom’s closet,” he says. Ferraro employs proxies to shop on his behalf, going into stores, developing relationships, and eventually buying items secretly bound for the resale market.

“We all do it,” says Ferraro, chain-smoking out the window of his Soho showroom. He’s 36, a former club manager and relative elder statesman to the younger crop of resellers. “I was always on eBay, hustling like that,” he says. “It was always, like, my passion, whereas I was working nightlife just to pay the bills. Then COVID came and everyone’s getting their checks, so they’re buying more shit. So I was just pumping out more listings, buying stuff in Japan.” Ferraro shows me a parade of rarities: a custom kimono, a green crocodile-leather backpack studded with dagger zippers, a leopard-print beanbag chair, and a floor-length fur coat with a two-foot leather cross down the back listed for $225,000.

There is friendly competition among him and the other top resellers. If you are someone with a rare pair of jeans, “you’re not gonna just text me,” he says. “You’re gonna text Raph. You’re gonna text Legos.” It can be stressful. “People really made this their life. It’s my life. A lot of people live off this now. They quit their jobs, and they do this full time. So if jeans come up, people are fighting over them.”

This past winter, Ferraro got an alert from his security system at 4 a.m. When he opened his phone to check the footage, “I see fucking four guys in here with ski masks, and my heart dropped. And I’m like, ‘Fuck! Call the cops! We gotta get over there now.’” The group had planned the heist meticulously: Dressed as construction workers with vests and gloves, they pulled up to the showroom in a Ford SUV and carried a ladder to the scaffolding outside. “The ladder didn’t work, so they climbed the scaffolding,” Ferraro says. They broke a window and went in with bags ready to go, “just dumping it in. So the alarm is screaming. I think they really wanted to get more, but you can tell they were nervous.” They tossed bags of clothes off the fire escape to their getaway driver. On the way out, they split up and turned off their phones, he says, “because they got pinged by the cops and stuff. Super-thought-out.” They were long gone by the time Ferraro got to the showroom, where he found the floor covered with broken glass. “This was, like, a heartbreaking moment, bro,” he says. “They took over $1.2 million of stuff, which was, like, 60 pairs of jeans.”

Eventually, four people were arrested. One of them, a 21-year-old named Abdallah Diaby, turned out to be an agented model with over 90,000 Instagram followers. He showed up to court wearing thousands of dollars of John Varvatos necklaces and $1,500 Balmain biker jeans. (He has pleaded not guilty.) Ferraro was glad to see them prosecuted but frustrated that his clothing was never recovered, even though his store was insured. “None of the items have ever come up, which is insane because, bro — I’d say I’m the top, original, No. 1 reseller in the world, so everyone comes to me with specialty items. Lenny Kravitz jeans, Drake jeans, they put their name in them.” Even the noncelebrity custom jeans would have been findable given production variance between pairs. “My shit is so one-of-one. It was a bad place to rob. If they robbed a Louis Vuitton, they’re never gonna find it. There’s gonna be too many; that shit’s in rotation. So I don’t know what their plan is with it.” He claimed the cops offered the defendants time off their sentences if they revealed where they stashed or sold the clothes, to no avail. “They’re facing five to seven years, and they’re still saying they don’t know where it is. I’m like, Come on, bro.”

Theft is an increasing problem for the resellers. Recently, a pair of 17-year-olds came into Jiang’s shop trying to sell him goods that, he learned later, were stolen from a different reseller. They also, as it turned out, were casing the joint. A few days later, one of them broke in through a window at night and made off with over a million dollars’ worth of jewelry and pants. Jiang reached out to a resellers group chat and asked members to be on the lookout lest any of his pieces resurface. Sure enough, he soon got a ping from a reseller in Switzerland, where one of the alleged thieves had flown to try to move his items. “They are good,” Jiang says. “They know how to climb walls and stuff. Like, it’s crazy.” Still, he adds, they left fingerprints, and he believes they’ll be arrested. Jiang is planning on moving his showroom to a more secure location.

There’s another less tangible risk for the resellers: If the bubble pops, they will be left holding warehouses full of literal bags. After all, Chrome Hearts is now so overexposed, and the resale market so hot, that the brand is at risk of becoming a parody of itself. Recently, someone on r/MensFashion posted a picture of Chalamet and Kylie Jenner wearing Chrome Hearts jeans with orange crosses captioned “Chrome Hearts is the new Ed Hardy.” A better comparison, though, might be Supreme, whose once-frenzied resale market collapsed under its own weight after its late-2010s peak. “You kind of have to tell when your investment is over,” Gabriel Prensena, a young menswear influencer, tells me. He’s been posting his Chrome Hearts hauls for years and, like many young people, treats his designer-clothing trove as something akin to a basket of stocks to be bought and sold. Now, he’s wondering if the market is looking bearish. He’s begun trimming his Chrome Hearts collection “because I have a scary feeling the value is going to go down sooner than later.” The brand, to him, has started to feel gauche. “It’s one of those things that’s, like, you see the logo and then you automatically correlate it with some sort of money-slash-wealth.”

The resellers know their living depends on decisions being made by a company over which they have no control. “Longevity-wise, I think it all depends on a few factors,” Badalov says. “If they start making more shit, they’ll fuck up the market, obviously. And if there’s more inexperienced people or just money-hungry people selling bullshit, it’s not going to kill the market, but it’ll drive a lot of customers away.” And as with any bubble, even a brief dip in prices could spiral into a full-scale sell-off as spooked resellers try to unload their product ahead of a collapse. At the same time, the scarcity of the items means the market will never really be saturated. In one YouTube video, a Miami-based reseller who goes by the handle Chrome Plug shows off a one-of-one duffle bag he hopes to sell for $100,000. “This is what we’d call blue-chip Chrome. This is your Microsoft. This is your Tesla. This is your eBay and Amazon of Chrome. Your price will only go up,” he says. “It will never go down because there’s people that have spent a lot of money that were all kind of in conglomeration, holding the prices up together and making sure that we’re able to still get the price that we need for items like this.” In other words, at the very top, Chrome Hearts resellers buying from one another is enough to keep the prices elevated.

Badalov is trying to pivot to futureproof his empire. He recently started offering something like concierge services for people new to being rich. “You focus on the experience,” he says. “If you have a guy buying a $100,000 pair of jeans, he’s going to want to buy a $100,000 watch. He’s going to want to go to a cool restaurant. He’s going to want to book a private trip.” He’s had takers. But in the short term, he’s confident in his clothing stock: “People were saying Chrome was going to die two years ago. There’s nothing else to say about that.”

items.title: The Butt Runneth Over
items.description: Three months ago, Dylan, a.k.a. Glute Max Guy, set out on a simple mission: “Glutemaxxing until my butt gets too big for my pants.” He’d been working out for a decade but tended to neglect his lower body. He wasn’t motivated solely by aesthetics, he said, but
items.author: Allison P Davis
paragraphs: Three months ago, Dylan, a.k.a. Glute Max Guy, set out on a simple mission: “Glutemaxxing until my butt gets too big for my pants.” He’d been working out for a decade but tended to neglect his lower body. He wasn’t motivated solely by aesthetics, he said, but “I didn’t want to have the Hank Hill ass that most men seem to be content with. I wanted to look and feel athletic.” He thought posting every day would help him stay consistent.

Dylan is a fairly average guy: brown hair, brown eyes, a beard; he watches reality TV with his wife. He often works out in his condo or a basic gym, and he approaches his glutemaxxing methodically. Six days a week, he posts his workouts: three sets, 12 reps. He eats one gram of protein per pound of body weight (around 200 grams total); he takes ten to 15 grams of creatine a day.

There is nothing even close to thrilling about the pursuit of this ass. Yet the comments under his TikToks and Instagram Reels are full of men lobbing thirsty compliments and women asking for tips. The enthusiasm inspired Dylan to start the Glute Max Club community, sort of like a Patreon, where people chat about their own glute journey and follow along with his. Yes, his ass has gotten bigger, he reports. So has his follower count.

Dylan is but one man moved to action by the ass Zeitgeist. On television, even the most macho, hetero-coded shows, such as Paradise and Reacher, feature long shots of men’s bare cheeks — as did the horniest romance, Heated Rivalry, which turned a quiet appreciation for the male ass into a loud, panting yearning for juicy cakes.

Different eras have had different ideal butts: the square, flat bottom of the ’80s, like Patrick Swayze’s, was followed by the tight little tush of the ’90s. In the 2010s, the focus shifted to a woman’s pliant, movable butt, and the Brazilian butt lift surged in popularity as people tried to achieve it. Heated Rivalry can be said to have had a hand in repopularizing the male butt and informing its current ideal. Now when people say they want a butt, it’s a high, muscular bubble butt, or a “hard football booty,” says Azelion, a New York–based photographer who claims his own gets him a lot of attention on Sniffies and Grindr. It’s the ass of a cheeked-up hockey player, of soccer stars like Jude Bellingham, of tennis juggernauts Frances Tiafoe or Carlos Alcaraz. A cake so firm the cheeks look like they could crush a windpipe, it’s not an ass a Kardashian could call a plastic surgeon to replicate. The people want the bum of an athlete, one that sits atop strong thighs and requires tracking macros to build.

Now that athletes are embracing style — see the pregame fit check in most professional sports — some brand designers are taking notice of their sportier bodies.“People aren’t afraid to show it off,” says Ian Bradley, a stylist and fashion consultant. For Bradley, it’s become easier in the past six years to find pants that fit men with thick thighs and huge asses. “Generations of Black football players struggled to find pants,” he says with a sigh, but now he has a few go-to brands; he points to Thom Browne, who dresses LeBron James, and Zegna, a favorite for formalwear. “There are more options, even in high fashion. Not everyone is just doing a Hedi Slimane cut — no shade.”

Still, high fashion has been slower to evolve. Designers seem to understand that butts are the moment, but few are rushing to send more clappable cheeks down the runway. This past February, Gucci’s artistic director, Demna, dressed men in bum-snuggling pants that drooped so low they would have been pornographic if the models had any sort of ass. Prada’s spring 2027 show had men in pants as tight as Lululemon leggings, yet the cheeks were too microscopic to even fill those out. Emily Dawn Long, an upstart brand, seized on the moment with a butt-crack-centric collection, but the butts wearing it were barely there. Where were the fluffy cinnamon rolls I’ve been lusting after? Fashion is not quite reading the room, because the room is full of people making awooga noises over recent photos of Hudson Williams in Balenciaga pants: The trousers’ draping is best showcased on a firm apple ass. There is a disconnect, in other words, between the kind of butt we desire and the kind of butt designers are willing to dress.

For real men off the runway, it’s actually a hard time to find yourself in a butt deficit. At 39, Tom was pursuing, as he puts it, the typical Fire Island gay body with the help of a trainer. Through bodybuilding, he had sculpted a “pretty nice booty for a white guy,” he says, which became slightly less nice when he had to stop seeing his trainer during COVID. Then came the GLP-1, which he’s been on for years. Now, at 45, his butt is as “flat as a pancake.”

“I catch myself in the mirror sometimes, and I’m like, Oh my God, I have old-man butt,” Tom says. He’s trying to build it back through four-times-a-week workouts with two dedicated leg days. He eats protein. He takes creatine. He does a “million squats and dead lifts and hip thrusts and all these things that are supposed to activate your glutes.” But no matter how many he does, he just has “this sad, deflated whoopee cushion for a butt,” he says woefully. And still he tries.

Seeing your fat ass as an asset isn’t particularly new to women or gay men. What feels most revelatory in this era of ass fetishization is that more straight men have come to understand that a good backside can be as impressive as a well-developed torso.

At a party, I polled a group of straight, married men and their wives about their butts. A woman volunteered that her husband had started going to Pilates. One man lamented how only recently, as women he knew kept talking about the “butts on the hockey show,” did he realize how supremely flat his own ass is. It’s making him insecure.

Another one of the husbands has started developing his naturally big butt. Glute fitness, he notes, has been credited with improving longevity. Still, he’s not totally comfortable with the “nasty little move” he has to do at the end of a squat to ensure glute activation. He demonstrated, suddenly squatting down and popping up with a dramatic clench of his ass cheeks and an audible moan that made him, and everyone else, delighted but uneasy. I worried about him using the gym’s hip-thrust machine.

Azelion, the photographer, has noticed the current booty culture feels very straight. “You have a group of men who are realizing that women and gay men are responding positively to it, so it’s kind of like, ‘Wait, I have something to offer, too,’ ” he says. The proliferation of straight men on TikTok and Instagram pursuing perfect glutes, he says, has “changed the landscape of what it means to have a nice ass (for worse).”

I’ve noticed this too. Glutemaxxing has turned the basic desire for a good ass into an unnecessarily complicated quest to make one’s butt muscles as big, hard, and strong as possible. It can often feel like the erotic instinct for an ass worth lusting after has been sublimated into a whitewashed wellness obsession.

The math should be simple: three muscles (gluteus maximus, medius, and minimus), two firm cheeks, one perfect ass. And yet glutemaxxing requires an astonishing number of Romanian dead lifts, Bulgarian split squats, cable kickbacks, hip thrusts, glute bridges, elevated sumo squats. The number of ways one can fail to fully activate one’s glutes, the calculations of how much protein and fiber and creatine to consume, could lead to a certain kind of mania.

When I scroll Fitness Instagram or TikTok (sometimes for my own gains, other times because, well, butts are nice to look at), I am inundated with male trainers who seem to be the disciples of the original Glute Guy, Bret Contreras, who allegedly invented the hip thrust 20 years ago after watching MMA fighters fling their opponents off with their hips. I’ve screenshotted tips from @thelabootybuilder, a bro who helps women “grow their peach, inch by inch,” and become grotesquely obsessed with @iamnunzi, who has the exact snatched waist to round ass ratio I find to be my personal ideal. I am impressed and repulsed by how he wears the spandex workout shorts that lift and separate your ass cheeks and unsettled by how the conversation is one macro away from sounding like a pro–RFK Jr. fitness regimen.

Something vital gets lost when the goal is a perfect marble-statue butt. It’s beautiful to look at — and look we do — but the life force is gone when optimization enters the conversation. What is the point of a juicy booty if we’ve glutemaxxed the eroticism out of it? Is it still a desired object when its pursuit has been divorced from desire? I sometimes sense that though more straight men want bigger butts, the sexiness of an ass has become secondary to its functionality. You’re building your glutes so can pick up a heavy box at age 60? What about so you’ll have something for someone to grab on to? Straight men’s need to optimize their butts has arguably ruined butts.

Not according to Jacob, 29, who started working out his butt to alleviate hip problems. His glutes were weak, and he wanted to make them strong. He and his friend Yianni started getting into glute workouts. The workouts turned into a friendly competition, which has grown to include some 30 friends participating in something called the Great Cake Competition.

He laid out all the details for me: They took official measurements at the start. He made a Strava-like app that includes 3-D renderings and growth charts. A photographer took glamour shots for before and after pictures. He got custom thongs for all of his friends, and when they do the final measurements in November, the winners will get plaster casts of their own asses.

As a result of growing his ass, Jacob has spent a long time getting really heady about what growing an ass can do for humanity. He’s moved away from the realm of fitness and function and developed a philosophical outlook on the whole thing. He sees the butt as the epicenter of his spiritual power — the root chakra. Unlocking his glutes is an act of self-acceptance and a way to achieve freedom from shame. That shame, he adds, is at the core of a lot of men’s lack of interest in engaging with their glutes.

The longer we talk, the more reasons he lists for the revolutionary potential of building a butt: It’s counter to Ozempic culture (“Everyone should eat as much as they can and make their asses as big as they can!”); it’s a way to ground himself physically — to align himself with the earth. The glutes aren’t just the key to longevity but an antidote to the ills of the manosphere. “The ultimate power comes from restraint and groundedness, which are representative of the ideals of masculinity I think we should be venerating,” Jacob says. If more men did, he thinks, society would move away from fascist applications of power.
And here I thought the men’s butt moment was about sex.

items.title: Your Daily Horoscope by Madame Clairevoyant: October 20, 2026
items.description: Any existing problems in your relationships could be amplified today, thanks to tension between Venus and Pluto (in Scorpio and Aquarius, respectively). Long-simmering jealousies and resentments, in particular, could make everyone (including you) act out. Don’
items.author: Claire Comstock-Gay
paragraphs: Any existing problems in your relationships could be amplified today, thanks to tension between Venus and Pluto (in Scorpio and Aquarius, respectively). Long-simmering jealousies and resentments, in particular, could make everyone (including you) act out. Don’t be surprised if the people around you become manipulative or passive aggressive in an attempt to get what they want. The best course of action right now is to acknowledge these feelings out loud. The more you can bring your “bad” emotions out into the open, the less power they’ll have over you.

You may struggle to see things clearly today — and to react proportionately. If you catch yourself lashing out over innocent mistakes or blowing up over minor inconveniences, take a beat. Seek advice from a trusted friend — ideally one with a bit more distance from the situation — and get a much-needed reality check. It’s not your fault if your feelings are intense today, but it is your responsibility to handle them. And before you ask for help, make sure you’re willing to listen — especially if their take differs from yours.

You probably won’t realize it, but you might be uncharacteristically competitive today. You’ll want to test even your strongest, most supportive relationships. You’ll be driven to prove you’re the best, the smartest, and the most deserving, and you might inadvertently hurt the people you care about in your quest to do so. Try to take a step back and remember that you will all thrive best when you thrive together. Remind yourself that life is not a zero-sum game; you can lift one another up so that everyone benefits.

If you’re feeling frustrated or unfulfilled today, be careful not to let resentment creep in. You might tell yourself that if others had only supported you more, you’d be farther along in your career; if others had appreciated you more, you’d be less lonely. But even if you’re thinking clearly — and you’re probably not right now — wallowing in bitterness won’t lead you anywhere good. Instead of feeding your own agitation, focus on taking action to create the change you need.

Don’t let your pursuit of excitement today lead you to make any rash decisions. You’ll likely have little patience for anything boring or mundane today, so your instinct might be to opt for quick thrills, even if they’re unhealthy ones. But try to ignore the inner voice telling you to stir things up just for the sake of it. If you create drama, it might be fun for a moment or two — but you’ll probably regret it before long. Try not to create extra messes that you’ll only have to clean up later.

What you crave most right now — as far as your relationships are concerned — is loyalty and trust. So much in life is uncertain; you want the people in your life to be dependable, easing your stress rather than adding to it. Just remember that it’s nobody else’s job to cater to you, devoting themselves entirely to your happiness and comfort. Take a moment to check in with yourself to make sure your expectations aren’t unreasonable. Your friends can be steadfast and devoted, even if they aren’t always behaving precisely the way you want.

You may be tempted to get involved in other people’s problems today. Your intentions are good: You genuinely want to help them work things out. You imagine that, because you have a more objective point of view, you’re the perfect person to step in. But consider that you might be overestimating your own abilities. You probably won’t manage to swoop in, instantly find a solution, and be the hero. If anything, you may end up getting more entangled and stressed out than you envisioned. So think twice before interfering.

Today, you might be quick to assume that anyone who’s irritating you is doing so on purpose. The people interfering with your plans seem to be intentionally making your life more difficult. But in reality, they probably aren’t thinking of you at all: The issue likely isn’t malice but carelessness. That’s no excuse — the effects of their behavior on you remain the same either way — but being clear about the source of it can help you address it more effectively.

Be aware you might feel guilty for spending time or energy taking care of yourself today. You’ll imagine you “should” be putting others first — only a fundamentally selfish person would be so worried about their own needs! Others might attempt to reinforce this thinking, particularly if they’re the ones benefiting from your self-sacrifice. But if anyone tries to make you feel bad for having needs or boundaries of your own, treat them with healthy skepticism. Generosity is important, but you don’t have to run yourself ragged in order to be a good person.
Sagittarius Daily Horoscope

You might be more inclined than usual to keep your feelings to yourself today. Maybe you need time to process things internally before you share them, or maybe you’re not in the mood to listen to everyone else opining on your problems. But recognize that others might interpret your reticence as secrecy; they might jump to the conclusion that you have something to hide. It might help to reassure your friends that you’re in a quiet mood today — but if they aren’t convinced, that’s their problem, not yours. Don’t let anyone pressure you to speak up before you’re ready.

Without meaning to, you might make the people around you feel criticized today. When you express your own opinions with confidence, others might imagine that you’re trying to browbeat them into agreeing. If you express pride for your own life choices, others might think you’re judging them for making different ones. You don’t have to soften your words if you don’t want to — but understand that people are sensitive right now, and adjusting your message accordingly might help you communicate more effectively.

If anyone in your life acts smug and self-satisfied today, you’ll have the strong urge to set them straight. If you get the impression that anyone thinks they’re somehow “better” than you, you’ll see it as your mission to prove them wrong. Up to a point, there’s nothing wrong with reminding people that you shouldn’t be underestimated — as long as you’re careful not to take it too far. The people who seem most full of themselves right now are probably the ones who are secretly the most insecure, so try not to be too harsh.

In general, you try to assume that people have good intentions. In most cases, you’d rather give the benefit of the doubt to someone who doesn’t deserve it than go through life suspicious of everyone. Today, though, you might be more guarded than usual, highly sensitive to even the slightest indication that people want to pressure or manipulate you. Trust your gut: This is one time when it’s probably best to err on the side of caution.
