items.title: Christina Applegate Says She Was Misdiagnosed With MS
items.description: Christina Applegate is “back at square one” after her doctor told her she’d been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Applegate shared the news in a two-part episode of her MeSsy podcast on Tuesday, her first back since taking a hiatus in March. The retired a
items.author: Olivia Craighead
paragraphs: Christina Applegate is “back at square one” after her doctor told her she’d been misdiagnosed with multiple sclerosis. Applegate shared the news in a two-part episode of her MeSsy podcast on Tuesday, her first back since taking a hiatus in March. The retired actress shared that her doctor recently said, “Congratulations, you don’t have MS.” She told her co-host, Jamie Lynn Sigler, that even though everyone else was “so happy” about the news, she’s “not happy at all.”

“You don’t get misdiagnosed and then all of the sudden I’m better,” Applegate said. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie! If anything, I’ve gotten worse. So I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me.”

Applegate was initially diagnosed with relapsing-remitting MS in 2021. She told Sigler, who was diagnosed with MS at 20 years old, that a diagnosis felt like an “answer to everything that was going on” with her body. Applegate added that she has “every symptom of someone with MS” but that, as she recently learned, there are also “many things that mirror MS.”

“I feel like I let everybody down, you know?” an emotional Applegate said. “It’s this weird feeling because I became this— you and I, the poster children for MS. And everything I was doing. I had a reason. I had a fucking reason as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason and it’s very unnerving and it’s very confusing for me.”

In the second part of the episode, Applegate talked about the emotional toll of both her illness and subsequent misdiagnosis. “I’ve gone through a great depression because of it,” Applegate said, noting that she “lost everything” following her initial diagnosis. “I get really emotional because it stopped my life. I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to the doctor’s office. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said, ‘You don’t have MS.’ Nothing magical happened.”

Applegate said that her doctors are about to begin an investigation into what she might actually have. In the meantime, she’s focusing on small ways to “find the love in life again.” “I’ve still got a lot of physical issues,” she told Sigler. “But I’m finding ways to make my room joyous and make sure that my doors are open and I can hear the birds and the fountain outside. I always have a flower in my hair.”

items.title: What’s the Wicker Husband Really Made Of?
items.description: Oh, you’re a fan of wicker? Name three fibrous materials that it is traditionally made from. The viral new erotic fairy tale Wicker, about a lonely fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who receives a sentient sex-god basket husband (Alexander Skarsgård), has women sudd
items.author: Cat Zhang
paragraphs: Oh, you’re a fan of wicker? Name three fibrous materials that it is traditionally made from. The viral new erotic fairy tale Wicker, about a lonely fisherwoman (Olivia Colman) who receives a sentient sex-god basket husband (Alexander Skarsgård), has women suddenly lusting over woven furniture. They’re rushing to the 4DX screenings; they’re speculating about the precise feel of “wicker ween.” But these bandwagon basket cases are so infatuated they haven’t asked the real question: What if the Wicker husband isn’t even wicker at all?

After the film’s trailer dropped two months ago, Deborah Needleman — former T magazine editor who absconded from magazine journalism a decade ago for a blissful life of basket-weaving — sounded the alarm that something was off. “Why is a dude woven in an English fishing village not made of willow — or even rush?!” she wrote in an Instagram post displaying one of the Wicker promo photos. (In the movie, he’s said to be willow.) Even worse, she pointed out, the Wicker husband appeared to be plaited, not woven, “from lacquered bamboo or phormium.” (Phormium is a type of New Zealand flax plant.) “Not to go all Emily Wilson and the odyssey on this,” she concluded, having already gone all Emily Wilson.

Maybe you think this is pedantic — as if this kind of nerdy “drama” isn’t half the fun of following a period movie like this one. If you’re in deep enough to worry about splinters during wicker sex, you should know what your beloved is made of.

Over the phone, Needleman explained that in the basket-weaving community, wicker is understood to be a weave, not a material. It is created with a technique called “stake and strand” — essentially, strands of material are woven horizontally above and under upright stakes. “It’s a little bit like loom weaving,” she said. Meanwhile, the Wicker husband is plaited, with strips laced diagonally in an over-and-under pattern. Fellow basket-weavers in Needleman’s comments weighed in: Lewis Prosser, a Cardiff-based “absurdist basket-maker” who has plenty of experience making humanoid figures, commented that he looked “classy and leathery, like a rawhide bullwhip,” adding, “This is what happens when people stray from buff willow, all the bark fetishists come out the woodwork!”

At the end of the day, Needleman clarified, “I think most basket-weavers are just psyched that this obscure thing that we all nerd out on is the hot hero protagonist in a movie,” she says, adding that the studio behind the costume, New Zealand’s Weta Workshop, is well-respected and that some interpret wicker as a general category of basketry and furniture.

In a statement, Weta prosthetic makeup designer Joe Dunckley stated that the traditional wicker-weaving style “doesn’t naturally provide the flexibility required for a moving human performer, so we needed to adapt and deconstruct traditional techniques.” Even so, he adds, “We still consider the character part of that broader wicker and basketry tradition.” Wicker directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Houston Fischer gave Dunkley and Weta’s lead makeup effects artist, Sarah Rubano, a whopping 18 months to research for the movie. They recruited Jasmin van Lith to be their lead weaver, supported by a team of other craftspeople, designers, and technicians, including some who had just wrapped up work on the last Avatar movie. The team used 3-D animation software to scan human faces then produced physical weave samples that could adapt to that movement; those weaves were factored into the design. Approximately 95 percent of the final costume was 3-D printed then painted to look like wicker.

Dunkley said that they drew from weaving techniques from all over the world, including traditional basket-weaving and New Zealand harakeke (flax) weaving: “For example, the nipples were created using a hat-making weave technique,” he says. They also studied how real woven willow behaves and factored that into the design.

Rest assured, I had already asked about the Wicker ween in an earlier conversation. Dunley strained for the best way to answer: “That was, relatively, um, last minute,” he says. The directors didn’t plan on shooting below the waist but changed their mind after presented with the opportunity to shoot in a river. Dundley said they collaborated with Wicker’s costume designers, András + Attila, who employed a “different technique” for the other half. “The weave itself on their side was a version of puff paint, which was quite remarkable.”
Well, there you have it. Stay safe, ladies.

items.title: Tinashe Is The People’s Pop Star
items.description: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.
items.author: Nolan Feeney
paragraphs: All month long, Bustle’s annual The Entertainers Issue is celebrating the performers and creators who lit up our screens and beyond in 2026.

The work of a Popstar never ends. On the eve of her eighth studio album in late September, Tinashe had a release party to attend in New York City, but she and her team also had some last-minute business to settle: finalizing social media posts to spread the word. “We went to some Asian fusion restaurant and were just on our phones,” Tinashe recalls, offering a snapshot of the big night. “When it drops, you have to be locked in. The post got to go up on eight different platforms.”

No one can accuse the 33-year-old of not putting in the hours. Since she started self-releasing mixtapes in 2012, the singer has never taken more than two years to release a new body of work. There have been highs — a generational turn-up anthem in “2 On”; unexpected streaming hits in “Nasty” and “No Broke Boys” — but also her share of roadblocks. She split from her previous label in 2019 over creative differences that, she’s said, whittled down her confidence. And though she subsequently burnished a reputation as a genre innovator on lean, kaleidoscopic projects like BB/Ang3l and Quantum Baby, her perma-underdog status remained.

Until now. Popstar received the best reviews of her career, including an eye-popping 9.0 score from Pitchfork, and debuted at No. 6 on the Billboard 200 — her first top 10 debut on that chart. Next spring, she’ll play some of the biggest shows of her career yet when she opens a pair of stadium dates for Harry Styles.

Tinashe took a victory lap this month by making a surprise appearance during Charli XCX’s headlining set at Austin City Limits. “It’s an amazing feeling when people who have been working and creating art in this game for a long time receive their flowers,” Tinashe says of her “B2b” and “Drop That Kitty” collaborator (who also knows firsthand how it can take a few albums for the world to catch up to your brilliance). “Charli’s rise to mainstream success as someone I consider a peer has been so heartwarming and inspiring to witness, and I’m thankful to be able to share these experiences together.”

Popstar’s warm reception settled some of the existential questions that have hung over Tinashe’s career — questions the album also grapples with directly: Can she summit the pop world while still pushing at its limits? Are ambition and talent enough in a fickle music industry known for routinely crushing spirits? Across its 16 tracks, Tinashe works through her feelings about her career while swerving between sonic extremes. Lead single “Too Easy” serves up TRL-era spectacle with a winking music video about the disposability of pop stars. On “Melatonin,” she trades the stage for the DJ booth, rejecting classic song structures for a chopped-up techno workout. By the end of the ride, she’s reckoning with her “oldest daughter” angst over a simple acoustic guitar.
“I’m the thread of connectivity between all of the different things that I love,” Tinashe says. “And my different projects, them really feeling like me is just a result of them coming from my brain.”

That’s the upside of taking the long road: There’s no question who’s in the driver’s seat. “I’m excited to be a part of spearheading these conversations about what pop is and expanding people’s minds and narrow definitions,” she says. “I hope we can continue to diversify and continue on this trajectory.”

“Popstar” was the first song I made for this record and my mission statement. I always came back to that one as the North Star, thematically. I didn’t know I wanted to name the album Popstar at the time, but I knew that was the tone that I was setting. Relationships, love — that has been a super afterthought in this season of my life, so I wanted to keep it really focused on what’s going on in my life: a ton of work and dealing with how I feel about it.

Over the course of the next two years, I did a bunch of sessions, made a bunch of songs. Some of them I wasn’t loving the direction of. For a while, I was kind of like, “Eh, I don’t really know where I’m going with this.” Then around the holidays of last year, I went into my creative cave, which is my favorite way to make songs — to really isolate myself and lock in. Basically, that week, I made 10 of the records on this project.
On the club-ready standout “Melatonin”:

Every day I’m just trying to challenge myself, and the people that I’m with, to do something that is unexpected. I got in the studio with my friends Nick [Weiss] and Zack [Sekoff] and was like, “I’ve got a bunch of a cappellas from different songs that I’ve been working on that I keep on deck in case we want to flip it or try to make something out of it.” That’s really what it started with: just a little piece of vocal, and we started building around that.

I love working with people who are down to get weird. That keeps me on my toes, and I think that’s when I get the best output: when I feel a little bit challenged and intrigued by a piece of music, and it’s not just super straightforward or easy.

I’d unsubscribed from it because I’ve never really had external validation in this type of way. I’ve never even sniffed the top 10 of a [major] Billboard chart. So that isn’t something that I even like to know, let alone be concerned with. I was surprised by the reaction, honestly. People are like, “Why are you surprised?!” And I’m like, “Why wouldn’t I be surprised?” The album doesn’t feel particularly different from a creative standpoint. I think the reception is the difference, which is exciting to say the least.
On the #UpliftTinashe trend:

It’s so nice and wholesome. I think my fans have been ready to see this critical reception. A lot of them have been riding with me for a really long time, and they’re very, very passionate about their love for me. I think it felt very validating for them as a fan base as well. So it was really cute to see.

I was reading a thread on Twitter recently where someone posed the question like, “How did you get into Tinashe? What was your thing?” And all the responses were super different, which I thought was so interesting. It went from, like, “I saw her on Rent Live!” to “I saw her open for Nicki Minaj in 2015” or “I heard ‘2 On’ on the radio in Dubai.” Some people were like, “I found out about her last week!” It was a really fun thread to dig through.

I’m chronically online, so I’m on all the social media apps. I don’t have beef with any of them. I actually love Twitter. I’ve always been a fan of Twitter, and I’ll always call it Twitter, too. I spend a lot of time on there. The news — absolutely not. But the conversation is great there. I think you can get a more nuanced [take] than on other platforms.
On her famous productivity:

I think it’s a couple things. I’m really impatient — when I have ideas, I like to get them out there. And then on a spiritual level, I really feel like you have to put things out into the universe in order to receive feedback from the universe. I’m a big believer that you have to release in order to get new ideas, which is my favorite thing about what I do. I’m a big perfectionist, but it never holds me back from dropping content. The content got to come out. I’ve never been trepidatious to drop a new project.
On opening for Harry Styles next year:

I’m most excited for a brand-new audience. I haven’t opened for someone on a tour in a long time. So that’ll be a new experience — and a new challenge, to see how they receive me. Playing a stadium will be another challenge because it’s so massive, and I think it’s in the round. I mean, I’d love the budget for 100 dancers — we can’t afford that. [Laughs.] We’ll just make it make sense. We always put on the best show that we possibly can given what we got. That’s the vibe: Make the best of every situation.

items.title: I'm The "Luckiest Girl Ever" But Can't Shake My Doubts About My Boyfriend
items.description: Q: I’m starting to think my boyfriend and I aren’t that compatible, but I’m also worried I’m self-sabotaging. We’ve been together for two and a half years and lived together for one. On paper, I should be the luckiest girl ever. He is incredibly kind, caring,
items.author: Sophia Benoit
paragraphs: Q: I’m starting to think my boyfriend and I aren’t that compatible, but I’m also worried I’m self-sabotaging. We’ve been together for two and a half years and lived together for one. On paper, I should be the luckiest girl ever. He is incredibly kind, caring, and funny. I have never been treated this well or felt this secure in a relationship. My friends and family tell me that I’ve hit the jackpot, but sometimes I can’t shake the feeling that something isn’t right.

For example, we disagree heavily on politics. Since we started dating, he has changed a lot of his views and even stated that he would take time to learn more about politics if it would make me happy. But something makes me feel put off and I wonder if he would have the same beliefs if it weren’t for our relationship. His friends share his original beliefs.

Another thing is work. When I met him, he was completing a master’s degree. Now, a year into his career, he often talks about quitting to do blue-collar work. I don’t have anything against that, but I am becoming a doctor, and he makes comments that I will be able to support him. I’d like to be able to take care of my parents and travel a lot, so I worry about him financially.
I’m torn because I do really love him and think he is an amazing person, but I don’t want to rush settling down (we’re 24). I just don’t know how to answer if he is the person for me. Please help!

A: This may not be a great comfort to you, but you are facing a very common problem. A lot of times, we believe we should only break up with someone if things are bad, rather than wrong, or even wrong-ish. That’s not true. You are allowed to leave a good situation, or even a great one. I often think about what author Cheryl Strayed wrote in her Dear Sugar advice column to five women who were considering ending their relationships. Her thesis? "Wanting to leave is enough.”

No matter what your family and friends say, a “perfect situation” may not be perfect for you. Unfortunately, you do not get a letter in the mail from the DMV when your relationship crosses the line and is too much work to be worth it. You won’t get a Partiful invite to leave him when the universe discovers that he is not The One. So, yes, you do have to pay attention.

However, I must tell you that your job in a relationship is not to ferret out whether it will last for eternity as quickly as possible. Your job is simply to understand whether you are sufficiently happy now. (A lot of heavy lifting, of course, is being done by the word “sufficiently.”)

What do you want — and expect — to get out of your time on Earth? In the words of Joan Didion, “Every day is all there is.” If your closest friend or your future child were questioning this relationship, what would you whisper in their ear?

Our happiness is not the responsibility of our partner. But how many days a year of feeling upset — or anxious or miserable or even just “off” — about a relationship are too many? Is it acceptable to experience five? What about 20? 150? (I think we can agree 150 is too much.)
Not all great things that can fit in your life are right for you. You don’t have to stay just because someone is good to you. In fact, that is actually the bare minimum.

Now, let’s get into some specifics. On the subject of politics, someone’s views are actually a direct representation of their values. Even “boring” stuff, like an opinion on where the city should build the new bridge, reveals what they care about. Will people be forced to move if it’s built in a certain neighborhood? Will it be built on the habitat of endangered species? What social services will get cut in order to pay for the bridge?

I think it’s fair to question the legitimacy of his new stances, especially because he’s saying he’ll read up on politics if that would make you happy, but he hasn’t actually done it. Is this same man going to suggest he would load the dishwasher if it would help you out around the house? I sure hope not!
And when it comes to money, it’s more than fair to not want to bring home the bacon for two — especially if this is a preference that he is voicing only through little comments or jokes.

Unfortunately, you do not get a letter in the mail from the DMV when your relationship crosses the line and is too much work to be worth it. You won’t get a Partiful invite to leave him when the universe discovers that he is not The One. So, yes, you do have to pay attention.

You do not need to figure this out now. Or next month. There is no hurry. You can enjoy the good parts of your relationship while continuing to encounter information that will help you decide either way. If you need to go, you will. You do not have to get everything right, certainly not the first time — and almost all of life is the first time.

So, how do you sift out the noise and see your life clearly? My advice to you is this: Make a firm commitment to trusting yourself in every possible situation. Take a jacket or leave it in the car? Trust yourself. Buy the concert tickets or wait until the day of? Trust yourself. Decline to be a bridesmaid to your toxic friend or spend your vacation days on her wedding? You know what to do.

You’re building a muscle. Tell yourself — even if you fear it’s not true — that you believe in your own abilities and insights. Know that even if you make a decision you later regret, you are capable of pivoting, and if necessary, surviving the consequences. You can always run out to the car and get your jacket.
