Of course, human beings have always outsourced some agency into shared structures, be they laws, public health systems or institutions. This has largely been to our benefit. But today our technologies capture attention, predict behaviour, automate choice and monetise our impulses, while keeping our bodies anchored to the machines on which we increasingly rely. These coordinating systems are often extractive and indifferent to our flourishing. We might imagine we’re escaping the body, but the technologies that make this seem possible depend on mines and cheap labour and come at a planetary cost. And if our technologies weaken the feedback loop between our bodies and the world, they may weaken it in both directions. At its worst, we become less sensitive not only to what the world is doing to us, but to what our own actions are doing to the world.
The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day

We have engineered novel digital and commercial environments that can habituate harmful impulses in our bodies. As our bodies refit themselves in response to the unhealthy architectures we’ve engineered, we can find ourselves in a spiral of self-harm.

Recent work by the neuroscientist Kent Berridge and colleagues has shown how the brain systems that tell us we enjoy something and the systems that drive us to pursue this can drift apart. In other words, what we find ourselves craving and what we enjoy can end up at odds. When these systems become disrupted, the body’s learned patterns fall out of alignment with the satisfaction that once justified them.

Influential models of drug addiction describe a progressive shift from prefrontal control to the striatum, a deep part of the brain involved in actions that become automatic over time. As such, addiction is a change from thoughtful self-command to more habit-driven control. Nowadays, addictions might not come only in the form of obvious candidates like alcohol and nicotine, but also smartphones and chatbots. The bodily gifts that allow us to learn can train us into patterns that diminish our freedom to act otherwise.

I have come to believe that our bodily deskilling is, in many ways, a loss of faith in what it is to be alive. A life of physical effort and friction is not only unavoidable if we want to be as resilient and capable as possible, but it is, in a nontrivial sense, the source of our intelligence.

Our intelligence is sustained through communication between the body and the world as we sense, assess and learn from what we encounter. Such gifts are shared with other life-forms too. Unlike the human kind of phenomenal consciousness, embodied intelligence is found wherever there is a living body. Even a lowly bacterium can sense chemical differences across time, retain a short molecular memory of what it has encountered, and alter its movements. The trees and grasses I brush past as I go on my walk are also hard at work learning from each changing day, modifying their growth and defences based on prior experiences. Many of us view them as lesser agents than the computer programs we’ve invented, if we consider them at all. But this is not based on the available evidence.
If you can no longer navigate the world and recall in flesh how to act, then you will not be liberated by technology, but ruled by it.

items.title: A good sceptic has more than doubt and less than certainty | Aeon Essays
items.description: How tightly should you hold your beliefs? You face the question several times a week without noticing. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach. Most of us swing betwe
items.author: Massimo Pigliucci
paragraphs: How tightly should you hold your beliefs? You face the question several times a week without noticing. Hold them too loosely and you don’t stand for anything, hold them too tightly and you become the sort of person no argument can reach. Most of us swing between the two and have no vocabulary for the ground in between. A Roman lawyer worked one out, under pressure far worse than anything we are likely to face, and it is still the best answer available.

The time is early 45 BCE, the place a villa near Lucrine Lake, northwest of Naples, in southern Italy. One of the most fascinating and controversial figures in the entirety of Western history, Marcus Tullius Cicero, is finishing writing a book that will be known as the Academica, where he explains the nature of sceptical philosophy and why it is so crucial not just to the advancement of human knowledge, but to living a good life.

It is a strange moment to retire into one’s villa to write. The Roman Republic, so beloved by Cicero, is about to be destroyed by aspiring autocrats: Julius Caesar, a longtime friend and now a political opponent, has declared himself dictator for life, a move that will soon lead to his assassination on the Ides of March 44 BCE. On the personal front, Cicero has recently divorced Terentia, his wife of 30 years, and a few months ago his beloved daughter Tullia died from complications following childbirth. You would think a man whose private and public worlds are collapsing so dramatically would hardly have the focus to write philosophy. Yet for Cicero such writing is a form of therapy, and the treatises he produces will influence medieval Christians, Renaissance authors, and the Founders of the American Republic.

Cicero managed all this because of his adopted philosophy, ‘Academic Skepticism’, so-called because it characterised, for the period from 266 to 90 BCE, the Academy originally founded by Plato. He used to be treated as a mere populariser, a gifted Roman relaying Greek ideas he did not really own, but scholars abandoned that uncharitable verdict decades ago as it became clear that Cicero argued and decided among his sources rather than simply transcribing them. He also built a Latin philosophical vocabulary from scratch, and much of the abstract terminology of European thought descends from his coinages. On the question that mattered most to his own school – whether a sceptic may hold opinions, and on what terms – his position was his own and differed from those of his teachers. What is true is that he philosophised in public, and tested his conclusions in the courts, in the Senate, and eventually against a death sentence. That is not popularisation: it’s philosophy done at street level.

Which is why he is worth your time now. What follows is partly the story of a man, but mostly a usable method: a way of holding beliefs that is neither the performed humility of the professional doubter nor the armoured certainty of the person who has ‘done their own research’. Cicero had a name for it – probabilia – and I think you will find it very useful any time you have to assess the validity of a notion and make a decision about it.
A genuine sceptic, confronted with compelling new evidence, updates – whereas the contrarian does not

‘Sceptic’ comes from the Greek skeptikos, meaning enquirer, and has a long and serious pedigree in philosophy. Yet, since the 1990s, the term has been hijacked by science-denial movements, giving us oxymorons like ‘climate sceptic’, ‘vaccine sceptic’, and ‘evolution sceptic’.

These movements understood that ‘sceptic’ has cultural prestige: it sounds rigorous, independent-minded, and anti-establishment, so they colonised it. The move was brilliant and corrosive, as it reframed denial as enquiry. The difference shows in practice: a genuine sceptic, confronted with compelling new evidence, updates – whereas the contrarian does not: they shift goalposts, raise new objections, or ignore what they cannot explain, all while citing studies selectively and appealing to the handful of dissenting experts cherrypicking the evidence. Their doubt is not the productive Socratic doubt that opens enquiry but a rhetorical shield that forecloses it. These self-styled sceptics are in fact dogmatists, having reached their conclusions in advance and thereafter simply engaging in rationalisations.

On the other side, a certain strand of scientism has overcorrected by demanding certainty as the price of admission for any belief worth holding, deploying ‘follow the science’ as a conversation-stopper rather than an invitation to enquiry. That is not how real science works either.

Both pathologies make the same mistake: they treat doubt and certainty as the only two options. Neither leaves room for what we actually need: calibrated confidence, the ability to say This is the best available account, I will act on it, and I remain open to being wrong. What is missing, then, is a philosophy of provisional but committed belief, a philosophy Cicero already worked out, in Latin, 2,000 years ago.

It began with a visit to Rome, in 87 BCE, by the then-head of the Platonic Academy, Philo of Larissa, having fled Athens amid political upheaval that eventuated, ironically, in the Roman sack of the city. Cicero, 19 years old and already a prodigy in oratory and law, went to hear Philo and was transfixed. What the visitor taught was not the abstract metaphysics of Plato but something more practical: a method based on the Socratic tradition of enquiry, the radical idea that wisdom begins in recognising the limits of one’s own knowledge.

The Academic Skeptics called their school the New Academy, to distinguish it from the Old one started by Plato. Arcesilaus and Carneades – the great sceptics of the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE – had pushed Plato’s and Socrates’ dialogical method toward a radical conclusion: we are unlikely to achieve certainty, because human knowledge comes from our senses and from reason, both of which are fallible.

Crucially, they did not conclude that we should therefore believe nothing whatsoever. Carneades introduced the concept of the pithanon (a Greek word) – the persuasive, the plausible – as the proper standard for action. Cicero translated the word into Latin as probabile (plural probabilia, from which we get the English ‘probable’) and built his whole epistemology on it.
What Cicero deployed was not a generic mood of open-mindedness but a graded, checkable procedure

Cicero’s own formulation is plain. In the Academica, he separates his school from the dogmatists in a single sentence: others declare that certain things are settled and fixed, whereas ‘we hold many things to be probabilia, which we can easily follow but can scarcely affirm.’ Follow easily, affirm rarely. The entire method is encapsulated by that asymmetry.

The term probabilia does not mean ‘probable’ in the modern, quantitative statistical sense, but something closer to ‘worthy of approval’: a claim that has withstood scrutiny, coheres with the available evidence, and a reasonable person would assent to while remaining open to revision. It is enough to act on.

Nor is ‘probabilia’ a single, undifferentiated category, and this is the important part usually left out. Carneades graded impressions (ie, preliminary judgments) by how much scrutiny they had survived. At the first level, an impression simply strikes you as a bit more likely to be true than not. At the second level, it rises to being persuasive. At the third, it is ‘undiverted’, meaning that nothing else you believe conflicts with it. At the fourth and highest level, it is also thoroughly examined, essentially the result of scientific investigation. Trivial matters need only the first or second grade; a medical decision or a criminal verdict demands the third or fourth. What Cicero inherited and deployed, then, was not a generic mood of open-mindedness but a graded, checkable procedure.

That grading is where the Academic parts company with the other great sceptical school of antiquity, Pyrrhonism, which counselled suspending judgment on most issues and otherwise acting according to how things appear to be while following local customs. There are three differences between the two approaches: first, the Academic assents, in a weakened but real sense: they approve the claim, argue for it, and carry the responsibility if it proves wrong, whereas the Pyrrhonist withholds approval and merely goes along. Second, the Academic ranks: appearances are sorted by how much testing they have survived, and some genuinely turn out to be better than others, while to the Pyrrhonist appearances arrive with no comparative weight attached – one is just as good (or bad) as another. Third, the two schools want different things: the Pyrrhonist pursues ataraxia, meaning tranquility, and suspension of judgment is his means to it. The Academic is still after truth; they simply doubt they will ever be able to certify that they have reached it. One is a therapy for anxiety, the other is a research programme conducted by a fallible animal that nevertheless needs to act in the world.

Cicero is explicit in the Academica: the wise person acts on the best available view, not because they are certain it is true, but because suspending all judgment would make life impossible. We are not the kind of people who think nothing is true, say the Academics; we are the people who say that some falsehoods are mixed in with truths, so similar to them that we have no sure criterion for judging, so we can assess only provisionally.
Strip away the Latin and the toga, and the Academic method comes down to a handful of habits, all of which can be practised, starting today:

- Say how confident you are, not just what you think. ‘I believe X’ is nearly useless. ‘I believe X, at about 7 out of 10, and here is what is holding back the other 3’ gives your interlocutor something to work with and gives you somewhere to move in the light of new evidence or better arguments.

- Grade your beliefs by how hard they have been tested. Most of what any of us believes sits at Carneades’ second level: it merely struck us as persuasive. Reserve confident action for what has been through the third and fourth levels.

- Separate your values from your empirical beliefs. That children should not go hungry is a value and may be held firmly. That a particular school-meals programme reduces hunger is an empirical claim, to be held only as firmly as the evidence warrants. Conflating the two is what makes people defend failing policies as though their integrity depended on it.
- State in advance what would change your mind. If nothing would, you do not have a belief, you have an identity.

- Argue the other side properly. The Academy’s signature exercise was arguing in utramque partem, on both sides of a question. Carneades notoriously did it in Rome in 155 BCE, defending justice one day and demolishing it the next. The point was not cynicism but that you do not truly know what you believe until you have built the strongest case against it yourself.

- Act anyway. The sceptic who treats uncertainty as a reason to postpone action has missed the point entirely. Uncertainty is the permanent condition of humanity, deciding effectively within that is a skill we can all benefit from.

- Treat being wrong as data rather than disgrace. If you follow these sceptical rules of thumb, you will change your mind from time to time – or at least ought to. The question is whether you experience that as humiliation or as the method working.
None of this was merely theoretical for Cicero. It informed every major decision of his life, including the most contested one.

As Consul – the highest office in Republican Rome – in 63 BCE, he faced a conspiracy to overthrow the government led by a disgruntled senator, Lucius Sergius Catilina, who was in the field threatening Rome with an army. Cicero gathered what intelligence he could and acted on probabilia. He laid the evidence before the Senate, which passed the senatus consultum ultimum, an emergency decree authorising the consuls to take whatever measures the safety of the state required. Cicero then put the fate of the captured conspirators to a full senatorial debate, in which Caesar argued for imprisonment and Cato the Younger for death. On the constitutional understanding that Cicero and the Senate majority held, the executions that followed were lawful. That understanding was contested, then and since: citizens had a right of appeal, and several years later Cicero was driven into exile by a (retroactively applied) law framed precisely to assert that he had violated it. Nothing here settles whether he was right, and I am not arguing that he was. What is instructive is his method of arriving at a conclusion: he acted on a judgment he knew might be mistaken, claimed no certainty he did not have, and then spent the rest of his life defending the decision rather than disowning it. That is Academic Skepticism under fire – not paralysis, nor reckless certainty, but consequential commitment to the best available judgment, including its costs.
Cicero knew he might be signing his death warrant, but the probable good outweighed the probable cost

Once removed from public life by Caesar’s dictatorship, Cicero retreated to his estates and wrote philosophy at extraordinary speed: De natura deorum, De divinatione, Academica, De finibus bonorum et malorum and the Tusculan Disputations, among others. De divinatione applies Academic Skepticism to superstition and mysticism, and is now considered the first treatise ever written on the difference between science and pseudoscience. His method there is recognisable to any working scientist. He does not dismiss out of hand the augurs and haruspices who read entrails and interpret the flight of birds. He examines them: what is the mechanism by which an animal’s liver predicts a battle’s outcome? Is there a genuine pattern of successful prediction, or only cherrypicked successes remembered after the fact? On each count, the evidence fails to compel assent. Crucially, he leaves open the possibility that the gods communicate through omens, concluding only that the evidence falls short of the standard he would demand anywhere else. Two thousand years before Carl Sagan’s dictum that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, Cicero was practising the same discipline and applying it to cherished Roman institutions. That is intellectual courage, not academic hedging.

The letters he exchanged with his friend Atticus in the months before his death are the most instructive documents Cicero left. Knowing that Mark Antony wanted him dead, he debated whether to flee, whether to return to Rome, whether to trust the young Octavian (the future emperor Augustus): reasoning under uncertainty, weighing probabilities, deciding anyway. When he returned and resumed attacking Antony in the discourses known as the Philippics, he knew he might be signing his death warrant, but the probable good outweighed the probable cost. He was murdered on 7 December 43 BCE. His last words, to the legionnaire sent to kill him, were: ‘I am stopping here. Come over, soldier. There is nothing right about what you are doing, but at least make sure you cut off my head properly.’
Is the Academic Skeptic approach worth revisiting and applying today? Very much so, at least in three areas.

First, science – contrary to what you may have heard – does not run on certainty. Scientific knowledge is not a collection of established facts, it is a provisional consensus of the best-tested theories, each held subject to revision. Thomas Kuhn showed that scientific paradigms shift over history, and Imre Lakatos argued that scientists rightly persist with research programmes despite anomalies they cannot explain, revising peripheral hypotheses before abandoning a theory’s core. What science practises is structurally identical to Cicero’s probabilia: the best current views, held with proportionate confidence, open to revision. Modern Bayesian probability theory (elaborating the theorem Thomas Bayes set out in the 18th century) formalises the same insight: priors updated by evidence, never certainty, always proportionality. The mathematics is new, but the wisdom is not.

This is not relativism, the view that theories are mere social constructs. Quite the opposite: modern philosophy of science describes a process by which science converges on progressively better accounts of reality, not by marching from certainty to certainty but by eliminating worse hypotheses and refining better ones. The scientist, like the Academic Skeptic, never claims final truth, but it doesn’t follow that anything goes. Interestingly, the sociologist Robert K Merton in 1942 described science as a kind of ‘organised scepticism’.

Second, democracy requires the willingness to be persuaded. Deliberation is possible only if citizens hold their political views as probabilia rather than as dogma, and the current political crisis is partly an epistemological one. Of course, there was never a golden age of reasonable citizens. But the measurements are unambiguous about the direction in which we have been moving: roll-call analyses of the US Congress show ideological overlap between the parties shrinking from the 1970s and effectively gone by the 2000s, while survey work by Pew and others documents a sharp rise since the 1990s in partisans holding consistently ideological positions and viewing the other side as a threat to the nation. Much of the change, moreover, is affective rather than programmatic: partisans have diverged on actual policy far less than they have come to dislike one another, which is exactly the sort of commitment that evidence cannot touch, and social media and the fake-news economy have accelerated it.
Developing a crystallised self that never updates is not integrity: it is rigidity dressed up as character

What would a genuinely probabilist citizen look like? They would hold strong political commitments, since probabilia are not wishy-washy and can be acted on with conviction. But they would distinguish their values from their empirical beliefs about how the world works. Suppose someone supports a universal basic income. The value underneath it – that no one should live in destitution in a wealthy society – is theirs to hold firmly. That a basic income is the best instrument for delivering it, however, is an empirical bet, and the trials now running in several countries might prove that bet ill-founded. The probabilist citizen would then be capable of saying, without shame: ‘I thought this would work; it does not appear to; therefore I am updating my view.’ That is not ‘flip-flopping’, it is exactly the cognitive posture that makes democratic persuasion possible. It is in fact a form of consistency: following the evidence wherever it may lead.

Third, on a personal scale, Cicero’s epistemology is an argument against the seductions of fixed identity. The person who has ‘found their truth’ and stopped questioning is not wise; they have surrendered to what Simone de Beauvoir, in The Prime of Life (1960), called ‘that conscious venture into lunacy known as a “philosophical system”,’ from which its adherents derive an obsessional attitude endowing their tentative patterns with universal insight and applicability. The well-examined life is one of continuous calibration and revision: strong-enough commitments to act with integrity, loose enough to update when the evidence changes.

This is countercultural in an age that prizes authenticity in the sense of having a fixed self, and urges us to own our identity. Cicero would have found that to be self-congratulatory. He changed his mind about friends, alliances and tactical judgments, and worried about it, as his letters make plain. But developing a crystallised self that never updates is not integrity: it is rigidity dressed up as character. The Ciceronian person is recognisable by a willingness to be embarrassed by earlier certainties, and by treating that embarrassment not as failure but as evidence that enquiry is working.

He was wrong about the Republic – it fell anyway. But he went on acting as though it could be saved, because that was the best available view on his analysis and worth acting on, and his legacy survived in the books he wrote in the shadow of Antony’s thirst for revenge.

The genuine sceptic is not the person who doubts everything, nor the person who demands proof before believing anything. It is the person who has learned to hold their best views with exactly the right strength of grip: firmly enough to act on them, loosely enough to let go when the evidence turns. That is what probabilia means. It is harder than dogmatism and harder than nihilistic doubt, but Cicero thought it the only honest stance available to a finite human being. He was probably right.

items.title: A scientist’s search for answers about Amanita muscaria gummies | Aeon Essays
items.description: In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies.
items.author: Eric Leas
paragraphs: In late summer 2023, I found myself in a smoke shop looking at a package of ‘magic mushroom’ gummies.

That phrase, magic mushrooms, usually calls to mind one type of mushroom: those containing psilocybin, the compound showing promise as a therapy for depression, addiction and other psychopathologies. But these gummies were not psilocybin. Instead, the packaging described Amanita muscaria, the red-capped, white-spotted toadstool of fairy-tale forests, iPhone keyboards and Super Mario.

I knew a little about the folklore of Amanita muscaria. I had first seen it discussed in an episode of the show Hamilton’s Pharmacopeia (2016-21), which begins with a claim I now hear often: that Amanita muscaria may be among the oldest human intoxicants. The New York banker-turned-ethnomycologist R Gordon Wasson, whose Life magazine essay from 1957 introduced psilocybin mushrooms to a mass Western audience, certainly took this idea seriously. In his book Soma: Divine Mushroom of Immortality (1968), he argued that the Vedic soma – a ritual drink in ancient Indian religions – was made from Amanita muscaria. The mushroom has also been linked, sometimes carefully and sometimes wildly, to the origins of Santa Claus, Viking berserkers and even Christianity. Some believe its other name, ‘fly agaric’, stems from its use as a natural pesticide for house flies; the word muscaria is also derived from the Latin word musca, meaning fly. Some scholars have linked Amanita muscaria to Lewis Carroll’s mushroom scene in Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865), in which the Caterpillar tells Alice that ‘one side’ of the mushroom will make her taller and the other shorter, though Carroll does not identify a species.

But I wasn’t standing in that smoke shop holding one of these products as a folklorist or looking to lose myself in Carroll’s ‘golden afternoon’. I am a public-health scientist, and my questions were pragmatic: what exactly was in this package? Could it hurt someone? Were these products legal?
The first thing I did was what I usually do. I went to the scientific literature. And down the rabbit hole I tumbled.

Although manufacturers use the term ‘magic mushrooms’, the main psychoactive compound in Amanita muscaria is not pharmacologically interchangeable with psilocybin; the two drugs do not act on the brain in the same way.

The body converts psilocybin into psilocin, the substance that actually produces its psychedelic effects. Psilocin switches on serotonin 5-HT2A receptors, proteins on the surface of brain cells that respond to the chemical messenger serotonin. These receptors are concentrated in the cortex, the brain’s outer layer, and especially in the prefrontal cortex, the region behind the forehead involved in such functions as attention, perception and our sense of self. The receptors sit on the big output neurons that broadcast to the rest of the brain, and switching them on makes those cells fire harder. Brain scans of people on psilocybin show what follows: networks that normally run in step with each other come apart, and regions of the cortex that rarely signal to each other begin to. What people report from the inside is a change in perception rather than false perception – surfaces that appear to move, colours that intensify, time that stops running at a fixed rate.
Muscimol killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl

Amanita muscaria works through a different system. Its principal psychoactive compound, muscimol, acts primarily on GABA-A receptors – part of the brain’s main braking system – quieting neuronal activity rather than amping it up. That puts muscimol broadly on the inhibitory side of brain chemistry, the same signalling system influenced by central nervous system depressants such as benzodiazepines and alcohol. The experience is still ‘psychoactive’, but it can look quite different. Clinical reports of Amanita intoxication describe drowsiness and dream-like states, impaired balance and coordination, confusion and disorientation, sometimes alternating with agitation, as well as visual or auditory hallucinations. In severe cases, people can become profoundly sedated, delirious or lose consciousness. In other words, rather than the characteristic alterations in perception associated with psilocybin, Amanita can produce a much less orderly mixture of sedation, hallucination and confusion.

The risks are different too. When my colleagues and I began looking at the toxicology, the numbers startled me. By the crude measure toxicologists often begin with – the LD50, or the dose required to kill half the test population – published estimates suggested that muscimol administered orally killed mice at a lower dose than nearly all commonly used psychotropic drugs we examined, including fentanyl. As a vegetarian, I found the exercise grim, and translating animal doses to humans is always imperfect. But these were safety signals we took seriously.

That was the first turn in the rabbit hole. The next was dosing. If companies were selling Amanita muscaria gummies and chocolates in ordinary retail settings, then somewhere, implicitly or explicitly, someone had made a decision about dosing. A gummy contains some amount. A package contains some total amount. A label tells a consumer to take one piece, or half a piece, or perhaps more. A certificate of analysis from products submitted to a laboratory can provide an amount per gummy. Those numbers can feel reassuring simply because they are printed on a package. They also imply that someone knew enough to choose a dose for the desired effect.
I wanted to know whether that chain existed.

So, I started with a simple question: are there human studies showing what muscimol does at different doses? The best answer to this would have come from controlled studies in which multiple human participants were given standardised doses under observation, with careful reporting of effects and adverse events. I could not find that literature in the usual places. I could find toxicology estimates, case reports, historical accounts and ethnobotanical discussions. But a modern dosing study, the kind one would want before placing psychoactive candies near a cash register, was not there.

Eventually, I came across the proceedings from a symposium I had not known about: the Ethnopharmacologic Search for Psychoactive Drugs, held at the University of California, San Francisco, from 28 to 30 January 1967. The time and place stood out to me immediately. Two weeks earlier, a couple of miles away in Golden Gate Park, Timothy Leary had told the Human Be-In crowd to ‘turn on, tune in, drop out’, a phrase that would become shorthand for the moral panic that soon surrounded psychedelics and particularly LSD. The symposium also opened with a letter by Albert Hofmann, the Swiss chemist best known for synthesising LSD and who had also led the work identifying psilocybin and psilocin as the active compounds of Psilocybe mexicana. The symposium covered compounds from many psychoactive plants and cultures, including a lecture on nutmeg delivered by Alexander Shulgin – the San Francisco Bay Area biochemist who is remembered most infamously (and perhaps unkindly) for his rediscovery and popularisation of MDMA (aka Ecstasy).
A mid-century scientist, dosing himself, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies

Near the end came a session on Amanita muscaria. In the final part of the final lecture, I found what I had been searching for – something resembling a dosing guide. It came from a report of a self-experiment with pure muscimol by Peter G Waser – a Swiss pharmacologist who later served as rector of the University of Zurich – under observation by a Swiss psychiatrist named Jules Angst. Waser repeatedly dosed himself with pure muscimol dissolved in water to establish a range of effects. This was not a modern dosing study. It was stranger than that, and I think it is worth hearing Waser’s language directly because it captures both the scientific seriousness and the unease of the moment:

Curiosity is one of the main qualities of a scientist, and this may be the reason why a pharmacologist watching the behaviour of his animals under certain drugs wants to know more about the emotions and changes in reaction they produce. Another reason is ethical. We have to foresee the accidents and dangerous actions new compounds of general interest may produce on man. My report on some experiments done on myself by ingesting ibotenic acid and muscimol under careful psychiatric control may give you an unauthoritative view on this.

At 5 milligrams taken orally in water, Waser reported little effect beyond a feeling of laziness. At 10 milligrams, however, he described a mild intoxication beginning about 90 minutes later, with dizziness, loss of coordination and elevated mood. He did not experience hallucinations, although he noticed slight changes in taste and colour vision, followed by muscle twitching and then sleep with dreams. Within two to three hours, he reported feeling normal again – rested and able to work – and said he slept deeply the following night.

At 15 milligrams, the effects were stronger and began more quickly, after about 40 minutes. Waser reported dizziness severe enough that he could not walk with his eyes closed, along with slurred speech, diminished appetite and taste, and increasing difficulty concentrating. His visual perception also changed: images of situations he had seen minutes earlier seemed to repeat themselves, and sounds sometimes appeared to echo. Most disturbing to him were repeated involuntary muscle contractions. At times, he wrote, he felt as though he had lost his legs, although he specifically distinguished the experience from the vivid, colourful hallucinations he had experienced with LSD. After falling asleep and awakening several hours later, he felt dull and uncertain rather than refreshed, although the muscle twitching had diminished. His blood pressure rose only slightly during the psychoactive period. In preliminary analyses conducted by the Swiss chemist Conrad H Eugster, muscimol appeared to be detectable in Waser’s urine after the self-experiment, although Waser cautioned, at the time, that the finding still needed confirmation.

What I found was upsetting, but not that surprising. Dosing recommendations from product manufacturers, including the one I found at that smoke shop, appeared to resemble that old self-experiment. While I have no way to confirm it, I have a strange feeling that this mid-century scientist, dosing himself under observation and reporting on it at a famous drug conference, may have produced numbers that later travelled into a marketplace of gummies and chocolates sold to consumers who likely have no idea where the guidance came from.

I wish I had been able to speak with Waser himself, but he died in 2010. In 2024, I did exchange emails with Angst, the psychiatrist who had supervised the experiment. Angst was 97 and not in good health, but he confirmed the point that mattered most to me: Waser had come to Angst for supervision as a precaution. Waser’s own later writing suggests why. Recalling the experiments, Waser described the experiences at high doses as unpleasant and even potentially life-threatening.

Convinced of questionable dosing standards in this marketplace, my line of enquiry returned to the potential harms – were there products on the market that contained enough muscimol to seriously harm someone?

I found a product with a very high reported amount of muscimol. It was a gummy product, one in a benign-looking package that did not have childproofing or clear warnings. I began doing the calculation no one wants to do. If a young child ate the entire package, mistaking it for candy, could they die? I took the reported amount of muscimol, the toxicology estimates (the LD50), a conversion used to translate dosing between species, and the average weight of a small child. The result looked bad. Bad enough that I did not quite trust myself. So, I called a friend, Matthieu Rouffet, a medicinal chemist and the dean of science at a local college, who does toxicology calculations more often than I do. I wanted him to tell me I had made an error. Instead, he was alarmed too.

There is a rare moment as a scientist when you encounter an empirical finding and it becomes emotionally charged. Before, it might just have been intellectual curiosity and your training that drove you to it. After, you feel a sense of responsibility. This was one of those rare moments for me. Perhaps this finding was especially emotionally charged for my friend Matthieu and me because we are fathers of young children. When I made the calculation, my daughter was only a year old. It could have just been the sleep-deprived delirium of early fatherhood, but I felt a moral responsibility to act.
The broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole
Were there policy levers I could pull? It was complex because Amanita muscaria fell into the gap between the categories – not a controlled substance, not a food, not quite a supplement.

Unlike psilocybin, Amanita muscaria and muscimol were not scheduled under the US Controlled Substances Act, and they also did not appear to be controlled under comparable drug laws in most countries, with a few exceptions. The Netherlands treated Amanita muscaria and Amanita pantherina (which also contains muscimol) as controlled substances, and, in the US, manufacturers generally acknowledged Louisiana as a state where sales were restricted. One manufacturer’s legal guidance listed prohibitions in countries including Brazil, Thailand, Australia, Romania, Russia, Sweden and Ukraine. But the broader pattern appeared to be permissiveness by omission or legal loophole.

This was an argument I had seen a few years earlier, when I wrote about the ‘hemp loophole’. It emerged from the 2018 Farm Bill legalising hemp, defined largely by its low level of delta-9-THC, the main intoxicant in cannabis. Some manufacturers saw an opening: if the law restricted just delta-9-THC, they argued, other intoxicating cannabinoids derived from legal hemp could still be sold. One was delta-8-THC, often produced from hemp-derived CBD, a nonintoxicating cannabinoid. Soon delta-8 gummies, vapes and candies were turning up in gas stations, smoke shops and online stores. The industry’s argument was essentially this: if the starting material was legal hemp and the finished product stayed below the federal limit for delta-9-THC, it did not have to be sold through the regulated marijuana market, with safeguards such as age restrictions and testing for potency.

The Amanita muscaria market seemed to be borrowing a similar playbook. The claim was not that Amanita muscaria gummies had been proven safe. It was that they were not psilocybin, not scheduled, and not clearly prohibited.

However, drug scheduling was only one possible policy lever. Food and dietary supplement law was another. Many Amanita muscaria products were being sold as if they were ordinary foods or supplements, but I could not find publicly available notifications showing that Amanita muscaria or muscimol had been accepted as a new dietary ingredient in the US or elsewhere.
Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all

Given the toxicology and case reports mentioned above, that absence mattered. The issue, here, was not whether someone could pick a mushroom in the woods and take it home to eat – that’s unambiguously legal. The issue was whether a company could extract, concentrate, flavour, package, advertise, and sell a psychoactive compound in candy-like forms without meeting basic consumer protection standards.

They didn’t appear to be meeting this standard, and so there was legal recourse. Regulators could clarify whether these products could be commercially manufactured and sold at all under dietary supplement and food laws. If sales were not allowed, they could take the products off the shelves. If sales were allowed, they could require product standards such as age restrictions, child-resistant packaging, maximum-dose rules, warning labels, restrictions on cartoons or candy-like marketing, and standardised testing for potency, contaminants and undisclosed drugs. They could also require labels to state what was in the package in units that were interpretable.

Now, with a clear safety concern and a clear pathway for legal recourse, my colleagues and I wrote a paper, published in a peer-reviewed journal, and we began raising awareness on the subject. I issued a press release with my school at the University of California, San Diego, which helped to generate some national media coverage including in The Washington Post and on NPR. I also contacted colleagues at the Department of Justice in my home state of California. They put me in touch with the consumer-safety division that would eventually build an investigation of several brands selling Amanita muscaria-branded products in the state, including one that led to the seizure of more than 95,000 mushroom chocolate bars from a warehouse in San Diego County.

By late 2024, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) had also reached its own conclusion about Amanita muscaria in food, offering a perspective that confirmed my own. In a scientific memorandum, FDA toxicologists concluded that Amanita muscaria and three of its active constituents, including muscimol, do not meet the criteria for safe use in food in the US.

There’s another side to the story. Some people believe the mushroom helps them. There are books and online communities organised around microdosing Amanita muscaria, often motivated by purported benefits based on, and following dosing information derived from, survey responses or anecdotal reports. The health claims tend to cluster around sleep, anxiety and the possibility of reducing dependence on benzodiazepines or other sedatives. Muscimol’s pharmacology makes some of this plausible in a broad mechanistic sense. A compound acting primarily on the GABA-A receptors could, in theory, have sedating effects that are therapeutic. Even our forerunner Waser alludes to this in his self-experiment. That account also mentions the findings of his colleague Eugster, who held a patent on a method of synthesising muscimol, which is currently assigned to the pharmaceutical company Novartis. Less toxic analogues of muscimol have also been explored as pharmaceuticals; gaboxadol, for instance, was discovered by the Danish chemist Povl Krogsgaard-Larsen. But the benefits and harms of these substances have never been rigorously tested to this day.

A thousand testimonials about the use of Amanita muscaria do not tell you what is in a gummy from a particular batch made by a particular company. They do not establish a safe range for children, older adults, pregnant people, people taking other medications, or anyone who eats more than the label recommends because the product looks harmless.
Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room

This is one of the tensions running through the modern conversation about psychedelics and plant medicines like Amanita muscaria. Some proponents of plant medicine argue that science should not be treated as the only legitimate way of evaluating the veracity of therapeutic claims. They point to traditional and Indigenous uses of psychoactive plants and fungi, sometimes over millennia, and ask why randomised controlled trials should outrank lived experience, ritual knowledge or community practice.

I take that argument seriously. Western medicine does not own all wisdom, and therapeutic approval pathways are limited. Many plant medicines will struggle through conventional drug approval because they cannot be easily patented, because no company has an incentive to fund the studies, or because they belong in a ceremonial setting that is not transferable to a randomised trial. If the only knowledge we recognise is knowledge that can be monetised through drug development, we will miss a great deal.

But the Amanita muscaria products sold in smoke shops are not simply traditional plant medicines being used in traditional contexts. They are commercial products in a modern marketplace. They are manufactured, packaged, branded, advertised, and shipped. They borrow the language of science, from microdosing to certificates of analysis, when it helps them. Once a substance is turned into a consumer good, science and capitalism are already in the room. The question is whether they will be used with integrity.

The distinction between plant medicine and a commercial market became painfully clear with the recall of Diamond Shruumz-brand chocolate bars, ice-cream cones and gummies sold by Prophet Premium Blends, based in Santa Ana, California. In 2024, federal agencies investigated 180 cases, including three potential deaths, tied to products marketed with mushroom language and sold in the same broad retail ecosystem of gas stations, smoke shops, hemp-derived cannabinoid stores and online sellers.

In their recall notice, Prophet Premium Blends indicated that the adverse events may have been due to elevated levels of muscimol. But product testing complicated that story. Muscimol did not appear in all products and could not explain all the reported symptoms. Instead, testing found a shifting mixture of substances across products, including psilacetin, a near chemical cousin of psilocin first disclosed in a patent by Albert Hofmann and Franz Troxler in 1961. Unlike psilocin and psilocybin, psilacetin is not always listed by name in controlled-substance schedules, though it may still be regulated under analogue laws or broader drug-control provisions. Some samples also contained psilocin, pregabalin (a prescription medication), and compounds related to the psychoactive root, kava. The result was not a simple story about muscimol toxicity. It was a more troubling story about a marketplace where consumers could not reliably know what psychoactive substances they were consuming.
That, to me, illustrates the central ethical issue I see in the conversation about modern psychedelics and plant medicines.

People can argue about whether adults should be allowed to use psychedelics or plant medicines. My own view is that adults should generally have wide latitude over what they put in their own bodies. But they also have a right to know what they are putting in their bodies, as well as the known benefits and risks. A person cannot meaningfully consent to ingesting one thing while being sold another. They cannot weigh risks that are hidden from them inside of mislabelled gummies. They cannot dose carefully when the dose is uncertain and the active ingredient is undisclosed. The right to alter one’s consciousness does not include a company’s right to deceive.
Psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it

And while there are many stories about the purported benefits of plant medicines like Amanita muscaria, there are also stories about the harms of this marketplace. The most impactful story I’ve learned about came from Ashley Glover, who contacted me through email in 2024.

Ashley first wrote to me after reading my peer-reviewed article. Her only brother Andrew Davenport died on 23 June 2024, she said, after consuming a Diamond Shruumz mushroom bar. What stood out in Ashley’s emails was not only the grief, but the difficulty of getting the justice system to recognise what might have happened. She wrote that a witness who was with Andrew had insisted that the bars made him sick. She wrote that an opened box of Diamond Shruumz bars was recovered near his body. She also wrote that his initial toxicology report did not show hard drugs or alcohol, and that his prescribed medications were described to the family as being at normal therapeutic levels. But the medical examiner, she said, had not saved the box or bars for testing and the explanation relayed to her was blunt: no one overdoses on magic mushrooms.

That sentence has stayed with me because it captures the potential danger of a category error. If the product had been treated as a psilocybin mushroom, its risk could be dismissed before the relevant chemistry was even known. But these products were not psilocybin mushrooms. They were manufactured psychoactive goods whose contents could vary, whose labels could be incomplete, and whose compounds were difficult for forensic scientists to detect.

Ashley told me that biological samples from Andrew were eventually sent for specialised testing. Whether those results can establish causation is a legal and forensic question, and I do not want to claim more than the evidence can support. But her account shows the public-health problem in human terms. Once a consumer product enters the marketplace without reliable safety evidence, accurate labelling and adequate testing capacity, the uncertainty does not end at the point of sale. It follows the consumer, the family, the medical examiner, the investigator, and anyone trying to reconstruct what happened after an adverse event leaves questions in its wake.

I began this investigation with a question that seemed narrow enough for an academic paper – should unregulated sales of Amanita muscaria products prompt a public-health response? The answer, to me, became an unequivocal yes. But the journey was stranger than the paper could contain.

I did not set out to become the public-health scientist warning people about the fairy-tale mushroom, sounding alarmist or like a teetotaller. I am not opposed to research on psychoactive substances or to responsible use among adults. If anything, the therapeutic promise of psilocybin is part of why Amanita muscaria bothered me; psilocybin was creating a halo around other mushrooms, and manufacturers were exploiting it in ways that I saw as unethical and dangerous.

The lesson I took from Amanita muscaria was not that altered states are inherently dangerous or that science should flatten every human encounter with plants or fungus into a risk calculation. It was simpler than that. If a company sells a psychoactive product to the public, especially in forms that look like candy, it should be transparent about what is in the product, and have evidence that the product can be used without unreasonable harm. This should not be a radical standard. It should be the minimum requirement for sales.

items.title: The Year of the Difficult Dad
items.description: A triad of films this year spotlights stories of estranged daughters navigating the overbearing egos of toxic, difficult fathers
items.author: Meg Walters
paragraphs: A triad of films this year spotlights stories of estranged daughters navigating the overbearing egos of toxic, difficult fathers

The great auteurs loom large in our collective imaginations. Look back through the years, and you’ll be greeted with a long line of Important Artists – towering, imposing, and, for the most part, male. Look a little closer, though, and you may see other hazy figures lurking on the outskirts. Almost a century ago, Virginia Woolf presented a thought experiment in her seminal A Room of One’s Own: if Shakespeare had a sister, and if she was a writer, would we know her work? (No: she’d be too busy cleaning and mending and cooking and having babies and generally facilitating the art made by the men in her life, of course.) Though we’ve made strides, Woolf’s point remains shockingly relevant: who gets to make art within a family and how does that art get to be made? A new slew of films this year ask us to reconsider the great male auteur through the eyes not of his sister, but rather his daughter.

Joaquim Trier’s Sentimental Value and Rodrigo Sorogoyen’s The Beloved paint portraits of renowned film directors facing up to their failings as their grown-up daughters take on roles in their films. Meanwhile, in Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland, real-life novelist Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler) is forced to reckon with his shortcomings when presented with the perspective of his daughter Erika (Sandra Hüller), a writer in her own right. In each story, we see a daughter serving the artistic vision of her father – and each collaboration paves the way for a destabilising personal and artistic reckoning.

In Fatherland, Thomas and Erika embark on a heavy father-daughter roadtrip. It’s 1949 and Thomas is taking his manifesto on the “new Germany” on tour during his first trip back to the country since he fled amid the rise of fascism before the war. In tow is Erika, his assistant, but also editor, translator, coach, administrator, stylist, and press manager all-in-one. When they receive some traumatic family news, Thomas buries himself deeper in his work, leaving Erika to pick up the emotional labour and reflect on the efficacy of her father’s mission. Pawlikowski lets the growing tension, both of an ideological and personal nature, build between them in a series of unspoken moments: A car ride clouded with tense silence. A party where Erika, alone, eyes her father amid a throng of fans.

This interrogation of the ego of the male artist, of his inability to face up to real trauma, is a common theme across this year’s father-daughter films. In Sentimental Value, director Gustav Borg (Stellan Skarsgård) wants his daughter Nora (Renate Reinsve) to take on a role inspired by his own mother in a film about her suicide. Despite his egotistical attempt to grapple with how this trauma affected him, he seems unable to face up to his own role as an absent father in Nora and her sister’s lives.

In a similar vein, The Beloved sees director Esteban Martinez (Javier Bardem) avoiding the difficult truth that he abandoned his daughter Emilia (Victoria Luengo) and her mother in pursuit of his own artistic ambition. Feeling guilty, perhaps, he invites Emilia to star in his next film. As production gets underway, the layers of pain, resentment and regret between them unravel in brutal ways. In one particularly unpleasant scene, Gustav terrorises his cast, forcing them to film a dinner party scene over and over again. When Emilia calls him out, he demands she eat and eat and eat until she’s almost sick.

There is a common pattern across these films: daughters left behind by their brilliant fathers and these fathers returning to their daughters a little too late, when the niggling guilt becomes unavoidable. Erika and her siblings are unable to compete with Thomas Mann’s obsession with his own art. Klaus, his son, was a needy boy, Thomas says in a moment of anger. “I wonder why,” comes Erika’s retort. These are portraits of daughters desperate to win love that wasn’t freely given – no psychology degree needed to see why they follow in their fathers’ footsteps. But when these father-daughter pairs do work together, the truth must out.

After days of silence, Erika’s viewpoint comes out in a short, sharp exchange. Thomas is a “cold-hearted narcissist,” she exclaims, too obsessed with his own legacy to face up to real trauma. Nora, too, is clear-sighted about her father’s shortcomings. After he gives a diatribe on how “artists need freedom” to create anything valuable, she asks him if he means they can’t have children. “You two are the best thing that happened to me,” he says hollowly. “Then why weren’t you there?” she demands. And Emilia finally forces her father to look at himself clearly too. “Answer me without stories. Do you know what it meant to me that you’re not in my life?” she asks him in their final scene together. “Yes,” he can only reply.

Each daughter reveals an uncomfortable truth to her father: that his art, though brilliant, might just have been his own way of avoiding his own failings – both as an artist and as a father. This father-daughter artist trope comes at an interesting time. Our collective relationship to the great male artists of both past and present is shifting. So, too, are the expectations we place on a new generation of fathers. It’s worth noting that these three films are directed by men – men who perhaps have felt the impact of these shifts. It is no longer acceptable to allow women in the family to facilitate art, then disappear when they’re no longer needed. Similarly, young women are no longer able to accept poor parenting from fathers simply because they happen to be men with artistic ambition. Each film offers a portrait of this shift as older generations, particularly men, find themselves facing up to new ideas and new standards from the women in their lives. After all, who better to hold up a mirror than their daughters?

Ultimately, each film resists the urge to condemn outright but seeks to push back against the misogyny embedded in the cult of male artistry and find new ways of doing things. The problems are exposed and, in the end, imperfect solutions are found. Fathers and daughters struggle on, finding a way forward on shaky new footing. Emilia and Esteban share a tearful farewell on the final day of filming. Nora and Gustav actually begin their project and manage to share a smile. Thomas finds a way to experience his pain and Erika is right there with him. A generational shift such as this one can be confronting. But perhaps we will be left with better art – and better fathers – as a result.

items.title: AnOther Loves: An Exhibitionist Boot
items.description: Loewe’s new Storm boot offers ample opportunity to show off your pedicure without getting your feet damp
items.author: George Pistachio
paragraphs: Loewe’s new Storm boot offers ample opportunity to show off your pedicure without getting your feet damp

Britain has had its hottest summer on record, with 33 days above 30°C and lawns turning the colour of toast. Today the rain is back, the grass is green again and our wardrobes have some catching up to do. Enter Loewe’s Storm boot. For all intents and purposes, it is a Wellington, only completely transparent, stamped with an enormous Loewe logo and more suited to Paris than shovelling muck in a muddy field. The Wellington boot itself began life as a leather riding boot commissioned by the Duke of Wellington before rubber versions arrived in the 19th century; now in a new iteration, its practicality gives way to exhibitionism. For their Spring/Summer 2026 debut at Loewe, Jack McCollough and Lazaro Hernandez introduced a transparent pointed shoe whose effect changed depending on the sock worn underneath. For Autumn/Winter 2026, the idea has stretched out and become downpour-ready, and sans sock, there is now an opportunity for an Alexander Skarsgård-style slutty-toes moment without getting your feet wet from the rain. From Spring/Summer to Autumn/Winter, McCollough and Hernandez have rather neatly solved the seasonal transition. Just add socks.
The Loewe Storm boot is available to buy now.

items.title: Death and Entrances
items.description: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
items.author: Susannah Frankel
paragraphs: This story is taken from the Autumn/Winter 2026 issue of AnOther Magazine:
Among the earliest and most famous depictions of a female nude is the Venus of Willendorf.

There are many Venuses, a broad – and obviously retrospective – nomenclature for figurines originating from the Upper Palaeolithic period, dating back 10,000 to 40,000 years. The Venus of Willendorf is carved in oolitic limestone. Standing a mere 11.1 centimetres tall, she is reputedly 30,000 years old. She has swollen breasts and a protuberant belly, both suggestive of pregnancy. Many thousands of words have been written about her. Is she, in fact, pregnant? Is she an ancient fertility doll, designed to be held in the hand of prospective or birthing mothers? Is she not pregnant at all but a symbol of beauty as it was perceived at that time? Also conjecture: the perspective of this Venus and more than a few of her Venus sisters, the fact that she has no facial features, or indeed feet, has led some to surmise that her creator was female – she is a self-portrait. Of course, nothing is proven. The issues this little Venus’s provenance raises, though, seem pertinent now for Harley Weir, whose exploration of the female form – and just the female – including her own, has led to some of the most striking and evocative imagery of the past decade.

In the history of art, depictions of pregnant women are few and far between. They are predominantly seen through the eyes of male artists. Their bodies are either hidden – through the medieval and Renaissance periods it was the fashion for women to wear voluminous clothing – or idealised. The Madonna is the most prevalent of all pregnant females in art history – the mother of all art historical clichés? – and her baby’s conception was immaculate. In myriad portrayals, myriad Annunciations, that purity is signified by the presence of a white dove. Of that same era, for many years critics speculated that the female figure in Jan van Eyck’s The Arnolfini Portrait (1434) was pregnant. Emblems of fertility – a carving of Saint Margaret of Antioch on a chair by the bed, ripe oranges, a symbol of prosperity but also fecundity, on the windowsill – are present in the painting’s background. The fullness of her famous green dress has since been attributed to the extravagance of its fabrication, however. Three-dimensional laser scans of Leonardo da Vinci’s Mona Lisa (1503–17) captured some 20 years ago now are not so easily dismissed. A fine gauze veil – or guarnello – seen over her dress, until that point hidden by aged varnish on the painting’s surface, is typical of those worn by soon-to-be or new mothers of that time. Representation of pregnant nudes in classical painting, meanwhile, are likely negative. Titian’s masterpiece Diana and Callisto (1556–59), which hangs in the National Gallery in London, is the best known. Nymph Callisto’s shaming, the revelation of her naked, pregnant body and subsequent fall from chastity, is subject to the goddess Diana’s fierce disapproval. Raped by Jupiter, Callisto was later transformed into a bear by that god’s wife, Juno. Or so the story goes.

A few centuries on, and modern artists from Gustav Klimt to Pablo Picasso and Lucian Freud painted (and sculpted) pregnant women, but always – inevitably – from a distance. Klimt’s Hope paintings, dated 1903 and 1907–08, of his favourite model Herma were executed against her better judgment, and the earlier rendition, portraying her naked surrounded by mythical monsters, caused a scandal. Picasso’s 1950 sculpture La Femme Enceinte was inspired by his partner at the time, Françoise Gilot, who had recently given birth to their second child, Paloma; he used ceramic bowls and pitchers to create the figure’s rounded breasts and stomach. Freud’s portraits of pregnant women, some carrying his own children, were forensic in their attention to detail: the subject as specimen.

It wasn’t until the last century that female artists’ representations of pregnancy began to enter the gallery setting. Paula Modersohn-Becker’s nude self-portrait of an imaginary pregnancy in 1906, Alice Neel’s paintings of pregnant women, clothed and nude, in the Sixties and Seventies and Chantal Joffe’s pregnant self-portraits are impassioned in their bid for reclamation, showing not only pregnancy’s beauty and power but also its complexity. For the first time, there is a sense of women’s alienation from their own bodies antepartum, for their feelings of intense love alongside, and never unreasonably, fear.

Harley Weir is no stranger to the self-portrait. Her 2022 Beauty Papers monograph, dedicated to “all the dolls in the world”, is an unflinchingly visceral – at times grotesque – representation of the tropes of femininity and the preconceptions those raise. Four years on, and ten weeks pregnant, Weir began to regularly take pictures of herself naked or near-naked in the relative privacy of her bedroom. At 32 weeks a further, more studied series was taken, including portraits of Weir, now helped by John Kelleher, her husband and the father of the baby, and of a body double wearing a pregnancy belly and Harley Weir mask. With styling by her friend and longtime collaborator Georgia Pendlebury, these images serve as Weir’s visual response to her physical and emotional transition at a time that may be as challenging as it is joyful. And intimate, but: “The real private self isn’t this though,” she says. “It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait.”
SUSANNAH FRANKEL Do you know the Venus of Willendorf? She’s got no feet. People think a woman may have made her.

HARLEY WEIR Because she’s looking down at her body? I’ve been documenting my pregnancy from week ten and there are a lot of looking-down pictures and also looking up in the mirror. When you’re pregnant there are so many blind spots. My husband helped take many of the pictures for that reason. The series is called Death and Entrances because, from what I’ve read, it’s like an ego death. You’re giving birth but you’re also dying, you change. I felt, physically in this story, as if I was wearing a disguise.

That’s something I think connects back to the Venus of Willendorf, this idea of a woman looking down at a body that is powerful, but also unfamiliar. During pregnancy, your body becomes the most visible thing about you, but at the same time it can feel like it no longer belongs. Here, I don’t have my usual breasts, I don’t have my usual stomach. I felt almost free from the shame of being nude because the bump isn’t me or us.

SF The physical state of pregnancy is extreme. We are taught from an early age to control our bodies and our body image. When you’re pregnant, you surrender that control. Perhaps your body is preparing you for becoming a mother, because once that happens your life is not your own in the same way.

HW Yes, it feels like that. It feels good. I’ve always been self-conscious about my breasts because they were so small. Now they are engorged and full of stretchmarks, but I don’t care who sees them. They’ve become functional objects. And there’s a safety in that. I feel much more at ease. I love being this blob that will bring purpose to someone new and it in turn gives my body purpose, a reason for its irregular shapes that before felt like deformities.
SF Is there any fear involved?

HW There was a lot more at the beginning. But I’m still at the stage where you don’t really know what’s about to hit. I’m in the phase where I feel this is the baby, it’s this bump. But no, the baby is going to come out and rock my world.
SF Have you looked at the way pregnant women are represented in art?
HW I haven’t seen much pregnant art – especially from the past. There’s the Virgin Mary, but we rarely see her pregnant. She didn’t even have sex. The virgin and the mother.
SF There’s that – the Christian ideal – but also some quite violent portrayals.

HW I have to say I can’t think of one classical painting where you see a pregnant woman. Klimt maybe. My mother talks a lot about how, even when she was younger, you had to cover the bump up, you couldn’t show it freely. I feel now we’re having a renaissance for mothers. The mother is more celebrated. I didn’t feel secure enough to be having a kid until now. And I’m getting on. I’ll be 38 when it comes out.
SF People called me a geriatric mother. I was 37.
HW But they’ve changed it now.

HW I would have been, but they stopped using that term recently, which is great. I do think this is an amazing moment for mothers. On Instagram there are so many inspirational women sharing their motherhood stories. Once you get pregnant your algorithm knows and they’re everywhere. So many cool mothers online, which I feel is something you wouldn’t have seen in the early Noughties. Mothers were dismissed or hidden. There was the fear of overpopulation and that having children was bad for the environment,

I used to hear that a lot. Now in the west fewer people are having babies, pregnancy is a positive thing again. It goes in cycles, I suppose. I’ve just finished reading Born [The Untold History of Humanity by Lucy Inglis]. It’s fascinating how attitudes shift. During the Roman Empire, people would kill unwanted babies, by “exposure” – especially girls.
SF In China and Japan they are now rolling out financial incentives to persuade people to have babies.
HW Exactly. First China wasn’t allowing more than one baby. Now there aren’t enough. For now, it feels like we’re in a baby-positive cycle.
SF The death part of the equation is the old you saying goodbye to your old life.

HW And saying hello to the mystery of what is about to begin. I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed.

SF You’ve photographed yourself before. How much of that process is about showing yourself to the world and how much is it about introspection, working out what, in this case, your pregnancy means for you?
“I have already said goodbye to my old body. It’s all very physical now. The changes being made are visual, my insides are yet to be rebirthed” – Harley Weir

HW My life is already very bump-forward. Wherever I go, it’s the focal point of conversation. It’s hard not to be obsessed by the pregnancy. At one point people argued that because the baby takes so much nutrition, the mother’s brain shrinks by 20 per cent. Now they are calling it rewiring. I’m rewiring. And my way of coping with things is photography – it’s like therapy. It’s a way for me to work out those ideas and also to detach from them. I was thinking how I’m kissing goodbye to this flat-chested girl and becoming a woman. The pregnancy at this stage is visual, the changes are reflected in the mirror. Every Wednesday I read my update that tells me how big the baby is.
SF How big is your baby now?
HW Honeydew melon. You know, it’s so silly. Apparently, there’s a dog one too.

SF How interested are you in the relationship between us as voyeurs and you as the subject? I looked at Beauty Papers. That’s overtly sexual, about fetishising women. This is almost more like you fetishising your own pregnant body.

HW I do think there’s something in the fact that I’m still a sexual being. In old tropes you become a mother and your sexiness was stripped from you. Almost as some kind gesture of respect that we never asked for. That’s what is interesting about fashion. It’s been a way to explore the female – that’s what I do. There are also many personal secrets tucked away inside the images, where they often look overly sexual – rarely my first thought, if thought about at all. There’s an undercurrent of personal meaning. Some images in the story are overlaid with pictures from my dad’s favourite beach. That’s seaweed. Mother earthing. My dad has Benson’s disease, so he’s not able to communicate any more. But I still want to include him in my life in ways that I can. It’s sad when I think of how good he would have been as a grandfather.
SF This story is so intensely autobiographical. Do you think all of your work is?

HW It is. I graduated from art school in 2010. I loved emotive art and started as a painter, which seemed to be the most primitive and uninteresting trade at the time. There was a bit of a backlash against people like Tracey Emin – who wore their heart on their sleeve. People whose work was too autobiographical, too self-involved. I loved her diary works and felt a kinship to them but my era was having a conceptual moment that I didn’t fit in with. I will always be an artist first but fashion allowed me to continue to use emotive language more freely and the impulse has never left me. There’s a picture of me with a pushchair on fire. I wanted to express the fear of being a bad mother. That’s my neighbour’s shed. It’s like a doll’s house. The dream gone wrong.
SF Very few artists have represented fear in pregnancy. Probably because they are mostly men, so maybe it’s not their place to look at that.
HW Yes, that was nice. They left it for us.
SF But being pregnant can be really frightening at times.

HW Part of the story I wanted to show was my thoughts of, oh God, am I going to be a bad mother? Am I going to drop the baby? Am I not going to love the baby? Am I going to have postpartum depression? What’s amazing is that there is so much information about those things now and people talk about it all the time.
SF That anxiety goes on for ever, I think. Did working with a body double in a mask feel strange to you?

HW So strange. Every time I look in the mirror now, I see the mask. It’s terrifying. When you ordinarily look in the mirror you see what you want to see. You think you look good or you think you look terrible. It doesn’t matter what you actually look like. I asked Chaïm, who made the mask, to get all the bits and bobs in there. Go hard on the skin blemishes. I knew they were there but when you actually see them looking back at you, it’s quite grotesque. My face like a piece of meat, you really see it that way. When I show the photos to people, they can’t understand that it’s not me in those pictures.
SF Did you do it for purely practical reasons?

HW Not only. There is something very laborious about taking a self-portrait, the tripod, the focusing etc, but I also wanted to divide myself – the divided self. She was supposed to be the idealised version of me, unstretched and glossy. It’s a shame we didn’t have more time with Anna, who wore the suffocating mask along with the fake bump and wig. There was so much more fun to be had.
SF The image with the snake is referencing Avedon’s Nastassja Kinski and the Serpent [1981]?
HW Yes. I thought that was funny. It’s my “pregnancy picture”.
SF You know the thematic of this issue of the magazine is cliché?

HW So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask.
That’s a real snake crushing me in the picture. I put make-up on in that one too, to cover the pigmentation on my face, to be the idealised pregnant woman for her pregnancy shoot.
SF And there’s an apple in another image. Eve’s apple.

HW Yes. Purity lost. And for taking the apple we must suffer in childbirth. But I actually feel purer than ever. There’s something in the body becoming so functional, it’s before shame. The instinctiveness and the nakedness of breastfeeding, for example, feels like that moment before the apple when there was no shame attached to the naked body. There’s one really disturbing breastfeeding image, the masked me breastfeeding me, the idea of a mother still needing a mother. There’s also me breastfeeding from John. Which takes the breast even further away from the sexual, because he doesn’t have one. It’s about becoming dependent on each other in a new way as a family and recognising that we all need to be nurtured.

SF You are photographing something that is transient, and by photographing it you’re fixing it in time. I suppose that is what photography is more generally, but it feels somehow more pronounced in this context.

HW The permanence is scary sometimes. I only thought about showing my child these images today. I thought maybe the baby never sees these. It’s very different because it’s still inside me. Baby out, different.
SF Do you think about that often, with explicit imagery?
HW I think about it all the time, but I try to be free. I don’t always get it right and people correct me. I like that conversation though.
SF Do people ever talk about your nudes, or look at your nudes, in a way that makes you feel uncomfortable?

HW It’s hard to put yourself out there and be judged. The real private self isn’t this though. It’s still a performance, especially in a self-portrait. Looking back, I realised I was trying to seem approachable, not too attractive or too sexy. But I’m obviously aware of the camera and that annoys me. I wanted to catch myself in a real state, but because I’m the one taking the photograph, that’s almost impossible. Some pictures are ugly because I felt I should include them, so I wouldn’t seem vain, which is probably the vainest thing you can do. In one I’m standing nicely, in another I’m slumped and badly postured. Sometimes I feel I can be quite vulgar. That’s part of me, letting people see a little too much. Not necessarily deliberately.

“So much of what I do is about cliché. The tropes of being a woman are so clichéd. If you want to put a signal out, it’s as simple as a little make-up and people treat you totally differently – it’s a totally different day, a different mask” – Harley Weir
SF And you don’t lie awake at night thinking about that.

HW Sometimes. You don’t want to read the comments too much. I don’t put much on Instagram for that reason. I would say that I have some boundaries, but the idea of vulgarity is something I subconsciously play with a lot. Or at least it seems my tolerance is higher than most. There is me covered in milk with my legs up. It reeked, because it came from France in a heatwave with Leana the make-up artist. I was trying to photograph what the baby would see coming to get the milk. Unfortunately, I didn’t get a linea nigra, the dark line that can appear when pregnant, apparently as an arrow to direct a new born to the breast.
SF There’s also the cliché of the earth mother, and that huge power, but equal to that is vulnerability.

HW Since I’ve become obviously pregnant, when I’m not with John, I don’t like walking around at nighttime. I want to be with my husband. I know most people are not thinking bad thoughts, but I feel vulnerable. There’s something of the mother earth in the photo of me feeding the fawn. This instinct to nurture, but also suggestive of how exposed motherhood can make you feel. I read that, in England, they used to use puppies to keep the milk supply going if your baby was away from you, fawns or pigs in other countries. And if your milk wasn’t working, they would bring round a donkey or a goat for the baby to suckle from.
SF Some of your self-portrait imagery displays a complete lack of vanity.

HW Art and fashion both rank quite high in the thoughts of the self. Oddly with fashion, being the voyeur that I am, possibly the less self-absorbing of the two. It’s so much about the other. It’s rare to see the photographer. We’re like ghosts haunting the image but we are never really there. I often photograph some of the most attractive people in the world and then sit with retouching comments to make them look even more attractive.
