So it’s hard to think, damn I look hot here, because in my mind, by comparison, I look like a gremlin. Me looking vain as hell to the public is probably me thinking I look real and unfiltered. It’s hard to be objective when it’s me in front of the lens but I like to think I show both sides. Perfection isn’t interesting.

Styling: Georgia Pendlebury. Hair: Alex Brownsell at Streeters using KEUNE and BLEACH LONDON. Make-up: Leana Ardeleanu at Artlist using MAKE UP FOR EVER. Mask: Chaïm Vischel. Manicure: Lauren Michelle Pires using Le Vernis in Garconne and La Crème Main by CHANEL BEAUTY. Set design: Phoebe Shakespeare. Casting: Gabrielle Lawrence for People-File at MiniTitle. Model: Anna Ramfel. Talent: John Kelleher. Studio manager: Melissa Arras. Lighting director: Jordan Lee. Photographic assistants: Chiara Croserio and JJay Johnson. Styling assistants: Ethan Barbara, Michiel Heemskerk and Stoyan Chuchuranov. Hair assistant: Tommy Stayton. Make-up assistant: Gwen Ryan. Set-design assistants: Freya Purkhardt and Keelin Coyle. Charting fashion from the 19th century to the Nineties to now, the stylist Panos Yiapanis combines garments from his own personal archive with pieces from Pieter Mulier’s five-year tenure at Alaïa. The approach connects Yiapanis, Mulier and Azzedine Alaïa himself – all collectors of historical and contemporary fashion – via a shared passion for clothes of the past, present and future.

items.title: Swizz Beatz's furniture collection for CB2 was designed to help people 'tune into themselves'
items.description: For Kasseem Dean, the Grammy Award-winning rapper and producer best known as Swizz Beatz, furniture and family go hand in hand. He remembers, as a kid growing up in the Bronx, the squeak of the plastic that covered his grandmother’s couch and the ritual that a
items.author: Anna Fixsen
paragraphs: For Kasseem Dean, the Grammy Award-winning rapper and producer best known as Swizz Beatz, furniture and family go hand in hand. He remembers, as a kid growing up in the Bronx, the squeak of the plastic that covered his grandmother’s couch and the ritual that accompanied her record cabinet, which also conveniently concealed adults-only barware.

‘Furniture’s always been a language of family,’ Dean tells Wallpaper* from his home in Harlem, one of several the mogul owns alongside his wife, fellow Grammy-winner Alicia Keys. ‘For me growing up, it was like, “Come sit down, come have a talk.” But furniture was always to be respected as well.’

All of those memories, not to mention decades spent amassing one of the world’s most significant collections of Black art, have informed Dean’s latest venture, a furniture collection in partnership with the contemporary home decor brand CB2. The collection, which comprises furniture, lighting and decorative accessories, is appropriately named for the producer’s family: Casa Dean. ‘I didn't want to just do something just to do it,’ Dean says. ‘My thing was more like, if we're gonna do it, what's the concept? What hole are we filling? And how can this inspire people?’

Dean’s fascination with design grew as he found success as a teenager, first as a DJ and later, at the ripe age of 18, the producer of DMX’s hit ‘Ruff Ryders' Anthem’. Dean jokingly recalls decorating his first home: ‘At that time there was no taste involved. It was just like, is it expensive? OK, I need that couch. What's the name brand of it? Gucci? OK, let's get it.’

But as his renown grew, Dean began to develop his own taste. ‘My style has grown tremendously throughout the years from travelling and seeing different walks of life,’ he says. ‘I'm just a creature of culture.’

In the Casa Dean collection, those sensibilities manifest in the line’s variety of colours, textures and silhouettes. There’s a curvaceous chair in a woolly taupe shearling; a linear console table topped with red enamel; a green velvet modular sofa with a gently swooping silhouette; artwork created in collaboration with artist Megan Gabrielle Harris; and bubbly barware in smoked crystal.

‘I love where I landed with the diversity of the collection and the colours and the palettes,’ Dean says. ‘That took guidance. That took being open-minded and not just coming in with the fake celebrity energy. I was more of a student.’
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

That’s because designing furniture didn’t come into the picture until recently. Keys’ nail tech, the celebrity manicurist Dawn Sterling, introduced Dean to a mutual connection at CB2. ‘Next thing you know, I was in Chicago looking at fabrics,’ the rapper jokes.

Working alongside designer Evan Jerry of Studio Anansi, the collection began to evolve. ‘Swizz was especially thoughtful about the experience of each piece. How does a sofa sit? How does a material feel? How does the furniture encourage people to gather and connect?’ says Andrea Erman, CB2’s senior director of design and development for housewares. ‘He was equally interested in the emotional experience of a space as he was in the visual impact.’

‘People take furniture so [lightly], but just with this hands-on process with CB2 and their amazing team that they surrounded me with, I really got a front-row seat to the movie called “furniture”,’ Dean adds. The Dean family even got a front-row seat: he and Keys would review drawings and photos at the family dinner table.

Each piece in the Casa Dean collection is meant to foster what Dean calls ‘the creative home’. There are items that especially resonate with him, like the ‘Lam-Louie’ credenza, named for his father, who also worked as a DJ alongside hip-hop pioneer Cool Herc, that doubles as a DJ set-up. And a chair that’s designed exclusively for solo daydreaming. His favourite colour, British racing green, pops up throughout.

‘I just want people to just tune into themselves with this collaboration,’ Dean reflects. ‘The world is moving so fast and there's so much uncertainty that when you sit on this couch, or when you plug your set-up into this DJ set, or put some ice in this amazing bucket, you're doing it to reflect yourself.’

Anna Fixsen is a Brooklyn-based editor and journalist with 13 years of experience reporting on architecture, design, and the way we live. Before joining the Wallpaper* team as the US Editor, she was the Deputy Digital Editor of ELLE DECOR, where she oversaw all aspects of the magazine’s digital footprint.

items.title: CMF bring their playful minimalism into portable audio with Speaker S and Speaker M
items.description: With their milk carton-inspired form factor and on point selection of colour finishes, the new Speaker S and Speaker M from CMF offer up a tantalisingly affordable piece of audio equipment for the younger generation. This is the first time that CMF – Nothing’s
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: With their milk carton-inspired form factor and on point selection of colour finishes, the new Speaker S and Speaker M from CMF offer up a tantalisingly affordable piece of audio equipment for the younger generation. This is the first time that CMF – Nothing’s India-based sub-brand best known for their smartphones, watches and headphones – has ventured into the realm of portable audio.

The two sizes are self-explanatory (half a litre and a litre, for those still thinking about milk), and the speakers play nicely with each other via a special Stereo Mode and Party Mode, encouraging you to acquire a pair. In fact, it’s more of a set, given CMF have lived up to their name and dug deep into their palette bag to conjure up four delightful hues for each size, White, Dark Grey, Orange and Turquoise.

More playful in tone than Nothing, which tends to over-emphasise the tech within, CMF is about reduce functions to the most minimally appropriate forms. Both speakers therefore have simple and swappable front panels and knobs to further mix up the available chromatic options. On top of that, the company is encouraging 3D-printer owners to go while and add another layer of personalisation.

Both speakers include Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity, strong IP68 protection dust and water resistance rating and have an impressive maximum battery life of up to 18 hours in ideal conditions. Naturally, the larger speaker is the louder, with the smaller S targeted at desk workers who want a colourful audio companion that looks good even when there’s nothing on.
Both come with an Ultra Bass mode and can be further tuned through the Nothing X app. Charging is via USB-C, which also offers audio compatibility for ultra-low-latency playback (good for gaming).

The sizing guide suggests a Speaker L might be in the works for even more power, but for the time being you’ll have to make do with the custom-tuned 45 mm full-range driver and dual passive radiators in Speaker S (up to 10W output) and a dual-driver (25W woofer and 10W tweeter) in the Speaker M.
CMF Speaker S, $59, CMF Speaker M, $109, nothing.tech, @nothing

Jonathan Bell has written for Wallpaper* magazine since 1999, covering everything from architecture and transport design to books, tech and graphic design. He is now the magazine’s Transport and Technology Editor. Jonathan has written and edited 15 books, including Concept Car Design, 21st Century House, and The New Modern House, and co-edits the long-running things magazine weblog.

items.title: The Sony Walkman is back – and its latest models cost up to £4,299
items.description: Sony was once the GOAT of all things related to portable audio, a title it’s had to relinquish in the face of hundreds of new challengers. Whilst the Japanese giant made hay in the compact cassette and CD era, it subsequently struggled valiantly with its super
items.author: Jonathan Bell
paragraphs: Sony was once the GOAT of all things related to portable audio, a title it’s had to relinquish in the face of hundreds of new challengers. Whilst the Japanese giant made hay in the compact cassette and CD era, it subsequently struggled valiantly with its superior but overlooked MiniDisc format and then watched everything go to pot as mp3s rose in popularity and Apple stepped forward to create the definitive player and ecosystem.

It’s not that Sony ever stepped back from the format, or that its mp3 players haven’t been any good, but for two and a half decades the zeitgeist has largely passed it by. With renewed interest in all things mp3, from affordable ultra compact players to a new wave of premium players from the likes of Astell&Kern, Sony wants to be back in the game.

These are updated versions of Sony’s two premium Walkman models, the NW-WM1ZM3 and NW-WM1AM3. They sit at the very pinnacle of Sony’s portable range, with prices to match, and compare only to a handful of other dedicated mp3 players. In short, we’re in true audiophile territory here, and whilst those of not blessed with golden ears will thrill to upgrades like the larger 5.5” touchscreen and 31-hour battery life, the real improvements are under the skin.

Build quality is clearly second to none, and Sony hasn’t scrimped on components either. To minimise noise and maximise sound quality, the company has used materials like oxygen-free copper and gold-plate. This is particularly evident in the NW-WM1ZM3, which uses a precision-machined, gold-plated oxygen-free copper (OFC) chassis (and a gold surface finish to match).

It’s joined by the NW-WM1AM3, which has to make do with aluminium-alloy for the main chassis (with gold-plated OFC on the rear). Improvements to power supply and circuitry is said to bring other big audio quality wins, with Sony’s onboard DSD Remastering Engine capable of upgrading digital files to give them a more analogue quality.

All this is slightly undermined by Sony decision to only cite playback times using low-quality 128kpps mp3 files, anathema to most fans of high-fidelity (although good for over 60,000 songs, given the player’s onboard 207GB of storage). Even if you only use files in the maximum lossless FLAC format, the new Walkmen are still good for around 10,000 songs. Streaming audio abilities also come as standard.

Alas, we’re in the realm of perception now, and while both players have characteristically high-quality finishes, a straightforward interface that combines a touchscreen with physical transport and volume buttons, the positive improvements netted by the circuitry, hand-soldering and absence of oxygen will only make a difference to a very small coterie of hardcore audiophiles.

items.title: Apple's Designers of Tomorrow invite us to slow down
items.description: 'Good design minds are always, fundamentally, surprising,' says Rodman Primack, who returns as curator for this year's Designers of Tomorrow at Design Miami Paris. 'It’s why we need them: not for the mundane - to find the most efficient choice - but to offer a
items.author: Ali Morris
paragraphs: 'Good design minds are always, fundamentally, surprising,' says Rodman Primack, who returns as curator for this year's Designers of Tomorrow at Design Miami Paris. 'It’s why we need them: not for the mundane - to find the most efficient choice - but to offer an idea that deviates from the standard.'

Led by Apple in collaboration with Design Miami Paris, the showcase brings together four emerging design practices from around the world to create original works around a theme. This year's topic, Design for Presence, seems particularly pertinent in the era of the attention economy.
Apple's Designers of Tomorrow 2026 explore presence

Displayed across a panelled room in Paris’ Hôtel de Maisons, the thoughtful, highly crafted objects reflect this theme, inviting us to slow our pace – to bask in the soft glow of a lantern by Egyptian-Danish architect Salem S. Charabi, listen to the ceramic beaded fringe on Brooklyn-based designer Isabel Rower’s chair, marvel at the intricacy of Seoul-based artist Yoonjeong Lee’s table and lamp, or share a moment of connection within Mexican design studio Parafernalia’s expandable seating area.

Primack – a designer, curator, former creative director of Design Miami and co-founder of Mexico City gallery AGO Projects – sees a common desire to make something meaningful, despite the four studios’ ‘fundamentally different’ approaches, materials and local contexts.

'I do think designers, not just this years cohort of Designers Of Tomorrow, are seeing that our lives need shape and boundaries and that they can help us by creating objects and circumstances that allow for grounding, for communion with ourselves or each other by inviting contemplation, or the sharing of an experience, or actual presence through physical sensation,' he reflects.

The 2026 cohort was handpicked by a jury made up of figures working across the creative industries – including Alexandra Cunningham Cameron, Fabien Cappello, Jennifer Dunlop Fletcher, Minjae Kim, Hun Chung Lee, Marion Mailaender, Nifemi Marcus-Bello, Jennifer Roberts, and Apple’s Molly Anderson. All four of the selected practices used Apple tools and platforms, from iPads to Apple pencils, to develop their pieces.
Wallpaper caught up with each studio to find out how this new generation of designers is thinking about materiality, making and human experience.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.
Salem S. Charabi, Cairo, Egypt

Charabi's lantern, 'The Emergence of Light', is made from everyday materials found around his Cairo studio, including a limestone base and a banana paper diffuser. The lantern's delicate skeleton frame is made by stacking date palm fronds using a traditional Japanese method.
Wallpaper*: How did the idea for 'The Emergence of Light' emerge?
Salem S. Charabi: Our first point of gathering was around the fire. I wanted to create this totem of light, to celebrate the moment the days turns to night.
W*: Can you tell us about the making process?
SC: Each strand is an octagon in profile – just 3 millimetres wide, split by hand, and carefully drilled. The ends are then sharpened with a chisel to interlock.

For this project, every component had to be mapped out in detail. I sketched and did all the 3D modelling on my MacBook Pro. It was a complex process getting everything to fit just right — from the carving of the stone and the paper moulds, down to the delicate base.
W*: How will it encourage people to slow down?
SC: I think innately, observing light slows us down. The way its reflected on the moon, the way it may hit the crown of a tree. It makes us wonder.
Isabel Rower, New York, USA

The dramatic proportions of Rower's 'The Padded Chair 1860' draw on 18th- and 19th-century papier-mâché furniture and objets d’art. Its high-gloss finish stands in sharp contrast to its ceramic beaded fringe, chosen for the appealing sound it makes when brushed.
W*: How did 'The Padded Chair 1860' begin?

Isabel Rower: A few years ago I took a photograph of a boudoir chair from the 1860s in the Musée des Arts Décoratifs in Paris. I found the form highly unconventional and I was drawn to its dramatic fringed skirt. When faced with the prompt of ‘Design for Presence’, I felt that this chair was the perfect object to revisit. Ceramics are not simply a medium but a transmission of thought: a way of communicating ideas and variations through touch, and of constantly reworking the material to generate something new.

I was interested in how swapping the textile fringe of the historic object for a skirt of over 1,500 ceramic beads would not only bring it into a contemporary present, but would bring the person sitting into a state of presence.
W*: How do you imagine the piece will encourage people to slow down?

IR: I investigate emulation and the stories of surfaces, drawing from 18th and 19th century papier-mâché furniture and objets d’art. The chair will offer a passage from the surface to interior histories. The sound of the ceramic beaded fringe when brushed against brings awareness to its materiality. It also works to bring the body that is brushing against it into a space of curiosity and presence. It moves sitting from being a passive activity to an activating one.
Yoonjeong Lee, Seoul, South Korea

The base of Lee's 'New Form' – a wooden table with an integrated lamp – is made from roughly 5,000 thin sheets of stacked veneer. Sheets of paper serve as a lampshade held in place by a trio of worn-down pencils that have been given new life as hardware.
W*: How did 'New Form' take shape?

Yoonjeong Lee: I’ve been making nails for a long time. The reason is simple: I wanted to turn something called a 'fitting', a mere part, into something more meaningful and independent. My work is about looking closely at objects that need to be seen differently.

One day, I was looking at a pencil that was almost used up, and I noticed its shape looked like a nail. A pencil doesn’t disappear as it wears down. It stays on in a new form: as a letter, as knowledge, as music. For me, it stayed on as a nail.
I made a nail from the worn-down pencil and used it as hardware. That small piece of hardware became the starting point, and the work took shape step by step from there.
W*: How does the theme, 'Design for Presence', show up in the work?

YL: I approached the future differently. Usually, we set a goal first, picture what the result will look like, and plan the process around it. I stepped back from that and focused on what I was doing right now. I finished the smallest unit in front of me first, and decided the next step based on the result. What we build by focusing on the present adds up to the future. Tomorrow is built on what I did today.

I spend more time looking at what’s around me, and I think that improves my focus on the moment and the quality of my work. This piece was made that way too. It started from one pencil nail. I chose materials that suited it, and used them to decide what the piece would do. I made the wood for the pencil nail from scratch as well.

Instead of carving a log, I stacked thin veneer, one layer at a time. These choices built up one by one, and the piece came together. The finished piece shows the theme, but I think it also matters that I practiced this year’s theme myself, through the process.
W*: How do you imagine people interacting with your piece?

YL: Grand, heavy, epic narratives are certainly important in their own way. But I like a modest ripple. Something moderate, small, slight, yet with an unexpected impact. That’s why I work with familiar objects and prefer physically small ones.

My pencil and nail works are small, so people sometimes walk past them in the exhibition space without noticing. That’s not a problem. If I can share a moment with the person who does find them, that is enough. I think a work made with a focus on something small has a certain pull. At first the overall form catches the eye, but gradually it draws people closer to the small details.

As people look at the pencil nails, each material, and the many layers of the wood, what makes up the whole slowly begins to come into view. When people realise that the pencil nail was originally a pencil, I hope some of them will remember the pencils they used.

A pencil carries memories that many people share, but within that, everyone has their own personal ones. I can’t predict which memory it will be. But following that memory, even briefly, can be a way of staying in the moment, or with the time that has passed.
Parafernalia, Monterrey and Mexico City, Mexico

Parafernalia founders Genki Matsumura and Sebastián Zorrilla conceived 'MonoAmbiente 1' as an intimate setting, where two people can converse, play chess, or share a drink. When not in use, the expandable seating area – consisting of a table and two stools and featuring acid-etched stainless steel surfaces – can be neatly folded away.
W*: Where did the idea for 'MonoAmbiente 1' come from?

Parafernalia: We interpreted 'Design for Presence' as an invitation to look at the different ways presence can occur: in solitude, in our relationship to our surroundings, and in moments shared with others. This led us to explore an object that could move between these states, from a landscape that invites observation when closed, to a space for conversation and shared activity when deployed.

Conversation is rarely an isolated activity. We talk while we play, eat, drink, walk, or cook. In this piece, the accompanying activities create the conditions for dialogue rather than defining it. The deployment of the piece marks a shift from solitary observation to shared occupation, from looking to participating.
W*: How did the theme ‘Design for Presence’ shape your choice of materials?

Parafernalia: The material selection was mainly based on what we’re personally interested in at the moment, and the decision was cemented once we determined that etched stainless steel could embody different intentions and qualities, from the decorative to the functional, and that these characteristics would be present in the piece. The high contrast graphic nature of the process invites onlookers to observe with a bit more attention, a bit more closely.
W*: How do you imagine people will interact with your piece?

Parafernalia: For starters, we imagine the piece will be difficult to digest at first – there's a lot going on. The piece is deployable, it is a foldout table and 2 stools that nest underneath, completing the landscape etched in the steel. This produces curiosity and invites close inspection. It makes taking your time and slowing down a necessity in order to fully understand the what’s going on.

We hope it will be fully interacted with, and explored with curiosity. A lot of thought was put into the different details in different parts of the piece and we expect the discovery of each one to be an activity in itself.
Design Miami and Apple Designers of Tomorrow is on view at Design Miami Paris, 21-25 October 2026
Hôtel de Maisons, 51, rue de l’Université, 75007 Paris, France

items.title: Potato Head’s new Balinese store is a model for ‘post-consumption retail’
items.description: Balinese hospitality brand Potato Head opens the Good Times General Store, its first dedicated retail space, designed in collaboration with its longstanding creative partner, the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA). Building on the pair’s shared explora
items.author: Yoko Choy
paragraphs: Balinese hospitality brand Potato Head opens the Good Times General Store, its first dedicated retail space, designed in collaboration with its longstanding creative partner, the Office for Metropolitan Architecture (OMA). Building on the pair’s shared exploration of circularity, the project marks the most developed expression yet of their commitment to using design as a vehicle for social and environmental good.
The Good Times General Store at Potato Head, Bali

Conceived as a model for ‘post-consumption retail’, the store challenges the conventional relationship between retailer, product and consumer. ‘The retail landscape is increasingly defined by experience rather than the possession of physical objects. Today, value lies less in what we own and more in what we feel and participate in,’ says David Gianotten, managing partner at OMA.

The new structure sits between the Desa Potato Head Bali hotel, which marked the beginning of the creative partnership more than a decade ago, and its beach club, an early expression of Potato Head’s distinctive approach to hospitality and design (which also extends to nightclub Klymax Discotheque). The store offers a new point of entry, both literally and figuratively, for visitors who may be less familiar with the brand’s established hospitality and entertainment offerings.

Gianotten describes the building’s material language as ‘contemporary-traditional’, integrating local building traditions into contemporary design. Roofing thatch is reinterpreted as an exterior finish, and rammed-earth walls feature smooth and bush-hammered finishes that reveal the earth’s raw character and the craftsmanship involved.

The rectangular structure is organised into five linear bays, bringing together products and opportunities to engage with the processes behind them. The first three bays present objects by independent makers from Indonesia and beyond, Potato Head’s in-house apparel and ‘Wasted’, a collection developed with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homeware. The remaining two focus on making: a natural-dye studio that uses food and plant waste, and a workshop for experimenting with recycled plastic collected by waste-pickers across Bali and Java.

The workshops sit at the heart of the store’s retail concept, with lightweight, movable elements allowing the interior to be reconfigured for different uses. ‘We see the space as something that will continue to develop through the people who use it,’ says Dan Mitchell, creative director of Potato Head. ‘The flexibility allows us to change the scale and use of different areas, to bring together the different expressions of the brand: music, art, design, food and wellbeing.’

‘The idea is to encourage people to think more consciously about consumption without diminishing the pleasure,’ says Gianotten. ‘The principle of “Good Times, Do Good” has guided our collaboration from the beginning.’ Over the years, their work has evolved into an ecosystem in which hospitality, design and environmental responsibility inform one another.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

Next in Potato Head’s creative universe is a sanggar in Bali, a space for learning and practising the arts, with a focus on the performing arts. ‘It’s going to be a bamboo dome (designed by Indonesian architect Nano Uhero),’ says Ronald Akili, the driving force behind Potato Head. ‘The team will work with artists from across Indonesia and Balinese performers to develop programmes and residencies.’ A design centre is also in the works, with a materials library, exhibition spaces and studios for designers to undertake residencies and develop new work. Both projects are scheduled to open in 2027.

Yoko Choy is the China editor at Wallpaper* magazine, where she has contributed for over a decade. Her work has also been featured in numerous Chinese and international publications. As a creative and communications consultant, Yoko has worked with renowned institutions such as Art Basel and Beijing Design Week, as well as brands such as Hermès and Assouline. With dual bases in Hong Kong and Amsterdam, Yoko is an active participant in design awards judging panels and conferences, where she shares her mission of promoting cross-cultural exchange and translating insights from both the Eastern and Western worlds into a common creative language. Yoko is currently working on several exciting projects, including a sustainable lifestyle concept and a book on Chinese contemporary design.

items.title: A conversation with Eileen Myles for Apartamento magazine issue #37
items.description: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful w
items.author: Valeria Tusquets
paragraphs: Marfa: ‘For a time I / stole trays / from hotels / & now I steal / cups’ writes Eileen Myles in ‘Göteborg’, a poem which becomes a love letter to desire itself. I wonder if any of the stolen objects exist in Eileen’s real world: ‘Yeah, and it was a beautiful wooden tray. That lives here’. Despite famously moving to New York City to become a poet in 1974, a metropolis which serves as the backdrop for much of their work, in this instance, ‘here’ is Marfa, Texas. Situated in North America’s largest desert with a population currently under 2,000, Marfa became a magnet for creatives after the artist Donald Judd moved there from New York in the ‘70s, and there has been an uneasy truce between outsiders and locals since then. Jokingly referred to as their ‘fortress of solitude’, Eileen’s Marfa home looks like many on their street, with a pickup truck parked outside a chain-link fence and little city blocks of prickly pear cactus dotted around their lot.

Eileen’s work has been translated into dozens of languages, and they have published more than 20 books across poetry, fiction, and nonfiction, earning them a Guggenheim Fellowship and an Andy Warhol Foundation Arts Writers Grant. One of Eileen’s many superpowers as a writer is their ability to marry first-person narrative with more ephemeral truths, or, as they say, ‘trusting the mechanism of desire…[the] desire for certain language to sit over some curve of a moment’. This realness, coupled with writing about a character named ‘Eileen Myles’, has also led to being flattened by labels—another Charles Bukowski or Patti Smith—as they slid between poetry and prose. ‘I have a specific system that downplays grammar in a lot of ways’, they say, but their system of delaying any easy resolution is also grammatical; there’s a really tight thought, but they don’t let it resolve immediately. We are taken away, shown something new. The action is deferred until the text realises its necessary climax.

Inside their home, cut-outs between rooms create a flow where kitchen peeks into office peeks into bedroom peeks into living room. A big picture window in their office, paid for when the show Transparent bought some of Eileen’s poems and based a poet character on them, looks out into the yard towards their ‘writing shack’ which sports a clawfoot bathtub, a bench press and weights, and a desk facing double sliding doors out onto the porch where we sit and sip Topo Chico. While access to DC Comics’ original Fortress of Solitude is controlled by a key carved from super-dense dwarf star material weighing half a million tonnes—imagine lifting 100 elephants or the weight of a small cloud—Eileen’s own abode is guarded by three desert-coloured pups who sound an imposing alarm when we pull up.

items.title: PRE-ORDER: Making a Show, Sabine Marcelis
items.description: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed
paragraphs: Making a Show is a photobook with Dutch artist and designer Sabine Marcelis, published on the occasion of her first museum exhibition at Museum für Gestaltung Zürich, Sabine Marcelis—Light and Color, on view from October 30, 2026 to April 4, 2027. Photographed by Mattia Balsamini inside Sabine’s Rotterdam studio in the months before the opening, the book documents an exhibition in transit: light, colour, and material stretched, poured, altered, and refined until they reach the simplicity that is Sabine’s fingerprint. Smashed mirrors, pink resin slabs, perfect droplets—all part of a symbiotic world, where the work produced inside the studio is in constant conversation with the hands that supply it from outside. Alongside, curator Damian Fopp grounds the book with a written introspection on living inside her universe as the show took shape, declaring by the end that ‘what appears effortless is anything but’. Punctuated by WhatsApp messages and email snapshots between Sabine’s team and the museum’s, Making a Show distils the incantatory movement of an exhibition in the making and the infrastructure of people behind it.

Sabine Marcelis is a Dutch artist and designer based in Rotterdam. Working across installations, objects, and spatial projects, she explores light, colour, and material, collaborating closely with a network of local manufacturers to push each to its limits. For the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival 2026, Sabine designed one of the headlining large-scale art installations, an immersive temporary installation titled Maze. She has also received multiple Designer of the Year honours (2020–2024) and her works are part of permanent museum collections worldwide, including MoMA, the Stedelijk Museum, and the Vitra Design Museum. Sabine Marcelis was previously featured in Apartamento magazine issue #21. Find her story from our digital archive here.

Mattia Balsamini is an Italian photographer based between London and Milan. After joining David LaChapelle’s studio in 2010 as a studio assistant and archivist, Mattia went on to develop personal and editorial projects through collaborations with institutions including MIT and NASA. His work has been exhibited at the Triennale di Milano, MAXXI, the Sandretto Re Rebaudengo Foundation, and the Italian Cultural Institute in San Francisco.

items.title: The Complete Works of Le Chateaubriand (2006–2026)
items.description: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photoc
paragraphs: This is the story of Le Chateaubriand, the Paris bistro that broke every rule fine dining had. In 2006, Inaki Aizpitarte and Frédéric Peneau took over a humble, century-old bistro in Paris’ 11th arrondissement. Untucked shirts, stubble, blaring music, a photocopied piece of paper as a menu: punk star chef Inaki and his disciples triggered a tsunami of gastronomic insurrection, launching ‘bistronomy’ and its devious subculture. Le Chateaubriand, originally published in French in 2024 and now translated into English by Florence Beretta and Christine Muhlke, is a memorialisation of their labyrinthine quest for adventure, experimentation, and a really good time.

Inside, a chorus of your favourite chefs’ favourite chefs, critics, regulars, and fundamental players document the uncanny dishes, drunk escapades, Michelin stars, and one-star reviews of a restaurant so notorious the conformists loosened their buttons for it.

As Inaki bows out, two decades later, he leaves behind a mythical record of an indisputable marathon to achieve something unheard of in the 2000s kitchen: freedom. At Le Chateaubriand, the customer is not always right.

Chef Inaki Aizpitarte, the son of Basque immigrants, grew up in Besançon and Bordeaux in the south of France. In 1999, at the age of 27, he travelled to Tel Aviv where he began washing dishes in a restaurant kitchen and discovered his passion for cooking. He moved to Paris in the early 2000s, where he worked at various establishments across the city, including Le Petit Marguery, La Fourchette des Anges, Ishtar Café, Le Café des Délices, La Famille in Montmartre, and Le Baratin. He then helped launch the restaurant at the MAC VAL contemporary art museum in Vitry-sur-Seine.

In 2006, he opened Le Chateaubriand at 129 Avenue Parmentier. His second venture, Le Dauphin, opened in 2010, two doors down from Le Chateaubriand. More recently, he opened Petit Grill Basque, this time in Saint-Jean-de-Luz, in the French Basque Country. Over the years, Aizpitarte has become widely regarded as the ‘godfather of bistronomy’, helping to redefine the Parisian dining scene through his distinctive, informal approach to fine dining.

items.title: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G
items.description: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag
paragraphs: Twenty-One Conversations with Architects by Arquitectura-G has been added to your shopping bag

Twenty-One Conversations with Architects brings together more than a decade and a half’s worth of interviews conducted by Barcelona-based architecture firm Arquitectura-G, published in Apartamento magazine since its very first issue in 2008. Expansive, technical, submerged, the book threads together some of architecture’s most singular minds, crossing decades, archives, disciplines, and countries, and placing multiple generations of architects side by side in a single volume. What started as a takeover of the magazine’s architecture section has now become something else entirely: a portrait of the studio itself, their own obsessions surfacing across every conversation—questions of scale, ambiguity, hedonism, bathrooms, dances, the house as a laboratory. As they open these interviews to the anthology, the architects unfold a series of choices in houses and homes that are deeply personal to those who conceived them, united by their fundamental questioning of universal needs answered by universal forms. What ties these houses together is something beyond architecture—less about having built them, and more about having gone on living inside the questions they raised. Twenty-one conversations later, Arquitectura-G draws each architect into a new one—curated together, and compiled by Moisés Puente, they are now asked to speak to each other across time.

Arquitectura-G is a Barcelona-based architecture studio founded in 2006 by Jonathan Arnabat, Jordi Ayala-Bril, Igor Urdampilleta, and Aitor Fuentes. Their practice spans ephemeral installations, residential projects, retail, and urban planning, with work published widely in international media. In 2015 they received the prestigious 2015 Mies Van der Rohe Award for Emerging Architects. They also teach, returning to the school where they first met. Since 2008 they have edited the architecture section of Apartamento magazine, a collaboration that also traces the development of their critical thinking.

items.title: ADRIEN BRODY - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star
paragraphs: Special rendezvous with the precise American movie star

Twenty-two years after he became the youngest ever winner of a best actor Oscar, for ‘The Pianist’, Adrien Brody has gone and done it again, this time taking home an Academy Award for his deeply moving performance as Hungarian architect László Toth in ‘The Brutalist’. What makes it all the more remarkable is that only a few years ago Adrien had all but given up acting. The awards are much deserved, of course. Adrien, 52, is an intense and uniquely gifted actor, which also makes him entertaining company. He doesn’t do things in half measures. He’s all in, all the time, and not afraid to speak his mind. In the following story Adrien engages in some energetic verbal ping-pong and gets dressed up in fashion by his friend Thom Browne. It captures some of the essence of what makes him such an incredible performer.
From Fantastic Man n° 40 – 2025
Photography by ILYA LIPKIN

The instant Adrien Brody sweeps into the room, he begins to express what I will soon come to think of as his resting affect: a kind of intense but fuzzy gratitude. “I just got back from London yesterday night,” he tells me. “Feeling very blessed with all the love that’s been coming my way. It’s a really special moment. It really is.” Maybe it’s just for now, in these hectic weeks promoting ‘The Brutalist’ ahead of the Academy Awards, but it’s with words like these that Brody seems at his most comfortable, and throughout our conversation he will periodically return to similar sentiments, restating and expanding upon them with evident sincerity.

With other kinds of words, though, it will often come to feel as though there are fault lines everywhere. Seconds after this initial declaration, I ask Brody – my question intended as little more than small talk to fill the empty space between us as we greet each other and take our seats – whether it feels like he’s being carried away in a whirlwind. He responds – not just in his words but in his body language too – as though he’s being somehow misunderstood or as though something wonderful is at risk of being spoiled.

“No, it’s not that at all,” he says, correcting me firmly. “No, my feet are on the ground. I’m ultra-present. I’m ultra-present and able to reciprocate the love. It’s different. Being older gives you a degree of perspective. It’s been a very long time since I’ve had an opportunity to do the work that I’m yearning to do. And the work is completed. So this is just something magical.”

Brody will prove to be engaging, fascinating company, and a man with plenty to say. In our conversation there will also be moments where he exudes a sense – verbally, but also through a repertoire of expressions that seem to hover between saddened and harried – that the world doesn’t quite get him.

What I then find myself wondering is whether such a sensibility might be a consequence of setbacks and reversals he has faced along his idiosyncratic chosen path, or whether it’s such a sensibility which sends you down that path in the first place. Conversely, I also find myself wondering whether it’s exactly this kind of off-kilter mindset which, when everything comes together in just the right way, somehow fuels Brody’s singular ability to inhabit and transmit a role like ‘The Brutalist’s’ László Toth with such compelling, all-consuming mastery.

It was back in 2019 when Adrien Brody was first given the script of ‘The Brutalist’, the expansive tale of a visionary Hungarian architect who escapes the Holocaust and makes his way to America, where he finds a new life – one of opportunity, but also one with horrors all of its own. Brody read it in the apartment he and his partner, fashion designer Georgina Chapman, then had in Manhattan. “I found myself very moved by the writing and the breadth of the storytelling, the complexity, the flaws of the character,” he remembers. “The opportunity for me to play someone that is experiencing so much and contending so much in life [was] wonderful. And I did consider parallels of László’s lived experience with my mother’s and my grandparents’ journey.” Brody’s mother, whose maternal grandparents were rounded up and taken to Auschwitz, survived the war in Budapest. She escaped in 1956, at the age of 13, buried under corn in a horse-drawn cart as she and her parents crossed the Austrian border. In New York, Brody grew up around his Hungarian grandparents. “So that, too, definitely is evident to me in reading it – saying: ‘Wow, I’m quite right to play this character.’”

After reading, Brody met with the director, Brady Corbet, who had written the script with his professional and personal partner, the filmmaker and actor Mona Fastvold, for brunch downtown. “A very long meeting – conversed a lot about lots of things,” Brody recalls. Nonetheless, he learned in due course that another actor had been chosen. “The message comes from your agent,” he says. “It’s either you get the message or they hope you’ve forgotten.” That’s the pattern. “I mourned the loss of this one,” he says. “I did not have expectations that it would be what it is today – I still mourned the creative loss of what I wanted to pour into it.”

Brody makes clear that over his career he has learned that this will happen, and maybe even why. “As an actor, you may be right for certain roles and you’re not necessarily eligible for them,” he says. “Even if you are quite a well-known actor and quite a successful actor. Because there are all these factors that are out of your control. You know, there are lists, and lists are based on a number of things that one might deem as an indication of success. Right? You know, consistent box office earnings are the primary reason you would be on the top of a list. But if you do make experimental choices and interesting choices in an artistic pursuit in a business, it’s not met with the same appreciation as, you know, your mother might have for your varied tastes.”

Brody points out that he’s balanced experimentation with “big blockbuster movies,” and that he enjoys those too. “But I like the range,” he says, and his suggestion seems to be that too much range has consequences. “I’m aware of how it has made certain things, such as this even, challenging,” he says. “Where I’m probably the most right performer for the role, but I wasn’t deemed valuable enough.”

This time, thankfully, everything eventually worked out. The film’s shoot was delayed several times, in part because of Covid, and by the time the project fell back in place the actor previously scheduled to play László Toth, Joel Edgerton, was no longer available. Brody heard from his agent that the role was back in play. Even then, it wasn’t as though Brody simply got a call saying the part was his. “No, not at all,” he says. “Not at all.” In the end, though, it was. Finally given the chance, he threw himself into it. “I knew we were making something special,” he says. “I wish I knew why things come when they do. This moment is because we’re very fortunate – all of us who have been involved in this project – that every collaborative creative element lifted up the other.”

It’s around now, a few minutes into our meeting, when another question seems to throw Brody, though this time the person asking is not me. It is the waiter, asking what Brody might like to eat or drink. From Brody’s reaction, you could easily think that he finds such an inquiry – at a pre-booked table by the window in a high-end New York hotel bar – somewhat perplexing. He talks aloud through this latest dilemma. “I’m not sure what I’m needing,” he says, then considers one kind of option. “I’m happy to have a drink,” he weighs, “but I’m also not needing it just yet.” He expands this thought. “I don’t really need anything.”
After vacillating further, he orders an oak milk decaf latte.
“Not too much milk,” he adds. “Just nice and strong.”

That ‘The Brutalist’ would allow Brody such a remarkable professional and creative renaissance is all the more marked given the place he has described finding himself in in recent years: sufficiently dejected by the opportunities coming his way that he had, unannounced, more or less turned his back on movies. As he recently put it, “I didn’t announce I was retiring, but I stepped back.” For a time, he concentrated on other artistic pursuits that he found more fulfilling, principally painting.

“I’ve been doing this so long, since I was a boy,” he says when I ask about that period. “There’s an ebb and flow in everything, in your own creative connections and personally, professionally in life, right? So I also was not under any illusion that it should just flow. But I found it oddly challenging to be up against things like this. I feel that I’ve proven my range. I’ve worked. The reason it seems inconsistent is I’ve been consistent in trying to break out of the box of subjective perception of what I am capable of doing, or what I represent for a character, or physically. Whatever it is. Too specific, often. And they find that…” He pauses, considering his words. “There’s a safer option, basically.”
“It wasn’t being reciprocated, for whatever reason,” he says. “It wasn’t. What I had to give was somehow not understood or not of value. I didn’t feel that I was of service and of value.”
How did that lack of reciprocation make him feel?

“I didn’t feel like I needed to prove that I was worth it. If I wasn’t, I’m going to go do something else that makes me feel good. I work primarily to feel connected and to feel immersed in something creative. And I handle my side of the bargain.”
I ask him whether he feels like he does all this for the same reasons as his peers do it.

“I mean, I would think so,” he says. “Like what? Like what reason?” Then he supplies his own answer. “I think anybody who cares about what they’re doing, which is such personal work – you have to embody the role. You have to ingest it and live it and feel it and be it. And you can only do that well if you feel it and believe in it.”
But, I put to him, my gut feeling is that a lot of actors, including some very talented people, may have a slightly more detached or casual relationship with their work.
“Yeah,” acknowledges Brody, and he laughs in a way that’s tricky to read. “I’m not detached enough. Or casual, I guess.”
I point out that, although I’ve only known him for 20 minutes, my sense is that he doesn’t want to be.
When I further echo this – suggesting out loud that he wants to be like he is – the notion seems to spark something in Brody, this time in a more helpful way.

“You know, it’s funny,” he says. “When I was young, there were a lot of tough kids in my neighbourhood, and I was always very sensitive. I was always amazed at how certain ones weren’t empathetic. You know, how they would torture ants and things when we would play, and how they got pleasure out of that. I was littler than them, and I didn’t really want to say all the time, like, ‘Why are you going to hurt…?’ because they’ll just pick on me. And I was always kind of aware that it was harder. It was harder to be more sensitive.”

From the age of four, Brody grew up in the New York suburb of Woodhaven, Queens, and he has occasionally alluded over the years to various rough aspects around the edges of this experience of growing up in a neighbourhood suffering from high levels of drug and gun crime. He compares it in general terms to his life these days: “Now, I have no one in my life that isn’t on the path that I feel we should all be on. But I think growing up in Queens I didn’t know anyone, really, who was on the path.”
And yet, I point out to him, it sounds as though while he’s grateful for what he didn’t end up doing, he still feels slightly romantic about that world.

“I am a little nostalgic for it,” he agrees. “It wasn’t terrible. It was also another time. Like, the whole world was different, let alone New York City. It was different. There were no [mobile] phones. I was on the street very young. I was taking the train. I was riding bikes with a bunch of kids around the neighbourhood. I was getting into trouble. I was kind of left on my own. I didn’t have a pager or a phone with a tracker on it. I wasn’t seeing what kids were doing on social media and living a better life, and ‘Why don’t I have these sneakers?’ I just lived. Lived.”

Following up on what he’d just said, I ask him what trouble he was getting into; this will be another of those moments where the mood shifts. “Here we go…” he says. But he nonetheless offers a response.
“I was around a lot of…yeah, a lot of stuff,” he says. “It was a lot of hardship…and there was a lot of… It was wild. It was just a wild time. You know, I was a good kid…but I was around a lot.”

There are a lot of long pauses in this answer, and as he speaks I feel like I can almost see all the things Brody is remembering but not saying flashing across his eyes and around the edges of his mouth. It’s quite a show. If I could transcribe everything he thought of between those sentences, I suggest to him, it would be quite a paragraph, wouldn’t it?

“It would be,” he confirms, and his laugh seems one of genuine shared amusement. “Yes. It sure would. And I’d love to share wonderful stories with you. Just somehow things always get taken out of context. I never would brag about doing things that…you know, whatever.”

We leave that there, but one of his mother’s books offers a fascinating snapshot into a different side of Brody’s childhood. His mother, Sylvia Plachy, is an acclaimed documentary photographer. ‘Unguided Tour’ was published in 1990, the year Brody turned 17. It’s far from a family album – it contains a dizzying variety of evocative photos, many taken around New York and quite a few in Eastern Europe, alongside occasional portraits of interesting notables (amongst them William S. Burroughs, Louise Bourgeois, Jorge Luis Borges, Claude Lanzmann, Hubert Selby Jr. and Tom Waits) – though there is one image of a joyous young Brody in a pool with his grandfather. But there are occasional pieces of text placed next to photographs, and several images are accompanied by words Brody apparently said to his mother when he was very young. (Brody is referred to throughout as Mishi, the name his mother used to call him.)

This, for instance, is from 1977, when he was four years old: “Mommy, I had a very sad dream. I was in a restaurant with a grown-up girl and I really liked her. She even bought me ice cream. But when we came out she just crossed the street and left me, and I’m not allowed to cross the street by myself. She just said good-bye and I don’t know why she left me. I loved her even more than I love you. I’m going to sing a song about it: ‘She left me and I don’t know why she left me, I really loved her.’”

And this is from the following year, when he was five: “Mommy, I had a bad dream; men made out of metal were after me with their metal ray guns. But then my nose started bleeding, I shouted ‘Time Out!’ and they all stopped.”
When I mention these to Brody, I comment that it sounds like he was a strange kid.
“I don’t think it was that strange,” he counters. “It was imaginative.”
What kind of four-year-old, I ask him, tells a fully realised story about a girl not being in love with him, or a five-year-old about men of metal coming at him?
“I don’t know,” he says. “This one.”
I reiterate: Not everyone, I promise you.

“But you think it’s strange?” he says. I point out that I like that he said those things. “Okay, good. It’s unusual – I don’t disagree. Yeah, it’s something.” After we talk a little more, he adds: “They sound like me. It sounds like something I would come up with.”
And that, I point out, is what I’m trying to understand.

“You can see that I’m an actor,” he reflects, “and that was her intuition.” He seems to be casting forward from age five to a famous pivot point in his life: when he was eleven, his mother was sent on assignment to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts, and when she saw their young people’s programme she thought it might suit her son. That’s how Brody started acting. He talks more about those qualities he had as a child. “I can see a lot of things, and I can see circumstances – imagine them fully,” he says. “Quite fully in emotion. I think those are qualities that are necessary to inhabit others. I am quite empathetic, and I think that’s been cultivated through that process.”
But it’s interesting, I say, that he was like this when he hadn’t yet had any training.

So where do you think it comes from? “No idea,” he says. “Just there.” But then he offers what seems like a suggestion. “My parents treated me with respect as a child. They didn’t treat me like a child.”

Brody has said that his parents saw acting as a way of keeping him out of the trouble that might have subsumed him in the neighbourhood. When I ask whether this was a big impulse, he says no at first but then offers up a surprising detail. “My dad considered me going to a military academy at one point. He knew what was around. Both of them understood that I needed some kind of creative outlet, that I was very creative. And that’s what’s evident in those things: that I had a very imaginative mind, a very curious mind. And hanging out on the block wouldn’t have given me a leg up in that space. It would suppress it, ultimately.”

Brody enjoyed some success right from the start. Aged 14, he was a lead in a TV movie, ‘Home at Last’, playing a New York orphan shipped out west. The following year, he was cast, if only for a day, by Francis Ford Coppola in his portion of ‘New York Stories’. A variety of roles followed before, at 23, he landed a wonderful, improbable opportunity. The director Terrence Malick was a legend, partly because 20 years earlier he had stopped making movies. The filmmaking world was abuzz with news that Malick was planning to return with an adaptation of James Jones’s World War II novel about combat in the Pacific, ‘The Thin Red Line’. It seemed as if the whole of Hollywood wanted to be in the movie. After Brody met with Malick – they talked for two hours in a hotel near where we are now, looking down at the skaters in Central Park – he was cast as one of the leads.

There’s a version of the script online, apparently close to the one Malick used when they all headed off to Australia to shoot for half a year. Brody’s character’s name, Corporal Fife, appears in the script 315 times. Fife speaks on 127 separate occasions. “We shot six months,” Brody recalls, “and we did many embellishments.”

In the lead-up to the release of a film Malick was yet to show to anybody, Brody did press interviews as the hot new young star he now was presumed to be. Malick did call him at one point and mentioned that his role had been “reduced,” but nothing even slightly prepared him for the truth. Just before the film’s release – still a grand secret – Brody was invited to what he was told was a private screening in New York. He took his parents. It wasn’t a private screening – selected press were there too – and as the film’s nearly three hours unspooled in front of everyone, Brody discovered that Malick had completely changed his movie in editing. Brody’s character appeared on screen for only a few minutes, and you could count the fleeting lines he spoke on one hand.

Brody has often talked about this as a formative experience and a key moment in his story, but today he seems less willing to reflect on it. “You want to get into all the past and the hardships. I don’t think about them. I don’t harp on them. You can reference them all you like, but I don’t harp on them,” he says.

I point out that the whole point of talking about any of this is to provide context to his role in ‘The Brutalist’ being such a triumph. And though it’s a little awkward to raise, I feel like he should know that I’ve spent much of the last eight years writing a book about events during the Holocaust in Lithuania and how one deals with the aftermath (the recently published ‘No Road Leading Back’), which, in a very different way, processes some of the same themes that lie at the heart of ‘The Brutalist’. We talk about that for a while. “It’s good to represent these stories,” he says respectfully.

Eventually I tell him that I should ask him some more annoying questions about his past. “It’s not annoying – it’s really not,” he says, and returns to the subject of ‘The Thin Red Line’. “It’s just, to then read it again – this moment, this terrible situation…” Even so, whether or not because of the break we have had, Brody addresses the situation with some thoughtfulness. “I do feel like you asked me why and how things happen,” he says. “And I don’t know, but that happened for a reason. You know what I mean? And that shaped me. It shaped my journey. It gave me a great understanding of loss as it pertains to my work. And had potential to be very detrimental to my future and the work that I’ve dedicated my whole life to. I gave everything to that project, too. Unquestioningly.”
It could have broken you, I point out.

“Yes,” he exclaims. “I was 23! But my dad always has a really great perspective of it.” (Brody’s father, Elliot, is a retired history teacher.) “He said: ‘That movie, as painful as it was for you, made a lot of people know about you in your business. Whether they saw your work or not, they knew about you.’ And he’s right. But I was concerned one could make the assumption that I must not have been good enough for the part. You have this iconic filmmaker who hasn’t made a movie in all these years, and then you have an actor who out of nowhere gets this thing – he must not have been good enough. And that’s what I felt. Like, I had no way to prove my side of this.”

Thankfully, at least through the lens of history, not too long a time passed between what could have been a debilitating humiliation and Brody’s first unequivocal triumph: playing the central figure in Roman Polanski’s ‘The Pianist’, based on the true story of a Polish-Jewish musician, Władysław Szpilman, and his desperate struggles to survive in the Warsaw ghetto during World War II. “It was profound – and also out of nowhere, you know,” Brody says. “It was only a few years from where I thought: ‘I may never work again.’”

To me, Brody seems like the kind of high-wire actor who, in a film that works less well, can sometimes appear stranded; you can almost viscerally feel the disconnect between the film he’s imagined and the film that is. But when everything works it’s the opposite: he entirely inhabits a character in a way which is mesmerising without being showy. So it is in ‘The Brutalist’; so it was in ‘The Pianist’. “It was nothing I had experienced,” he reminisces. “You know, I had such a responsibility throughout the making of it, saddled with the need to faithfully represent a survivor’s story and what it speaks to of the enormity of loss. And [as] a young man, I had to deeply immerse and understand that level of loss that was so profound that I didn’t have an understanding, really. I opened up a portal to a depravity and the horror and cruelty that exists. My association to darkness was very different prior to that. So that was a big shift. Darkness and light. And finding light through darkness…”

At this very moment, something remarkable happens. Presumably in response to the dwindling daylight outside, just as Brody says the phrase “light through darkness,” the lighting in the hotel bar suddenly surges to about twice its previous level of brightness.
“See!” he declares. “I have a way about me!” He looks delighted. “If we did that on the take,” he says, “that would be in the movie!”

For his role in ‘The Pianist’, Brody was nominated for an Oscar for the first time. The other four nominees – Jack Nicholson, Michael Caine, Daniel Day-Lewis and Nicolas Cage – had all previously won Oscars, and in the weeks beforehand, as the major precursor awards were announced, Brody won none of them.
But on the evening, it was his name that was read out. He became – and to this day remains – the youngest winner of the best actor trophy.

“Time did slow down,” he says. “I remember that. I remember that feeling where it literally warped down to something. It was enormous. It was enormous. And it was a real outpouring of love. That room lit up. And there I was, surrounded by so many people I admire, and all the influential people in my industry. And I just… I was plucked from obscurity. I had been working and toiling away as an actor for 17 years. And overnight” – he laughs – “I was now successful. In the world’s eyes.”

‘The Brutalist’ is now on the same awards circuit. So far, it is going well. A couple of weeks before we met, Brody gave an emotional speech after winning best actor at the Golden Globes. It is, of course, a strange quirk that the two roles towering above all others in his career, as different as they are in most respects other than the commitment and intensity he brings to them, are both connected to the Holocaust.

It’s also the kind of low-hanging fruit ready-made for awards show hosts, and in the first few minutes of the Golden Globes, during comedian Nikki Glaser’s opening monologue, she said, “Oh, look! It’s two-time Holocaust survivor Adrien Brody.” As the camera fixed on his face, Brody gamely grinned and blew Glaser a kiss.
As I watched, I tell him, I wondered whether he was wincing slightly inside.

“Of course,” he says. “Of course. You know the nature of her humour. Of course. I feel very privileged to have been able to speak to this horrific time in my work. Such great depths. And there’s been a lot of ancestral loss and struggles, and I don’t take it lightly, obviously.”
Not long before Brody leaves the bar, I ask him what he thinks his talent is. He takes some time before he starts to speak.

“I’ve managed to not lose the imaginative quality of my youth through my experiences in life,” he tells me. “And I can apply that similar curiosity and enthusiasm to my work, and my encounters with others. And it gives me a sense of freedom. And I can incorporate that into my work, and the process of doing my work. I can find, I can access, things that I find quite fulfilling and real, that shed light on lots of things in my work and in life. So that is what I’m most grateful for.”
I ask him when he’s happiest.
“When I’m working,” he says. “When I’m immersed in something creative. The most alive, yes. Definitely not on vacation or something. I don’t know. I’m more happy working.”

He says he doesn’t yet know what he will do next. “There are a few things that are interesting,” he says. (Naturally, those lists will be looking much better for him right now.) Even aside from ‘The Brutalist’, in recent times Brody’s world seems to have opened up a little. When he renewed his focus on acting after his unannounced break (he has credited Chapman with nudging him in that direction), he began to make distinctive contributions to TV shows, most notably ‘Peaky Blinders’, ‘Succession’ and ‘Poker Face’, and renewed his ongoing relationship with Wes Anderson, now five films deep. Brody also co-wrote, produced and starred in a dark revenge movie, ‘Clean’, and wrote its music. (He has been making beats for many years.) There’s another script he’s writing, inspired by a painting he saw in Madrid’s Prado museum. And, for that matter, he wants to get back to his own painting. “I have no time to do anything at the moment, unfortunately,” he says ruefully. “Like, literally no time. I would like a window to paint a little.”

Brody made a documentary, too, several years back: ‘Stone Barn Castle’, about the seven-year renovation of a building he owns in upstate New York. He showed the film once at the SXSW festival, but it hasn’t been seen since, and he tells me he wants to redo it sometime, change the structure and the storytelling. “I envision another iteration before it’s something to share publicly,” he explains. “But I have an enormous amount of footage.” And, like so many things, it may have already found its worth in another way.

“It’s fascinating,” he says of the documentary, “especially in context of me playing an architect, having spent a good seven years toiling away and trying to bring a building back to life and integrate all these architectural elements. And my aesthetic, which is quite unique, influenced from Eastern sources and modern things – that, too, probably informed some connection with my character.”

As he further explains the connection between the renovation and his most recent landmark character, I realise that Adrien Brody could just as much be talking about his life. And maybe that’s the point.
“The need to complete it,” he says. “And not letting it get the best of me. And all of the stuff you have to overcome to get there.”

Chris Heath, as mentioned in the preceding interview, is the author of the recently published book ‘No Road Leading Back: An Improbable Escape from the Nazis and the Tangled Way We Tell the Story of the Holocaust’. It was voted a 2024 book of the year by ‘The Washington Post’.

items.title: AI WEIWEI - FANTASTIC MAN
items.description: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger
paragraphs: The extraordinary artist makes monumental installations of a radical and provocative nature, telling the truth about China and putting his very life in danger

The Turbine Hall at London’s Tate Modern is one of the world’s most coveted exhibition spaces, and the next artist to fill it is Ai Weiwei. Although a veteran of major art events such as Documenta 12 and the 48th Venice Biennale, in his home country of China Ai Weiwei is as much known for his activism as he is for his aesthetics. Based in Beijing, where he is under constant surveillance, the artist brazenly flouts the law to bring his view on modern day China to the rest of the world. He is an avid user of fashionable social networking sites, and on an average day he tweets approximately 107 times.
From Fantastic Man n° 12 — 2010
“Okay, let’s start,” says the artist Ai Weiwei, greeting me with a wide smile.

It’s 9am on a sunny Beijing morning – so much for creative types sleeping late – and Ai Weiwei has already been up and at it for several hours. Given his reputation, I assume he’s been irritating the Chinese government and tickling his legions of followers by way of his famously acerbic Twitter feeds. (Consider: “The system doesn’t follow the law. The people don’t believe in the law. So who’s out of luck?”)

I have made what’s been called the ‘ritual pilgrimage’ to the compound Ai designed and built for himself in the city’s northeast outskirts. It’s a journey previously taken by the likes of Gerhard Schröder, Diane von Furstenberg and countless others who fancy themselves sophisticated and international. From the centre of town, you go past unremarkable high rises and light industry zones, beneath highway overpasses and railroad tracks and, finally, along a quiet, gingko-lined road. A blue metal door marks the entrance to Ai’s fabled home and studio, which he shares with his wife, the artist Lu Qing, and which these days also happens to be under surveillance by Chinese authorities.

Inside, the word FUCK is mounted on a garden wall in big neon letters. Otherwise, the scene is quite tranquil. Ai is sitting next to a pleasant, grassy lawn framed by cypress trees, antique stone fragments and thickets of bamboo. He’s accompanied by a member of his 30-or-so-person studio – a young woman, Germanic, I’d say, possibly Scandinavian – and several of his unconfirmed number of cats and dogs. (“We don’t really know how many we have,” he admits.) Ai has close-cropped hair, an unruly beard and an ample belly that together define what you might call the Ai Weiwei look. Wearing a periwinkle T-shirt and shorts, he politely leads me across a patio and into his loft-like, grey-brick home.
“That’s Du Du,” he starts off, catching me glancing at another free-roaming canine as we sit down at a huge wooden table.
“Yeah. And there’s Danny,” he adds, pointing to a female cocker spaniel. “We also have two of her children here.”
Ignoring his pet-naming decisions, I ask how his day is going.

“Normally, I give two interviews in the morning, but today I only have yours,” he says, continuing the small talk. Ai is known to be accessible. “Don’t hesitate to ask me anything you’d like,” he offers.

Ever since 2006, when the architect Jacques Herzog first insisted that I try to meet him – they had collaborated on the design of Beijing’s Bird’s Nest stadium, a project Ai later disavowed as a “fake smile” serving Communist propaganda – the Chinese artist, architect and dangerously outspoken activist has been a distant yet recurring motif in my life.

There he was, popping up at the architecture biennale in Venice and at exhibition openings in Beijing – always with an entourage and rarely without an assistant videotaping his every move. Once, I briefly interviewed him over a bowl of beef noodles. Another time, I visited his studio on a day I was told he wouldn’t be there, only to find him typing away at his computer.

Ai has a knack for being somewhere even when he isn’t. He infiltrates things. As part of a massive, high-concept exercise, he took over Documenta 12 in Kassel, Germany, in 2007 with no less than 1,001 ordinary Chinese whom he’d flown in for the occasion. Earlier this year, he helped organise a protest march on a highly symbolic thoroughfare in central Beijing. The demonstration was totally unauthorised and quickly halted by police, but at least one Communist Party newspaper covered it – and guess whose name was on the photo credit?

Ai, 53, is a conceptual artist who’s become known for his activism and an activist whose provocations verge on art. He named his studio Fake Design, but it’s really his life that his art imitates, and the other way around. This October, Ai will become the latest artist to transform London’s Tate Modern as part of the museum’s blockbuster series of Turbine Hall installations. For many, he’s the godfather of contemporary Chinese art, the man – no, the concept – around which an intriguing image of China begins to emerge.

So who, or what, exactly is Ai Weiwei? A figure of controversy in his home country, for a start. “In China, the newspapers and magazines used to report on me a lot – but mostly fashion publications,” he tells me. (I kid you not: as I write this, a friend has stopped by my home, randomly wearing a Comme Des Garçons T-shirt emblazoned with a watermelon and the words THANKS TO AI WEIWEI.)

“People on the internet have seen me on CCTV” – the Chinese state television network – “and said, ‘Weiwei, what the fuck? You’re on CCTV,’” he says. “Maybe they’re using old programmes, but it’s a big joke because I’ve been censored by them. Officially, they cannot mention my name.” Programmes must sometimes slip through the cracks.
What about the Tate installation? What are you doing for that?
“I really can’t talk about it; they even asked me not to talk to you in particular about this.”
So now you’re being censored by the Tate?
“Partially,” he says with an ironic chuckle.

The proper way to address Ai Weiwei is, in fact, Ai. The Chinese place their surnames first; his is pronounced like ‘eye’. But mostly, Weiwei (‘way-way’), as many call him, is an enigmatic yet omnipresent abstraction, an iconoclastic artist and philosopher whose contours are hard to grasp. He works in a range of media, from sculpture, installations and photography to architecture, film and, for lack of a better word, “actions”, while at various times moonlighting as an antiques trader, gallerist and curator. Until recently, he was also the proprietor of Qu Nar (“Go Where?”), a restaurant specialising in the cuisine of Zhejiang province, at which he frequently held court before it was demolished to make way for a new development last year.

As for his art, Ai is unapologetically irreverent and sardonic. He can be seen flipping his finger at the White House and Eiffel Tower in his well-known Study of Perspective photographs, and he has painted the Coca-Cola logo on ancient pots. All the while, his work often relies on earlier wreckage, the kind of creative destruction that defines China’s contemporary crossroads. There’s Dropping a Han Dynasty Urn (1995), a photographic triptych in which he smashes a 2,000-year-old vase. And Map of China (2003), a hulking, geographically correct sculpture made of wood salvaged from demolished Qing dynasty temples. Ai hits a nerve shared by Chinese and non-Chinese alike. As the artist later puts it: “What does ‘China’ mean?”

Nowadays, however, the more pressing question may be just how far he can push the Chinese authorities. Ai has become a gigantic thorn for the powers that be, a vocal critic of the government – for its corruption, human rights shortcomings and other injustices – in a country where life has been known to get difficult for vocal government critics. He doesn’t go about it quietly and misses few opportunities to act or speak out. During our first interview, he tells me how one week earlier, he’d driven into the mountains to rescue an activist who he says was abandoned there after being beaten by secret police. “He announced it on Twitter, said he didn’t know where he was,” Ai says of the man, an advocate for migrant workers. “We had to go out and find him.”
Then, during our second meeting, he’s interrupted by a phone call. “That was the people from the earthquake area,” he says. “They’re still calling me.”

‘The earthquake’ refers to Ai’s biggest cause to date – more specifically, the thousands of children who died in the 7.9-magnitude tremor that roiled China’s Sichuan province in May 2008. Most of the area’s young perished when their schools collapsed, as a result of shoddy construction that was widely attributed to the negligence and corruption of local officials. Fearing the ensuing outcry, the government silenced protests and failed to produce the names, or even a tally, of the victims.

In response, Ai sent an army of volunteers to the region to help fill the gap. The list they produced grew to more than 5,200 names. Even two years later, Ai daily sends out the names of the victims via Twitter on their birthdays. (Twitter is technically blocked in China, though that’s easy to get around.) For a recent exhibition, he covered the façade of Munich’s Haus der Kunst with 9,000 coloured backpacks forming a quote in Chinese characters taken from one of the children’s mothers. He’s flung open his doors to the press while producing documentaries about the tragedy; they are part of a series tackling a range of issues. “We’ve sent probably 50 or 60 thousand documentaries out on DVD for free,” Ai says, “though millions have seen them on the internet.”

Last year, Chinese censors shut down the popular blog Ai had started writing in 2005. “We had maybe over 50 million readers,” he laments. Meanwhile, he says his email accounts have been hacked, his bank accounts investigated, and his home staked out by mysterious men in parked cars; the latter have since been replaced by closed-circuit cameras.

“The machines are much friendlier,” he says, nodding toward a pair of surveillance cameras, mounted on telephone poles that are aimed at his front gate. “Before that, the guys waiting outside weren’t so nice.” (Even as a mark, Ai is a true gentleman, having once asked his surveillants if they might like some water. When they reacted poorly, he called the police on them.)

If it sounds like Ai is flirting with martyrdom, he’s got the scars to prove it: two of them, on the right side of his head. In August 2009, Ai was in the Sichuanese capital of Chengdu to attend the trial of a fellow earthquake activist when police broke into his room at the Anyi Hotel. It was the middle of the night, and according to Ai, he was roughed up and suffered a blunt blow to the head.
