items.title: Marco Rubio’s Wild, Wild West
items.description: When Barack Obama went to Athens in mid-November, 2016, on his last state visit as President, he celebrated democracy. The speech he delivered in the Greek capital, at a ritzy opera hall perched next to the Saronic Gulf, came only eight days after Hillary Clin
items.author: Ishaan Tharoor
paragraphs: When Barack Obama went to Athens in mid-November, 2016, on his last state visit as President, he celebrated democracy. The speech he delivered in the Greek capital, at a ritzy opera hall perched next to the Saronic Gulf, came only eight days after Hillary Clinton lost the Presidential election to Donald Trump; Obama, an era-defining leader, now mulled the likely unravelling of his legacy. His remarks evoked a world on edge, beset by growing social and economic divides and the uneven effects of globalization. But he clung to an optimistic theme, hailing the “rocky hills” of Athens as the birthplace of democracy, the incubator of such concepts as citizenship and equality before the law. He acknowledged that democracy in the Athens of antiquity was “far from perfect,” not unlike that of his own nation at its founding, but said that democracy was a “flame first lit here” that had “never died.” And, he insisted, the yearning for democracy reflected a universal dream. “We’ve been told that these are Western ideals,” Obama said. “We’ve been told that some cultures are not equipped for democratic governance and actually prefer authoritarian rule.” But, he said, his travels around the world during eight years in office showed him that that was not the case, that the “basic longing to live with dignity, the fundamental desire to have control of our lives and our future . . . burn in every human heart.”

When Marco Rubio, the Secretary of State, went to Athens last week and gave a speech, he mentioned the word “democracy” just twice in almost thirty minutes. Instead, standing upon the Pnyx, a hilly outcrop that overlooks the Acropolis, he tub-thumped for the West. He declared ancient Greek city-states as “the birthplace of the greatest civilization in the world,” the font not of universal value but of an exceptional cultural legacy that belonged to Europe and the United States—and not many others. Rubio turned to Plato and invoked the ancient idea of thymos—“the fire of passion, strength, courage, pride,” as he put it, that gives life to a civilization—and placed the Greek hoplites who resisted the advances of the Persian empire at Thermopylae (never mind that they were Spartans, not Athenians) in a line of great men that included Christian martyrs and the defiant Texans who perished at the Alamo. Their bravery, sacrifice, and loyalty to a greater cause, Rubio argued, were distinctly Western characteristics, rooted in an ennobling spirit that he claimed was under threat from those who have made nationalism “a dirty word” and taught children to be “ashamed” of their countries. “Now we take the West’s conception of these things—heroism, honor, duty—we take these things for granted,” he said, before offering a riposte to Obama’s idealism of a decade before. “We assume that these somehow are universal to all people in all times and in all places. They are not.” In his telling, European nations, gripped by mass migration and the torpor of liberalism, faced a civilizational “inflection point” and had to “awaken” from their “long slumber”; the West had to maintain “its place at the head of the world” and resist a “future of atrophy and servitude and decline.”

In all this, Rubio is doing his best to inhabit the Zeitgeist of right-wing politics in the United States. He no longer has time for the neoconservative internationalism of John McCain or George W. Bush, and instead walks a path paved by conservatives such as by James Burnham, who in the nineteen-sixties saw liberal élites as complicit in the “suicide of the West,” and Pat Buchanan, who wrote, in the twilight of his career, at the beginning of this century, of “the death of the West” by immigration and demographic replacement. Of course, the West itself is a nebulous concept, one that was wholly absent from the ancient Greek and Roman luminaries who ground its canon. It entered political parlance in the nineteenth century, as Europeans sought ways to create distance between themselves and Russians, while also gesturing to bonds across the Atlantic. It took a more concrete geopolitical form in the Cold War, undergirded by the NATO military alliance. After the fall of the Soviet Union, the West, for a time, became more capacious, linked to principles of liberal democracy that could take root anywhere.

Rubio’s idea of the West is both messier and simpler, populated by muscular explorers and conquerors, from Alexander the Great and the Frankish king Charlemagne to the conquistador Hernán Cortés and the frontiersmen of the American West. Rubio doesn’t seem interested in the Athenian legacy of civic institutions and models for self-governance that appealed to the Founding Fathers. In his speech, the West is more defined by whom it does not encompass—chiefly, tyrannical Persians who tried to absorb Greece’s stubborn city-states, and their modern-day descendants in Iran, described by Rubio as “radical mullahs” who propagate a “cult of death.” There is no space in Rubio’s narrative for any more sophisticated reading of the past, any recognition of the profound interconnections between societies that already existed in the age of Pericles, or of the pivotal roles that the medieval philosophers and scientists of the Islamic world played in helping proliferate the knowledge of the ancient Greeks into European Christendom. Paul Betts, a professor of modern European history at the University of Oxford, said Rubio seemed to instrumentalize Athens as “a justification for adventurism, national power, and even imperial expansion.” Forget Obama’s visions of democracy—here was Trump’s deferred annexation of Greenland and his deepening vassalage of Venezuela. “It’s a Trump-era rereading that somehow ancient Greece is recast as the political foundation for a new American mission in the world,” Betts told me. Tom Malinowski, a former U.S. diplomat and congressman, was more blunt. The text of Rubio’s speech “belongs on the syllabus of every class on the intellectual foundations of fascism,” he wrote.

For those following the Washington horse race, Rubio’s speech was seen as a soft launch for a potential Presidential challenge in 2028, a statement to the MAGA base at home that he can carry Trump’s banner in the years to come. He reminded his audience of the American ambition to rebalance trade relationships, reassert control over global supply chains, bolster military spending, and “fight for dominance” over the industries and technologies of the future. “We choose the unapologetic pursuit of national power,” he said in Athens. But onlookers abroad already know that. The Trump Administration offers constant reminders to the rest of the planet—and, especially, to erstwhile allies in the West—of both the narrowness of its world view and the vastness of its sense of primacy. For months, it bullied and scolded other countries not to purchase Russian oil, even slapping tariffs on some that did, before turning around, this past week, and announcing its own plan to import hundreds of thousands of tons of Russian diesel, infuriated top European diplomats, who see this as another blow to their collective efforts to buttress Ukraine.

Trump’s conspicuous rapport with the Kremlin undermines the unity of the archetypal geopolitical West. So do other moves: just a day after his Athens speech, Rubio announced sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court, an institution stoically defended by many European governments. The White House, in its stated national-security strategy, is sour on the whole project of the European Union and sees itself as being in league with anti-establishment, far-right factions. Although they are ascendant in some countries, these “patriotic” parties don’t yet reflect dominant majorities in Europe, where Trump, on the whole, is hopelessly unpopular. Michael Kimmage, the director of the Kennan Institute, in Washington, D.C., and the author of “The Abandonment of the West: The History of an Idea in American Foreign Policy,” saw Rubio’s speech as taking place in “a remarkably ironic set of circumstances.” The U.S.’s top diplomat conjured “a cardboard notion of the West, taken from a very selective set of references,” Kimmage told me, which “doesn’t really speak to Europeans,” doesn’t “resonate in any meaningful way within the United States”—where pan-Hellenism isn’t exactly a feature of mass culture—and which belies “a transatlantic relationship that is deteriorating.” (Rubio’s grandiose oratory was also undercut by the apparent tawdry self-dealing of the Trump Administration; allegations surrounding an inappropriate payment request by Kimberly Guilfoyle, the Trump-appointed U.S. Ambassador to Greece, shadowed Rubio’s visit last week and compelled Guilfoyle to resign her post on Tuesday. Guilfoyle has denied wrongdoing.)

Still, Rubio is not an outlier. His speech in Athens is part of a wider phenomenon in global politics that scholars have dubbed “civilizationism,” in which great powers engage with one another as “civilization”-states, marked by distinct cultural identities and political styles. They don’t have to clash, as the late political philosopher Samuel Huntington famously envisioned after the end of the Cold War, but the divergence of their interests and the difference of their cultures suggest a world shaped by competing spheres of influence. The Chinese President, Xi Jinping, has already launched a formal Global Civilizations Initiative that pads this world view with reams of Communist Party jargon; India, too, sees itself as a civilization-state, with commensurate weight on the world stage. Even the centrist French President Emmanuel Macron, who wants a more united, empowered Europe to hold its own, is wont to speak about the Continent in civilizational terms. Hans Kundnani, a visiting professor at the European Institute of the London School of Economics, argues that civilizationism reflects a retreat from universalist ideas not only in the United States and its allies but also in countries in the Global South that found their freedom in the twentieth century. In the more overtly illiberal moment in which we find ourselves today, with international law proving tougher to enforce and human rights more difficult to protect, talk of civilizations is rising. “There’s a blurring of the distinction between democracies and authoritarian states,” Kundnani told me. “At a time of democratic backsliding, thinking in civilizational terms is an alternative way of legitimating the actions of states.” In a Foreign Affairs essay, Leonard A. Schuette, a fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, anticipated Rubio’s speech. The new right’s idea of civilization “is not based on a creedal understanding of Western identity as rooted in a shared set of principles that anyone, regardless of origin, can espouse, such as constitutional democracy, liberty, and equality,” he wrote. “Instead, for thinkers on the New Right, the West is defined by a specific geographic territory, a shared ancestry, and Christianity.”

Rubio advocated a gentler version of this blood-and-soil, identitarian vision of the West, which, most of the time, gets voiced by conservatives in baldly dehumanizing terms—for example, through calls for the deportation of illegal immigrants, or the depopulation of unwanted brown kids from college football stadiums. At the same time that Rubio was in the Greek capital, a coterie of far-right Western leaders had convened across the sea, in Jerusalem, for the annual National Conservatism conference, which included a motley cast of followers of Vice-President J. D. Vance, Trump’s heir apparent. There, the nationalist instincts driving Rubio’s speech found more vociferous expression. Amichai Chikli, Israel’s diaspora minister—who, out of a shared antipathy toward Muslims and liberals, has made controversial overtures to the same European far-right parties whose ideological forebears participated in the Holocaust—urged his compatriots “to smash political correctness, unite around our national movements, the only natural order in which our freedom has any meaning, and destroy once again the Tower of Babylon.”

“Civilization” is one of the favorite words of these sorts of politicians, more committed to supremacy than to democracy. But, as a rallying cry of the American right, it’s language that rings more hollow by the day, given the excesses of the past two years, the brutalization of migrants and protesters, the bullying of weaker countries, the repeated turns to unprovoked war and displays of force, and the garishness of an Administration that plans to live-stream a public execution later this year. Sebastian Gorka, a White House official focussed on counterterrorism, told the audience in Jerusalem that right-wing forces find themselves “in a war between civilization and barbarity.” He may not be on the side he thinks he is. ♦

items.title: James Dolan Is Doing All He Can to Kill the Knicks’ Vibe
items.description: Just about every single Knicks development since they won the title last June — remember that? They won the title? It was incredibly awesome! — has been negative. And it has all been Jim Dolan’s fault. Of course it has.
items.author: Will Leitch
paragraphs: Just about every single Knicks development since they won the title last June — remember that? They won the title? It was incredibly awesome! — has been negative. And it has all been Jim Dolan’s fault. Of course it has.

One of the primary reasons team president Leon Rose and the rest of the Knicks brass were able to build the championship roster they did — and they won the championship! The Knicks! Woooooooooo!!!! — was that, for the first time really since he took over ownership of the team, Dolan stayed out of things. Maybe he was busy with the Sphere or all the wonderful political activity he’s involved with, or maybe those hard-rockin’ tours exhausted him. Regardless of the reason, the Knicks’ usually meddling owner stayed mostly absent and/or silent as Rose meticulously constructed the Knicks into the NBA champions (woooo!!!) they became last June.

Inevitably, that era has come to an end. We saw the beginning of its demise during and after the Finals: There was Dolan’s vibes-destroying invitation to President Trump to attend game three; his stupid fight with the mayor over watch parties outside MSG; his relentless megalomania at both the trophy presentation and the parade. All of that was essentially harmless, though — Dolan was always going to put himself front and center once the Knicks finally broke through and act like their success was a testament to his leadership rather than a direct refutation of it. He’s Jim Dolan. He’s a huge freaking goober.
But this offseason, Dolan’s clownishness started affecting the actual team itself.

Just four days after the title win, Dolan gave an interview to (fellow meathead) Craig Carton on WFAN, in which he opined that it would be “suicidal” for the team to go over the second apron — essentially, the NBA’s maximum salary cap, which you can spend above but which leads to penalties if repeated. His comments were in direct opposition to the plan that Rose and the front office, who want to keep this team together as long as possible, had put together. The ramifications of Dolan’s stance were immediate. Mitchell Robinson, the Knicks’ quixotic but defensively dominant center, signed with the hated Boston Celtics then took some parting shots at New York on his way out the door.

It got more ominous after that. Karl-Anthony Towns and Josh Hart — who you may remember being, uh, kind of important parts of last year’s team — are due contract extensions, and it’s not difficult to understand why each of them would be expecting more money, what with the championship they just won (woooo!!!). Towns, in particular, is due a big raise, considering how much he elevated his game after coming over from Minnesota; we are, after all, almost certainly talking about a future Hall of Famer here. Towns was even reasonable about his demands about a possible extension at Knicks Media Day, hinting he’d be willing to take less than maximum to help out the team. (When asked if he thought the Knicks title was a point of evidence that he deserved that extension and raise, KAT said, perfectly understandably, “Uh, no shit, Sherlock?”)

But Dolan’s reaction — and it’s key to separate this from Rose’s response — was not to roll up his sleeves and come to an agreement that most outside observers believed was in reach. Instead, he tabled all talks for either a Towns or Hart extension “until later in the season,” a move most saw as a slap in the face to both players. “Simply put, I want to do something that can keep the team together and work with the Knicks and also values me,” Towns said in response to the statement. “None of those things have come close to happening.” If the extension talks don’t resume, the Knicks may have to consider trading Towns in January lest they potentially lose him for nothing.

That, friends, is how one might ruin the vibes of the happiest moment in New York sports this century, and surely longer. It took Dolan three months. Oh, and he brought back Isiah Thomas too. It’s so nice to have Dolan paying attention to the Knicks again, isn’t it?

As the new season begins on Tuesday night against the 76ers and this new free agent they signed, a fella named James, you can see why all this could put Knicks fans (of which I very much am one) in a foul mood. This is a team that is in its prime, one that has every opportunity to go out and win another title this year, one that’s considered the favorite, at the very least, to win the Eastern Conference again. It’s exactly the sort of team that you spend to keep together, even if it means going over the dreaded apron. Dolan has been spending (his dad’s) money recklessly for decades, and now this team is where he decides to draw the line. It’s infuriating.
Except … well, I will confess … this Knicks fan is having a hard time getting too angry about it.

I have been waiting my entire life for the Knicks to win the NBA title. (WOOOOOOOO!) What happened last June was one of the most truly rapturous moments of my sports-fan life, and I suspect it was one of yours too. I would like to see the Knicks win another title this year: I legitimately think they do have a chance. (And I don’t think KAT’s ultimately going anywhere anyway.) I know Dolan is messing things up, and even if he weren’t, honestly, I’d be irritated just to have to look at his stupid face. But I am not going to let that dunce take away my joy on this, and you shouldn’t either.

The Knicks just won the title! (WOOOOOOOOO!!!!!!) It was just the greatest thing. And it’s something we get to have for the rest of our lives. We know it can happen now: It just did! All the happiness that last June brought, all the love you felt, all the ways it knitted so many communities together, that feeling that if this could happen, maybe there was a little hope for this world just yet — that was all real, and it can never, ever be taken away from us. It gets to live forever.

Yeah, it’s a huge bummer that Dolan has stuck his big fat head in the middle of everything again. But even if he screws up the Knicks moving forward — and I’m still not sold that he can — it’s already too late for him to blow this whole thing up. Because it already happened. The fucking Knicks won the championship! It’s going to take a lot more than Dolan to wipe this smile off my face. The new Knicks season is about to begin, and maybe it will go well, and maybe it won’t. But we already won. We already won. Wasn’t it incredible? Wasn’t it just the most wonderful thing? Wooooooooooo!!!!

items.title: Trump Helps Out by Dropping Antisemitic Slur at Kansas Rally
items.description: Donald Trump’s approval ratings are so low that Republican candidates have to consider whether his presence on the campaign trail is more of a help than a hindrance. Many Republicans have been distancing themselves from the president, and he just embarked on a
items.author: Margaret Hartmann
paragraphs: Donald Trump’s approval ratings are so low that Republican candidates have to consider whether his presence on the campaign trail is more of a help than a hindrance. Many Republicans have been distancing themselves from the president, and he just embarked on a campaign tour that avoids traditional battlegrounds in favor of several deep-red states. The idea is to boost GOP base turnout in these districts, which Republicans didn’t even have to think about defending in previous elections.
Trump kicked off his red-state swing in Kansas on Monday night. And judging from his performance, candidates set to welcome him in the Carolinas, Florida, Iowa, and Georgia should brace themselves.

The president’s goal at the Park City, Kansas, event was to boost Senator Roger Marshall, a GOP incumbent who has found himself in an unexpectedly tight race against Democrat Adam Hamilton, though Republicans haven’t lost a Senate race in the state since 1932.

Trump played all the rally hits, like musing about U.S. generals’ physical attractiveness, rambling about getting a “perfect score” on a cognitive test, and complaining, “Nobody appreciates how great a president I am.”
But the part that’s making headlines today is Trump defending Marshall by insisting he’s not “some kind of a Shylock-type guy.”

To state the obvious, the president of the United States casually dropping a term that’s widely considered an offensive stereotype about Jews is not great. (Marshall is not Jewish, which would have made this even worse.) Shylock, a Jewish moneylender, is the antagonist in Shakespeare’s The Merchant of Venice. The ADL noted:
What’s particularly interesting about this incident is that it was like an onion of things Trump shouldn’t be saying.

First, while Trump is certainly not the only politician to get in trouble for using the term Shylock, he should definitely know that it’s offensive, since Jewish groups called him out for using the slur at another rally in July 2025. At the time, Trump said he wasn’t aware it’s seen as antisemitic. “I’ve never heard it that way,” he said. “To me, Shylock is somebody that’s a money lender at high rates.” But apparently he still didn’t remove it from his vocabulary.

Second, Trump was bringing up a story Marshall would really like voters to forget. Last month, the New York Times reported that while he was working as an obstetrician before entering politics, Marshall’s practice sued more than 700 patients over unpaid medical bills. This led to some of his patients having their wages garnished or even being arrested. (The piece opens, memorably, with a poor couple being taken into custody on Easter weekend as their grandchildren prepared for an egg hunt.)

Trump actually suggested that someone on his team urged him not to get into the whole “Marshall allegedly shook down poor patients for owing him as little as $101” thing. The president segued into the topic by saying, “I have to say this. Somebody said, ‘Oh, don’t say it, nobody believes it.’ But I have to say it because I believe it’s appropriate.”

So if you’re a Republican candidate planning to host the president in the next two weeks, you should know that in addition to his usual rally antics, he might just bring up a damaging story you warned him not to discuss, and throw in an attention-grabbing slur for good measure. You’re welcome!

items.title: Can Ossoff Help Elect a Black Woman Governor of Georgia?
items.description: One of the most inspiring Democratic political stories of the 2026 midterm elections is the likely success of freshman U.S. senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia. In a state Donald Trump carried by more than 3 percent two years ago, Ossoff, a relatively progressive Je
items.author: Ed Kilgore
paragraphs: One of the most inspiring Democratic political stories of the 2026 midterm elections is the likely success of freshman U.S. senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia. In a state Donald Trump carried by more than 3 percent two years ago, Ossoff, a relatively progressive Jewish Democrat from Atlanta, looks to be running away with a reelection win over MAGA Congressman Mike Collins. He’s also making himself (willingly or not, since he denies any interest in a 2028 race) a dark-horse prospect for the presidency thanks to his viral fiery attacks on Trump and the GOP for systemic corruption. And it’s possible his popularity could help deliver another historic feat in Georgia.

Ossoff, who was widely expected to be a prime GOP target this year, has instead built so strong a lead over Collins that Republicans appear to have decided against throwing good money after bad by committing the resources their candidate would need to catch up with the incumbent in spending or in the polls. Silver Bulletin’s polling averages show Ossoff leading Collins by 9.1 percent. But Republicans have a better chance for victory in Georgia’s other marquee statewide race. With two-term GOP governor Brian Kemp facing term limits, his party’s nomination went to previously little-known health-care tycoon Rick Jackson, who spent over $100 million of his personal fortune to make and then win a runoff over Trump endorsee and Lieutenant Governor Burt Jones after a campaign featuring extensive mutual mudslinging. With grudging if general GOP support (which is fine by Jackson, who is running as a poor-boy-who-made-good “outsider” candidate), Jackson has now unleashed another personally financed ad blitz on Democratic nominee and former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms. And he’s outspending Bottoms by an estimated 7-to-1 margin.

The contest is reminding a lot of observers of the last two Georgia gubernatorial contests between Kemp and Democratic voter-mobilization wizard Stacey Abrams. In 2018, Abrams came tantalizingly close to breaking a GOP gubernatorial winning streak dating back to 1998. But in a 2022 rematch, Kemp won by a 53 percent–to–46 percent margin (and this was after he easily dispatched a Trump-backed rival in the primary). It was easy to mark up both Abrams losses to the reluctance of white Georgia voters to elect a Black woman to the position. But the racial interpretation of the 2022 vote was complicated by the concurrent Senate reelection of Ossoff’s Black colleague Raphael Warnock, and complicated even more by the fact that Warnock’s opponent was Black football legend and Trump crony Herschel Walker, whose personal problems caught up with him in a big way.

Bottoms does not have Abrams’s iconic status in Georgia Democratic politics, but she was universally regarded as a national rising star when she was elected Atlanta’s mayor in 2017; she even made the short list of candidates to become Joe Biden’s 2020 running mate. But her one term as mayor was marred by the same racial tensions and rising violent-crime rates that beset many cities during the COVID pandemic, and she lost the chance for a smoother second term (which she would have definitely won) by retiring and taking a sub-Cabinet job in Biden’s White House.

Still, Bottoms solidified a comeback bid earlier this year by beating a large field to win the gubernatorial nomination without a runoff, even as Republicans battled and bickered, and she led Jackson in scattered early polls. Then came the inevitable barrage of negative ads from Jackson, some blasting Bottoms for “abandoning” Atlanta to go to Washington and others exploiting an incident from her tenure wherein anti-police protesters burned down a Wendy’s restaurant and a child was murdered in the subsequent violence. Clearly Republicans are also hoping that Bottoms’s close association with Atlanta city government will hurt her and Democrats generally in the rest of the state (and also in Atlanta’s suburbs), where fear and resentment of the megacity is chronic.

Thanks to his largely unopposed advertising, Jackson now leads Bottoms narrowly in recent polls. A new survey from the Atlanta Journal-Constitution shows Jackson up among likely voters by one point (46 percent to 45 percent), with the billionaire achieving some success in describing himself as more of a protégé of the very popular Kemp than the unpopular Trump. So unsurprisingly, the big question has become whether the high-riding Ossoff can loan some support and money to his hard-pressed ticket mate. He’s certainly making an effort. In September he transferred $3.6 million to a coordinated campaign account backing the Democratic ticket (and there could be more of that if Republicans continue to abandon Collins), and he has been barnstorming with Bottoms. Next week former president Barack Obama will give both Democrats a lift at an Atlanta campaign rally.

There’s a lot at stake for Ossoff in Bottoms’s success. If Jackson wins, Democrats may be cool to any Ossoff ’28 talk on grounds that his Senate seat is too precious to risk on a presidential run. Such an outcome could also feed concerns that other candidates (possibly even Warnock, who has recently spent some time in early 2028 primary states) could do a better job of mobilizing the southern Black voters needed to take back the White House two years from now.

Conversely, if Bottoms wins with a notable assist from Ossoff, it will represent a major racial and gender breakthrough in Georgia politics for which he will receive significant credit. Abrams was the first woman (Republican Karen Handel came very close in 2010, before going on to defeat none other than Jon Ossoff to win a congressional seat in 2017), and the first Black pol, to win a major-party gubernatorial nomination in Georgia; Bottoms is the second. If she can overcome Jackson’s bankroll, a biracial blue sweep would firmly reestablish Georgia as a purple state and potentially the southern foundation for a winning presidential coalition in 2028 and beyond. And if Ossoff does choose to run for president in 2028 or later (he’s only 39), he’d likely have an ally in a Governor Keisha Lance Bottoms.

items.title: Costume Sketches from ‘The Devils’
items.description: What did you get up to during your school vacation? In the summer of 1970, an 8-year-old Vicki Russell was “playing a slave girl, pushing a great big truck full of plague victims.” Her parents? The visionary director Ken Russell (Altered States, The Boy Friend
items.author: Douglas Greenwood
paragraphs: What did you get up to during your school vacation? In the summer of 1970, an 8-year-old Vicki Russell was “playing a slave girl, pushing a great big truck full of plague victims.” Her parents? The visionary director Ken Russell (Altered States, The Boy Friend) and his frequent costume designer collaborator Shirley Russell. While her classmates were at the beach, or running around play parks, Russell, now a costume designer herself, was getting a front-row seat to an industry she’d soon be a part of. She was on set of The Devils—a controversial, ecclesiastic horror movie that, 55 years later, is about to be seen by a whole new audience.

The film, loosely based on the real life demise of a priest accused of witchcraft after a collective of nuns become “possessed” by his spirit, starred Oliver Reed and Vanessa Redgrave, and, until recently, has never been seen the way its director intended. But now, in a 4K remastered version (released this Friday in the US, and from October 30 in the UK), sequences deemed so controversial that they were left on the cutting room floor have been salvaged and re-added. They contain things that would make any modern horror auteur wince.

Thankfully, 8-year-old Vicki didn’t witness the horror of what her family was making as she dotted around the set. “It was like Disneyland to me,” she tells me over the phone, recounting memories of learning how to ride horses at the guidance of the film’s horse wrangler. In addition to her brief on-screen appearance, Russell spent a lot of time on the set of The Devils with her mother in the costume department, poring over the wildly designed and cultivated garments that captured the 17th century French era the film was set in.

But it all began months earlier, in the Russell family home in Portobello Road. “Half of their bedroom was mom’s studio where she would be drawing [these garments],” Russell says. “You could just see them coming together from these historical references.” She’d sketch them out in ink, dissect each piece and hone in on the details. You can see it in these sketches, presented here for the first time ever.

“She was fast because she knew her history of fashion so well,” Russell says of her mother’s process. “I think she just had to understand the character and what drove them.” The Devils had plenty of bombastic outfits to balance out the plainness of plague victims and peasants. Even then, the outfits were striking: regal dresses, pompous religious wear, and costumes for dancers that made them look like stars and birds. In the restored version, framed by sets from the master of British cinema Derek Jarman, you can see all of them in perfect detail.

After working on a project, the costumes Shirley Russell created would end up in a costume house of her own making: The Last Picture Frock in Shepherd’s Bush, West London. Russell recalls it being known as “one of the best in Europe.” Inevitably, some of the costumes in The Devils were destroyed during the fiery and untameable shoot; existing only on celluloid and in these sketches. A handful, including the regal red dress worn by Georgina Hale (seen below), will be included in an exhibition coming next year, to mark what would be the 100th birthday of Ken Russell.

It’s the blessing of Russell’s life to have followed in the footsteps of her artist parents, working alongside her mother in the costume department on several films, and eventually collaborating with her father as the lead costume designer on the 1986 film Gothic. “I’ve worked with him since I was 18-months-old, playing Oliver Reed’s daughter in Debussy, wearing period costume. Okay, he had a temper, but I knew it was just a rage and it would pass. But he absolutely loved the creative process, and he really loved costumes and set design.” He might have been her dad, but he also, she says, was “a very funny and brilliant man to work with.”
‘The Devils’ is in US cinemas for a one week engagement from Friday October 16. It opens in the UK on October 30.

items.title: Gisele Bundchen Interview: Motherhood, Happiness, Modeling Career
items.description: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
items.author: Steff Yotka
paragraphs: This story appears in i-D 377 “The Mother Issue” available now at select retailers and online.
photography COLLIER SCHORR

When she was 15 years old, Gisele Bündchen left Horizontina, Brazil, and moved to Tokyo to become a model. It was 1995. She didn’t speak Japanese or English. To reach her parents, grandparents, and five sisters, she used an international calling card on a landline phone. She would speak to them every 15 days, exactly.

“It was, in a way, liberating because I felt like I was living life,” Gisele says, thinking back to getting lost on the subway, navigating teenage growing pains, and learning how to integrate into a foreign reality. “I was experiencing life.”

Thirty-one years later, there is little of life Gisele hasn’t experienced. She walked her first major runway show for Alexander McQueen in 1998, and for the next decade was a regular on the catwalk for Gucci, Dolce & Gabbana, Versace, Valentino, and Marc Jacobs. She signed an advertising contract with Dior, posing for Nick Knight amongst bubbles and saddle bags, then another with Dolce & Gabbana for its glittering perfume The One, and then another with Victoria’s Secret. She routinely wore the brand’s Red Hot Fantasy Bra—estimated to be worth $15 million in 2000.

Gisele was the Forbes highest-paid model for 12 years in a row, from 2005 to 2016. Her own website estimates she has appeared on an unprecedented 1,200 magazine covers (this issue will be her seventh for i-D). She walked the runway during the 2016 Olympic Opening Ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, released multiple singles, and has appeared in a handful of movies, from Taxi (2004) to The Devil Wears Prada (2006). Gisele has fundraised for Lotus House, Save the Children, The Red Cross, and more. In 2016, Taschen published a book commemorating her 20 years of modelling, retailing for $700 and selling out in one day. The cover shot is by Irving Penn of a nude Gisele. (“I still have the note from him saying that it was wonderful. ‘You did great.’”) Inside are now-legendary photographs by Steven Meisel, David LaChapelle, Inez and Vinoodh, and Juergen Teller. Gisele has published one autobiography and one cookbook, which is to say nothing of the digests she posts on Instagram to her 22 million followers. She is so famous and so known, from Brazil to Tokyo to New York to Mars, that it would be impossible for any one of us to calculate exactly where we know her from or how many times we’ve seen her face.

And yet, for Gisele, who turned 46 in July, those wandering Tokyo days are among her most special. “My whole thing is going back to that,” she tells me, tucked into an armchair in a white tank and jean shorts. “How can I create more of that reality in my life?”

You see, despite being the object of so many gazes, Gisele prefers to set hers on the sun, the sea, the sky. She was born on a farm in Brazil, surrounded by her grandparents, parents, sisters, and pets. Now, 6,900 kilometres away, she’s recreated that paradise in Northern Miami with her children Benjamin (16), Vivian (13), and a baby boy (16 months), her husband Joaquim, and a pair of dogs.

“Life is a gift,” she says. “I think I have so much joy in my life because I really see the ordinary as the extraordinary… The sun rises every day. You can walk around and be grateful for it, or you can just be disconnected from all these incredible things. You can be robbed of your life if you think life is this”—she mimics looking down at her phone—“and you forget life is so much more.”
She smiles, sipping from her room-temperature water. “Anyway, I’m sure you have more questions for me.”
Because we got into the meaning of life and Gisele’s very philosophy of being so quickly into our first meeting, here’s what happened in the lead-up—minutes one through seven:
1. I enter Gisele’s small ranch home a couple blocks from her larger, beachfront estate. I am promptly served her homemade granola and her proprietary tea (warming, like dark chocolate and honey).
2. Alfie, her gigantic German Shepherd, comes in first and gives me the once-over. “He’s my protector,” Gisele smiles, kicking off her sandals and wrapping me up in a hug.

3. “You smell amazing,” she says, and I just give her the bottle of perfume in my purse. She asks if it has parabens, and I say I don’t know, and she tells me never to use anything with parabens, especially on your wrists or neck. It’s been three months and I am still too embarrassed to research: Does Maison Louis Marie’s scent Aboukir have parabens?
4. She checks my astrological vibe to make sure this interview will go well: “What’s your sign?” she asks squarely.
“Cancer. I knew we’d talk about it. I read you’re a Cancer, Scorpio Moon. What’s your rising?”

“Oh, go girl! I don’t even know how I ended up doing this job. If you let me, I would just never leave my house, because I’m a crab. And with the Scorpio Moon, for me, if it’s not deep, I don’t want to talk about it.”

That’s the guiding premise of being Gisele: Always searching for depth, connection, and meaning. In some way, modelling was the perfect job for her—homey, crablike tendencies notwithstanding—because it allowed her to find connections the world over. The high-low of the industry, which led to anxiety attacks in her mid-20s, was the impetus for Gisele’s soul searching. “Shit happens to all of us, but I think I don’t stay there,” she says of the down days. “I learned how to meditate. It’s like you can take a step back: You can be having an experience and observing yourself having that experience at the same time.”

Meditation led her to yoga, which she practises routinely, and then to Pilates and then to jujitsu. Recently, she has added weight training. “I do weights three times a week. I do Pilates once or twice a week. I do yoga two or three times a week. I work out every day because, for me, working out—I don’t see it as something I have to do. I see it as something I get to do,” she says. “It doesn’t matter if I’m surfing, if I’m playing volleyball with my daughter, if I’m paddleboarding. Whatever it is, I feel like it’s a moment of being.” She bares a bicep. “Now for the first time in my life, I can do pull-ups.”

Early this summer morning, she took her baby to the park. Much like his older half-siblings, he has picked up on Gisele’s connectivity and generosity. “I have to show you this video.” For the first time, she whips out her phone and opens her camera roll. As she scrolls through—I promise I’m not trying to peek!—I realise almost every photo is of her kids. “He’s so funny,” she says of her son, captured waddling around the park with a paper towel. “I mean, he’s 16 months and he saw that I was cleaning the park—because Miami, it’s so damp all the time!—and he wanted to participate and he felt really good about it,” Gisele beams, watching her tiny son dry off the slide, the seesaw, the swing.

“Kids give us this opportunity to live again, to be more present and to experience life again. To do it maybe differently than we’ve done it before.” She pauses. “I don’t know. I find every little thing so amazing.” Gisele goes on to show me videos of Benny DJing in his bedroom, his baby brother dancing by his side. She has pictures of Vivi playing volleyball (“She’s amazing!”) and dancing with friends. She scrolls to a dancing video. “I mean, what is better than this? This is my daughter and she’s like, ‘Mum, let’s do a dance class.’ So this is us doing a dance class. I’m not so great,” Gisele laughs, “but look at her and her friend—and that’s her mum’s friend.”

She quickly scrolls through about 20 more videos before she chucks her phone away. “By the way, I don’t know if you noticed, my phone doesn’t ring. There’s no alarms. It never rings. It’s liberating.”

A silenced iPhone and spending all day with her family is a far cry from the past 30 years of Gisele’s life. To briefly summarise the lore: Her mother enrolled her, her twin sister Patí, and younger sister Gabriela in modelling classes in Brazil. Gisele was later scouted to participate in the Elite Model Look competition, and in 1995, she placed second. From 1996 to 2016, life didn’t stop—she spent the better part of her 20s and 30s at the white-hot centre of it all: Fashion, fame, celebrity, paparazzi, and money. She was signing bigger contracts than other models, getting bigger media attention, becoming an entity bigger than Gisele Bündchen from Horizontina, Brazil. She was, by 2004, a supermodel, capital S. Everything about her sparkled.

“I’ve experienced the rat race. I was on the hamster wheel in my early 20s,” she says. “I won Model of the Year at 19. I worked so hard from 14 to get to that place, I felt like I couldn’t say no [to major jobs].” And sure, Gisele encountered so much of the bullshit so many models of the ’90s and ’00s did. She tried not to let her industry’s lack of protection faze her. “Even though I wasn’t going to the parties, I was doing 360 days [of work a year]. I wanted to be the best that I could be every day. I wanted to bring my best.”

We start to look through some of her runway fits from her catwalk days and she sparks up with delight. “Girl, it was very tight inside. You couldn’t really move so much—but, I mean, look how he made you look!” she cheers of a supersized Fall 2004 Christian Dior look by John Galliano. “I’m forever grateful to McQueen, I’m forever grateful to John. I was always so excited to do the Dior shows because I never knew what I was going to look like.”

She singles out a Galliano show for Dior held at Versailles. “This was 60 years of Dior and I wasn’t even doing shows anymore. John was like, ‘Please, Gisele. This is all my muses and it’s going to be the 60 years, it’s to be in Versailles.’ I was like, ‘I must do it,’” she remembers. “Look at these shoes. It was like a platform without a heel. I was walking on cement, like bricks. It was crazy. I was like, ‘Am I going to fall and break my ankle?’”

But that’s the thing about Gisele: Even if she’s struggling to walk or struggling to feel beautiful—as she often recounts of that first-ever McQueen show, where she hit the runway topless with a trompe l’oeil white tank painted on by Val Garland, rain falling and her lashes dripping into her eyes—she is always going to do her best. “I didn’t say no or complain because people were giving me the opportunity,” she reflects. “I came in, I did my job, I went home… and I think what I really appreciate and really enjoyed about fashion is that it got me to access and experience different sides of me. I really wanted to be the best canvas for the creatives. I felt like it was my way of contributing.”

But working in the oil-slick glossy world of new millennium modelling meant that few people saw Gisele as a full person—because of her beauty, her chameleonic qualities, and her prowess, she was quickly regarded as an idol. Nice to look at, nothing to say. The first time she appeared in i-D, on the cover in December 1998, she wasn’t interviewed. Instead, the photographer who took the picture was, and here’s what he had to say about the smart and vibrant Gisele: “She’s certainly gorgeous. I’d marry her.”

Her “godfather” in the turbulent fashion industry was Steven Meisel. (Are you surprised that the greatest model of her generation would find kinship with the greatest photographer of his?) In one of the earliest pieces of press about Gisele, a New York Magazine article from 1999, Meisel already saw her as more than a body to stand in front of his lens. He felt her spirit. “Gisele is able to change because she wants to—it’s not in her looks; it’s in her mental process. She is malleable and is willing to be a silent screen star because she understands that modelling is acting,” he told the mag. He later wrote the foreword for her Taschen book, and she still speaks of him as her guardian angel. “I’m grateful for him. I don’t think I would have been the model that I was if it wasn’t for him, for real. We got to play together. I shot with him every week.”

And yet, after weekly Meisel shoots, over 130 Vogue covers, and decades on billboards and TV ad spots, Gisele wanted more. Well—maybe not more in the way you and I might think of it. She wanted to actually enjoy what she’d accomplished, and that meant leaving the fracas behind. After a decade in Boston, she relocated here, to Florida, to co-parent her older children and set up a new world of sea and sun and sand. Being mum, practising gratitude, taking care of herself and her community have become more valuable than any seven-figure ad job: “I say no to 99 percent of the jobs I’m offered because, when I put it on the scale, I’m like, ‘Am I going to miss my daughter’s volleyball game? Am I going to miss going to the park with my son? Am I going to miss my son DJing?’”

That’s why, with the exception of a few trips to her home in Costa Rica, to see family in Brazil, and recently, to Tahiti, Gisele rarely leaves Florida. “Having a baby at this moment of my life is such a gift, because I’m in a different place. I don’t have anything to prove. I don’t feel like I really, quite frankly, care.”
“I’m not defined by other people’s opinions,” she continues, firmly. “I feel like I get to choose how I want to live my life.”

Being alive today can feel like a quest for more: Make more money. Diversify your portfolio. Get PRP+ to be more beautiful and then Ozempic to be more svelte. Become a brand and use that brand to become more famous. Every day of your life can be used to sell something or say something or self-improve. I don’t think I have ever encountered a person more satisfied with exactly how her life is than Gisele. She has a lot, sure, but it’s long been enough. She’s done a lot, sure, but she’s not looking back. She’s been everywhere, yeah, but she isn’t driven by getting in your face.

She’s not a brand. She’s not an entrepreneur. She’s not a self-help guru—even though I tell her she should have a podcast. She’s not forcing Gisele-dom down our throats and, in some way, it seems like she doesn’t really want to be famous at all. That she’s financially well-off, she tells me, is just an opportunity to take care of her sisters and her family. She doesn’t want fancy clothes. She hasn’t been to New York in over two years and she’s not eager to come back.

“At the end of the day, this is your temple, this is your life, this is your journey. How do you want it to look? What do you want it to be? Who defines success?” she asks, as concerned in that moment with my well-being as with her own. “What is success? Some people say success is power, money, fame, more. Some people say success is being able to spend time with your kids, to have food on your table, to have a home to live in, to have great relationships and actually enjoy every day. I find that, quite frankly, much more successful than…” she trails off, not eager to point a finger. “It’s up to each person to define, because when I was in my 20s, success was different than what I feel today.”
“What do you want your legacy to be?” I ask as we’re wrapping up our conversation.

“In the end, I ended up having the best time. I ended up enjoying it all, staying in it, learning from it, and growing up in it. It’s been a blessing. However people see me, that’s okay with me. I want to look back and think, ‘I really enjoyed this journey. I really loved fully. I really experienced every emotion. I really had meaningful relationships. I tried to make the world a better place, and I made my surroundings more harmonious and loving and beautiful.’ I want my kids to feel like I was a great mum and that I helped them become the best version of themselves. I want to feel like I lived striving to be the best version of myself. Hopefully, I can look back and say I did it.”

Today, after I pack up my things and head for Miami International Airport, she’ll go to a birthday dinner. It’s a rare night out for Gisele, and after decades of no carbs and no dairy, she might have some of her friend’s homemade sourdough. “What’s better than bread and cheese? Oh my god, I don’t know!” she laughs. Tomorrow, she’ll wake up early to paddleboard. She’s worried about me not seeing the sea one last time before I get on a plane back to New York, but she’s calmed when I tell her I spent two hours on the beach this morning. As I wheel away my little suitcase and say goodbye, she pops her head out the front door with a final blessing. “Live the life you want to live! Everything else is going to shake out.”

items.title: The Democratic Socialists of America Are Threatening to Dump Nithya Raman
items.description: Nithya Raman, the Democratic Socialist of America member running to be mayor of Los Angeles, is at risk of losing support from her local DSA chapter.
items.author: Maxwell Adler
paragraphs: Nithya Raman, the Democratic Socialist of America member running to be mayor of Los Angeles, is at risk of losing support from her local DSA chapter.

The Democratic Socialists of America’s national leadership is considering stripping Raman of the endorsement she received from its Los Angeles chapter in August, citing her refusal to explicitly embrace the Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions movement against Israel.

The DSA’s National Political Committee has determined that its Los Angeles chapter violated national rules when it endorsed Raman in August because local DSA leaders didn’t ask the candidate whether she supported BDS. National leaders are now considering proposals to rescind the endorsement and prevent the LA chapter from using its resources to support her campaign.

But local DSA leaders are pushing back. In a message to members, obtained by Vanity Fair, LA chapter co-chairs Leslie Chang and Sean Wakasa acknowledged that they failed to include a mandatory question about BDS during their endorsement process, calling it an “oversight.” But they insisted Raman’s positions on Palestinian rights have “evolved significantly” and that she’s aligned with the organization on this issue. The local chapter also said they have requested a written statement from Raman’s campaign asking her to clarify her position.
Raman’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment. The National DSA declined to comment.

The dispute could present a problem for Raman, who rode DSA support to an upset City Council victory in 2020 but has since frustrated some DSA members with her positions on policing, housing development, and Israel.

Locally, losing the endorsement could strip Raman of volunteers and organizing infrastructure just weeks before her runoff against Mayor Karen Bass. But the rupture could also complicate her opponents’ efforts to portray Raman as an uncompromising far-left radical.

In the last few months, Raman and Bass have both been courting supporters of Spencer Pratt, the conservative reality television personality who got 26% of the vote in June’s primary by running an anti-establishment, tough on crime campaign. Some Pratt voters might actually look favorably on Raman if she refuses to endorse BDS in order to secure DSA-LA’s support.

Jason Oppenheim, the luxury real estate broker best known for his role on Selling Sunset, was intrigued by Pratt and Raman this election cycle. He attended campaign events for both candidates and recently interviewed Raman on Graham Stephan's podcast. Like a lot of other more politically centrist Angelenos, Oppenheim is apprehensive about the DSA’s rise but he’s encouraged by Raman’s willingness to break with the organization on policy. He told VF that losing the DSA endorsement could actually help Raman. “To a lot of moderates, a DSA endorsement is a net negative,” he told VF. Raman, he argued, already has a lot of progressive support and should be courting the Pratt and Rick Caruso voters.
Nationally, the fight raises a larger question about how much ideological compromise the DSA will accept in its pursuit of electoral power.

Just yesterday, The New Yorker published a story about how the DSA is embracing political pragmatism over ideological purity in an attempt to gain some real governing power, and they highlighted DSA-LA’s endorsement of Raman as evidence of that shift in thinking.
More than 900 local DSA members voted to endorse Raman. There’s currently a petition circulating among them urging national leaders to respect their vote to endorse Raman.

When Vanity Fair profiled Raman earlier this year, her team asked us to qualify a line in the story about Raman accepting an endorsement from a Pro-Israel group (Democrats For Israel-Los Angeles) in order to specify that it wasn’t from AIPAC. Then at last week’s mayoral debate, Raman quoted Ronald Reagan. The trouble with trying to please anti-zionist socialists and Reagan Republicans? You risk alienating both.

items.title: Burberry’s Next Print? A Watercolor by King Charles III
items.description: King Charles III, as we know, has a keen sense of style. In addition to being named one of the best-dressed men by various magazines, the monarch has also forged collaborations with some of the most renowned fashion houses, creating collections infused with hi
items.author: Laura Scafati
paragraphs: King Charles III, as we know, has a keen sense of style. In addition to being named one of the best-dressed men by various magazines, the monarch has also forged collaborations with some of the most renowned fashion houses, creating collections infused with his aesthetic vision and a commitment to sustainability.

This time, however, the king wanted to go a step further, personally designing the central motif of the fifth collection born from the well-established collaboration between Burberry and Highgrove Gardens—the gardens surrounding the private residence of King Charles III and Queen Camilla, managed by The King’s Foundation, the charitable foundation established by King Charles and dedicated to nature conservation and sustainability.

Specifically, the king created a watercolor depicting Birkhall, the British royal family’s private country residence in Aberdeenshire, Scotland, on the Balmoral estate, which was reproduced on some of the pieces in the capsule collection. The result is a beautiful chromatic ode to the unmistakable English countryside and its dreamlike atmosphere.

King Charles’s artwork stands out on an intarsia-knit wool sweater and a silk scarf. The entire collection is embellished by Burberry’s iconic House Check pattern, reimagined in a laurel green palette created exclusively for this collection. Among the key pieces of Highgrove x Burberry are the Waterloo trench coat, the Mayfair trench jacket, a car coat, a quilted jacket, and an intarsia-knit sweater, along with a range of accessories.

It’s a collection that, in addition to being a pure reflection of British style, aims to be a guardian of artisanal excellence—a value shared by the fashion house and the royal family. The main fabric and linings of the trench coats and car coats are, in fact, made in England using gabardine composed of 100% organic cotton.

This attention to detail and sustainability has always been a key value for the monarch and his ongoing commitment to environmental protection, a commitment particularly evident in the gardens of Highgrove. Considered among the most inspiring and innovative gardens in the United Kingdom, they now host educational workshops that teach young people traditional skills linked to cultural heritage and craftsmanship.
Originally published in Vanity Fair France.

items.title: Benedict Cumberbatch, Jude Law, and More Celebrate at the British Museum Ball
items.description: In the days before the second annual British Museum Ball, there was plenty of chatter about the event: who would be there; what everyone would be wearing; how exactly the artist Es Devlin would transform the Queen Elizabeth II Great Court, said to be the large
items.author: Nate Freeman
paragraphs: In the days before the second annual British Museum Ball, there was plenty of chatter about the event: who would be there; what everyone would be wearing; how exactly the artist Es Devlin would transform the Queen Elizabeth II Great Court, said to be the largest covered public square in Europe. It helped that Frieze London and Frieze Masters opened Wednesday, injecting a jolt of art mania into Regent’s Park. Then on Friday came the news that the British Museum had received a gift of 30 million British pounds (around $40 million) from “a single, long-standing supporter,” money independent of the funds raised by the gala that will go toward renovations known as the Masterplan—a massive endeavor described in a press release as one of “the most ambitious cultural redevelopment projects undertaken anywhere in the world.”

As the ball began Saturday, more than 850 figures from the worlds of art, fashion, film, and British society arrived in Bloomsbury—including London mayor Sadiq Khan, a co-chair of the event, and Mick Jagger, who took the stage at the event to proclaim, “All of us here tonight are the custodians of this wonderful museum. We hope to continue and inspire generations of artists, inventors, historians, and new Mozarts.” (Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart famously visited the British Museum when he was a nine-year-old prodigy, presenting the institution with a motet he composed, in English, while in London.) Benedict Cumberbatch and Jude Law were also on hand. The two stars performed a version of Letters Live, an epistolary routine in which each actor read from a series of correspondence.

Devlin’s installations included three large-scale sculptural interventions, one of which paid homage to the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum after a truly herculean loan agreement with France. Following dinner, Wyclef Jean performed.

For those in town to soak up the art and culture at Frieze London, this was a pretty spectacular way to wind up the week. “At the heart of everything we do is our ambition to make the British Museum more welcoming, and inspiring for everyone,” said Dr. Nicholas Cullinan, director of the museum, “and this evening has been a wonderful celebration of that shared vision.”

items.title: Muna Safe After Tour Bus Catches Fire on California Highway
items.description: A tour bus carrying the members of Muna caught fire on the freeway in Burbank, California, on Monday. The scene was captured on camera by local station KTLA, which reported the incident shut down several lanes on the busy roadway.
items.author: Charisma Madarang
paragraphs: A tour bus carrying the members of Muna caught fire on the freeway in Burbank, California, on Monday. The scene was captured on camera by local station KTLA, which reported the incident shut down several lanes on the busy roadway.

The station said the driver reportedly did not realize the bus was on fire when the California Highway Patrol got a call at 8 a.m. about a flaming bus on the southbound 5 freeway. After the bus pulled over on an off-ramp, the Burbank Fire Department was able to put out the fire.

Muna shared a photo from KTLA’s coverage on their social media alongside a caption: “the band MUNA as seen on the news this morning.” The band said that “many personal items were lost but we’re all safe, thank goodness.”

In the comments section, musician Naomi McPherson wrote, “If anyone could help me find the grandchild of the warlock whose curse is wreaking havoc on my life so that I can carry em up the mountain & fulfill the prophecy/undo the curse that has befallen me that would be much appreciated.”

Back in September, Muna announced that McPherson, who plays guitar, synths, and sings in the band, would need to miss several tour dates to look after their mother, Harriet, who was in the terminal stages of a cancer battle. Muna also paid tribute to Harriet in the post, calling her “one of the greatest, most wise and loving people.”

McPherson is back on the road with Muna for their Gets So Hot Tour, which kicked off Sept. 25 in Philadelphia. The band has one more show at Red Rocks Park and Amphitheatre outside of Denver on Oct. 21 before heading to Europe for another month of concerts.

items.title: The 10 Best Jane Austen Adaptations, Ranked
items.description: Let’s talk about truths universally acknowledged. Men with fortunes want wives. Being happy in marriage is often up to chance. And Jane Austen’s body of work makes for undeniable magic on the screen.
items.author: CT Jones
paragraphs: Let’s talk about truths universally acknowledged. Men with fortunes want wives. Being happy in marriage is often up to chance. And Jane Austen’s body of work makes for undeniable magic on the screen.

When Austen published her first novel, Sense and Sensibility, anonymously in 1811, there was no way for her to know that her books would remain cultural touchstones for over two centuries. But the timeless yet deceptively modern nature of her work — lush family dramas and earnest romances woven with strong critiques about the place of women in England’s early-19th-century elite — has given Austen’s stories more than staying power in the world of literature: It’s made them ripe for adaptation and reinterpretation.

Some cinematic treatments of Austen’s books thrive on strict adherence to her words and world-building. Others keep the dialogue but experiment with an irreverent treatment of the costuming or setting. And still others use Austen’s stories as a jumping-off point to explore an entirely new world, centering viewers in the familiar emotional tethers while allowing them to see their favorite characters in new contexts.

With the latest Austen adaptation in theaters now — a new version of Sense and Sensibility, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and George MacKay — we’ve conducted a rigorous review of modern interpretations of her books for both film and television. Here, our highly unscientific ranking of the 10 best Austen adaptations.

- ‘Mansfield Park’ (1999) Austen’s third novel follows downtrodden child Fanny Price as she’s sent from her poor household to live with wealthy family members, and the consequences that follow her feeling out of her place her entire life. It takes a dedicated Austenhead to adore the book where her dowdy and quiet main character falls in love with and eventually marries her cousin, which might explain why this adaptation takes the character in a different direction. Actress Frances O’Connor imbues Fanny with way more spine than she has in the text. The film also explicitly addresses how the Price family’s wealth was built on the backs of slaves, adding historical context that makes the criticisms baked into Austen’s work an integral part of the plot.

- ‘Persuasion’ (1995) Austen’s saga of broken engagements and late-in-life love has a bit more going on than her most popular books. There are mistresses, Navy captains, family fortunes lost and regained, and a heroine who’s closer to middle age than the fresh blush of youth. But this adaptation thrives on production choices that keep it grounded. There’s little makeup, the costumes are period-accurate, and Ciarán Hinds gives a standout performance — all of which helps the story feel almost indistinguishable from the book. This is the type of Austen adaptation that you don’t boo when your teacher puts it on at school.

- ‘Bride and Prejudice’ (2004) A not-universally-acknowledged truth: Many movies get better when people SING. Directed by Gurinder Chadha, Bride and Prejudice tracks the modern-day love story of Lalita Bakshi, a young Indian woman bound by familial expectations, and Will Darcy, an American friend who puts his foot in his mouth at a wedding by calling arranged marriages backward. The film, set in London, India, and Los Angeles, turns Austen Bollywood, with an explosion of dance numbers, memorable songs, and a double-wedding ending.

- ‘The Lizzie Bennet Diaries’ (2012) If adaptations are all about form, The Lizzie Bennet Diaries might be the most inventive. The web series from Hank Green imagines a modern version of the Bennet family, with stay-at-home grad-student Lizzie narrating the story through vlogs for her thesis project. This is the adaptation that might give Lizzie’s best friend Charlotte the most prominent role; in the vlogs, Charlotte is both director and editor, and remains in Lizzie’s life throughout the story. The clever approach helped make it the first digital series to ever win an Emmy Award.

- ‘Fire Island’ (2022) It’s a shame Austen died before learning about the gay nexus that is New York’s Fire Island. It’s full of things she loved: drama, intrigue, passionate romance, and plenty of balls (albeit maybe not the kind she most often wrote about). Lucky for us, Joel Kim Booster figured out just how much the queer summering grounds and Austen had in common. This rom-com retelling of Pride of Prejudice starring Booster, Bowen Yang, Conrad Ricamora, Margaret Cho, and Matt Rogers puts new faces to Austen’s familiar characters, placing them alongside Grindr, the Meat Locker, drug use, naked house parties, and sweet sunset countdowns.

- ‘Pride and Prejudice’ (1995) The common nickname for this BBC miniseries of Pride and Prejudice makes its draw clear: This is “the Colin Firth one.” Its place in the history books is helped along by Jennifer Ehle’s Elizabeth — whose refusal of Mr. Darcy’s first proposal is so full of indignation that it practically singes the green patterned wallpaper. (It was celebrated in the viral 2015 meme “Rest in pieces, Mr. Darcy,” which soundtracks Ehle’s refusal scene to the beat drop of DJ Snake and Lil Jon’s “Turn Down for What.”) But Firth, as Darcy, also does some heavy lifting. Practically every actor who’s ever stepped into the landed gentryman’s boots knows how to make him gloomy, impenetrable, and brooding. Firth made him awkward and angry — a choice that makes Darcy’s eventual marriage to Elizabeth feel well earned.

- ‘Sense and Sensibility’ (1995) Before he gave us The Ice Storm, Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon, and Brokeback Mountain, director Ang Lee tackled Austen’s first novel, adapted by and starring Emma Thompson as the sensible Elinor Dashwood. Hugh Grant is at his most charming and bumbling as the object of her affections, Edward Ferrars, while Kate Winslet and Alan Rickman play the slowly blossoming lovers Marianne Dashwood and Colonel Brandon. Thompson won an Oscar for adapted screenplay, but it’s Lee’s knack for emotional restraint and tension that make this period romance a high point of the genre.

- ‘Emma’ (2020) Yes, most people remember Gwenyth Paltrow’s cherubic 1996 screen version of Emma, complete with ringlet curls and a bow and arrow. But the Autumn de Wilde-directed iteration, starring Anya Taylor-Joy, manages to deliver on the most essential aspect of Austen’s book. The titular Emma is beautiful. But she’s also impulsive, spoiled, and, at times, incredibly cruel to the people around her. Taylor-Joy perfects Emma’s look of shame. And armed with sizzling chemistry between her and Johnny Flynn, as George Knightley, and hysterical character work from Josh O’Connor and Mia Goth, this Emma sings.

- ‘Sense and Sensibility’ (2026) Director Georgia Oakley, I was unfamiliar with your game. This new version of Sense and Sensibility proves just how timeless Austen’s work remains. Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles (daughter of Samantha Morton) put the power of sisterhood on stark display in this pastoral version of the author’s classic. They’re helped along by a quiet George MacKay, whose sad eyes lend the film a romantic, tragic air, and a borderline riotous Fiona Shaw, who’s an Austen expert at this point. (She played Lady Russell in the 1995 adaptation of Persuasion and will play Lady Catherine de Bourgh in Netflix’s six-part Pride and Prejudice coming in December.) The end result is a film that manages to strike a balance between epic romance and rousing comedy, packaged in the way Austen adored best — a simple tale about what people are willing to do for love.

- ‘Pride and Prejudice’ (2005) Two decades after its premiere, the Joe Wright-helmed Pride and Prejudice is the blueprint for Austen adaptations. The cast is full of heavy hitters, including Keira Knightly as Elizabeth Bennet, the late Donald Sutherland as Lizzie’s father, Matthew Macfadyen as Mr. Darcy, Rosamund Pike as poor Jane Bennet, Judi Dench as Lady Catherine, and Jena Malone and Carey Mulligan as the youngest Bennet girls. But it’s Wright’s treatment of landscape that makes this film a sleepover staple. The woods breathe, the rush of the air feels like it blows off the screen and right into your living room, and the foggy English countryside transports viewers into Austen’s lived world.

items.title: The Diplomat Recap: Advisory Board, Assemble
items.description: The what-could-have-been vibe of “The Dead” is agonizing. If Todd were not so loyal to and trusting of his wife, who is unfortunately also POTUS, he might have been a valued member of the advisory board Kate assembles with Stuart and Eidra. The outcome of Kate
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: The what-could-have-been vibe of “The Dead” is agonizing. If Todd were not so loyal to and trusting of his wife, who is unfortunately also POTUS, he might have been a valued member of the advisory board Kate assembles with Stuart and Eidra. The outcome of Kate’s conversation with Vaughn might have been the same, but perhaps if she could have trusted Todd to attend without trumpeting Grace’s warships ultimatum (even one flimsily disguised as an offer of help), he’d have offered an insight that was sufficiently reassuring to get her to accept Kate’s offer of a joint mission to retrieve the bodies of the Russian submariners.

Instead, Kate gets her hopes up for nothing, and the shiny new upgraded security clearance she acquires for Todd may wind up coming back to bite her. Boo! I think another part of what leads Todd to back delivering Grace’s entire message to Vaughn — “tell the Russians to stay out of her yard, or I’ll send warships to do it for her” — over Kate’s preferred plan of only delivering the first half is that he hasn’t seen Grace at her reactive, high-handed worst in one of the high-security Zooms yet. He’s seen enough to make him concerned; he tells Kate what anyone with eyes has already seen many times, that Grace has been different since the shooting and that “there’s a lot less nuance in her perspective and in the way that she talks about things.” This seems to me, a person whose vast medical expertise comes from her decades-long enrollment in such rigorous programs as the full-season runs of ER and Call The Midwife, like a problem that is preventing her from carrying out her duties as the Commander-in-Chief and Chief Executive of the nation. My second bold take of the day is that it’s essential for anyone in those roles to be in command of the facts and capable of working with others to arrive at good solutions to the problems they face. Grace seems to hope for escalation at every turn and is recklessly determined to bring it about. Meanwhile, Hal too often dumps gas on the fire when he ought to be pumping the brakes.

Todd also mentioned feeling shut out from Grace’s thoughts and decision-making process; of course he’s been unsettled and worried as well as resentful. This puts him in good, if uncomfortable, company with Billie, who tells Hal about how the week previous, she was in the middle of a negotiation of the Labor HHS budget, when she received a push notification about the President having approved the $200 billion budget without her. Intentional humiliation? Forgetfulness? Is one any better than the other?

Kate manages to convince Todd to raise the issue of the warships ultimatum with Grace before they meet with Prime Minister Vaughn, and for one tantalizing moment it seems as though reasonableness may prevail. Admittedly, Kate’s (and my) hopes were a little too high to start with. Todd isn’t a seasoned diplomat or political operative, and on top of that, Grace confides that part of why she wants him in London is to show the world that she’s not afraid for him to be in the place where she was nearly murdered. She is afraid, though, and that shared confidence with Todd is a significant one. He can’t bring himself to not do what the President has asked, because she is also his wife.

Once Kate’s Todd hopes are dashed, and she can tell that Stuart told Eidra about her blackmailing Trowbridge, it becomes easier for her to take the big step of reading them both into all of the gory details going back to the attack on HMS Courageous. The levels of shock Stuart experiences…whatever the State Department is paying him, they should triple it immediately. If Kate’s not going to have regular friends, these two, who work alongside and care about her, will make a solidly trustworthy advisory board. Good for her for finally saying out loud that she may be in over her head and incapable of seeing clearly enough to know that she’s working for “a culture of consistent lawlessness”. And good for Stuart and Eidra for confirming her new perception of the situation and facilitating a new plan to circumvent Todd’s participation in her conversation with Vaughn. I love when a plan comes together!

I also love this scene between Kate and Vaughn at the latter’s family home in her constituency. We only see it at nighttime in this episode, but it’s a very impressive old pile, the kind of place you stick with even though it’s impossible to heat or cool consistently and nothing really works anymore. Having opened her home in the middle of the night, Vaughn once again strikes Kate (and me) as the very picture of decency and good faith. The character is written to be very likable and worthy of respect, and Jodie Whittaker brings a really effective extra oomph of warmth and humor to her performance that makes her consistent refusals to accept Kate’s proposals even more striking.

Grace Penn wants Vaughn to revoke her permission to the Russians as a secret-keeping courtesy to the U.S.? It would have been a courtesy for Grace to mention to Trowbridge that she’d ordered the U.S. Navy to remove the Poseidon, but she didn’t. Vaughn hasn’t given up the Americans, though; she has not told the Russians about the Poseidon, largely because it would seem unbelievable that “our closest allies would do that to us without our consent.” She’s so calm, and not in Trowbridge’s usual way of seeming as though he was holding himself back from flying into a rage through force of will. She’s just a very grounded person who is communicating thoughtful decisions.

Kate’s new idea, for a joint mission between the U.S. and Royal Navies to carefully retrieve the bodies of the dead from the submarine and tell the Russians it’s all been entombed in concrete, also fails. Not on its merits, which Vaughn agrees are quite good, but because of the number and scale of betrayals of trust the U.S. has inflicted on the U.K. From her perspective, “The fundamental character of your country has sufficiently changed that we have no idea what you will do next.” She’ll take her chances with the predictable Russians instead, thank you very much. And that’s the end of that. As planned, Kate doesn’t issue the warships ultimatum, and once back at Winfield House, tells Todd he’s welcome to sit in on her conversation with Grace.

Todd is not thrilled that Kate went to speak with Vaughn without him, but there’s no time for him to get into that just yet. Instead, it’s time for Kate to lie her face off by confirming that she issued Grace’s ultimatum, and that Vaughn agreed to call the Kremlin to revoke her permission for Russian ships to enter British waters.

• That final moment with the secure link video call is the first moment that Gannon learns of Todd’s new role as Special Envoy with higher security clearance. The chain of communication in the Penn administration really is something else.

• One tiny glimmer of a good thing for Stuart as he learns one appalling fact after another: he can recover his good opinion of the late President Rayburn, who was not involved in the bombing of HMS Courageous, after all.

• What a sweet relief to see Stuart and Eidra resolve their conflict about the status and future of their relationship. I particularly liked the proposal to discuss from Eidra – all those post-its in the breeze of her desk fan and the legal pad sun held aloft reminded me of Max Cohen’s thousand yellow daisies-based proposal to Lorelai in Gilmore Girls. The song playing on her desk speaker in this scene is Prince’s classic slow jam “Adore”. Solid pick.
• Eidra taking the measure of the young Vaughn who asks for a jammy dodger before delivering a cool “no”. One of my favorite little moments of the season so far.

items.title: The Diplomat Recap: Is She Your Wife or Is She the President?
