items.description: Kate Wyler is not having a great week. It’s not enough to have inadvertently prompted the British prime minister to resign. Oh, no; now she must await a new PM’s election, establish and manage a new relationship with a new administration, and process her roili
items.author: Sophie Brookover
paragraphs: Kate Wyler is not having a great week. It’s not enough to have inadvertently prompted the British prime minister to resign. Oh, no; now she must await a new PM’s election, establish and manage a new relationship with a new administration, and process her roiling emotions at having set that whole mess in motion, all while babysitting the Second Gentleman. Bonus first-act plot twist: Said gentleman plans to move into Winfield House and the embassy, has a million questions, and is prone to leaping to wild conclusions. For her part, Bethan Vaughn (the very welcome Jodie Whittaker) steps into Nicol Trowbridge’s shoes at No. 10 with an approach nearly 180 degrees apart from her predecessor. Where he was impulsive (“Ruled by his tempers,” as she puts it), Vaughn is thoughtful and measured, the type of leader who thinks and “consults the graybeards” in her cabinet before making a big decision. What a concept! Are the scales tilting ever so slightly toward measured normalcy? Come on. That’s not what we’re here for.

Both Vaughn and Todd have tremendous potential as maybe-allies for Kate. She’s pretty good at moving Todd where she needs him to go, and he can and does offer insights into Grace’s psyche that nobody else can or will. His suitability for the role is also sharply limited by his understandable loyalty to Grace. Last season, I remarked that Kate is very isolated. She doesn’t really have a trusted chum on this assignment, and she’s stuck confiding in Hal (who is always playing an angle) and unable to do the same with any of the likely candidates in their circle, like Billie. Grace is, at best, her frenemy; Roylin is dead; and Thema Asseidu-Dennison is grieving. Eidra has the best potential — they have a good rapport and she’s read into most of the sticky situations Kate gets herself into — but is a bit too co-worker-y to be Kate’s ride-or-die, and they both know it. Vaughn is bright, warm, funny, capable, self-aware — A+ friend material, if only Kate were not the representative of a government that has attacked a British aircraft carrier, stolen a nuclear superweapon and lied about it, and blackmailed her predecessor.

Kate’s first meeting with Vaughn goes well; they hit it off immediately and part on good terms. It was a strange nothingburger in every other respect, though, as Vaughn spent most of their whopping four minutes together in a funny little song-and-dance with her civil-service secretary, Elaine, who knocks on the door so quietly she can scarcely be heard. It’s a solid time filler and saves Vaughn from having to address anything on Kate’s agenda, especially the content of the congratulatory call she took from her counterpart in Russia. Things get even more alarming when Eidra can’t reach Tom Libby and reports start rolling in that Vaughn is dismissing everyone in Trowbridge’s government who’d had a significant relationship with Kate and her team. Robyn Palmer, while not exactly forthcoming, fills in enough of the gaps in her brief conversation with Kate that the game board comes into sharper focus.

She gets an even crisper twenty-twenty view of the state of play at that evening’s Royal Society gala held in Todd’s honor. In light of recent events, Prime Minister Vaughn has serious concerns about the U.S. relationship with the U.K. and is taking steps to insulate the nation from the unpredictability of its closest ally. She’s permitted the Russians to enter U.K. waters to retrieve the bodies of their dead submariners; when they find that the Poseidon is missing, she says that might put the U.S. in a major security crisis, “and while I do not take that lightly, the last thing I hope to do is make security calculations on your behalf, just as I know you won’t do on mine.”

By my rough calculations, Vaughn is better at her job than Trowbridge was by approximately 82 fafillion percent. She’s calmly, firmly holding up a mirror to Kate, showing her the logical consequences of her actions. Kate keeps saying she’s on the U.K.’s side, but how can she be, when, at the behest of Grace and Hal, she has lied, withheld information, and coerced their government into doing the U.S.’s bidding? That’s actually being the swaggering bully Trowbridge accused the U.S. of being in the previous episode. Kate is more isolated than ever, and more than ever, what she needs is good advice from trustworthy sources. She’s always been a good soldier, doing her best to put the mission first in the name of serving the greater good, but Grace’s orders keep pushing her further and further from anything recognizable as the greater good.

Todd may be Kate’s best bet for a trusted sounding board, especially once they start speaking openly about his likely role as special envoy to the United Kingdom, but he’s also a very mixed bag. He’s clever and kind and seems sincere in his desire to be useful, but he’s also nosy and gossipy, and shares his musings with his wife, who is also the president. Kate sure is throwing up a lot — could she be pregnant? Vaughn stonewalled her about the call she received from Russia — what’s going on there? In fact, what’s going on with Russia in general? Grace is delighted and titillated by Todd’s speculation, and in the middle of a G7 Summit preparation meeting with Billie and Gannon, quietly asks Hal if Kate is pregnant. This little game of highly consequential telephone is a lot to deal with on top of everything else Kate is managing and deciphering. I want to put an extra-fine point on this detail, too: The president of the United States ignored her own chief of staff and secretary of state during a meeting to prepare for their first G7 as a team to have a sidebar conversation about the most personal aspect of her vice-president and British Ambassador’s relationship.

So yes, Grace continues to Grace. She doesn’t just ignore Gannon and Billie; she dismisses their concerns about her planned announcement of a ban on Chinese computer chips, talks over them, and cuts them all off, saying, “Can we stop pretending we’re not in charge? I find it exhausting.” This increasingly frequent defaulting to autocratic behavior combines alarmingly with the almost bloodthirsty pleasure she takes in Trowbridge’s downfall and Kate’s role in it. She actually congratulates Kate and jokes that were it not illegal, she’d appoint Kate to her own post.

Who knows what Grace will think of Todd eventually confirming Hal’s denial of any pregnancy, but Kate has to go to extreme rhetorical lengths to convince him of it, telling him in two separate conversations that her nausea and vomiting are the result of reflux, not morning sickness. Eventually fed up to the back teeth with his refusal to drop the subject, she yells that the real problem is the work she’s doing on behalf of his wife. Sometimes puking is a sign of pregnancy, but in this case, “it’s just the garden variety wave of nausea people get when they’ve overthrown a democratically elected leader!”
If dread-driven nausea is contagious, then poor Frances, unintentionally overhearing this in shocked dismay just outside the door to Kate’s study, is sure to be its next victim.

• Stuart and Eidra have their first big disagreement since getting back together, and it’s a doozy. Eidra pushes her tendency to get glib and sarcastic rather than risk being vulnerable and honest to its farthest limits. Turns out, that pushes Stuart to his limits, too. After she monologues about what a drag it would be to use one of her few individual conversations with the CIA director to request retrofitting Stuart’s house to meet her security needs, concluding with a salty “ew,” Stuart quietly turns away and heads upstairs. Revisit this one tomorrow, lovebirds.

• Turns out Grace asked the head of Todd’s Secret Service detail to plant the special envoy idea. Are we surprised? At all? She needs him out of her hair, and they both need him to feel competent and not an object of Grace’s disdain.

• I recall that early on last season, Hal suggested that Kate shift from her ambassadorship to a brand-new role as special envoy to Europe. It came with tons of potential but no specifics as to budget or brief. What are the odds that these are problems Todd runs into in his own tenure as special envoy?

• Kate Wyler is somewhere between 45 and 55 years old. I get Todd wondering for a few minutes about Kate being pregnant, but a man who fumbled a multimillion-dollar NIH grant and his postmenopausal wife should be capable of a tiny bit of pregnancy-likelihood math before continuing to hang out on the conclusion they jumped to.

• I love the gowns costume designer Jenny Gering has put Keri Russell and Jodie Whittaker in for the gala. Russell always shines in something sleek, and her black column dress makes for a very elegant battle dress. The long sleeves, sweeping A-line skirt, and slightly quilted effect on Whittaker’s black-and-gold number are bold visual reminders of Vaughn’s strategic reserve in her conversations with Kate.

items.title: Gram Parsons Tribute Concert at Troubadour to Feature Emmylou Harris, Elvis Costello, Black Crowes, Margo Price and More
items.description: The “Grievous Angel” will be getting a salute from a lot of grateful angels when an all-star tribute concert honoring the late Gram Parsons takes place at the Troubadour on Nov. 11, three nights before the country-rock pioneer is inducted into the Rock & Roll
items.author: Chris Willman
paragraphs: The “Grievous Angel” will be getting a salute from a lot of grateful angels when an all-star tribute concert honoring the late Gram Parsons takes place at the Troubadour on Nov. 11, three nights before the country-rock pioneer is inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame.

One of Parsons’ key collaborators during his lifetime, Emmylou Harris, leads the bill, along with Elvis Costello, who helped make a new generation aware of his work by recording his songs in the early 1980s (and who has often harmonized with Harris himself). Others on the star-filled lineup include the Black Crowes, Margo Price, Grace Potter, Jesse Welles, the Head and the Heart, Madison Cunningham, Jim Lauderdale, Harper Simon and Grahame Lush. Longtime L.A. favorites the Beachwood Sparks will serve as the house band… or as “cosmic accompaniment,” as the show’s poster art has it.

The concert — officially billed as “A Song for Gram: Celebrating Gram Parsons’ Induction into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame” — is being co-produced by Gram’s daughter, Polly Parsons, Vector Management and Rolling Stone editor-in-chief Shirley Halperin, in conjunction with the Gram Parsons Estate and the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame.
Tickets go on sale Thursday at 10 a.m. PT via AXS. The show will benefit the Friendly House Foundation and Backline, Los Angeles-area organizations supporting addiction and mental health concerns.

Demand will undoubtedly quickly outstrip supply for the show, which Polly Parsons tells Variety will be a “you had to be there” affair. Although some past tributes to her father have taken place in larger venues, Polly says that “it was really important for all of us that we do it somewhere legendary that resonated in the storyline of Gram, and Gram played the Troubadour quite a bit. My hope is that we will be doing more shows in the future. If we get that kind of support, that’s the direction we’ll go, larger venues — maybe an anniversary show at the Santa Barbara Bowl again in a couple years.”

Polly is alluding to the last significant Gram Parsons tribute she spearheaded, which was 22 years ago — a two-night affair at the Universal Amphitheatre and Santa Barbara Bowl dubbed “Return to Sin City” that featured artists including Keith Richards, Lucinda Williams, Steve Earle and Norah Jones. That run of 2004 tribute shows was immortalized on DVD.

“The concert that we were able to do 20 years ago was really a special moment, and I think that we’re coming into another really important moment with Dad’s induction and his 80th birthday, so I thought it would be really nice to get some good folks together and just kind of mark that moment,” Polly says. Her father’s 80th birthday is Nov. 5, less than a week prior to the Troubadour show.

“For me personally,” she says, “it’s beautiful to have the opportunity to celebrate my father’s music with Emmylou Harris in attendance. She wasn’t able to make the first one [in 2004]. This is such an incredible time to honor the music that they created together and to be able to share that in person. And Elvis Costello has been a champion of Gram Parsons, as Chris Robinson and the Black Crowes have been for so many years, and I’m excited for them to have this opportunity to do this in a different setting. I’m also really excited at how many young musicians were so incredibly excited to jump on board with this project. It’s definitely a torch that gets passed from generation to generation, and the fan base is just as passionate as they’ve ever been. Gram is kind of a North Star for this genre of music, and it means a lot, not only that it survived decades of changing times, but remains beloved by people that enjoy authentic music and Americana.”

Polly Parsons has two big jobs to which she devotes her life: first, “I focus my efforts on working with men and women in recovery, walking them through the process of getting to the other side of addiction.” And then, naturally, “nurturing my father’s music and legacy for his grandchild and for the people that love what his vision was and what he stood for.”

The Rock Hall induction already marks a significant and long-sought milestone. “He has a really solid team around him now that I’ve been able to put together in the last three years, and they’re all visionaries and all extremely passionate, and we just really look forward to what’s coming. There’s some good stuff on the way. I’ve been able to put together a really meaningful publishing move that I think will revitalize his music and his catalog, along with the campaign that we put together for getting him finally inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame. People have tried, but it wasn’t until this last couple years of focus that I realized that if we were ever gonna get him nominated, this was the time to really lean into that. His musical family really supported me in that mission, and the team of people that are around me now, we were able to make that happen. So it’s just a lot of passion and hard work and dedication, and running a healthy, vibrant, legacy musical estate for Gram Parsons is really much more about what you say no to than it is what you say yes to.”

items.title: ‘Mayor of Kingstown’ Season 5 Drops Release Date and First Look Photos at Jeremy Renner’s Final Episodes
items.description: “Mayor of Kingstown,” the Taylor Sheridan-created crime series starring Jeremy Renner, will return for its fifth and final season on Jan. 15.
items.author: Selome Hailu
paragraphs: “Mayor of Kingstown,” the Taylor Sheridan-created crime series starring Jeremy Renner, will return for its fifth and final season on Jan. 15.

Accompanying the news, Paramount+ released 15 photos from the season, which picks up “in the wake of Tracy’s murder and the vengeance visited upon Callahan by Mike (Renner) and Kyle McLusky (Taylor Handley),” per the official logline, which continues: “FBI agent Russell Hardy (David Morse) arrives in Kingstown searching for the ‘fugitive’ Callahan. A true lawman, Agent Hardy threatens to unearth all of Mike’s sins and secrets, and disrupt Kingstown’s tenuous balance of power.”

Along with Renner, Handley and Morse, the cast includes Edie Falco as Nina Hobba, Laura Benanti as Cindy Stephens, Hugh Dillon as Ian Ferguson, Tobi Bamtefa as Deverin “Bunny” Washington, Derek Webster as Stevie, Necar Zadegan as Evelyn, Nichole Galicia as Rebecca and Lennie James as Frank Moses.

Sheridan co-created “Mayor of Kingstown” with Hugh Dillon, and both serve as executive producers Antoine Fuqua, David C. Glasser, Ron Burkle, David Hutkin, Bob Yari, Michael Friedman, Dave Erickson, Wendy Riss, Evan Perazzo, Michael Slovis, Regina Corrado, and Keith Cox. Erickson also serves as showrunner for the series, and Sheridan directed the series pilot. Paramount Television Studios, 101 Studios and Bosque Ranch Productions produce the series.
See the first look photos above and below.

items.title: Netflix Sets Release Date for Rob Lowe Documentary ‘The Outsider’
items.description: Netflix is gearing up for a Rob-Lowe-filled holiday season with the release of the actor’s documentary, “Rob Lowe: The Outsider,” and new video episodes of his podcast, “Literally! With Rob Lowe.”
items.author: Tanya Fedak
paragraphs: Netflix is gearing up for a Rob-Lowe-filled holiday season with the release of the actor’s documentary, “Rob Lowe: The Outsider,” and new video episodes of his podcast, “Literally! With Rob Lowe.”

Set to release Nov. 24, “Rob Lowe: The Outsider” traces Lowe’s career from his breakout roles in “The Outsiders” and “St. Elmo’s Fire” to his Emmy-nominated performance on “The West Wing” and how he maintained his Hollywood career. The documentary is directed by Chris Smith (“Tiger King”) and executive produced by Marc Gurvitz, Jon Liebman and Zoe Rogovin. Chris Smith, Sydney Schwartz and Stacy Smith for Library Film produce.

Lowe’s podcast, “Literally! With Rob Lowe,” will be available to stream Dec. 3 in a new partnership with SiriusXM, Netflix and Lowe. More than 30 library episodes will be available on the streaming platform, where new video episodes will be released every Thursday. The actor created and hosts the podcast, also executive producing alongside Nick Liao, Adam Sachs and Jeff Ross. Team Coco’s Sean Doherty produces with associate producer Sean Calvano.

The news comes in anticipation of Netflix’s holiday comedy film “In A Holidaze,” which premieres Dec. 2 and also stars Lowe, as well as “Dance Moms” alumna Maddie Ziegler. Based on the novel by Christina Lauren, the pen name for writing partners Christina Hobbs and Lauren Billings, Ziegler plays a young woman stuck in a holiday time-loop that forces her to relive the same Christmas at her family’s cabin until she finds what brings her true happiness.
Graham Phillips and Elias Kacavas also star in the film, which is directed and written by Tiffany Paulsen. Leslie Morgenstein and Elysa Koplovitz Dutton of Alloy Entertainment produce.

items.title: Why Netflix Fired Dan Lin
items.description: “Everyone is collateral damage.”
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: “Everyone is collateral damage.”
That’s how one top Netflix insider summarized another bloody Monday at the streamer, which saw Dan Lin ousted as the company’s head of film.

Following last week’s 6% workforce reduction at Netflix – which claimed victims including chief content officer Bela Bajaria and Lin’s right-hand Doug Belgrad – consensus said it was a matter of time before co-CEO Ted Sarandos would show Lin the door.

It took a day. On the heels of the Bajaria news on Thursday, Sarandos rang Lin on Friday to tell him he’d been dismissed, three sources told Variety. The exec kept his head up and pressed on through the weekend, appearing at Saturday’s Academy Gala (in the same room as Sarandos) and at a Sunday tastemaker screening to support the filmmakers of “La Bola Negra.” As has been summarized in many articles about the Netflix purge, creative leadership at the company is being overhauled amid poor stock performance and declining user engagement on the platform. Peter Rice, the veteran film and TV executive, will now preside over and shake up the platform’s content.

Competing narratives are flying about why Lin was let go, but they arrive at the same conclusion: In the end, it wasn’t working. This, despite Lin meeting his mandates to curb spending and make movies that resonated with subscribers. In firing Lin and Bajaria and ushering in Rice, some say Sarandos was desperate to sell a story about growth to Wall Street (Netflix’s quarterly earnings report drops Tuesday). Others say Lin could not dance fast enough to find the balance between sticky streaming titles and theatrical release experiments (in fairness, he made it halfway through a five-year deal, barely enough time to get a casting announcement together by today’s standards). There are also some interesting leaks around tension he’s said to have with A-list filmmakers like Greta Gerwig and Ben Affleck, which we’ll get to.

The Lin era at Netflix was framed around austerity, both by the town and in some ways by “The Lego Movie” producer himself. A June profile in the New York Times declared Lin was done “coddling” Hollywood, bragging he did not “fawn over stars or write blank checks.” The implication was that his predecessor Scott Stuber had overpaid for talent and too-ambitiously committed to a new Netflix movie release every week in 2022. Those efforts scaled back gradually until Stuber exited in mid-2024.

Lin entered with a red pen and a machete, the lore goes, in hopes of emphasizing quality over quantity. Some find it convenient that Stuber’s legacy is still being kicked up, perhaps to provide cloud cover for decisions made by Lin and his former boss Bajaria. Amid the noise of the current Netflix layoffs, it’s important to remember that the prevailing logic at Netflix for a long, long time was “we don’t give a shit about theatrical,” said one colorful studio source. Releasing movies in theaters was never part of the Netflix business model. Stuber paid premiums to get filmmakers like Martin Scorsese, Alfonso Cuarón and Rian Johnson on the service. He also worked with fervor to make the theatrical exhibitors accept Netflix titles in any capacity. While they refused at the time, individuals familiar with Sarandos said Stuber laid the groundwork for the inevitable – that the only way to create value around movies is to put them in theaters first.

Lin brought this logic to fruition in convincing Sarandos that family-driven IP should receive robust, exclusive theatrical windows before moving on to streaming, individuals with knowledge of Lin said. We’ll see the results next year when Gerwig’s “Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew” and “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory” come to cineplexes.

Where Netflix once organized its internal film teams by the budget range of projects they worked on, Lin grouped his executives according to genre expertise. He also moved swiftly to program release windows left empty by Stuber’s exit (“Nonnas,” “Happy Gilmore 2,” “The Thursday Murder Club”). He spent one day of his work week with the Netflix animation team, where he installed Hannah Minghella as a leader. For the core slate, Lin is credited with wooing Alan Ritchson (“War Machine”), Matthew McConaughey and Ben Stiller for upcoming projects.

In the weeks before his exit, reports said Lin clashed with filmmaker Affleck (director of the just-released “Animals”) over the use of his AI platform InterPositive. Perhaps more consequential was a rift with Gerwig this summer over the upcoming “Narnia.” The movie represents a $250 million theatrical-first gamble.

Four sources with knowledge of the matter said that, indeed, Lin and Gerwig had a falling out during a Zoom call about the project earlier this year. On a virtual meeting populated by numerous Netflix executives, Lin is said to have been “dismissive” to the director in conversation about the progress of the film. Lin is known in town to be incredibly fair, but at times obtuse in his frankness. Word travelled fast around Netflix that the meeting had gone south, at which point sources said Bajaria called Gerwig’s producer Amy Pascal to smooth things over. Two sources also said that Gerwig’s new, all-powerful CAA agent Bryan Lourd went to Sarandos directly over the faux pas. Lin was subsequently disappeared from the film, all sources concurred, and Belgrad stepped in as the primary Netflix exec overseeing the project (until, of course, he was laid off last week).

None of the sources suggested the incident led to Lin’s firing. One Lin defender said he’s never “afraid to talk about how to make a movie better.” Another person familiar with the company said there are any number of filmmakers who could say the same about Lin’s delivery. While it may be juicy to speculate that Gerwig’s follow-up to the game changer “Barbie” could be troubled, don’t forget that the industry doubted that Margot Robbie film right up to opening weekend. “Barbie” grossed $1.44 billion at the worldwide box office and became the highest-earning release in the history of Warner Bros. Pictures.

While talk will instantly turn to Lin’s replacement (is it Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy? “Probably,” said one high-placed source), don’t shed too many tears for Lin. He ascended to Netflix from a successful, self-made business in Rideback.

“When I took this job, Bela gave me a simple piece of advice: Be yourself,” Lin wrote in a Monday memo obtained by Variety. “You work here because it’s personal. Because of that unspoken pact between your individual passion for movies and the audiences we serve. To them, movies aren’t about business. They’re about feeling something.”
And the truth about his tension with Greta Gerwig over "Narnia"

items.title: Christina Applegate Reveals She Was Misdiagnosed and Does Not Have MS: “I Haven’t Gotten Better … I’m Back at Square One”
items.description: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast after some time away to reveal that she was misdiagnosed and does not, in fact, have MS.
items.author: Jackie Strause
paragraphs: Christina Applegate returned to her podcast after some time away to reveal that she was misdiagnosed and does not, in fact, have MS.

Applegate revealed in a two-part episode of her MeSsY podcast that she co-hosts with Jamie-Lynn Sigler, who has multiple sclerosis (MS), that, in 2021, she was being tested for “everything under the sun,” but not MS right away. She had brain and spinal MRIs, and a spinal tap, which determined that she had RMS, which was, at the time, “on the low scale.” However, Applegate said she was getting progressively worse. The doctor then showed her the lesions on her brain, almost 40, she said, and “that was it. That was my answer to everything that was going on” at the time.
Applegate revealed her diagnosis in August 2021, at age 49, sharing publicly that she had been diagnosed a few months prior.

On her podcast episode released on Tuesday, she said that after her diagnosis, she then leaned on the MS community, which includes her co-host, and started infusions that went on for years, wreaking “havoc” on her body. A “couple of years ago,” however, Applegate said, her doctor wanted to take her off of the infusion and monitor her B cells. When her B cells didn’t change, that’s when they began a study into her diagnosis.
Thanks to new technology around brain MRIs, Applegate recently learned she was misdiagnosed.
“She came into my room and she said, ‘Congratulations, you don’t have MS. Congratulations.’,” she recalled, fighting back tears.
Applegate said everyone else was so happy but, “I’m not happy at all.”

“You don’t get misdiagnosed, and then all of a sudden, I’m better,” she added. “I haven’t gotten better, Jamie. If anything, I’ve gotten worse in some ways. So I’m back at square one where I don’t know what’s going on with me, and that’s going to be an online investigation that my doctors are going to get into to find out what has been happening since 2021. Why did this happen? I have every symptom of someone with MS — every single one.”

Applegate said there is a high number of misdiagnoses with MS, even after years of infusions like she had. She began crying while saying, “I feel like I let everybody down. I became, you and I, the poster children for MS. I had a reason — I had a fucking reason — as to why my day sucked every day. And now I don’t have a reason, and it’s very unnerving and very confusing for me.”

Applegate continued to say she’s currently in a state of shock. “It’s a mind fuck, for sure,” she told Sigler. The investigation into her health is so new, she said, that next week she begins a process that will involve her being her own advocate and finding the right specialists.
“I needed some time to process that, but I also needed me time, after the book and some health stuff that was going on,” she said. “I just needed time to find the love in life again.”

She said it “hurts to get out of bed; it hurts to stand up. I’m still sleeping all the time. I’ve still got a lot of health issues. But I’m finding ways to make my room joyous and make sure that my doors are open and that I can hear the birds and the fountain outside.”

Applegate and Sigler said they will have experts on to respond to the news but that their podcast will also still be an entertaining space for the two of them to discuss the things that bring them joy (like Bravo shows and Andy Cohen). Ultimately, she said she’s not relieved, but Sigler pushed her to be curious. “Your reaction is very human and real, and I think one that anyone would share,” said Sigler, then insisting that Applegate look forward to doing a little dance, “a little shuffle,” over not having MS.
“I’ve been talking about that damn jumping for so long!” Applegate said, with a laugh.
In the second part of Tuesday’s podcast, the co-hosts brought on Dr. Marwa Kaisey, an associate professor of neurology at Cedars-Sinai in Los Angeles, to unpack the news and discuss what’s next.
Applegate grew emotional towards the end of that conversation when reflecting on what she’s lost since being diagnosed six years ago.

“I lost everything. I lost my job,” she said. “It stopped my life. I still have to use wheelchairs when I go to doctors offices. I can’t walk from the car to the room. I’m still in this. Nothing magical happened when she said ‘You don’t have MS.’ So what do you say to someone like that? What do you say to someone who has lost their abilities and here we are, we don’t know. I guess I felt comfort in having a name. I felt comfort in having an answer and a community. I still am a part of it.”

items.title: Roseanne Barr Breaks Silence on High-Stakes TV Return: “Who Wants a Number One Show?”
items.description: It would be completely reasonable if Roseanne Barr, 73, packed it up and retired. But she feels she has one more show in her — even if she has to pay for it herself. The question remains whether anyone will buy it.
items.author: Seth Abramovitch
paragraphs: It would be completely reasonable if Roseanne Barr, 73, packed it up and retired. But she feels she has one more show in her — even if she has to pay for it herself. The question remains whether anyone will buy it.

At her peak, she was the most powerful woman in television. Her “domestic goddess” standup character became a favorite of Johnny Carson’s. She eventually earned $1 million per episode on her ground-breaking sitcom Roseanne, a ratings juggernaut for ABC in its original run from 1988 to 1997.
Controversy was never very far from Barr, who has been open about her own mental health issues and defiantly outspoken about her politics, which have grown increasingly right wing and conspiratorial.

But nothing came close to 2018, the year ABC abruptly canceled a highly rated Roseanne reboot after Barr published an offensive tweet about former Barack Obama advisor Valerie Jarrett, who is half-Black, saying she looked as if “muslim brotherhood & planet of the apes had a baby.” The show was retooled as The Conners, killing Barr’s character off via a drug overdose, and aired for seven seasons. Eight years later, Barr maintains the tweet wasn’t racist and that she was criticizing Jarrett for being sympathetic to the Iranian regime.

Shunned by Hollywood, Barr is now going the indie route, with a self-financed single-camera sitcom called Meemaw: A Modern Day Fable. In the show, based loosely on her life in Texas Hill Country, she plays the matriarch of a mixed-race family (Drea de Matteo plays her daughter, Omar Gooding plays her son-in-law) who runs afoul of the law trying to raise funds for her granddaughter’s bat mitzvah. Randy Quaid is also in the mix as a local sheriff.

The Hollywood Reporter got a sneak peek of Meemaw, which sees Barr running amok in thrift store furs at rooster fights — closer in tone to trailer park comedy like My Name is Earl than the three-camera repartee of Roseanne.
Barr called THR for a wide-ranging conversation about her career, her cancellation, and her hopes of a comeback.
What’s Meemaw: A Modern Day Fable about?
It’s about a patriotic grandmother who is the matriarch of a mixed-race prepper family in Texas.
Black and white. Her son-in-law is Black and her daughter is Jewish and Cuban.
Somebody who’s prepared for the end of the world.
Is that based on your own life?
Yeah. I’m a prepper. I live in Texas. Everybody’s a prepper here.
I heard there’s a bat mitzvah involved in the plot?

She knows that she’s got to give her granddaughter a bat mitzvah because that’s part of their Jewish culture. So one day she gets a message from the good Lord that she’s got to take things into her own hands if she wants to be able to afford the greatest bat mitzvah that’s ever been in Bovine, Texas.
Which probably wouldn’t be that expensive.
And she uses everything at her command, which is her multi-religious prayer group, and her formerly dormant sexuality.
It’s no longer dormant? Who’s she sleeping with?
Well, you have to watch. But Randy Quaid does play my romantic interest.
This isn’t filmed in front of a live studio audience like Roseanne was?
No, it is not. I haven’t really showed it to anybody yet. But it is so funny. It’s the funniest shit I’ve ever done, and I had a ball and I play a really wacky old lady this time.
Randy Quaid is pretty wacky on social media. What’s he like on set?
I’m in love with him and I wish he would leave his wife and marry me. I enjoyed making out with him so much that I wrote extra scenes where we would make out.
What’s the plan now with the show? Where can we see it?

Anybody who wants a number one show and is smart enough to take a number one show. I don’t know why they don’t want a number one show and why they hate a number one show and why they would destroy a number one show. But if they do want a number one show, I got it.
How did you pay for this? Did you pay out of pocket?
I whored my ass up and down Hollywood Boulevard. [It was actually a co-production between Barr and Just the News founder John Solomon, who split production costs evenly.]
You mentioned reaching out to Elon Musk about this project.
I don’t know why he hasn’t called me or returned my calls. I mean, of all people on earth, I’m the one he should call, but I don’t know.
Oh, hell, honey, I’m always about the union and wages for the American workers. Hell yeah. I never changed on that. That’s why I’m no longer a Democrat.
Let’s go back to when Roseanne returned to ABC in 2018. It premiered to 18 million people.
No, it did not. Bitch, it did not, bitch. It premiered to 28 million people.
Sorry, I was talking same-day viewing. The audience did grow substantially when you factored in delayed viewing.
You better update your files, Mr. Man.
Honestly, I’m happy I got it wrong just to hear you call me bitch.
Oh my God. I haven’t even had my morning cocktail yet. I’m twitchy.
Did those ratings make you feel vindicated about your appeal to mainstream audiences?

I didn’t think of it that way. I thought of it like, “Oh my God, the American people are wanting to see something that talks to them again.” I lined up with the, what do they call it? The zeitgeist. I mined the zeitgeist again. I knew I hadn’t lost my connection to people’s hearts.

I was so excited to go back and say something new that hadn’t been said about the working people of the backbone of this country. And they didn’t like it, ever, the people at the network, and they tried to derail me. I see that now. They tried to derail me every step of the way. Meemaw is everything that they would not allow me to do.
It sounds like this show is letting you heal from a lot of the pain of what happened with the Roseanne reboot.

Absolutely. And a lot of the healing happens through my scenes with Omar Gooding, who plays my son-in-law. He’s also a standup comic and he’s a Black man. I met a lot of resistance casting Black actors.
You mean Black actors didn’t want to audition for you?
We had a lot of really great Black comedians audition for the role. A lot of people said no, they wouldn’t. “How could any Black person work with me?” That hurt me.
Let’s talk about the Valerie Jarrett tweet that got you fired. You’ve maintained that you didn’t know she was Black. Can you explain?

It was not a racist tweet. It wasn’t about race, it was about politics. What it really was was a three-month conversation between myself and journalists in Iran who were talking about attacks mostly on Iranian women in the streets.

And what I meant was the Muslim Brotherhood, of which Valerie Jarrett is part. [Barr offers no evidence for this allegation.] Planet of the Apes is my favorite movie. [Screenwriter] Rod Serling said it was an analogy for what the Nazis did to the Jews. I always called the government in Iran Planet of the Apes, because that is exactly what they do. In the movie Planet of the Apes, a militarized police force arrests human beings for speaking and reading, and that is exactly what they did to the women of Iran. That is a movie about fascism, it is not a movie about Black people.
You said something happened before the tweet that made you feel you’d lost control of the show. What was it?

I called the head writer and said, “When are we getting back together to outline season 2?” Because I was pretty much the ceremonial head writer, right? It was my show, and I outlined and went over every script in the writers’ room that season. And the guy says to me, “Oh, the writers are already back.” I couldn’t believe what I was hearing. I said, “How long have they been back?” “Oh, at least a month. But all the writers, they really want you to drop by.” These are the words that hit me so hard. It was like getting hit with a board. I knew at that moment, “Oh my God, they have taken my show. I gave them a number one show, they have taken it away from me.”
What was [producer] Tom Werner‘s role in this?
Seems like [he was behind it].
Why had you clashed with him during the original run of Roseanne?

Because he was trying to steal my show. He tried to fire me off my own show and steal it from me then. Man, it goes deep, man. So I had a couple beers, take Ambien, go to bed, have my computer in bed with me, which I always do because I can’t sleep. I wake up and that’s where my brain’s at. They’ve taken my show. I was feeling sorry for myself. Christ, this is the reward I get for giving them a number one show, that they take it from me. (Werner did not respond to a request for comment.)
How did you learn you were fired?

At 8:00 a.m., my boyfriend goes, “Hey, ABC’s on the phone.” And I go, “Why?” He goes, “Because you tweeted something.” And I said, “I deleted that.” He goes, “Well, they’ve got it and they’re saying it’s racist.” And I said, quote, and everyone in the house heard me, I said, “Muslim is not a race.” And my boyfriend says, “No, they say she’s Black.” And I’m like, “Oh, fuck. What?”
And so I called ABC back and they put me through, and it was Ben Sherwood. And first thing he says to me is, “What possible excuse can you have for the egregious thing you have done?”
And so I just swallow hard and I go, “Well, I thought she was white.”

And I just knew. So I go, “Don’t cancel my show. You’re not going to cancel my show, are you?” I go, “I will do anything. I will go on any of your news shows. Let me explain. Let me explain what I meant. Let me apologize.”
And he says to me, “Well, we’ll just have to wait and see how the community handles this.”

I remember it being almost immediate that somebody sends me Wanda Sykes’ tweet saying, “I have to get off of this show. Roseanne’s a racist.” But she was already off the show, because she had been complaining that the show was “humanizing Trumpers.”

Then Sara Gilbert goes, “I am so embarrassed by another cast member.” Such an insult from the person who wrote her lines in all those years and made her the executive producer so she could “protect me.” And those two tweets, once they were public, the next step was the show’s canceled.
What was involved in The Conners continuing? What did you have to do to allow that to happen?

ABC demanded that they would only make [the show] if I were not [in it]. And they called me and said, “You have a choice to make: You can sign off on letting us do a show without you [or everyone is out of a job.]”

The only thing that mattered to me at the time is I said, “I want you to say I’m not a racist and that you know I’m not a racist and that my whole life has been about fighting racism and that you know it.”

And [Werner] said, “I will do that once you sign away your rights. And also I promise you, if you sign away your rights for this season, that we’ll make sure that everybody knows you did it to save the jobs of the crew.”
The Conners ran for seven seasons. You didn’t get paid for the subsequent ones?
Did you have any say in how they wrote you off?

They decided to kill me with opioids because in the first episode of that, Dan and Roseanne are kind of making a drug deal. I really wanted to talk about the opioid crisis in our country. So they killed me with an opioid overdose. Wow, I’m really grateful that they didn’t have me robbing an orphanage or raping some kids. That was a nice way to kill America’s mom. Drug overdose.
It was all insulting on so many fucking levels, not ever even considering what that character meant to people who still come up to me on the streets and say, “You were my mom.”
How do you get along with your former castmates, John Goodman and Laurie Metcalf?
You’re not in contact with them at all?
That’s kind of sad. I assumed you guys were like a family.

And then this whole thing bubbled up recently with Michael Fishman, which was very hard to watch. [Fishman said Roseanne was “rightfully canceled,” while Barr shot back, calling her TV son “a little worm.”]
Nobody is more brokenhearted than me. I just choose to remember the fun and the good times. My son called Goodman and asked him to do a cameo on Meemaw and he declined.
Chuck Lorre put out a memoir and said he was made to write scripts for Roseanne that were credited to Tom Arnold. Tom came out swinging in response. Who’s telling the truth?

Unbelievably — I don’t think you’ll hear me say this often — but Tom Arnold is telling the truth for once. Talk about the paradigm switch here. Tom Arnold is defending me. I have to thank him for that. That’s the first time he’s done something right by me in his fucking life. Thanks, Tom.
Can I ask how much you were making at the height of Roseanne? I read somewhere it was like $20 million a season.
I made $1 million an episode.
Like Friends, Charlie Sheen-level money.
No, I made a million way before them all in the ’90s.
What happened to all that money?
I still got quite a bit of it. The rest of it, I had some divorces and some legal problems and I had some people help themselves to a lot of it.
How much do you have left?
I got a lot left. I ain’t hurting for money.
Let’s end with something a little fun. A speed round of some of your most memorable chapters. Your performance of the national anthem in 1990.

Yeah, I didn’t sing so good. I call that a tragic singing accident. I had gone on Johnny Carson the night before and told him I was going to do it, and Johnny says to me, “Whatever you do, don’t start too high.” He goes, “Bob Goulet started too high and it was a disaster.” I had practiced it so many thousands of times, but I didn’t know that much about singing. About five notes in I thought, fuck it, I’ll just try to make it funny. Bad, bad, bad, bad idea.
I mean, you’re obviously not a singer. Why would they even ask you in the first place?
Because Tom Werner owned the Padres and it was working woman’s night and him and Tom Arnold, friendly they became, and said, “Oh, Roseanne would be the perfect person to sing it.”
Do you have any memories of making She-Devil with Meryl Streep?

I really loved acting. And I loved the Teamsters. I didn’t get any scenes with Meryl. And we both complained to the director. We had one brief scene, but me and Meryl were like, the posters were showing us fighting and we’re like, “We want to get in a girl fight!” I said, “I want to fucking pull Meryl Streep’s hair and smash her fucking face in the dirt! Come on, let me do it!” And they wouldn’t. She wanted to beat the shit out of me, too. We thought it’d be funnier than hell.
You won the Emmy for best actress in 1993. Do you remember that night?
I was having a nervous breakdown.
You used to run around with Sandra Bernhard and Madonna, didn’t you?
Yeah, a little bit. The best person that I ran around with was Lisa Marie Presley.
Did she ever talk to you about Michael Jackson?
Yeah. She said he was the best lay she ever had.
No, I’m not. She said he was the best lay and he had it going on. She said he told her all the things girls want to hear.
Yeah. She never lied about shit like that. She told me about Nicolas Cage and his business. She told me everybody she was with and their business, the size of it and the use and all of it.

items.title: R.J. Mitte’s Mother Opens Up About His Tragic Passing to Help Other Families (While Clarifying Speculation About His Finances, Career and Fiancée)
items.description: Dyna Mitte is taking one step at a time.
items.author: Chris Gardner
paragraphs: Dyna Mitte is taking one step at a time.

The mother of R.J. Mitte is walking through unimaginable grief after discovering her son Monday at his Texas home after he took his own life at age 34. The blow gave way to highs of hearing how much of an impact he had on the lives of those touched by his acting work on shows like Breaking Bad or his advocacy on behalf of the disability community, but hasn’t been without more lows of waking up each day without him.

The week ended as R.J. Mitte was remembered during a Celebration of Life ceremony at the Mitte Center in Brownsville, Texas, where hundreds filled the seats (and an overflow building) to share memories and emotional tributes. Dyna chose to not stand at the podium because she was more focused on supporting her other child, R.J.’s little sister Lacianne Carriere, and allowing others the chance to speak on his behalf.

But hours after the ceremony, she got on a Zoom with The Hollywood Reporter for the purpose of honoring her only son while offering advice to families out there that may one day see red flags like she did. “Listen to your children. Watch for the signs. Be in tune with them, be there for them and be willing to get help when it’s needed,” she said. Dyna Mitte was also keen to clarify online speculation and rumors about the state of his career and finances and an reported feud with his fiancée.

I’m taking one step at a time. It’s a difficult thing for a parent to lose a child, and then to face the day of the actual celebration of life. It takes a lot out of you. I’m glad to do this [interview], but I’m tired and emotional. I feel a little beat up emotionally, but I think this is important.
You’re speaking today in part because you want to help other families that may be struggling. What do you hope people take away from your experience?

It’s important for parents to realize that there may be big signs or small signs. If you notice, even in conversation, that there are struggles or questions, be really in tune with your children and take the steps you can to help.
You didn’t speak at the celebration of life today. What led you to that decision, and what might you have said if you had been able to speak?

It’s hard enough to plan a funeral or a celebration of life — to know that you’re waking up without your son or daughter and will never see or hear them again. I’m in a slightly different situation because I can watch his movies or listen to his speeches, but that in itself is overwhelming. To then stand up and share all of that with people was not something I felt prepared to do on that particular day.
I also have a daughter who is devastated. We didn’t know whether she was going to speak, but she wanted to. She had a difficult time throughout the service, so I needed to be there to support her.

There were so many people who could have spoken that we could have been there for days or weeks. We tried to choose people who were close to R.J. and had meaningful relationships with him. I speak about my children every day and how wonderful they are, so I thought I would let other people share their memories of him.
Was there a particular moment, memory or comment from the service that stood out to you?

Everything did. Every picture in the room had a different meaning to each of us. Family members were sharing stories and feelings before and after the celebration, and everyone who spoke honored R.J. The room was filled with producers, directors, casting agents, agents, managers and publicists. For an actor, that says a lot. All of those people traveled to be there for him. Everything had meaning to me, and I think R.J. was looking down and understood that it all had meaning for him, too.
What would it have meant to R.J. to see all of those Hollywood friends and collaborators in attendance?

Well, first of all, I know there’s been some speculation that his career had taken a dive or this and that. And honestly, I want to straighten that out right now. They used to say, “You may do a thousand auditions before you land one job.” Well, obviously it doesn’t work that way today. Of course, COVID made things kind of slow but things picked back up. But honestly, R.J. had three movies that have already come out this year. He has two more coming out. He has already signed deals on several new movies that he was going to be filming. There were talks of different things. He had a book coming out. He had a food truck he was starting. He had a lot going on.

To answer the question, I do believe R.J. did see [the support today]. I do believe that when we get to heaven, God rolls back the curtains and reveals some things. I’m sure he rolled back those curtains and R.J. saw today exactly who was there, who honored him. I’m sure he laughed about things. I’m sure he joked about things. He probably was the one pulling the back of my hair and making me twitch. But I do believe R.J. was incredibly proud, and I’m sure that he was weeping and hearing all the wonderful things that were being shared about him. R.J. would’ve been proud of each and every moment.

Thank you for clarifying. I know there had been a lot of commentary swirling around on social media, some of it in reference to things that happened years ago, including a financial situation involving a representative that had taken some money?
There had also been speculation about a financial situation involving a manager. That happened years ago, had already been resolved, and was not related to what happened now.
Hearing you talk about all of the movies he had upcoming, the food truck, everything to look forward to, does it make it harder to process why he left?

When something is tormenting you — whether it’s for an hour, a day, a week or a month — I think people can have weak moments. I believe that’s what happened in this case. That doesn’t mean he hadn’t been having personal struggles. He had been opening up to me, to his sister, to family members and to people on his team. I don’t know what else to say other than that it wasn’t something we expected. A mother should never have to find her child that way. It’s a hard pill to swallow.
You’ve said that you noticed warning signs and encouraged R.J. to seek therapy. What can you share about what those signs looked like?

It wasn’t necessarily about specific actions. It was more about the conversations we were having — not just with me, but with his team and friends. There were concerns. That’s why I encouraged him to talk to a counselor. It’s always good to have an outside counselor, a third party with no “skin in the game,” as we say in the South. I told him to talk to a therapist and share his feelings and how he saw things. A therapist could tell him what they saw and heard without having a personal stake in it.

Parents should listen to their children and watch for signs. I thought R.J. was in a place where we had gotten over the hump and that he was OK. It wasn’t until he didn’t answer the phone that I recognized it as a red flag, because we talked regularly.
You are such a close family. Finding your beloved son the way that you did must be traumatic. Are you getting support and therapy yourself?

Yes. I’ve already talked with a therapist about my feelings and everything that’s happening. I have one therapist in Texas, where I live, and another in Los Angeles when I’m there. I had even spoken with a therapist ahead of time about the signs and conversations we were having and how to approach those subjects.
There has been speculation about R.J.’s relationship with his fiancé and reports about who was invited to the celebration of life. Is there anything you want to clarify?

I can share certain things, but some things are private and are not my story to tell. I don’t know all of the conversations between the two of them. I can say there were struggles, but those conversations were private between R.J. and me and between him and his friends. She moved in December, and they had only seen each other three or four times since then. I don’t know what those conversations were after she moved. I had not spoken with her about not coming to the funeral. She had asked one of R.J.’s friends on the day I found my son, but at that point we didn’t even know what was happening. No plans had been made. That’s all I can share about it.
What was R.J. like as a child? Must’ve been pretty special to have been raised to grow into this advocate and activist that changed so many lives?

R.J. was adopted at three days old and was the light of my life. He was a very smart child who started speaking words at nine months. He was always an achiever, and he lit up a room with his big smile. He was also laid-back and incredibly giving. If another child wanted his toy, he would give it to them. If a child got hurt and started crying, he would go check on them. He was passionate and caring from an early age.

His grandparents also had a strong influence. I grew up with a grandmother who was a children’s minister and a mother who worked in education. When R.J. and his sister were young, we gave them allowances and asked them to set aside 10 percent as a tithe and another 10 percent in a charity bank. Every Christmas, they chose a child from a giving tree, Make-A-Wish or another organization and spent that money on the child they had selected. They learned that because they were fortunate, they needed to give back. They learned to recognize that other people might be less fortunate and to lend a helping hand.

As R.J. grew older and lived with a disability of his own, he developed an even deeper understanding. At Shriners Hospitals for Children, he would meet children with different disabilities and take time to visit them, talk with them, laugh with them and make them laugh. He understood what they were going through because he was going through it, too.

That passion carried into his acting and advocacy. He spoke out for actors with disabilities and worked with organizations including Shriners Hospitals for Children and United Cerebral Palsy. He raised money, spoke around the world and advocated for inclusion and diversity in the workplace and education system. He believed everyone should have the opportunity to audition for a role, whether it was written for a disabled character or not. He fought hard for that. He wanted to change the world and make it better for everyone.
What did you learn about the impact R.J. had on people after his death?

In the first few days, I received more than a thousand messages. People weren’t asking for details. They were telling me what R.J. had meant to them. One person said, “You’ll never know. I met your son on the street, and you’ll never know how he changed my life.” Another person said they had met R.J. at a college while contemplating suicide, and by the end of their interaction, they felt able to make it another day.

People from other countries called to talk about the impact he had made. He had traveled to Lithuania to speak about disabilities in education, to Russia to speak about disabilities in the workplace and to Washington, D.C., to lobby for disability rights. For the first couple of days, there was almost no sleep. I was inundated with people sharing his accomplishments, and I had to sit back and realize, “My son did this. My son was able to change lives.”

That’s why it’s so important to be in tune with your children, listen to them and be willing to say that they need help. We need to shine a light on mental illness, depression and the importance of being there for one another. The world lost a bright light this week, and that light happened to be my son.
How do you reconcile R.J.’s own struggles with the fact that he helped so many other people?

He’s still helping people. This is what he would expect me to do. He would want me to raise awareness. I feel as though he’s looking down at me and saying, “Yes, Mom, this is a hard pill for you to swallow, but you’re going to talk about it and make some changes on my behalf.” There is no shame. He was an incredible young man.
When did you first realize that R.J. was a star?

I think we’re talking about two different stars. He was a star, but I’m talking about the shining star in the sky. What makes someone a celebrity or a star? R.J. never believed he was better than anyone else. He never identified himself as a celebrity. He simply loved acting and loved working with producers. Vince Gilligan allowed him to shadow different departments on Breaking Bad, and R.J. learned about every part of filmmaking — the producer, director, cinematographer, actor, lighting, camera and everything else. He understood that great things happen when people work together.
R.J. never thought, “I’m this actor — look at me.” He believed we’re all human and all in this together. He saw everyone as a friend and as someone he worked with on the same level.
You’ve said that R.J. lives on through his work. Have you been able to watch any of it since his death? Can you watch Breaking Bad?

I’ve watched Breaking Bad all the way through twice. I’ve always watched R.J.’s work at least once, although R.J. himself didn’t watch his own work. He didn’t like hearing himself. Early on, I asked his manager about that. He told me that if actors watch themselves and criticize what they’re doing, they may change their approach, so you don’t want them to change their natural acting. I would watch him on set and give him feedback, and we would talk about his projects.

I don’t know when I’ll sit down and watch one of his movies, but I will. Since Monday, I’ve watched the videos people have been posting. I find comfort in still hearing his voice, seeing his smile and watching his eyes light up when he talks about something passionately.
Is another celebration of life being planned in California?

We don’t have all the details worked out yet. Because R.J. worked so diligently in South Texas, we knew we needed to have something there, and it was an incredible day. The building reached maximum capacity, and the city opened an overflow building that also reached capacity. After calls came in from Los Angeles, New York and around the world, we knew we needed to do something somewhere else. Los Angeles seemed like the logical place because so many people who wanted to attend were there, including directors, producers, actors and crew members who had worked with R.J.

We’re working on it now. It looks like it will probably be Oct. 30, but the details are not final. I’ll do whatever I can to make sure R.J. is honored and that his legacy lives on. The city is already discussing programs, and actors have reached out about helping ensure his legacy continues.
In closing, right now on this emotional day from where you’re sitting, what advice can you give parents who may be worried about their children?

Even if you think your child needs counseling — whether they want to go or not, whether they’re an adult or a minor — you find a way to get them there. That would be my biggest message. Listen to your children. Watch for the signs. Be in tune with them, be there for them and be willing to get help when it’s needed.
Interview edited for length and clarity.

One of the women described her encounter with Brand as "frenzied" and "violent," and another told the court that she was anally raped. The disgraced star denies all of the claims made against him.

items.title: I Went Freediving With a $6,000 Tudor Watch on My Wrist
items.description: “When I dive deep, I think about nothing. Nothing.” So says Morgan Bourc’his, a French-born world-champion freediver. I was in Marseilles on the Côte d’Azur to learn the basics of freediving, a sport for which timing is both essential and something that must b
items.author: Oren Hartov
paragraphs: “When I dive deep, I think about nothing. Nothing.” So says Morgan Bourc’his, a French-born world-champion freediver. I was in Marseilles on the Côte d’Azur to learn the basics of freediving, a sport for which timing is both essential and something that must be ignored.

Though Bourc’his can hold his breath for well over seven minutes, I, a mere mortal, cannot. Perhaps with a bit of training, I thought, I could extend my time to a respectable few minutes? Certainly it helps that Tudor—Bourc’his’s principal sponsor and the underwriter of this French excursion—had equipped each of us journalists with a heavy-duty, highly waterproof Pelagos 42-mm dive watch.

Alas, it turns out that one isn’t meant to think much about time when underwater. Unlike SCUBA diving, in which one tracks bottom and decompression time through the use of a dive computer or watch, freediving doesn’t actually have much to do with time, at least not during the actual dive. When you’re pulling yourself downward from a rope attached to a buoy at the surface, it’s best to have a clear mind free of distraction. If one is competitive—as world champion Bourc’his was during his career—then the numbers that really matter are those of depth.

Even so, Bourc’his is zen-like when using his Pelagos to time our practice sessions, which consist of lying facedown, hands on the edge of a pool at a villa situated along the Marseilles coast, as he times progressively longer intervals. Beginning with just 15 or 30 seconds, we end with a “personal record” interval, in which I achieve something like 2:25. Satisfied with this progress, I wonder what it’ll be like trying it in the ocean, with waves, weather…and maybe sharks.

Of course, time—and timing—does play an important role in freediving. But not the way you’d expect. “When you are in this state of mind of slowing down, time seems to be very long,” explains Bourc’his. “You are completely linked to the present moment, and nothing passes through your brain. You say, ‘Okay, I think I probably dived for two minutes and 30 seconds. But no—it was four minutes. You forget [time] completely. You check after the dive for the information.” The idea of slowing down time—and slowing down oneself—looms large in the practice of freediving.

The push-pull between the consciousness of time and the dissociation from it pervades Bourc’his’s freediving practice as well as his life. Still, he keeps his original blue-dialed variant Pelagos around for even his most audacious attempts. During a freedive in the frigid waters off the coast of Norway, he found himself staring facedown at a pod of some 20 humpback whales as they passed silently beneath him. “It was like a train—a never-ending train passing by me,” he says. “I was alone with my wetsuit and wearing my Pelagos, and that’s probably one of the most iconic and amazing memories I have.”

Most people, of course, will never test a Pelagos the way that Bourc’his tests his, but it’s good to know that it could come along if you suddenly decided to pursue a career as a three-time world-champion freediver. Launched at Baselworld in 2012, the Pelagos was conceived from the ground up as a flagship, highly technical timepiece made for serious divers. It came in titanium, measured a large 42 mm in diameter, carried a depth rating of 500 meters, and featured a spring-loaded self-adjusting clasp on its matching bracelet.

Over the years, the Pelagos has evolved, shedding its earlier ETA movements in favor of in-house calibers and adding both smaller and larger sizes to the collection. The relatively new Pelagos Ultra, which debuted at Watches and Wonders 2025, measures 43 mm (also in titanium) and features a whopping 1,000 meters of water resistance, plus a helium escape valve (HEV). For Bourc’his, it has particular appeal. “The Ultra is probably my favorite one today,” he says, noting that only small changes in diameter and thickness yielded double the water resistance. In fact, Tudor presented him with a one-of-one example, engraved on the caseback with an image of him suspended in the water during his final World Championship dive.

As a freediver, Bourc’his also has a unique relationship to time, which makes him an especially interesting partner for a watch brand. He is the tour guide into freediving for journalists, retailers, and collectors in Tudor’s orbit, teaching them that, ultimately, mastering the sport means letting go. “Today, performance means for everybody to be faster, to be higher,” he says. “And here, if you want to perform, you have to slow down. You have to do a lot of things with softness and slowness. This is the paradox of the activity.”

Out in the open ocean, just off the coast of Marseilles, Bourc’his is a calming force. With the blue Pelagos strapped to my wrist, I enter the warm water, secure in the knowledge that this talisman has brought me good luck thus far—but trying, all the same, to forget about time. After several middling practice attempts, I realize that if I’m going to hit the modest goal of five meters I’ve set for myself—the height of a tall single-story building—I’m going to have to descend feet-first, rather than headfirst. This involves wrapping the aforementioned line around my fins and pulling myself hand-over-fist downward, stopping at each pull to equalize my eardrums—a practice I’m used to from scuba diving. “Why did you stop?” he questions me after I turn around and head for the surface after just a few meters during a practice run. “You held your breath in the pool for over two minutes. You have plenty of time. Breath is not the issue.”

He’s right, of course. But holding one’s breath while floating in a calm pool and out in the open ocean are two completely different worlds. After two days of practice, however, I get the hang of it, descending deeper and deeper each time I try. Finally, on my last attempt—during which I’ve been tasked with removing a card from the bottom of the buoy and taking it back to the surface—I spend two minutes breathing calmly, then descend, Pelagos on my wrist. Though the pressure builds in my left ear, I remain calm, equalize, and feel the bottom of the rope hit my fins. I grab the card, rip it free from its rubber band, and swim quickly for the surface.

While Bourc’his’s competitive career is behind him, he still spends an inordinate amount of time freediving. Unlike with scuba, the beauty of freediving is that it can be done with barely any equipment. A diver like Bourc’his can effectively disappear into the environment. A mechanical watch is one of the few tether points to the topside world of technology and objective measurement for a freediver like him.

Really, Tudor’s role in freediving (and its partnership with Bourc’his in particular) is almost more of a totem—a signifier of the man-made environment to which the diver belongs. Disconnected from urgent reminders of missed meetings, pending RFPs, and an overflowing inbox, you’re consumed by the ocean, free to experience nature as a child might. Then, finally—when you’re ready—a glance down at your wrist reminds you of the surface, and you swim homeward.
“Freediving is a nice school about the knowledge of yourself in this sport—in daily life also,” says Bourc’his. “Slowing down is not just ‘I do nothing.’ You know? It’s a way to organize your life.”

items.title: Magnesium May Not Reach Your Brain, Despite Supplement Label Promises
items.description: Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throu
items.author: Adam Obr
paragraphs: Most of us probably don’t think about how much magnesium we’re consuming, but our bodies couldn’t function without it. We each typically contain about 25 grams of magnesium, more than half of which is stockpiled in bones. The rest is distributed in cells throughout the body, taking part in hundreds of essential chemical reactions, including building DNA and proteins and sending signals within our nervous systems and between our brains and the rest of our bodies.

But just because our cells—and especially our neurons—need magnesium doesn't mean that extra magnesium will make them function any better. Not only that, but ingesting more of the element doesn’t mean it’s reaching your brain or really any specific part of your body.

In supplement pills, magnesium isn’t just on its own but part of a compound usually called a “magnesium salt.” This must dissolve to release Mg²⁺, the ionic version that our bodies use. How much of this actually gets into your system—versus gets excreted—depends on a variety of factors including the dose, your stomach contents, and how much magnesium is already in your body. In other words, the higher the dose, the less magnesium gets absorbed.

That’s all if the supplement dissolves in the first place. Magnesium oxide, which is usually the basis of the cheapest pills offered, doesn’t break down all that easily. In reality, magnesium oxide supplements mostly act as laxatives, drawing water into the intestines to flush out the excess salt.

This is where the marketing comes in. There are other types of magnesium compounds that do dissolve better. Magnesium citrate, for example, has been shown to have the highest bioavailability in laboratory tests. Despite the fact that all these salts still break down in the intestine, some supplement labels also claim that their specific chemical blend targets the magnesium directly to certain parts of your body, like your muscles or your brain.

These claims are often based on experiments using rodents, and the animals are typically supplied with magnesium long-term at higher doses than found in a pill. One study in rats found that a salt called magnesium L-threonate increased the amount of magnesium in the brain and improved some manifestations of learning and memory. This is the basis of some of the more overzealous marketing in the supplement world, which proclaims that this special salt will take the magnesium right to your brain.

There are some human studies, but that’s not really what they say. A few small randomized trials reporting improvements in some cognitive tests or sleep have been conducted—but there are several important caveats. Some studies tested a mixture of substances, lasted for only a few weeks, or analyzed a very limited number of outcomes. Many of these studies can also not be considered independent, because they were funded by supplement manufacturers or led by their staff.

Moreover, the studies—for extremely understandable reasons—didn't measure magnesium content in the brain. So maybe a little more sneaks into your gray matter, but based on the scientific understanding of how these salts are processed, in all likelihood, a brain-focused magnesium supplement is still just an expensive laxative.
This story originally appeared on WIRED Czech Republic and Slovakia and has been translated from Czech.

items.title: 10 Breakthrough Technologies 2026
items.description: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies
items.author: Amy Nordrum
paragraphs: 10 BreakthroughTechnologies

Our reporters and editors constantly debate which emerging technologies will define the future. Once a year, we take stock and share some educated guesses with our readers. Here are the advances that we think will drive progress or incite the most change—for better or worse—in the years ahead.

Sodium-ion batteries, made from abundant materials like salt, are emerging as a cheaper, safer alternative to lithium. Backed by major players and public investment, they’re poised to power grids and affordable EVs worldwide.

AI coding tools are revolutionizing how we write, test, and deploy code, making it easier and faster to build sophisticated websites, games, and other applications than ever before. Just be sure to double-check what they come up with.

Nuclear power already provides steady electricity to grids around the world, without producing any greenhouse-gas emissions. New designs rely on alternative fuels and cooling systems or take up less space, which could get more reactors online faster.

Every day, millions of people interact with AI chatbots. Some of them form what feel like close, personal bonds with the bots. There’s mounting evidence that this can be dangerous, and politicians are finally waking up.

When he was just seven months old, baby KJ became the first person to receive a personalized gene-editing treatment. A clinical trial is now planned, and bespoke gene-editing drugs could be approved within the next few years.
Growing banks of gene information on extinct creatures are providing clues to new treatments and suggesting solutions to climate change—and may help save endangered species.
Mechanistic interpretability

Nobody knows exactly how large language models work, which means we don’t have a clear idea of their limitations. But that’s changing: Clever research techniques are giving us the best glimpse yet of what’s really going on inside the black box.

Space tourism may seem fanciful, but this might be the year paying customers can finally check into a room with a galactic view. The shiny new modules will also support research missions by scientists and space agencies.

Screening embryos for genetic diseases is relatively common practice in fertility clinics today, and it can give potential parents some peace of mind. Now, though, new startups are making bold claims about using similar techniques to predict certain traits, including intelligence.
Hyperscale AI data centers

The race for AI supremacy has supercharged data centers. Hyperscale AI data centers pack powerful computer chips into synchronized clusters that work like giant, high-speed supercomputers—sizzling hot, power-hungry behemoths pushing infrastructure to its limits.
10 Breakthrough Technologies

MIT Technology Review’s annual list of 10 Breakthrough Technologies aims to help our audience know which emerging technologies are really worth paying attention to right now. Our editors and reporters pitch advances that they think should make the list, and we discuss and debate the merits of each over the course of several months.

We look for breakthroughs that will have a broad impact and make meaningful differences in our lives and work. We give equal consideration to those that we think will have a positive effect or bring negative consequences. Every year, we have to pass on many worthy candidates. Here’s what didn’t make the list this year.

This is the 25th year we’ve produced this list. Predicting the future is tough and we don’t always get it right. Look back through our archives to see what’s worked out—and what hasn’t. Or read this special analysis by an MIT researcher about some of the flops.
