In 2016, then–FBI director James Comey infamously made two announcements about the investigation of Hillary Clinton’s emails, one just 11 days before the election. We’ll never know for sure, but Comey’s public statements might have swung the outcome of the 2016 presidential contest. Clinton certainly believes they did.

And in October 2024, one month before Election Day, Jack Smith dropped a 165-page filing that detailed various misdeeds by Donald Trump around his effort to steal the 2020 election. Smith apologists note that a judge ordered him to make his filing (suggesting he had no say on the matter of timing); they omit that Smith specifically requested that the judge reverse the established rules of criminal procedure and permit him to file his brief before the defense filed its papers — which enabled him to file just before Election Day rather than after.

The historical lesson is that DoJ’s 60-day rule is an important discretionary safeguard, and only bad things await when it is bent or broken. A Justice Department spokesperson attempted to justify the timing of the Omar search with linguistic gymnastics: “The standard is purpose, not proximity to Election Day. Department policy does not require the Department to stop ongoing work during an election season.” But nobody argues that DoJ should cease all work on cases around candidates before an election; the long-standing practice simply would have prosecutors refrain from publicly visible enforcement actions during that time if they can safely be conducted after the election. And the claim that the relevant standard is “purpose, not proximity” is bogus. No prosecutor — Comey, Smith, or current Attorney General Todd Blanche — would ever acknowledge an intent to influence an election. And the rule is designed to prevent even the appearance of interference, regardless of underlying purpose.

The best explanation here is that the Justice Department under Trump and Blanche simply doesn’t care about the 60-day rule. That’s their imperative; the attorney general absolutely has the power to ignore a long-standing, internal prudential practice, and Blanche has risen to the top of the law enforcement world by trampling on tradition and trashing DoJ’s political independence. But it’s an especially dangerous principle to abandon, as Comey and Smith have shown us before when their preelection prosecutorial actions could have influenced the outcome of razor-thin presidential contests.

Another wrinkle: Omar is a sitting U.S. representative, and the Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause provides that members of Congress cannot be prosecuted or questioned over their legislative activities. The magistrate judge who approved the search warrant reportedly has therefore required DoJ’s investigative team to follow a cumbersome filtering procedure. First, prosecutors from outside the Omar investigative team must review all documents seized from Omar’s home; if any materials relate to her legislative work (which has been defined broadly by the courts), then those materials must be filtered out and kept away from Omar’s prosecutors. The arrangement will create a bureaucratic headache for the investigative team and could deny prosecutors access to materials they might otherwise find helpful. But it’s reasonably designed to protect both Omar’s constitutional rights and the investigation itself from becoming tainted by improperly accessing protected information.

The problem here isn’t necessarily the investigation of Omar itself; it’s the timing of the search warrant on the brink of an election. Omar might be guilty of some crime, or perhaps not. We’ll find out, eventually. Either way, the Justice Department has done institutional damage to itself, yet again, by letting politics drive its prosecutorial tactics.

items.title: How Steve McQueen Became the King of Cool
items.description: “When I did The Great Escape,” movie icon Steve McQueen once said, “I kept thinking, if they were making a movie of my life, that's what they'd call it—‘the great escape.’”
items.author: Hadley Hall Meares
paragraphs: “When I did The Great Escape,” movie icon Steve McQueen once said, “I kept thinking, if they were making a movie of my life, that's what they'd call it—‘the great escape.’”

McQueen had a lot to escape: a devastating childhood, a host of inner demons. He parlayed these tensions into a career as a dangerous dreamboat in classic films including Bullitt, The Thomas Crown Affair, The Cincinnati Kid, The Sand Pebbles (for which he was nominated for a best actor Oscar), and The Getaway. A talented race car driver, martial arts enthusiast, pilot, and notorious ladies’ man, he has become a cultural icon, the definitive king of cool. “His special, unique talent was his ability to balance his inner heat (his emotional rage, his distrust of older authority figures, and his defiance of them) and his cautious, careful, catlike wariness that so beautifully translated to the screen as the ultimate in cool,” Marc Eliot writes in 2011’s gossipy Steve McQueen: A Biography.

But in 1986’s My Husband, My Friend: A Memoir, McQueen’s first wife, Neile Adams McQueen, exposes the fallible human behind the iconic star, with beautiful (and at times brutal) honesty, grace, and just a tad bit of righteous anger. Along the way she describes the stars who populated their world: Marlon Brando, Princess Grace, Howard Hughes, Elvis Presley, Suzanne Pleshette, Sharon Tate, Shirley MacLaine, Frank Sinatra, Faye Dunaway, Candice Bergen, and even Princess Margaret.

What unfolds is a heartbreaking, at times haunting story about a little boy who strove to become a legend, and the woman who understood his manic, at times reckless drive. “Like a gambler, he had a desire to conquer the odds,” she writes “and when that failed, he still reveled in simply having been part of the excitement to begin with. The element of danger was as necessary to his survival as breathing.”

“I came from a world of brute force,” Steve McQueen once said of his life, per Eliot. Born Terrence Stephen McQueen on March 24, 1930, in Beech Grove, Indiana, he was the product of a quickie marriage between Terrence, a deadbeat circus stunt pilot, and Julianne, a wayward teenager (whom Eliot claims was a sex worker) on her way to alcoholism.

Terrence split almost immediately, and Julianne deposited her small son on the Missouri farm of her Uncle Claude, a stoic, kindly old man. The beautiful, sullen boy was an energetic dreamer who often longed for his mother. “He told me that sometimes, during especially cold mornings,” Neile writes, “he would curl up with the cows as soon as he had finished milking them.”

Like something out of a Steinbeck novel, McQueen’s early quiet childhood shattered when he ran away to join the circus. He eventually ended up in Los Angeles with Julianne, where he was brutally abused by her partner. Angry and defiant, McQueen became a full throttle juvenile delinquent, and his mother sent him to the California Junior Boys Republic in Chino. After finding fame, he’d continue to visit and support the institution throughout his life.

“During holiday periods when the boys were allowed to go home, Steve would invariably be the only boy left at school,” Neile writes. “There he would wander the grounds alone, barely able to contain the pain that tore his heart.” At 16, he was in Greenwich Village with Julianne before taking off to become a sailor—complete with a phony able-bodied seamancard. He jumped ship in the Dominican Republic and worked as a towel boy in a brothel before bumming around the U.S. working odd jobs.

After two steadying years in the Marine Corps, McQueen made his way back to New York City with a chip on his shoulder and a smoldering anger masked by surprisingly boyish charm and boundless energy. “I’ve knocked around a lot,” he noted, “and there’s nothing very romantic in it.”

Throwing himself into the bohemian life in Greenwich Village, McQueen survived as a dishwasher, petty thief, and amateur boxer before a girlfriend suggested he join her at Sandy Meisner’s legendary Neighborhood Playhouse.

McQueen had found his calling. “They put me on the stage with a girl—a dilettante from Long Island—and we were supposed to improvise an argument. Well, she hit me,” he later remembered, per Eliot. “She hit me hard and I couldn’t stand it. I hit back as hard as I could and knocked her cold. Man, it was Panicksville!” Rather than being appalled, Meisner was impressed, and McQueen became a serial student, studying with Uta Hagen and Lee Strasberg and building his resume in summer stock and television.

In 1956, he was starting an unsuccessful stint starring on Broadway in a Hatful of Rain when he ran into Neile Adams, a musical theater star of Broadway hits like Kismet and The Pajama Game. “Suddenly, blond fella-with-dog caught my eye,” Adams writes. “’Hi!’ he said as he looked me over. I stared. Hmmm. Nice-looking I thought. As the groups passed by me, he stood directly in my path. ‘You’re pretty.’ ‘Oh, thank you. So are you.’”

“In a very unusual way our lives paralleled each other’s in texture if not in content,” she continues. Like McQueen, she had never known her father, and her mother, a famous hula dancer, left her to grow up in Manila with a kind old man while she was on tour. During World War II, Adams was part of the Philippines resistance before spending years in a Japanese concentration camp. Her mother then sent her to Rosemary Hall in Connecticut (the same high school McQueen’s future wife Ali MacGraw attended, Neile cheekily notes), and from there her dancing career began.

Within weeks, the two beautiful theater kids were madly in love. “He had an adorable smile and wonderfully piercing blue, blue eyes,” Neile recalls, “which were now simultaneously crinkled in laughter and embarrassment and quite unexpectedly taking me to someplace I had never been.” The unpredictable, motorcycle-riding McQueen taught type-A Adamshow to “live,” she says. In turn, she mothered and supported him—financially and emotionally—even though friends constantly told her that the bad boy would ruin her career and her life.
They married on November 2, 1956, only four months after they first met. “I LOVED this man!” she writes. “I liked the way he made me feel. I danced to his music. Together we burned brightly.”

In 1958, McQueen hit paydirt when—with his wife’s help—he scored the role of bounty hunter Josh Randall on the TV series Wanted: Dead or Alive. The show was a hit, and McQueen soon earned a role in the film Never So Few, starring Frank Sinatra. Old Blue eyes enormously admired McQueen’s spunk and spark. At the film's preview, Sinatra slapped his costar on the back and said, “It’s all yours, kid!”

The McQueens were overjoyed. They ran out of the screening room deliriously happy. "Honey, I think we're gonna make it!" Adams said—but her husband hushed her: "Not so loud. They might hear you and put the whammy on me before I even get started!"

Adams subsequently neglected her own career, devoting herself to motherhood: their daughter Terry was born in 1959, and son Chad came a year later. It was just where Steve wanted his “old lady” to be. “For the quintessential male chauvinist pig—and I say that with much affection—that was the ideal!” she writes.

At the same time, Adams diligently guided McQueen’s career, prepared his peyote, and participated in his schemes, such as getting in a planned car accident to spur contract negotiations. She also smoothed over his increasing tantrums and feuds with everyone from Yul Brynner during filming of The Magnificent Seven to his frenemy James Garner on location shooting The Great Escape.

She also overlooked his affairs with costars like Lee Remick, though in her book, she can’t help being catty about Natalie Wood’s failed attempts to seduce McQueen during the filming of Love with the Proper Stranger. (According to both Eliot and Adams, years later, the two would actually have an affair.) Despite putting up with so much, she is clear that McQueen gave much in return. “For all his toughness, Steve was a little boy,” she writes. “He was also a man who found emotional safety in me and his children. He was tender, sentimental, sensitive, dominant, strong and steady as a rock.”

His adoring children would echo that sentiment as well. “[McQueen was a] complicated soul,” Chad later noted. “But I guess that comes from him not having a dad. I got the good end of the stick on that deal. He was great.”
"We movie stars are different, you know,” McQueen liked to joke. “We shit crushed pineapples!"

But as McQueen skyrocketed from it-boy to superstar in the late 1960s, Adams saw the man she loved losing his boyish sense of humor—and himself. He spent nights with his so-called “fuck-flings” at his buddy Elmer Valentine’s night-club Whisky A Go Go and did tons of cocaine supplied by hairstylist-to-the-stars Jay Sebring, whose influence Neile resented. (Eliot claims Sebring and McQueen also participated in threesomes with Sebring’s girlfriend, Sharon Tate.)

My Husband, My Friend is in many ways a cautionary tale, a blueprint of what fame can do to a damaged person who is not equipped to deal with the spotlight. McQueen was proving increasingly that fame and fortune had gone to his head. He got obsessed with building an empire, started Solar Productions, and became a tyrant both on set and off. Drugs and alcohol became a daily habit, and his womanizing got worse in 1968, when he learned he was on a scurrilous “list” of secret gay men in Hollywood. “Steve became possessed,” Adams writes. “His ego couldn't handle the innuendo. It seemed to violate everything he stood for—most notably his macho image… That, plus the drug culture and the sexual revolution, conspired to draw him into a midlife crisis.”

Adams poignantly writes of her own torment. Though her husband was self-destructing, he made her feel guilty every time she tried to help him. In 1968, things came to a head when to surprise McQueen for his birthday during the filming of Bullitt. Waiting for him in his San Francisco hotel room, she noticed a woman’s hairbrush with long, blonde strands in it—and instantly believed that McQueen was having an affair with costar Jacqueline Bisset. (Bisset has denied ever having an affair with McQueen.)

Afraid to leave him, Adams watched her husband repeatedly betray his character. He turned down Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid because he couldn’t bear not to have billing over his longtime nemesis (and sometimes friend) Paul Newman; he gave blowhard interviews where he pontificated badly about politics. All the while, he professed that he and Adams were the perfect couple. “He was getting all that free love from the outside,” she writes. “Coming home and having to work for love seemed unfair to him.”

On August 9, 1969, Jay Sebring and Sharon Tate were murdered by the Manson family. McQueen was supposed to be with them on the night they were killed; his life was saved when he met up with a “little chickie,” and never showed up at the house on Cielo Drive. Unsurprisingly, after the murders, his paranoia ramped up exponentially. “Steve never went anywhere without a gun now,” Adams writes. “Even I had to sleep with a gun under my pillow—as per Steve's direction.”

In the summer of 1970, Adams and the children went to join McQueen in the South of France where he was filming Le Mans, his long planned passion project about a famous 24-hour auto race. Adams was highly disturbed by what she found. McQueen was out of control: sleeping around recklessly, abusing the crew, highly paranoid. He informed her that he would be sleeping with multiple women even while she was visiting, since they were “kinda separated.” That night, he cradled his wife in his arms. "I'm sorry I hurt you, baby,” he said. “I really don't mean to. I want you to know I love you. But I gotta do what I gotta do."

Things only went downhill from there. High on cocaine, he began to casually ask Adams if she had ever cheated on him. He then convinced the staunchly anti-drug Adams to take a bump and began quizzing her more. Fed up and high, she finally admitted to a brief affair with an unnamed, Academy Award-winning actor (whom Eliot asserts was Maximilian Schell).

McQueen went ballistic. What followed was a horrific night of physical and mental spousal abuse, which Adams describes in searing, emotional prose. McQueen abused her the whole night, including pointing a gun at her head, a pattern which would continue during her entire visit to France. During this nightmare, she discovered that she was pregnant, and went to London to have an abortion.

The abuse cycle continued back in Los Angeles as Adams desperately tried to save her marriage. to no avail. She finally told McQueen she had to leave him. He understood, and told her, “I love you and I will always love you.”

Officially divorced in 1972, Adams rediscovered her love of dancing and performing as McQueen plunged headlong into his headline-making affair with, and eventual marriage to, Ali MacGraw (whom Adams liked enormously). The remarkably, borderline unbelievably forgiving Adams became good friends with her ex-husband. During a visit to his “bachelor pad” in the Beverly Wilshire Hotel in 1976, she even slept with him again, overwhelmed by McQueen’s charm:

Within a few minutes, as I stepped into my car, I heard the whistle that time had made so familiar and the “Hey, Nellie!” that inevitably accompanied it. I looked up to find him on the balcony of his hotel suite. I laughed, shook my head, and said, “It’s Neile, as in kneel down, you creep!” A wide grin spread over his face. “I love you, baby.” Our eyes locked for a few seconds and I understood that he meant it. “I love you, too, honey. See you soon.”

It seems Adams felt sorry for McQueen. By then, he had become an out-of shape-recluse. (Famously, he once said “I would rather wake up in the middle of nowhere than in any city on earth.") His reckless actions had burned many bridges. As she became stronger, Adams watched the man she had loved retreating from the world. But the two still co-parented well, and developed a teasing relationship, with McQueen sneakily making sure to marry his last wife, model Barbara Minty, before Adams married her second husband Alvin Toffel in 1980.

That same year, it became apparent that McQueen was dying of mesothelioma, a rare lung cancer. He began earnestly making amends with those he loved. Adams, usually so conciliatory, plainly voices her disgust with the unethical Mexican clinic which gave McQueen false hope, and side-eyes his late-in-life turn to Christianity. When she visited him for the last time in Mexico, McQueen hoarsely professed his love: "I'm sorry I couldn't keep my pecker in my pants, baby. I never loved anyone more than I loved you. And that's the truth."

Steve McQueen died on November 7, 1980. According to Eliot, at his funeral Adams joked that "Steve liked to fuck blondes, but he married brunettes." Tragically, their daughter Terry died in 1998, and their son Chad died in 2024. Adams survives; she’s 94 years old.

Forty-six years after his death, Steve McQueen is still considered the King of Cool, a patron saint for adventurous desperados everywhere. "Man, I do like to live,” he once said. “Life is good and I mean to take a big slice!"

items.title: MAGA’s Petit Trianon? Katie and Stephen Miller’s House on a Military Base
items.description: One night in late August, Washington’s ruling class piled into the home of Katie and Stephen Miller for a party. There were White House staffers, law enforcement officials, and what felt like the entire Cabinet of President Donald Trump’s second administration
items.author: Aidan McLaughlin
paragraphs: One night in late August, Washington’s ruling class piled into the home of Katie and Stephen Miller for a party. There were White House staffers, law enforcement officials, and what felt like the entire Cabinet of President Donald Trump’s second administration. Hibachi chefs erected onion volcanoes and squirted sake into the mouths of guests. On the lawn, a mechanical bull bounced shrieking children into the air. The occasion was Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt’s birthday, and a cake made to resemble the Briefing Room lectern was served alongside cookies with “No More Questions” written in icing. With events like these, Katie has turned the home she shares with Trump’s most powerful aide into one of the most gossiped about party addresses in this strange new Washington.

She may not mean to, but Katie is reviving an ancient Washington tradition. In the days before Trump’s hostile takeover of the capital, there was a quaint idea that partisan warfare was left at the drawing room doors. “When the five o’clock bell rang on the Hill, in the old days, that’s when they’d get out the bottles of bourbon and start drinking together,” says Sally Quinn. “And then they’d move on to the dinner parties.” Such parties, often thrown by the grandes dames of Washington in their palaces dotted around town, were an opportunity for political rivals to meet in fizzing comity over catered meals and coupes of Bollinger. These hostesses greased the gears of power in the capital, and an invitation to their dinners was a chance to rub shoulders with Cabinet members and ambassadors and, occasionally, a bona fide celebrity. Ina Ginsburg, the Courrèges-clad convener, even managed to lure Andy Warhol down the Acela Corridor for dinners at her Georgetown mansion.

That kind of dining-table diplomacy has been extinguished by a decade of MAGA-fied political combat. Trump’s movement has never been fond of bipartisan bonhomie, and there’s always been something a little silly about his officials mingling with the press (“the enemy of the people”) or political opponents (“evil,” “scum,” “lock them up”) anyway. “When Trump got elected the first time, that’s when the whole thing fell apart,” says Quinn. “That’s when people stopped talking to each other.”

But at the home of the Millers, who live on a military post south of the White House, a new kind of partygiving has emerged. Over the summer, Katie hosted a bash in celebration of Todd Blanche’s confirmation as attorney general along with that birthday party for Leavitt, which tripled as a goodbye party for the soon-to-depart press secretary and a celebration of Stephen Miller, whose birthday lands the day before. There were “almost 100 people there,” one regular guest of the Millers’ tells Vanity Fair. “It’s almost the whole Cabinet. Sometimes we joke: ‘Do we need a designated survivor for this one?’”

At these executive functions you might find the Rubios, the Hegseths, the Burgums, and Kash Patel with his fiancée, Alexis Wilkins. They are major productions. Katie has hired pizza trucks for the backyard, bartenders to serve cocktails, and even livestock: One of her children’s birthday parties featured a petting zoo with donkeys and other assorted animals. Katie strives to use catering companies that adhere to the teachings of the Make America Healthy Again movement, one regular guest says, which encourages the consumption of raw milk and the avoidance of seed oils. Though there is an exception: A shaved ice truck that uses syrups that partygoers say contains one of the food dyes against which Robert F. Kennedy Jr. is on the warpath.

“Love her or hate her, when she says she’s going to do something, she does it far better than you would ever expect,” Karoline Leavitt tells Vanity Fair. “And that is true of her party planning. She goes over the top. It’s always a family-friendly affair, and she invites everyone. She’s super welcoming. She’s a really good host.”

And what about Stephen, a man better known for his droning demagoguery than his warmth? A man of whom my colleague Evgenia Peretz once wrote: “Rarely has a face been such an apt illustration of the person inside”? According to Leavitt, he’s a different man when hosting: “I will say this too: People wouldn’t expect this of him, but when he’s in his home or in dad mode, he is super warm and fun.”

Katie’s reputed conviviality presents a similar contrast to her persona on X, where she has amassed 250,000 followers. Her caustic posts target the left, the press—she recently called a BBC presenter “a retard”—and competitors of Elon Musk, like Sam Altman. (The latter campaign began after she started working for Musk; according to Stephen Miller’s financial disclosure, Katie owns more than $1 million in xAI stock.) On Instagram, between clips from her podcast, The Katie Miller Podcast, she channels the more soft-focus social footprint of lifestyle influencers. In a recent post, she films with one hand while using the other to fill a Le Creuset with the ingredients that would ordinarily make up a slow-cooked brisket. (Katie Miller declined to be interviewed for this story.)

Yet there is a distinct difference between Katie and the hostesses of yore. Whereas her forebears used dinner parties as a sterling silver route to power, friends of the Millers who spoke with Vanity Fair say she started hosting at home to avoid the hostility they say greets high-visibility Trump officials out in town. “They need to do something to blow off steam because they’re not welcome in public,” says one. “They can’t go to any venue without being assaulted. They have to do this stuff in Camelot.”

Despite the allusion, the Kennedy era this is not. It’s a political movement animated by its protagonists’ hostility towards political opponents and their desires to enact sweeping changes to public life without public consequences, including imperial monuments constructed extralegally in the capital to honor a leader whom the local population does not like. So the best course of action, they seem to believe, is to avoid the local population.
“It’s hard for anyone in the Trump administration,” says Leavitt. “So why not just create our own parties with our own friends?”

This all dates back to the first term, when a small farm-to-table restaurant in Virginia called The Red Hen asked Sarah Huckabee Sanders, then Trump’s press secretary, to leave. This was a scarring experience for the socially insecure MAGA set, and Fox News covered the moderately newsworthy incident with the same zeal as CNN tracking Malaysia Airlines Flight 370. The climate has only gotten more heated since, and as a consequence, some members of the Trump administration tend to avoid the kind of socializing, well-watered by wine, that once made the Washington machine buzz along.

“This group of Republicans in particular has a fair amount of disdain for the culture of DC,” one Trump official tells me. “People keep their circles pretty tight. It’s out of distrust for the city. It’s out of necessity.”

For the Millers, the trouble started at their home in northern Virginia. “We were great neighbors,” Katie would later insist on a podcast. “We improved the value of our neighborhood.” Some neighbors seemed to disagree. They wrote protests in chalk on the pavement outside the Millers’ home—“Stephen Miller is destroying democracy,” read one—and distributed leaflets listing the address. “It was no longer safe for our children to play in our front yard,” Katie said. The couple put their house up for sale and moved in late 2025 into a home on a military installation in Washington.

The base’s residences have historically been reserved for military brass. But in Trump’s second term, an increasing number of his top officials have opted to move onto the heavily fortified post, which features a micro-suburbia of colonnaded Beaux Arts homes for which officials pay a monthly rent. This settlement has resulted in a kind of MAGA utopia, a fortified Xanadu where children can play in the front yard. There’s nary a chalk-wielding liberal in sight, and the attorney general might pop by for Sunday dinner. “At the military base now, the kids are so happy, they can run free,” Katie told the Ruthless Podcast earlier this year. “They love seeing soldiers. It is a once-in-a-lifetime experience.” A White House official tells Vanity Fair the Millers do pay rent for their home, though they declined to disclose the rate; The New York Times previously reported that officials pay a “fair market rate,” which can range from $4,500 to $6,500.

Not that White House aides living on a base is uncontroversial, and Democrats on Capitol Hill have questioned Trump’s officials on their use of military housing. “They’re reserved for military who have earned those quarters from fighting in wars and defending our country,” says Quinn, an Army brat whose father, Lt. Gen. William W. Quinn served in World War II and raised the family on Fort Myer in Virginia. “They should not be used for people in the White House. It’s an abuse.”

The Millers’ neighbors include a number of high-ranking Trump administration officials, from Jeanette and Marco Rubio to Pete Hegseth and his wife, Jennifer Rauchet, a former Fox News producer turned informal adviser at the Pentagon, all of whom have been regular guests at the Miller household.

Katie’s ability to bring these people together has attracted interest beyond her circle of friends. Earlier this year, when Paramount Skydance chief David Ellison was chasing approval from the Trump FCC to merge his company with Warner Bros. Discovery, he decided to host a dinner party “honoring the Trump White House.” He tapped Katie to help organize it and determine the guestlist, The Atlantic first reported in May. By coincidence, at the time of the Paramount dinner, Katie was reportedly in talks with the company about an acquisition of her podcast, which features major interviews with Cabinet members and business titans.

It doesn’t hurt for bookings on The Katie Miller Podcast, sources say, that Katie’s husband is Trump’s imperious deputy chief of staff. For one longtime Trump ally who knows the Millers, Stephen’s position is part of the calculation when Katie calls. “I’ll say I love her publicly, but the truth is I can’t fucking stand her,” the ally says. “But if she asks you to go on the podcast, or come over for dinner, you say yes, because Stephen Miller is the second-most powerful person in the world.”
Editor's Note: This story originally referred to the program Katie Miller hosts as The Katie Miller Show, but it's The Katie Miller Podcast. We regret the error.

items.title: Richard Riehle, Character Actor and 'Office Space' Scene-Stealer, Dead at 78
items.description: Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor best known for memorable turns in Office Space, Bridesmaids, Glory, and Casino, has died, Variety reports. He was 78. A cause of death was not immediately available.
items.author: Jon Blistein
paragraphs: Richard Riehle, a prolific character actor best known for memorable turns in Office Space, Bridesmaids, Glory, and Casino, has died, Variety reports. He was 78. A cause of death was not immediately available.

Riehle worked extensively across film and television, amassing more than 400 credits during his career, according to IMDB (with the database noting he has 10 additional upcoming projects). Though he scored his first screen roles in the Seventies, Riehle spent the early part of his career doing regional theater around the U.S., especially in the Pacific Northwest.

It wasn’t until the late 1980s that his onscreen career picked up, especially after he was cast in the celebrated 1989 Civil War drama Glory. Another important part was in the 1992 crime thriller The Public Eye, where Riehle met Joe Pesci, who helped him get a role in Martin Scorsese’s 1995 classic, Casino.

During the Nineties, Riehle popped up in movies like The Fugitive, and TV shows like Quantum Leap, Murder, She Wrote, and L.A. Law. In 1992, he appeared on an episode Star Trek: The Next Generation; over the coming decades, he would work on other franchise shows like Star Trek: Voyager and Star Trek: Enterprise.

One of Riehle’s most enduring performances was in the 1999 comedy Office Space, as Tom Smykowski, a product manager with a dubious job as a conduit between customers and engineers who tries to stave off a firing by proclaiming in one scene, “I have people skills!” Another classic scene found Tom explaining his supposed million-dollar idea, the “Jump to Conclusions” mat — a literal mat with different conclusions written on it “that you could jump to” — to his unimpressed colleagues.

“[I]t was just an amazing group of people,” Riehle told The AV Club of working on Office Space, though he did note that the Jump to Conclusions mat had apparently disappeared. “And that’s including [director] Mike Judge! I saw him when he brought me in for Extract, and it was very nice. We had a nice chat, and that’s one of the things I asked him: ‘Where’s the Jump to Conclusions mat?’ He said, ‘It disappeared.’”

Riehle continued to work extensively over the next couple of decades, appearing in shows like The West Wing, ER, Psych, and Drunk History; he also had an extensive recurring role on the sitcom Grounded for Life. Meanwhile, Riehle’s film credits include Transformers: Age of Extinction, Pee-wee’s Big Holiday, and Bridesmaids.

items.title: Trump Plans to Target Americans Behind on Student Loans
items.description: While Donald Trump’s administration has largely neutered the Department of Education, the agency is still doing what it can to extract even more money from financially encumbered young people.
items.author: Nikki McCann Ramirez
paragraphs: While Donald Trump’s administration has largely neutered the Department of Education, the agency is still doing what it can to extract even more money from financially encumbered young people.

According to a Monday report from The Washington Sun, the Trump administration is preparing to roll out — after the midterms, of course — new policies aimed at penalizing nearly 10 million student loan recipients who have defaulted on their payments. The plan includes proposals to hire debt collectors and garnish the wages and benefits of borrowers.

The plans revive past efforts by the administration to target student loan borrowers, who have seen a steady increase in defaults amid persistent inflation, stagnated wage growth, and a general cost of living crisis two years into Trump’s second term. Previous attempts by the administration to target student loan borrowers had been quietly shot down as the Treasury and Department of Education debated who would manage the national student debt.

Sources told The Washington Sun that the plan is set to roll out after the midterms. Naturally, announcing that the federal government plans to target largely low-income borrowers shortly before an election, as Republicans are getting pummeled over increased prices, was seen as a bad idea.

The plan is part of a larger effort to limit what types of students have access to federal student loans in the first place. Last week, the administration announced that it will seek to limit students pursuing low-income degrees from borrowing federal funds. The new Student Tuition and Transparency System (STATS) holds that “undergraduate programs will be required to demonstrate that their graduates earn more than the typical high school diploma holder, and graduate programs will be required to demonstrate that their graduates earn more than the typical bachelor’s degree holder.”
Otherwise, enrolled students would not be eligible for federal loan programs.

Experts warn that the new restrictions could severely impact careers in social and civil services, as well as the arts. Over the weekend, a former judge in the Bankruptcy Court for the District of Arizona said in an interview with CNBC that the changes the Trump administration has already made to the federal borrowing system — including creating unrealistic federal loan caps for students under the 2025 reconciliation bill — will “most likely increase” the rate of bankruptcy filings.

“Once the Education Department was gutted in 2025, there were few, if any, employees who could approve the debt modifications through one of the offered programs,” the judge added. “As a result, it has become harder to reach a settlement with the Department of Education,” on outstanding debt.

Under Secretary of Education Linda McMahon — the estranged wife of World Wrestling Entertainment founder Vince McMahon — who has no background in education, the department has cut roughly half of its workforce. The majority of those positions were within its student-aid division and the offices of civil rights enforcement. The latter oversaw investigations into allegations of discrimination against students and educators, particularly people of color, women, and other minorities. The cuts stopped investigation in their tracks as the administration pivoted resources toward enforcement action against supposed discrimination against white students and educators.

With major elections just a few weeks away, the cost of basic necessities is becoming a near-unbearable burden for a growing number of Americans. Instead of directing its energy toward the ever-increasing, exploitative growth of tuition rates across the country, or reforming a predatory federal and private student-loan system, the Trump administration is instead focusing its efforts on targeting those caught in its web. It’s an abysmal argument to make right before a referendum on your first two years of governance, which may explain why the administration reportedly wants to keep the plan buried until after voters cast their ballots.

In the meantime, the president and his allies continue to make dubious promises of $5,000 tariff “dividends” if voters reward them with a Republican House and Senate. Elon Musk is also pledging stock shares for every American child … but not until next year. They’re loud about the things they never plan to actually follow through on, but you can bet your last dollar that just like their cuts to healthcare funding and food stamps, their plans to keep punishing low-income Americans will almost always find their way into legislation.

items.title: ‘The Debut,’ ‘Ink’ Among Evolution Mallorca Highlights as Festival Celebrates 15th Edition: ‘We Want the Island to Be a Thriving Film Destination’
items.description: Back in 2012, actress-turned-director Sandra Lipski wanted to crown a successful festival run for her debut short film “Going Down” with a screening in her hometown of Mallorca, but was surprised to realize the thriving island did not have its own film festiva
items.author: Rafa Sales Ross
paragraphs: Back in 2012, actress-turned-director Sandra Lipski wanted to crown a successful festival run for her debut short film “Going Down” with a screening in her hometown of Mallorca, but was surprised to realize the thriving island did not have its own film festival. Rather than wait for it to happen, she decided to start one herself. The result is Evolution Mallorca, celebrating its landmark 15th edition this year and taking place between Oct. 28 and Nov. 4.

Lipski was born in Germany, but moved to her family on the Spanish island as a young girl, later heading to Los Angeles to pursue a career as an actor. When the 2008 writers’ strike hit Hollywood, the actress was on the cusp of a big break. “That was very frustrating for me as an actress because that was the year I had a lot of big things coming out,” she tells Variety when recalling the origins of the festival. “I then said I would just do my own short film, which I did. Then I spent 2010 travelling to a lot of festivals.”

“I was so confused about Mallorca not having a film festival,” she adds. “Living in the U.S., there was a film festival in every tiny town, and it felt obvious to me the island would have one because it felt like the perfect festival location. I was very young at the time and just decided to try it and see what happens. I pulled some friends together, many Europeans who, like me, were born somewhere else but grew up here, and we created a very well-rounded team.”

In the years since its inception, Evolution Mallorca ballooned into a destination festival showcasing the best of cinema produced in the region but also attracting major international names. Guests who have attended previous editions include Danny DeVito, Annette Bening, Paul Haggis and Jessica Hausner. This year’s edition is set to be another glitzy one, with the festival honoring “Conclave” director Edward Berger, “Black Swan” cinematographer Matthew Libatique, “Inglourious Basterds” actress Diane Kruger, and “Triangle of Sadness” star Iris Berben.

This year’s line-up will feature over 100 projects across its program, with the festival boasting its largest feature film selection to date. International highlights include Jesse Eisenberg’s “The Debut,” Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” Paweł Pawlikowski’s “Fatherland,” and the opening gala in Jordan Firstman’s Cannes-dazzler “Club Kid.”

“We try having more glamorous, notable films in our international feature film section, films that have won awards from other festivals and already have a strong seal of approval,” says Lipski. “We need this section as it works as a helium balloon lifting the festival towards a wider audience. But, just a millimeter away, we are pushing the debut feature section and Made in Baleares, which is what Evolution is all about: giving a platform to and celebrating upcoming filmmakers.”

Notable films amongst the Made in Baleares section, which celebrates local cinema, include the world premiere of Juan Sut’s “Torna,” a co-production between Mexico and Mallorca following a young man who learns the house his dad left him in Mallorca is inhabited; Danna Ayelén Bosch García’s doc “Un Darrer Capfico,” exploring the intimate bond between Mallorcans and the sea; and Marga Melià’s “Putting Up With Paradise,” which revisits talks with Mallorcan artists to provide a critical, human look at the island’s past and future.

“What makes Evolution special is that these films all stand next to each other,” emphasizes the festival director. “They are all equally important to us and give the festival its soul of diversity and inclusion, reaffirming our mission of giving a platform to new voices.”

The director also says she has seen certain themes emerge in the section: overcrowded islands, housing issues for the local younger generation and finding a balance with tourism. “I don’t think it can go away; I think we just need to find a way to deal with it,” she says. “The island needs tourism as it is a main source of income, but we need to contain it so that local life is not forgotten.”

Lipski also notes the festival’s continued mission of platforming short films, which speaks directly to Evolution’s origins. “These are important filmmakers because they will be the future of the industry. And we have names like Renée Zellweger and Michael Keaton in the program, directing their first shorts. I always say: Don’t underestimate the power of a short film.”

Evolution also has a key differentiator with its Cinematography Focus, a section celebrating the art, vision, and craft of cinematography. This year’s program will be led by Cinematography Icon Awardee Matthew Libatique and delivered in collaboration with British Cinematographer and Camera & Light Magazine. Activities include a hands-on lighting workshop, an exclusive Icon Talk with Libatique, and a timely panel discussion on the female gaze in cinematography. Previous editions have welcomed and honored some of the world’s most influential cinematographers, including Ed Lachman, Erik Messerschmidt, Anthony Dod Mantle, Phedon Papamichael and Oona Menges.

Speaking about the origins of the section, Lipski says that, on the festival’s 10th anniversary, she sat down with her team – which includes her husband, cinematographer Rainer Lipski – to understand how they could celebrate the craft within Evolution. The director says there are festivals dedicated to cinematography, like Cameraimage, but she couldn’t find other film festivals with intensive programs focused on professionals. “It has really grown into a meeting point for cinematographers from all around the world,” she notes.

The festival director is also a big supporter of promoting Mallorca as a shooting destination, as well as underscoring how great a location it is to host a film festival. “In the last decade, Mallorca has really boomed in terms of production,” she says. “It’s also a sanctuary for celebrities, which is not why I do the festival here, but it’s a helpful point in showing how accessible the island is from all over the world. We are very well-connected and in a very desirable place in the south of the Mediterranean. It’s very similar climate-wise to Los Angeles, and that’s how the industry started in LA, because the climate was so perfect.”

“People just love to come,” she adds. “The island has amazing infrastructure in terms of hotels, production companies, equipment… You can find everything here. I think it’s time to give it more of a push to show that to people. We have an event called Mallorca Go, which happens on the last weekend of the festival, where we take the visiting producers and filmmakers somewhere on the island. This year we are taking them to Calvià, a municipality in the southwest that has proclaimed this year to be its year of cinema and is inviting more film shoots. We want the island to be a thriving film destination.”

items.title: Dan Lin Out as Netflix Film Chief
items.description: Dan Lin has been dismissed as Netflix‘s head of film after almost three years, multiple sources tell Variety.
items.author: Matt Donnelly
paragraphs: Dan Lin has been dismissed as Netflix‘s head of film after almost three years, multiple sources tell Variety.

Even if expected, it’s a significant shoe to drop following a layoff bloodbath last week at the streamer. Roughly 1,000 employees got the chop, capped by the shock firing of chief content officer Bela Bajaria. Lin was let go at the start of the weekend, two sources added, and will address his teams throughout the day on Monday. The executive attended Saturday’s Academy Gala, and was spotted Sunday evening at a tastemaker screening for “La Bola Negra” on the Netflix campus.

A Netflix spokesperson had no immediate comment on the matter. It’s unclear who will replace Lin, though an announcement is expected in the coming days. Mike De Luca and Pam Abdy, the former heads of the Warner Bros. Motion Picture Group, have been widely speculated to be speaking with the streamer about a possible role at the company.

Netflix is embarking on a major creative restructuring after months of headlines citing engagement problems and stock stagnation — all in the aftermath of its defeated bid for Warner Bros. — namely in hiring the seasoned film and TV executive Peter Rice to replace Bajaria. In the days leading up to his ouster, Lin watched as layoffs claimed his right hand Doug Belgrad and the film vertical’s indie head Sheroum Kim.

Lin’s ascension to the top Netflix film job turned heads in 2024. The accomplished producer sat atop a thriving self-made business in Rideback. That production house is best known for building the animated “Lego” film franchise, Stephen King’s “It” adaptations and the “Sherlock Holmes” movies.

He departed Rideback to replace longtime film lead Scott Stuber. In a June sit-down with The New York Times, Lin said that he greenlit or acquired 88 movies for Netflix up to that point, with the standouts being “Apex,” “Emelia Perez,” “Here Comes the Flood” and “The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.”
Jack Dunn contributed to this post.

items.title: ‘You Can See Everything’ Sets Oscar Campaigns for Best Picture, Supporting Actress and More Categories
items.description: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: SPOILER ALERT: This article contains major spoilers for “You Can See Everything,” now playing in theaters.
“You Can See Everything” may rewrite the rules of the Oscar season.

Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s A24 documentary, which follows the Theranos founder through the 34 days before she reported to prison and keeps rolling afterward, opened to a staggering $15 million over the weekend, a number most nonfiction films never see in a full run. It’s also boasting a record-setting 99 on Metacritic, 98% on Rotten Tomatoes and holding a 4.7 (out of 5) on Letterboxd and 9.4 on IMDb (as of Monday, Oct. 19). If the IMDb score holds, it will surpass the longstanding No. 1 “The Shawshank Redemption” (1994) as the highest-rated film of all time.

In addition to being eligible for best documentary feature at the 99th Academy Awards, the film will also be submitted across the board as seen on A24’s awards site: best picture (Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, Tatiana Bears, Maggie Ambrose and Jack Davis), director (Fielder and Oppenheim), production design (Alex DiGerlando and Rebecca Meis), cinematography (David Bolen), costume design (Katina Danabassis), film editing (Adam Locke-Norton), makeup and hairstyling (Stephanie Pasicov and Kerrie Smith), sound (Paul Hsu and Richard Carlos) and original score (Ari Balouzian).

Variety confirmed exclusively after the film made its surprise world premiere (and general existence became known) at the Telluride Film Festival that Amanda Seyfried, credited in the film as Elizabeth Holmes, is eligible for the Academy Awards in the acting categories. Seyfried, who also appears as herself while reprising her Emmy-winning turn as Holmes from “The Dropout,” will be campaigned in the supporting actress category. If she lands the nomination, it would be her second, following “Mank” (2020). She would get there for playing two people at once: herself and the woman she already won an Emmy statue for playing.

Fielder, credited as himself, may be eligible to submit as a performer, but Variety has confirmed he won’t. The decision sidesteps a bit of history that has never gone a performer’s way: no actor has been nominated for an Oscar for playing himself. The closest the Academy came recently was with another A24 title, “Sing Sing” (2024), in which co-writer and star Clarence Maclin, a formerly incarcerated man playing a version of himself, built a real case for supporting actor and was ultimately overlooked. Fielder’s possible Oscar recognition would be in three categories — best picture, documentary feature and directing.
Christopher Abbott, who also appears in the film as Holmes’ spouse, Billy Evans, in recreated scenes, is also eligible for acting consideration in the supporting actor category.
Sources close to the awards campaign say the acting push will center on Seyfried regardless.
No documentary has ever been nominated for best picture in 98 ceremonies. The zeitgeist says this one can be. The awards circuit that usually paves the way is another matter.
We are in uncharted waters.
Golden Globes: Not eligible based on current written rules, but there could be an avenue.

The Globes don’t recognize documentaries, which means no picture, no director and no Seyfried. The film cannot be submitted in any category. However, with the acting eligibilities lingering, sources share the group may consider it for this upcoming run. That doesn’t mean it can be eligible across the board. And then in that case, do they consider it a drama or comedy/musical?
Critics Choice Awards: Eligible across the board, including the acting races.
That makes Critics Choice the only major stop this season where the performances in “You Can See Everything” could get significant recognition before Oscar nominations.
Actor Awards: Not eligible but could they make an exception?

The ceremony formerly known as the SAG Awards does not recognize documentaries, since they aren’t narrative films, even with the narrative recreations woven throughout this one. Seyfried’s path to a supporting actress nomination looked like it would skip the precursor vote by her fellow actors. However, the committee that rules on films is said to be looking at the film to see if it can, in fact, be eligible.
BAFTA: Still a bit of a question mark but it doesn’t look promising.

The current rules and guidelines indicate the film can submit in the top categories, but sources say BAFTA may not go for it. Whether Seyfried and Fielder can enter the acting races is less clear. However, indications suggest it may ultimately be eligible for recognition if the voters choose to go for it.
Writers Guild of America: Not eligible.

The film has no credited screenplay, which isn’t unusual for a documentary but isn’t universal either. Michael Moore’s “Bowling for Columbine” famously won the WGA’s original screenplay prize more than 20 years ago. That won’t be the case here, so “You Can See Everything” won’t be eligible for the Oscars‘ original or adapted screenplay categories.
Directors Guild of America: Eligible in both top categories.

This is where it gets interesting. The DGA has a separate documentary category, and its top prize is labeled for directors of a theatrically released feature film. Questions began percolating because of RaMell Ross, whose “Hale County This Morning, This Evening” was nominated for documentary feature at the Oscars before his narrative debut, “Nickel Boys,” was entered in first-time feature director at the DGA, a category he went on to win.

This is Fielder’s first directorial credit for a documentary feature, but that isn’t the case for Oppenheim, who helmed “Spermworld” (2024) and “Some Kind of Heaven” (2020). Therefore, the film won’t be eligible for first-time feature director. However, Oppenheim makes his narrative feature directorial debut with the A24 thriller “Primetime” starring Robert Pattinson, Merritt Wever and Skyler Gisondo. He will be vying for one of the five slots in that category.

More importantly, under the forward-facing rules, Fielder and Oppenheim are eligible for the DGA’s top award in addition to the documentary prize. That means they could take a slot otherwise slotted for Christopher Nolan (“The Odyssey”) or the other directing duos in the race, including Los Javis (“La Bola Negra”) and Phil Lord and Chris Miller (“Project Hail Mary”).

The guild that represents film editing separates theatrical feature films into four categories: drama, comedy, documentary and animated. Per the rules, “You Can See Everything” would have to choose a category to submit to. A similar situation occurred with Jonas Poher Rasmussen’s animated nonfiction film “Flee” (2021), which was submitted to the guild as a documentary and nominated by ACE Eddie.
ASC (American Society of Cinematographers): Eligible, but only as a documentary.
Per the rules for the highest award for cinematographers, “All Documentary Feature Films and Documentary Series Episodes must be submitted in the Documentary Award category.”
Producers Guild of America: Eligible for both the theatrical motion picture award and the documentary prize.

Add it up and you get a contender with no conventional map. Best picture winners typically announce themselves through the guilds, with a PGA win, a DGA nod, an Actor Awards ensemble slot and a Globe or two along the way. “You Can See Everything” likely won’t be at the Globes. The actors can’t nominate it. BAFTA would be a stop if the rules hold. That leaves the DGA, PGA and Critics Choice as the only places the film can win a top prize and signal whether it’s a historic nominee or something bigger.
And this raises a bigger question: What if the first documentary nominated for best picture goes all the way to the top prize?

A few studios are trying to frame the race as David vs. Goliath regarding how they can possibly topple Christopher Nolan’s billion-dollar sensation “The Odyssey.” What if this is actually Odysseus vs. Elizabeth Holmes?
A caveat that applies to all of the above: every voting body and guild writes its own rules, and any of them can convene a committee to revisit eligibility. So all of these are subject to change.
Holmes built a company on the promise that one test could see everything. Awards season has at least six major contests, and as of now, none of them can agree on what they’re actually looking at.

items.title: Jaafar Jackson on Playing His Uncle in ‘Michael,’ Losing the Original Third Act and the Upcoming Sequel: ‘My Job Is to Come Prepared’
items.description: Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office.
items.author: Clayton Davis
paragraphs: Two years before a frame of “Michael” was shot, Jaafar Jackson wrote down a list of goals. One was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross $1 billion at the worldwide box office.

Antoine Fuqua’s film, which opened April 24, became the first biopic in history to surpass $1 billion worldwide and Lionsgate’s biggest release ever. It also made a star of Jackson, who had never acted professionally before.
“I was pretty emotional,” he tells Variety. “I know how proud Michael would be of that, because he was someone who wanted to break many records.”

On this episode of the Variety Awards Circuit Podcast, Jackson opens up about leading the blockbuster “Michael,” navigating the Oscar buzz surrounding his performance and what he hopes comes next after a career-defining year.

Jackson, 30, is sitting down with Variety just two days after wrapping his second film, “Supermax,” opposite Will Smith, following 40 days of shooting in Australia. He’s candid about the life that led him here. Growing up in a house filled with 30 or 40 relatives every holiday, he dreamed of becoming a golfer, not a performer. He didn’t fully grasp the weight of his last name until he was about six, watching his father and uncles take the stage as the Jackson 5 at a reunion concert in New York and hearing the crowd erupt.
He has fond memories of his family, especially his late uncle. One of his earliest recollections of Michael is asking him for Starbursts — specifically the pink and red ones, his favorite flavors.

Bringing Michael to life, however, took two years of preparation before Jackson officially landed the role: building his own archive of songs, demos, journals, rehearsals and performances; working with acting coach Angela Gibbs; and immersing himself in the techniques of Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen. Nailing his signature voice and tone came first. After the young Jackson sent producer Graham King an unsolicited voice note speaking as Michael, he had a coach the next day. The hardest part came with learning his signature movies, particularly when performing the footwork for “Bad,” which is what closes out the film.
But what does it mean to reenact your own family’s history?

Colman Domingo plays a grandfather who, Jackson says, was gentler with him than with his father, Jermaine. Nia Long, who plays his grandmother Katherine, would touch his hand in certain scenes the way his grandmother did in real life. His father Jermaine insisted on watching the film for the first time at its Berlin premiere, surrounded by an audience. And the next day, he called his son and told him, he couldn’t tell him apart from his late brother.
Jaafar is just trying to take this all in.
Read excerpts from his episode below.
The interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.
You’re here two days after wrapping a movie with Will Smith. Is that correct?

That’s correct. I was in Australia for about 40 days, an incredible experience, to shoot my second film and to shoot outside the country, since we shot all of “Michael” in Los Angeles. It was a whole new experience, with a new crew, a new cast and a character completely different from Michael. That excited me.
So you didn’t dance or sing in this movie?
No, no, not at all. It’s completely different.
You were born in Los Angeles in 1996. What was your childhood like growing up as a Jackson, and when did you first understand what that name meant to the world?

I grew up with a lot of siblings and cousins who visited on weekends and every holiday. About 30 to 40 family members were at the house, so we had lots of game nights and family cookouts, with music playing. I didn’t really realize who my family was until I was around six, when I saw them perform in New York for their 30th anniversary. Hearing the fans scream, I was scared because I didn’t understand how intense it was to see people react to someone like that.
I first saw that when my dad and uncles came out on stage as the Jackson 5, and that’s the first memory I can recall of, “Oh, they’re important in some way. They have a huge fan base.”
A very important follow-up. What games did you play on family game night, and how competitive does it get in the Jackson household?

It was always Pictionary. Boys versus girls, no doubt. It was pretty competitive, because the boys always like to brag. I think our streak was like 15 years. I think it was unfair. There are a lot more boys in the family.
You started making music around 12, and your debut single, “Got Me Singing,” came out in 2019. Did you always see yourself as a musician first?

No. Growing up, I was only focused on golf. I started playing when I was around 4. My dad gave me golf balls to throw before I could properly swing a club, because I was so young. I fell in love with it. He got me a coach to train with once a week, then I joined a young golf club and started playing tournaments and did some charity tournaments with my father. I committed to it full time, every day, until he brought me to a recording studio and had me sit and watch him create from scratch. That shifted what I wanted to do. That was the turning point.
What’s your earliest memory of your Uncle Michael? Not the icon. Just Uncle Michael.

Asking him for candy. He always had candy machines or stacks of candy in the movie theater, and I had a problem with an addiction to Starbursts at that age. Pink and red. I would eat too many as a kid. I remember always asking him for candy and wanting to play. He always had the latest games and game consoles, and we’d play hide-and-seek.
In that house, it must have been impossible to find him.
He was the best at it. It was just fun, free-roaming and a blast all the time.

“Michael” became the first biopic to cross $1 billion worldwide, and it’s Lionsgate’s biggest film ever. Sorry you set that bar for yourself. Do you remember where you were when you heard and who called to tell you?

I was at home, and I spoke with Antoine [Fuqua] and Graham King individually. We were discussing how crazy a milestone that is. Going into it, you hope and dream it’ll be that successful. I remember that two years before production even started, I wrote down a list of goals I wanted to accomplish and one was to beat “Bohemian Rhapsody” and cross the $1 billion mark. When it did that, I was pretty emotional. I was proud of it, because I know how proud Michael would be. He wanted to break many records, and I couldn’t be more grateful that this did.
I imagine you walking the earth, stalking Rami Malek. “I’m coming for your record, man.”
No, he’s great. I actually got to meet him in Paris during Fashion Week. He couldn’t have been nicer.

Let’s talk about “Michael” Part 2. Lionsgate’s Adam Fogelson has said production could start at the end of this year or early next, with a release targeted for 2027 or ’28. Where do things officially stand? Is anything on your schedule?

I haven’t been told anything concrete, but whatever decision is made, I’m more than ready to get back into it and excited for where that goes. I haven’t been told a date or anything solid yet. As far as my schedule, it’s open.

Leading up to the release, there was a lot of reporting about the original third act, which dealt with some sensitive subject matter. What was it like, as an actor, to lose material you had already shot and performed, knowing that footage would never see the light of day?

It was a massive shoot. I’ve heard many stories from other actors about how much you shoot on a project that doesn’t make it into the final picture. In the editing room, you go through scenes looking for specific performances or takes and things change constantly. So going in, I knew not everything we shot would make it into the final picture. But for me, it was the most rewarding experience because even the things that weren’t used, the experience I got from them, made me a better actor. I feel like that will happen many more times with other projects. You wish a certain performance was in there and it’s not. That’s something you have to deal with when making a film.

You’re in a best actor conversation with some people like Ryan Gosling, Pedro Pascal, Matt Damon and John Malkovich. How are you approaching your first Oscar campaign? Even the movie’s detractors seem to agree: “But Jaafar is great.”

It’s been a crazy and surreal experience, and it’s all gone so fast. I’m taking it a day at a time. Having those conversations and being here speaking with you has been a great honor, and I’m learning so much. Whatever the studio has in mind, I’ll be there to support the film in any way I need to and I’ll be happy to do that. It’s an exciting time, and it inspires me to want to do more work and challenge myself in many different ways. To be in that conversation is definitely an honor.
Did you know awards season was like this? That you’d have to go through all these campaign stops?
Not to that extent. You hear stories, but it’s a great experience to feel it and see it firsthand.
What did you have to learn from scratch, and who taught you the Michael-isms and the Michael moves?

It started with dissecting and creating a library of footage of Michael. A library of all his songs, demos, writings and journaling, performances and rehearsals. I immersed myself in that every day. It became a full-time job, while I also worked on acting with Angela Gibbs, my head coach, who steered me in the right direction, put me in acting classes and brought in other coaches. I read books on classic teachers like Stanislavski, Meisner and Uta Hagen and studied different approaches, because there are many tools you can use, but they don’t work for every actor. I researched different ways to approach a scene, picked my favorites and then developed new ones that might work for Michael, like the dancing. It was a full immersion, a process that took about two years until I actually knew I had the role. Then it was a different energy and confidence, knowing I had it.
Our chief film critic, Owen Gleiberman, wrote in his review that you got Michael’s tentative, high, sugary voice just right. Did you find the voice first or the movement first?

The voice came first. The movement was harder. I believe the voice was the first thing that convinced Graham because I sent him a voice note out of nowhere, over text, of me speaking as Michael. He called me and said, “Getting you a coach tomorrow.” That was the turning point.
Fans keep circulating the side-by-side of your “Bad” tour rehearsal with the 1988 concert. What was the hardest move to replicate?

The hardest thing was feeling that true freedom on stage, so it didn’t feel rehearsed or choreographed. It’s very fluid, and that came from repetition, doing it over and over in rehearsal, so when I shot it that day, I could be completely free. I wasn’t thinking about the next move. I was present in the moment. That was the most fun part. But in rehearsal, the most challenging thing was going up on your toes, because doing it over and over hurts you. I did, many times. That move was a problem for me. I had a whole new respect for ballet dancers. Their toes are probably the strongest part of the body.
Colman Domingo plays your grandfather, Joe Jackson. What was it like to film those scenes, knowing your own father lived through many of those tougher moments?

It was eye-opening to act alongside Colman, then see him as my grandfather and have that full-circle moment. It was so seamless. He’d arrive on set, I’d arrive and we’d get right into it. No rehearsals. I loved that, because we discovered things with every new take and Antoine would guide it or let us play. I grew up with a different side of my grandfather, a softer side. He was strict here and there. If you didn’t put your dishes away, he’d make sure you did or finish all your cereal. But the grandfather my father grew up with was more strict and disciplinary and wanted to keep them together as a group. It was a different time, growing up in the ’60s and parents disciplined their kids differently. Seeing how Colman channeled that, telling so much through his stillness, his eyes and the tone of his voice, was amazing to witness.
Seeing it brought to life on screen would be difficult for anyone. How did it feel to be in a scene recreating something that, in theory, could be traumatic for your dad and your whole family?

Of course it’d be very personal, making a film about your own family and then having them watch it. I remember being really nervous about my family going to see it. I didn’t know if I wanted to sit there with them, because I didn’t want to be in my own head about what they thought of my performance. I just wanted them to enjoy it for themselves. Seeing a film about your own family can make a lot of people uncomfortable because you have your own idea of what that is, and it’s hard to capture it in a two-hour film. But the response I got from my family was incredible, and it made me emotional to get those phone calls from my cousins, even my younger cousins who are 12 and 13 and my uncles and aunts. They were so supportive, and I was happy I could bring that emotion out in them and bring them together to experience it.
What did your father say when he saw the film for the first time?

I saw him get emotional because he first saw it at the Berlin premiere, with the crowd, with the fans. I said, “Dad, you sure you want to wait to see it there?” He said, “I’m sure.” He wanted to see it with the audience. I felt a little nervous for him, but he loved it. He had tears when he got on stage afterward. He called me later that night or the next day to say how incredible it was to see his son playing his brother and not be able to tell the difference in so many moments. I told him how high a compliment that is, if I can convince him, me being his son, that I’m actually his brother in that film. It brought back a lot of memories. He said how much he misses Michael and his smile, and that seeing me on screen brought back the presence I brought to some of those quiet moments, especially the energy in the “Bad” performance. He was incredibly proud. That’s the highest reward, to get that from your parents and your family.

We’re at the tail end of Hispanic Heritage Month. In a clip that went viral earlier this year, you said, “I’m half Colombian and a lot of people don’t even know that.” Your mother, Alejandra, was born in Bogotá and you’ve talked about weaving Latin music into your early songs. What does being half Latino mean to you, and how have Latino audiences responded?

The response from the Latin audience has been amazing. I wish I’d had a chance to go down to South America or Mexico City, where I know the response to “Michael” was through the roof. As someone half Colombian, I sometimes feel embarrassed that I don’t know any Spanish. It’s not too late to learn. My mom still has a full Colombian accent, which I love. Every time I call her, I tease her about it. My Colombian side of the family is fairly small compared to my father’s side, and they’re still in Bogotá. I have some family in Mexico I don’t see often, but we keep in touch. My mom makes Colombian food every now and then. That’s a reminder, with the holidays coming up. I haven’t been to Colombia since I was 14, so I plan on going soon. The last time I was in South America was Brazil in 2019. It’s beautiful, and I love that part of the world.

There are complicated feelings around this movie, about where it ends and where part two should go. As a family member who sees Michael through that lens, what’s your message to people who have their own idea of what Michael was about, including the more complicated discussions and allegations from his life?

Finding out who Michael was is in his music. It’s in his lyrics. It’s in the poems he wrote, the videos, the messages he put out, the talks he gave on panels and at universities. It’s in what he devoted so much time to: charities, visiting other countries and visiting countless children. Part two, I can’t say, because I don’t know. It’s not up to me. My job is to come prepared and deliver the best performance I can. But to know Michael, it starts with the music.
10 QUESTIONS WITH JAAFAR JACKSON
- Childhood nickname? Art.
- Something you loved as a kid that you can’t believe you were into? Tarantulas. I have one as a pet now. And toy soldiers. I used to imagine battles with toy soldiers.

- Karaoke song or shower song? I’ve never done karaoke. I’m too shy. I feel like I’d be judged completely. In the shower, I don’t have a favorite. I hum different melodies or make weird instrument sounds if there’s an echo.
- Alternate title for “Michael?” It’d have to be a song title. I’m going to go with “Man in the Mirror.”
- Secret talent? Juggling.
- Favorite ice cream flavor? Easily McConnell’s Sea Salt Cream & Cookies.
- The one item you couldn’t live without? I can live without my phone. Maybe Apple TV, for my movies. I have a big movie collection.
- What TV show or film in history do you wish you’d been a cast member of? “Troy.” Not Brad Pitt’s role, because he played that so well. Hector.
- Fictional character you most relate to or admire? I’m going with Black Panther.

- Favorite piece of advice you’ve received? Not to be jaded. To enjoy the most simple things in life, and that there’s beauty in front of you at all times. Just being present to look at it, not getting taken away by the illusion of what’s in front of a screen, that dopamine intake. Be present, find beauty everywhere and stay curious, with wonderment. You find happiness and joy there a lot more than in other places.
Do you remember who told you that?
It wasn’t told to me verbally. It was through a note I found that was written by Michael. The way I found it, I felt like I was supposed to hear that.

Variety’s “Awards Circuit” podcast, hosted by Clayton Davis, Jazz Tangcay, Emily Longeretta and Michael Schneider, who also produces, is your one-stop source for lively conversations about the best in film and television. Each episode, “Awards Circuit” features interviews with top film and TV talent and creatives, discussions and debates about awards races and industry headlines, and much more.
