items.title: Gwyneth Paltrow Sets First Lead TV Role in A24 Drama ‘The Apology’ at Netflix
items.description: Gwyneth Paltrow has taken her first-ever lead television role in an upcoming A24 drama series titled “The Apology,” which has landed a two-season order at Netflix.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Gwyneth Paltrow has taken her first-ever lead television role in an upcoming A24 drama series titled “The Apology,” which has landed a two-season order at Netflix.

The Oscar winner will play Evelyn Amspoker, whose son was murdered 18 years ago in a cold case that gripped the nation. “When a stranger suddenly appears and confesses, justice finally seems possible,” per the logline, until Evelyn and her husband, Caleb, learn the killer may get off with a reduced sentence. “Faced with that unbearable truth, Evelyn and Caleb decide to take matters into their own hands.”

The show hails from creator, showrunner and writer Joe Murtagh (“The Woman in the Wall”) and director Thomas Vinterberg (“Another Round”). Joe Hipps of Cut To executive produces alongside Murtagh, Vinterberg and Paltrow. A24 is the studio.

While Paltrow’s filmography includes star-making turns in “Emma,” “Sliding Doors,” Shakespeare in Love” and “The Talented Mr. Ripley” — as well as major roles in the “Iron Man” franchise and “Marty Supreme” — her career on television is less illustrious. Paltrow had a five-episode run on “Glee” as Holly Holiday and had a supporting role in Ryan Murphy’s Netflix series “The Politician.” She has guest starred in random projects but has never led a small-screen title.

The ambitious two-season order for “The Apology” comes amid an executive shake-up at Netflix, which followed an announcement that the company was laying off 6% of its employees. Chief content officer Bela Bajaria was ousted from the streamer last week and was replaced with Peter Rice, while head of film Dan Lin left the company on Monday morning. Meanwhile TV boss Jinny Howe, who oversees U.S. and Canada scripted series, has weathered the storm.

items.title: Netflix Earnings Preview: Not the Time to Chill
items.description: Netflix doesn’t need its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday to get anyone’s attention. It already has had all sorts of eyes and ears in Hollywood and on Wall Street on it for days. After all, the global streamer has been in the headlines with its largest
items.author: Georg Szalai
paragraphs: Netflix doesn’t need its third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday to get anyone’s attention. It already has had all sorts of eyes and ears in Hollywood and on Wall Street on it for days. After all, the global streamer has been in the headlines with its largest layoffs in years, hitting around 6 percent of its workforce, and the surprise replacement of chief content officer Bela Bajaria with Peter Rice.

The flurry of changes came after Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos had lamented at the Bloomberg Screentime summit on Sept. 30 that “overall, we’re not growing as fast as I want us to, and we’re working on making that move faster.” The message seems to be: This is not a time to chill.

Indeed, the streamer’s engagement momentum has been disappointing Wall Street analysts and management alike, with intense competition for audiences’ attention from the likes of YouTube and TikTok as the background. As a result, Netflix shares have been trading near their 52-week low of $65.08. And some analysts have further reduced their stock price targets on the streamer.

Among Netflix’s third-quarter content slate were the likes of 72 Hours With Kevin Hart, The Whisper Man, The Hawk, the final season of Outer Banks, Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, The Gentlemen season 2 and Home Run Derby.

Some on Wall Street expect recent price increases to bolster the latest quarterly results, while others wonder if the job cuts and executive changes are an admission of increased concerns about a lack of content momentum and a further weakening of engagement.

Expect Netflix’s Tuesday results and earnings call to attract much attention from analysts and investors looking to dissect commentary on anything from content strategy changes to rev up the content engine again and engagement trends to how advertising and other new revenue initiatives are shaping up.
Here, The Hollywood Reporter has compiled some of the analyst projections and questions for Netflix’s third-quarter earnings report.
Analyst: Brian Pitz, BMO Capital Markets
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $125 from $135

Takeaways: Netflix’s content chief change led Pitz to pare back his financial estimates, also resulting in a lower stock price target. “Peter Rice will replace Bela Bajaria as chief content officer, suggesting to us that engagement trends may have softened further in the third quarter, leading us to reduce our estimates,” the expert explained. “Sensor Tower’s app data and a shift in chief content officer implies muted engagement growth in the third quarter, suggesting near-term results could remain challenged as Netflix cuts 6 percent of its workforce.” He lowered his third-quarter and fourth-quarter revenue estimates by about 1 percent each and also reduced his 2027 revenue forecast by around 1.5 percent, “reflecting softer engagement trends.”

Growth challenges in the core U.S./Canada business remain “the key focal point,” the analyst emphasized. “Investors fear that Netflix’s U.S./Canada segment lacks a near-term catalyst supporting revenue acceleration, especially as view-hours declined in the second quarter.” Calling advertising “the clearest acceleration lever,” he noted that “our model conservatively does not assume a U.S./Canada revenue acceleration until 2029. While we see the ramping advertising business as the clearest driver of eventual growth acceleration, we believe live sports, bundling, and video games offer additional levers that could pull that acceleration forward.”

Pitz is also still bullish on Netflix’s competitive positioning. “Among surveyed U.S. streaming consumers, 75 percent subscribe to Netflix and 37 percent called it their preferred streaming service, more than twice the nearest competitor,” he shared. “Additionally, 76 percent of Netflix subscribers use the service multiple times a week, underscoring the near-daily frequency.” His conclusion: patient Netflix investors should benefit. “While Netflix may struggle to drive meaningful near-term outperformance, investors with duration will be rewarded as Netflix scales into a leading performance ad platform over time.” Or as he summarized in the title of his report: “Still Near-Term Pain, But Attractive Long-Term Gain.”
Analyst: Alicia Reese, Wedbush Securities
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $90, down from $105

Takeaways: “A New Path is Being Laid; It May Take Time,” the analyst summarized in the headline of her preview note, urging investor patience. So why the price target drop? “Our price target still bets on the advertising ramp, layered with games, podcasts, and eventually performance marketing,” she explained. “However, it may take longer with the significant changes underway.”

The optimism in her take: “Engagement remains central to the bear case; however, ad revenue matters more. Ad revenue remains on track to double to roughly $3 billion in 2026, and Netflix is actively making changes that should address both its engagement issues and shift dollars from heavy infrastructure to more focused content spend.”

Reese’s estimates assume 5 percent year-over-year growth in total global subscribers, “with net paid additions of 2.2 million, a 500,000 drop in the U.S./Canada and modest increases elsewhere.” She also projects an increase, compared to the second quarter, in average revenue per member, driven by “higher prices and subscription retention, plus growing ad spend driven by better targeting and stable CPMs.”
Analyst: Michael Morris, Guggenheim
Stock rating and price target: buy, $80, up from $75

Takeaways: Yes, there are challenges, Morris also acknowledged, citing “continued investor concern, particularly focused on revenue trajectory and content slate.” But he pointed out that Netflix’s stock has been trading at 22 times his 2026 earnings estimate, “in line with the broader market, and a 25 percent discount to Alphabet and Meta on 2027.” As a result, “we see an attractive price for sustainable core growth and potential return on incremental initiatives.”

In the third-quarter update, he sees one key investor focus on “core revenue pacing and average revenue per member outlook in the face of challenging content comparisons and no scheduled engagement or membership update.” A potential positive would be any “evidence that platform expansion (podcasts, short-form, games, distribution partnerships) is showing incrementality,” he added.

Morris is also curious about management’s “outlook for content investment allocation or [a] trajectory change given that management does not plan to ‘take a pause on margin expansion to spend more on content.'”
Analyst: Sean Diffley, Morgan Stanley
Stock rating and price target: overweight, $80, down from $83

Takeaways: “As the number of things vying for our attention is increasing at an accelerating rate, it becomes harder to drive meaningful hours of engagement and time spent across different forms of media & entertainment,” the analyst emphasized in his report entitled “Ice Age: Dawn of the Dinosaurs?” “While once the disrupter, challenger and share taker, Netflix now finds itself on the other side of the chasm and seemingly has to fight harder to remain relevant.”

Explained Diffley: “Stagnant viewing hours and lack of a big English-language hit have been the primary drivers of weakness. A stronger slate and more sports should drive urgency.” And he pointed to “recent green shoots,” such as East of Eden, a Disney licensing deal, Indian content and Netflix’s TF1 deal in France.

The expert also addressed the engagement debate that “has lingered nearly all year, [but] has reached a fever pitch in the last few months, particularly as YouTube continues to take share of total viewing time.”  While calling this “a real debate,” he suggested that Netflix was not facing “a broken model,” as the goal should be “weighing quality and variety enough.” His conclusion: “Netflix remains one of the largest premium entertainment platforms globally, with engagement spread across an increasingly broad mix of scripted series, films, licensed content, live events, video podcasts and games. We believe the next leg of the story is less about maximizing hours at any cost and more about increasing the frequency of reasons to open Netflix, improving discovery, and monetizing each hour more effectively through advertising.” In other words: YouTube may win the showdown in terms of total viewing hours, but Netflix could “remain highly advantaged in premium, intentional entertainment engagement.”
Analyst: Mark Mahaney, Evercore ISI
Stock rating and price target: outperform, $110, recently up from $100

Takeaways: The analyst expects a financially in-line third quarter, but mentioned one key risk looking ahead. “In July, the third-quarter guide came in below the Street on every line,” he explained. “A repeat on the fourth quarter is the main risk to the stock reaction. Fourth-quarter catalysts include the [recently unveiled] U.K. price increase, NFL Thanksgiving Eve and Christmas games, and the WWE launch in Japan.”

Could revenue actually surprise on the upside? “We view the Street’s revenue estimate of $12.9 billion as reasonable to modestly conservative at +12 percent year-over-year and +3 percent quarter-over-quarter,” Mahaney wrote. “Netflix has landed within about 1 percent of its revenue guide in each of the last eight quarters. Recall, the third quarter is the first full quarter of the first-half price changes; in the U.S./Canada, second-quarter growth of 10 percent reflected only a partial-quarter benefit.”

On the earnings call, the expert will be listening out for all sorts of color. Among key topics, he mentioned: “Is engagement softness becoming a revenue problem? Netflix moving its What We Watched report to annual cadence makes retention and pricing commentary the main proof point.”
Analyst: John Blackledge, TD Cowen
Stock rating and price target: buy, $100

Takeaways: The analyst predicted 10 percent-plus revenue growth and rising profit margins “over the next few years, consistent with Netflix’s financial objectives.” After all, “while the investor narrative has remained focused on recent soft engagement trends, Netflix is seeding emerging engagement vectors (live, podcasts, etc.) that could lift engagement and drive member growth and retention,” Blackledge explained.

But what about the near-term challenges? “We acknowledge that Netflix engagement growth has been soft, in our view likely a product of broader expansion of social media and short-form video,” the analyst wrote. “However, we’re bullish on Netflix’s push into podcasts and promotion of their Clips vertical video feature, as we believe these efforts can incrementally drive penetration and engagement among mobile viewers throughout the day.”

He also touted the results of a recent survey. “We asked our surveyed consumers which platform they use most often to view video content on their TV, and Netflix held the top spot in the third quarter through August with 23 percent of respondents, followed by YouTube (19 percent) and Amazon Prime Video (9 percent),” Blackledge noted. “We think Netflix’s broad catalog across multiple genres creates a durable advantage over time.”
Analyst: Daniel Kurnos, StoneX Financial
Stock rating and price target: hold, no price target

Takeaways: “The setup has arguably deteriorated since the last print, with shares down 14 percent in September alone as third-party data continued to show share loss to YouTube and as co-CEO Ted Sarandos conceded … that Netflix is ‘not growing as fast as I want us to,'” Kurnos highlighted.

But he also pointed to “a back-loaded live calendar which we think is underappreciated,” including “the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, Fury-Joshua streaming globally from Cardiff, and a Christmas Day doubleheader.”

Kurnos shared what he will be curious about, noting: “We will be listening for early 2027 content spend framing, live rights appetite beyond the NFL, ads progress toward and beyond around $3 billion, and whether forward margin guidance fully absorbs more aggressive future spending plans.”

items.title: The Six Things You Don’t See In ‘You Can See Everything’
items.description: [Spoilers galore! But come on, you want them.]
items.author: Steven Zeitchik
paragraphs: [Spoilers galore! But come on, you want them.]

So you’ve gone out and watched You Can See Everything, joining the nearly 2 million people this weekend who drank in the Nathan Fielder–Lance Oppenheim investigation into the mad psyche of Elizabeth Holmes. You gasped in the theater, you turned to a friend or a new friend unable to believe what you just saw, you found yourself still marveling at the moments in the parking lot and restaurant, you texted your other friends both annoyed and superior that they haven’t seen it yet. Go ahead, pick up your phone right now, someone you know has just written back “yeah, I need to see it” while you shake your head at their deprivatory laziness.

But even after all that discussing, all that plumbing, you still have questions about what the duo henceforth known as Fieldenheim have created. We all have questions. Heck, Fielder himself has questions. “I am still struggling to this day to understand what I went through,” the director told a New York Film Festival audience last month. He said he and Oppenheim disagreed about the meaning of nearly everything that happened between Holmes and her husband Billy Evans.
But there are some verifiable facts, no matter Holmes’ and Evans’ postmodern take on truth. So here are six key points you’re likely curious about, unpacked to sate your twitchy curiosity.
So how did this movie even happen, you wonder. How was Holmes convinced to do it? She didn’t need to be. Here’s how it went down.

It actually began with A24. Company executives met with Holmes after she called them looking for exposure (lest you think she was just minding her own business when Hollywood came along. Hey, at least she has taste). “It was to have people see who she is,” Evans recently said in response to a question about why they wanted it. But the parties couldn’t come to an agreement, so by the boards the project went.

Then, something spooky. Fieldenheim were — wait for it — at L.A.’s Magic Castle during a visit that Oppenheim took from NYC. During an improv bit, someone from the audience called out Holmes’ name. “Hey, that reminds me, I heard A24 is mulling a Holmes movie!” Oppenheim said to Fielder when the show ended. Shortly after, Fielder placed a call to A24’s offices in NY, and the pair were on the case. Or, at least, on some weirdness they thought could probably never be a movie.

So who are the two A24 execs who met with filmmakers and Holmes-Evans, as the movie reconstructs? The studio isn’t saying, but one thing worth knowing: the person who ran docs for the studio and helped guide the project earlier on is…no longer there. Yes, she was not at the company to see everything. That would be Emily Osborne, laid off last year as A24 shelved its doc division. (She’s still an executive producer on the film.)

By the way, like all good wannabe lawyers, you may have watched the whole handwring about whether the Holmes-Evans unit would get paid and thought: isn’t there a law against that — against a convicted criminal profiting from their crime? There is. Or there was — the Son of Sam Law. But California struck it down a number of years back. So had the couple continued pushing for payment, it likely would have been fine even for Holmes to get paid directly. Think of all the blood-testing machines it could’ve funded!
Does the Alleged Rape Incident Kinda Explain Everything?

It comes and goes so fast you find yourself still processing it five minutes later. Did Holmes’ father say that everything changed for his daughter when she was raped? That degree of trauma could clearly make someone dramatically pull back, hide behind a false persona so thick even they’ve lost track of what’s beneath.

So what’s the real story? Is Holmes a rape victim? Yes, she has said she is — and that it changed everything. Back at her trial in 2022 she spoke tearfully about an incident when she was at Stanford in the fall of 2003, at 19. The alleged incident, she said, sent her on a work-constantly, my-startup-must-succeed-at-all-costs path (she founded Theranos and dropped out of college later that academic year).

What do public records say about the event? The Santa Clara County sheriff’s office had gotten a call late one October night that a student named Elizabeth Holmes was reporting an on-campus sexual assault, at a frat house. Deputies were dispatched, according to a document NPR obtained as part of a California Public Records request. We don’t know where the investigation went from there.
Holmes also alleged that Sunny Balwani — her former boyfriend and Theranos COO who was convicted of fraud and is currently incarcerated too — sexually abused her. Balwani has denied the allegations.
Those details certainly contextualize a lot of Holmes’ behavior; whether they excuse it is up to you. But no such context exists for Billy. Which brings us to…
Who the Hell is Billy Evans and Is It True He Is an AI Who Came Into Existence Thanks to a “Design an Evil Trust-Fund-Bro” Prompt?

No. Maybe. Probably not. We don’t know in great detail what Evans’ source of wealth is in the film — just that he has one, and that this makes him uber-credible because he doesn’t need anything from Holmes.  Or so he’d like us to believe, shades of Larry David and his unattractive-spouse bit.

Of course rather than making us think “oh, he’s privileged, he wasn’t after Holmes for the money,” what we really think is “oh, he’s privileged, he thinks he can get instant fame by leveraging his notorious wife and then yelling at people who don’t sign up for the ride.” (Evans’ recent appearance with the low-key folks on the All-In podcast — having quite a film year, by the way, after their cameo cringily yukking it up at the death of Twitter in Musk — doesn’t exactly boost his credibility.)

Here’s something to know about Evans: the Evans Hotel Group that his grandparents founded some 70+ years ago (The Lodge Terry Pines, the Bahia Resort Hotel and the Catamaran Resort are its three properties) has gotten into plenty of hot water with local groups in Southern California. Citizens’ orgs said an expansion of the Bahia, for instance, took away public access to Mission Bay. Which gives Evans and Holmes frolicking on an endless expanse of beach at their Del Mar rental an added pungency. The family also sued unions in San Diego because they didn’t like how said unions were trying to stop the expansion. The suit was dismissed.

But hey, Evans is in biotech now. Yes, the new blood-testing company talked about in the 2023 section of the film was indeed founded the next year. It’s called Haemanthus — like Theranos, but with some extra Haman — and Evans is the CEO. The company actually is working with a legit technique known as Raman spectroscopy but at least as of May 2025 only seems to have one patent. Blood-testing from the people who brought you Theranos, what could go wrong?
Amanda, I’m Going to Take You By Surprise and Make You Realize

You know that scene where we first see Seyfried, when she’s sitting there on the couch watching the Holmes footage at the start of the third act and you almost blink in disbelief? “Wait…who…could it…is it?” Well, that happened in real time — that’s the first meeting she and Fielder actually had. In fact so realtime there were no plans to have Seyfried come in and play Holmes in those reconstructions we would later see. Fieldenheim just wanted her to react to what they shot and maybe provide some talking-head commentary/clarity. Little did they know that the scene would become, well, a rehearsal for the eventual Rehearsal.

N.B. That farm Fielder visits Seyfried where the animals are fed (and fart). That’s an animal rescue that the actress and longtme partner Thomas Sadoski founded and live in in upstate New York with their two kids. It’s a pretty rad place — a 501(c)(3) nonprofit on which they’ve saved and housed elderly or endangered ducks, goats, donkeys, cats, chickens and horses, funding the place themselves. They thus don’t take donations, but Seyfried has done work for at least one animal-rights group that is public-facing, the anti-kill shelter Best Friends Society. If you donate money, you’d probably save a living being, unlike whatever time you’re not saving using a Theranos device.
Anyway, Seyfried and Sadoski announced a split after that footage was shot. Hopefully she got to heal there too.

Besides some pretty chill movies, A24 excels at spinning off memes. Hereditary memes, Uncut Gems memes, memes contrasting its movies with Costco hot dogs. The company thought — we all thought — they had a good one with that close-up two-shot of Fielder and Holmes on the couch. It had already been repurposed many times.

But when the final history of our era is written and the one true artifact remains, that artifact will, of course, be a meme of Holmes making eggs. So banal; so revealing. There is no one way to whisk eggs. But Evans thinks there is, and he is about to joystick Holmes into doing it that way.
So the SNL sketches are coming; so are the Oscar bits. An omelet station will never be the same again.
Like, why would we deceive you?

Federal Prison Camp Bryan, where Holmes is being held, already comes off as a mysterious place in the film, doesn’t it? (We still have vending-machine questions.) You don’t know the half of it. The facility has incarcerated a true motley crew of inmates — Ghislaine Maxwell is currently there, former Real Housewife Jen Shah just got out of there in August, and Jenna Ryan, the Texas realtor and convicted Jan. 6 rioter who’s had some seriously wild things to say as she tried to become a right-wing influencer, was released from there last winter. When’s the doc of that place?

The women’s prison is a very low-security facility (one reason Maxwell’s transfer there as a sex offender provoked outrage) and generally holds people with sentences shorter than five years. The compound, about 100 miles outside Houston, has fewer staff than other federal facilities because the inmates are not generally considered violent risks. Family and anyone else approved by the inmate can visit every Saturday and/or Sunday. The prison sits in a residential neighborhood of craftsman-esque homes and singing mockingbirds, and the grounds have even been reported by neighbors as almost seeming like a park. (You may have gotten that vibe from the last scene.)

Holmes, per her sentence, shouldn’t be out until 2034. But a judge ruled earlier this year that because she didn’t cause “substantial financial hardship” to victims she can get out some four years early, in 2030. Meanwhile a Theranos investor who was defrauded by Holmes says he was alerted by the Justice Department that, likely because of good behavior, Holmes is actually headed for a halfway house in Austin as soon as this summer — giving her and Fieldenheim just enough time to plan a sequel for 2028.

items.title: Oscar Predictions via Feinberg Forecast: Scott’s Mid-October Charts and Dissection of the Race
items.description: A NOTE FROM SCOTT It’s been a busy few weeks since the last update of the Feinberg Forecast. In that time, I finally saw — or was released to acknowledge having seen — almost all of the high-profile awards hopefuls that were not yet on the charts, among them A
items.author: Scott Feinberg
paragraphs: A NOTE FROM SCOTT It’s been a busy few weeks since the last update of the Feinberg Forecast. In that time, I finally saw — or was released to acknowledge having seen — almost all of the high-profile awards hopefuls that were not yet on the charts, among them Artificial, Mr. Irrelevant, Wildwood, NAZA, 14th and The Social Reckoning. At this point, the only biggies that are still off the books are Dune: Part Three, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Madden and Werwulf.

I also was on the ground at the Toronto, Zurich and Newport Beach film festivals (but unfortunately not at the New York, London or Middleburg film fests, which also took place since the last update), all of which attracted impressive showings of awards-contending talent. In Toronto and Zurich, I was able to get a stronger sense of how awards hopefuls are playing with non-American members of the Academy, which is of particular interest given the massive influx of Oscar voters based outside of the U.S. in recent years. There were Academy members numbering in triple-digits at both events, and the organization’s CEO was on hand for Zurich’s excellent Summit, the “Davos of the film industry.”
This past weekend, two important awards hopefuls debuted in theaters: A24’s You Can See Everything and Netflix’s La Bola Negra.

Unsurprisingly to any of us who caught its world premiere at the Telluride Film Festival, reactions to Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s Elizabeth Holmes documentary have been ecstatic. The film has a 99 percent critical score on Rotten Tomatoes and a 4.71 rating on Letterboxd, the latter a new record; it grossed an astounding $15 million in its opening weekend, the biggest debut from fewer than 1,000 locations since 2006’s Borat and the biggest doc debut since 2004’s Fahrenheit 9/11; and Academy members — even from the frustrating documentary branch — are flipping out for it.

Indeed, some Oscar voters saw it at an early L.A. screening at the Academy Museum on Oct. 6, after which doc branch members Ryan White and AJ Schnack described it on social media as “brilliant” and “incredible,” respectively, and short films/feature animation branch member Travon Free called it “one of the best things I’ve ever seen in my life.” Many other members turned out for its official Academy screening in L.A. on Oct. 18 — more, I’m told, than had ever previously turned out for a documentary — where it played through the roof.

For anyone wondering if the film is eligible for recognition beyond the best documentary feature Oscar category, I refer you to my Sept. 7 piece entitled “Nathan Fielder’s Off-the-Wall Elizabeth Holmes Doc Could Click With Academy — and Land Picture and Acting Noms,” and to the charts below.

As for La Bola Negra, its theatrical debut came amid a tremendously turbulent period for Netflix, with layoffs impacting some 6 percent of the company’s workforce including chief content officer Bela Bajaria, film chief Dan Lin and Kelly Caton, the head of series awards strategy and publicity since 2019. In the face of this, Netflix’s formidable film awards team is forging ahead with the rollout of the Spanish-language epic that is their strongest contender this awards season. It is set for the longest exclusive theatrical window of any film in the company’s history, 47 days, and it is the first film for which the company is publicly reporting box office receipts. The initial numbers are very strong: La Bola Negra debuted in four theaters in L.A. and New York and scored the second-highest per-screen-average ever for a non-English-language film, $69,375, behind only 2019’s Parasite.
Following the fall film fests, there has been a huge uptick in events bringing together Oscar hopefuls and Oscar voters.

I recently moderated post-screening convos in L.A. with the likes of La Bola Negra’s Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, Elsinore’s Andrew Scott, Fjord’s Cristian Mungiu and Possible Love’s Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu. More excitingly for voters, other recent moderators have included Emmy Rossum (with the writers/directors and stars of La Bola Negra following a Sept. 10 New York screening), Greta Gerwig (with The Invite’s Olivia Wilde and Rashida Jones after a Sept. 27 London screening), Jessie Buckley (with Elsinore’s Andrew Scott, Simon Stone and Stephen Beresford following an Oct. 9 London screening) and Demi Moore (with Long Day’s Journey Into Night’s Jessica Lange after an Oct. 16 L.A. screening).

The Academy hosted receptions in Toronto (on Sept. 11 for all of its members who are based there or happened to be in town for the Toronto International Film Festival), L.A. (on Sept. 17 for new members), the Bay Area (on Sept. 23 for new members) and London (on Oct. 10, during the London Film Festival, for new members). These attracted not only the invited members but also some familiar faces as those members’ plus-ones, such as Obsession’s Inde Navarrette and Curry Barker, Club Kid’s Jordan Firstman, Artificial’s Monica Barbaro and Andrew Garfield, Being Heumann’s Ruth Madeley, The Liberation’s Carrie Coon, Give Me the Ball! subject Billie Jean King and the whole La Bola Negra contingent — a somewhat cynical but effective way for Oscar hopefuls to get into rooms packed with Oscar voters.

And this past Saturday night, countless Oscar hopefuls packed the Academy Museum of Motion Pictures in L.A. for the Academy Museum Gala, the Met Gala of the West Coast, which raised $14 million for the institution, and also provided a great opportunity to see and be seen by Oscar voters. Honorees included Michael’s Colman Domingo and The Odyssey’s Charlize Theron, and the featured performer was Taylor Swift, who is in Oscar contention for “I Knew It, I Knew You,” the Toy Story 5 original song that she co-wrote with Jack Antonoff, which was, not coincidentally, among the tunes featured in her four-number set.
A few final notes about things that have happened since the last Forecast before we get to the latest one…

We exclusively broke several important developments related to awards classifications: Obsession’s submission for Golden Globes consideration as a musical/comedy, as opposed to a drama, and the lead versus supporting acting determinations for La Bola Negra, Paper Tiger, Possible Love and Tender Loving Care.

We’ve also posted new episodes of my Awards Chatter podcast — which I hope you’ll subscribe to, for free, on Apple or Spotify — with Penélope Cruz (La Bola Negra, Bunker and The Invite), Andrew Scott (Elsinore), John Leguizamo (The Odyssey) and Inde Navarrette (Obsession). This week, I’ll be posting a new episode with Jordan Firstman (Club Kid). And I’ll soon be posting two other episodes that I recorded over the weekend, in front of audiences at the Newport Beach Film Festival, with Aaron Sorkin (The Social Reckoning) and Emmy Rossum (Furious).

Finally, we’re about to take the podcast on the road and would love to see you if you happen to be in the neighborhood — at the Virginia Film Festival on Oct. 23 with Jessica Lange (Long Day’s Journey Into Night) and at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival on Oct. 25 with Danny Boyle (Ink). And if you’re in Savannah, don’t miss my annual ‘Docs to Watch’ panel, on Oct. 28, with the directors of 10 of the year’s most outstanding documentary features, including the man of the hour, You Can See Everything’s Nathan Fielder!

items.title: CNN Shocker: Christiane Amanpour to Exit News Channel Next Year
items.description: CNN is losing one of its highest-profile anchors and correspondents next year.
items.author: Alex Weprin
paragraphs: CNN is losing one of its highest-profile anchors and correspondents next year.
Christiane Amanpour will scale back her work at CNN over the next few months, and leave the channel entirely next June. CNN CEO Mark Thompson shared the news in a note to staff Monday morning.

“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” he wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Amanpour has been with CNN for 43 years, becoming perhaps its most famous foreign correspondent, and a staple of its lineup.

Why Amanpour is leaving is not clear, but the announcement comes just weeks after Skydance completed its acquisition of Warner bros. Discovery, bringing CNN into its fold. Thompson will continue to lead CNN for the time being, though longer-term anything could happen.

“After many months of thought and a few sleepless nights, I have decided to separate from CNN, my partner of 43 fantastic years!” she said in a statement. “I will end my daily shows across CNN and PBS at the end of this year, while continuing to maintain a weekly show on CNN through May and working on a smooth transition through June.

Amanpour had publicly expressed concern with the takeover, saying at an event in May that “Clearly I’m concerned, and I’m not sure how much I’m allowed to say about a corporate thing that’s under way, but I am obviously, as a person, as a journalist with a record, concerned, and I’m concerned based on what’s happened to the other things that [Ellison has] taken over already, like CBS News.”

For now, she will gradually pull back on her CNN International show this year bfore it ends next May. She will continue to host her podcast The Ex Filed, which she co-hosts with her ex-husband and former U.S. diplomat and Assistant Secretary of State Jamie Rubin. The podcast is not produced by CNN.

“I want to thank all the amazingly talented people I’ve worked with throughout this incredible journey. Especially my beloved show teams and field crews,” she continued. “From my very first big exciting assignment covering the First Gulf War, to the horrors of the Bosnian War, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukrain and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor.”
You can read Thompson’s note to staff below.
I’m writing today with news about a CNN icon – and our dear friend and colleague – Christiane Amanpour.

After more than 43 years at CNN, Christiane has decided that the time is right to begin a new chapter. Early in 2027, she will scale back her CNN International show, Amanpour, to once a week. The program will conclude in May, and she will leave CNN at the end of June.

Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months. Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.

Christiane has been a household name around the world for decades. Yet she began more than 40 years ago not as one of the biggest stars in CNN’s history, but as a news desk assistant in our Atlanta newsroom. Famously, one of her bosses told her back then that she didn’t have what it took to become a foreign correspondent – or to hold any on-air role at all. Boy, did she prove him wrong!

It would be impossible to list all of her reporting triumphs, exclusive interviews, awards and broadcasting firsts, or the many other accomplishments that have made her one of the most trusted and beloved journalists anywhere. We will make sure to share and celebrate them all before she departs next year.
In the meantime, on behalf of the entire CNN leadership team, I want to thank Christiane for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship.

items.title: Feeling Stuck? A Denim Shirt Is Probably the Answer
items.description: The best denim shirts for men have reached heights far beyond their humble beginnings. Popularized in the early 20th century by the ranch hands and roughnecks of the American frontier, the rugged button-up has long since earned its place in the canon of hard-w
items.author: Jeremy Freed; Gerald Ortiz
paragraphs: The best denim shirts for men have reached heights far beyond their humble beginnings. Popularized in the early 20th century by the ranch hands and roughnecks of the American frontier, the rugged button-up has long since earned its place in the canon of hard-wearing, easy-going menswear classics. Unlike the plaid flannel, white tee, or chore coat, the denim shirt has managed to work its way into the snooty, sartorial upper echelons of tailoring, too. These days, some boast spread collars for tucking under a lapel or shell buttons to balance a lustrous wool gabardine blazer, but all are ready to add a hit of workwear-inspired swagger to your everyday lineup.

Just look at fellas like Steve McQueen, Tupac Shakur, and Pedro Pascal, who’ve made the denim shirt an essential part of their wardrobes. (And that’s to say nothing of Ralph Lauren, who’s been schooling the world on how to wear a denim shirt with panache for over 50 years.)

These days, there’s a wider array of denim shirts than ever before, from authentic sawtooth western joints crafted from Japanese selvedge to cozy flannel-lined jacket hybrids to elevated riffs done up in crisp white Italian cotton. Try one with a blazer and weathered khakis or as one-half of a Canadian tuxedo, and don’t be surprised—or remotely disappointed—if you find yourself reaching for it day after day. Rest assured, you’re in good company.
The Best Men's Denim Shirts, According to GQ
Best Denim Shirt Overall: Levi’s Barstow Western Denim Shirt

If it’s authenticity you’re after, you’d best go straight to the source. Levi's has been outfitting folks in sturdy cotton workwear since 1853, and no other brand has a better claim to establishing blue denim as a mainstay of Americana style. Unlike their iconic dungarees, which became popular with miners and railway workers in the late 1800s, denim shirts didn’t become part of the Levi’s catalog until the 1930s, when they were adopted by ranch hands, cowboys, and city slickers looking to ape their rugged frontier style.

True to those origins, this version features authentic vintage details like western pockets, pointed front yokes, pearl snap placket with faux mother-of-pearl buttons, and a just-right mid-blue rinse. As in the 1930s, there’s no better way to add a dash of western swagger to your look without going full Midnight Cowboy.
Best Upgrade Denim Shirt: J.Crew Medium Weight Denim Shirt

Real ones know that sometimes the best shirt isn’t just a shirt. It’s one that can play different roles at the drop of the hat, from everyday button-up to light jacket to rough-and-tumble work shirt. J.Crew’s classic denim shirt has been in its catalog for as long as this writer can remember and it’s obvious why. The denim ain’t flimsy. It’s sturdy and densely woven, but softened into a vintage feel with a few different washes. The double flap chest pockets, pencil slot, cateye buttons, and contrast double-needle stitching come together to tie in the workwear inspiration, and the relaxed-but-not-sloppy silhouette make it perfect for wearing as a light layer or on its own.

It feels like the kind of shirt you’d be happy to acquire from your grand pappy, or find hidden deep within your favorite vintage store, ready to synchronize with every pair of pants you throw at it. And for a smidge above a hundred bucks—and very often on sale—that’s a lot of shirt for a truly reasonable price.
Best Budget Denim Shirt: Wrangler Iconic Denim Regular Fit Snap Shirt

Contrary to what you might believe, many of menswear’s well-established style icons are propped up by humble garments. There are, no doubt, plenty that rely on designer names and cutting edge labels, but elder statesmen and young bucks alike know to toss in some everyman garments to ground their style. Oftentimes, that’s a Wrangler western shirt. From Bruce Springsteen to the guy that’s playing him, the shirt have passed muster with cool guys for generations and made countless hopefuls way more stylish along the way.

At just about forty bones, the snap button western supplies heaps of style, much more than you’d think. It’s been in Wrangler’s lineup for generations and remains relatively unchanged which means they actually look vintage straight out of the box. If it’s not clear, that’s a very good thing.
Best Denim Shirt for the Office: Todd Snyder x Hamilton Chambray Long Point Collar Dress Shirt

Your buttoned-up corporate office may not allow jeans, but they probably never said anything about denim dress shirts. We’re all for a western shirt under a blazer, but that’s not what we’re talking about here. Denim, employed with the right details and cut, can be as elegant as a crisp poplin and ready to stroll down the cubicle aisles or even a red carpet. Todd Snyder’s collaboration with multi-generational shirtmakers Hamilton have made one of the most distinguished shirts we’ve seen and can make any diehard denim junkie expand their understanding of the tough-natured fabric.

It features a substantial pointed collar, hand-carved mother-of-pearl buttons, a split yoke, and a classically tailored silhouette. Toss it under your best-fitting suit with a silk foulard tie and a pair of derbies, and your boss will have no choice but to acknowledge your superiority—or at least won’t put you on their shit list.
Best Denim Shirt for Denimheads: Sugar Cane 8oz Denim Western Shirt

The Western shirt may have been invented in the Wild West but—as with so many pieces of the classic American wardrobe—it was perfected in Japan. Formed in a Japanese factory that originally produced garments sold to US military bases, Sugar Cane makes both reproductions of vintage Americana as well reinterpretations suited to the modern market. This western shirt takes its cues from vintage western shirts with its slanted snap chest pockets, real mother-of-pearl inlay snaps, double-needle stitching, and western yokes, and crafts it all out of a hefty 8-ounce pure-indigo-dyed Japanese denim.
How We Test and Review Products

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.
We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.
Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)

items.title: I'll Give Up Desert Boots When You Pry Them Off My Feet
items.description: The trend cycle moves at a breakneck pace; the second you decide to hop onboard, the ship has already sailed. While clothes seem to have more of a never ending deluge of trend shifts, shoes can also be hard to keep up with. In the footwear space, there are a f
items.author: Leon Hedgepeth
paragraphs: The trend cycle moves at a breakneck pace; the second you decide to hop onboard, the ship has already sailed. While clothes seem to have more of a never ending deluge of trend shifts, shoes can also be hard to keep up with. In the footwear space, there are a few options that come to mind that are trend-proof and never kowtow to what’s “in”: the Clarks Desert Boots happen to be one of those shoes.

The Desert Boot was officially launched in 1950 by Nathan Clark, the great-grandson of the company’s founder, after he noticed officers in Burma wearing rough suede boots with crepe rubber soles. Seventy-six years later, one of the defining features of the Clarks Desert Boot is its bouncy rubber crepe sole. It differs from other chukkas, which can use leather soles or other sturdy rubber outsoles. Desert boots are also unlined and super flexible, a detail that adds to its endearing casualness.

As someone who prides himself on not jumping on trends, I figured that with fall finally in the air, and fresh foliage on the ground, now’s a good time to revisit this footwear stalwart. They are still one of the best boots thanks to their malleable nature; they can be worn with a variety of jackets or different washes of jeans, chinos, and work shirts. Below is a breakdown of how I styled my pair three different ways.
Outfit 1: The Autumnal Go-To

If Mother Nature didn’t exist, I’d dress like this year-round. The cola suede colorway on the Desert Boots makes them an easy neutral to pair with just about anything in your fall wardrobe. Ecru is one of my favorite shades to wear, as it always pairs well with brown hues, and my Jungmaven tee has that washed-down, vintage T-shirt feel that drapes perfectly.

For denim, these 1947 LVC 501s have been getting a lot of wear lately. I actually think they did a great job with the pre-darning and mending on these jeans, which gives them a hint of character without looking like a homemade distressing attempt.

This has easily been one of my go-to outfits for making the transition between seasons a little easier. The mornings start brisk, temperatures jump up around noon, and suddenly you’re trying to figure out which season it is, which is why a good piece of knitwear on standby is never a bad option.

A denim shirt and chinos are about as safe as an outfit can get, but you’ll never regret wearing some version of this, or at least that’s what I keep telling myself. Ever since becoming a dad five years ago, my denim-shirt collection has multiplied tenfold. They’re versatile, easy to wash, and somehow look better the more stains and rips they collect—and built for parenthood.

I’m wearing mine with some baggy chinos from Gap, which, I must say, might take the crown from the J.Crew Giant Chino in my humble opinion. I’ve been wearing this combination while working from home, running errands, and walking to pick my son up from school. It’s comfortable, but still gives the illusion of effort.

Maybe it’s the Midwesterner in me, but there’s something so liberating about wearing a long-sleeved shirt, jacket, and shorts this time of year. I once saw an artist featured in Mr Porter’s The Way I Dress video series from back in the day who went sockless with his Desert Boots, and I understand it now. That’s the beauty of the unstructured upper and the comfort of the crepe rubber sole: they make going sockless feel a little less questionable.

The shorts from Filson have a decent amount of volume, but they don’t feel too baggy. Maybe I’ve been looking at too many old Banana Republic catalogs, but there’s something about this combination that feels interesting. All I need now is a Land Cruiser and an expensive pair of binoculars.

items.title: The Best Belts Prevent Everything From Going South
items.description: The best belts for men keep your slacks from going south, but they also make them sing, in the most stylish way possible. Other than saving you from an embarrassing wardrobe malfunction, belts can be the difference between a fine outfit to a divine ensemble, i
items.author: Leon Hedgepeth; Gerald Ortiz
paragraphs: The best belts for men keep your slacks from going south, but they also make them sing, in the most stylish way possible. Other than saving you from an embarrassing wardrobe malfunction, belts can be the difference between a fine outfit to a divine ensemble, injecting your getups with a jolt of cowboy swagger or disheveled-heartthrob cool.

That's not to say you should ditch your low-key leather joint for a garish WWE Championship Belt—unless you are, in fact, worthy of the title. But you definitely should apply the same care and attention to your belts that you do every other piece of clothing in your closet—especially given how, when styled correctly, they're typically the first thing someone hones in on when they look at you. To help you invest in some leather that'll last, we went deep on the best belts for men to keep you looking sharp—and your pants right where they belong.
The Best Men’s Belts, According to GQ
Best Belt Overall: Maximum Henry Oval Standard Belt

When Maximum Henry Cohen launched his eponymous label in 2012, I doubt he pictured himself outfitting style icons like Robert Pattinson and Timothée Chalamet—but here we are. Fourteen years later, his brand has crossed into Hollywood, collaborated with leading Internet menswear personalities, and also notably partnered with the most discerning boutiques, who proudly display his handmade belts right on their shelves.

They do it because the belts are true pieces of craftsmanship. They’re cut, dyed, stitched, and waxed to order in their Long Island City studio, and made from 100% Belgian vegetable-tanned leather with sturdy hardware. Take this one: At 1.5” wide, it’s the perfect daily driver, whether you’re pairing it with raw denim jeans or paper-thin chinos. The additional beauty of this brand? No two pieces are exactly alike, so each belt is already unique, though you’ll make it even more so as the patina builds with every wear. With Maximum Henry, you’re getting a piece that’s truly yours—not some cookie-cutter belt from the nearest outlet store.
Best Budget Belt: Journeyman Full Grain Leather Belt

For a little over $50, you can snag both black and brown belts from Journeyman. And don’t let the price fool you: Made in the U.S. from full-grain leather at a sturdy 1.5” width, this belt gets all the fundamentals right. It’s an ideal pick if you’re just dipping your toes into the belt game—not only does it keep your wallet happy, but the classic color options and silver single-prong buckle make it as versatile as they come. More good news? The brand backs it with a lifetime warranty, making it a stress-free investment. And here’s the kicker: the buckle is removable, so you can swap it out someday for that vintage one you scored at the flea market.
Best Dress Belt: Morjas Leather Belt

Belts tend to distract from a suit, especially if you went to great lengths to tailor your suit to perfection. That isn't to say you can't wear a belt with a suit, but your belt should match the energy of the suit. Ideally, that means leather with a sheen that matches the suit fabric, about 1.25" thick, and with a buckle that's elegant without stealing the show. Hence, this Morjas belt.

Morjas might be better known for its shoes, but its belts have also quietly become a stylish guy-favorite for their upscale look and their approachable price point. The leather is a supple, full-grain calf leather that has just enough texture to pair with most suit fabrics, from a classic gabardine to twills and tweeds. The stitching adds an element of depth, while the gently curved brass buckle is handsome, but not showy. At $150, it's certainly an upgrade from most belts in the mall, but it's definitely worth the splurge.
Best Braided Belt: Anderson's Woven Suede Leather Belt

Family-owned Italian accessory brand Anderson’s has been turning out some of the world’s finest belts for nearly 65 years—and they’re still doing it all from a workshop in Parma, Italy. Their secret sauce? A mastery of Italian leather, a playful approach to design, and a commitment to a rigorous 100-step production process that guarantees every belt shipped out meets its high standards. (Yes, that’s 100 steps for a single belt. Quality, my friend, doesn’t come easy.) All of this is also why retailers like Mr. Porter don't just buy two or three Anderson's styles—they buy twenty or thirty.
Best Suede Belt: J.Crew Italian Suede Buckle Belt

With more warm-weather outfits, a smooth, shiny, dark leather belt can feel a little… sweaty. Suede is the solution. To help, J.Crew chose to produce their suede belt in what some say are the two best varieties—Chocolate brown or snuff. We’re all winners for it, especially when the result comes in at sub-$100. And while that lower price point might be cause for quality concerns with a dressier style, for a belt you'll ideally be wearing to and from a park picnic, the more you rough it up the better.
Best Belt for Fashion Guys: Our Legacy Leather Belt

Honestly, Our Legacy’s belts are one of the main reasons menswear guys started paying closer attention to belts again. Just as their Camion series managed to perfect the kind of shoes every guy wants to wear right now, their semi-braided Western belt has an unmistakable presence at most fashion gatherings and has spawned a series of imitations.

But the original remains the strongest. OL’s belt is a neat 2cm wide, with a metal pin, Western buckle closure, metal keeper, and metal hardware tips that all combine for a sort of punk, sort of rodeo vibe. Simply put, this belt takes any outfit in a number of complimentary directions—and don’t worry, it won’t bite.
Best Belt for GQ Cover Stars: Artemas Quibble Roebling Belt

What do Steven Yeun, Sergio Pérez, and Paul Mescal all have in common? Well, aside from rocking the cover of GQ, they’ve also each been spotted wearing belts from Artemas Quibble. The masterminds behind the label are husband-and-wife duo Natasha Chekoudjian and Jason Ross, who have also designed belts for some of fashion’s biggest names: Calvin Klein, Helmut Lang, and Rick Owens.

Each belt is handmade, and you, the buyer, get to choose the hardware and leather color. The belts feature materials like reclaimed leather, repurposed brass, and antique textiles, combining for a perfect blend of raw materials and avant-garde aesthetics. The strap itself is 1.25” wide, but the buckles? Unlike anything you’ve ever seen. Seriously, if "presence" had a dictionary image, this would be it. It’s the kind of belt that could easily work for A-listers today, cowboys of yesteryear, and maybe even a Spartan or two before that.
What to Look for in a Great Belt

What, exactly, differentiates a so-so belt from a truly superlative one? It’s more than just enough holes (though that’s a good place to start). Homing in on the materials at play is especially key. Are you looking for full-grain leather that’s durable and business-ready? Or maybe a braided suede for a relaxed, just swung-off-the-horse vibe?

Once you've got that figured out, it’s time to choose between widths (casual belts usually clock in at around 1.5 inches wide; formal belts 1.25 inches), and buckle types (clean and classic buckles skew formal; rugged, D-ring buckles skew casual).

Finally, and perhaps most importantly: figure out your proper waist size. Pros tend to go about 1 or 2 inches up for a fit that’s snug but not restrictive, which also leaves a little room for any winter weight anybody reading this definitely won’t gain.

items.title: The Best Corduroy Pants Swaddle Your Legs in Pure Bliss
items.description: Just as the mighty Mitochondria produces energy for your cells, the best men's corduroy pants produce all the heat your fall outfits need. Constructed of evenly spaced rows of thick cotton “wales,” corduroy will always be warmer than conventional denim, though
items.author: Louis Cheslaw; Daniel Varghese
paragraphs: Just as the mighty Mitochondria produces energy for your cells, the best men's corduroy pants produce all the heat your fall outfits need. Constructed of evenly spaced rows of thick cotton “wales,” corduroy will always be warmer than conventional denim, though it could—and should—be worn with the same reckless abandon as your favorite just-thrown-on jeans.

Frankly, they’re also just a joy to wear. The real magic of wearing corduroy is something you can only feel once you’re swaddled in it. Like corduroy shirts, corduroy pants have real heft to them, bathing your legs in all the warmth and cuddly energy of a weighted blanket without, well, the excess weight.

That said, not all corduroy pants are created equal—right now, for example, it’s all too easy to end up with an overly tapered option that hugs the legs too closely. Luckily, there's also no shortage of options in handsome cuts and colors, all of which are more than worth adding to your fall rotation this season, and every autumn after it. These are 13 of the best men's corduroy pants you can buy right now.
The Best Corduroy Pants for Men, According to GQ
Best Corduroy Pants Overall: Polo Ralph Lauren Whitman Relaxed Fit Corduroy Pant

As the long arc of menswear zigs and zags, one thing never changes: Ralph Lauren doesn't scrimp on the essential details, and menswear nerds keep coming back for them. In this case, Ralph's designers have sourced sumptuous corduroy and let it spread out a little, with two pleats and an added coin pocket. Both rear pockets have buttons for added security, and while it's hard to see in the image above, all colorways come with a lovely cuff at the hem. All of this for just $200 (or $198 at Ralph), and the knowledge that if you fall in love with this cut, known as the Whitman, it also comes in a chino fabric for summer.
Best Corduroy Pants to Replace Your Jeans: Levi’s 555 Relaxed Straight Corduroy Jeans

Levi’s: synonymous with denim, but also pretty good at everything else. For proof, peep this pair of corduroy pants, cut from the same block as the brand's classic, beloved 555—essentially the neatness of the iconic straight-fit 501, but with some much appreciated extra room throughout. They're 100% cotton, so the knees won't ever sag out, and our favorite detail has to be that colorway, a gray-brown that will sit perfectly against a navy or black knit. (Levi's calls it ‘Smokey Taupe.’)
Best Corduroy Pants for the Office: Todd Snyder Relaxed Wide Wale Corduroy Pant

If there’s any potential knock against corduroy, it’s that the fabric can read a bit casual. And sure, in some highly formal settings, the average pair of corduroy pants might make you feel like a schoolboy in a room of Miss Trunchbulls. Not these Todd Snyder pants though, mainly thanks to their incredibly elegant sheen, black color, and relaxed fit that helps them wear almost more like suit trousers. (It also means they're one of the more comfortable pairs on this list, as well as being the most formal.) One more note for the nerds: The 8-wale corduroy used here is a touch wider, making them even more satisfying to run your hands over during stressful Q3 budget meetings.
Best Corduroy Pants for Fashion Guys: Agolde Fusion Straight-Leg Cotton-Corduroy Trousers

In recent years, the Agolde brand has started to really gain the attention of fashion guys, simply because its jeans are just that good. Naturally, that extends to its corduroys: A plum-gray hue, 100% cotton fabrication, lovely drape along the inseam, and all made in the USA. Simply put, these get Agolde medal from us (Sorry.)
Best Corduroy Pants for Menswear Nerds: Mfpen Generation Straight-Leg Cotton-Corduroy Trousers

Fear not! While many mfpen trousers err on the actually-quite-wide side of ‘Straight Leg,’ these represent a new, closer fit for the brand. But that isn't the point here: The jumbo cord is. For indeed, a closer look will reveal that these aren't just any old corduroys, but some of the widest wales our jean-faring eyes have ever had the good fortune to see. Jumbo cords, for a jumbo grail.
More Corduroy Pants We Love
How We Test and Review Products

Style is subjective, we know—that’s the fun of it. But we’re serious about helping our audience get dressed. Whether it’s the best white sneakers, the flyest affordable suits, or the need-to-know menswear drops of the week, GQ Recommends’ perspective is built on years of hands-on experience, an insider awareness of what’s in and what’s next, and a mission to find the best version of everything out there, at every price point.

Our staffers aren’t able to try on every single piece of clothing you read about on GQ.com (fashion moves fast these days), but we have an intimate knowledge of each brand’s strengths and know the hallmarks of quality clothing—from materials and sourcing, to craftsmanship, to sustainability efforts that aren’t just greenwashing. GQ Recommends heavily emphasizes our own editorial experience with those brands, how they make their clothes, and how those clothes have been reviewed by customers. Bottom line: GQ wouldn’t tell you to wear it if we wouldn’t.
We make every effort to cast as wide of a net as possible, with an eye on identifying the best options across three key categories: quality, fit, and price.

To kick off the process, we enlist the GQ Recommends braintrust to vote on our contenders. Some of the folks involved have worked in retail, slinging clothes to the masses; others have toiled for small-batch menswear labels; all spend way too much time thinking about what hangs in their closets.

We lean on that collective experience to guide our search, culling a mix of household names, indie favorites, and the artisanal imprints on the bleeding-edge of the genre. Then we narrow down the assortment to the picks that scored the highest across quality, fit, and price.

Across the majority of our buying guides, our team boasts firsthand experience with the bulk of our selects, but a handful are totally new to us. So after several months of intense debate, we tally the votes, collate the anecdotal evidence, and emerge with a list of what we believe to be the absolute best of the category right now, from the tried-and-true stalwarts to the modern disruptors, the affordable beaters to the wildly expensive (but wildly worth-it) designer riffs.
Whatever your preferences, whatever your style, there's bound to be a superlative version on this list for you. (Read more about GQ's testing process here.)
Why Buy Corduroy Pants This Fall 2026?

Unlike most jeans, corduroy pants totally pass muster in more formal environments, too. Think of them as winterized—or just simply better—chinos: Their unmistakably soft, nubby fabric offers texture and depth, where standard khakis feel more pedestrian (dare we say… forgettable).

items.title: Every Must-See Look From the Victoria's Secret Fashion Show 2026
items.description: On October 18, the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show returned to Los Angeles for the first time in 19 years. “It’s the city of angels!” the brand’s creative director, Adam Selman, said gleefully over Zoom a week before the event. “It just felt right.”
items.author: Carolyn Twersky Winkler
paragraphs: On October 18, the Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show returned to Los Angeles for the first time in 19 years. “It’s the city of angels!” the brand’s creative director, Adam Selman, said gleefully over Zoom a week before the event. “It just felt right.”

The California homecoming wasn’t the only exciting return on Sunday night. The show also featured the return of the decadent diamond-covered Fantasy Bra after eight years—modeled by none other than Kylie Jenner who made a surprise appearance as proud boyfriend Timothée Chalamet and mom Kris Jenner looked on from the front row. There were several OG models who returned for the event, including Rosie Huntington-Whiteley’s first VS moment in 16 years, and Elsa Hosk hitting the runway again after almost a decade. Despite these revivals, Selman was adamant that the event is more focused on the future than the past. “This is not a heritage show,” he said.

His comment came as the Internet broke into a tizzy over casting news in the days leading up to the show. “We’re trying to thread the needle between the old and the new,” Selman explained. That means welcoming back some models of yore, while also allowing room for new women to join the VS family.

One of those new women was Solange Omon, winner of the YouTube docuseries “Angels Among Us,” which followed Selman, Paloma Elsesser, Gigi Hadid, and Ashley Graham on a nationwide casting call to find Victoria’s Secret’s newest Angel. “It was probably one of the most challenging but most rewarding things I've ever done in my career,” Selman said of the process, which invited 1200 women to compete for a spot in the lineup and a contract with IMG Models.

Omon walked the runway alongside Victoria’s Secret stalwarts including Alessandra Ambrosio, Candice Swanepoel, and Adriana Lima. They were joined by Hadid, Alex Consani and Liu Wen, models who capped off a whirlwind fashion month with the lingerie show. “I love that the girls are walking in Paris and then coming to us,” Selman said.

The 2026 iteration of the spectacle—kicked off by Bella Hadid—boasted a seasonal theme, with women walking the lucite runway in lingerie that transported viewers through a year in a matter of minutes. “Each season is tied to an emotion or a feeling,” Selman said. “So spring is tied to desire and obsession and summer is high heat. It's fast and it's bold.” Autumn, with its corsetry and lace wings, was all about romance, while two winter sections saw models adorned in luxe furs and silver-tipped sets. An intermission in the cyclical journey featured a vintage Victoria section with a vibrant display of slip dresses. “We heard that people loved our slip dresses from the past and collect them, so we did reissues,” said Selman. The Pink halftime show rounded out the offerings and allowed It girls like Quen Blackwell and Trinity Rodman to take on the runway in ready-to-wear.

The Selman-constructed seasonal voyage featured a live soundtrack with Megan Thee Stallion, Katseye, and Megan Moroney, who performed on the runway alongside the models. W’s Originalscover star Tate McRae sang her new single “Housewife” for the first timein shimmering red lingerie. She shared the stage with those walking the summer portion of the show, including Gigi Hadid with her paillette-fringe wings.

As the winter snow thawed under the heat of the runway lights, the show closed in its usual celebratory fashion. Models returned to the runway one last time for a final lap and bow as Chalamet, Nicole Kidman, and Tinashe provided the applause, cementing another Victoria’s Secret Fashion Show in the history books.
