Few pedestrian malls survived into the 21st century, even as pedestrian zones wove their way into the fabric of cities around the globe. This month, a 1km stretch of London’s Oxford Street will be pedestrianised, finally resolving a longstanding debate about the love-it-or-hate-it high street.

Today, cars once again get caught in the gridlock on downtown Vancouver’s Granville Street. But over the summer, a five-block stretch of this once-bustling, now-struggling road was closed to traffic and opened to people. Originally planned as a short-term intervention to create an outdoor gathering space during the 2026 Fifa World Cup, the plein-air party proved so popular that the city council voted to extend the experiment until 7 September.

Just as the barricades, picnic tables, café seating, outdoor games and public art have been stowed away for winter, there are now calls to bring it back – perhaps for good. “We envision ourselves potentially doing this year-round and longer term,” Councillor Lisa Dominato told the CBC. “Hopefully next summer.”

As the enthusiasm in Vancouver attests, North America has a newfound interest in opening streets where people can stroll and linger. After years of dithering, Seattle has finally banned private cars from the street fronting its famed Pike Place Market for much of the year, while Madison, Wisconsin turned State Street into a pedestrian zone last year. Philadelphia also pedestrianised a stretch of the Benjamin Franklin Parkway earlier this year.

The sometimes-tired, 20th-century pedestrian malls that have persisted are now being rethought. Calgary’s Stephen Avenue completed the first phase of its revitalisation project in late June this year. Civic leaders in Minneapolis are debating how to revive Nicollet Mall, a signature Lawrence Halprin design which James Corner Field Operations previously spruced up. These refreshed versions can be called “the pedestrian mall 2.0” and are part of what the University at Buffalo’s School of Architecture and Planning professor Kelly Gregg describes as “a new moment of questioning the prioritisation of automobiles”.
Pedestrian mall 1.0: Urban renewal and small-city success

Beginning with two blocks of Kalamazoo, Michigan’s Burdick Street in 1959, more than 200 cities across North America converted their streets into pedestrian malls in the mid-20th century. Out went the asphalt and lane markings, and in came trees, benches, water fountains and artful pavers.

Austrian-American architect Victor Gruen – who aimed to recreate the pedestrian experience of his native Vienna – was the mastermind behind the revamp in Kalamazoo, as well as revitalisation plans in Fresno, California; Fort Worth, Texas; Rochester, New York; and Honolulu, Hawaii. Cities flush with federal urban renewal money eagerly hired him and his peers to keep shoppers coming downtown instead of heading to the shiny new malls on the urban fringe – many of which Gruen also designed.

In the end, however, the shopping malls prevailed. “It was a losing strategy economically,” says Gregg, adding that the design of pedestrian malls was “unable to counter the massive economic restructuring that cities were facing”.

The response was sometimes swift. Toronto’s summertime Yonge Street Mall, for example, only lasted four years from 1971 to 1974. And sometimes, it was agonising: Chicago’s State Street Mall limped along for nearly two decades until city leaders put the strip out of its misery in 1996, with a redesign that allowed car traffic and reduced the width of pavements. The city’s downfall was banning cars and bikes but still allowing buses. Instead of ambling along a pleasant street, Chicagoans had to choke on fumes. (Minneapolis is grappling with the same issue today.)

Big cities, such as Toronto and Chicago, were outliers with most pedestrian malls flourishing in smaller towns. While not all survived – Gruen’s mid-century designs were erased from Kalamazoo in 1998 and scrubbed from Fresno in 2017 – one common thread among those that have persisted is a university. Pedestrian malls have thrived in places such as Pearl Street Mall in Boulder, Colorado and The Ithaca Commons in New York state, where students create a steady stream of foot traffic.
Pedestrian mall 2.0: Big-city revival

Pedestrian malls in charming college towns have had an easier run than those in big cities that grapple with higher rates of retail vacancy, property crime, rough sleepers and open-air drug use. It was public safety perception that partly doomed the 20th-century’s pedestrian malls, as the absence of car traffic began to make the streets feel less safe.

The new wave of pedestrian malls, however, is not fixated on bringing customers into a bygone era of downtown shopfronts. “Downtowns are no longer just about retail,” says Gregg. “The pedestrian malls that have adapted are more focused on entertainment, bars and restaurants.”

This was definitely the case on Vancouver’s Granville Street, a designated entertainment district where one in four shopfronts is vacant. “We are fighting very hard to save this street,” says Jane Talbot, the president and CEO of the Downtown Vancouver Business Improvement Association. “We know that people love this street and that when we give them a reason to come to Granville Street, they will.”

Downtown Vancouver’s team programmed a summer of activities in the temporary pedestrian zone: free cotton candy, outdoor DJ sessions, an International Cat Day celebration, a Belmont Cameli lookalike contest, a morning baby rave for families. The list might resemble the lineup on a cruise ship but today’s North Americans are drawn downtown by intensive programming.

In Vancouver’s case, the hyperactivity during the frenzied summer months is part of the city’s seasonal rhythm before winter hibernation, as well as an astute political move. A short-term move towards pedestrianisation “is a tactic that helps with the people who don’t want it,” says Talbot. “They’re far less likely to push back on a seasonal approach.”

The flip side, warned Gregg, is that cities can get stuck in a “permanent temporary” state, unwilling to invest in quality design. New York’s former transportation commissioner Janette Sadik-Khan pushed to close Times Square and five blocks of Broadway to cars in 2009, which is widely considered the vanguard of 21st-century pedestrianisation in North American cities. It took almost a decade, however, to replace flimsy, fold-up café furniture with Snohetta-designed stone benches. As urban design critic Diana Lind writes, “Increasingly, when I see moveable chairs in a public space, I feel that it’s a cop out.”

One city bucking the trend is Denver, whose 16th Street Mall was a late arrival but one that came with star power: architects IM Pei and Henry Cobb collaborated with landscape architect Laurie Olin. The stretch opened in 1982 to public adulation and design plaudits for its “character-defining carpet of diamond-patterned, charcoal-grey, light-grey and Colorado-red granite pavers” inspired by Navajo blankets and rattlesnake skin.

Almost a year ago, the downtown street reopened after a $175m (€151m) revamp that replaced ailing locusts with a healthier tree canopy, upgraded underground utilities and added seating and play areas. By December of last year, the strip was back to pre-2020 levels of vibrancy, according to the Downtown Denver Partnership. But it had also dropped an important moniker in a key sign of the times: it’s just 16th Street now – no “mall” to be found.

items.title: Shibuya is changing – but in Tokyo’s trend capital, disruption is the only constant
items.description: Tokyo’s Shibuya neighbourhood said goodbye to one of its most famous institutions this week when Seibu department store closed its doors after 58 years. Thousands turned out in the final weeks as operations wound down. Some came to snap up a bargain – towels,
items.author: Fiona Wilson; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: Tokyo’s Shibuya neighbourhood said goodbye to one of its most famous institutions this week when Seibu department store closed its doors after 58 years. Thousands turned out in the final weeks as operations wound down. Some came to snap up a bargain – towels, kitchenware and handbags were piled high and going cheap – while many regulars came for a last visit to Top’s café. People of all ages (myself among them) came to take snaps of the Showa architecture, a postwar style that many are belatedly waking up to just as it’s being demolished across the city. Elegant design details, such as the staircases and the arched walkways that connected two of the buildings, were well worth recording.

For a generation, Seibu was the place that shaped Shibuya’s position at the heart of Japan’s youth culture. It opened in 1968, just as Japan was rebuilding its confidence after the Second World War and the economy was booming. Seiji Tsutsumi, son of the wealthy founder of the Seibu Railway company, established the retail space close to Shibuya Station. It helped to launch the careers of young Japanese fashion designers who were given space in Capsule Corner, where Shiro Kuramata created transparent plastic display pods to showcase his clothes. Seibu stocked international names but championed homegrown brands such as Issey Miyake, Comme des Garçons and Yohji Yamamoto. It also had all the other obligatory features of the Japanese department store – the basement food hall, the rooftop play area and, of course, the pet shop.

Shibuya has been responsible for many fashion trends, from Shibuyakaji (Shibuya casual) fashion in the 1980s to Shibuya-kei (Shibuya style) music in the 1990s. It was the epicentre of gyaru culture, whose startling look featured exaggeratedly loose socks and mahogany tans. Shibuya became the place to be in the 1970s, with the opening of era-defining shops such as Parco, Tokyu Hands and fashion emporium Shibuya 109.

The crowds are still here but the retail landscape has changed. Seibu is no longer the cultural force that it once was. Shibuya 109 still throngs; Parco was demolished but reopened in 2019 with its cultural programme of exhibitions, plays and cinema still intact. Tokyu Hands – which rebranded as Hands in 2022 – continues to thrive but the Shibuya branch is closing for good in November. The shop has always been hard to define: you could buy a hamster (I did) or a reconditioned boom box – and rely on its well-informed staff to know exactly which type of glue or kitchen cleaner worked best. You could while away hours there on a rainy weekend.

Though there are many other branches, the one in Shibuya is the mothership, a multi-story wonder on a cramped corner site. Real-estate company Hulic will redevelop the site as a luxury hotel. As someone who visits Hands at least once a week, it’s hard to imagine Shibuya without it.

Some feel that Shibuya is losing its uniqueness, its streets dotted with global chains and its distinctive department stores gone. Even the famous scramble crossing is now besieged by tourists, as police try to shepherd stragglers who are determined to get the perfect photo. Still, it doesn’t do to be too curmudgeonly about change. Perhaps it’s more realistic to see Shibuya as a place that belongs to whoever goes there. After all, transformation and novelty were always part of the district’s appeal. Just across from Seibu, the finishing touches are being applied to Japan’s first multi-story wooden retail complex, designed by Foster + Partners. Another chapter begins.
Fiona Wilson is Monocle’s Asia editor. For more opinion, analysis and insight, subscribe to Monocle today.

items.title: Looking good and feeling great: Our October issue examines the rewards of a sharp appearance beyond mere aesthetics
items.description: There are many people who will tell you that being cool just doesn’t matter. That, while style might be a nice add-on, it’s really not something that you should be spending too much time thinking about. That appearances are fundamentally irrelevant.
items.author: Andrew Tuck; Kate Lucey
paragraphs: There are many people who will tell you that being cool just doesn’t matter. That, while style might be a nice add-on, it’s really not something that you should be spending too much time thinking about. That appearances are fundamentally irrelevant.

But they are wrong. How things look and making places that are cool can be a positive, potent driver in everything from economics to architecture and urbanism. One place that seems to have cottoned on to this is New Zealand’s largest city.

Poor old Auckland has been the target of some rather waspish comments over the years. Travel writer Paul Theroux described arriving in the city a few decades ago as like “touching down on a distant star”. When former Singapore prime minister Lee Kuan Yew came to town in the 1990s, he’s said to have described Auckland as “shut”. Now, I’m sure that many Kiwis were indifferent to these arrows and the city was happy to be the urban equivalent of a dad in flares but other residents understood the damage that this inflicted – including a brain drain that saw numerous people leaving to find fun and opportunities in Sydney, London and Los Angeles. Change was needed and, over the past 20 years, the city has been rebuilt, with its post-industrial waterfront taken back for public use. As we go to press, it’s also preparing to open the largest infrastructure project in the country’s history.

The City Rail Link is New Zealand’s first underground metro system and comes with a series of beautiful stations that have been attracting thousands of visitors on special preview days. Its imminent unveiling was a good cue for us to send reporter Gordon Peake to assess how the city got its new look and how being a bit cooler is changing perceptions.

The often-surprising impact of beauty in the things that we build and make is a recurring idea in this issue. It certainly runs through a wonderful interview by Grace Charlton with Lebanon-born, Paris-based architect Lina Ghotmeh.

I first met Ghotmeh when she participated in our Quality of Life Conference in the French capital in 2022. I was transfixed by her ability to rise above the fray to talk about what architecture can do for people and countries; coming from a nation scarred by wars and infighting had clearly given her both clarity of thought and a determination to deliver change. It’s a mindset that has resulted in Ghotmeh winning competitions to design everything from a perfect factory (for Hermès) to national exhibition pavilions (for Bahrain at Expo 2025 in Osaka). Now, she’s redesigning the Western Range galleries of the British Museum in London that house objects from ancient Greece, Egypt and Rome.

Reading her interview, you will immediately sense her ability to harness design to deliver so much more than just an efficient exhibition space. “How do we allow a piece of architecture to become a place that builds our knowledge, that allows you to experience the work better but also to open up to dialogue?” she asks. “The museum is not a static place that just showcases objects from the past. It’s also a contemporary place that has to allow for debate and learning from our ancestors.” It’s designed as a Trojan horse to deliver big ideas that will stay with visitors forever.

Debate and learning have been common threads in Monocle since our launch in 2007 – the first issue went on sale on 14 February that year. Over the coming months, in the run-up to our 20th-anniversary celebrations, we will be putting the spotlight on some of our own history.

This month’s Expo pages document what has become a key part of our brand: our annual Quality of Life Conference, which this year unfolded in Lisbon. The event is the magazine brought to life; a display of all the topics that we care about but also a moment when we are able to underline some bigger ideas – that listening is good, that we can find some of the best answers in fields beyond our own. And that, yes, being cool can be a good thing.
If you would like to send me ideas, thoughts or style tips, I can always be found at [email protected]

items.title: Emmanuel Macron Addresses The Nation Following Violent Protests Across France
items.description: The images, from Paris, Marseille, and Lyon, have been seen around the world. Amid protests across France against the soaring cost of living and in support of education—following weeks of mobilizations by high school and college students—rioters have overshado
items.author: Kahina Sekkaï
paragraphs: The images, from Paris, Marseille, and Lyon, have been seen around the world. Amid protests across France against the soaring cost of living and in support of education—following weeks of mobilizations by high school and college students—rioters have overshadowed demands that are reminiscent of those of the Yellow Vests. On one hand, the official protest: a largely peaceful gathering, with signs bearing humorous messages and cultural references. On the other, violence, looting, and burned-out buildings—such as the Limoges city hall, which was devastated by flames.

Emmanuel Macron spoke on Sunday evening in a televised address, even though the entire political establishment—including the declared candidates for his succession—had already commented extensively on the events.

“Watching these images, we all asked ourselves: What are they thinking? How can French people do this to France? Why burn down the Limoges city hall, the tourist office in Lyon, storm the Marseille city hall, or attack the prefect’s residence in Bordeaux? How could they have gone this far? Nothing justifies it, nothing explains it. Nothing excuses it,” the President of the Republic began.
He announced that Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu would chair a crisis task force starting Monday, in particular to address the concerns of business owners whose establishments were vandalized.

“Those who destroyed property must pay, those who looted must reimburse, and those who sought to bring down the Republic will be held accountable,” he continued, calling for “exemplary” legal action. “We will be unyielding toward rioters and all those who engage in violence. Listening and dialogue do not mean weakness or impunity.”

According to Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, more than 2,000 people were arrested across France, and more than 600 police officers and firefighters were injured. One protester died in Paris after falling ill, according to Le Parisien.

“Our responsibility is therefore twofold: to listen to the anger and address its causes, and to firmly uphold republican order. We must neither confuse legitimate demands with violence, nor must we allow violence to prevent these demands from being heard,” he continued, calling on “all political parties, professional organizations, and labor unions to unequivocally condemn all acts of violence and call for calm.”

“All those who are telling you today that the urgent need is to take to the streets, to protest, to create disorder, have only one goal: to undermine the Republic and hijack the debate,” Macron continued. “The choices about the future that you—and we—will have to make in six months are essential. And France is a great democratic force. It deserves these debates. They must take place in public forums. They must involve the political parties, not take place in the streets through violence.”
The Presidential Election on Everyone’s Mind

“Our country deserves a fair presidential election in six months. It is also being decided right now, through a spirit of responsibility,” Emmanuel Macron insisted, as all political parties speak out against the government in the wake of the attacks.

On the left, Paris’s Socialist mayor, Emmanuel Grégoire, said he was awaiting “explanations” from Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez, as sporadic looting continued Sunday evening in the capital. “There’s no need to stage all this—the Greens are very clear: we condemn all violence,” Marine Tondelier wrote on X following the president’s address, while Manuel Bompard, the coordinator of La France insoumise, stated on LCI that Emmanuel Macron had “spoken without saying anything.” “It’s absolutely irresponsible to take the podium tonight just to say nothing,” Bompard added.

Edouard Philippe, former Prime Minister and presidential candidate, was not convinced by the speech. “Like millions of French people, I would have preferred decisions and initiatives to restore order and reestablish state authority, to punish looters and rioters, and to outline a detailed plan for resuming dialogue with high school students and labor unions. Our country needs strong leadership,” he posted to X.
His successor and opponent, Gabriel Attal, urged people to “learn all the lessons from these events.”

“The scenes of violence are unbearable. The scenes of looting of our stores and town halls are disgraceful. The scenes of chaos are a provocation against state authority. Nothing can justify these actions,” he wrote.
Jordan Bardella, president of the National Rally, described the president’s statement as “lamentable.”
“This cowardly and disoriented administration has nothing left to say to the French people, nothing left to offer them. It no longer even has the strength to protect them,” he posted on X.

Bruno Retailleau (Les Républicains), concurred on the same platform. “The President of the Republic appears completely overwhelmed," he wrote, adding that Macron appears “incapable of using the force of the state to counter the mayhem threatening the Republic.”
Originally published by Vanity Fair France

items.title: Trump's Crunch-Time Message: New Mexico Should Be Renamed 'New America'
items.description: Golf courses, Jon Husted’s fat dumper, and demands to rename “New Mexico.” There are only 15 days until the midterms, and Donald Trump is locked in.
items.author: Nikki McCann Ramirez
paragraphs: Golf courses, Jon Husted’s fat dumper, and demands to rename “New Mexico.” There are only 15 days until the midterms, and Donald Trump is locked in.

On Monday, with early voting already underway in more than half a dozen states, the president should be focused on boosting Republicans’ closing message to disillusioned voters around the country. Instead, he is upset that New Mexico is called New Mexico.

“New Mexico should immediately change its name to New America,” the president wrote on Truth Social. “We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America! The name would add great value and prestige to the State! Home Values and Incomes would rise, and you would be even prouder while saluting our beautiful American Flag! Maybe even the Crooked Elections, that New Mexico is known for, would become honest again!”

If New Mexico becomes New America, does that mean everything else in the union is Old America? Is it an admission that the rest of us are washed, that we need to scrap the whole thing and start over? Who’s to say?

It’s not the first time Trump has made such a demand. In September, he claimed on Truth Social that “many people” (who are most definitely real and plentiful) “suggested changing the name of New Mexico, one of the great vote cheating states of all time, to NEW AMERICA.”

The call builds on Trump’s efforts to rename stuff, part of a series of lazy attempts to goad our supposed allies in North America and create an illusion of geopolitical dominance without actually doing any work. This includes attempting to rebrand the Gulf of Mexico as the “Gulf of America” and Lake Ontario as “Lake America.” He’s also recently used, perhaps less seriously, changing the name of the Atlantic Ocean to the “Ocean of the Americas” or “Trump Ocean.”

The president’s fixation on New Mexico is just part of a longer string of erratic campaign-trail moments in the past few days — many of which run completely opposed to the priorities and messaging being put out by Republican candidates. The president, whose D.C. construction projects have been deeply unpopular with the American public and rife with allegations of financial mismanagement and corruption, announced last week that he is moving forward with plans to take over a public golf course in Washington.

“You have a golf course right now: it’s old, tired, beaten up, it’s useless,” Trump told reporters on Monday. “It doesn’t do much business. We want to do something great for Washington. We’re going to basically build a better golf course. It’s going to be one of the great courses.”
The president has been similarly unfocused on the stump. Last week in Kentucky, he went on an extended rant about how beautiful he found the body of Ohio Sen. Jon Husted.

“I don’t do this with men very often,” Trump said. “I started examining his body because I didn’t know he was a great athlete. And I looked and I watched up and down. I looked at his ass. I looked at his shoulders, I looked at his feet, I looked at his hand, I looked at his jawline, studying … I then patted him on the shoulder, and it was like a piece of steel.”
Very good, sir. The price of diesel just hit $6. Hopefully no one notices.

items.title: Jon Stewart to Remain ‘Daily Show’ Host Through 2028
items.description: Jon Stewart will continue to lead “The Daily Show” through 2028.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Jon Stewart will continue to lead “The Daily Show” through 2028.

The host has extended his contract with the Comedy Central series for another two years and will continue to man the desk through the next presidential election. Stewart’s contract was set to end at the end of 2026 after signing a one-year renewal in November 2025.

Stewart will remain part of the rotating lineup of hosts that includes Ronny Chieng, Josh Johnson, Jordan Klepper, Michael Kosta and Desi Lydic, with Troy Iwata and Grace Kuhlenschmidt as non-hosting correspondents. He also stays on as an executive producer with showrunner and executive producer Jen Flanz and Stewart’s longtime manager, James “Baby Doll” Dixon.

Stewart last renewed his contract just a few months after Comedy Central parent company Paramount was acquired by Skydance Media. His new extension comes weeks after the David Ellison-led conglomerate closed on a merger between Paramount and Warner Bros.

Stewart made his hosting debut on “The Daily Show” in 1999 and left in 2015. Trevor Noah took his place as anchor of the satirical news program before he stepped down in 2022. After Stewart returned to “The Daily Show” in February 2024, ratings went up. According to metrics provided by Paramount, the show is the most-viewed cable program across social media in 2026.

“Jon Stewart is a generational talent and ‘The Daily Show’ continues to be one of the most influential franchises on television and a cornerstone of Comedy Central. We are excited to continue our partnership with Jon and his award winning news team,” said George Cheeks, co-chair and chief content officer of Skydance TV.

items.title: ‘Running Point’ Co-Creator Mindy Kaling Joins Season 3 Cast
items.description: Mindy Kaling, writer, executive producer and co-creator of “Running Point,” has picked up one more title on the Netflix show: star.
items.author: Ethan Shanfeld
paragraphs: Mindy Kaling, writer, executive producer and co-creator of “Running Point,” has picked up one more title on the Netflix show: star.

Kaling is stepping in front of the cameras for Season 3 in the recurring role of Divya, an outspoken, confident CEO of a popular gambling app. Per the character description, “Much like Isla (Kate Hudson), she’s proudly the first female leader in her male dominated field. Their similarities end there with Divya becoming a thorn in Isla’s plans all season.”

Production on “Running Point” Season 3 is underway in Los Angeles. Kate Hudson will direct the first episode, marking her television directorial debut. Returning cast includes Drew Tarver, Scott MacArthur, Brenda Song, Fabrizio Guido, Chet Hanks, Toby Sandeman and Justin Theroux, with recurring actors Ray Romano, Uche Agada, Ken Marino and Jay Ellis.

“Running Point” follows Isla (Hudson), a former party girl and college dropout who is unexpectedly left in charge of her family’s pro basketball team. In Season 2, she is “no longer the surprise choice to lead the Los Angeles Waves, she’s the one everyone is watching,” per the logline. “With the franchise finally rebounding after last year’s scandal, Isla is determined to prove she’s not just keeping the seat warm for her brother Cam (Justin Theroux). What she doesn’t know is that Cam is quietly maneuvering behind the scenes to reclaim his post, turning every misstep into ammunition. As she tries to balance the pressure of running a franchise with devoting time to her personal life, every decision on and off the court counts. To survive the family power plays and the scrutiny of the board, she’ll have to rip up last season’s game plan and come up with a whole new playbook if she wants to close out the season on top.”

The sports comedy series hails from writers and executive producers Kaling, David Stassen (who also showruns) and Ike Barinholtz. Hudson, Howard Klein, Jeanie Buss and Linda Rambis also serve as EPs. The series is produced by Mindy Kaling’s Kaling International in association with Warner Bros. Television. Kaling and Stassen are both under overall deals with WBTV.

items.title: Agents and Indie Producers Argue Incentives Alone Won’t Fix Hollywood’s Ills
items.description: It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.
items.author: Gene Maddaus
paragraphs: It doesn’t mean much to anyone under 45, but for older folks in Hollywood, the term “fin-syn” evokes a golden age of mansions, yacht parties and cutting-edge TV.

The FCC’s “financial interest and syndication” rules forced TV networks to buy shows from superproducers like Norman Lear and Grant Tinker rather than making them in-house. And ever since the FCC did away with fin-syn 30 years ago, producers and agents have been longing for its return.

Now, with momentum building behind a U.S. film incentive, they are hoping the moment is ripe to recreate fin-syn for the streaming era. They argue it would bring a jolt of creativity and a spirit of enterprise to a business stuck in a creative slump.

The major agencies — WME, CAA and UTA — announced last week that they are forming a coalition with production companies including Imagine Entertainment and Legendary to push for legislation that would force streamers to buy at least 50% of their original content from independent producers. The legislation would also limit the length of licensing terms, reviving secondary markets that have largely withered away.

Their message is that Hollywood ails not only from runaway production, but also from a consolidated ecosystem that limits creativity and makes it harder for producers, writers and actors to profit from their labor.

“The tax incentive may change where the production shoots, but it doesn’t change who owns and profits from it,” argued Ken Ziffren, co-founder of Ziffren Brittenham LLP, who has been campaigning for a restoration of fin-syn for decades. “We think the tax legislation only goes so far to help our industry and it’s not a complete effort, and it can’t be a complete effort, unless it’s paired with a modernized ownership framework.”
Jeff Sagansky, a producer, investor and longtime fin-syn supporter, argued that overseas incentives are not the only reason that U.S. production jobs are going away.

“They’re also going away because of the way the streaming business has consolidated around four players,” he said. “They act as an oligopoly. They’ve got incredible pricing power,” saying the streamers are ordering 30-40% fewer hours of programming than they were a few years ago.

Getting the idea through Congress will be an uphill battle, and will face adamant opposition from Netflix, Amazon and the other streaming platforms. The effort also has the potential to sow division within an industry that has united behind the goal of passing the first-ever federal film incentive.

Supporters wanted to some version of their ideas into the tax credit bill that was introduced to much fanfare in September. But while they had some positive meetings, they were ultimately rebuffed. They are now aiming for 2027, when Democrats are expected to take control of at least one of the houses of Congress.

Rep. Laura Friedman, a co-author of the tax incentive as well as a former producer, said in a statement that she sympathizes with producers’ concerns about industry consolidation and the threat to diverse voices in entertainment.

“My focus right now is on passing our bipartisan national film tax credit bill to put film and television workers back on the job, but I look forward to continuing to work with stakeholders to ensure the industry is vibrant for the future,” she said.

The Streaming Innovation Alliance, which includes Netflix and other streamers, issued a statement on Thursday calling the proposal a package of “blunt government mandates” that would “only dampen production and discourage creative risk-taking.”

The Federal Communications Commission adopted the fin-syn rules in 1970, when there were only three TV networks. The rules prevented networks from owning syndication rights in their shows, and later, from owning shows that aired in primetime. The rules are credited with leading to an era of groundbreaking TV, including “All in the Family,” “The Mary Tyler Moore Show” and “The Cosby Show.”
The repeal of the rules in the mid-90s spurred a wave of vertical integration, as Disney acquired Capital Cities/ABC and Viacom acquired CBS.

Arguing that the end of fin-syn had killed off independent production, a group called the Coalition for Program Diversity urged the FCC to reinstate a version of it. In 2002, the coalition — led by Ziffren — sought a new regulation that 25% of primetime programming come from independent producers. In a deregulatory era, such pleas fell on deaf ears.

Nowadays, streamers typically either make shows themselves or buy from the handful of other major studios. When they do buy from indie producers, they typically take all rights for 10-20 years, locking the producers out of the option of selling into secondary markets.
Mark Vahradian, producer of the “Transformers” franchise and other films, argued that streamers are so powerful that they can dictate those terms, and that dynamic ultimately hurts consumers.

“There’s no incentive for the creators to go out and build something brand new,” said Vahradian, a founding member of Producers United. “That’s why they’re only making sequels and franchise titles. They own those and have no motivation to say ‘Why don’t we do something new?’”
For years there wasn’t much opportunity to do anything about it. But with President Trump vowing to “save” Hollywood from a dramatic downturn, fin-syn supporters see an opening.
The initiative would require an act of Congress, as the FCC’s ambit is limited to the public airwaves.
Andrew Long, a senior fellow at the Free State Foundation, a free-market think tank, argued that the streaming marketplace is far more diversified now than the three-network era of the 1970s.

“It’s hard to find factual predicate that would justify this kind of government intervention in the video distribution marketplace in 2026,” Long said, adding that it could raise First Amendment concerns. “I think there would be high scrutiny, and I think that given the state of the marketplace and the options available, it might not pass muster.”
But Rich Shuter, head of business affairs at UTA, argued that consolidation leaves his agency’s clients without much leverage — and viewers without much choice.
“We’re going back to a situation where you have these streaming conglomerates controlling all the content the country is viewing,” Shuter said. “They’re determining what is being produced.”
Shuter said that more risk-taking will lead to a more vibrant ecosystem.
“We don’t want to stall the federal tax credit from being passed as quickly as possible,” he said. “We hope the administration and Congress recognize this is a supplemental benefit.”

items.title: Netflix Film Head Dan Lin Out
items.description: Dan Lin is out as Netflix‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter.
items.author: Mia Galuppo
paragraphs: Dan Lin is out as Netflix‘s film chief, sources tell The Hollywood Reporter.

The news comes as the streamer cuts from its uppermost ranks and implements layoffs that will affect roughly 1,000 people, the company’s biggest cut since 2022. Prior to Lin, chief content officer Bela Bajaria was exited, along with VP of film Doug Belgrad and a series of high-ranking television executives.

It is unclear who will assume Lin’s role, but the understanding is that Peter Rice, who took over the chief content officer post, will be in charge of finding new leadership. Netflix did not immediately reply for comment.

Lin joined Netflix in 2024, taking over from then film chief Scott Stuber. Under Stuber, Netflix became known as the place where name filmmakers could land big budgets and paydays as the traditional studios implemented more cost-conscious spending practices. During this time, the streamer consistently ended up with best picture nominations, but top awards have notoriously evaded Netflix films.
Lin, who was hired by Bajaria, was brought in to curb spending while (ideally) increasing the quality of the entire film slate, not just the titles from big-name directors.

Under Lin, the streamer‘s movies division was reorganized by genre, with deputies like Kira Goldberg, Ori Marmur and Jason Young handling films that fell under categories like sci-fi, rom-com and family film. Netflix began offering more mid-size films that have been ignored by theatrical players, including big book adaptations like Remarkably Bright Creatures and People We Meet on Vacation, as well as mid-budget action films like Apex and The RIP.

(This is not to say that Netflix’s Lin tenure was without big swings — see: Greta Gerwig‘s Narnia movie due out next year or David Fincher’s The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth— but the offerings no doubt slowed.)

Lin came from his production company Rideback, which minted the $1 billion grossing Aladdin and was involved in the hit It movies as well as The Lego Movies. He departed the company when he joined Netflix, leaving partners at the helm who found another $1 billion hit with last summer’s live-action Lilo & Stitch.

As of late, the streamer hasn’t been able to capture audience interest, at least at the rate co-CEO Ted Sarandos would like, with viewership and subscriber growth stagnant. Under Rice‘s leadership, Netflix will focus on “creating big, buzzy hits,“ as Sarandos wrote in his memo to staff.

After the initial news broke, Netflix confirmed the news, and shared statements from, Lin and Sarandos. Lin said, “It’s been a great privilege to lead this incredible team and work with amazing filmmakers and talent to bring their movies to the world. Thank you to Ted, Greg [Peters] and Bela for the opportunity.”

Sarandos added: “I started working with Dan well before he joined us in 2024 and his strength as a producer was always clear. Once he joined Netflix, I saw up close how his dedication to quality filmmaking, rigor around dealmaking and strategy, and collaborative spirit elevated our film business. I’m grateful to Dan for everything he’s done for Netflix films.”
Oct. 19, 10:16 a.m. Updated with statements from Lin and Sarandos.

items.title: Feds Got Warrants to Use Fake Cell Towers to Hunt Down Don Lemon’s Producer
items.description: US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, c
items.author: Dhruv Mehrotra
paragraphs: US law enforcement agents obtained authorization to use a controversial surveillance device capable of intercepting cell phone signals to find and arrest a 21-year-old college student who helped produce journalist Don Lemon’s coverage of an anti-ICE protest, court filings show.

The former student, Jerome Richardson, who has since graduated from Temple University, is among 39 people charged with conspiring to violate worshippers’ civil rights and interfering with religious worship at Cities Church in St. Paul, Minnesota, in January. Protesters said they targeted the church’s January 18 service because one of its pastors, David Easterwood, also led ICE’s St. Paul field office. Those charged include journalists Georgia Fort and Lemon, a former CNN host, who say they were there to cover the demonstration.

Twelve days after the protest, judges in two states began signing warrants authorizing agents to use so-called cell-site simulators, commonly known as Stingrays or IMSI catchers, to target Richardson’s phone: one in Minnesota on January 30 and another in Pennsylvania the next day. The purpose, his lawyers wrote in a motion seeking to exclude the tracking evidence, was “locating and arresting him.”

Agents also applied for cell-site simulator warrants targeting the phones of Fort and Jamael Lundy, then a Minnesota State Senate candidate. They separately sought pen register orders, which can log the numbers a phone contacts, for Fort and a number WIRED traced to Lemon. It's unclear whether a judge approved any of those applications.

The records reviewed by WIRED do not establish whether investigators actually deployed a cell-site simulator to locate Richardson or whether judges approved the applications targeting Fort and Lundy. In a July letter filed in court, Fort’s lawyers said prosecutors “did not know” whether the surveillance applications had been authorized or had yielded evidence.

Cell-site simulators impersonate cell phone towers to locate a target’s phone. In doing so, they can also collect identifying information from any nearby cellular device, including those belonging to people who aren’t suspected of a crime. That indiscriminate collection has made the devices controversial among privacy advocates, who describe them as dragnet surveillance tools.

The use of cell-site simulators has long been shrouded in secrecy. FBI records released in 2023 showed that police borrowing its simulators had to agree to keep details of their use secret, even in court. Privacy advocates have long warned that the devices could be turned against protesters and journalists.

“Using an advanced surveillance capability such as a cell-site simulator against members of the free press for reporting stories that are unfavorable to the president is an appalling attack on the First Amendment,” says Cooper Quintin, senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, a tech-focused civil liberties nonprofit. Quintin has spent years researching the devices and developing tools to help people detect them. Using EFF’s detection software, WIRED found evidence suggesting a cell-site simulator was deployed near the 2024 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, though who operated it and for what purpose remain unknown.
Attorneys for Lemon, Lundy, and Fort did not respond to requests for comment. Richardson’s attorneys declined to comment on the record.

The previously unreported warrants are a product of a campaign of contentious investigative tactics waged by federal agents in pursuit of people connected to the protest at Cities Church. According to court records, the Department of Homeland Security demanded journalists’ telephone and YouTube records under a customs authority that requires no prior judicial approval. Agents also sought records identifying everyone who had purchased a particular beanie at REI in the Minneapolis–St. Paul area over a period of more than two years. Defense attorneys have identified 92 customs summonses and are challenging the government’s authority to issue them.

The cell-site simulator warrants raise serious questions about both the accuracy of the information investigators presented to judges in their effort to obtain authorization for surveillance tool’s use, as well as why they sought such intrusive tracking to find Richardson in the first place.

The affidavits supporting the applications to track Richardson claimed video showed Fort, Lemon, Richardson, and others “chanting with agitators.” Prosecutors have since conceded that Lemon and Fort did not chant. According to her lawyers, the government acknowledged that the false claim appeared in at least 15 warrant affidavits.

DHS policy says cell-site simulators are deployed only “in the fraction of cases in which the capability is best suited to achieve specific public safety objectives,” but it’s unclear what specific public safety reason justified its use in this case. Investigators obtained a second simulator warrant to locate Richardson, then a senior at Temple University, two days before he walked up to a federal courthouse in Philadelphia and voluntarily surrendered. He was released on bond that afternoon.

The Justice Department responded to WIRED’s request for comment by writing in an email that the department “speaks through its court filings.” DHS declined to discuss ongoing investigations or investigative methods and referred questions to the US Attorney’s Office for the District of Minnesota, which did not respond to a request for comment.

The warrant was signed January 31, the same day Richardson posted a YouTube video saying he expected to enter federal custody “in the coming days,” suggesting he had no intention of fleeing. It is unclear whether the warrant preceded the video, leaving questions about why investigators sought such an intrusive tool to find someone who was publicly anticipating his arrest and whom prosecutors agreed to release the day he surrendered.
While Richardson’s suppression motion asks to suppress evidence obtained from the phone tracking, it does not specify whether agents used a simulator or obtained evidence through either.

A former federal prosecutor who spent a decade working on counterterrorism cases says using a simulator to locate someone is not necessarily unusual. But based on the court records they reviewed about Richardson’s case, they called the government's tactics aggressive: “I don’t understand why it would be at all necessary.” They spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record

Richardson, a St. Paul native, had led an NAACP chapter at 16 and served as executive director of Minnesota Teen Activists, according to his fundraiser’s organizer. He described his work for Lemon as handling logistics and connecting him with local contacts. He drove the journalist to Cities Church, where Lemon livestreamed the demonstration and interviewed protesters and churchgoers. Prosecutors allege Richardson joined chants and obstructed congregants.
In his video, Richardson defended his role. “I was proud to support his work,” he said of Lemon. “This is the price of being unapologetic about humanity and love of Christ.”

The government’s initial effort to obtain arrest warrants met resistance from judges. A magistrate judge refused five of eight warrants, and after an appeals court rejected the Justice Department's bid to override that decision, the department withdrew its request. In a filing with the appeals court, the chief judge wrote that two of the five “were not protestors at all; instead, they were a journalist and his producer” and that there was “no evidence that those two engaged in any criminal behavior.” Prosecutors later secured a grand jury indictment on January 29.

The way the government chose to arrest some defendants has also drawn objections from defense lawyers. Lemon’s attorneys say in court filings that prosecutors rejected their offer to arrange his surrender; agents instead arrested him shortly before midnight at a Beverly Hills hotel while he was covering the Grammy Awards. Fort’s lawyers say agents arrested her at home rather than allowing her to turn herself in.

items.title: Microplastics React With Water, a New Study Says. That’s a Problem for Biology
items.description: One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.
items.author: Jorge Garay
paragraphs: One of the reasons plastic has become so ubiquitous is that, generally, it’s very chemically stable, meaning it does not readily react with the substances around it. That’s why this material is so often used for food packaging and water bottles.

The same was thought to be true of microplastics—those tiny pieces of debris that break off from larger plastic objects and which, according to numerous studies, have spread to virtually every ecosystem on the planet. But scientists at Columbia University and UC Berkeley have just discovered that water can make the surfaces of microplastics chemically active and turn them into a potential hazard.

According to the findings of the article published in Nature, this activity can trigger the spontaneous formation of chemicals capable of altering other molecules, like those that are essential for living organisms. The phenomenon, the authors note, occurs even under normal environmental conditions, without the need for sunlight or other agents that cause plastic degradation.
So how can microplastics be so reactive when bigger plastics generally aren’t? The scientists suggest this has to do with the greater available surface area for these reactions to occur.

“As plastic fragments into smaller and smaller particles, its surface area increases enormously,” Wei Min, a professor of chemistry and biomedical engineering at Columbia University, said in a press release. “Then microplastics change the water that surrounds them, generating high-energy, reactive radicals that very likely contribute to biological damage that we see in animals and potentially in humans as a result of microplastic exposure.”

Among these potentially dangerous chemical products—called reactive oxygen species—a variety known as hydroxyl radicals stands out. They are particularly dangerous because they can snatch electrons from the proteins and fats that make up cell membranes, disrupting their structure and function. These “are textbook examples of the kinds of molecules that can damage animal and human tissue,” added Naixin Qian, a postdoctoral researcher in Min’s lab who helped lead the research.

Our body has some defenses against this kind of damage. This is the biological function of the buzzy molecules known as antioxidants. These neutralize the reactive chemicals, but if the reactive compounds greatly outnumber antioxidants, this line of defense can be overwhelmed.

This can develop into a scenario called oxidative stress, leading to the damage of cells. Previous research had already identified oxidative stress among the cellular responses associated with exposure to microplastics, although the mechanisms responsible for this damage are not yet fully understood.

The extent to which microplastics have pervaded our bodies remains an open debate, with some of the more sensational findings having been called into question. But if even a small amount of microplastics are present in our tissues, they could be reacting with the water in our bodies.

The researchers were particularly concerned with the potential effects on blood, which is largely composed of water. If contact with this fluid can chemically activate the surfaces of microplastics, their presence inside the body could pose an additional danger beyond that of the pollutants they carry or release.

When the researchers exposed red blood cells extracted from mice to different types of microplastics, the cells became deformed and ruptured—a phenomenon known as hemolysis. The effects were greater with plastics that were more reactive with water, indicating that this activity was the cause of cellular damage.

Research into the effects of microplastics has long focused on other chemicals leaching from the particles or on their physical effects, often considering the plastic itself chemically inert. The larger pieces generally are, but these findings challenge the assumption that what is true of plastic on a grand scale is also true of the microscopic pieces it breaks down into.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

items.title: Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon
items.description: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.
items.author: James Temple
paragraphs: In the middle of an especially warm July in 2021, a wildfire ignited in a thick forest of black spruce and peeling paper birch trees on the northern campus of the University of Alaska, Fairbanks.

The blaze, possibly sparked by lightning, burned across the dry carpet of feather mosses and lichen before climbing into the crowns. By the time fire agencies responded, flames had reached 12 feet in length and sent up a 500-foot column of smoke.

A few days shy of the five-year anniversary of the Yankovich Road Fire, I followed three members of the Alaska Fire Science Consortium into the boreal forest, walking along cross-country ski trails lined by feathery field horsetail.

In 2024, the organization, which hosts presentations to keep wildfire managers abreast of new developments in fire science, helped turn the area into an educational walking trail, with interpretive signs posted along the route. About a half-mile in, the horizon opened up as we reached a sparse stand of naked, blackened tree trunks, stripped of needles and neighbors.

Hilary Shook, the coordinator of the consortium, stepped off the trail with her thaw probe, a T-shaped pointed metal rod used to detect the upper boundary of the permafrost, the ancient layer of frozen soil that underlies 15% of the land around the Northern Hemisphere and stores roughly twice as much carbon as the atmosphere.

A test of the ground just outside the burn scar hit the concrete-like layer about a foot below the surface. But as Shook applied pressure here, where the fire had burned away the moss and organic-rich topsoil that insulates the permafrost, the probe plunged at least three times deeper into the ground.

“That was an immediate effect of the fire,” said Alison York, the outgoing coordinator of the organization, who was standing nearby. “When we monitored right after, it had already thawed quite a bit.”

This rudimentary tool, offering a measure of depth from a single point in the earth, reveals an escalating problem across the far north. As climate change fuels increasingly frequent and severe fires in the planet’s northern latitudes, they’re accelerating the thawing of more and more permafrost. This allows the organic matter to break down and release powerful greenhouse gases that contribute to a spiraling climate feedback effect, propelling more warming, more fires, and the loss of still more permafrost.

Most dramatically, intensifying wildfires in Canada released more carbon than the nation’s combined fossil fuel emissions in 2023. As in Alaska, many of these megafires occur in vast remote areas where the policy is to let them burn so long as they don’t threaten human habitats. Yet if intensifying fires and warming are left unchecked, the world’s boreal forests and permafrost could increasingly transition from giant carbon sinks into massive sources of atmospheric carbon.

Now, international teams of researchers across the US, Canada, and elsewhere are scrambling to understand what’s at stake, financially as well as ecologically. They’re looking at preventive measures, like controlled burns, and studying the potential to rapidly detect and extinguish wildfires before they grow out of control. They’re even exploring what was once unthinkable: sending in human firefighters not to save lives or structures, but to protect one of our planet’s great stores of carbon.

“We need to figure out a better way to live with wildfire," says Brendan Rogers, a senior scientist at the Woodwell Climate Research Center, one of the main organizations driving the loosely collaborative research effort. “I do think that it can make a meaningful difference."

Woodwell, the University of Victoria’s Polis Institute for Ecological Governance, and the nonprofit Alaska Venture Fund are now partnering on a multimillion-dollar initiative known as North Fire to study and raise public awareness about the potential benefits of these interventions, MIT Technology Review can report.

The idea is complicated and controversial for a number of reasons. Wildfire is a natural and necessary component of healthy forest ecosystems. Preventing or suppressing fires across huge stretches of largely unmanaged Arctic-boreal forests and tundra would take vast resources. And it’s not yet clear how much of a difference such interventions would make in emissions.

Ultimately, the mere fact that researchers are considering such extreme interventions into natural systems is a grim reflection of the dangers we’ve placed ourselves in by continuing to generate more and more greenhouse-gas emissions each year. Those threats are forcing us to grapple with increasingly difficult questions that involve ever steeper trade-offs: What’s the best way to spend our finite resources and dwindling time to avoid the worst dangers of climate change? And when, if ever, is it okay to put people in possible danger to reduce broader risks to the world?
Emissions from forest fires have risen 60% around the world since 2001—but they’ve nearly tripled across the boreal forests in the far north.

This stretch of the globe is warming as much as four times faster than the rest of the planet, drying out the landscape. In addition, lightning strikes that set off fires have ticked up sharply as warmer air increases the convective energy in the atmosphere, driving the updrafts that trigger thunderstorms.

In that sense, humans have already interceded in these otherwise natural ecosystems by producing the greenhouse-gas emissions that are increasing temperatures, subjecting forests to fire patterns well outside healthy historic norms.

“To me, that outweighs the existential dread of ‘Should we or should we not intervene?” says Kate Hayes, an assistant professor at Western Washington University, who is working with Woodwell to study the emissions benefits of fire interventions. “We’ve already intervened, arguably. And so from here, it’s a little bit of a Band-Aid on a bullet wound.”

The permafrost that encircles the northern latitudes, underlying large stretches of Canada, Greenland, Siberia, Scandinavia, and other Arctic nations, stores around 1.5 trillion tons of carbon, much of which froze in place millennia ago. The steady global rise in temperature, however, has already shrunk the footprint of Arctic permafrost by about 12 % since 1850, with that loss rapidly accelerating during the last 50 years.

By 2100, fire-driven thawing of permafrost could release about the equivalent of nearly 80 billion tons of carbon dioxide, under high warming scenarios. That’s more than half the emissions that fires will release from the direct combustion of vegetation, according to a January study. And it would be on top of more than 400 billion additional tons that could be released through thawing from general warming over that period.

Despite its growing contributions to climate change, only a minority of the models that have informed the UN’s major climate reports to date include the gradual loss of permafrost through warming temperatures, and none incorporate the abrupt collapse and accelerated thaw that can often occur after fires and heat waves. In light of those phenomena and other powerful and undercounted climate feedback effects, we’re almost certainly underestimating how rapidly the planet will warm up, as scientists warned in a paper earlier this year.

These warming-driven emissions are a “massive blind spot,” says Brian Buma, a senior climate scientist at the Environmental Defense Fund and a coauthor of the paper, who is working to develop tools that could help fire agencies decide which fires to prioritize.

As escalating fire and permafrost emissions become significant additional contributors to climate change, some researchers have begun to explore what it might cost to take on the responsibility of preventing them, in much the way we’ve sought to cut the pollution from power plants, vehicles, and factories.

A 2022 paper in Science Advances, led by researchers at Woodwell and the Union of Concerned Scientists, found that making greater efforts to put out boreal fires could be a cost-effective climate solution—comparable to, or even cheaper than, addressing emissions by building wind turbines, solar farms, or carbon-sucking factories.

Those economic findings were instrumental in getting more researchers to take the idea of tackling fire emissions seriously, says Peter Frumhoff, a coauthor of the 2022 paper and now a senior science policy advisor at Woodwell.

For several years now, Woodwell researchers have been in discussions with forest managers, fire agencies, Indigenous communities, and other groups across Alaska to communicate the potential of this approach.

It hasn’t been an easy sell, given the constrained resources and tightly defined mission of the federal and state agencies responsible for combating fires in Alaska. The general policy there is to allow fires in remote territories to burn unless they present a direct danger to communities.

“Those agencies are tasked with protecting life and property now, and to a lesser extent natural resources,” says Randi Jandt, a fire ecologist at the Alaska Fire Science Consortium. “But they’re not tasked to save the world.”
There was one notable early success, however.

The Yukon Flats National Wildlife Refuge is an 11-million-acre patchwork of wetlands, forests, and bogs. The foothills sit above a particular type of frozen soil known as yedoma. It’s an especially deep, ice-rich, and carbon-dense form of permafrost, composed of massive wedges of silty, wind-blown sediments frozen during the late Pleistocene, which ended about 11,700 years ago. (It also presented ideal conditions for preserving mummified remains of woolly mammoths.)
“It took kind of the last ice age to accumulate,” Hayes says. “So there’s no rapid way to re-accumulate it. We can’t really put it back.”

In 2019, the region suffered a series of devastating fires that burned some 750,000 acres. After an Alaska Fire Science Consortium meeting at which Woodwell scientists highlighted the possible climate benefits of more aggressive fire suppression, the refuge's then manager, Jimmy Fox, began exploring the possibility of putting out blazes when they threatened that permafrost, whether or not they threatened human habitations.
The early reaction was not encouraging.
“You’re going to have people jumping out of airplanes with parachutes to save frozen woolly mammoths—and maybe dying from that?” he recalls being asked.

But eventually, he persuaded managers at the US Bureau of Land Management’s Alaska Fire Service to carry out a pilot project on a 1.6-million-acre section of the Yukon Flats. They agreed to try to put out fires there if they had the resources available and believed they could contain a blaze within 72 hours.
Woodwell and its partners agreed to study how that change affected permafrost loss and fire emissions, in the hope of making the case for similar programs elsewhere.
It wasn’t clear the pilot program would survive after Donald Trump was reelected, particularly once the DOGE initiative retroactively cut the public funding for that research collaboration.
But in February, the federal government formally preserved the program and broadened its rationale to include goals like protecting habitat diversity, water quality, and air quality.

One of Woodwell’s main tasks now is determining when and where fire agencies should step in. Crucially, excessive efforts to stamp out fires in the past have allowed the buildup of dry plant material that fuels more severe fires later.

“We’re not going after all fires all the time,” says Rogers over lunch in a sunny courtyard on the Stanford University campus, where Woodwell and EDF hosted a workshop on potential fire interventions in January. “We can’t do that. We don’t want to do that. We shouldn’t do that. So how do we prioritize our resources?”

Woodwell and its collaborators are working to answer that question by developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across interior Alaska. The plan is to eventually expand it across much of Canada as well.

These maps will highlight the locations of rich reserves of yedoma and other forms of permafrost, forecast where fires are most likely to break out in the next 10 to 15 years, and predict how they’re likely to behave and spread.
“Our ultimate goal is to get a layer that can tell us, if a fire were to occur, what areas are most vulnerable to high carbon emissions, permafrost thaw, permafrost degradation,” Rogers says.
In response to a question about potentially putting firefighters at risk, Rogers stressed in an email that it’s “a very serious issue that needs careful consideration.”

He added that early fire detection technologies, preventative fire stewardship practices, improved fire suppression planning and other measures can all help to reduce dangers to firefighters as well as communities.

Once areas of particular risk are identified, the first option is to take measures to prevent fires there, or at least to reduce the odds that they’ll become major ones. That generally entails using heavy equipment or intentional, controlled fires to clear away vegetation that could fuel new fires, or to create fire breaks that might check their spread.

Indigenous tribes carried out what’s known as cultural burning for thousands of years to reduce fire dangers, clear land for crops, and more. The practice was widely outlawed across North America beginning in the 1800s, though those rules have loosened in recent years.
Both cultural and prescribed fires, however, remain controversial because they can burn out of control. And even if they remain contained, the fires can still produce smoke that wafts into towns.

But rushing around to put out blazes after they’ve started will never get Alaska ahead of its surging wildfire problem, says Edward Alexander, cochair of the Gwich’in Council International, which represents the Indigenous Gwich’in peoples of the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, and Alaska.
“There’s not enough money in the world for this to be a chainsaw-and-ax problem,” he says. “This country is too big up here.”

Alexander, who also serves as senior Arctic lead at Woodwell, argues that Alaska should encourage much greater use of cultural burning to reduce the risk of conflagrations and the emissions that come with them.
“We need mild fire, not wildfire,” he says.

The North Fire initiative will include several additional pilot research projects, including an effort to study the potential for cultural burning to reduce climate and fire dangers near Fort Yukon, Alaska.

The plan is for a wildland firefighting crew operated by the Council of Athabascan Tribal Governments, a consortium in the Yukon Flats region, to carry out cultural burns there next spring, Rogers says.

Researchers at Woodwell and the University of Alaska, Fairbanks, will then collect and analyze data flammability, carbon levels, and permafrost over several years, in the hopes of learning more about what such interventions do.
Similarly, the Polis researchers at the University of Victoria plan to study how adding fuel breaks, by logging or switching to less flammable trees, alters fire risks in British Columbia.

The broad aim of the North Fire initiative is to accelerate research and expand community involvement “in a way that helps us scale this as a meaningful global natural climate solution on a rapid timeline,” says Erin Harrington, a partner at the Alaska Venture Fund, a philanthropy focused on environmental, economic development, and Indigenous issues.
Detecting fires from space

Other observers, including Jandt, believe the bigger opportunity to reduce fire emissions and preserve permafrost may lie in the “initial attack.” That means marshalling planes, tankers, and firefighters to stamp fires out at the first sign of them, before they’ve had the chance to turn into conflagrations.
Once fires reach a certain size, it takes much more time to contain them—and the job becomes far more dangerous.

Accelerating response times is one of the chief promises of the FireSat satellite constellation, which is expected to begin delivering fire data at least twice daily from around the world to Woodwell, a handful of fire agencies, and other early adopters by the end of this year. The system will eventually include more than 50 satellites circling the globe, equipped with high-resolution cameras and thermal sensors that can detect smaller, lower-temperature fires than existing satellite systems, down to as little as five by five meters (16 by 16 feet).

Currently, it can take days to spot fires. But once the full constellation is in place, likely in the early 2030s, FireSat should be capable of detecting and providing updated images of fires anywhere in the world every 20 minutes or less.

The first prototype satellite launched in 2025, and three operational ones went into orbit in July. The Earth Fire Alliance, the nonprofit that manages the constellation, expects to launch four more by the end of next year.

A number of similar systems are also coming online. German-based OroraTech has launched 18 of its fire-detecting satellites in the last year and a half. Similarly, Canadian agencies are planning to launch their own satellite constellation, dubbed WildFireSat, beginning in 2029.
But as these systems produce more and more detections across the globe, it’ll become increasingly essential to build tools that can filter through that information.

EDF is supporting and collaborating on several projects that could potentially help with that, and it ultimately intends to develop an AI-powered triage tool that could help fire agencies prioritize responses as FireSat and other fire-spotting tools come online.

"All of this is kind of like building the data ecosystem around FireSat, so that when they start popping out “fire start here, there, fire start here, fire start there,” we won’t be like, ‘Oh shit, there’s fires everywhere,’” Buma says. “We’ll have a framework. It won’t be perfect, obviously. We’ll have to improve it, but we’ll have the machinery to incorporate those data.”
But faster detections and decisions do only so much. Regions would still need to get firefighting personnel and resources to those fires fast enough to prevent them from burning out of control.

“Say we have the full FireSat constellation up and running, and it spots a fire that just broke out in one of these sort of high-priority, highly vulnerable areas,” I said to Rogers and Frumhoff during our conversation in that Stanford courtyard. “How might we deploy firefighting resources to a remote area fast enough for it to matter in that scenario?”
“I think the answer, unfortunately, is that it depends,” Rogers responded.

Ideally, he said, we would have fire management policies in place that allow for putting out fires with a high risk of producing climate-warming emissions. In addition, regions could install more firefighting personnel and resources across more operational centers, strategically placed in locations that allow them to get to those blazes fast.

Frumhoff stresses that Woodwell isn’t promoting any particular companies but says there are additional technologies “in the mix of conversations” that might help to prevent or rapidly put out fires as well.
Those possible approaches include seeding clouds to suppress lightning strikes and pre-positioning autonomous firefighting helicopters to respond rapidly to high-emissions-risk fires.

Sikorsky, a Lockheed Martin company, is developing and testing autonomous versions of the Black Hawk helicopter, equipped with thermal sensors and water tanks. It is collaborating with Rain Industries, a startup based in Alameda, California, that has developed software to track shifting conditions and steer unpiloted aircraft through the process of putting out wildfires.
The company says it has talked to fire agencies and the “broader Alaska fire community” about the potential use of its technology but declined to name any specific entities it has interacted with.

“The twin climate tipping points of the yedoma permafrost and the boreal forest, and the fact that it’s completely underresourced at the moment, from my perspective does make it an ideal use case for autonomous aircraft,” says Max Brodie, chief executive officer of Rain.
Advancing technologies can only do so much if governments’ fire prevention and suppression policies don’t prioritize preserving carbon.
And that will remain a hard sell given the costs of managing extensive areas of land that nations have historically left largely alone.

The 2022 Science Advances paper estimated that additional fire suppression efforts would cost about $12.63 per metric ton of prevented carbon dioxide emissions—a number that drops when the carbon in permafrost is taken into account, according to upcoming research.

But that would still add up to about $7 billion in additional spending this decade to keep Alaska’s fire emissions at their historical levels, and another $7 billion to $50 billion over the subsequent 30 years as fire severity continues to rise.
Frumoff stresses that those figures just reflect what the researchers found it would cost to preserve the status quo, which is not necessarily what the policy goal would be.

But widening the scope of where we put out fires will inevitably create a big added cost for fire agencies that are already notoriously underfunded in the US. While Alaska produces about half the nation’s wildfire emissions, it receives around 4% of federal firefighting funds.

The US Wildland Fire Service provided a prepared statement in response to an MIT Technology Review inquiry asking whether preserving carbon could or should become a priority in certain fire management decisions. The roundabout reply suggests that this isn’t the agency’s prime concern: “Firefighter and public safety are the top priorities for the U.S. Wildland Fire Service.”

Frumhoff says it’s possible that landowners or government agencies could eventually use carbon markets to defray some of the additional costs. Woodwell has also had multiple conversations with Alaska’s federal legislators about the value of preventing catastrophic wildfires and the need to increase the “total pot” of public funding, he says.

A few days after walking through the fire scar in Fairbanks, I drove slowly along a crumpled stretch of Stampede Road, just north of Denali National Park, where the underlying permafrost had melted without the aid of fire.
I arrived at a cramped wooden cabin to meet with Michelle Mack, a regents professor of ecosystem ecology at Northern Arizona University.

Mack studies how fire is altering ecosystems in the high northern latitudes as the region grows warmer and drier, and she sometimes collaborates with Rogers and other scientists working on the push to protect permafrost in other areas of research. But she’s unsure how much these interventions will accomplish as climate change continues.
“I’m an empiricist, and at this point, it’s not clear to me that the empirical evidence suggests that we can actually have any impact on these fires,” she says.

She expects there will be clear cases where we could and should act fast to put out fires and “keep carbon in the ground.” She points to the example of the 2007 Anaktuvuk River Fire, a massive tundra fire on Alaska’s North Slope that might have been extinguished with relative ease in its early days but was instead allowed to burn until the winter snows put it out nearly three months later. Over that time, it ripped across 400 square miles and, Mack’s research showed, released more than 2 million tons of carbon into the air.
“I feel like that’s the low-hanging fruit, something that doesn’t cost much—and that’s where the technology for detection I think is really important,” she says.
But she adds that fires in boreal forests can rapidly spread in unpredictable ways, frustrating efforts to quickly extinguish them even when they are spotted right away.

In addition, rapidly putting out a fire one season doesn’t necessarily reduce the fire risk for a given forest, so suppression may simply kick the “fire can” down the road—delaying but not preventing an inevitable loss of carbon, Mack says.

Her thinking more recently shifted “a little” after she came across an earlier modeling paper that showed some encouraging findings on the potential of early suppression to reduce the footprint of boreal fires. But she says that prevention through forest thinning, prescribed burns, and the introduction of less flammable deciduous trees to create “living fire breaks” is probably a more promising path than technology-augmented suppression.
“If we could solve this with a techno fix, that’d be great,” she says. “But what if we solved it with nature?”
Rogers, in an emailed response to Mack’s concern, said that the interventions they’re exploring, which do include both prevention and suppression, “can make a real difference.”

“I certainly agree that some fires are much easier to suppress via initial attack than others,” he wrote. “That said, until I see data showing me otherwise, I believe there is strong potential to bend the curve with management.”

EDF’s Buma acknowledges there are a number of unknowns, including how quickly agencies could act on faster detections from satellites—and how big the political obstacles will be to making necessary changes to fire management policies.
“We can’t overpromise what’s possible. We don’t know what’s possible,” he says. “It’s all new. But we’re in a new climate and have to consider trying new things.”
