items.title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
items.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.
items.author: James O'Donnell
paragraphs: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.

But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September.

The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us.

Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would.

Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.

These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn.

If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans.

The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.

How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions.

That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example.
Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do.

These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

items.title: Lush Apple, Cozy Vanilla, & The Scents We're Loving This October
items.description: Lush Apple, Cozy Vanilla, & More New October Fragrances
items.author: Karina Hoshikawa
paragraphs: Lush Apple, Cozy Vanilla, & More New October Fragrances

At Refinery29, we’re here to help you navigate this overwhelming world of stuff. All of our market picks are independently selected and curated by the editorial team. All product details reflect the price and availability at the time of publication. If you buy or click on something we link to on our site, Refinery29 may earn commission.
TATE BY TM TATE 01 Eau de Parfum

Pop star Tate McRae has officially entered the perfume chat with her debut fragrance, Tate 01. This aromatic woody scent opens with fresh bergamot and bright clary sage before unfolding into lush white florals and a warm, creamy dry-down of amber, tonka, and sandalwood.
D.S. & Durga Resurrected Corpse Flower Eau de Parfum

Inspired by perfumer and co-founder David Seth Moltz’s chance encounter with a funky corpse flower at the Brooklyn Botanic Garden, Resurrected Corpse Flower reimagines the unconventional bloom with notes of green olive, Madonna lily, tuberose, freesia, and deep bog cedar.
The Nue Co. Moon Rice Eau de Parfum

The newest addition to The Nue Co.'s lineup of wellness-focused functional fragrances comes in the form of Moon Rice, a creamy floral with smooth notes of cardamom milk, zingy bergamot, calming lavender, rice accord, and a base of amber, musk, and sheer woods.
Heretic Parfums Thornapple

Lush green leaves, warm saffron, and a crisp apple accord mingle with two of the year’s breakout scent trends: grounding tea and juicy plum. A base of frankincense, oakmoss, and musk adds a dark, earthy edge, making this the ultimate forbidden fruit.
Ôrəbella VANILLA'S TOUCH Body & Hair Perfume Mist
Bella Hadid’s latest Ôrəbella creation pairs light-as-air vanilla with fluffy marshmallow and romantic florals before settling into a warm, skin-close finish of soft woods and musk.
Skylar Fated Flame Eau de Parfum
The latest fragrance from Leah Kateb’s Skylar pairs decadent cherry purée and chocolate ganache with woody oud, creamy sandalwood, and warm amber.
Le Monde Gourmand L'Essence Shirin Eau de Parfum
Le Monde Gourmand’s newest fragrance, created in collaboration with influencer Cyrus Veyssi, is a floral musk that pairs juicy pomegranate with lush jasmine and a warm, sensual amber-musk base.

Lifestyle brand Sidia is making its debut in fine fragrance this month with The Strike, a portable, refillable scent atomizer that lets you choose among three of the brand’s signature scents: warm and cozy Braless, earthy Soaked, and sunny Midas.

items.title: Transitioning made me happy, but it came with a high price | Psyche Turning Points
items.description: I was 19 when I first considered becoming a trans woman. I grew up in a household of women: my parents divorced when I was four, so it was just me, my mother and four sisters. ‘Deepen that voice!’ my uncles constantly reproached me. ‘You’re too delicate! Don’t
items.author: André Aram
paragraphs: I was 19 when I first considered becoming a trans woman. I grew up in a household of women: my parents divorced when I was four, so it was just me, my mother and four sisters. ‘Deepen that voice!’ my uncles constantly reproached me. ‘You’re too delicate! Don’t walk like a girl!’ I’d realised from an early age that I was gay. In elementary school, there was a boy with whom I would hold hands in secret. One day we kissed; a teacher saw and scolded us. That’s when I began to understand this was wrong, though I didn’t know why.

My mother didn’t know how to deal with this. ‘I won’t accept a little faggot for a son,’ I heard her say countless times. She struggled with mental illness, including body dysmorphia, and rarely left the house; she thought people were laughing at her for being overweight. By the time I was eight, I was doing everything on my own – grocery shopping, going to the bank, taking the bus. During these errands, I’d sometimes stop at newsstands and admire the male bodies in magazines, fall in love with the princes in the cartoons.

Looking back, I realise that, for an effeminate, mixed-race, lower-middle-class boy on the outskirts of Brasília, there was always a predator lurking: a neighbour, a relative, someone with bad intentions. When I was 13, we started attending an evangelical church. There was no sense of belonging there either, for me; I was always seen as the guilty one. The pastor there would approach me and ask if I was homosexual.
‘The devil is preparing you for this,’ he warned. ‘You have to pray and fast.’

Once, I was at the home of a pastor who lived next to the church. We were counting flyers that would be distributed before a religious event. Night had fallen. The pastor went to the bathroom and returned in his underwear. Realising his intentions, I fled without saying a word. I left the church after that. That’s when I started spending time around the trans women in Brasília.

I would hang out with them in the industrial zone in Taguatinga, near the Coca-Cola factory, and in the red-light districts in the central parts of the city. Theirs was a world full of contradictions. They lived in houses owned by pimps, to whom they paid a daily fee to live on the properties and work in the streets. There was loud laughter and there was loud makeup – everything felt like a party. There were big egos and intense competition over looks, but food and wigs were freely shared. Once, when a trans woman returned home beaten by a client, the others came together to pay for her food, medicine and her share of the fee owed to the pimp.

By the time I was 16, I’d left home to live with a boyfriend. He was 16, too. Where we lived, in the gay ghettos, there were a lot of fights. But no one messed with me because they knew the trans women would defend me. When you’re young, you’re always looking for a sense of belonging you didn’t find in your own family. I found it in the trans women who accepted and welcomed me.

Some people experience body dysphoria from a very early age – what they see physically isn’t what they actually feel. For others, the possibility of being trans arises only later in life, when they can choose to be something other than who or what they are. I belong to the latter category: it was only after years of living alongside trans women that I began to realise I could be one, too.

My first attempt at transitioning was short-lived – three months into taking hormones, I stopped. My decision had less to do with my gender identity than the ways in which I thought changing it would foreclose possibilities for me. Simply put, I did not want to become a sex worker – often the only means of income for the trans women around me. It is a profession accompanied by a great deal of violence and psychological trauma; most trans women I knew used drugs to cope with that life. I liked their world, I liked being with them, but I didn’t like the situations they found themselves in.

Ten years later, after much reflection, I decided once more to transition. This time, I resolved to follow all the steps to fully become a woman. I began psychological counselling, then hormones under medical supervision. I’d already set aside the funds I’d need, through years of working at a beauty salon in an upper-middle-class neighbourhood in Brasília, a place specialising in hair extensions. The clients there were supportive, even if some found it strange. Some gave me earrings, makeup, clothes, even lingerie. Others asked whether I would now turn to sex work.

Within months, my body began to change. I was also studying nursing at the local university and when I returned for the second semester, I looked like a different person. When I got my breast implants, I was euphoric – I felt I would be a woman only after getting implants and wearing a dress. The other students complimented me, peppering me with questions. Some teachers ignored me; one insisted on calling me by my dead name. She’d never liked me, actually.
My social life changed drastically. People stop inviting you to birthdays and barbecues

As my body changed, I felt both fear and joy. My mother cried when she saw my breasts. I think they were tears of frustration but that didn’t bother me. I don’t think my mother ever stopped loving me – she worried only about the prejudice I would face. My sisters were happy that I was happy. I was happy: I was building a whole new self.

Maintaining a feminine appearance is expensive. Your hair has to be silky, straight and long, nails manicured, makeup flawless, clothes beautiful – not to mention the laser hair removal, hormone treatments and plastic surgeries. In order to ‘pass’ – that is, look more feminine so that society would be more accepting – I must have spent more than $25,000. Then, there are expenses you wouldn’t think to account for: occasionally, in order to avoid harassment, you can’t take the bus and you have to take a taxi. You even have to choose where you live carefully.

Despite all these efforts, my social life changed drastically. People stop inviting you to birthdays and barbecues – one friend told me she didn’t invite me because her relatives were evangelicals. She said she wanted to protect me from the possibility of being offended by them. Some began watching my every move, suspicious I would flirt with their boyfriends. It’s as if you’re no longer trustworthy; everything suddenly revolves around sexuality. Once, my friend and I were pelted with eggs on the street. Another time, I was at a nightclub and kissed a guy. Then a girl told him I was trans. He said he was going to the bathroom and would be back. I never saw him again.

After two years of living as a trans woman, I decided to reverse my transition. The truth is, there wasn’t a single day I wasn’t afraid for my life. For many people, gender transition is a vital necessity, but for me it wasn’t. It was a choice I’d made, and I’d made it happily, but it came with costs: the constant shadow of violence, estranged and murdered friends, the high price of upkeep.
I began to wonder whether it was worth going through all that just to be a woman.

For 18 consecutive years, Brazil has topped the global list of countries with the highest number of murders of trans people. Last year, there were 80 documented homicides of trans people. We wake up prepared for war every day. One friend – we called her ‘little whore’ because she was all of five feet tall, 22 years old and sweet – was seen on the street getting into a client’s car, but she never returned. We know she was murdered, but we don’t know how or why. Another, Paula Maia, became a quadriplegic after an attempt on her life, but what ultimately killed her was the industrial silicone she’d used to modify her body – a primitive, painful and irreversible procedure. Another named Julia died after being attacked by an older man who lived in the red-light districts; he would go out with some of the sex workers but had a habit of humiliating trans women: ‘You’re ugly, you’re fat, you’re not worth what you charge.’ Julia argued back once, so he stabbed her.
Life as a trans woman is far riskier than as a gay man
Nothing happened to him. I see him on the street sometimes because he lives near my salon.

I sought counselling for a while and began to ask myself: Why can’t I go back? Little by little, I began telling people about my decision. Some tried to dissuade me, others chastised me for being indecisive, while others, such as my evangelical family, readily supported me – to them, it was a sign of ‘liberation’. Almost everyone understood, however, that life as a trans woman is far riskier than as a gay man.

Some asked if I had become evangelical. This is common in Brazil, where the evangelical population is booming: people who detransitioned after converting, fed false promises that everything would be different for them after, or those who’d fallen into drug use or become homeless and were offered support only on the condition that they stop being trans. I’ve seen how that goes. For many people, religion is a pretext to gain social acceptance because it’s extremely difficult to deconstruct something you’ve built and suddenly declare: ‘I don’t want this anymore and I’m going to change.’ Not everyone has that courage.

I began saving up once more, this time to pay for the removal of my breast implants. If it’s expensive to become a trans woman, it’s also not cheap to stop being one. I’ve heard from others who would like to consider doing so but lack the money or job prospects to do so. A woman named Aline who lived in southern Brazil reached out to me at the time, saying she too wanted to detransition. But it was difficult for her as she’d already altered her jaw, nose and forehead.

It’s been 10 years since I stopped identifying as a trans woman. I was happy with my trans body, and I’m happy now too. It was an experience I wanted to have, and it changed my outlook on life. Trans life in Brazil can be very cruel, but it also offers a sense of belonging. It was important for me to have had that. When you actually live through it, you realise the price is high – some are willing to pay it, while others are not. Those who criticise me don’t understand this is my existence, my decision, and every human is unique.

items.title: The Renaissance gun, from diabolical device to popular militias | Aeon Essays
items.description: If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed i
items.author: Catherine Fletcher
paragraphs: If you were asked to think of a gun owner, then Lorenzo de’ Medici – the celebrated patron of Renaissance art – would probably not be the first person to come to mind. In fact, however, Lorenzo ‘the Magnificent’ owned five portable firearms, which are listed in his 1492 postmortem inventory. Guns and gunpowder were controversial. In art and literature, they were labelled the Devil’s work, and were perceived as fundamentally unchivalrous. Yet within half a century, by the early months of 1539, Lorenzo’s descendant Duke Cosimo de’ Medici had 91 firearms in his Florentine storerooms. Somehow, in the courts of late-Renaissance Italy, the gun had become an acceptable, even valued, weapon.

Beyond the palazzi of the peninsula’s towns and cities, guns were also making inroads into more ordinary lives. There were no standing armies in the 16th-century Italian states. Their wars were fought through temporary mobilisations, and with considerable help from companies of mercenaries. Yet as the 1506 provision that established the Florentine militia made clear, ‘little hope’ could be placed ‘in foreign and hired arms’. Far better to establish a new magistracy with ‘full authority and power’ to enlist men from Florentine territory, at least 10,000 of them. One in 10 of these men were to be equipped with firearms, and 500 handguns (schioppetti) should be kept in the Palazzo della Signoria (the city hall, now known as the Palazzo Vecchio) along with ‘such money as should be necessary for the schioppetti’, presumably to purchase gunpowder and shot. Three or four companies (bandiere) entirely of schioppettieri might also be established.

This militia, most often noted for the role of Niccolò Machiavelli in its foundation, was to be organised after the fashion of the Germans, in whose cities there was a centuries-old tradition of civic defence and a duty on every male citizen to maintain suitable arms for the purpose. In fact, one of the Florentine militia’s early constables was German (a Giovanni Tedesco); another (Giliberto Spagnolo) came from Spain, a country making the running in the use of small arms on the battlefield. Giovanni Tedesco arranged target practice for his company, which from 1508 was extended more generally among the militia, with exercises taking place on a monthly basis.

Militias were not new but, by the 1490s, large-scale foreign military intervention on the Italian peninsula was giving a new impetus to their development, as was the growing importance of infantry in the military context. In Friuli, where Venetian lands bordered Ottoman territory, the militia were using handguns from the 1490s, and city guards across the Italian peninsula were soon provided with guns too. The growth of militias was the single most important factor in the proliferation of firearms in 16th-century Italy. This is too early a period for the kind of autobiographical writing that would tell us what these men made of the process, but there was certainly ample encouragement to become familiar with firearms and acquire shooting skills.

The backdrop to these developments was the decades of war in which France and Spain contended for hegemony on the Italian Peninsula. In the 1480s, while pitching his services to the duke of Milan, Leonardo da Vinci, highlighting his potential as a military engineer, wrote:

I have also plans of mortars most convenient and easy to carry with which to hurl small stones in the manner almost of a storm; and with the smoke of this cause great terror to the enemy and great loss and confusion.

By the turn of the century, Spanish arquebusiers – named for the long, wooden-stocked gun with which they were armed – were doing precisely that on the battlefields of Italy. As the conflicts of 1494-1559 rolled on, the rulers of the peninsula’s multiple states promoted shooting in the interests of civic defence and military preparedness and, as they did, their own use of firearms shifted too.

The Medici were not the only leading family of Renaissance Italy to take an interest in this new military technology. In 1538, the duke of another Italian city-state, Urbino, described a novel firearm as ‘very dear to me’. Such appreciation, however, ran counter to the dominant image of guns in the period’s literature. Leonhard Fronsperger, once a captain of the ducal armoury in Munich, wrote of gunpowder as ‘indispensable’, but also as ‘horrible’ and ‘unmanly’. Ludovico Ariosto’s epic poem Orlando Furioso (1532) described guns as a ‘foul and pestilent discovery’, weapons through which ‘no more shall gallantry, no more shall valour prove their prowess’. Only in edgier texts, like the swashbuckling memoirs of the goldsmith and sculptor Benvenuto Cellini, did anyone hint that guns were fun. ‘Frightened’ by a plague that hit Rome in the early 1520s causing thousands of deaths, Cellini ‘began to seek relief in a sport that I found very enjoyable’. In between sketching the city’s ancient ruins, he shot pigeons. He developed his own gunpowder recipe, and boasted of his ‘really good marksmanship’, claiming to be able to shoot ‘200 yards point-blank’. This is probably exaggerated, but just as relevant is Cellini’s explanation that, by getting him out into the fresh air to go hunting, and combating his ‘naturally melancholy disposition’, his gun ‘brought me more gain than loss’.

The textual enthusiasm of both Cellini and the duke of Urbino finds a material counterpart in a growing culture of luxury weapons. The aesthetics of these high-end guns helped firearms fit into a court culture that valued beauty and craftsmanship. They were decorated with classical gods, Christian figures and mottoes, and images of the hunt, while the novelty value of combination weapons such as spears with miniature guns attached appealed to the Renaissance sense of fun.

Records of gun ownership in elite households, too, tell a different story from the literary sources. It is at court that wheellock guns – a groundbreaking technology that allowed concealed carry – first leave traces. Leonardo’s sketches of their mechanisms (probably developed in Germany) can be seen in the Codex Atlanticus. Expensive, convenient and modern, wheellocks seem to have become a status symbol. The standard military firearm of this period, the matchlock, was fired by means of a lighted cord (the match) that ignited the powder when the gun was triggered. But the wheellock was a self-lighting mechanism that avoided the need for a lighted match. It was a more complex and therefore more expensive technology, and could be unreliable (probably especially if produced on the cheap). On the other hand, wheellocks had advantages in hunting, avoiding as they did the glow and smell of the burning match cord which might alert prey to a hunter’s presence.
Designs echoed court imagery: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, biblical figures

By the start of 1539, Duke Cosimo de’ Medici owned four wheellock handguns made in the German style that he (or more likely his bodyguards) took with him when he travelled. Not a decade on, a wheellock appeared in the first portrait of a European ruler with a handgun: Titian’s equestrian portrait of the victorious Emperor Charles V after the Battle of Mühlberg, in which Charles is shown ‘in the manner in which he went against the rebels’, that is, in the garb of the wheellock-toting Spanish cavalry.

The aesthetic qualities of high-end firearms helped guns blend into the wider courtly environment. Designs echoed imagery common to the court: hunting scenes, battles, motifs from ancient history and myth, or biblical figures like Judith. A wheellock pistol made in Germany and dated 1548 features a figure of the Roman heroine Lucretia along with a Christian motto and image of the Crucifixion. By this time, guns were finding new uses in Europe’s religious wars: far from the Devil’s weapon, they were a means of asserting true Christianity against the heretics.

Back at court, novelty weapons such as the match-fired combination pollaxe and gun in the Royal Armouries, or the boar-spear with two small guns attached given to Cosimo de’ Medici, engaged with a fashion for wider theatrical and festival machines aimed at provoking wonder in their audience. These firearms functioned as marketing devices, promoting their makers – and perhaps also the cities or states of their makers – as potential providers too of the thousands of weapons that might be commissioned for use in war. A striking indication of their acceptability in elite culture comes in 1553, when Mantuan officials began to make ceremonial presents of firearms to the city’s duke in place of the crossbows they had previously given. That the gun could now appear in these ritual contexts shows it had truly arrived.

In wider society, luxury decoration was out of reach, but other factors favoured an expansion of gun ownership. Florence was not the only state to establish or revive a civic militia. In the context of long-running on-off war, it made sense for rulers across Italy to mobilise citizens and equip them with up-to-date weapons. Alongside requirements for militia drill went contests to incentivise the acquisition of shooting skills. Farmers found guns useful for pest control; hunters used them too. Thus, in the 1520s and beyond, more and more Italian states formalised or expanded their militia. Giovanni Moro, a Venetian official who had previously handled military supplies, proposed in 1525 the formation of a citizen militia of 12,000 men, of whom two-thirds would use firearms; these men would receive powder and lead for practice, and a contest would be held three times a year to encourage them. This would be, said Moro, to the ‘honour and utility’ of Venice, and of ‘great benefit’ when it came to conserving Venetian territory.

Such ambitious plans didn’t always succeed, as two cases from Tuscany show. Jacopo Pessina’s detailed study of military organisation in the Republic of Siena estimates that in the last 30 years of the republic (1525-55), between 20 and 33 per cent of adult men served in the militia, with each 500-strong battalion including 150-200 arquebusiers. A report from 1543, however, suggested that the militia was not fit for purpose, lacking not only sufficient men but also the necessary firearms and helmets. The case of Florence, moreover, where the last republican government of 1527-30 fell to the Spanish-backed Medici party after a long siege, shows the limits of a city militia in the face of a foreign army. Anticipating attack, the republican government issued new ordinances for the militia, instituting training in the use of arquebuses, and shooting contests. During the siege of 1530, artisans from shoemakers to cutlers were equipped with arquebuses. They did not, however, prevail against the much better-resourced Spanish army. Still, governments across Italy continued to expand their militia, which made firearms increasingly available to men of all social ranks.
‘Every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’

If militia service provided one route to familiarity with firearms, so did the related rise of shooting contests. In 1506, Venice introduced a competition to encourage the development of handgun skills among the archers serving on its naval galleys. In 1518, the first prize was 16 arms-lengths of damask fabric, worth 32 ducats, along with 6 ducats in cash. In 1520, the Republic of Lucca instituted a thrice-yearly shooting contest in order to ensure that its citizens were prepared for defence, the founding decree urging them to prefer ‘death over the loss of dear liberty and the reduction of their fatherland to servitude’. Prizes included a silver cup worth almost 20 ducats, and six arms-lengths of damask worth 5 ducats. Soldiers’ pay could be less than 30 ducats a year, so these were generous rewards. Contests, however, were not only about financial incentives. They were also about establishing an acceptable social image for the firearm, just as the iconography of luxury weapons had done at court. The language of the Lucca decree, for example, offered a new and more positive discourse of the gun, as a weapon for the defence of liberty.

Hunting was another context in which guns became familiar not just for elites but more widely. In 1552, for example, a cowherd named Vincenzo obtained a licence from the Bologna authorities that allowed him to carry arms, including a gun for the purpose of hunting. It came with the standard caveat that the weapon must not be carried in churches, at festivals or in markets. These were busy environments where an accidental misfire had higher risks than out in the countryside, and where a generalised ban on arms-bearing (staff weapons such as pikes were also included) made policing more straightforward. Such wide access to guns, however, was a matter of concern. The anonymous author of a proposition for international gun control observed, probably in the late 1570s, that if the Italian princes did not take action soon, then ‘there will be no place nor state where people are safe, given that every low herdsman or shepherd you meet in the countryside today has a wheellock arquebus over his shoulder’.

As guns became more common, so did their appearance in the criminal records. By 1600, firearms had become the predominant weapon used to commit homicide in Bologna. That said, they still accounted for only a third of offences, and in interpreting the figures we should bear in mind the relative lethality of guns when compared with other weapons. In fact, across the broad range of gun crime, it was still relatively rare to come across cases where guns were directly used in planned homicide. More commonly, they were used to threaten: the ideal outcome for the highwayman who shouts: ‘Your money or your life!’ is to ride away with the money without firing a shot.

Many of the historic investigations feature possession of illegal guns and/or their use to intimidate. In a 1554 case near the northern Italian city of Brescia, Valerio Soncino and a gang of 20 men ‘armed with various weapons, including arquebuses’, scaled the walls of a property belonging to Valerio’s brother Annibale, and ‘with various threats’ forced two of his stewards to bring them carts, which they loaded up with goods, stealing in addition cattle and a horse. The robbers got only five miles, however, before they were halted by some villagers who had got wind of what was happening and sounded the alarm. In the ensuing violence, two men and a woman among the villagers were injured. Here, the primary use of the guns was to frighten people into doing as they were told, not to kill them. That is not to say, however, that the proliferation of firearms was not risky. Criminal records from Bologna describe a case in 1575 in which an elderly woman named Giovanna was killed by a man named Pierantonio Fangarezzo; Fangarezzo had been looking over an arquebus (perhaps an early variety of flintlock) to see how it worked when it accidentally went off.
In some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership

People engaged in, or considering, political violence also used firearms. The distinction between criminal and political activity was not always straightforward. The system of exile in the Italian states – in which offenders were banned from their home territory and had their property confiscated – often made banditry an attractive option (hence the overlap between the concepts in Italian, where the word bandito is also used for an exile). Civic authorities were particularly keen to police weapon ownership when it posed a risk to the regime. The early years of Medici ducal rule in Florence (formally established in 1532) saw numerous confiscations of illegal weapons: Girolamo di Filippo Bonciani and Francesco di Piero Serragli, for example, fell foul of the law after an arquebus was found under the straw of their former stable. Some of these weapons were probably planted by city officials, but opponents of the regime might reasonably have decided to arm themselves in case of an uprising (for which there were several precedents).

Dissidents in Brescia (a subject city of Venice) also obtained weapons: testimony from 1539 shows how one alleged firearm offender, Antonio Maria, was accused of saying several times that ‘he desired nothing more than that the Emperor and the King of France should make an accord against our Venetian lords, and that he hoped to come with them to sack Brescia.’ Antonio Maria was further accused of ‘continually keeping in his house exiled men of a bad sort, who go out killing on the streets’; he had in his house around 25 guns of different types. While we typically learn about these cases from regime records, by reading between the lines it becomes clear that at least in some notionally criminal cases there was also a political motivation for gun ownership.

People in northern and central Italy owned guns for several reasons: to participate in militia service, for hunting and livestock control, and for criminal activity. Some of this ownership was purely practical: a gun would more reliably than the alternatives kill the fox eating your chickens. Some of it had political motivations, whether to defend the liberty of one’s own fatherland or to oppose a tyrannical overlord. By the middle of the 16th century, a lot of people had guns. It is challenging to establish quite how many. Based on population estimates and numbers enrolled in the militia, the historians Michael Mallett and John Hale estimated that one in 15 rural households in Venetian territory would have had a firearm following the establishment of the militia in the later 1520s: ‘the government’, they observed in Military Organisation of a Renaissance State (2009), ‘was calculatedly accepting a risk to public order’. By 1540, the ruler of Modena required that one in three countryside households should have a gun. These calculations concern militia service, however, and other people may have bought guns second-hand from soldiers, or won them via gambling.

Later in the century, larger cities had shops where guns might be mended and probably also purchased. A 1559 proclamation issued in Bologna in anticipation of riots declared that ‘shopkeepers, who sell those polearms and arquebuses, must store them in their shops in such a way that they are not ready to use’. There is no reason to think that the anonymous author who complained of wheellock-toting shepherds was greatly exaggerating the extent of proliferation.
Guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership

Certain moments in wartime no doubt accelerated access to firearms. Besides the 1529-30 Siege of Florence, records of the defensive provisions in Ferrara of 1552 (when the city was likewise preparing for a possible siege) show that, out of 520 households equipped with armour, pikes, arquebuses and morions, more than half (270) had a gun. Included in this list are 18 female heads of household, of whom six had guns. This raises the question of how many women were gun-owners more generally. The answer seems to be rather few. Sieges were emergency situations in which gender norms might temporarily be suspended, such as when the women of Siena took responsibility for repairs to the city walls. Outside the wartime context, Joe Tryner’s study of court records in Bologna turned up only a single example of a woman with a firearm, and nothing in my wider survey of source material has suggested that was untypical.

In contrast, guns did come to be associated with masculinity. In The Fruit of Liberty (2013), Nicholas Scott Baker argued that the siege of 1529-30 was a particular turning point for elite identity, redefining notions of masculinity from those associated with practices of civic governance to something more ‘rugged, militaristic’. This was particularly apparent in changing clothing styles, to which the bearing of new types of arms might be added. Focusing on Florence after 1537, in Masculinity, Arms and Armour (2020), Victoria Bartels identifies guns as one factor in shifting performances of masculinity, noting that they increased the danger attached to ‘routine bouts of aggression’ that had traditionally been employed to settle disputes between men. In the context of the Italian Wars (and specific local conflicts within them), guns had a role to play in changing ideas about gender, both in general and with reference to images of rulership. This is confirmed in the account of Benvenuto Cellini, whose self-aggrandising narrative of his participation in the Italian Wars includes a comment he made to a companion, Alessandro del Bene, to persuade him to stick around and shoot back at an invading army during the 1527 Sack of Rome: ‘Now you’ve brought me here, we must show that we’re men.’

Over the course of the 16th century, familiarity with firearms grew. It was increasingly expected that men would be able to use a gun: the expansion of militias was a key factor here alongside direct soldiering experience. The acquisition of skills in shooting was positively encouraged through civic contests with generous prizes. Rhetoric about the importance of guns for civic defence and for the maintenance of honour and liberty offered a counterweight to more negative images of gunpowder weapons as diabolical, unchivalrous or impious. Guns were useful for protection of livestock from predators as well as for hunting more generally. In turn, their ready availability also made them accessible for use by bandits, during vendettas and indeed for political violence. However, their lethality shifted the dynamics of violent encounters: so effective were guns as a threat that in some cases they may have prompted victims to give up without a fight. On the other hand, with increasing proliferation came an increased risk of both accidents and casual use in interpersonal violence. Yet not all gun ownership was enthusiastic. Some applicants for arms licences evidently felt constrained to carry guns in self-defence, and cultural ambivalence about these weapons remained long after they became common objects.
As firearms became more familiar, it was as much a decision not to be a gun owner as to acquire the new technology.

items.title: Step inside this minimalist Nigerian beach house for a taste of lagoon living
items.description: The sculptural, white volumes of this Nigerian beach house effortlessly nod to the white sands beyond, as it sits idyllically placed on the coastline of Ikaare Island, off the Lagos lagoon. The project, designed by architect, curator and past Wallpaper* Awards
items.author: Ellie Stathaki
paragraphs: The sculptural, white volumes of this Nigerian beach house effortlessly nod to the white sands beyond, as it sits idyllically placed on the coastline of Ikaare Island, off the Lagos lagoon. The project, designed by architect, curator and past Wallpaper* Awards nominee for Best Private House 2023, Tosin Oshinowo, blends crisp modernity, local design language and a site-specific approach; welcome to OA House.
Explore a new Nigerian beach house by Tosin Oshinowo

The project is a private retreat, a four-bedroom Nigerian beach house, conceived specifically around its seaside setting. The entire home's orientation - from windows to the outdoor areas, including a generous swimming pool deck - is designed to look out towards the plot's clean vistas of the Atlantic Ocean.

The same goes for the house's heart, its living space, which opens up to the outdoors and was approached as an 'open, breezy pavilion,' the architect explains. A hot tub and outdoor seating areas all cleverly, slowly create a 'gradual transition from the house to the shoreline,' Toshinowo adds.

The architecture is 'deliberately restrained.' This brings a welcome freshness, as it sits across the minimalist landscape - white sands, green palms and blue sea. It also creates a pared-down, flexible and calming backdrop for living and relaxing for its residents.

This simplicity becomes a key feature, defined by simple, smooth, matte off-white walls, timber floors and an aqua-green pool. The region's bright sun and distinctive vegetation frame the volumes' presence on the beach.

The ground floor hosts the main living spaces, opening up towards the water views. Bedrooms are also located on this level, but placed towards the plot's rear (yet still facing the pool) for privacy and a more cocooning feeling, facing away from the vastness of the ocean.
Upstairs, more bedrooms feature their own private terraces, offering moments of contemplation as residents can take in the coastal landscape.
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

'This project is particularly special because its narrow site became an opportunity to create an engaging visual transition through the property. The house remains true to our minimalist aesthetic, with a calm, cohesive palette of subtle off-white tones across the floors, walls, and exterior ceilings, complementing the surrounding landscape and the aqua colour of the pool,' Oshinowo says.

'No two homes are ever the same when designed for private clients. Residential architecture lets us explore the extraordinary diversity of possibilities within the world’s most fundamental architectural typology, shaped by each client's individuality, lifestyle, and relationship with place.'

Ellie Stathaki is the Architecture & Environment Director at Wallpaper*. She trained as an architect at the Aristotle University of Thessaloniki in Greece and studied architectural history at the Bartlett in London. Now an established journalist, she has been a member of the Wallpaper* team since 2006, visiting buildings across the globe and interviewing leading architects such as Tadao Ando and Rem Koolhaas. Ellie has also taken part in judging panels, moderated events, curated shows and contributed in books, such as The Contemporary House (Thames & Hudson, 2018), Glenn Sestig Architecture Diary (2020) and House London (2022).

items.title: Can a chic new London bar make pétanque cool?
items.description: London Fields might best be known as an after-hours destination for dive-bar martinis and small plates, but Circle13 is aiming to bring a new dimension to the area’s social offering. Recently opened by winemaker and cocktail veteran Marc Sarton Du Jonchay (A B
items.author: Lisa Wright
paragraphs: London Fields might best be known as an after-hours destination for dive-bar martinis and small plates, but Circle13 is aiming to bring a new dimension to the area’s social offering. Recently opened by winemaker and cocktail veteran Marc Sarton Du Jonchay (A Bar with Shapes for a Name, New York’s Gage & Tollner) and former international pétanque player Monty Quaia, the space – taking residence in one of Mentmore Terrace’s railway arches – aims to bring the more than 100-year-old French sport to East London, along with an equal focus on Basque cuisine and low and no-ABV highballs.

'Pétanque has always had the reputation of being for older people, and that’s partly true but it’s also slightly unfair to the game because there are lots of subcultures playing and making it their own,' says Quaia. 'London Fields is already one of the hubs of pétanque in London. We're convinced that the future of the game is making it a bit younger, a bit more fun, and appealing to people like us and our friends.'

In keeping with this outlook, Circle13 has been designed with a thoroughly modern aesthetic in mind. Helmed by experiential designer Joseph Stone, whose work spans high-end residential design and product launches for brands including Google and Nike, its interiors have been curated to reflect the visuals of pétanque itself, where silver balls are thrown onto pitches made of gravel or grass.

'The image we’ve based everything on is as though you’re looking down at pétanque balls on a gravel surface. All of the materials have an earthy backdrop with steel cut through; the back of the bar has a sandy tile, but then the bar slices through it,' explains Stone. 'We’ve taken the elements of pétanque and expanded them, riffed off them, and tried to create a contemporary take on them all.'

Though gaming bars are increasingly rife in the city, Circle13 have approached their brand with a notably different ethos. 'The competitive socialising [scene] is great because having an activity makes it less about excessive drinking. But my biggest gripe is that they're generally quite tacky and the activity isn't coming from people that care about it, so it always feels a bit inauthentic,' says Quaia. Instead, the core mantra of Circle13 is “rebellious simplicity”. 'Petanque is so simple and it refuses to be more complicated, so we wanted everything to reflect that,' he continues.

Spatially, that means creating areas – a front seating space with cocktail tables, a bar area with high stools, pétanque pitches both indoors and out, and a secondary arch for events – that work individually but have a 'porosity' between them. 'When you're having a drink in the front area, there are screen breaks [around the pétanque pitch] at head height so you can see the game through them. Then we also worked with our friend Darran Prior from There’s Light on the expanded lighting design. We've tried to hero each area, illuminating the bar so it’s focused on groups of two, and making sure the pétanque pitches have a really nice diffused light so they have a kind of amphitheatre energy,' explains Stone.

'Pétanque can really be quite fun and chic so the idea is that you should have your sexiest picture in the pétanque pitch with the screens around it, with the lighting above when it's soft,' laughs Quaia. 'We want it to be on everyone's Hinge profile and for it to be known for being the place to get you a nice photo taken.'
Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox.

The space has been designed in a modular fashion, with most features – from the screens around the pétanque pitch to the bar set-up in their second events arch – able to be rearranged depending on the night. Situated down a side road of E8, the frontage of the building has been kept open and welcoming, with floor-to-ceiling glass that allows the warm light of the interior to invite people in. 'We could have easily gone for the speakeasy feel, where you have a door and a single light and, as you go in, the world opens up in front of you. But because of it already being an industrial-feeling street, having that bigger aperture into the space was really important,' says Stone.

Staff uniforms are equally as considered, with plans for an adjacent merch line in place. A former tailor at Paul Smith, Quaia wanted to focus on 'streetwear with a sports background', working with Lithuanian streetwear brand Püga73 to develop a capsule collection of four pieces. 'Petanque has gone through many different phases, from the south of France rich guy with chinos and cigars, into something sporty with tracksuits, but none of them really spoke to us as modern Londoners,' he says.

The 'rebellious simplicity' also extends to their food and drink menu, headed up by Du Jonchay and chef Sean Donnelly. From the kitchen, Basque-centric pintxos are designed for snacking and sharing, featuring a variety of skewers, toasts and croquetas. Their pork belly and date skewer is a best-selling mix of savoury and sweet, while slices of home-baked Basque cheesecake make up their sweet offering.

Though their drinks menu still features ‘hard’ drinks, including a negroni sour and a mezcal toreador – a twist on a margarita using apricot – Circle13 have purposefully prioritised a less potent drinking culture. Here, non-alcoholic drinks are placed front and centre, with the option to add alcohol as a secondary concern. They’re purposefully kept at a very reasonable price point too: non-alcoholic cocktails are all priced at £6, with low-ABV highballs and spritzes coming in at £8.50.

'If you're not drinking, generally everything is based on non-alcoholic spirits which are more expensive in some cases than the boozy version. It makes no sense to us when there are already so many drinks in the world that don't have alcohol in them and are delicious,' Quaia reasons. 'We want it to highlight some of the ridiculousness of the industry, where £20-plus drinks and £8 pints are becoming increasingly more common.'

It all combines to create a venture that feels quietly radical, where a love of pétanque has brought about a new kind of bar, and a different way to socialise. 'We’re going to be launching different programs. We want to have Tuesday takeovers with different young chefs from Michelin kitchens, giving young people a chance to be creative and do something in the same way that we've been given a chance to open the space,' says Quaia. 'Rather than just trying to sell pétanque as a sport, we want it to be a social experience.'
Circle13, 369-370 Mentmore Terrace, London E8 3SD

items.title: Yes, Stone Island Just Made Six of the Same Jacket
items.description: Streetwear, as a culture, has a funny relationship with craft. As a scene, it is still very much so beholden to trends and their cycles, leaving the finer (or nerdier) points of garment construction to be reserved for the “heads.”
items.author: Maya Kotomori
paragraphs: Streetwear, as a culture, has a funny relationship with craft. As a scene, it is still very much so beholden to trends and their cycles, leaving the finer (or nerdier) points of garment construction to be reserved for the “heads.”

Stone Island’s first NO SEASONS collection since 1994 is a meditation on the kind of material obsession often overlooked by the masses. (No, Stoney isn't a "streetwear" label, but its clothes are synonymous with street-level cool and what is streetwear if not for everyone?) Initiated by founder Massimo Osti in 1989, Stone Island's NO SEASONS series is exactly how it sounds; clothing means to last beyond whatever may be en vogue at the time.

To the layperson, it may look like Stone Island just released six identical grey jackets. But Stone Island is defined by nuance and most importantly, material. Up close, NO SEASONS makes much more sense.

Rendered in varying interpretations of the brand’s proprietary Piombo — a prismatic grey tone — each jacket becomes an example of the brand’s textile nerdery and garment dyeing wizardry that solidifies Stoney in the eyes of the roadman as well as the “head.”

From pressure-dyed polyester to glossy coated nylon, each of these NO SEASONS jackets is shaped by a history of experimentation and a borderline obsessive devotion to refining the details. Put simply: the flex isn’t the silhouette, it’s the stuff you may not even see at first, but will definitely feel.
The original NO SEASONS project ran from 1989 to 1994. What made now the right moment to revisit this concept?

Stone Island Design Team: The modernity of Massimo Osti’s approach to design is still striking. We wanted to refer to what he had already developed while working with current material evolutions. Each NO SEASONS piece is meant to continue a conversation between convention and experimentation at the core of Stone Island.
The collection centers around a single jacket expressed through six different fabrications. Why was it important to focus on a single silhouette?

Despite sharing the same aesthetic, the jackets have completely different personalities and characteristics, achieved through compositions, finishes, dyeing processes and constructions that emphasize the specific qualities of each material.
All six jackets are presented in the same color. And why Piombo?

The initial idea of using all the same color was to focus attention on the details of the garment, and each different material. The final products are not actually the same color, but a more chromatic result achieved through the different dyeing processes that correspond to the specific fabric types we used.

We initially thought that the most iconic color of all could be black. However, we realized that choosing a Piombo tone would better emphasize the different materials and their different levels of absorption. The final product is something specific to our dyeing processes.
Each fabrication has a distinct history within Stone Island. How did the team decide which six fabrics would represent No Seasons today?

We wanted to select iconic materials for the brand that could communicate different aspects of Stone Island's material research and history. The six are Tela Resinata, Nylon Prismatico, Mussola Prismatica, Raso Gommato, Panno, Nylon Crinkle, and David.

Tela Resinata is an evolution of Tela Stella, the only material used for the first Stone Island collection in '98. The fabric is coloured in a pieced form using pigments and then garment-washed to create an uneven appearance. Nylon Prismatico evolves Mussola Prismatica into a new nylon-based version, maintaining the highly glossy appearance of the surface. The Raso Gommato, one of our most versatile materials, has been renewed with a new type of transparent matte polyurethane coating, which we then garment-dyed.

Panno evolves the military wool fabrics used across numerous past collections through the special KDf treatment, which allows for a more contemporary use with raw-cut edges. It was selected for its mixed wool and nylon composition, which gives it an authentic yet contemporary appearance. Nylon Crinkle has become an essential material in our collections due to its versatility and functionality; it’s intended to be an everyday wear piece.

Lastly we have David, which is such an iconic material. We also wanted to complement the other cotton, nylon and wool fabrications with a polyester garment, which has always posed a challenge with the complexities of its dyeing process. We also wanted to emphasize the versatility of this material by adding a detachable inner layer with the rope system, as we consider David to be an all-season material that can be used all year long.
Given the dramatically different constructions, what were the biggest challenges in achieving a consistent Piombo expression? Were there any surprises?

Although we are now highly experienced in managing polyester dyeing, it is always complex to achieve a specific color nuance with the David fabric. The pressure-dyeing process at 130°C requires specific dyes and adjustments in order to reproduce the desired tones. Piombo is also a complex color for the dyeing process, as all our dye recipes are composed of three pigments combined to create a new, unique color. If not properly controlled, the result can easily skew more red or blue than the desired tone.

Our Nylon Prismatico material has a unique color absorption: intense, full and glossy, created by the specific grooved structure of the external polyurethane layer. Due to the brushed hand of the material, the resulting color effect is unique and particularly special to us. Raso Gommato absorbs different color nuances on the external cotton satin face and on the internal polyurethane side, which takes on a deeper and more opaque color tone due to the new transparent rubber coating.
What did success look like?
We always like each garment to retain and respect its own characteristics. Although the overall aesthetic may appear consistent, there are small details and adjustments specific to each piece.
What does NO SEASONS reflect about Stone Island’s modern approach to material research and garment development?

We hope it communicates our constant research into functionality and our obsessive focus on product rather than trends. We look at function, research and good product design with obsession, never with nostalgia for the past, but always with the aim of developing toward the future.

items.title: Киты-бутылконосы, возможно, заботятся друг о друге, когда болеют
items.description: Биологи выяснили, что киты-бутылконосы поддерживают друг друга при болезнях и голоде
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: Биологи выяснили, что киты-бутылконосы поддерживают друг друга при болезнях и голоде

Северные бутылконосые киты поддерживают более тесные социальные связи, когда голодают или болеют. К такому выводу пришла группа исследователей под руководством Хэла Уайтхеда из Университета Далхаузи в Галифаксе (Канада), пишет New Scientist.

Открытие стало неожиданным, так как у млекопитающих социальные контакты обычно связывают с лучшим состоянием здоровья. Наблюдения согласуются с описаниями поведения этих животных, оставленными ранними китобоями. В отчёте 1882 года командир китобойного парохода Eclipse Дэвид Грей указал, что стадо не покидает раненого сородича, пока тот жив.

Северные бутылконосы (Hyperoodon ampullatus) относятся к малоизученному семейству клюворылых китов, обитают в изолированных районах океана и большую часть времени проводят в глубоких погружениях за кормом. Поэтому изучать этот вид сложно.

Команда Уайтхеда наблюдает за локальной популяцией северных бутылконосов с 1980-х годов. Эта группа держится над глубоким подводным каньоном. За 37 лет учёные накопили базу фотографий, сделанных в моменты, когда животные поднимались к поверхности. Особей различают по отметинам на плавниках, что даёт возможность отслеживать их жизнь на протяжении десятилетий, пояснил участник исследования Сэм Уолмсли из Принстонского университета.

Специалисты фиксировали, выглядит ли кит упитанным или истощённым, используя это как показатель здоровья. Примерно 11% животных в каждый конкретный момент времени находились в плохом состоянии. Чтобы составить карту социальных связей, исследователи отмечали, с какими спутниками киты попадали в кадр.

Уолмсли ожидал увидеть положительную связь между социальными контактами и здоровьем, как это описано у многих млекопитающих — от мышей до павианов. «Если кит в плохом состоянии, возможно, ему просто нужно сосредоточиться на том, чтобы добыть достаточно кальмаров или рыбы для выживания», — рассуждал он. Однако ослабленные особи имели больше социальных партнёров, чем обычно для этого вида, и держались в более крупных группах.

Причины такого поведения пока неясны. По словам Уолмсли, больные киты могут активнее искать общество других, либо животные, уже находящиеся в больших группах, вынуждены сильнее конкурировать за пищу. Ещё один вариант состоит в том, что «киты притягиваются к особям в плохом состоянии, возможно, оказывая им дополнительную поддержку».

items.title: Новая ИИ-платформа поможет женщинам контролировать лечение при ЭКО
items.description: В Сеченовском университете создали ИИ-помощника для женщин, проходящих ЭКО
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: В Сеченовском университете создали ИИ-помощника для женщин, проходящих ЭКО

Студенты Сеченовского университета совместно с выпускником кампуса вуза и «Школы 21» разработали цифровую платформу ReProduct для женщин, проходящих экстракорпоральное оплодотворение (ЭКО). Сервис помогает контролировать лечение, хранить медицинские документы и справляться с тревогой на разных этапах процедуры. Об этом ТАСС рассказали в пресс-службе университета.

Платформа сопровождает пациентку от начала протокола ЭКО до подтверждения беременности. В ней можно вести календарь лечения, отмечать симптомы и получать персонализированные напоминания о приёме препаратов и визитах к врачу. Сервис также объясняет этапы процедуры и помогает подготовить вопросы для консультации со специалистом.

Отдельная функция ReProduct — ИИ-компаньон. Он отвечает на вопросы о лечении, разъясняет медицинские термины и оказывает эмоциональную поддержку. Разработчики уделили особое внимание периоду ожидания результатов процедур, когда тревожность может усиливаться.

«Мы хотели создать инструмент, который поможет женщине чувствовать себя более уверенно на протяжении всего протокола ЭКО. В этот период особенно важны понятная информация, возможность отслеживать ключевые этапы лечения и эмоциональная поддержка. ReProduct объединяет эти возможности на одной платформе», — рассказала автор идеи проекта Анастасия Шатилина.
В команду также вошли Татьяна Усачёва, Ева Титкова, Денис Анискин и Асельдер Саидов, выпускник совместного кампуса Сеченовского университета и «Школы 21».

При этом ИИ-помощник не заменяет врача — медицинские решения по-прежнему принимают специалисты. В дальнейшем разработчики планируют добавить инструменты анализа симптомов и оценки состояния пациентки, которые помогут определить, когда следует обратиться за медицинской помощью.

items.title: Бразилец продал всё ради встречи с девушкой, которая оказалась создана ИИ
items.description: В Бразилии мужчина проехал 2000 км к женщине, которая оказалась сгенерирована ИИ
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: В Бразилии мужчина проехал 2000 км к женщине, которая оказалась сгенерирована ИИ

В Бразилии мужчина проехал почти 2 тысячи километров ради встречи с женщиной, на которой хотел жениться. Однако его возлюбленная оказалась сгенерирована искусственным интеллектом, пишет The New York Post.

49-летний каменщик Эдимар Роша Мартинс впервые наткнулся на аккаунт девушки в 2020 году. На странице появлялись ролики, в которых она рассказывала, что она одинокая хозяйка фермы и ищет спутника жизни. Мужчина отметил, что у него ни разу не возникло сомнения, что женщина может быть ненастоящей.
Мужчина решил ехать к девушке в штат Минас-Жерайс. В октябре этого года он продал все свои вещи, чтобы хватило денег на дорогу.

Когда Мартинс прибыл на место, ему сообщили, что этой женщины не существует. У мужчины закончились деньги, и он обратился в мэрию. Там он рассказал социальному работнику, как оказался в Минас-Жерайсе. Ему купили билет домой.
Создатель аккаунта позже выложил видео, в котором сообщил, что героиня создана ИИ для продвижения товаров в соцсетях. Он также отметил, что никогда не переписывался с Мартинсом.

items.title: В США выдали ордер на арест Рауля Кастро
items.description: В США выдали ордер на арест бывшего лидера Кубы Рауля Кастро
items.author: Александра Копылова
paragraphs: В США выдали ордер на арест бывшего лидера Кубы Рауля Кастро
В США генеральный прокурор штата Флорида Джеймс Утмайер заявил о выдаче ордера на арест бывшего лидера Кубы Рауля Кастро. Его обвиняют в сговоре с целью совершения убийства первой степени.

20 мая Минюст США предъявил Кастро и пяти кубинским военным обвинения по делу об инциденте с двумя сбитыми в 1996 году гражданскими самолётами, которые принадлежали гуманитарной организации Brothers to the Rescue. Им вменяют уничтожение воздушного судна и убийство четырёх человек.
Джеймс Утмайер заявил, что Рауль Кастро отдал приказ сбить самолёты. Поэтому выдан ордер на арест экс-лидера Кубы.

Раулю Кастро 95 лет. Вместе со своим братом Фиделем он участвовал в свержении правительства Фульхенсио Батисты в 1959 году. Он занимал пост министра обороны, а в 2008-м сменил заболевшего брата на посту главы государства. Фидель Кастро скончался в 2016-м. Сам Рауль Кастро покинул пост президента в 2018 году, но по-прежнему сохраняет политическое влияние на Кубе.

Давление на Кубу со стороны США усилилось после январских событий в Венесуэле, которая была ключевым партнёром острова. Вашингтон объявил Кубу угрозой и ввёл дополнительные пошлины для стран, поставляющих ей нефть. В ответ кубинские власти объявили режим международного чрезвычайного положения, а президент Мигель Диас-Канель заявил о готовности к обороне.

items.title: Леденцы вместо одной зубной пасты: в России разработали новые средства от кариеса
items.description: Учёные КубГМУ разработали леденцы и фиточай для профилактики кариеса
items.author: Виолетта Ефимова
paragraphs: Учёные КубГМУ разработали леденцы и фиточай для профилактики кариеса

Учёные Кубанского государственного медицинского университета разработали два средства для профилактики кариеса — леденцы и фиточай. Они должны помогать сдерживать рост бактерий, вызывающих заболевание, и поддерживать здоровье зубов и дёсен. Об этом ТАСС сообщила доцент кафедры терапевтической стоматологии вуза Екатерина Запорожская-Абрамова.

Леденцы изготовили на основе изомальта — подсластителя, который не ферментируется микрофлорой полости рта и помогает поддерживать нейтральный уровень кислотности. Для фиточая исследователи выбрали экстракты листьев и плодов зизифуса, а также плодов жимолости. По замыслу авторов, эти компоненты должны помогать корректировать микрофлору, сдерживать рост нежелательных бактерий и уменьшать воспаление.
«Разработка позволит эффективно останавливать рост кариесогенных бактерий и повысит приверженность пациентов к лечению благодаря своей удобной форме», — отметила Запорожская-Абрамова.

По словам исследовательницы, сочетание двух средств может сделать профилактику кариеса эффективнее, чем использование одной зубной пасты. Леденцы и чай обеспечивают длительное высвобождение активных компонентов в полости рта, где они должны действовать непосредственно на проблемные участки.

По данным Всемирной организации здравоохранения, нелеченый кариес постоянных зубов есть примерно у 2,5 млрд человек в мире. Поэтому поиск новых способов профилактики остаётся важной задачей стоматологии и фармацевтики.
Разработка КубГМУ пока находится на этапе доклинических испытаний.

items.title: Открытие Grott Base, татарский бранч в «Айне» и алтайский ужин в «Матрешке»
items.description: Не успели моргнуть, как пролетело лето, моргнули еще раз — и золотая осень уже позади. На смену ей пришел сезон дождей, но мы не унываем и продолжаем искать поводы выбраться из дома даже в самую неприветливую погоду.
items.author: Злата Лапшина
paragraphs: Не успели моргнуть, как пролетело лето, моргнули еще раз — и золотая осень уже позади. На смену ей пришел сезон дождей, но мы не унываем и продолжаем искать поводы выбраться из дома даже в самую неприветливую погоду.

В еженедельном дайджесте «Большого Города» мы собрали главные ресторанные новости недели. Рассказываем про открытие Grott Base, тыквенное меню в Megobari, масштабное обновление в «Ладо», сезонные новинки в Copen 57, Tokyo Sushi, «Бибирево» и других, новые завтраки в Atlantica. А также о гастрольных вечерах Киока Огава из Японии в Motto Azabu, татарском бранче «Чирэм» в «Айне», краснодарского «Пресс» в Sur и алтайского ресторана «Сосны» в «Матрешке».

За московским открытием стоит ресторанный холдинг Grott из Екатеринбурга, известный по проектам Grott Brewery Bar и Norra Rök. Grott Base стал его флагманом в столице. В новом ресторане традиции гастрономии и гостеприимства Урала соединяются с кухней живого огня и вниманием к каждому продукту.

Оформлением пространства занималась екатеринбургская архитектурная мастерская RIM.VIII во главе с Григорием Заславским. В интерьере — дерево, кожа, керамика и фактурная штукатурка, а центром пространства стала барная стойка, напоминающая тлеющий очаг. На минус первом этаже расположился уютный погреб, куда можно спуститься за настойкой или бокалом пива.

За кухню отвечает бренд-шеф Никита Кузьменко. Здесь пекут собственный хлеб, готовят в хоспере и смокере, выдерживают мясо и ферментируют продукты. Барную карту разработал шеф-бармен Сергей Шаньгин. В меню: квас из хлеба собственной выпечки, ферментированные газировки, настойки и авторские коктейли, а также импортное пиво и сидр.

В гастропространстве «ИНО» на Гоголевском бульваре стартует «Лаборатория вкуса» — ежемесячный гастрономический проект, посвященный исследованию сезонных продуктов. В каждом выпуске команда «ИНО» будет выбирать один ингредиент и вместе с приглашенным шефом раскрывать его потенциал через разные техники приготовления, текстуры и сочетания. Первым продуктом проекта станет белый гриб, а приглашенным шефом — Тимофей Сулима.
Стоимость ужина — 6 000 рублей. Начало в 19:00.
Оленина с белыми грибами и копченым желтком
Говяжье ребро BBQ с белыми грибами и сыром чеддер
Шоколад, смородина и белые грибы
Грибное парфе с черным трюфелем
Черная треска с мисо и белыми грибами
Коктейль или моктейль «Белые грибы и мисо»
Киш с белыми грибами, фундуком и мороженым из камамбера
Винная дегустация в «Радио»
22 октября, ул. 2-я Бауманская, 9/23, стр. 3

В «Радио» пройдет дегустация вин со всех уголков мира, чтобы гости познакомились с разными сортами и терруарами, сравнили игристое и тихое вина и открыли новые горизонты виноградной лозы. Проводником в винный мир на этот вечер станет Илья Сармаев — друг проекта и специалист по вину.
В качестве гастрономического сопровождения команда «Радио» подготовит закуски, которые подчеркнут вкус каждого вина: антипасти из разновидности сыров, оливок, хумуса и цельнозернового хлеба.
Стоимость дегустации — 5 000 рублей.
Ужин «Цирк и море: что готовит шеф на яхте» в «Цирке»
22 октября, Цветной б-р, 21/7

Бистро «Цирк» запускает серию ужинов с локальными проектами, гастроэнтузиастами, фермами и винными хозяйствами. Первый ужин — «Цирк и море: что готовит шеф на яхте» — пройдет в формате à la carte. За общее меню будут отвечать шеф «Цирка» Денис Демьянов и шеф-повар яхтенного проекта MayakSail Ольга Петухова. В этом меню будет представлена гастрономическая карта тех мест, в которых удалось побывать команде на многочисленных регатах.
